docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
Hardware security is the foundation upon which all software security rests. Without trust in the hardware, no software guarantee can be meaningful. This book provides a comprehensive reference covering every major area of hardware security – from the most fundamental primitives (TPMs, PUFs, TRNGs) to cutting-edge developments in post-quantum cryptography and AI hardware security.

Every chapter follows a rigorous structure: it begins with the threat landscape and motivating attack, explains the architecture with block diagrams, dives into both FPGA and ASIC implementations with real resource numbers, surveys every major commercial and open-source solution that exists today, walks through solved problems, and closes with exercises to test and deepen understanding.

docs.title: Who This Book Is For
docs.text:
This book is intended for:

  • Hardware security engineers designing security into chips and systems

  • Software engineers building security systems on top of hardware primitives

  • Security researchers investigating hardware attack techniques and defenses

  • Students studying hardware security, embedded systems, or cryptography

  • CTF participants tackling hardware hacking challenges

  • Industry professionals in automotive, IoT, medical, aerospace, and telecom sectors

docs.title: What This Book Covers
docs.text:
This book covers 36 hardware security technology areas organized into logical groups:

Foundations (Chapters 1–5) TPM, HSM, PUF, TEE, and Hardware Root of Trust. Attack Defenses (Chapters 6–9) Side-channel attacks, hardware Trojan detection, secure boot, and TRNG. Platform Security (Chapters 10–14) FPGA security, IOMMU/DMA protection, memory security, anti-tamper, and attestation. Domain-Specific Security (Chapters 15–20) Automotive, PQC, JTAG debug, crypto accelerators, key management, and IoT. Authentication and Identity (Chapters 21–23) Secure elements, FIDO2/WebAuthn, and cryptocurrency wallets. Network and Architecture (Chapters 24–26) Network processors, CHERI capability hardware, and RISC-V security. Industry Solutions (Chapters 27–36) Formal verification, supply chain, 5G, medical, ICS/SCADA, biometrics, satellite, AI/ML, USB/Thunderbolt, and wireless. Emerging Technologies (Chapters 37–39) Confidential computing hardware (Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, ARM CCA), hardware security design flow and EDA tools (from RTL to silicon), and chiplet and heterogeneous integration security (UCIe, DICE identity, HBM3 encryption).

docs.title: Conventions Used
docs.text:
Each chapter uses:

  • TikZ block diagrams to visualise architectures

  • Code listings in C, Python, Verilog, assembly, and shell

  • Comparison tables for all existing solutions (FPGA LUTs, ASIC area, speed)

  • Solved Problems with step-by-step worked solutions

  • Exercises ranging from short-answer to open-ended design challenges

  • Note: Note boxes for important definitions and facts

  • Warning: Warning boxes for common mistakes and security pitfalls

  • Tip: Tip boxes for practical implementation advice

docs.title: 1.1 Introduction and Historical Context
docs.text:
The Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is a dedicated security microcontroller standardized by the Trusted Computing Group (TCG). It provides hardware-rooted cryptographic measurements, remote attestation, sealed storage, and key management that cannot be subverted by software adversaries, even under complete operating system compromise.

Note: A TPM is a hardware root of trust: its private keys and operations execute on dedicated silicon isolated from the host CPU. Software cannot extract TPM-protected keys or forge TPM-signed attestation structures.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Historical Timeline
docs.text:
• 1999: IBM TCPA founded with Compaq, HP, Intel, Microsoft; TPM 1.0 spec drafts

  • 2003: TCPA reorganized into Trusted Computing Group (TCG); TPM 1.1b released; Atmel, Infineon, STMicro begin production

  • 2005: TPM 1.2 – Direct Anonymous Attestation (DAA) and locality model

  • 2007: TPM 1.2 mandatory for Microsoft Vista Designed-for-Windows logo

  • 2014: TPM 2.0 published – algorithm agility, three-hierarchy key model

  • 2015: ISO/IEC 11889:2015 ratified as international TPM 2.0 standard

  • 2016: TPM 2.0 replaces 1.2 in Windows 10 hardware requirements

  • 2021: Microsoft mandates TPM 2.0 for Windows 11

  • 2022: TCG post-quantum proposals: ML-DSA (Dilithium), ML-KEM (Kyber), XMSS

docs.title: 1.2.2 PCR Banks and Extend Operation
docs.text:
Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) are the cornerstone of TPM integrity measurement. TPM 2.0 maintains one bank per hash algorithm, each with 24 registers (indices 0–23) initialized to all-zeros at power-on (TPM2_CC_Startup with TPM_SU_CLEAR).

The extend operation is irreversible:

\[\text{PCR}[i]_{\text{new}} = H\!\bigl(\text{PCR}[i]_{\text{old}} \;\|\; M\bigr)\tag{1.1}\] Table 1.2. Standard PCR Allocation – TCG PC Client Platform Profile v1.05 PCR Content Extended By 0 CRTM, BIOS firmware, Host Platform Extensions BIOS/UEFI 1 Host Platform Configuration (DMI, SMBIOS) BIOS/UEFI 2 Option ROM Code (PCIe, NIC firmware) BIOS/UEFI 3 Option ROM Configuration and Data BIOS/UEFI 4 MBR / UEFI Boot Manager code BIOS/Bootloader 5 Boot Manager configuration and data BIOS/Bootloader 6 State Transitions, S3/S4 wake events BIOS 7 Secure Boot Policy (PK, KEK, DB, DBX) BIOS/UEFI 8–15 OS loader (GRUB2, Windows Boot Manager) Bootloader/OS 16 Debug register (software-resettable) Application 17–22 DRTM (Intel TXT / AMD SKINIT) Firmware 23 Application-specific measurements Application

docs.title: 1.2.3 Key Hierarchy: Three Permanent Hierarchies
docs.text:
TPM 2.0 organizes all keys in three hierarchies backed by 256-bit hardware seeds.

Figure 1.2. TPM 2.0 Key Hierarchy with Permanent Hardware Seeds Endorsement Key (EK) Derived from ehSeed via TPM2_CreatePrimary. EK cert in NV 0x01C00002 (RSA) or 0x01C0000A (ECC). EK private key never leaves the TPM. Storage Root Key (SRK) Derived from shSeed. Persistent handle 0x81000001. Wraps child keys stored outside the TPM. Attestation Identity Key (AIK) Restricted signing key (restricted|sign). Signs only TPM-internal TPMS_ATTEST structures. Requires Privacy CA certification. Platform Key (PK) Administrative key in Platform Hierarchy; used during manufacturing.

docs.title: 1.2.4 NV Storage
docs.text:
• Capacity: 64KB user NV (SLB 9670); up to 256KB (ST33KTPM2XSPI)

  • Index handles: Owner 0x01000000–0x01BFFFFF; Platform 0x01800000–0x01BFFFFF

  • NV types: ORDINARY (byte array), COUNTER (monotonic), BITS (set-only), EXTEND (hash-extend-only), PIN_PASS/PIN_FAIL

  • Factory: 0x01C00002=RSA EK cert; 0x01C00004=EK template; 0x01C0000A=ECC EK cert

docs.title: 1.2.5 Authorization Sessions
docs.text: HMAC Session Password/HMAC auth; HMAC over session nonces proves authValue; replay-protected. Policy Session Flexible conditional: TPM2_PolicyPCR (PCR binding), TPM2_PolicySigned (external ECDSA), TPM2_PolicyCounterTimer (time gate), TPM2_PolicyCommandCode, TPM2_PolicyOR. Trial Session Computes policy digest offline without authorizing; used during key creation. docs.title: Infineon SLB 9670 – Industry Reference Chip
docs.text:
The SLB 9670 is the most widely deployed TPM 2.0 chip in enterprise notebooks (ThinkPad, EliteBook, Latitude):

  • Process: 22nm HKMG CMOS; Package: QFN-28, \(10\,\text{mm}\times 10\,\text{mm}\)

  • Interfaces: LPC 33MHz and SPI 43MHz (pin-strap selectable)

  • RSA-2048 keygen: \(<1\)s; RSA-2048 sign: \(<100\)ms

  • ECC P-256 ECDSA sign: \(<10\)ms; AES-256: \(>100\) MB/s hardware-accelerated

  • Supply: 1.8V or 3.3V; Active: \(<10\)mA; Standby: \(<10\) \(\mu\)A

  • Temp: \(-40^{\circ}\) to \(+85^{\circ}\)C industrial

  • Cert: CC EAL4+ (BSI-DSZ-CC-0782); FIPS 140-2 Level 2

  • EK cert: Pre-programmed; verifiable at pki.infineon.com

  • Eval board: Infineon IRIDIUM9670 SPI breakout (\(\sim\)$5 USD)

docs.title: AMD fTPM and Intel PTT
docs.text:
• AMD fTPM: ARM TrustZone in AMD PSP; all Ryzen/EPYC since Zen (2017); ms-tpm-20-ref firmware; NV in SPI flash

  • Intel PTT: ARC processor in Intel ME; 4th Gen Core (Haswell, 2013)+; NV in BIOS SPI flash

  • Qualcomm fTPM: Snapdragon 8cx Gen 3 (Windows on ARM); TrustZone secure world

Warning: fTPMs have larger attack surface than dTPMs. AMD PSP attacks (CVE-2021-26310) demonstrated arbitrary PSP code execution. A dTPM on separate silicon provides fundamentally stronger isolation.

docs.title: 1.4 Python Remote Attestation with tpm2-pytss
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os, hashlib
from tpm2_pytss import ESAPI
from tpm2_pytss.types import *

TPM_GENERATED_VALUE = 0xFF544347

def create_aik(ectx):
    in_pub = TPM2B_PUBLIC(publicArea=TPMT_PUBLIC(
        type=TPM2_ALG.ECC, nameAlg=TPM2_ALG.SHA256,
        objectAttributes=(
            TPMA_OBJECT.RESTRICTED | TPMA_OBJECT.SIGN_ENCRYPT |
            TPMA_OBJECT.FIXEDTPM | TPMA_OBJECT.FIXEDPARENT |
            TPMA_OBJECT.SENSITIVEDATAORIGIN | TPMA_OBJECT.USERWITHAUTH
        ),
        parameters=TPMU_PUBLIC_PARMS(eccDetail=TPMS_ECC_PARMS(
            symmetric=TPMT_SYM_CIPHER(algorithm=TPM2_ALG.NULL),
            scheme=TPMT_ECC_SCHEME(scheme=TPM2_ALG.ECDSA,
                details=TPMU_ASYM_SCHEME(
                    ecdsa=TPMS_SCHEME_HASH(hashAlg=TPM2_ALG.SHA256))),
            curveID=TPM2_ECC.NIST_P256,
            kdf=TPMT_KDF_SCHEME(scheme=TPM2_ALG.NULL)))
    ))
    handle, pub, _, _, _ = ectx.create_primary(
        ESYS_TR.ENDORSEMENT, TPM2B_SENSITIVE_CREATE(),
        in_pub, TPM2B_DATA(), TPML_PCR_SELECTION())
    return handle, pub

def generate_quote(ectx, aik_handle, nonce):
    pcr_sel = TPML_PCR_SELECTION(count=1, pcrSelections=[
        TPMS_PCR_SELECTION(hash=TPM2_ALG.SHA256,
            sizeofSelect=3, pcrSelect=bytes([0xFF, 0x00, 0x00]))])
    scheme = TPMT_SIG_SCHEME(scheme=TPM2_ALG.ECDSA,
        details=TPMU_SIG_SCHEME(
            ecdsa=TPMS_SCHEME_HASH(hashAlg=TPM2_ALG.SHA256)))
    return ectx.quote(aik_handle,
                      TPM2B_DATA(buffer=nonce), scheme, pcr_sel)

def main():
    nonce = os.urandom(32)
    print(f"Nonce: {nonce.hex()}")
    with ESAPI(tcti=None) as ectx:
        aik_handle, _ = create_aik(ectx)
        print("AIK created: ECC P-256, restricted|sign")
        quoted, sig = generate_quote(ectx, aik_handle, nonce)
        quoted_bytes = bytes(quoted)
        magic = int.from_bytes(quoted_bytes[0:4], "big")
        assert magic == TPM_GENERATED_VALUE, f"Bad magic: 0x{magic:08X}"
        print(f"Magic 0x{magic:08X} verified (genuine TPM)")
        ectx.flush_context(aik_handle)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 1.6.1 CVE-2017-15361: ROCA – Infineon RSA Weakness
docs.text:
Matus Nemec (Masaryk University) discovered Infineon RSA prime generation produces primes of the form \(p = k \cdot M + (65537^a \bmod M)\) for specific constant \(M\). This algebraic structure enables faster-than-expected factoring via Coppersmith methods.

  • Fingerprinting: Check \(n \bmod M_i\) for a specific list; \(>\)98% of vulnerable keys in \(<\)1ms

  • RSA-1024: \(\approx 2^{62}\) operations (feasible; demonstrated for \(\sim\)$40k AWS cost)

  • RSA-2048: \(\approx 2^{100}\) (weakened from \(2^{112}\); still infeasible)

  • Affected: Infineon SLE/SLB firmware \(<\)v7.x; Yubikey 4; Estonian e-ID

  • Fix: Firmware v7.x update; all affected keys must be regenerated

  • Detection: pip install roca-detect; works on any RSA pubkey or X.509 cert

docs.title: 1.6.2 CVE-2019-11090: TPM-Fail Timing Attack
docs.text:
Researchers (WPI, TU Graz, Univ. Lubeck) found non-constant-time ECC in Intel PTT and STMicro:

  • Intel PTT: 4-bit nonce leak per ECDSA-P256 signature; \(\sim\)1,000 sigs recover 256-bit key via HNP lattice + BKZ

  • STMicro ST33: \(\sim\)40,000 signatures needed

  • Attack: No physical access; timing via ioctl(/dev/tpm0); \(\sim\)4 hours on laptop

  • Root cause: Non-constant-time scalar multiply; conditional branch on nonce \(k\) MSB

  • Fix: Intel PTT microcode patch; STMicro firmware \(\geq\)70.0.18

docs.title: 1.6.3 Physical Bus Sniffing Attack
docs.text:
• Target: BitLocker TPM-only mode – VMK crosses LPC/SPI bus in cleartext during TPM2_Unseal

  • Equipment: Saleae Logic 8 ($149); PoC: github.com/FSecureLABS/bitlocker-spi-toolkit

  • Time: Under 5 minutes on laptop with accessible LPC debug header

  • Defense: (1) BitLocker PIN (policyauthvalue); (2) PCR[7] Secure Boot binding; (3) Pluton integrates TPM into CPU die

docs.title: 1.7 Post-Quantum Considerations for TPM 2.0
docs.text:
Current TPM 2.0 cryptography relies on RSA and ECC, both vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm on a large quantum computer. NIST finalized post-quantum standards in 2024: ML-DSA (FIPS 203), ML-KEM (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). TCG has initiated work to incorporate these into TPM 2.0 via new algorithm IDs.

Table 1.6. Post-Quantum Algorithm Candidates for TPM 2.0 Algorithm Type NIST Standard Public Key Signature/CT ML-DSA-44 (Dilithium2) Signature FIPS 204 1,312 B 2,420 B ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium3) Signature FIPS 204 1,952 B 3,293 B ML-DSA-87 (Dilithium5) Signature FIPS 204 2,592 B 4,595 B ML-KEM-512 (Kyber512) KEM FIPS 203 800 B 768 B CT ML-KEM-768 (Kyber768) KEM FIPS 203 1,184 B 1,088 B CT ML-KEM-1024 (Kyber1024) KEM FIPS 203 1,568 B 1,568 B CT SLH-DSA-128s (SPHINCS+) Signature FIPS 205 32 B 7,856 B XMSS (RFC 8391) Signature NIST SP 1800-25  68 B 2,500+ B LMS (RFC 8554) Signature NIST SP 800-208  60 B 1,460+ B

Note: ML-KEM and ML-DSA require larger NV storage and buffer sizes in TPM. TCG TPM 2.0 Rev 1.83+ introduces TPM_ALG_MLDSA (0x0044) and TPM_ALG_MLKEM (0x0045) algorithm IDs. NV index size cap may need raising from 2,048 to 4,096 bytes.

docs.title: 1.7.1 XMSS Stateful Hash-Based Signatures
docs.text:
XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) is attractive for TPM due to conservative hash-only security:

  • XMSS-SHA2_20_256: 20-level Merkle tree; \(2^{20}\) one-time signatures; 64 B public key

  • Statefulness: Leaf index must never repeat; requires NV counter with integrity protection

  • TCG proposal: NV index stores current leaf index; TPM2_NV_Increment atomically advances state

  • OIDs: XMSS OID 0x0000001 (XMSS-SHA2_10_256); defined in RFC 8391

docs.title: 1.10 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: PCR Extend Chain Calculation

A system performs a measured boot sequence. The PCR[0] bank uses SHA-256. Initially PCR[0] = 0x00...00 (32 zero bytes). Three measurements are extended in order:

  1. BIOS code hash: M1 = SHA256(BIOS_blob) = 0xABCD...1234 (32 bytes)

  2. Bootloader hash: M2 = SHA256(bootloader_blob) = 0x5678...ABCD (32 bytes)

  3. Kernel hash: M3 = SHA256(kernel_blob) = 0x1111...FFFF (32 bytes)

Compute PCR[0] after each extend operation and explain why PCR values cannot be forged. Solution: The PCR extend operation is defined as: \(\text{PCR}[i]_{\text{new}} = H(\text{PCR}[i]_{\text{old}} \| M)\)

Step 1 – After extending M1:

\[\begin{align*} \text{PCR}[0]_1 &= \text{SHA256}(\underbrace{00…00}_{32} \| M_1) \\ &= \text{SHA256}(32 \text{ zero bytes } \| \texttt{0xABCD...1234}) \end{align*}\]

Step 2 – After extending M2:

\[\begin{align*} \text{PCR}[0]_2 &= \text{SHA256}(\text{PCR}[0]_1 \| M_2) \end{align*}\]

Step 3 – After extending M3:

\[\begin{align*} \text{PCR}[0]_3 &= \text{SHA256}(\text{PCR}[0]_2 \| M_3) \end{align*}\]

Why forgery is infeasible: The TPM provides forward-only ratcheting. To forge a target PCR value \(T\), an attacker must find \(M^*\) such that \(H(\text{PCR}_{k-1} \| M^*) = T\). This is a preimage attack on SHA-256, requiring \(2^{256}\) operations. Furthermore, the TPM resets PCR values only on power cycle or TPM2_PCR_Reset (for resettable PCRs). Sealing a secret to PCR[0] = \(\text{PCR}[0]_3\) ensures it can only be unsealed on a system that booted the exact same BIOS, bootloader, and kernel in that order.

Solved Problem: Remote Attestation Protocol Design

You are designing a remote attestation system. A client machine (prover) has a TPM 2.0. A remote server (verifier) wants to verify the prover’s boot state. Design the full protocol exchange and identify what each message prevents. Solution: Protocol Steps:

  1. Provisioning (one-time): The TPM EK certificate (signed by Infineon/AMD CA) is registered with verifier. An Attestation Identity Key (AIK) is created: TPM2_CreatePrimary on endorsement hierarchy, then TPM2_Create with objectAttributes = fixedTPM|fixedParent|sign. The AIK public key is certified by the EK via TPM2_ActivateCredential.

  2. Challenge (verifier -> prover): Verifier sends nonce \(N\) (128-bit random value). Purpose: prevents replay attacks; each attestation is fresh.

  3. Quote generation (prover):

    tpm2_quote --key-context aik.ctx --pcr-list sha256:0,1,2,3,7 \
           --qualification $NONCE --message quote.msg --signature quote.sig

    TPMS_ATTEST structure contains: magic=0xFF544347, type=TPM_ST_ATTEST_QUOTE, qualifiedSigner (AIK name), extraData (nonce \(N\)), pcrSelect, pcrDigest.

  4. Verification (verifier):

    tpm2_checkquote --public aik.pub --message quote.msg --signature quote.sig \
                --pcr pcr.bin --qualification $NONCE

    Verifier checks: (a) AIK signature valid; (b) nonce matches; (c) PCR values match golden reference; (d) EK cert chain valid.

Security Properties Achieved:

  • Freshness: Nonce prevents replay of old quotes

  • Binding: fixedTPM|fixedParent ensures AIK cannot be exported and used off-device

  • Integrity: PCR values reflect measured boot chain; SHA-256 collision resistance

  • Authenticity: EK certificate chain roots to manufacturer CA (Infineon, AMD, etc.)

  • Privacy: AIK is pseudonymous; EK is not revealed to verifier (via ActivateCredential)

Solved Problem: FPGA Soft-TPM Resource Estimation

You need to implement a soft-TPM (TPM 2.0 compliant) on a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA. The design must support SHA-256, AES-128-CFB, RSA-2048, and HMAC-SHA-256. Estimate the FPGA resource usage and discuss trade-offs versus a discrete dTPM chip. Solution: Resource Estimation per Component:

Block LUTs FFs BRAMs DSPs SHA-256 (unrolled) 1,800 512 0 0 AES-128-CFB 1,200 256 0 0 RSA-2048 (Montgomery) 2,500 800 2 16 HMAC-SHA-256 200 64 0 0 TPM command dispatcher 800 400 1 0 NV storage controller 300 200 4 0 SPI slave interface 150 100 0 0 TRNG (ring oscillator) 120 80 0 0 Total 7,070 2,412 7 16

On Artix-7 XC7A100T (101,440 LUTs, 126,800 FFs, 135 BRAMs, 240 DSPs), utilization is approximately: 7,070/101,440 = 7.0% LUTs; 2,412/126,800 = 1.9% FFs; 7/135 = 5.2% BRAMs; 16/240 = 6.7% DSPs. Expected operating frequency: 75–100 MHz on Artix-7 speed grade -1.

Trade-offs vs Discrete dTPM:

  • Cost: Artix-7 XC7A100T  $50; SLB9670  $3. FPGA only makes sense in custom SoC.

  • Certification: Discrete SLB9670 is EAL4+ certified; FPGA soft-TPM has no certification.

  • Physical security: Discrete TPM has active shielding, sensors; FPGA has none by default.

  • Flexibility: FPGA can add PQ algorithms (ML-DSA) without hardware change.

  • Speed: RSA-2048 key generation: dTPM  2s; FPGA @100MHz  0.8s with DSP optimization.

Solved Problem: TPM Policy Authorization for Multi-Factor Sealing

Design a TPM 2.0 policy that seals a disk encryption key such that it can only be unsealed when: (1) Secure Boot is enabled (PCR[7] has a known value), AND (2) The user provides a PIN (6-digit numeric password), AND (3) The TPM has not been rebooted more than 10 times since the last unlock. Write the tpm2-tools commands and explain each policy primitive used. Solution: Policy Design using TPM2_PolicyAND:

TPM 2.0 uses a policy session where each primitive extends the policy digest. Multiple conditions are AND-ed by sequentially applying policy commands in the same session.

# Step 1: Start a trial policy session to compute policy digest
tpm2_startauthsession --policy-session -S session.ctx

# Step 2: PCR[7] policy -- Secure Boot PCR must match golden value
tpm2_policypcr -S session.ctx --pcr-list sha256:7 --pcr-digest $PCR7_GOLDEN

# Step 3: Policy auth value -- require PIN input at unsealing time
tpm2_policyauthvalue -S session.ctx

# Step 4: Policy NV counter -- NV index 0x01500001 must be <= 10
# First create the NV counter index:
tpm2_nvdefine 0x01500001 --size 8 --attributes nt=counter|ownerwrite|ownerread
# Then add NV counter policy (counter value <= 10):
tpm2_policynv -S session.ctx --index 0x01500001 --operand-b 10 --operation le

# Step 5: Save the computed policy digest
tpm2_policygetdigest -S session.ctx -o policy.digest
tpm2_flushcontext session.ctx

# Step 6: Create sealed object with this policy
tpm2_createprimary -C o -c primary.ctx
echo -n "MY_DISK_KEY_32BYTES" | \
tpm2_create -C primary.ctx -L policy.digest -i - -u sealed.pub -r sealed.priv
tpm2_load -C primary.ctx -u sealed.pub -r sealed.priv -c sealed.ctx

Unseal procedure (must satisfy all three conditions):

tpm2_startauthsession --policy-session -S session.ctx
tpm2_policypcr -S session.ctx --pcr-list sha256:7 --pcr-digest $PCR7_GOLDEN
tpm2_policyauthvalue -S session.ctx
tpm2_policynv -S session.ctx --index 0x01500001 --operand-b 10 --operation le
tpm2_unseal -c sealed.ctx -p session:session.ctx+hex:313233343536  # PIN=123456
# Increment reboot counter
tpm2_nvincrement 0x01500001

Policy Primitives Explained:

  • TPM2_PolicyPCR: Binds policy to current PCR values; PCR[7] reflects Secure Boot state per UEFI spec

  • TPM2_PolicyAuthValue: Requires caller to provide correct authValue (the PIN) at unseal time

  • TPM2_PolicyNV: Compares NV index value against operand; operator le enforces max 10 reboots

  • AND semantics: Each primitive extends the same session digest; all must be satisfied sequentially

docs.title: 1.11.1 TCG TPM 2.0 Profile for Automotive (2024)
docs.text:
The Trusted Computing Group published the TCG TPM 2.0 Automotive Thin Profile in 2024, targeting ISO 26262 functional safety requirements and AUTOSAR integration. Key additions relative to the standard PC Client profile include mandatory HSM-to-TPM binding, support for CAN/Ethernet transport (MCTP over PCIe), and a reduced command set optimised for latency-critical boot.

Table 1.8. TCG Automotive Thin Profile vs. PC Client Profile (2024) Feature PC Client Profile v1.05 Automotive Thin Profile Transport LPC / SPI / I2C MCTP over PCIe / SPI PCR banks SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 SHA-256, SHA-384 (mandatory) NV storage \(\geq 8\) KB \(\geq 4\) KB (resource-constrained) Boot latency target No requirement \(< 50\) ms cold-start Functional safety Not addressed ISO 26262 ASIL-B reference AUTOSAR binding No SecOC + TPM-Attestation API

Note: Automotive TPMs must survive \(-40^{\circ}\)C to \(+125^{\circ}\)C operation and AEC-Q100 Grade 1 qualification. Infineon SLB 9760 and STMicro ST33G1M2ARC are the primary AEC-Q100 certified TPM 2.0 parts as of 2025.

docs.title: 1.11.2 Microsoft Pluton: Integrated TPM Replacement
docs.text:
Microsoft Pluton, co-designed with AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm, eliminates the separate TPM die by implementing TPM 2.0 semantics inside the main CPU package:

  • AMD Ryzen 6000 / 7000 / 8000 series: Pluton core in Zen 3+ and Zen 4 die; firmware delivered via Windows Update (UEFI capsule), decoupled from BIOS vendor

  • Qualcomm Snapdragon 8cx Gen 3: Windows on ARM laptops; Pluton shares TrustZone fabric with Qualcomm fTPM

  • Security gain: No LPC/SPI bus means bus-sniffing attacks (Section 1.11) are architecturally impossible; Pluton communications traverse the CPU interconnect fabric

  • DICE integration: Each Pluton instance generates a DICE Compound Device Identifier (CDI) per boot stage per TCG DICE Layering Architecture v1.1

  • Limitation: Pluton firmware is closed-source and updateable by Microsoft; some enterprises prefer auditable discrete dTPMs for compliance reasons

Warning: Pluton implements the TPM 2.0 command set and passes tpm2-tools workloads transparently. However, the internal key hierarchy and attestation chain differ from a discrete Infineon/STMicro TPM. Verify EK certificate chain format before deploying existing attestation infrastructure against Pluton devices.

docs.title: 1.11.3 CVE-2023-1017 and CVE-2023-1018: TPM 2.0 Reference Buffer Overflows
docs.text:
In early 2023, researchers at Quarkslab disclosed two critical stack buffer overflows in the TCG reference implementation of TPM 2.0 (libtpm2-0-dev, ms-tpm-20-ref):

Table 1.9. CVE-2023-1017 / CVE-2023-1018 Vulnerability Summary CVE Details CVE-2023-1017 Out-of-bounds write in CryptParameterDecryption; malformed TPMT_SYM_CIPHER can write 2 bytes past a stack buffer CVE-2023-1018 Out-of-bounds read in the same function; leaks up to 2 bytes of adjacent stack memory Affected ms-tpm-20-ref \(<\) Feb 2023 tag; libtpms \(<\) 0.9.6; swtpm \(<\) 0.8.1 CVSS 8.8 (High) – requires authenticated TPM session, local attacker Fix Bounds check added to UINT32 unmarshallSize in Part 3 command parsing Impact vTPM deployments (QEMU/KVM, Azure Hyper-V) prioritised patching; discrete hardware TPMs use vendor firmware – not directly affected

Tip: Always deploy virtual TPM stacks (libtpms, swtpm, ms-tpm-20-ref) from distribution packages with active security maintenance. Pin to a minimum version of libtpms \(\geq 0.9.6\) in container images and VM hypervisor configurations.

docs.title: 1.11.4 faulTPM: AMD fTPM Voltage Glitch Attack (2023)
docs.text:
Researchers at TU Berlin published faulTPM in 2023, demonstrating physical extraction of AMD fTPM secrets via voltage fault injection on the \(V_{\text{core}}\) rail:

  • Target: AMD Platform Security Processor (PSP) running fTPM firmware on Ryzen laptops (2019–2022 era)

  • Method: \(\approx \$200\) crowbar glitcher injects sub-microsecond \(V_{\text{cc}}\) spikes during PSP firmware execution; causes missed comparisons in signature verification

  • Result: Full extraction of Storage Root Key (SRK) hierarchy seed (shSeed); all keys wrapped under SRK are recoverable

  • Attack time: 2–3 hours of automated glitch iteration

  • Mitigation: AMD PSP firmware update (AGESA 1.2.0.8+); Pluton-based devices are immune (CPU die voltage glitch does not cross security isolation boundary as easily)

Warning: TPM-only BitLocker (no PIN) is vulnerable to faulTPM on affected platforms. Enforce BitLocker Network Unlock PIN or PCR+PIN policy on enterprise laptops with AMD Ryzen pre-2023 processors. Check AMD advisory AMD-SB-7031 for affected AGESA versions.

docs.title: 1.11.5 Post-Quantum Migration: FIPS 203/204 in TPM 2.0 (2024–2025)
docs.text:
NIST finalised the first post-quantum standards in August 2024:

Table 1.10. Post-Quantum Standards and TPM 2.0 Algorithm ID Assignments (Draft) FIPS Standard Algorithm TPM2_ALG_ID (draft) Status FIPS 203 ML-KEM-512/768/1024 (Kyber) 0x0045 TCG proposal 2024 FIPS 204 ML-DSA-44/65/87 (Dilithium) 0x0044 TCG proposal 2024 FIPS 205 SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) TBD Under review RFC 8391 XMSS / LMS 0x0022 (existing) Supported TPM 2.0 Rev 1.83

TCG Technical Committee WG-Platform published a Post-Quantum Cryptography for TPM 2.0 whitepaper in 2024 outlining a hybrid migration path:

  1. Phase 1 (2024–2026): Add ML-KEM for key encapsulation alongside existing ECC; hybrid ECC-P256 + ML-KEM-768 KEMs for key exchange

  2. Phase 2 (2026–2028): Introduce ML-DSA for AIK signing; hybrid ECDSA + ML-DSA attestation quotes

  3. Phase 3 (2028+): Deprecate RSA-2048 and ECC in high-assurance profiles

docs.title: 1.11.6 Open-Source TPM Ecosystem Updates (2023–2025)
docs.text:
Table 1.11. Open-Source TPM Software Ecosystem (2023–2025) Project Latest Maintainer Key Update libtpms 0.9.6 (2023) IBM / Stefan Berger CVE-2023-1017/1018 fix; ML-DSA draft swtpm 0.8.1 (2023) Stefan Berger CVE fix; QEMU 8.x integration ms-tpm-20-ref Feb 2023 Microsoft CVE fix; Pluton firmware base wolfTPM 3.x (2024) wolfSSL ML-KEM draft; Raspberry Pi 5 support tpm2-tss 4.1 (2024) TCG / Fedora FAPI improved; EAT token support tpm2-tools 5.7 (2024) TCG tpm2_policytemplate new command tpm2-pytss 2.3 (2024) William Roberts Python 3.12; ML-DSA stub API

Tip: The wolfTPM library is the recommended choice for bare-metal embedded TPM integration (STM32, Raspberry Pi, Zephyr RTOS) with no Linux dependency. It supports Infineon SLB9670 over SPI with a footprint under 30 KB Flash.

docs.title: 1.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Describe the difference between a dTPM (discrete TPM), fTPM (firmware TPM), and vTPM (virtual TPM). What are the security trade-offs of each in terms of physical attack resistance, certification level, and performance?

  2. A PCR bank uses SHA-1 (20-byte digest). Starting from PCR = 0x00...00, three measurements M1, M2, M3 are extended. Write the mathematical formula for PCR[0] after all three extends. Why is SHA-1 considered insufficient for new TPM deployments?

  3. Explain the Endorsement Key (EK), Storage Root Key (SRK), and Attestation Identity Key (AIK) in TPM key hierarchy. What makes the EK unique per device? Why can the AIK be used for attestation instead of the EK directly?

  4. You want to seal a 32-byte secret so it can only be unsealed when PCR[0], PCR[2], and PCR[7] have specific values. Write the complete sequence of tpm2-tools commands for (a) sealing the secret and (b) unsealing it. What happens if the system is booted from a different bootloader?

  5. The CVE-2017-15361 (ROCA) vulnerability affected Infineon TPM firmware versions below v7.x. Explain the mathematical weakness in Infineon’s RSA key generation and why RSA-1024 keys were practically factorable. Was RSA-2048 broken? Justify your answer.

  6. Compare the authorization session types in TPM 2.0: Password session, HMAC session, and Policy session. For a production disk encryption deployment, which session type should be used for TPM2_Unseal and why? What does the HMAC session protect against?

  7. Design a remote attestation solution for a fleet of 10,000 IoT devices, each with an Infineon SLB9670 TPM. Your solution must: (a) provision EK certificates at manufacturing time, (b) perform daily attestation, (c) detect firmware tampering. What infrastructure is required?

  8. TPM NV storage has a total capacity of approximately 8 KB on most discrete TPMs. A developer wants to store 16 different X.509 certificates (each 1,200 bytes) in NV storage for certificate pinning. Is this feasible? If not, propose an alternative architecture using TPM capabilities.

  9. Explain how Microsoft’s Pluton security processor differs from a traditional discrete TPM. What specific attack does Pluton prevent that an LPC/SPI-connected TPM cannot prevent? Name a processor family that includes Pluton.

  10. A post-quantum migration requires adding ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium3) to a TPM 2.0 implementation. ML-DSA-65 has a public key size of 1,952 bytes and signature size of 3,293 bytes. What TPM 2.0 structures and buffer limits need to change? Reference specific TCG spec sections.

  11. You are given a Raspberry Pi 4 with an Infineon SLB9670 TPM 2.0 HAT. Using Python and tpm2-pytss, write a program that: (a) reads PCR[0-7] (SHA-256 bank), (b) creates an RSA-2048 signing key, (c) signs a message, (d) verifies the signature. Provide the complete code.

  12. The TPM-Fail attack (CVE-2019-11090) used a timing side-channel to extract a 256-bit ECC key from Intel PTT using approximately 1,000 ECDSA signatures. Explain: (a) what information leaked per signature, (b) the lattice reduction technique used (HNP), (c) what fix was applied, (d) how constant-time implementation prevents this attack.

docs.title: 2.1 Introduction
docs.text:
A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a physically and logically tamper-resistant hardware device that safeguards cryptographic keys and performs cryptographic operations within a secure boundary. HSMs are mandatory infrastructure in banking, PKI, code signing, cloud key management, and government classified systems. They enforce the principle that private key material never leaves the hardware boundary in plaintext form.

Key properties of an HSM:

  • Tamper resistance: Active sensors detect intrusion; keys are zeroized on attack

  • Tamper evidence: Visible seals or enclosures that show if the device was opened

  • Secure key generation: On-board TRNG with continuous health tests (NIST SP 800-90B)

  • Cryptographic acceleration: Hardware engines for RSA, ECC, AES, SHA at high throughput

  • Audit logging: Tamper-evident logs for all key operations (required by PCI HSM)

  • Authenticated access: Multi-factor, M-of-N operator authentication with smart cards

Note: Unlike a TPM (which is a passive co-processor bound to one host), an HSM is an active network appliance or PCIe card providing cryptographic services to multiple clients simultaneously via PKCS#11, JCA/JCE, or vendor APIs.

docs.title: 2.2 FIPS 140-3 Security Levels
docs.text:
FIPS 140-3 (superseding FIPS 140-2 in 2019) defines four security levels for cryptographic modules. It aligns with ISO/IEC 19790:2012 and ISO/IEC 24759:2017.

Table 2.1. FIPS 140-3 Security Levels Summary Level Requirements and Examples Level 1 Basic cryptographic security; no physical security beyond production-grade components. Allows software-only implementation. Example: OpenSSL FIPS module on generic server. Level 2 Tamper-evidence: tamper-evident coatings or seals; role-based authentication. Example: Thales Luna T-Series PCIe, Yubico YubiHSM 2. Level 3 Tamper resistance with response: zeroizes keys on physical attack attempt; identity-based auth; physical/logical separation of interfaces. Example: Thales Luna Network HSM 7, Utimaco CryptoServer Se50. Level 4 Complete envelope of protection; environmental attack protection (voltage, temperature); EFP/EFT. Example: Thales payShield 10K, IBM 4769, Utimaco SecurityServer.

Warning: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 is the minimum required for most PKI root CA HSMs and banking key management systems. Level 4 is required for PIN-entry device (PED) master keys in payment processing.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Internal Components
docs.text: Table 2.2. HSM Internal Hardware Components Component Typical Implementation Function Main processor ARM Cortex-A9 @ 800 MHz Command processing, PKCS#11 dispatch, access control Cryptographic accelerator Custom ASIC / FPGA AES-256, RSA-4096, ECC P-521 at hardware speed TRNG PTG.2 (BSI AIS-31) ring oscillators Entropy source; continuous health test per SP 800-90B Secure SRAM Battery-backed 256 KB SRAM Key cache; zeroized on tamper or power loss Flash storage 64 MB NOR flash (encrypted) Firmware, key blobs, audit logs; MK-encrypted Tamper sensors Temp, voltage, light, mesh, drill Trigger zeroization; EFP/EFT attack detection PED interface USB smart card reader PIN entry device for operator authentication (ISO 9564) Battery Li-Po 3.7V, 5-year life Maintains SRAM key cache when main power removed Environmental sensors Temperature: -20 to +70 C Detect forced cooling/heating attacks (FIPS L4)

docs.title: 2.4 PKCS#11 API
docs.text: PKCS#11 (version 3.0, OASIS standard) is the primary API for interacting with HSMs. It defines a platform-independent C interface: CK_FUNCTION_LIST_PTR.

docs.title: 2.4.1 AES Key Generation and Encryption
docs.text:
#include <pkcs11.h>

CK_FUNCTION_LIST_PTR pFunctionList;
CK_SESSION_HANDLE hSession;
CK_OBJECT_HANDLE hKey;

/* Initialize PKCS#11 library (Thales Luna, SoftHSM2) */
C_GetFunctionList(&pFunctionList);
pFunctionList->C_Initialize(NULL_PTR);

/* Open session and login */
CK_SLOT_ID slotId = 0;
pFunctionList->C_OpenSession(slotId, CKF_SERIAL_SESSION|CKF_RW_SESSION,
                             NULL, NULL, &hSession);
CK_UTF8CHAR pin[] = "user-pin-here";
pFunctionList->C_Login(hSession, CKU_USER, pin, strlen((char*)pin));

/* Generate AES-256 key inside HSM */
CK_MECHANISM keyGenMech = { CKM_AES_KEY_GEN, NULL, 0 };
CK_ULONG keyLen = 32;  /* 256 bits */
CK_BBOOL trueVal = CK_TRUE, falseVal = CK_FALSE;
CK_ATTRIBUTE keyTemplate[] = {
    {CKA_VALUE_LEN,   &keyLen,   sizeof(keyLen)},
    {CKA_TOKEN,       &trueVal,  sizeof(trueVal)},
    {CKA_ENCRYPT,     &trueVal,  sizeof(trueVal)},
    {CKA_SENSITIVE,   &trueVal,  sizeof(trueVal)},
    {CKA_EXTRACTABLE, &falseVal, sizeof(falseVal)},
};
pFunctionList->C_GenerateKey(hSession, &keyGenMech, keyTemplate, 5, &hKey);

/* Encrypt data with AES-256-GCM */
CK_GCM_PARAMS gcmParams = { iv, 12, NULL, 0, 128 };  /* 128-bit auth tag */
CK_MECHANISM encMech = { CKM_AES_GCM, &gcmParams, sizeof(gcmParams) };
pFunctionList->C_EncryptInit(hSession, &encMech, hKey);
CK_ULONG cipherLen = plaintextLen + 16;
pFunctionList->C_Encrypt(hSession, plaintext, plaintextLen, ciphertext, &cipherLen);

Tip: Always set CKA_SENSITIVE = TRUE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE = FALSE on sensitive keys. The HSM hardware enforces this: C_GetAttributeValue for the key value will return CKR_ATTRIBUTE_SENSITIVE.

docs.title: 2.4.2 RSA Key Pair Generation and Signing
docs.text:
/* Generate RSA-2048 key pair inside HSM */
CK_MECHANISM rsaGenMech = { CKM_RSA_PKCS_KEY_PAIR_GEN, NULL, 0 };
CK_ULONG modBits = 2048;
CK_BYTE pubExp[] = { 0x01, 0x00, 0x01 };  /* e = 65537 */
CK_OBJECT_HANDLE hPub, hPriv;
CK_ATTRIBUTE pubTmpl[] = {
    {CKA_MODULUS_BITS,     &modBits, sizeof(modBits)},
    {CKA_PUBLIC_EXPONENT,  pubExp,   sizeof(pubExp)},
    {CKA_VERIFY,           &trueVal, sizeof(trueVal)},
};
CK_ATTRIBUTE privTmpl[] = {
    {CKA_SIGN,        &trueVal,  sizeof(trueVal)},
    {CKA_SENSITIVE,   &trueVal,  sizeof(trueVal)},
    {CKA_EXTRACTABLE, &falseVal, sizeof(falseVal)},
};
C_GenerateKeyPair(hSession, &rsaGenMech,
                  pubTmpl, 3, privTmpl, 3, &hPub, &hPriv);

/* Sign with RSA-PSS SHA-256 */
CK_RSA_PKCS_PSS_PARAMS pssParams = { CKM_SHA256, CKG_MGF1_SHA256, 32 };
CK_MECHANISM signMech = { CKM_SHA256_RSA_PKCS_PSS, &pssParams, sizeof(pssParams) };
C_SignInit(hSession, &signMech, hPriv);
CK_ULONG sigLen = 256;
C_Sign(hSession, message, messageLen, signature, &sigLen);

docs.title: 2.6 Key Ceremony Procedures
docs.text: A key ceremony is a formal, witnessed, and audited procedure for generating, transporting, or destroying cryptographic keys. It is required for Root CA key generation, HSM master key setup, and KMS initialization.

docs.title: 2.6.1 Root CA Key Generation Ceremony
docs.text:
1. Pre-ceremony preparation:

    • FIPS 140-3 L3+ HSM verified (seal check, firmware hash, certificate chain)

    • Air-gapped room with Faraday shielding; no network connectivity

    • Key custodians selected: 5-of-8 Shamir Secret Sharing threshold

    • Hardware tokens (smart cards or USB security keys) issued to each custodian

    • Video recording, independent auditors, and a notary present

  2. HSM initialization:

    • Factory reset + new partition; generate new HSM domain master key via TRNG

    • Domain master key split into 8 shares using Shamir Secret Sharing

    • Each share encrypted to a custodian smart card (RSA-4096 or ECC P-384)

    • Smart cards distributed to geographically separate custodians

  3. Root CA key generation:

    • 5 of 8 custodians insert smart cards; HSM decrypts and reconstructs domain key

    • C_GenerateKeyPair(RSA-4096) on HSM; CKA_EXTRACTABLE = FALSE

    • Self-signed Root CA certificate generated inside HSM

    • Public key exported; signed ceremony report generated

  4. Verification and documentation:

    • Audit log printed and signed by all participants and auditors

    • Root CA certificate fingerprint verified against HSM log

    • HSM backup created; backup tokens stored in separate secure locations

Warning: The ICANN Root KSK Ceremony for DNSSEC is performed using an Entrust nShield HSM in a highly secure facility. It is publicly webcast and involves 14 Trusted Community Representatives across 7 global sites. Missing the ceremony requires a formal exception report.

docs.title: 2.7 Payment HSM Operations
docs.text:
Payment HSMs (PCI HSM v3.0 certified) implement the ANSI X9.24 retail financial services key management standard. They use a key hierarchy based on Zone Master Keys (ZMK) for inter-bank key exchange.

Table 2.4. Payment HSM Key Types and Operations Key Type Abbreviation Function Zone Master Key ZMK Encrypts other keys for inter-bank transport (TR-31 key blocks) Terminal Master Key TMK Encrypts PIN Encryption Keys; shared between acquiring bank and POS terminal PIN Encryption Key PEK Encrypts customer PIN blocks (ISO 9564 format) from POS terminal to host PIN Verification Key PVK Generates/verifies IBM PIN Verification Value (IBM PVV) or Visa PVV Card Verification Key CVK Generates/verifies CVV/CVC value printed on payment card Message Authentication Key MAK MAC for ANSI X9.19 transaction authentication Base Derivation Key BDK Derives DUKPT (Derived Unique Key Per Transaction) device-specific keys

docs.title: 2.7.1 PIN Processing Flow
docs.text:
1. Customer enters PIN on POS terminal keyboard (encrypted in PEK by HSM inside POS)

  2. Encrypted PIN block transmitted with transaction to acquiring bank

  3. Acquiring bank HSM translates PIN block from PEK to ZMK encryption

  4. Issuing bank HSM translates PIN block from ZMK to PVK encryption

  5. Issuer HSM verifies PIN using PIN Verification Value (IBM PVV or Visa PVV)

  6. Approval or decline sent back through network

docs.title: 2.8 Python Interface: PyKCS11
docs.text:
PyKCS11 is a Python binding for PKCS#11 that works with SoftHSM2, Thales Luna, Utimaco, and any compliant HSM.

import PyKCS11
from PyKCS11 import Mechanism, CKM_RSA_PKCS_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_SHA256_RSA_PKCS_PSS
from PyKCS11.types import CKA_MODULUS_BITS, CKA_TOKEN, CKA_SIGN, CKA_SENSITIVE

# Load PKCS#11 library (SoftHSM2 for testing, Thales/Utimaco for production)
lib = PyKCS11.PyKCS11Lib()
lib.load('/usr/lib/softhsm/libsofthsm2.so')

# Open session and login
slot = lib.getSlotList(tokenPresent=True)[0]
session = lib.openSession(slot, PyKCS11.CKF_SERIAL_SESSION | PyKCS11.CKF_RW_SESSION)
session.login('user-pin')

# Generate RSA-2048 key pair in HSM
pub_template = [
    (CKA_MODULUS_BITS,    2048),
    (CKA_TOKEN,           True),
    (PyKCS11.CKA_VERIFY,  True),
]
priv_template = [
    (CKA_TOKEN,           True),
    (CKA_SIGN,            True),
    (CKA_SENSITIVE,       True),
    (PyKCS11.CKA_EXTRACTABLE, False),
]
pub_key, priv_key = session.generateKeyPair(
    Mechanism(CKM_RSA_PKCS_KEY_PAIR_GEN),
    pub_template, priv_template
)

# Sign a message using RSA-PSS SHA-256
message = b'Hardware Security Module demo message'
pss_params = PyKCS11.RSA_PKCS_PSS_Params('sha256')
signature = session.sign(priv_key, message,
                         Mechanism(CKM_SHA256_RSA_PKCS_PSS, pss_params))
print(f'Signature ({len(signature)} bytes): {bytes(signature).hex()[:32]}...')

session.logout()
session.closeSession()

docs.title: 2.10.1 Differential Power Analysis (DPA) on HSMs
docs.text:
• Attack: Measure power consumption during AES key schedule; statistical correlation with key bits

  • Countermeasures: Random insertion of dummy operations; balanced logic (DPL); power line filtering

  • Reference: Kocher, Jaffe, Jun 1999 (original DPA paper); ANSSI RGS B3 DPA requirements

docs.title: 2.10.2 Offline PIN Brute Force (ANSI TR-39)
docs.text:
• Risk: If PIN verification key (PVK) extracted from compromised HSM, offline PINs can be guessed

  • 4-digit PIN space: Only 10,000 combinations; exhaustive search in milliseconds

  • Defense: VISA PVV uses 3DES with 4-bit result from 11-digit PAN+PIN input; limits false positives

  • Countermeasure: HSM access control and PCI HSM require M-of-N for PVK access

docs.title: 2.10.3 API-Level Attack on Thales RG7000
docs.text:
• Discovery: Anderson and Bond (Cambridge, 2003) found API-level flaws in Thales/IBM HSMs

  • Attack: Combine Exportkey + Translate commands to extract keys in cleartext

  • Principle: HSM commands individually secure; combinations create logical vulnerabilities

  • Fix: API reformulation; explicit key type attribute flags; command access restrictions

docs.title: 2.10.4 Cold Boot Attack on Battery-Backed SRAM
docs.text:
• Attack: Freeze SRAM battery; remove chip; read key material at -60C (data retention: hours to days)

  • Countermeasure (FIPS L4): Mesh sensor wire over SRAM; voltage/temperature sensors trigger zeroization

  • Additional: Key cache encryption with ephemeral key; SRAM scrambling on power loss

docs.text:

docs.title: 2.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: FIPS 140-3 Level Selection for PKI Infrastructure

A government agency is deploying a new PKI with the following components: (a) Root CA that signs Intermediate CA certificates (once per year), (b) Intermediate CA that signs subscriber certificates (100/day), (c) OCSP responder signing (10,000 responses/day), (d) Code signing for software releases. Select the appropriate FIPS 140-3 level for each component and justify the choice. Solution:

  1. Root CA – FIPS 140-3 Level 4. The root CA private key is the most critical asset. Compromise would invalidate the entire PKI. Level 4 provides complete physical protection envelope, environmental attack protection (EFP/EFT), and tamper-response zeroization. The low volume (once/year) means performance is not critical. Recommended: Thales payShield 10K or IBM 4769 in an air-gapped facility.

  2. Intermediate CA – FIPS 140-3 Level 3. Level 3 provides tamper resistance with identity-based authentication. Performance at 100 sigs/day is trivially achievable. Physical separation of signing interface from admin interface is required. Recommended: Thales Luna Network HSM 7 or Utimaco CryptoServer Se50.

  3. OCSP Responder – FIPS 140-3 Level 3. 10,000 RSA signatures/day (0.12/s) is easily achievable. The OCSP key is a delegated signer; compromise allows forgery of revocation status but does not compromise CA key. Level 3 is standard for OCSP; Luna PCIe HSM or nShield Solo XC are suitable.

  4. Code Signing – FIPS 140-3 Level 3. Code signing private key compromise would allow malware distribution signed by a trusted key. Level 3 with strict access control (M-of-N authentication) and audit logging is required. YubiHSM 2 (Level 3) is suitable for small teams; Luna for enterprise scale.

Solved Problem: Key Wrapping and TR-31 Key Block Analysis

A payment processor needs to securely transport a new Zone Master Key (ZMK) from their HSM to a partner bank’s HSM. The key is AES-256. (a) What is a TR-31 key block and what fields does it contain? (b) Construct the key block header for this ZMK transport. (c) Why is simple encryption with the KEK insufficient? Solution: (a) TR-31 Key Block Structure: TR-31 (ANSI X9.143-2022) defines a key block format that binds a key to its attributes, preventing repurposing attacks (using a PIN encryption key as a MAC key, for example).

Field Length Example Value Version ID 1 char D (AES key derivation binding) Key Block Length 4 char 0112 (total block length) Key Usage 2 char K0 (Key Encryption Key / Zone Master Key) Algorithm 1 char A (AES) Mode of Use 1 char X (Key used for key derivation) Key Version Number 2 char 00 (no version assigned) Exportability 1 char S (Sensitive – exportable under KEK only) Number of Optional Blocks 2 char 00 Reserved 2 char 00

(b) Example TR-31 header for AES-256 ZMK transport: D0112K0AX0000000 Breakdown: Version D, Length 0112, Key Usage K0, Algorithm A (AES), Mode X, Version 00, Export S, Optional 00, Reserved 00.

(c) Why simple KEK encryption is insufficient:

  • No attribute binding: A simply-encrypted AES key can be repurposed as any key type

  • No integrity: Bit flips in the wrapped key are undetectable

  • No version management: Cannot distinguish key versions

  • Regulatory: PCI HSM v3.0 requires TR-31 format for all key exchange

TR-31 uses AES-CMAC to authenticate the header + key, preventing tampering.

Solved Problem: HSM Performance Design: Cloud HSM Cluster

A cloud application requires HSM-backed TLS certificates for 50,000 concurrent HTTPS connections. Peak new connection rate: 5,000 TLS 1.3 handshakes/second. Key type: ECDSA P-256 (used for TLS certificate private key). How many Thales Luna Network HSM 7 units are needed? Design the HA cluster. Solution: Performance Analysis:

Thales Luna Network HSM 7 specifications:

  • ECDSA P-256 sign throughput: approximately 10,000 signs/second per HSM

  • TLS 1.3 handshake with ECDSA P-256 requires: 1 ECDSA sign (server) + 1 ECDH derivation

  • ECDH P-256 throughput: approximately 8,000 derivations/second

  • Combined TLS ops: min(10,000, 8,000) = 8,000 handshakes/second per HSM

Capacity calculation:

\[\begin{align*} \text{HSMs needed} &= \lceil \frac{5{,}000}{8{,}000} \rceil = \lceil 0.625 \rceil = 1 \text{ for peak load} \end{align*}\]

For high availability (no single point of failure) and 100% overhead for failures:

  • Minimum: 2 HSMs in active-active cluster (Luna HA group)

  • Recommended: 3 HSMs (N+1 redundancy); 2 active + 1 standby

  • Geographic distribution: 2 units in primary DC, 1 in DR site

  • Luna HA group: automatic key synchronization; transparent failover in \(<\)1 second

  • Total capacity: 24,000 TLS 1.3 handshakes/second (3x HSM)

Architecture: Application servers connect via TLS to Luna Network HSM 7 using PKCS#11. Private key CKA_EXTRACTABLE = FALSE; certificate private key never leaves HSM. Luna HA library handles load balancing and failover transparently to the application.

Solved Problem: SoftHSM2 Development Workflow

You need to prototype an application that uses PKCS#11 for key storage before deploying on a real HSM. Set up SoftHSM2 on Ubuntu, generate an RSA-2048 key pair, sign a message, and verify it. Identify the limitations of SoftHSM2 versus a physical FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM. Solution:

# Install SoftHSM2 (PKCS#11 software HSM for development)
sudo apt-get install softhsm2 openssl gnutls-bin

# Initialize a new token
softhsm2-util --init-token --slot 0 --label 'DevHSM' \
              --so-pin 'admin-pin' --pin 'user-pin'

# List available slots
softhsm2-util --show-slots

# Generate RSA-2048 key pair using p11tool (gnutls)
p11tool --provider /usr/lib/softhsm/libsofthsm2.so \
        --login --set-pin 'user-pin' \
        --generate-rsa --bits 2048 --label 'MyRSAKey' \
        'pkcs11:model=SoftHSM

# Sign a file with the HSM key via pkcs11-tool
pkcs11-tool --module /usr/lib/softhsm/libsofthsm2.so \
            --login --pin 'user-pin' \
            --sign --mechanism SHA256-RSA-PKCS \
            --id 01 -i message.bin -o signature.bin

# Verify signature with OpenSSL
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify public.pem -signature signature.bin message.bin

Limitations of SoftHSM2 vs Physical FIPS HSM:

Property SoftHSM2 Physical HSM (FIPS L3) FIPS certification None FIPS 140-3 Level 3 Physical tamper protection None (pure software) Tamper-responsive envelope Key material protection AES-encrypted SQLite DB Battery-backed SRAM + mesh TRNG quality OS entropy (getrandom) Hardware RNG (BSI PTG.2) DPA/SCA resistance None Balanced logic, power filtering Audit logging None Tamper-evident audit log Performance CPU-limited (100s RSA/s) 10,000+ RSA-2048/s

SoftHSM2 is suitable for PKCS#11 API development and testing only; never use for production key material.

docs.title: 2.14.1 Entrust nShield 5s and 5c (2024): FIPS 140-3 Level 3 with PQC
docs.text:
Entrust released the nShield 5s (network appliance) and nShield 5c (PCIe card) in 2024, the first nShield generation achieving FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation. Key improvements over the nShield Connect 6000+ include post-quantum algorithm support and updated CodeSafe sandbox:

Table 2.8. Entrust nShield 5s Specifications (2024) Parameter Value FIPS validation FIPS 140-3 Level 3 (CMVP #4600+) RSA-2048 throughput 20,000 ops/s ECC P-256 throughput 40,000 ops/s Post-quantum algorithms ML-DSA-44/65/87, ML-KEM-512/768/1024 (firmware) Hybrid signing ECDSA P-256 + ML-DSA-44 dual-algorithm certificates CodeSafe SDK Version 13: RISC-V sandbox replacing ARM SC300 Key management Security World v14; backward-compatible with nShield 6000+ Throughput (AES-GCM) 20 Gbps hardware-accelerated

Note: Entrust Security World technology allows nShield 5s HSMs to share keys with older nShield Connect 6000+ units in the same cluster during migration. This enables zero-downtime hardware refresh for production PKI deployments.

docs.title: 2.14.2 AWS CloudHSM v3 and External Key Store (XKS) Integration (2024)
docs.text:
Amazon Web Services released CloudHSM v3 in 2024 and the External Key Store (XKS) integration for AWS KMS, enabling customer-managed HSMs to serve as the key authority for KMS:

  • CloudHSM v3: Multi-AZ cluster management improvements; automatic firmware update to FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware; new cloudhsm-cli replacing legacy CLI

  • XKS (External Key Store): KMS API calls proxied through customer VPC endpoint to on-premises or co-located FIPS HSM; key material never leaves customer hardware

  • XKS protocol: HTTPS proxy (TLS 1.3); PKCS#11 on customer HSM; KMS Encrypt/Decrypt translated to C_Encrypt/C_Decrypt

  • Latency: XKS adds \(\approx 5\)–20 ms per call versus \(<1\) ms for KMS-managed keys

  • Use case: Regulated sectors (financial, healthcare, EU data sovereignty) where key material must reside in customer-controlled hardware

Tip: XKS is not a substitute for performance-sensitive workloads. For bulk S3 server-side encryption, keep DEKs in KMS. Use XKS only for the root wrapping key (KEK) that protects data encryption keys, reducing call frequency to infrequent key wrap/unwrap operations.

docs.title: 2.14.3 PKCS#11 3.0 Standard (2023): Post-Quantum Mechanism IDs
docs.text:
OASIS published PKCS#11 Version 3.0 (officially OASIS PKCS11-v3.0) with formal post-quantum mechanism identifiers:

Table 2.9. PKCS#11 3.0 Post-Quantum Mechanism IDs (OASIS PKCS11-v3.0) Mechanism CKM ID Algorithm CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x00004200 ML-KEM-512/768/1024 keygen CKM_ML_KEM_ENCAPSULATE 0x00004201 ML-KEM encapsulation CKM_ML_KEM_DECAPSULATE 0x00004202 ML-KEM decapsulation CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x00004210 ML-DSA-44/65/87 keygen CKM_ML_DSA 0x00004211 ML-DSA sign/verify CKM_SLH_DSA 0x00004220 SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) sign/verify

The CKA_PARAMETER_SET attribute on key objects specifies the parameter set (e.g., CKP_ML_KEM_768 or CKP_ML_DSA_65).

docs.title: 2.14.4 HSM-as-a-Service: Azure Managed HSM and GCP Cloud HSM (2024)
docs.text:
The HSM-as-a-Service model matured in 2024 with significant updates:

Table 2.10. HSM-as-a-Service Platforms Comparison (2024) Service FIPS Level PQC Support 2024 Updates Azure Managed HSM FIPS 140-3 L3 Preview (ML-DSA) Sovereign key rotation; Managed Identity binding AWS CloudHSM v3 FIPS 140-3 L3 No (roadmap) Multi-AZ auto-failover; new CLI GCP Cloud HSM FIPS 140-2 L3 No Cloud KMS Autokey; HSM key attestation IBM Cloud HSM FIPS 140-2 L4 No z/OS CEX8 integration

Warning: FIPS 140-2 L3 vs. FIPS 140-3 L3 is not equivalent. The newer 140-3 standard aligns with ISO/IEC 19790:2012 and adds stricter entropy source requirements, software/firmware security, and physical attack testing. Verify the exact CMVP certificate number for each deployment, not just the self-reported level.

docs.title: 2.14.5 Thales Luna Network HSM 7.x PQC Firmware (2024)
docs.text:
Thales released a post-quantum firmware update for existing Luna Network HSM 7 hardware in mid-2024, enabling field upgrade of deployed units without hardware replacement:

  • PQC algorithms added: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87; ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768; SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s

  • Hybrid certificate support: Luna SDK 8.5 generates X.509 certificates carrying both an ECDSA P-256 public key and an ML-DSA-65 public key in a SubjectAltName extension

  • Migration tooling: lunacm command hagroup addmember transparently replicates PQC keys to all cluster members

  • FIPS status: PQC mechanisms are non-FIPS pending CMVP validation; existing FIPS-approved mechanisms remain available in parallel

docs.title: 2.14.6 HSM Post-Quantum Migration Strategy: Hybrid Keys and Dual-Algorithm Signing
docs.text:
Industry consensus (NIST IR 8547, 2024) recommends a hybrid approach during the transition to post-quantum cryptography in HSM deployments:

Table 2.11. Hybrid PQC Migration Strategy for HSMs Phase Timeline Action Inventory 2024 Audit all HSM-protected key types; classify by longevity requirement Hybrid KEM 2024–2025 Implement X-Wing (ECDH + ML-KEM-768) for TLS key exchange Hybrid signing 2025–2026 Generate dual-algorithm CA certs (ECDSA + ML-DSA) Validation 2026 Await CMVP validation of PQC mechanisms in HSM firmware Classical sunset 2028+ Deprecate RSA-2048 / ECDSA P-256 for long-lived keys

Note: The X-Wing hybrid KEM (IETF draft-irtf-cfrg-xwing) combines X25519 with ML-KEM-768 into a single KEM mechanism. It is the recommended hybrid for TLS 1.3 supported_groups extension in the 2024–2026 transition window.

docs.title: 2.15 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between tamper evidence, tamper resistance, and tamper response in FIPS 140-3 terminology. Give a physical mechanism example for each concept, specifying which FIPS level each mechanism corresponds to.

  2. A bank deploys a Thales payShield 10K HSM for PIN processing. The HSM uses 3DES for legacy PIN block encryption (ISO 9564 Format 0). PCI DSS 3.2.1 requires migration to AES by 2024. Describe the key migration procedure including key types, TR-31 key blocks, and HSM commands required.

  3. Describe the M-of-N smart card authentication scheme used in HSM key ceremonies. If N=7 and M=4, how many distinct groups of custodians can reconstruct the key? What are the security properties of Shamir Secret Sharing used to implement this?

  4. Compare the security architecture of AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, and Azure Managed HSM. For each: (a) which physical hardware is used, (b) FIPS level, (c) who holds the HSM admin credentials, (d) network isolation model.

  5. You discover that a deployed HSM has PKCS#11 attribute CKA_EXTRACTABLE = TRUE on the TLS private key. What are the security implications? How would an attacker exploit this? What procedure should be followed to remediate?

  6. Design a PKCS#11-based code signing service for a software company signing 500 releases per day. Requirements: (a) air-gapped signing workstation, (b) dual control (two engineers must approve each signing), (c) audit log with date/time/signer. Specify the HSM product, authentication mechanism, and workflow.

  7. Explain the Anderson-Bond HSM API attack discovered at Cambridge in 2003. What two specific PKCS#11 commands were combined to extract key material? What PKCS#11 attribute was missing that would have prevented this attack?

  8. A retail payment terminal uses DUKPT (Derived Unique Key Per Transaction) with Base Derivation Key (BDK) stored in an acquiring bank HSM. Explain: (a) how DUKPT derives unique keys per transaction, (b) what happens if the BDK is compromised, (c) why DUKPT is preferred over a shared PEK for large terminal deployments.

  9. Calculate the number of RSA-4096 sign operations per second possible on a Thales Luna PCIe HSM 7 (10,000 RSA-2048/s). Justify your estimate using operation count analysis. How many such HSMs are needed for a Certificate Authority signing 1 million certificates per day with RSA-4096?

  10. A post-quantum migration plan requires adding ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium3) support to an existing Thales Luna HSM infrastructure. What are the firmware update requirements, key size implications (1,952 B public key, 4,000 B private key), and PKCS#11 mechanism IDs? How would hybrid classical+PQC signing be implemented?

  11. Write a complete PyKCS11 Python script that: (a) initializes the PKCS#11 library, (b) generates an AES-256 key with CKA_EXTRACTABLE=False, (c) encrypts a 64-byte message with AES-CBC, (d) decrypts and verifies. Include error handling for CKR_PIN_INCORRECT and CKR_TOKEN_NOT_PRESENT.

  12. Describe the zeroization process for an HSM upon tamper detection. What triggers zeroization (list 5 sensors)? What is zeroized? What is the minimum time specification for zeroization in FIPS 140-3? After zeroization, what is the device state and recovery procedure?

docs.title: 3.1 Introduction
docs.text:
A Physically Unclonable Function (PUF) is a hardware security primitive that exploits manufacturing process variations inherent in semiconductor fabrication to create a unique, device-specific mapping from input challenges to output responses. PUFs serve as a hardware fingerprint – even two chips manufactured from identical masks will produce different responses due to nanoscale variations in transistor threshold voltages, wire widths, and oxide thicknesses.

Key properties of an ideal PUF:

  • Uniqueness: Two different PUF instances produce distinct responses to the same challenge

  • Reproducibility (Reliability): Same instance, same challenge produces the same response across temperature/voltage variations

  • Unclonability: No physical device can reproduce the PUF response profile, even the manufacturer

  • Unpredictability: Responses appear random; responses to unseen challenges are unpredictable

  • One-wayness: Cannot derive PUF physical parameters from observed challenge-response pairs (CRPs)

Note: PUFs are classified as Strong PUFs (exponential CRP space, e.g., Arbiter PUF with \(2^n\) challenges) or Weak PUFs (limited CRP space, e.g., SRAM PUF with one challenge per memory cell). Strong PUFs enable authentication protocols; Weak PUFs are used for key generation.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Operating Principle
docs.text:
An Arbiter PUF uses a race condition between two signal paths to generate a 1-bit response. An \(n\)-stage arbiter PUF provides a challenge space of \(2^n\) distinct challenges.

Each switch stage either passes signals straight or crosses them based on challenge bit \(c_i\). The arbiter samples which path arrives first, producing 1-bit response \(r\).

docs.title: 3.2.2 Additive Delay Model
docs.text:
The additive delay model represents path timing difference as linear in challenge parity products:

\[\Delta = \mathbf{w}^T \cdot \Phi(c)\]

where \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) is the delay weight vector and \(\Phi(c)\) is the \((n+1)\)-dimensional feature vector. The response is \(r = \text{sgn}(\Delta)\). This linear separability makes Arbiter PUFs vulnerable to logistic regression attacks.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Architecture
docs.text:
A Ring Oscillator PUF uses pairs of identically-designed ring oscillators. Due to process variations, each pair oscillates at slightly different frequencies. The PUF response bit is determined by which oscillator in a pair runs faster.

Note: FPGA implementation constraint: RO pairs must be placed in adjacent LUTs with identical routing constraints. Otherwise routing asymmetry dominates over process variation, reducing PUF uniqueness. Xilinx ISE/Vivado placement constraints: LOC and BEL directives.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Operating Principle
docs.text:
SRAM cells have a metastable state at power-up. Their initial value (0 or 1) is determined by transistor mismatch – the stronger transistor wins the race and sets the stable state. Each cell reliably powers up to its preferred value, creating a device-specific fingerprint.

  • Cell count: Typical SRAM PUF uses 8,192 cells (1,024 bytes); enrolled at device initialization

  • Reliability:  95-99% of bits are stable across -40 to +85 C and 1.8V-3.6V supply

  • Unstable bits:  1-5% of bits are near-metastable; masked out via enrollment helper data

  • Uniqueness: Hamming distance between two different devices:  50% (ideal random)

  • Key generation: SRAM startup values processed through Fuzzy Extractor to produce stable key

  • Products: NXP SE050/SE051, Intrinsic ID QuiddiKey IP core (used in Microchip SAME54)

docs.title: 3.5 Fuzzy Extractor
docs.text:
A Fuzzy Extractor converts a noisy PUF response into a stable cryptographic key. It consists of two algorithms:

  • Gen\((w)\): On first call (enrollment), generates key \(k\) and helper data \(P\) from PUF response \(w\)

  • Rep\((w', P)\): On subsequent calls (reconstruction), reproduces \(k\) from noisy \(w'\) using \(P\)

docs.title: 3.5.1 Implementation with BCH Error Correction
docs.text:
BCH codes are commonly used in fuzzy extractors for SRAM PUFs. A BCH\((n, k, t)\) code can correct up to \(t\) bit errors.

Table 3.1. Fuzzy Extractor Parameters for SRAM PUF Key Generation Parameter Value Notes SRAM PUF response size 2,048 bits 2K SRAM cells evaluated at power-up BCH code BCH(2047, 1024, 55) Corrects up to 55 bit errors in 2047-bit block Error rate assumption 12% bit error rate Conservative for -40 to +85 C, \(\pm\)10% voltage Raw SRAM bits used 2,048 bits For one BCH block Codeword bits \(n\) 2,047 bits BCH block length Information bits \(k\) 1,024 bits Bits available after ECC overhead Helper data \((n-k)\) = 1,023 bits parity check bits Public; does not leak PUF secret Output key after hash 256 bits SHA-256(Rep output) Security level 128 bits After accounting for helper data leakage

docs.title: 3.5.2 Fuzzy Extractor Python Implementation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import hashlib
from bchlib import BCH  # pip install bchlib

class FuzzyExtractor:
    def __init__(self, t=55, n=2047):
        """BCH(n, k, t) fuzzy extractor for SRAM PUF key generation"""
        self.bch = BCH(t, n)  # BCH with t error correction
        self.n = n

    def gen(self, sram_bits):
        """Enrollment: sram_bits is numpy array of 0/1 values (n bits)"""
        # Truncate to BCH block size
        raw = sram_bits[:self.n]
        raw_bytes = np.packbits(raw).tobytes()
        # Generate ECC syndrome (helper data)
        data_len = self.bch.data_len
        secret = raw_bytes[:data_len]
        ecc = self.bch.encode(secret)
        helper_data = raw_bytes[data_len:] + ecc  # ECC parity bits
        # Derive stable key via SHA-256
        key = hashlib.sha256(secret).digest()
        return key, helper_data

    def rep(self, noisy_sram_bits, helper_data):
        """Reconstruction: recover key from noisy readout + helper data"""
        raw = noisy_sram_bits[:self.n]
        raw_bytes = np.packbits(raw).tobytes()
        data_len = self.bch.data_len
        # Apply ECC correction
        ecc = helper_data[len(helper_data)-self.bch.ecc_bytes:]
        corrected, _ = self.bch.decode(raw_bytes[:data_len], ecc)
        if corrected is None:
            raise ValueError('Too many bit errors -- PUF decoding failed')
        key = hashlib.sha256(corrected).digest()
        return key

# Simulate SRAM PUF enrollment and reconstruction
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sram_enrollment = rng.integers(0, 2, size=2047)  # PUF startup values
fe = FuzzyExtractor(t=55, n=2047)
key, helper = fe.gen(sram_enrollment)
print(f'Enrolled key: {key.hex()}')

# Simulate noisy readout (5
flip_mask = rng.random(2047) < 0.05
sram_noisy = sram_enrollment ^ flip_mask.astype(int)
recovered_key = fe.rep(sram_noisy, helper)
print(f'Recovered key: {recovered_key.hex()}')
print(f'Keys match: {key == recovered_key}')

docs.title: 3.6 Machine Learning Attacks on PUFs
docs.text: Strong PUFs (particularly Arbiter PUFs) are vulnerable to machine learning attacks. Given a set of challenge-response pairs (CRPs), an attacker can train a model to predict responses to unseen challenges with \(>99\%\) accuracy.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Logistic Regression Attack on Arbiter PUF
docs.text:
• Method: Logistic Regression (Ruhrmair et al., 2010; Becker 2015)

  • Input: Challenge feature vector \(\Phi(c) \in \{-1,+1\}^{n+1}\)

  • Model: \(P(r=1|c) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \Phi(c))\) where \(\sigma\) is sigmoid

  • Training data: 10,000 to 100,000 CRPs collected via physical access or side-channel

  • Accuracy: 64-bit Arbiter PUF: \(>99\%\) with \(\sim\)10,000 CRPs

  • 128-bit: \(>99\%\) with \(\sim\)100,000 CRPs

  • XOR-n PUF: Requires \(10^n\) CRPs; \(n=8\) is currently at ML boundary

docs.title: 3.6.2 pypuf Machine Learning Attack Example
docs.text:
# pip install pypuf
import numpy as np
from pypuf.simulation import ArbiterPUF
from pypuf.attack import LRAttack2021
from pypuf.io import random_inputs

# Create a 64-bit Arbiter PUF instance (victim)
puf = ArbiterPUF(n=64, seed=0xDEADBEEF)

# Collect 20,000 challenge-response pairs (simulating physical access)
N = 20000
challenges = random_inputs(n=64, N=N, seed=42)
responses = puf.eval(challenges)

# Split into train/test
train_c, test_c = challenges[:15000], challenges[15000:]
train_r, test_r = responses[:15000], responses[15000:]

# Run LR attack
attack = LRAttack2021(
    puf, train_c, train_r, k=1,  # k=1 for single arbiter
    transformation='id', combiner='xor'
)
model = attack.fit()

# Evaluate accuracy on unseen challenges
model_resp = model.eval(test_c)
accuracy = np.mean(model_resp == test_r)
print(f'Attack accuracy: {accuracy:.1

# Compare: 2-XOR Arbiter PUF (more resistant)
from pypuf.simulation import XORArbiterPUF
xor_puf = XORArbiterPUF(n=64, k=2, seed=0xBEEF)  # 2-XOR
# Needs ~1M CRPs for k=2; ~10M for k=4

Warning: All Arbiter PUF variants (single, XOR, iPUF) have been shown vulnerable to ML attacks with sufficient CRPs. Only Weak PUFs (SRAM PUF, Flash PUF) or PUFs with CRP obfuscation (Controlled PUF) are currently considered ML-resistant for authentication applications.

docs.title: 3.11 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: PUF Uniqueness: Hamming Distance Calculation

An SRAM PUF is evaluated across 64 chips from the same wafer. Each chip produces a 512-bit response to the same challenge. The inter-chip Hamming distances are measured pairwise. The mean inter-HD is \(\mu = 49.8\%\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 2.1\%\). (a) Is this an acceptable uniqueness value? (b) What fraction of chip pairs have inter-HD \(> 55\%\) (indicating problematic overlap), assuming Gaussian distribution?

Solution: (a) Ideal uniqueness:

The ideal inter-HD is \(50\%\), meaning two random \(n\)-bit strings differ in exactly half the bits on average. \(\mu = 49.8\%\) is within \(0.2\%\) of the ideal, which is excellent. Accepted criterion: \(|\mu - 50\%| < 2\%\). Pass.

(b) Fraction with inter-HD \(> 55\%\):

Standardise: \(z = (55 - 49.8) / 2.1 = 5.2 / 2.1 = 2.476\).

From the standard normal table: \(P(Z > 2.476) = 1 - \Phi(2.476) \approx 0.0066\).

About 0.66% of chip pairs have inter-HD \(> 55\%\). For 64 chips, the number of unique pairs is \(\binom{64}{2} = 2016\). Expected number of problematic pairs: \(2016 \times 0.0066 \approx 13\).

Interpretation: These 13 pairs are not security failures—they merely mean those two chips produce unusually similar PUF responses. A fuzzy extractor with BCH code correcting \(t = 10\) errors on 512-bit responses would still produce distinct keys, since the HD difference (\(55\% \times 512 \approx 282\) bits differing) far exceeds the error correction capability of any practical code.

Solved Problem: Fuzzy Extractor: BCH Code Parameter Selection

An SRAM PUF produces 512-bit responses with intra-device HD \(\leq 12.5\%\) (i.e., the same chip measured twice differs in at most \(0.125 \times 512 = 64\) bits due to temperature/voltage variation). Select BCH code parameters \((n, k, t)\) to correct up to 64-bit errors in 512-bit codewords, and calculate the helper data length.

Solution: BCH code selection:

A BCH\((n, k, t)\) code over \(GF(2^m)\) with block length \(n = 2^m - 1\) can correct up to \(t\) errors. We need \(n \geq 512\) and \(t \geq 64\).

Choose \(m = 10\): \(n = 2^{10} - 1 = 1023\). For \(t = 64\) errors, the required parity-check bits: \(r \leq m \cdot t = 10 \times 64 = 640\) bits. Then:

\[k = n - r = 1023 - 640 = 383 \text{ information bits}\]

Practical choice: BCH(1023, 383, 64) corrects 64 errors in a 1023-bit codeword, providing 383 bits of secure key material.

Secure sketch construction:

  1. Enrollment: PUF generates reference response \(R\) (512 bits, zero-padded to 1023 bits). Encode: \(C = \text{BCH-Encode}(K)\) for a random 383-bit key \(K\). Helper data: \(P = R \oplus C\) (1023 bits, stored publicly).

  2. Reconstruction: PUF generates noisy \(R'\) (\(R' = R \oplus e\), \(\text{HW}(e) \leq 64\)). Recover: \(C' = R' \oplus P = C \oplus e\). Decode: \(K = \text{BCH-Decode}(C')\) (succeeds since \(\text{HW}(e) \leq t = 64\)).

Helper data size: 1023 bits \(\approx 128\) bytes, stored in non-volatile memory.

Security: Given \(P\) and up to \(n-k = 640\) parity bits, an adversary cannot recover \(K\) without the PUF (information-theoretic security from the fuzzy extractor construction).

Solved Problem: ML Attack: Logistic Regression Success Rate

A 64-stage Arbiter PUF is attacked using logistic regression with the additive delay model. The feature vector is \(\phi(c) \in \{-1, +1\}^{65}\). After training on \(N = 4000\) challenge-response pairs (CRPs), the model achieves 92% prediction accuracy on a held-out test set. How many additional CRPs are needed to reach 99% accuracy, assuming accuracy grows as \(\text{acc}(N) = 1 - A \cdot N^{-\alpha}\)? Estimate \(A\) and \(\alpha\) from the two data points: (1000 CRPs, 81%) and (4000 CRPs, 92%).

Solution: Fit the model: From \(\text{acc}(N) = 1 - A \cdot N^{-\alpha}\):

\[\begin{align*} 1 - 0.81 &= A \cdot 1000^{-\alpha} \Rightarrow 0.19 = A \cdot 1000^{-\alpha} \\ 1 - 0.92 &= A \cdot 4000^{-\alpha} \Rightarrow 0.08 = A \cdot 4000^{-\alpha} \end{align*}\]

Divide: \(0.19/0.08 = (4000/1000)^{\alpha} = 4^{\alpha}\).

\[4^{\alpha} = 2.375 \Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{\log(2.375)}{\log(4)} = \frac{0.3757}{0.6021} = 0.624\]

From first equation: \(A = 0.19 \times 1000^{0.624} = 0.19 \times 76.9 = 14.6\).

CRPs for 99% accuracy:

\[0.01 = 14.6 \cdot N^{-0.624} \Rightarrow N^{0.624} = 1460 \Rightarrow N = 1460^{1/0.624} = 1460^{1.603}\] \[\log N = 1.603 \times \log 1460 = 1.603 \times 3.164 = 5.072 \Rightarrow N \approx 10^{5.07} \approx 118{,}000 \text{ CRPs}\]

Conclusion: Approximately 118,000 CRPs are needed for 99% accuracy. For comparison, a Strong PUF with \(2^{64}\) possible challenges makes exhaustive CRP collection infeasible (years of operation). XOR-PUF designs increase the difficulty of ML attacks by a factor of \(\binom{k}{n}\) combinations.

docs.title: 3.12.1 Deep Learning Attacks on PUFs (2023–2024)
docs.text:
The machine learning threat to Strong PUFs has intensified with deep learning approaches that surpass classical logistic regression on XOR and iPUF variants:

Table 3.6. ML Attack Accuracy on PUF Variants (2023–2024 Literature) PUF Type Attack Method CRPs Required Accuracy 64-bit Arbiter PUF Logistic Regression \(\sim\)10,000 \(>99\%\) 4-XOR Arbiter PUF (64-bit) Deep MLP (3-layer) \(\sim\)200,000 \(>98\%\) 5-XOR Arbiter PUF (64-bit) ResNet-style CNN \(\sim\)1,000,000 \(>96\%\) iPUF (\(k=6\)) GAN-assisted attack (2023) \(\sim\)500,000 \(>92\%\) Weak SRAM PUF No ML attack (insufficient CRP space) N/A N/A

A 2023 paper from ETH Zürich introduced GAN-based CRP augmentation: a generative adversarial network trained on 50,000 real CRPs synthesises millions of plausible CRPs, dramatically reducing the physical access needed before offline model training. The generated dataset then trains a ResNet classifier to \(>97\%\) on 5-XOR Arbiter PUFs.

Warning: The security claims of any Strong PUF design published before 2022 should be re-evaluated against 2023–2024 deep learning attacks. Only Controlled PUFs (hash-obfuscated challenge) and Weak PUFs (SRAM PUF for key generation) currently withstand state-of-the-art ML adversaries.

docs.title: 3.12.2 New PUF Types: Memristor PUF and SRAM PUF in 3 nm Processes
docs.text:
Memristor PUF (resistive RAM based):

  • Exploits stochastic switching threshold variations in HfO\(_2\) RRAM cells

  • Demonstrated on TSMC 28 nm and Samsung 14 nm HBM stacks (2023 ISSCC)

  • Advantage: \(10\times\) higher cell density vs. SRAM PUF; non-volatile state

  • Challenge: retention at elevated temperature (\(>85^{\circ}\)C) causes bit drift; requires \(t > 100\) error correction

  • Uniqueness: \(48.2 \pm 1.8\%\) inter-HD across 200 test chips

SRAM PUF at 3 nm (TSMC N3E, 2024):

  • FinFET-to-GAA (Gate-All-Around) transistor transition changes mismatch statistics: threshold voltage \(V_T\) mismatch \(\sigma_{\Delta V_T} \approx 2.1\) mV (vs. 3.8 mV at 7 nm)

  • Lower mismatch reduces SRAM PUF startup reliability to \(\approx 93\%\) at \(-40^{\circ}\)C; requires stronger ECC (BCH \(t \geq 80\) for 512-bit block)

  • Intrinsic ID NVM PUF (2024): alternative entropy source from oxide trap density in N3E; avoids SRAM reliability degradation at advanced nodes

docs.title: 3.12.3 ISO/IEC 20897-1:2020 Updated Guidance (2024)
docs.text:
ISO/IEC TC47 published updated evaluation guidance for ISO/IEC 20897-1 PUF metrics in a 2024 corrigendum addressing advanced-node testing:

  • Temperature cycling: Evaluation now requires 3-cycle aging (\(-40^{\circ}\)C / \(+85^{\circ}\)C / \(+125^{\circ}\)C) to expose latent metastable cells before enrollment

  • Voltage margin testing: PUF must maintain \(< 5\%\) intra-HD at \(\pm 20\%\) \(V_{DD}\)

  • ML resilience assessment: New informative annex classifies PUFs as Class A (ML-resistant) or Class B (ML-vulnerable); only Class A permitted for authentication

  • Min-entropy lower bound: Minimum \(H_{min} \geq 0.85\) bits/cell mandated for Class A security; assessors must use NIST SP 800-90B estimators

docs.title: 3.12.4 PUF-Based Key Generation for Post-Quantum Algorithms
docs.text:
PUFs provide an attractive seed source for post-quantum key generation because the derived key is never stored in non-volatile memory:

Table 3.7. PUF Seed Requirements for Post-Quantum Key Generation Algorithm Seed Size PUF Bits Required ECC Overhead ML-KEM-768 (Kyber768) 32 bytes (256 bits) 512 raw bits (BCH) 256 bits helper data ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium3) 32 bytes (256 bits) 512 raw bits (BCH) 256 bits helper data SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s 48 bytes (384 bits) 768 raw bits 384 bits helper data X25519 / P-256 32 bytes (256 bits) 512 raw bits 256 bits helper data

The Intrinsic ID BroadKey 3.0 IP core (2024) implements the full FIPS 203/204-compliant derivation path: SRAM PUF \(\to\) BCH fuzzy extractor \(\to\) HKDF-SHA-256 \(\to\) ML-KEM/ML-DSA seed. BroadKey 3.0 is taped out on TSMC N5 and GlobalFoundries 22FDX.

Note: PUF-derived keys for post-quantum algorithms must satisfy the same entropy requirements as classical keys: \(\geq 256\) bits of min-entropy for 128-bit post-quantum security level. Verify min-entropy through NIST SP 800-90B assessment, not just statistical tests, before certifying a PUF for PQC key derivation.

docs.title: 3.12.5 NIST SP 800-90B Application to PUF Entropy Assessment
docs.text:
NIST SP 800-90B (Recommendation for Entropy Sources) is now the canonical framework for PUF entropy evaluation in FIPS-compliant products:

  • Min-entropy estimators: The ea_non_iid tool (NIST GitHub) computes the 10 independent estimators (collision, compression, Markov, …) from a raw PUF bitstream; the final \(H_{min}\) is the minimum of all estimators

  • Sample requirement: At least \(1{,}000{,}000\) raw bits from \(\geq 100\) devices across the full operating range must be collected

  • IID assumption: SRAM PUF bits are NOT independent and identically distributed (adjacent cells share supply rails); the non-IID path of SP 800-90B is mandatory

  • Conservative bound: NIST subtracts a 10-bit security margin from the estimated \(H_{min}\); a design targeting 128-bit security must demonstrate \(H_{min} \geq 138\) bits across 512 raw cells
