docs.title: 3.13 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Calculate the uniqueness and reliability metrics for a 128-bit RO-PUF implemented on 10 Artix-7 FPGAs. Describe the measurement procedure and specify the acceptable ranges for inter-HD (uniqueness) and intra-HD (reliability).

  2. An SRAM PUF has intra-HD of \(8\%\) at \(-40\)° C and \(18\%\) at \(85\)° C. Select BCH code parameters \((n, k, t)\) for a fuzzy extractor that reliably regenerates a 128-bit key across the full temperature range.

  3. Implement the pypuf logistic regression attack on a simulated 64-stage Arbiter PUF. Plot prediction accuracy vs. number of training CRPs (100 to 100,000). At what CRP count does the attack exceed 95% accuracy?

  4. A 5-XOR Arbiter PUF uses five 128-stage Arbiter PUFs in XOR combination. Estimate the number of CRPs needed for a logistic regression attack compared to a single Arbiter PUF. What neural network architecture could attack it?

  5. Describe the reliability-based attack on Arbiter PUFs. How does it exploit the intra-HD variability of “weak” challenges to recover model parameters without a conventional CRP dataset?

  6. Design a PUF-based key generation system for an IoT edge device using an ATECC608B. Specify: enrollment procedure, helper data storage location, key derivation (HKDF or KDF), and re-enrolment policy after a hardware replacement.

  7. Compare the security of Ring Oscillator PUF, SRAM PUF, and Arbiter PUF against (a) machine learning attacks, (b) cloning attacks, and (c) temperature/ voltage variation. Which is most suitable for a hostile-environment military device?

  8. Explain the controlled PUF construction that prevents a modelling attack by binding the challenge to a one-way function output. What hash function is used, and how does it affect the CRP distribution?

  9. A device uses a PUF-generated 256-bit root key as the DICE Unique Device Secret (UDS). Describe the full DICE CDI derivation chain from UDS to Layer 0 CDI, and explain how physical replacement of the SRAM chip changes the CDI.

  10. NIST IR 8214A defines a min-entropy floor for PUF outputs. Calculate the min-entropy per bit of a biased SRAM PUF where bit \(i\) is stuck-at-1 with probability \(p_i = 0.55\). What is the average min-entropy per bit across all cells?

docs.title: 4.1 Introduction
docs.text: A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is an isolated execution environment that provides security guarantees for code and data: confidentiality (data cannot be read by untrusted software), integrity (code/data cannot be modified), and attestability (remote party can verify the TEE state). TEEs represent a critical security primitive for cloud computing, mobile payments, and IoT.

docs.title: 4.2 TEE Landscape
docs.text: Table 4.1. TEE technologies comparison Technology Vendor Architecture Key Feature SGX Intel x86-64 Encrypted memory (EPC), DCAP TrustZone-A ARM AArch64/32 Secure/Normal world, OP-TEE TrustZone-M ARM Cortex-M TrustZone for microcontrollers SEV-SNP AMD x86-64 VM-level confidential computing TDX Intel x86-64 VM-level (Trust Domain) CCA ARM v9 Realm Management Extension Keystone RISC-V RISC-V PMP-based enclaves

docs.title: 4.3.1 Architecture
docs.text:
Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions) creates protected memory regions called enclaves:

  • EPC (Enclave Page Cache): Encrypted DRAM region (up to 512MB in SGX1, GBs in SGX2)

  • MEE (Memory Encryption Engine): AES-CTR encrypts EPC contents

  • MRENCLAVE: Measurement (SHA-256) of enclave code/data

  • MRSIGNER: SHA-256 of enclave signing key

docs.title: 4.3.2 SGX Instructions
docs.text:
ECREATE  -- Create an enclave (SECS page)
EADD     -- Add page to enclave
EEXTEND  -- Measure page content (extend MRENCLAVE)
EINIT    -- Initialize enclave (verify SIGSTRUCT)
EENTER   -- Enter enclave via TCS
EEXIT    -- Exit enclave
EGETKEY  -- Derive enclave-specific sealing key
EREPORT  -- Generate local attestation report

docs.title: 4.3.3 Remote Attestation (DCAP)
docs.text:
1. Application creates enclave; SGX generates REPORT

  2. Quoting Enclave signs REPORT -> QUOTE

  3. QUOTE sent to Intel PCCS (certificate cache service)

  4. Verifier checks QUOTE against Intel SGX Root CA

  5. Trust established: Enclave is genuine Intel SGX

docs.title: 4.4.1 TrustZone-A (Application Processors)
docs.text:
TrustZone-A partitions the system into Secure World and Normal World:

Secure World (S-EL1: OP-TEE OS, S-EL0: Trusted Apps)
  <- Monitor (EL3: ARM Trusted Firmware)
Normal World (EL1: Linux kernel, EL0: Applications)

NSS bit in bus transactions:
  NS=0: Secure transaction (Secure World only)
  NS=1: Non-Secure transaction (Normal World)

docs.title: 4.4.2 OP-TEE (Open Portable TEE)
docs.text:
OP-TEE is the open-source reference implementation of TrustZone TEE:

  • Trusted Apps: Run in S-EL0, isolated from each other via virtual MMU

docs.title: 4.4.3 TrustZone-M (Cortex-M33/M55)
docs.text:
For microcontrollers, TrustZone-M provides:

  • SAU (Security Attribution Unit): Configures secure/non-secure memory regions

  • Secure Entry Points: NSC (Non-Secure Callable) regions

  • No MMU required – uses MPU for isolation

docs.title: 4.5 AMD SEV-SNP
docs.text:
AMD SEV-SNP (Secure Encrypted Virtualization – Secure Nested Paging) provides VM-level confidential computing:

  • Memory encryption: Each VM has unique AES-128 encryption key

  • Memory integrity: RMP (Reverse Map Table) prevents hypervisor from remapping VM memory

  • Attestation: SNP Attestation Report signed by AMD SEV signing key

  • Use case: Azure Confidential VMs, GCP Confidential VMs

  • Projects: Enarx (TEE-agnostic runtime), Gramine (SGX library OS), Veraison (attestation)

docs.title: 4.10.1 Apple Secure Enclave (A17 Pro, 7nm)
docs.text:
The Apple Secure Enclave Processor (SEP) is a dedicated security subsystem in every Apple device since iPhone 5s:

  • CPU: Custom ARM-based processor (Cortex-M class ISA), physically isolated from Application Processor

  • Process node: 7nm on A17 Pro (iPhone 15 Pro); 3nm on A18 (iPhone 16)

  • Memory: Dedicated encrypted RAM, hardware-separated from AP memory bus via hardware firewall

  • Crypto engines: AES-256, ECC-P256/P384, SHA-2/3, TRNG (DRBG seeded from ring oscillators)

  • Boot: Immutable SEP Boot ROM -> SEP firmware (signed, verified before execution)

  • Keys: UID key (unique per device, blown at manufacture, never exported even to Apple)

  • Biometrics: Face ID and Touch ID templates stored and matched exclusively inside SEP

  • Attestation: SEP signs attestation statements for Apple KeyChain, Apple Pay, SE Attestation for MDM

docs.title: 4.10.2 Qualcomm Secure Processing Unit (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3)
docs.text:
The Qualcomm SPU is an isolated ARM Cortex-M core within the Snapdragon SoC:

  • Architecture: Dedicated ARM Cortex-M security processor; hardware memory firewall from AP

  • TEE OS: Qualcomm QTEE v5 (GlobalPlatform TEE Internal Core API v1.3.1 compliant)

  • Crypto: AES-256, RSA-4096, ECC-P256/P384, SHA-3, TRNG

  • Storage: Secure RPMB-backed replay-protected storage for tokens and biometric templates

  • Use cases: Fingerprint matching, Widevine L1 DRM, SIM authentication, Qualcomm Mobile Security

  • Separation: Hardware TZASC (TrustZone Address Space Controller) and XPU memory firewall

docs.title: 4.10.3 Samsung Knox Vault (Titan M2-equivalent)
docs.text:
Samsung Knox Vault (Galaxy S21+) implements a dedicated Secure Element physically separate from the AP:

  • Hardware: Separate security SoC (ARM SC300 core) + dedicated SRAM + embedded flash; own power supply

  • Isolation: Physical bus separation; no shared cache or DRAM with Application Processor

  • Crypto: AES-256, RSA-2048/4096, ECC-P256, ECDSA, SHA-256/512, hardware TRNG

  • Storage: Replay-protected secure storage for biometric templates, Samsung Pay tokens, lockscreen credentials

  • Certification: Common Criteria EAL 5+, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware module

  • Attestation: Knox Attestation API: ECDSA-signed report of device security state for Android Enterprise MDM

docs.title: 4.10.4 MediaTek TEE: TEEGRIS and Kinibi
docs.text:
MediaTek Dimensity SoCs implement TrustZone-A with either Trustonic Kinibi or Samsung TEEGRIS:

  • TrustZone: ARM Cortex-A cores; Monitor at EL3 (ATF); TEE OS at S-EL1

  • TEEGRIS: Samsung in-house TEE OS, GlobalPlatform compliant; Dimensity 9300+ and Exynos

  • Kinibi: Trustonic TEE; Dimensity 1200/9000 class; GP TEE API v1.2 compliant

docs.title: 4.13.1 SGX-Step: Controlled Page Fault Single-Stepping
docs.text:
github.com/jovanbulck/sgx-step exploits the fact that SGX does not protect against page fault injection by an untrusted OS:

  • Mechanism: Attacker clears present-bit (P=0) on enclave PTE; CPU raises #PF on each instruction; APIC timer provides single-instruction granularity

  • Effect: Single-step execution reveals instruction-level memory access pattern and enclave control flow

  • Exploit: Recover AES T-table lookup key-dependent indices; reveal RSA square-and-multiply private key bit sequence

  • Mitigation: SGX2 EMODPR/EACCEPT removes untrusted OS from PTE management; no complete fix for SGX1

docs.title: 4.13.2 CacheOut (CVE-2020-0549)
docs.text:
CacheOut (L1D Eviction Sampling) enables reading SGX enclave data via speculative L1D cache eviction:

  • Root cause: Speculative writes to L1D fill buffer leak stale data across privilege boundary

  • Impact: Cross-SGX-enclave and cross-VM data leakage; bypasses memory encryption (data leaked in plaintext in cache)

  • Mitigation: Microcode update + VERW instruction to flush fill buffers on privilege transition; Linux kernel 5.10+

docs.title: 4.13.3 LVI: Load Value Injection (CVE-2020-0551)
docs.text:
LVI is the inverse of Meltdown: inject attacker-controlled values into SGX enclave via speculative loads:

  • Mechanism: CPU speculatively uses stale fill-buffer or store-buffer value during enclave load; attacker data transiently used in enclave computation

  • Effect: Redirect enclave control flow speculatively; extract secrets via dependent timing measurement

  • Mitigation: LFENCE after every load in enclave code (up to 19x overhead); compiler flag -mindirect-branch=thunk

docs.title: 4.13.4 SGX AEPIC Leak (CVE-2022-21233)
docs.text:
Architectural (non-side-channel) leak of enclave data via uninitialized xAPIC MMIO registers:

  • Root cause: Reading certain xAPIC MMIO registers in legacy memory-mapped mode returns stale data from internal CPU register files

  • Impact: Approx. 16 bytes of enclave stack/heap per read; requires ring-0 privilege; direct architectural read

  • Mitigation: Disable xAPIC MMIO; enforce x2APIC mode via BIOS/kernel; Intel microcode update for affected Xeon SKUs

docs.title: 4.13.5 PLATYPUS: Power Side-Channel on Intel SGX (CVE-2020-8694)
docs.text:
Unprivileged Intel RAPL interface enables software-only power analysis of SGX enclaves:

  • Mechanism: Read /sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl energy counter before and after ECALL; compute delta-E; apply CPA with AES key hypothesis

  • Impact: Full AES-NI key recovery; full RSA key recovery; no physical access; no root required on pre-5.10 Linux

  • Mitigation: Restrict RAPL to root; kernel.perf_event_paranoid=3; Intel microcode disables unprivileged RAPL; Linux 5.10 patches intel_rapl_common driver

docs.title: 4.13.6 TrustZone Cache Timing Attacks
docs.text:
TrustZone world switches do not flush the shared L1/L2 cache by default, enabling PRIME+PROBE attacks:

  • Mechanism: Normal World PRIME-fills L1 cache sets; TA executes AES T-table lookup T[p[i] XOR k[i]] evicting primed lines; PROBE measures miss latency

  • Recovery: Since plaintext p[i] is known (chosen-plaintext), key byte k[i] = observed index XOR p[i]

  • Mitigation: (1) Flush L1 on world switch (3–5 us penalty); (2) ARMv8 AESE/AESMC hardware AES (register-to-register); (3) HACL* or BearSSL constant-time AES

docs.title: 4.14.1 Intel SGX ECALL/OCALL Example (C)
docs.text:
/* enclave.edl -- Enclave Definition Language interface */
enclave {
    trusted {
        public int ecall_seal_data(
            [in,  size=len]  const uint8_t *pt,  size_t len,
            [out, size=512]  uint8_t       *out,
            [out]            size_t        *out_len
        );
    };
    untrusted {
        void ocall_log([in, string] const char *msg);
    };
};

/* enclave.c -- Trusted code inside SGX enclave */
#include "sgx_tseal.h"
#include "enclave_t.h"

int ecall_seal_data(const uint8_t *pt, size_t len,
                    uint8_t *out, size_t *out_len) {
    uint32_t sz = sgx_calc_sealed_data_size(0, (uint32_t)len);
    if (sz > 512) return -1;
    sgx_status_t r = sgx_seal_data(
        0, NULL, (uint32_t)len, pt, sz, (sgx_sealed_data_t*)out);
    *out_len = sz;
    return (r == SGX_SUCCESS) ? 0 : -1;
}

/* app.c -- Untrusted host application */
#include "sgx_urts.h"
#include "enclave_u.h"

int main(void) {
    sgx_enclave_id_t eid;
    sgx_create_enclave("enclave.signed.so", 1, NULL, NULL, &eid, NULL);
    uint8_t sealed[512]; size_t slen = 0; int rv = 0;
    ecall_seal_data(eid, &rv, (uint8_t*)"secret", 6, sealed, &slen);
    sgx_destroy_enclave(eid);
    return 0;
}

TEE_Result TA_InvokeCommandEntryPoint(void *sess,

}

docs.title: 4.14.3 AMD SEV-SNP Attestation Report Parsing (Python)
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Parse AMD SEV-SNP attestation report (AMD ABI Table 21 v1.55)"""
import struct, json, sys

SNP_REPORT_SIZE = 0x4A0  # 1184 bytes

def parse_snp_report(raw: bytes) -> dict:
    if len(raw) < SNP_REPORT_SIZE:
        raise ValueError(f"Short report: {len(raw)}")
    version, guest_svn = struct.unpack_from("<II", raw, 0)
    policy  = struct.unpack_from("<Q",  raw, 8)[0]
    measurement = raw[0x38:0x38+48].hex()  # SHA-384 of guest FW
    host_data   = raw[0x68:0x68+32].hex()  # 32-byte host nonce
    chip_id     = raw[0x1A0:0x1A0+64].hex()
    sig_r = raw[0x2A0:0x2A0+48].hex()  # ECDSA-P384 R (little-endian)
    sig_s = raw[0x2E8:0x2E8+48].hex()  # ECDSA-P384 S
    return {"version": version, "guest_svn": guest_svn,
            "policy": hex(policy), "measurement": measurement,
            "host_data": host_data, "chip_id": chip_id,
            "sig_r": sig_r, "sig_s": sig_s}

def verify_vcek(report_bytes: bytes, vcek_pem: str) -> bool:
    from cryptography import x509
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ec import ECDSA
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.hashes import SHA384
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.utils import encode_dss_signature
    cert   = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(vcek_pem.encode())
    signed = report_bytes[:0x2A0]
    r = int.from_bytes(report_bytes[0x2A0:0x2C8], "little")
    s = int.from_bytes(report_bytes[0x2E8:0x310], "little")
    sig = encode_dss_signature(r, s)
    try:
        cert.public_key().verify(sig, signed, ECDSA(SHA384()))
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Verify failed: {e}"); return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raw = open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read(SNP_REPORT_SIZE)
    print(json.dumps(parse_snp_report(raw), indent=2))
    if len(sys.argv) > 2:
        ok = verify_vcek(raw, open(sys.argv[2]).read())
        print("Signature VALID" if ok else "Signature INVALID")

docs.title: 4.17 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: SGX Enclave Memory: EPC Size Constraint and Paging Overhead

An application developer wants to process a 2 GB dataset inside an Intel SGX v1 enclave for privacy-preserving analytics. Explain the EPC limitation and describe how the developer should handle data exceeding EPC size. What is the performance impact?

Solution: Intel SGX version 1 restricts the Enclave Page Cache (EPC) to a maximum of 128 MB (some BIOS/SKU configurations: 256 MB). Any enclave memory beyond the EPC limit must be paged out by the untrusted OS memory manager. When an EPC page is evicted:

  1. The MEE (Memory Encryption Engine) encrypts the page with AES-CTR and computes a MAC (GHASH or AES-CMAC) to ensure integrity on reload.

  2. The encrypted + MAC page is written to regular untrusted DRAM outside the EPC.

  3. On re-access, the page is loaded back, decrypted, and MAC-verified by MEE before the enclave can use it.

For a 2 GB dataset with 128 MB EPC, the working set exceeds EPC by 16x. Random access causes nearly every operation to trigger an EPC page fault. Measured overhead: 3–100x slowdown depending on access pattern.

Developer solutions:

  • Upgrade to SGX2 (Icelake+ Xeon): EPC up to 512 GB; EAUG allows dynamic EPC page addition without recreating the enclave.

  • Partition: split 2 GB into 100 MB chunks; use OCALL to request each chunk from untrusted host memory; process one chunk at a time inside EPC.

  • Use Gramine SGX library OS: its built-in virtual memory manager handles EPC paging transparently for unmodified applications.

  • Apply streaming algorithms (one-pass statistics, MapReduce-style processing) to minimize simultaneous EPC working set.

Solved Problem: OP-TEE Trusted Application: Device-Unique AES-256 Key Derivation

Implement an OP-TEE Trusted Application that derives a device-unique AES-256 key from the Hardware Unique Key (HUK). The key must never leave the Secure World. Describe the full approach using the GlobalPlatform TEE Internal Core API.

Solution: The HUK is accessible only to OP-TEE at S-EL1 via the platform abstraction layer (PAL). On Xilinx Zynq, the HUK is stored in eFUSE registers accessible only at EL3/S-EL1.

Step 1: Invoke OP-TEE System PTA PTA_SYSTEM_DERIVE_TA_UNIQUE_KEY to get a 32-byte HKDF output bound to the TA UUID.

uint8_t ta_secret[32];
invoke_system_pta_derive_key(ta_secret, sizeof(ta_secret));

TEE_ObjectHandle hkdf_key, aes_key_handle;
TEE_Attribute hkdf_attr;
TEE_AllocateTransientObject(TEE_TYPE_HMAC_SHA256, 256, &hkdf_key);
TEE_InitRefAttribute(&hkdf_attr, TEE_ATTR_SECRET_VALUE, ta_secret, 32);
TEE_PopulateTransientObject(hkdf_key, &hkdf_attr, 1);
TEE_DeriveKey(hkdf_key, &context_attr, 1, aes_key_handle);

TEE_StorageHandle sh;
TEE_CreatePersistentObject(TEE_STORAGE_PRIVATE,
    "enc_key_v1", 10, TEE_DATA_FLAG_ACCESS_WRITE,
    aes_key_handle, NULL, 0, &sh);
TEE_CloseObject(sh);

Security properties: HUK never crosses the Secure/Normal world boundary. Derived key is bound to device HUK and TA UUID. TEE Secure Storage uses AES-GCM encryption; RPMB provides hardware replay protection.

Solved Problem: AMD SEV-SNP vs Intel TDX: Four-Dimension Comparison

Compare AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX in terms of: (a) threat model, (b) memory encryption granularity, (c) attestation mechanism, and (d) VM live migration support.

Solution: (a) Threat Model: Both protect VM workloads from a compromised hypervisor/VMM. SEV-SNP additionally defends against malicious host BIOS and DMA attacks (IOMMU + RMP). Intel TDX introduces the TDX Module at SEAM privilege level above the hypervisor, providing architectural isolation.

(b) Memory Encryption:

  • AMD SEV-SNP: AES-128 per VM via AMD SME/TSME key table; RMP enforces one physical page -> one ASID ownership; prevents hypervisor aliasing at 4 KB granularity.

  • Intel TDX: AES-128-XTS per Trust Domain via MK-TME; physical address KEYID bits carry the TD key ID; TD page attribute bits prevent hypervisor from remapping TD pages.

(c) Attestation:

  • AMD SEV-SNP: AMD PSP generates SNP Attestation Report signed by VCEK (P-384 ECDSA); VCEK certificate from AMD KDS (kdsintf.amd.com); MEASUREMENT = SHA-384 of initial guest memory; HOST_DATA carries verifier nonce.

  • Intel TDX: TDX Module generates TD Quote signed by TDX Quoting Enclave (P-256 ECDSA); verified against Intel PCK via PCCS; MRTD = SHA-384 of initial TD state; RTMR[0..3] are runtime extend registers.

(d) VM Live Migration:

  • AMD SEV-SNP: Secure live migration via Migration Agent TA; encrypted pages re-keyed with destination PSP key; source and destination PSPs mutually authenticate.

  • Intel TDX: TD live migration in TDX Module 1.5 (Granite Rapids); TD Migration Agent Module handles key transfer; attestation MRTD preserved; RTMRs must be re-extended post-migration.

Solved Problem: TrustZone PRIME+PROBE Cache Timing Attack and Mitigations

Describe how a PRIME+PROBE cache timing attack against an OP-TEE TA performing AES-128 with T-tables works. Propose two mitigations with their performance tradeoffs.

Solution: Attack mechanics:

  1. PRIME: Normal World attacker fills L1 D-cache sets corresponding to the Secure World AES T-table virtual addresses (4 tables x 1024 bytes = 4096 bytes spanning specific cache sets).

  2. TRIGGER: Attacker calls TEEC_InvokeCommand; OP-TEE switches to S-EL1; TA executes round-1 AES lookup T[p[i] XOR k[i]] for i in 0..15. Each lookup evicts attacker data from specific L1 cache sets.

  3. PROBE: On return, attacker measures access time to each primed cache line. Cache miss reveals the T-table index used.

  4. Key recovery: Since attacker controls plaintext p[i] (chosen-plaintext), k[i] = observed_index XOR p[i]. All 16 key bytes recovered in roughly 200 invocations.

Mitigation 1 – Constant-time bitsliced AES: Replace T-table AES with bitsliced AES (HACL*, BearSSL ct-AES). All loads are fixed; access pattern is data-independent. Tradeoff: 2–5x slower than T-table AES.

Mitigation 2 – ARMv8 hardware AES instructions: Use AESE/AESD/AESMC intrinsics on Cortex-A53+ (ARMv8-A). AES rounds execute in vector registers; no memory loads after key schedule; immune to cache timing. Tradeoff: Requires ARMv8 hardware; still potentially vulnerable to power side-channel.

Solved Problem: Keystone RISC-V Enclave: PMP Configuration and Limits

Explain how Keystone uses RISC-V Physical Memory Protection (PMP) to implement enclave isolation. How many PMP entries are required per enclave, and what limits simultaneous enclaves on a SiFive U74?

Solution: RISC-V PMP: Hardware-enforced memory access control at Machine mode. Each PMP entry specifies pmpaddr (address), pmpcfg byte (R/W/X bits, address matching mode NAPOT/TOR/NA4, Lock bit L). Entries are checked in priority order; first match wins.

Keystone PMP layout for one enclave:

Entry 0 [LOCKED]: Security Monitor (SM) region
  pmpcfg = L | NAPOT | R=0 | W=0 | X=0
  Effect: No S-mode or U-mode code can access SM memory

Entry 1 [per-enclave]: Enclave physical memory (code + stack + heap)
  pmpcfg = NAPOT | R=1 | W=1 | X=1
  Effect: Enclave S/U-mode can access; OS (S-mode) cannot

Entry 2 [per-enclave]: UTM -- Untrusted Shared Memory for OCALLs
  pmpcfg = NAPOT | R=1 | W=1 | X=0
  Effect: Both enclave and OS can R/W (no execute)

Entry 15 [catch-all]: Full DRAM for OS
  pmpcfg = NAPOT | R=1 | W=1 | X=1

Entries per enclave: 3 (SM entry is shared). With 16 PMP total, 2 reserved: max \(14 / 3 \approx 4\) simultaneous enclaves on a 16-entry platform.

SiFive U74 (HiFive Unmatched): 8 PMP entries. Maximum: \(8 / 3 = 2\) simultaneous Keystone enclaves. RISC-V Smepmp extension (64 PMP entries) would enable 20+ concurrent enclaves.

Critical gap vs SEV-SNP: Keystone does not encrypt enclave DRAM. Cold-boot attack or DRAM bus probing reveals enclave data in plaintext. AMD SEV-SNP AES-128 memory encryption prevents this class of physical attack.

docs.title: 4.18.1 ARM CCA: Realm Management Extension (RMEv1)
docs.text:
ARM Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA) introduces a fourth world – the Realm – alongside Secure, Non-Secure, and Root worlds. CCA is available in Cortex-A710, A715, and X3 cores (ARMv9.2-A), and the RME hardware shipped in Apple A17 Pro (iPhone 15 Pro) and select Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 devices:

  • Realm Management Monitor (RMM): Executes at the new EL2 Realm exception level; manages Realm VMs; implemented by open-source tf-rmm (Trusted Firmware RMM)

  • Granule Protection Table (GPT): Hardware-enforced per-granule (4 KB) access control table managed by firmware; prevents Normal World hypervisor from aliasing Realm memory

  • CCA attestation: Realm VMs receive a hardware-signed Realm Attestation Token (RAT) in CBOR/COSE format; token includes realm measurement (SHA-512 of initial image), RIM/REM values, and platform certificate chain rooted in an ARM-signed root

  • iOS 17 use: Apple implements “Private Cloud Compute” on CCA-capable A17 Pro hardware; on-device ML inference Realms isolated from iOS kernel

Note: ARM CCA differs from AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX in one critical way: the Realm is isolated from both the hypervisor and the Secure World. This orthogonal isolation provides stronger separation guarantees for multi-tenant cloud workloads on ARM infrastructure.

docs.title: 4.18.2 Intel TDX 1.5 (2024): Improved Attestation and Nested VMs
docs.text:
Intel released TDX Module 1.5 with Granite Rapids Xeon (2024), bringing:

Table 4.6. Intel TDX 1.0 vs. TDX 1.5 Feature Comparison Feature TDX 1.0 TDX 1.5 RTMR count 4 (RTMR[0–3]) 4 + XFAM-extended RTMRs Nested VM support No TD Partitioning (L2 TDs) Live migration Experimental GA; TD Migration Agent Module Attestation quote size 4,653 bytes (ECDSA P-256) 5,120 bytes (with P-384 option) PCCS endpoint Intel-managed Customer-hosted PCCS supported Memory encryption AES-128-XTS AES-128-XTS + TME-MK

docs.title: 4.18.3 AMD SEV-SNP Improvements (2024)
docs.text:
AMD Genoa / Bergamo EPYC (Zen 4) introduced SNP_LAUNCH_UPDATE improvements:

  • VMPL (VM Permission Levels): Up to 4 VMPL tiers within a single SNP guest; allows a security monitor VM (VMPL0) to supervise application VMs (VMPL1–3) without exposing the hypervisor

  • REPORT_DATA field: Extended from 512 bits to 512 bits with VMPL-scoped nonces, enabling per-VMPL attestation

  • SNPGuest kernel driver: Merged into Linux 6.8; provides /dev/sev-guest for in-guest attestation report requests without hypervisor involvement

docs.title: 4.18.4 RISC-V Keystone 2.0 TEE Framework
docs.text:
The Keystone project released Keystone 2.0 in 2024 for SiFive U74 and the VisionFive 2 board:

  • SM (Security Monitor) v1.4: Supports RISC-V Smepmp extension (64 PMP entries) enabling \(\geq 20\) concurrent enclaves vs. 2 on a 16-entry platform

  • Attestation: DICE-based attestation using SM-generated ECDSA P-256 signatures over enclave measurement; compatible with IETF RATS RFC 9334

  • SDK: Keystone SDK 2.0 supports Rust enclave development via keystone-rs

docs.title: 4.18.5 OP-TEE 4.0 (2024): FIDO2 and Improved Secure Storage
docs.text:
Linaro released OP-TEE OS 4.0 with significant security additions:

  • FIDO2 / WebAuthn TA: Reference Trusted Application implementing CTAP2 protocol; biometric assertion generation inside Secure World; compatible with Android FIDO2 API

  • Secure Storage v2: Encrypted storage now uses AES-256-GCM (replacing AES-128-CBC) with hardware TRNG-generated per-object IVs; RPMB backing on eMMC/UFS

  • FF-A (Firmware Framework for Arm) support: OP-TEE can now co-exist with SP (Secure Partitions) under FF-A; enables hybrid OP-TEE + CCA deployments

  • OP-TEE on RISC-V: Experimental port for SiFive U54/U74 via M-mode security monitor; PMP-based world isolation

docs.title: 4.18.6 TEE Attacks: CacheWarp and TDXDown (2023–2024)
docs.text:
Table 4.7. New TEE Attacks (2023–2024) Attack Target CVE Description CacheWarp AMD SEV-SNP CVE-2023-20592 Write-back cache manipulation allows hypervisor to revert guest memory writes; bypasses SEV-SNP memory integrity for specific cache-flush sequences TDXDown Intel TDX CVE-2024-23953 DoS via malformed TDH.MEM.SEPT.ADD SEAMCALL; crashes TDX module, forcing VM termination AEPIC 2 Intel SGX CVE-2023-22655 Extended APIC bug family; SGX enclave register file leak via legacy MMIO reads

GlobalPlatform published TEE Protection Profile v1.3 (GPD_SPE_021) in 2024:

docs.title: 4.19 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between Intel SGX MRENCLAVE and MRSIGNER measurements. In what scenario should a developer choose MRSIGNER-based sealing? What is the security tradeoff from a key continuity and enclave update perspective?

  2. A cloud provider claims TEE-based protection. What specific attestation evidence must a tenant demand? List at least four fields to verify in an SGX QUOTE or SEV-SNP attestation report, and explain what each field proves about the platform state.

  3. Compare ARM TrustZone-A and Intel SGX isolation from the perspective of a compromised OS with root privilege. Which provides stronger guarantees? Consider: (a) memory access, (b) exception and interrupt handling, (c) shared L1/L2 cache side-channel exposure.

  4. Write pseudocode for the complete GlobalPlatform TEE Client API sequence to: (a) open a session to a TA by UUID, (b) invoke a command encrypting a 256-byte buffer, (c) close the session. Label each call as Normal World or Secure World transition.

  5. The PLATYPUS attack exploits Intel RAPL power measurements to extract SGX enclave keys without physical access. Explain why restricting RAPL to root is incomplete in a multi-tenant cloud. Propose a hardware-level countermeasure that prevents PLATYPUS without performance penalty for non-enclave workloads.

  6. Describe the AMD SEV-SNP Reverse Map Table (RMP). How does it prevent a hypervisor from aliasing one physical page into two VMs simultaneously? What CPU instruction validates the RMP during VM entry (VMRUN)? What happens if the RMP check fails?

  7. A developer wants to run Flask + SQLite inside SGX using Gramine. List four security-relevant entries required in the Gramine manifest file. What happens if the application attempts a syscall not in the manifest whitelist? How does Gramine intercept syscalls from the glibc vDSO path?

  8. OP-TEE supports multiple TAs running concurrently in S-EL0. Explain the isolation mechanism between TAs. What hardware feature prevents TA-A from reading TA-B heap memory? What occurs when a TA calls TEE_Malloc and the secure heap is fully exhausted?

  9. GlobalPlatform TEE v1.3.1 defines TEE_STORAGE_PRIVATE and TEE_STORAGE_USER. Explain their access control semantics. Which type should a Widevine L1 DRM key storage TA use, and why? What hardware backing provides replay protection on Android devices?

  10. Compare Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP attestation in four dimensions: (a) root signing key identity, (b) certificate retrieval endpoint URL, (c) measurement field semantics (what is measured and how), (d) nonce/freshness mechanism.

  11. An attacker executes SGX-Step against a naive RSA square-and-multiply implementation inside an enclave. Explain step-by-step how private key bits are revealed. Why is square-and-multiply vulnerable? Explain why the Montgomery ladder resists this attack.

  12. Keystone uses PMP for isolation without DRAM encryption. List three attack classes possible against Keystone but not against AMD SEV-SNP. For the most critical class, propose a concrete RISC-V ISA extension (specify mnemonic and semantics) that would close the gap.

  13. Design a complete threat model for a mobile payment TEE app on Qualcomm Snapdragon SPU. Enumerate: (a) assets and sensitivity levels, (b) three attacker classes with distinct capabilities, (c) one specific attack vector per class, (d) one concrete mitigation per attack with justification.

docs.title: 5.1 Introduction
docs.text:
A Hardware Root of Trust (HRoT) is the foundational security anchor from which all higher-level security guarantees are derived. Unlike software security, which can be subverted by compromised operating systems or hypervisors, an HRoT is implemented in tamper-resistant hardware that is trusted unconditionally. The chain of trust extends upward: the HRoT verifies the bootloader, the bootloader verifies the OS, and the OS verifies applications – each link cryptographically binding the next.

HRoTs provide three core capabilities: (1) Secure storage of keys, certificates, and secrets that cannot be extracted even with physical access; (2) Cryptographic operations (signing, verification, encryption) performed in isolated hardware; (3) Attestation – the ability to prove to a remote verifier that the platform is in a known-good state.

docs.title: 5.2 HRoT Architecture Components
docs.text: Table 5.1. Core HRoT architecture components Component Function Example Immutable Boot ROM First code on power-on; cannot be modified TSMC OTP mask ROM TRNG Entropy source for key generation Ring oscillator array AES engine Symmetric encryption/decryption AES-256-GCM hardware PKI engine ECDSA/RSA signing and verification ECC-P384 accelerator Secure key storage OTP fuses or battery-backed SRAM eFUSE, BBRAM Monotonic counter Anti-rollback; counts firmware updates 64-bit HW counter Lifecycle state machine Provisioning, deployment, field, EOL DMTF lifecycle model Secure debug JTAG lock/unlock via challenge-response JTAG authentication

docs.title: 5.3.1 Google Titan M2
docs.text:
The Titan M2 is Google’s in-house security chip, embedded in every Pixel smartphone since Pixel 6:

Google Titan M2 Specifications:
  Core: ARM SC300 (Cortex-M3 variant with security extensions)
  Process: Samsung 10nm LPE
  Memory: 8KB SRAM, 512KB NVM (flash)
  Crypto: AES-256-GCM, SHA-256/384, ECDSA P-256/P-384, TRNG
  Certification: Common Criteria EAL5+ (PP 0084)
  Interface: SPI to main AP (Tensor G2/G3)

  Key functions in Pixel 6+:
    - Android Verified Boot 2.0: verify Android partition signatures
    - Weaver: throttled PIN/password verification (10 tries then lockout)
    - Strongbox: Android Keystore HSM; Titan M2 as dedicated HSM
    - Secure element for Google Pay (OMAPI interface)
    - Rollback prevention: monotonic counter for Android version
    - Insider Attack Resistance: prevents Google from extracting user data

docs.title: 5.3.2 Microsoft Pluton
docs.text:
Pluton is a security processor co-designed by Microsoft, AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm, integrated directly into the main CPU die:

Microsoft Pluton Architecture:
  Integration: Inside AMD Ryzen 6000, Intel Alder Lake Core, Qualcomm Snapdragon SC8cx Gen3
  CPU: Dedicated Arm core; no separate die (anti-bus-snooping)
  TPM semantics: Pluton implements TPM 2.0 command set
  Updates: Firmware updateable via Windows Update (UEFI capsule)

  Security advantages over discrete TPM:
    - No PCIe/LPC/SPI bus (cannot sniff Pluton-CPU communications)
    - Anti-Spectre: isolated from main CPU; not affected by speculation attacks
    - DICE integration: each Pluton generates DICE CDI per boot stage
    - fTPM alternative: unlike firmware TPM, Pluton is hardware-isolated

  Key features:
    - RSA-2048/3072, ECC-P256/P384, AES-128/256, SHA-256/384
    - Monotonic counters, TRNG, secure storage (PNVRAM)
    - TPM 2.0 protocol: PCR extend, quote, seal, attest

docs.title: 5.3.3 NXP SE050 (EdgeLock Secure Element)
docs.text:
NXP SE050 Family:
  Core: ARM SC000 (Cortex-M0 derivative)
  Process: 40nm embedded NVM (SmartMX2 platform)
  Memory: 46KB EEPROM (user data), 10KB RAM
  Crypto: AES-128/256, SHA-256, ECC P-256/P-384/P-521, RSA-2048/4096
           ECDH, ECDSA, SCP03 (GlobalPlatform secure channel)
  Certification: Common Criteria EAL6+ (PP-0084)
  Interface: I2C (up to 400 kHz); SE05x-T1oI2C transport

  SE050B (most secure):
    - Physical attack resistance: fault detection, shielding mesh
    - Side-channel countermeasures: randomized execution, masking
    - Monotonic counter: 128 independent 32-bit counters
    - SE050 EdgeLock 2GO: cloud provisioning service for IoT devices

  Usage:
    i2cset -y 1 0x48 0x00 0x00  # Reset SE050 via I2C
    # Use OP-TEE se050 plugin or simw-top SDK for communication

docs.title: 5.3.4 Microchip ATECC608B
docs.text:
Microchip ATECC608B:
  Process: 0.18 um EEPROM (2KB user EEPROM, 16 key slots)
  Crypto: SHA-256 with HMAC, ECDSA P-256, ECDH P-256, AES-128
           (NO RSA -- ATECC is ECC-only)
  Interface: I2C (single-wire SWI also supported), 400 kHz max
  Certification: Common Criteria EAL2+ (FIPS 140-2 on 608C-TFLXTLS)
  Power: 150 uA active, 100 nA sleep (IoT optimized)

  TrustFLEX: Pre-provisioned configuration for TLS:
    - Slot 0: Device ECDSA private key (P-256, never exported)
    - Slot 1: Device certificate (X.509 DER encoded)
    - Slot 2: Root CA certificate
    - Slot 10: IO protection key

  Configuration command (cryptoauthlib):
    atcab_init(&cfg_ateccx08a_i2c_default);
    atcab_genkey(0, NULL);  // Generate key in slot 0
    atcab_write_pubkey(2, pubkey);  // Write companion pubkey
    atcab_lock_config_zone();  // Lock -- no further config changes
    atcab_lock_data_zone();    // Lock -- keys immutable

docs.title: 5.3.5 Infineon OPTIGA Trust M (SLB9670)
docs.text:
Infineon OPTIGA Trust M3:
  Core: ARM SC000 security controller (SLB9670)
  Process: 28nm embedded NVM
  Memory: 10KB RAM, 50KB user NVM (ECC-protected)
  Crypto: AES-128/256, SHA-256/384, RSA-1024/2048/4096,
           ECC NIST P-256/P-384/P-521, ECDH, ECDSA, TRNG
  Certification: Common Criteria EAL6+ (BSI-DSZ-CC-1190)
  Interface: I2C + SPI (optional)

  Key Differentiators vs ATECC608B:
    - Full RSA support (ATECC has no RSA)
    - Larger NVM (50KB vs 2KB)
    - Higher assurance (EAL6+ vs EAL2+)
    - Platform binding (bind OPTIGA to specific host board via OID)
    - Shielded connection: encrypted I2C channel (SHIELDED_CONNECTION)

docs.title: 5.4 OpenTitan: Open-Source HRoT
docs.text:
OpenTitan is a collaborative open-source project (Google, lowRISC, Western Digital, Winbond, Seagate) producing a verified, transparent HRoT design:

OpenTitan Earlgrey Block Diagram Components:
  Core: RISC-V Ibex (RV32IMC, 2-stage pipeline, 32KB I-cache option)
  SRAM: 512KB (execution) + 512KB (retention)
  ROM: 32KB ROM + ROM_EXT (verified extension in OTP/flash)
  Flash: 1MB information flash + 1MB data flash (ECC protected)
  OTP Controller: 1KB OTP for device secrets, lifecycle state, key derivation

  Security Peripherals:
    KMAC: SHA-3/SHAKE256 with key management
    CSRNG: CTR_DRBG (AES-256 based); NIST SP 800-90A
    EDN: Entropy Distribution Network (connects CSRNG to all consumers)
    ENTROPY_SRC: Hardware TRNG (ring oscillators + health tests)
    AES: AES-128/192/256-ECB/CBC/GCM (SCA-hardened masking)
    HMAC: SHA-256 hardware accelerator
    RSA/ECC: OTBN (OpenTitan Big Number accelerator): RSA-3072, ECC P-256
    ALERT HANDLER: Hardware alert management (fatal errors -> reboot)
    GPIO, UART, SPI, I2C, USB: Communication peripherals

  Build and simulate:
    cd $OPENTITAN/hw/top_earlgrey/
    fusesoc --cores-root . run --target=sim \
      --tool=verilator lowrisc:systems:top_earlgrey_verilator

  Run OpenTitan on FPGA (Xilinx CW310):
    ./util/fpga/cw310_loader.py --bitstream \
      build/lowrisc_systems_chip_earlgrey_cw310_0.1/synth-vivado/\
      chip_earlgrey_cw310.bit

docs.title: 5.5 DICE Architecture
docs.text:
TCG DICE (Device Identifier Composition Engine) provides layered device identity without requiring external PKI at manufacturing time:

DICE CDI Derivation Chain:

Layer 0 (Boot ROM / HRoT):
  UDS (Unique Device Secret): 256-bit secret in OTP fuse
  CDI_0 = HMAC-SHA256(UDS, SHA256(Layer0_FirmwareImage))

Layer 1 (First-Stage Bootloader):
  CDI_1 = HMAC-SHA256(CDI_0, SHA256(Layer1_FirmwareImage))
  DeviceID_KeyPair = KDF(CDI_0)  // ECDSA P-256 key pair
  Alias_KeyPair   = KDF(CDI_1)  // ECDSA P-256 key pair for this layer

Layer N:
  CDI_N = HMAC-SHA256(CDI_{N-1}, SHA256(LayerN_FirmwareImage))

Certificate Chain:
  DeviceID Cert: self-signed by DeviceID key (burn at factory)
  Alias Cert: signed by DeviceID key; contains Alias public key + FW digest

Security property: Compromising Layer 1 FW changes CDI_1 but not CDI_0.
  Verifier detects mismatch between expected and actual Alias cert.

RIOT Core (DICE reference implementation in C):
  DICECore_Init(uds, uds_len, cdi_out);
  DICECore_DeriveCDI(cdi_in, firmware_hash, cdi_out);
  RiotCrypt_SeedDRBG(cdi_out, CDI_LENGTH);
  RiotCrypt_DeriveEccKey(alias_key, RIOT_ECC_PRIVATE);

docs.title: 5.10 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: DICE CDI Chain: Compute CDI and Detect Compromise

A device uses DICE with 3 firmware layers. UDS = 0xDEADBEEF... (256-bit). Layer 0 hash = H0, Layer 1 hash = H1, Layer 2 hash = H2. (a) Write the CDI derivation formulas. (b) If Layer 1 firmware is replaced by an attacker, which CDI values change? (c) What does the verifier check to detect the compromise?

Solution: (a) CDI Derivation:

\[\begin{align*} CDI_0 &= \text{HMAC-SHA256}(UDS,\ H_0) \\ CDI_1 &= \text{HMAC-SHA256}(CDI_0,\ H_1) \\ CDI_2 &= \text{HMAC-SHA256}(CDI_1,\ H_2) \end{align*}\]

Each CDI cryptographically binds all lower-layer firmware measurements through the chain.

(b) Impact of Layer 1 compromise: If Layer 1 firmware changes to \(H_1'\):

  • \(CDI_0\): unchanged (Layer 1 hash not in \(CDI_0\) derivation)

  • \(CDI_1'= \text{HMAC-SHA256}(CDI_0, H_1') \neq CDI_1\): CHANGED

  • \(CDI_2'= \text{HMAC-SHA256}(CDI_1', H_2)\): CHANGED (cascading effect)

(c) Verifier detection: The device presents an Alias Certificate for Layer 2, signed by the Alias key derived from \(CDI_2'\). The Alias Certificate contains the firmware measurement \(H_1'\) in the SubjectAltName extension. The verifier:

  1. Checks that \(H_1'\) matches the reference value \(H_1\) stored in a trusted reference database.

  2. Since \(H_1' \neq H_1\), the verifier rejects the attestation evidence.

  3. The DeviceID certificate (signed at factory with \(CDI_0\)-derived key) is valid but the Alias chain reveals the firmware tampering.

Solved Problem: HRoT Monotonic Counter: Anti-Rollback Analysis

A firmware update system uses a 32-bit monotonic counter stored in OTP fuses (each bit is a one-way blow). The counter is encoded as a unary counter (each firmware version blows one more fuse bit). (a) What is the maximum firmware version supported? (b) Current version = 18. Attacker has version 15 firmware (older, vulnerable). Can the attacker install it? (c) Propose a firmware version policy to extend counter lifetime.

Solution: (a) Maximum version: Unary encoding uses 1 fuse per version increment. A 32-bit counter supports 32 distinct versions: version 0 (no fuses blown) through version 32 (all 32 fuses blown). Maximum firmware version = 32.

(b) Rollback attempt: The HRoT reads the current counter value (18 fuses blown). Before installing any firmware, it checks that the firmware’s embedded version number \(\geq\) current counter value. Attacker presents version 15 firmware: \(15 < 18\). The HRoT rejects the installation. Even if the attacker bypasses the software check, the counter value (18) in hardware prevents the device from booting firmware with version \(<\) 18.

(c) Extending counter lifetime:

  1. Sparse encoding: encode the version in binary (32-bit binary counter: supports \(2^{32}\) versions – but OTP fuses cannot be reset, so binary encoding doesn’t work for OTP).

  2. Two-level counter: use 8 fuses per major version + 24 fuses for minor. Supports 8 major \(\times\) 24 minor = 192 versions.

  3. TPM monotonic counter: TPM 2.0 NV counter increments without consuming fuses (backed by NVRAM with replay protection); supports \(>2^{32}\) versions.

  4. Rolling window: once counter reaches max, factory re-provisioning resets counter in OTP (requires physical return).

Solved Problem: OpenTitan Key Derivation: Creator and Owner Keys

OpenTitan derives cryptographic keys from two sources: the Creator Identity (manufacturing) and the Owner Identity (deployment). Explain the key hierarchy and how it isolates creator and owner keys even if the owner is malicious.

Solution: OpenTitan’s key manager implements a hierarchical key derivation based on DICE principles:

Key hierarchy:

  1. Root Key (CreatorRootKey): Derived from HW entropy (OTP secret) + ROM digest. Accessible only to ROM_EXT (creator-signed bootloader).

  2. Creator Identity Key: \(= \text{KDF}(\text{CreatorRootKey},\ \text{“CreatorIdentityKey”})\). Used to sign device certificates. Never accessible to owner software.

  3. Owner Intermediate Key: \(= \text{KDF}(\text{CreatorRootKey},\ \text{OwnerSeed} \| \text{“OwnerIntKey”})\). OwnerSeed is programmed by the owner during onboarding.

  4. Owner Identity Key: Derived from Owner Intermediate Key + owner firmware digest. Used by owner applications.

Isolation properties:

  • The owner never sees CreatorRootKey; key manager only outputs key-material sealed to specific key versions.

  • OwnerSeed is chosen by the owner but mixed with CreatorRootKey via KMAC – the owner cannot derive CreatorRootKey from OwnerSeed alone.

  • If owner firmware is compromised, it can only access Owner Identity Keys. Creator certificates and secrets remain protected.

  • DICE binding: each key derivation includes the measurement of the firmware at each layer, so a firmware change results in different derived keys (automatic key isolation per software version).

Solved Problem: ATECC608B Device Authentication in TLS 1.3

An IoT device uses ATECC608B for TLS 1.3 mutual authentication. The device holds an ECDSA P-256 private key in slot 0. Describe the complete authentication flow from TLS handshake initiation to certificate verification.

Solution: Pre-configuration (factory):

  1. Factory programs ATECC608B slot 0 with device ECDSA P-256 key (GenKey command).

  2. Device certificate (X.509, signed by factory CA with ECDSA P-256) is stored in ATECC608B slot 1.

  3. Root CA certificate stored in slot 2.

  4. Config zone locked: slots 0-2 are non-extractable; slot 0 is “sign-only” (private key never leaves chip).

TLS 1.3 Mutual Authentication flow:

  1. Client (IoT device) sends ClientHello with supported cipher suites (TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384).

  2. Server sends ServerHello + CertificateRequest + server certificate.

  3. Client sends its certificate (read from ATECC slot 1 via I2C: atcab_read_pubkey(1, cert_buf)).

  4. Server sends CertificateVerify: ECDSA signature over handshake transcript.

  5. Client must send CertificateVerify: compute SHA-256 of transcript, call atcab_sign(0, digest, signature) – ATECC608B signs with slot 0 private key.

  6. Private key never leaves ATECC608B; only the 64-byte ECDSA signature is output to the host MCU.

  7. Server verifies client signature against device certificate public key.

  8. TLS session established; subsequent traffic uses AES-256-GCM (computed on host MCU).

docs.title: 5.11.1 OpenTitan Earl Grey Silicon Tapeout (lowRISC, 2023)
docs.text:
OpenTitan Earl Grey completed its first commercial silicon tapeout in June 2023 at GlobalFoundries 180nm process, marking the world’s first open-source silicon RoT:

  • Tapeout partner: Google and lowRISC; co-fabricated at GF 180nm MEMS process (first tapeout) and TSMC 65nm (second tapeout, 2024)

  • Silicon validation: All 47 crypto-functional tests passing on silicon; OTBN (OpenTitan Big Number accelerator) validated for RSA-3072 and ECC P-256

  • Open-source significance: Full RTL, synthesis scripts, DV test suite, and silicon test reports published at github.com/lowRISC/opentitan

  • Production deployment: WDC (Western Digital) integrating OpenTitan RoT into data-centre SSD controller; Google Titan M3 roadmap includes OpenTitan core

  • Ibex RISC-V core: 2-stage pipeline, RV32IMCB; formal verification of security properties via Jasper; no speculative execution (immune to Spectre class)

Note: OpenTitan is the first hardware security chip whose complete design database (RTL, physical layout, DRC/LVS reports, and silicon test data) is publicly available. This enables independent security audits impossible for proprietary HSM/SE silicon.

docs.title: 5.11.2 Microsoft Pluton as Integrated Root of Trust (AMD Ryzen 6000+)
docs.text:
Pluton shifts the RoT from a separate die (TPM or SE) to an integrated subsystem within the main CPU package, delivering new security properties:

Table 5.5. Discrete TPM vs. Microsoft Pluton Root of Trust Property Discrete TPM (SLB9670) Microsoft Pluton Physical isolation Separate 22nm die On-die ARM core inside Ryzen Bus sniffing Vulnerable (SPI/LPC) Impossible (CPU fabric) Voltage glitching Possible (faulTPM) Harder (shared \(V_{\text{core}}\)) Firmware update Vendor OTA only Windows Update (capsule) DICE support Via TCG DICE spec Native DICE per boot layer TPM 2.0 compliance Full Full (TPM 2.0 command set) Open-source firmware No (vendor closed) No (Microsoft closed)

docs.title: 5.11.3 TCG DICE Layering Architecture v1.1 (2023)
docs.text:
TCG published DICE Layering Architecture v1.1 (TCG-D-2023-0000) with clarifications and new profiles:

  • DICE Open Profile: Defines an X.509-compatible certificate format for Alias CDI and DeviceID certificates; enables interoperability with existing PKI infrastructure

  • Multi-CPU: Guidance for multi-processor platforms (e.g., AMD PSP + host CPU) where CDI must be chained across security domain boundaries

  • DICE + SPDM: Integration profile with DMTF SPDM 1.3 (Security Protocol and Data Model) for server platform attestation; PCIe CMA-SPDM binding

  • RIOT Core v2.0: Updated reference implementation in C with ED25519 key derivation; supports DICE Open Profile certificate generation

docs.title: 5.11.4 NIST SP 800-193 Revision 2 Draft (2024): Platform Firmware Resiliency
docs.text:
NIST released the SP 800-193 Revision 2 draft in early 2024 updating the 2018 original with cloud and container platform guidance:

Table 5.6. NIST SP 800-193 Rev 2 Draft Key Updates (2024) Section Change 4.1 Protection Extended to cover cloud hypervisor firmware and container runtime integrity 4.2 Detection Added runtime integrity monitoring (dm-verity, IMA/EVM for container images) 4.3 Recovery Explicit DICE-based recovery attestation; recovery firmware must attest itself 5.1 HRoT OpenTitan and Pluton cited as reference implementations 5.2 Firmware update UEFI capsule update with FWTS (Firmware Test Suite) validation

Tip: NIST SP 800-193 Rev 2 is the most important firmware resiliency standard for server and cloud platforms. Compliance requires all three pillars: Protection (immutable root code), Detection (runtime integrity check), and Recovery (automatic authenticated recovery).

docs.title: 5.11.5 Google Titan M2 (Tensor G3, 2023): Secure Element Plus RoT Combo
docs.text:
The Titan M2 in the Pixel 8 (Tensor G3 SoC, Samsung 4nm) expanded its role:

  • Process: Samsung 4nm (upgraded from 10nm in Titan M1)

  • Secure Element integration: Titan M2 now acts as both the Android Strongbox HSM and the NFC secure element for Google Pay (replacing external NXP SE050)

  • Insider Attack Resistance (IAR) v2: Updated key management prevents even Google-signed firmware from extracting user biometric templates

  • Attestation v3: ECDSA P-384 (upgraded from P-256); certificate chain published at developers.google.com/android/attestation

  • Rollback counter: 8 independent monotonic counters for different firmware components (SE, HRoT, Android Verified Boot, Kernel)

docs.title: 5.11.6 Apple Secure Enclave (A17 Pro, 2023): 3 nm with Hardware Post-Quantum
docs.text:
Apple’s A17 Pro (iPhone 15 Pro, TSMC N3E 3 nm) introduced hardware-level PQC in the Secure Enclave:

  • PQC Key Agreement: ML-KEM-768 (Kyber) implemented in dedicated hardware accelerator within the SEP; used for iMessage PQ3 protocol (announced March 2024)

  • Hybrid protocol: iMessage PQ3 combines Curve25519 (classical) with ML-KEM-768 (post-quantum) for forward secrecy against “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks

  • SEP process: N3E 3 nm FinFET; SEP die area \(\approx 0.5\) mm\(^2\) estimated

  • Memory encryption: AES-256-XEX hardware engine for SEP SRAM; PUF-derived unique key per device

  • Boot ROM: Immutable 64 KB ROM with SHA-3/384 hash of SEP firmware; no field update of ROM possible

Note: Apple’s deployment of ML-KEM-768 in iMessage PQ3 (2024) is the largest-scale post-quantum cryptography deployment in production as of 2025, protecting over 2 billion active iMessage sessions with hardware-accelerated PQC in the Secure Enclave.

docs.title: 5.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between a Hardware Security Module (HSM) and a Hardware Root of Trust (HRoT). In what scenarios would you deploy each? Can an HRoT replace an HSM in a cloud server application?

  2. Google Titan M2 implements “Insider Attack Resistance” – even Google employees cannot extract user data from the device. Explain the cryptographic mechanism that enforces this property, referencing the Titan M2 key hierarchy and attestation model.

  3. OpenTitan’s ROM_EXT is a code extension beyond the immutable ROM. Describe how ROM_EXT is authenticated (by what key, using what algorithm) before execution. What happens if authentication fails? Can ROM_EXT be updated in the field?

  4. DICE generates a CDI per boot layer using HMAC-SHA256. Explain why using SHA256(UDS || firmware_hash) instead of HMAC-SHA256(UDS, firmware_hash) would be less secure. What specific attack does HMAC’s keyed construction prevent?

  5. A manufacturer provisions ATECC608B devices with a device-unique ECDSA key in a factory secure room. The CA private key is stored in a Thales Luna HSM. Describe the complete provisioning flow from device blank state to shipped device with a valid X.509 certificate.

  6. Microsoft Pluton is integrated into the CPU die, while discrete TPMs connect via SPI/LPC bus. Describe three specific attacks that are possible against a discrete TPM that Pluton eliminates by being on-die.

  7. Design an HRoT for an industrial controller (IEC 62443 SL-3). Specify: (a) hardware components (chip model, crypto algorithms), (b) secure boot chain (3 stages), (c) field update mechanism with rollback prevention, (d) attestation capability for OT network monitoring.

  8. A DICE implementation uses a 256-bit UDS stored in OTP fuses. If 5 fuse bits are read incorrectly due to manufacturing variation, the CDI derivation will produce a different result. Propose an error correction scheme for the UDS that (a) corrects up to 3-bit errors, (b) does not increase attack surface for brute-force UDS recovery.

  9. Compare the key storage mechanisms of Google Titan M2 (volatile SRAM + flash), NXP SE050 (EEPROM), and Microsoft Pluton (PNVRAM). For each, describe: (a) endurance (erase cycles), (b) retention (years), (c) tamper response.

  10. An HRoT must support 10 years of firmware updates with rollback prevention. The device has a 256-bit OTP fuse array. Design a version encoding scheme that: (a) supports at least 50 unique firmware versions, (b) enables cryptographic rollback prevention, (c) allows emergency downgrade with manufacturer authorization.

  11. Explain how the Lattice MachXO3D implements NIST SP 800-193 Platform Firmware Resiliency for protecting a server BMC’s SPI flash. Draw the data flow for the “Recovery” function when the BMC flash is corrupted by a malicious firmware update.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Side-Channel Attack Protection
docs.text: Note: Side-channel attacks exploit physical emanations from cryptographic hardware. Even theoretically perfect ciphers leak through power, EM, timing, and acoustics.

docs.title: 6.1 Side-Channel Attack Taxonomy
docs.text: Side-channel attacks (SCA) exploit information leaked through physical implementation. The taxonomy spans: power analysis (SPA, DPA, CPA, HO-DPA), timing, EM, acoustic, photonic, and cache-timing channels.

docs.title: 6.1.1 Power Analysis Attacks
docs.text:
CMOS logic dissipates power proportional to switching activity. The Hamming Weight (HW) model:

\[P(v)=\alpha\cdot\mathrm{HW}(v)+\beta+N,\quad N\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\]

The Hamming Distance (HD) model for register transitions:

\[\mathrm{HD}(x,y)=\mathrm{HW}(x\oplus y)=\mathrm{HW}(x)+\mathrm{HW}(y)-2\mathrm{HW}(x\wedge y)\]

SPA: Visual inspection of one trace. RSA square-and-multiply produces distinct per-operation patterns, directly revealing key bits.

DPA (Kocher 1999): Statistical attack over \(N\) traces. Partition by predicted intermediate bit \(b\): \(\Delta D=E[T\mid b=1]-E[T\mid b=0]\). Correct key produces a peak.

CPA (Brier 2004): Pearson correlation between hypothetical power \(v\) and traces \(T\):

\[\rho(H,T)=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(H,T)}{\sigma_H\sigma_T}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N(h_i-\bar{h})(t_{i,j}-\bar{t}_j)}{\sqrt{\sum_i(h_i-\bar{h})^2}\sqrt{\sum_i(t_{i,j}-\bar{t}_j)^2}}\]

Key ranking: \(\rho_k^*=\max_j|\rho_{k,j}|\); correct key \(\rho^*\to1\), wrong keys \(\approx0\).

HO-DPA: Combines \(d+1\) time points (product or absolute difference) to attack \(d\)th order masking.

docs.title: 6.1.2 Leakage Assessment: t-TVLA
docs.text:
ISO/IEC 17825 TVLA uses Welch t-test on fixed (\(x_f\)) vs. random (\(x_r\)) trace sets:

\[t_j=\frac{\bar{T}_{F,j}-\bar{T}_{R,j}}{\sqrt{s_{F,j}^2/N_F+s_{R,j}^2/N_R}}\]

\(|t_j|>4.5\) declares leakage at significance \(\approx2^{-20}\) (false positive \(2.8\times10^{-6}\) per sample).

Warning: \(|t|>4.5\) indicates information-theoretic leakage. All certified products must pass TVLA under ISO/IEC 17825 and CC AVA_VAN.5.

docs.title: 6.1.3 Timing and Cache Attacks
docs.text:
Kocher (1996): RSA decryption time varies with key bits through conditional Montgomery reduction. AES cache-timing attacks reveal T-table indices via hit (\(\approx 100\) cyc) vs. miss (\(\approx 200\) cyc) latency.

Spectre (CVE-2017-5753): Branch predictor training causes speculative out-of-bounds access; secret encoded in cache state, exfiltrated via Flush+Reload. Mitigated by retpoline and IBRS.

Meltdown (CVE-2017-5754): Out-of-order execution reads kernel memory; cache encodes value before exception. Mitigated by KPTI (Kernel Page-Table Isolation).

Flush+Reload (Yarom 2014): Flush shared line (clflush), wait for victim, time reload: hit (\(<200\) cyc) confirms access.

Prime+Probe: Fill cache set, wait for victim evictions, probe own lines. Works across VMs; no shared memory required.

docs.title: 6.1.4 EM and Acoustic Attacks
docs.text:
Near-field EM probes (Langer RF-U 5-2, 100 kHz–3 GHz) 1–2 mm above IC capture SEMA/DEMA traces. XY scanning (Thorlabs PT3/M, 0.5 mm steps) produces spatial leakage maps.

Acoustic attacks (Genkin 2014): switching regulator coil whine encodes RSA-4096 key computation. Consumer microphone at 44.1 kHz extracts key in \(\approx 1\) hour.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Boolean Masking
docs.text:
\(d\)th order Boolean masking splits secret \(s\) into \(d+1\) shares revealing nothing from any \(d\) shares:

\[s=s_0\oplus s_1\oplus\cdots\oplus s_d,\quad s_0,…,s_{d-1}\xleftarrow{\$}\{0,1\}^n,\quad s_d=s\oplus s_0\oplus\cdots\oplus s_{d-1}\] Figure 6.2. First-Order Boolean Masking (\(d=1\)). Secret \(s\) split into \(m\) (TRNG mask) and \(s\oplus m\). Both shares processed independently through \(f\); output XOR recombines. Any single share is uniform over \(\{0,1\}^n\), revealing nothing about \(s\).

docs.title: 6.3.2 Threshold Implementation (TI)
docs.text:
TI (Nikova et al., 2006) provides provably secure masking for nonlinear functions. Three properties:

  1. Correctness: XOR of all output shares equals the correct function output.

  2. Non-completeness: Each output share depends on at most \(d\) of the \(d+1\) input shares.

  3. Uniformity: Uniform input shares produce uniform output shares.

For AES SubBytes (degree 4 over GF(\(2^8\))), minimum 3 shares required for first-order TI. GF(\(2^4\)) tower field decomposition enables 3-share TI with 18 AND-gate evaluations per S-box.

Note: FPGA synthesis must not merge share domains. In Vivado, apply ( DONT_TOUCH = yes ) on share-boundary nets to prevent OPT_DESIGN from collapsing masking into unprotected logic.

docs.title: 6.3.3 Domain Oriented Masking (DOM)
docs.text: DOM (Gross et al., 2016) isolates computation domains via register stages. DOM-indep provides \(d\)th order security with \(d\) shares requiring \(\binom{d+1}{2}\) fresh random bits per AND gate.

docs.title: 6.3.4 WDDL: Wave Dynamic Differential Logic
docs.text: WDDL dual-rail encoding makes switching activity constant regardless of data. All gates produce both \(x\) and \(\bar{x}\) toggling every clock. Requires differential standard-cell library and balanced routing. On FPGAs, routing asymmetry degrades protection.

docs.title: 6.3.5 Physical and Algorithm Countermeasures
docs.text:
Clock randomization: Spread-spectrum oscillators (Cypress CY22393FZXC, SiTime SIT1533) modulate frequency \(\pm1\%\) at 20–100 kHz.

Power filtering: 100 nF C0G + 10 \(\mu\)F tantalum per VCC pin; Microchip MIC5504 LDO (PSRR \(>60\) dB).

Constant-time code:

/* Constant-time compare: no early exit */
int ct_memcmp(const uint8_t *a, const uint8_t *b, size_t len) {
    uint8_t diff = 0;
    for (size_t i=0; i<len; i++) diff |= a[i]^b[i];
    return diff;
}
/* Constant-time select: compiles to CMOV on x86 */
uint32_t ct_select(uint32_t cond, uint32_t a, uint32_t b) {
    uint32_t mask = (uint32_t)(-(int32_t)(cond != 0));
    return (a & mask) | (b & ~mask);
}
/* Shuffled SubBytes: randomize order to desynchronize */
void aes_subbytes_shuffled(uint8_t s[16], uint8_t perm[16]) {
    trng_fisher_yates(perm, 16);
    for (int i=0; i<16; i++) s[perm[i]]=SBOX[s[perm[i]]];
}
Table 6.2. Side-Channel Countermeasures Comparison Countermeasure Type Security Area OH Rand. Bits Boolean Masking (d=1) Algorithm 1st order 2x Low TI (3 shares, d=1) Algorithm 1st order 3x–4x Medium DOM-indep (d-th) Algorithm d-th order \(d^2\) High WDDL (dual-rail) Logic style 1st (ASIC) 2x+routing None Spread-Spectrum Osc. Physical Partial 5% area None LDO + Decoupling Physical Partial PCB area None Noise Generator Physical Partial 10% area Low Shuffling Algorithm Partial 1.1x Low

docs.title: 6.4 SCALib Python CPA Attack
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scalib.metrics import SNR, Ttest
traces = np.load("traces.npy").astype(np.float32)   # (N=5000, L)
pts    = np.load("plaintexts.npy").astype(np.uint8) # (N, 16)
SBOX = [0x63, 0x7c, ...]  # 256 AES S-box values
def hw(x): return bin(int(x)).count("1")
# Step 1: SNR leakage identification
labels = np.array([hw(SBOX[int(pt[0])^0xAB]) for pt in pts], dtype=np.uint16)
snr = SNR(nc=9, ns=traces.shape[1], np=1)
snr.fit_u(traces, labels.reshape(-1,1))
snr_v = snr.get_snr()
print("Peak SNR", snr_v[0].max(), "at", snr_v[0].argmax())
# Step 2: t-TVLA
ttest = Ttest(ns=traces.shape[1])
ttest.fit_u(traces[:2500], 0); ttest.fit_u(traces[2500:], 1)
t = ttest.get_ttest()
print("Max|t|=", abs(t).max())
# Step 3: CPA key byte 0
hyp = np.array([[hw(SBOX[int(pt[0])^k]) for k in range(256)]
               for pt in pts], dtype=np.float32)
T_c = traces-traces.mean(0); H_c = hyp-hyp.mean(0)
corr = (H_c.T@T_c)/(len(pts)*np.outer(hyp.std(0)+1e-12,traces.std(0)+1e-12))
print("Recovered key[0]=", hex(np.argmax(np.max(np.abs(corr),axis=1))))

docs.title: 6.7 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: DPA Trace Count from SNR

AES-128 on ATmega328P (ChipWhisperer-Lite CW1173, 16 MHz): SNR \(=0.04\) at S-box leakage. (a) CPA traces for 99% success. (b) Trace count vs. first-order attacker on 3-share TI. (c) Second-order attacker vs. TI. Solution: Part (a): \(\rho^2\approx0.0385\), \(\rho=0.196\):

\[N\approx\frac{\pi^2(1-\rho^2)}{4\rho^2}(\Phi^{-1}(0.99))^2\approx\mathbf{333}~\text{traces}\]

With alignment overhead: 500–1000 traces in practice.

Part (b): TI vs. first-order. TI uniformity: \(\rho=0\) exactly. First-order CPA fails; infinite traces required.

Part (c): Second-order attacker:

\[\mathrm{SNR}_2\approx\frac{(0.04)^2}{8}=2\times10^{-4},\quad N_2\approx66{,}800~\text{traces}\]

Summary: Unprotected \(\sim\)333 traces; TI vs. 1st-order: fails; TI vs. 2nd-order: \(\sim\)67k traces.

Solved Problem: CPA Key Recovery Step-by-Step

With 1000 power traces (5000 samples) from AES-128 on STM32F303 (ChipWhisperer UFO), recover key byte \(k_0\) via CPA. Solution: Step 1: \(v=\mathrm{SubBytes}(p_0\oplus k_0)\) – involves only \(k_0\).

Step 2: Hypothesis matrix H (1000 x 256):

\[H[i][k]=\mathrm{HW}(\mathrm{SBOX}[p_0^{(i)}\oplus k])\in\{0,…,8\}\]

Step 3: Pearson correlation (256 x 5000):

\[\rho_{k,j}=\frac{\sum_i(H[i][k]-\bar{H}_k)(T[i][j]-\bar{T}_j)}{\sqrt{\sum_i(H[i][k]-\bar{H}_k)^2}\sqrt{\sum_i(T[i][j]-\bar{T}_j)^2}}\]

Step 4: Key ranking: \(\rho_k^*=\max_j|\rho_{k,j}|\). Sort 256 keys descending.

Example: Correct key 0x2B: \(\rho^*=0.89\) at sample 347, rank 1. Wrong key 0x17: \(\rho^*=0.22\), rank 2.

Step 5: Full key. Repeat for \(k_1\)–\(k_{15}\). Total \(\approx2\times10^{10}\) MACs, \(\approx\)30 s on CPU.

Solved Problem: t-TVLA Threshold Analysis

NXP LPC55S69: \(N_F=N_R=10{,}000\) traces, 5000 samples, maximum \(|t|=3.8\). (a) Pass? (b) False positive rate at \(|t|>4.5\)? (c) Expected FP across 5000 samples? Solution: (a) \(3.8<4.5\): device passes. Recommend re-evaluation at 100k traces.

(b) \(P(|t_j|>4.5)=2(1-\Phi(4.5))\approx6.80\times10^{-6}\).

(c) \(E[\text{FP}]=5000\times6.80\times10^{-6}=0.034\ll1\). Threshold 4.5 chosen so \(E[\text{FP}]<0.05\) for 5000 samples.

Solved Problem: Design First-Order Masked AES S-box

Design first-order masked AES S-box for Artix-7 XC7A35T. Input: masked byte \(x\prime=x\oplus m\) and mask \(m\). Output: \(y\prime=S(x)\oplus m\prime\). Estimate FPGA resources and security requirements. Solution: Architecture: Canright Tower Field (2008). Decompose GF(\(2^8\)) as \(\mathrm{GF}(2^8)\cong\mathrm{GF}(2^4)^2\).

Step 1: Basis change \(B\) to \((x\prime,m)\) separately (linear). Step 2: Masked GF(\(2^4\)) multiplication with fresh random bit \(r\):

\[(c\oplus m_c)=(a\oplus m_a)(b\oplus m_b)+(a\oplus m_a)m_b+m_a(b\oplus m_b)+r\]

Step 3: GF(\(2^4\)) inversion (4 masked multiplications + 2 squarings). Step 4: Inverse basis + AES affine transform.

FPGA resources (Artix-7 XC7A35T):

  • 4 masked GF(\(2^4\)) multipliers (28 LUTs each) + squarings (16 each) + inversion: 200 LUTs

  • Basis change, AES affine: 64 LUTs; pipeline registers (3 stages): 128 FFs

  • TRNG (5 ring oscillators): 32 LUTs, 16 FFs

  • Total: 264 LUTs, 144 FFs, 0 BRAMs per masked S-box

Security requirements: Fresh TRNG bit per AND gate; DONT_TOUCH on share nets; formal verification with SILVER; post-layout TVLA at 1M traces.

docs.title: 6.8 FPGA Implementation of SCA-Resistant AES
docs.text:
Implementing masked AES on FPGAs is challenging due to glitches in LUT-based logic. The following table shows resource utilisation for various SCA countermeasure styles:

docs.title: 6.10.1 INCEPTION Attack: AMD Zen 3/4 Speculative Execution (2023)
docs.text:
INCEPTION (CVE-2023-20569) is a transient-execution attack discovered by ETH Zürich researchers affecting all AMD Zen 3 and Zen 4 processors:

  • Mechanism: Combines “Training in Transient Execution” (TITE) with “Rete” – a speculative execution technique that poisons the return-address predictor stack (RSB) using a specially crafted RET instruction sequence executed in a transient window

  • Effect: Arbitrary speculative code execution of attacker-chosen gadgets; can leak kernel memory across privilege boundaries; bypasses existing Spectre-BTI mitigations (IBRS/retpoline)

  • Affected: All AMD Zen 3 (Ryzen 5000, EPYC Milan) and Zen 4 (Ryzen 7000, EPYC Genoa); Intel processors not affected

  • Mitigation: AMD microcode update + kernel IBPB-on-VMEXIT enforcement; performance overhead 3–54% on database workloads; Linux 6.5+ includes mitigation

Warning: INCEPTION is the first transient-execution attack that bypasses all existing Spectre-v2 software mitigations on AMD hardware. Enterprises running AMD EPYC in multi-tenant cloud or database environments must apply AMD microcode update (AGESA 1.0.0.8+) immediately.

docs.title: 6.10.2 iLeakage: Apple M1/M2/A-Series Safari Side-Channel (2023)
docs.text:
iLeakage (published October 2023 by researchers at MIT, Georgia Tech, UT Austin) exploits a speculative-execution side channel specific to Apple Silicon:

  • Root cause: Apple M-series CPUs support speculative execution across process boundaries via shared L1-I and L2 caches without sufficient partition

  • Attack surface: JavaScript in a malicious Safari tab can speculatively read cross-origin iframe content; exploits the speculative fetch width of Apple’s A-Series (A14–A17) and M-Series (M1–M3) OoO engines

  • Demo: Leaked Gmail inbox content and auto-filled Instagram passwords from a separate tab in a controlled Safari browser session

  • Mitigation: Apple Safari 17.2 (released December 2023) adds process-isolation for cross-origin browsing contexts; hardware fix requires microarchitecture change

  • iOS 17 impact: iPhones affected but attack requires JavaScript to be enabled; no iOS exploit chain demonstrated publicly

docs.title: 6.10.3 RowHammer on DDR5 (2024): Target Row Refresh Failures
docs.text:
RowHammer attacks on DDR5 memory demonstrated in 2024 that the new on-die ECC (ODECC) and Refresh Management (RFM) mitigations are insufficient:

Table 6.6. RowHammer Mitigations on DDR4 vs. DDR5 (2024) Mitigation DDR4 DDR5 Target Row Refresh (TRR) Per-vendor, variable Standardised JEDEC TRRv2 Refresh Management (RFM) Absent JEDEC JESD79-5 mandatory On-die ECC Optional (some SKUs) Mandatory for DDR5 Attack threshold \(\sim\)70,000 activations \(\sim\)4,800 activations (2024 paper) Proof-of-concept flip Demonstrated Demonstrated (SMASH, 2024)

The 2024 SMASH paper (TU Delft) achieved bit-flips on DDR5 DRAM from JavaScript with only \(4{,}800\) row activations, well below the JEDEC Alert Threshold (ART) of \(32{,}000\). DDR5 on-die ECC corrects single-bit errors but masks flips from TRR monitoring, paradoxically enabling more reliable exploitation.

docs.title: 6.10.4 AEPIC Leak (2022–2023): Intel CPU Architectural Bug Leaking SGX Secrets
docs.text:
AEPIC Leak (CVE-2022-21233) is an architectural (non-side-channel) bug in Intel Sunny Cove and Ice Lake microarchitectures:

  • Root cause: The Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller (APIC) MMIO register space at physical address range 0xFEE00000–0xFEE00FFF contains uninitialized reads that return stale data from CPU internal register files

  • Affected: Intel 10th–12th Gen Core (Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, Alder Lake) with SGX; Intel Xeon Ice Lake-SP (server)

  • Leak rate: \(\approx 16\) bytes of enclave register file per MMIO read; requires ring-0 (kernel) privilege to access APIC MMIO

  • SGX impact: A malicious OS/VMM with root privilege can extract SGX enclave AES keys, RSA private keys, and ECDSA nonces in \(< 1\) second

  • Fix: Disable xAPIC MMIO; mandate x2APIC mode in BIOS; Intel microcode update for APIC register initialization

docs.title: 6.10.5 Composable Masking Schemes (2024): Hardware-Friendly d+1 Sharing
docs.text:
A 2024 paper from KU Leuven introduced “Parametric Masking Gadgets” – a framework for constructing composable \(d\)th-order secure Boolean masking schemes directly implementable in ASIC standard cells without glitch amplification:

  • Key result: Proved that a \(d+1\)-share AND gadget consuming \(\binom{d+1}{2}\) fresh random bits is composable and provably \(d\)th-order secure under the robust probing model (which accounts for CMOS glitches)

  • Implementation: AES S-box in GF\((2^4)\) tower field using 3-share TI achieves first-order security with only 4 fresh random bits per AND gate vs. 8 in DOM-indep

  • TVLA results: Post-layout TVLA at \(10^6\) traces with \(|t|_{\max} < 2.1\) on TSMC 28nm; first formal proof and empirical validation combined

  • Open-source: Reference Verilog released at github.com/KULeuven-COSIC/Masking2024
