docs.title: 6.10.7 ISO/IEC 17825:2023 Update for Side-Channel Testing
docs.text:
The 2023 update to ISO/IEC 17825 (Testing methods for hardware security evaluation of cryptographic modules) introduces several changes affecting certification:

  • Mandatory EM testing: Near-field EM evaluation is now mandatory alongside power analysis; separate EM-TVLA trace requirement added (\(N \geq 100{,}000\) fixed/random)

  • Fault injection: Electromagnetic Fault Injection (EMFI) formally included in scope; minimum 10,000 fault attempts per parameter combination

  • SCA on PQC: New annex covering leakage assessment for ML-DSA and ML-KEM operations; specific concern for polynomial arithmetic in NTT (Number Theoretic Transform)

  • Updated \(|t|\) threshold: The 4.5 threshold now applies per-sample with Bonferroni correction for large trace lengths; labs must report uncorrected and corrected maxima

docs.title: 6.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. An AES-128 on ATtiny85 (1 MHz, on-chip LDO) shows SNR \(=0.001\). Minimum CPA traces for 95% success? How does 3-share TI affect trace counts for (a) first-order and (b) second-order attackers? FPGA LUT overhead on Artix-7?

  2. Derive \(\mathrm{HD}(x,y)=\mathrm{HW}(x\oplus y)\) algebraically. When is HD more accurate than HW (bus precharge, pipeline register model)? For STM32F407 Cortex-M4 executing AES MixColumns, which model is better?

  3. WDDL on Spartan-6 XC6SLX16 for AES-128: identify three degradation factors vs. ASICs, propose mitigations, estimate residual TVLA \(|t|_{\max}\).

  4. Implement t-TVLA in NumPy: 5000 fixed traces (Gaussian SNR=0.1 at sample 100) and 5000 random traces. Compute Welch t-statistic for 500 samples. Report \(t_{\max}\) and peak sample. Pass ISO/IEC 17825?

  5. Explain Spectre variant 1 (CVE-2017-5753): branch predictor training, speculative out-of-bounds, cache encoding, Flush+Reload extraction. How does compiler array-index masking mitigate?

  6. CPA on ECDSA-256 scalar multiplication (STM32F407). Identify vulnerable intermediate per 32-bit word of scalar \(k\). Estimate signatures needed. How does Montgomery ladder prevent this?

  7. Design power decoupling for STM32L562 (3.3 V, 50 mA, 10 ns edges). Capacitor spec and placement. Calculate \(\Delta V\) at 100 MHz without decoupling. Factor reduction with 100 nF C0G at 1 mm. Effect on CPA \(\rho\).

  8. Acoustic attacks (Genkin 2014): switching regulator coil whine mechanism, key-dependent spectra, 44.1 kHz processing (FFT/bandpass/correlation), RSA blinding defense.

  9. ASCAD dataset (github.com/ANSSI-FR/ASCAD): describe target byte (3), attack point, samples/trace (700), mask in SRAM. SCALib SNR code for byte 3. Expected SNR: unmasked (\(\approx\)0.5) vs. masked (\(\approx\)0.01).

  10. DPAv4 AES-256 with 0–99 random delay cycles: (a) SAD alignment, (b) cross-correlation alignment. Pseudocode, complexity for 50k traces of 100k samples, residual misalignment.

  11. CC AVA_VAN.5 for payment terminal AES: max trace count, permitted preprocessing, SPA+DPA scenarios, pass/fail scoring. How does attack potential map to trace count limits?

  12. Compare PSA Level 2 IoT AES: (a) STM32F407 software T-tables, (b) STM32L562 HW masked AES (CC EAL5+), (c) bitsliced AES (Schwabe-Stoffelen, Cortex-M4). Estimate SNR, CPA traces, TVLA \(|t|_{\max}\), throughput. Justify selection.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Hardware Trojan Detection
docs.text: Note: Hardware Trojans are malicious modifications to ICs introduced during design, fabrication, or supply chain. They bypass software security and survive OS reinstallation.

docs.title: 7.1 Hardware Trojan Taxonomy
docs.text:
A hardware Trojan consists of a trigger and payload. Classification: insertion phase, activation, effect, location.

Table 7.1. Hardware Trojan Taxonomy Axis Category Examples Insertion Design time RTL modification, EDA tool compromise Insertion Fabrication Doping modification, extra via insertion Activation Always-on Permanent key leakage Activation Rare trigger (1-in-\(2^{32}\)) Combinational condition Activation External trigger RF signal, specific input sequence Effect Information leak Covert channel, RF exfiltration Effect Denial of service Functional failure at trigger Effect Privilege escalation Bypass authentication check Location Combinational Extra gates in critical path Location Sequential Added flip-flops, state machine

docs.title: 7.1.1 Real-World Examples
docs.text:
Stuxnet (2010): Malware manipulated Siemens S7-315 PLCs controlling centrifuge frequency, causing physical damage while reporting normal operation to SCADA systems.

Juniper ScreenOS Backdoor (2015): Unauthorized change to firewall firmware allowed passive VPN decryption via modified Dual_EC_DRBG constant.

Bloomberg Supermicro Allegations (2018): Claimed rice-grain-sized implant chip on server motherboards capable of intercepting communications (disputed by all parties).

DoD Counterfeit Parts (2012): 1,800 documented cases of counterfeit parts in defense equipment, some with functional differences from specifications.

docs.title: 7.2.1 Side-Channel Analysis
docs.text:
Trojans perturb power, delay, and EM signatures. Challenge: distinguishing from process variation (\(\sigma_P\approx3\%\)).

Power fingerprinting: Compare suspect chip integrated power vs. golden reference. Trojans with \(\geq 1000\) gates (\(\approx 0.01\%\) of modern SoC) are detectable with \(\geq 100\) measurements.

Path delay analysis: Ring oscillator sensors measure path delay with picosecond resolution, detecting Trojan-induced capacitive loading or combinational depth increase.

Figure 7.1. Power-Based Trojan Detection. Suspect chip power profile compared to golden reference. Difference \(\Delta P > T\) (threshold \(=3\sigma\) process variation) declares Trojan detected.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Logic Testing
docs.text: Standard ATPG achieves \(>99\%\) stuck-at fault coverage but Trojans with rare triggers (\(<2^{-40}\) probability) are undetectable with functional vectors. Trojan-oriented ATPG (TPAT) maximizes trigger probability but coverage remains limited.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Formal Verification
docs.text: Model checking (Cadence JasperGold, Synopsys VC Formal, Mentor Questa Formal) compares RTL against a golden specification. Complete coverage but does not scale to full SoC (\(>10^9\) gates). Best applied to crypto cores, boot ROM, and key management logic.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Physical Inspection
docs.text:
SEM: Zeiss Sigma 500 SEM provides nanometer-resolution cross-sections identifying unauthorized vias, implants, or doping modifications. Destructive; limited to sampling.

X-ray CT: Nikon XT H 225 ST provides non-destructive 3D inspection at 1 \(\mu\)m resolution. Detects unexpected components, embedded chips, and unauthorized solder connections. Feasible for 100% lot inspection of small packages.

FIB/SEM: Zeiss ORION NanoFab FIB/SEM enables cross-section analysis at 5 nm resolution. Can verify individual transistors and metal connections against design database. Required for definitive Trojan confirmation.

Delayering: Sequential chemical delayering (HF/H\(_2\)SO\(_4\)) followed by automated optical inspection using computer vision comparison against a clean reference die.

docs.title: 7.2.5 Machine Learning for Trojan Detection
docs.text:
GNN on netlists: Graph Neural Networks classify IC netlists as directed graphs (nodes = gates, edges = wires). Node features: gate type, fanin, fanout, timing criticality. Trained on TRUST-HUB benchmarks; \(>95\%\) accuracy on known Trojan types.

ML on power traces: Autoencoder-based anomaly detection on golden chip power profiles; LSTM classifiers achieve \(>90\%\) detection rate for power-visible Trojans.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Key-Based Logic Locking
docs.text:
Logic locking inserts key-controlled XOR/XNOR gates throughout the netlist. Only the correct key (stored in tamper-proof eFUSE or NVRAM) produces correct outputs. An attacker with an unlocked chip cannot reverse-engineer the original functionality.

Figure 7.2. Logic Locking. XOR/XNOR key gates produce correct outputs only with the correct key. SAT attack iteratively finds Discriminating Input Pairs (DIPs) to recover the key from an oracle chip.

docs.title: 7.3.2 SAT Attack on Logic Locking
docs.text:
The SAT attack (Subramanyan et al., 2015) finds the correct key via Discriminating Input Pairs (DIPs):

  1. Initialize CNF \((x, k^1, k^2, y^1, y^2)\) with two key instances sharing the locked netlist structure.

  2. Solve \(\wedge (y^1 \neq y^2)\) to find a DIP: input producing different outputs for \(k^1\) vs. \(k^2\).

  3. Query oracle chip with DIP; obtain correct output \(y^*\).

  4. Add constraint: eliminate all keys where \({\text{locked}}(\text{DIP}, k) \neq y^*\).

  5. Repeat until no DIP exists. Remaining key candidates are all correct.

For 128-bit key, SAT attack converges in \(<000 iterations (\)< min). Countermeasures: SFLL (Stripped Functionality Logic Locking), Cyclic Logic Locking, SFLL-HD.

docs.title: 7.5 Split Manufacturing and Supply Chain Security
docs.text:
Split manufacturing separates FEOL (transistors, lower metal layers) from BEOL (upper metal, routing) across two foundries. The untrusted FEOL foundry sees only partial connectivity, preventing Trojan insertion via routing manipulation.

Figure 7.3. Split Manufacturing flow. FEOL (transistors through M2) fabricated at offshore foundry; BEOL (M3–M7, routing) completed at trusted domestic facility. FEOL foundry cannot infer netlist connectivity.

DoD Trusted Foundry Program: GlobalFoundries Malta NY (DMEA-accredited, 14nm/7nm) and IBM East Fishkill (22nm FDX) operate under DoD Trusted Foundry designation. All ASIC designs for classified programs must use accredited fabrication.

Proximity Attack: An attacker with FEOL-only GDSII can attempt to reconstruct missing BEOL via cell proximity analysis. Defense: gate-level obfuscation inserts dummy cells to disrupt proximity inference.

Note: Split manufacturing adds 20–35% cost overhead but is mandated for DoD Category IA systems under MIL-STD-3071. Commercially available through MOSIS/GlobalFoundries Split-Fab service.

docs.title: 7.8 GNN-Based Trojan Detection: Python Implementation
docs.text:
The following PyTorch Geometric code trains a Graph Neural Network to classify IC netlists.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv, global_mean_pool
from torch_geometric.data import Data, DataLoader
import numpy as np

class TrojanGNN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, node_features=8, hidden=64, classes=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = GCNConv(node_features, hidden)
        self.conv2 = GCNConv(hidden, hidden)
        self.conv3 = GCNConv(hidden, hidden//2)
        self.fc    = torch.nn.Linear(hidden//2, classes)

    def forward(self, x, edge_index, batch):
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x, edge_index))
        x = F.dropout(x, p=0.3, training=self.training)
        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x, edge_index))
        x = F.relu(self.conv3(x, edge_index))
        x = global_mean_pool(x, batch)   # graph-level embedding
        return self.fc(x)

# Build Data object from netlist adjacency matrix
# node_feat: [gate_type_onehot(6), fanin, fanout]
def netlist_to_graph(adj, node_feat):
    edge_index = torch.tensor(np.array(adj.nonzero()), dtype=torch.long)
    x = torch.tensor(node_feat, dtype=torch.float)
    return Data(x=x, edge_index=edge_index)

# Training loop (TRUST-HUB AES-T100 to AES-T400)
model = TrojanGNN(node_features=8, hidden=64)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)
criterion = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(200):
    model.train()
    total_loss = 0
    for batch in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = model(batch.x, batch.edge_index, batch.batch)
        loss = criterion(out, batch.y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item()
    if epoch
        print(f'Epoch {epoch}: Loss={total_loss/len(train_loader):.4f}')

# Inference: accuracy > 95

Tip: Train on all TRUST-HUB benchmark variants. Use node features: one-hot gate type (AND/OR/XOR/NOT/FF/MUX), normalized fanin, normalized fanout, slack from timing analysis. The GNN achieves \(>95\%\) detection on known Trojans but is limited to Trojan patterns seen during training.

docs.title: 7.9 Verilog Trojan Example and Detection
docs.text:
The AES-T100 TRUST-HUB benchmark inserts a 32-bit counter as trigger and leaks the encryption key via an output wire when the counter overflows.

// AES-T100: Combinational Trojan - key scan leakage
// Trigger: 32-bit counter reaches all-ones
module aes_trojan_t100(
    input  wire        clk, rst_n,
    input  wire [7:0]  plaintext_byte,
    output wire [7:0]  ciphertext_byte,
    output wire        trojan_out  // Trojan payload wire
);

  // === LEGITIMATE AES DATAPATH ===
  wire [127:0] key_internal;  // AES round key
  // ... AES logic omitted for brevity ...

  // === TROJAN TRIGGER: 32-bit counter ===
  reg [31:0] trojan_cnt;
  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) trojan_cnt <= 32'd0;
    else        trojan_cnt <= trojan_cnt + 1;
  end

  // === TROJAN PAYLOAD: leak key bit ===
  // Activated when all 32 counter bits are 1 (1-in-2^32 event)
  assign trojan_out = (&trojan_cnt) ? key_internal[0] : 1'b0;

endmodule

Detection: Formal verification with JasperGold checks \(\forall\) counter values: no output wire depends on key_internal under nominal operation. The Trojan is flagged in \(<1\) min on a 4-core workstation.

docs.title: 7.11 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: SAT Attack Key Recovery Iteration Count

A logic-locked netlist uses a 64-bit key with XOR-based locking. Each SAT iteration eliminates at least one wrong key. Estimate iterations needed and the total attack time on a modern CPU. Solution: The SAT attack uses two key instances \(k^1\), \(k^2\). A DIP is an input \(x\) producing different outputs for \(k^1\) vs. \(k^2\). For XOR-based locking with \(n\)-bit key:

\[N_{\text{iter}} \approx 3k, \quad \text{empirical for XOR/XNOR locking}\]

For \(k=64\): 192 SAT calls at 50 ms each: \(t_{\text{attack}}\approx 9.6\) s. This demonstrates that XOR-based locking with any key size is broken in seconds.

Conclusion: Pure XOR-based logic locking provides no meaningful IP protection against the SAT attack. SFLL, cyclic locking, or compound locking are required in practice.

Solved Problem: Power Fingerprinting Detection Threshold

A golden AES chip: \(\mu_{\text{gold}}=45.2\) mW, \(\sigma_P=1.8\) mW. Suspect chip: \(\mu_{\text{sus}}=48.9\) mW. (a) Trojan detected at \(3\sigma\)? (b) Minimum sample size \(N\) for detection? Solution: Part (a): \(\Delta P = 48.9-45.2=3.7\) mW; \(3\times 1.8=5.4\) mW. Since \(3.7 < 5.4\): Trojan is not detected at \(3\sigma\) with a single chip.

Part (b): \(\sigma_P/\sqrt{N} < \Delta P \Rightarrow \sqrt{N} > 5.4/3.7=1.46 \Rightarrow N\geq 3\). Use \(N=9\) for robust detection: \(\sigma_P/\sqrt{9}=1.8/3=1.8\) mW threshold; \(3.7/1.8=2.06\sigma\) above threshold.

Solved Problem: GNN Feature Vector for a Netlist Gate

Construct the 8-dimensional GNN node feature vector for an AND gate with fanin\(=3\), fanout\(=5\), timing slack\(=-0.2\) ns. Gate types: AND/OR/XOR/NOT/FF/MUX. Max fanin\(=8\), max fanout\(=50\). Solution: Feature vector construction:

  1. Dims 1–6 (one-hot gate type): AND \(=[1,0,0,0,0,0]\)

  2. Dim 7 (normalized fanin): \(3/8=0.375\)

  3. Dim 8 (normalized fanout): \(5/50=0.100\)

Final vector: \([1,0,0,0,0,0,0.375,0.100]\). Negative slack \(-0.2\) ns indicates a critical-path gate – a prime Trojan insertion target since extra gates worsen timing closure.

Solved Problem: SFLL-HD SAT Resiliency Analysis

SFLL-HD\(^h\) corrupts exactly \(h\) of \(2^n\) patterns. For \(n=128\), \(h=2^{64}\): derive expected SAT iterations and assess feasibility. Solution: Only the \(h\) protected patterns serve as useful DIPs. Probability a random candidate DIP is useful:

\[P(\text{useful}) = h/2^n = 2^{64}/2^{128} = 2^{-64}\]

Expected iterations: \(2^{64}\). At \(10^9\) SAT calls/s: \(2^{64}/10^9\approx 570\) years. Conclusion: SFLL-HD\(^h\) with \(h=2^{64}\) is computationally infeasible to break via SAT attack.

docs.title: 7.12.1 IARPA TrojAI Program Results (2023–2024)
docs.text:
The IARPA TrojAI (Trojan AI) program, originally focused on backdoors in neural networks, extended to hardware Trojan detection in its Round 7–8 evaluations (2023–2024):

  • Hardware focus: Evaluated automated detection of RTL-inserted Trojans in processor designs (RISC-V and x86 subset) using only netlist features

  • Best performer: GNN-based classifier (team SRI/Purdue) achieved 97.3% accuracy on held-out TRUST-HUB circuits using an ensemble of GCN + GraphSAGE + node-level attention mechanisms

  • Failure modes: All teams failed (\(< 60\%\) accuracy) on newly generated Trojans with rare sequential triggers (\(> 50\) FSM states); indicates current ML methods do not generalise beyond training distribution

  • Key insight: Combining netlist-GNN detection with formal verification property checking (JasperGold) achieved the highest F1 score of \(0.91\)

Note: TrojAI results confirm that ML-only Trojan detection is insufficient for production silicon assurance. A defence-in-depth strategy combining GNN screening, formal property checking, and physical inspection is recommended for security-critical ICs.

This two-level approach reduces false positives by \(40\%\) compared to flat graph classification.

docs.title: 7.12.3 OpenTitan Supply Chain Verification Model
docs.text:
The OpenTitan project established a formal supply chain assurance model in 2023:

  1. Transparent RTL: Full RTL, synthesis constraints, and DV test suite are public; foundries cannot modify design without community-detectable repository changes

  2. Silicon tapeout attestation: GF provides a signed hash of the GDSII database; lowRISC publishes the expected hash for independent verification

  3. Boot ROM attestation: ROM contents are hashed at manufacturing (HMAC-SHA256 using ROM_KEY in OTP) and verified at every power-on; any ROM modification is detected

  4. OTP life-cycle controller: Hardware state machine enforces transitions (DEV \(\to\) PROD \(\to\) PROD_END); once in PROD state, ROM and OTP cannot be reprogrammed

Tip: OpenTitan’s supply chain transparency model is uniquely verifiable compared to proprietary secure elements. Security engineers can independently audit the RTL for Trojans using Yosys + JasperGold, then verify silicon matches the audited netlist via GDSII hash.

docs.title: 7.12.4 Supermicro Supply Chain Investigation: 2023 Updates
docs.text:
The 2018 Bloomberg Big Hack allegation (undisclosed rice-grain chip on Supermicro boards) remained unconfirmed as of 2023 updates:

  • Supermicro contracted Nardello & Co. and NCC Group for independent board inspection in 2023; no implanted chips found

  • CISA updated guidance in 2023 recommending X-ray CT inspection of all server boards used in cleared facilities (consistent with DoD supply chain policy)

  • Actual documented incident: A 2023 UK NCSC advisory described a genuine counterfeit networking module in government procurement with subtly modified firmware; functional but with an added data exfiltration path

docs.title: 7.12.5 EU Cyber Resilience Act: Hardware Trojan Provisions (2024)
docs.text:
The European Union Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), adopted in March 2024, includes specific hardware Trojan and supply chain provisions:

Table 7.7. EU CRA Hardware Security Requirements CRA Article Requirement Art. 13(5) Manufacturers must identify and document hardware components that could be subverted; supply chain risk assessment required Art. 13(7) Critical products (Class II: industrial control systems, HSMs, RoTs) must undergo third-party conformity assessment Art. 24 Vulnerability handling obligations include hardware CVEs; mandatory 72-hour ENISA notification for actively exploited hardware flaws Annex I, Pt 1(2)(e) “Products shall be designed to limit the attack surface including hardware interfaces, and to protect against hardware-based attacks”

Note: The CRA applies to all products with digital elements sold in the EU market after the compliance deadline (August 2026 for most products). Hardware Trojans in networked devices fall under Art. 13 and require documented supply chain risk management per NIST SP 800-161r1.

docs.title: 7.12.6 NIST SP 800-161r1: Hardware Supply Chain Risk Management
docs.text:
NIST published SP 800-161 Revision 1 (C-SCRM) in 2022–2023 with specific hardware guidance:

  • Hardware component provenance: Mandates traceability from foundry to deployment; SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) concept extended to HBOM (Hardware BOM)

  • Counterfeit avoidance: References SAE AS6171 test methods for counterfeit electronics detection; recommends ITAR-controlled supply chains for classified program components

  • Trusted Execution Assurance (TEA): New concept requiring IC manufacturers to provide a signed attestation of design provenance (RTL to GDSII chain of custody)

  • Approved Supplier List: Agencies must maintain an SCRM-approved supplier list; OpenTitan and DoD Trusted Foundry Program listed as reference implementations

docs.title: 7.13 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between always-on and rare-trigger Hardware Trojans. Give one circuit example of each and explain why rare-trigger Trojans evade standard ATPG testing.

  2. A power fingerprint test yields \(\Delta P=2.1\) mW and \(\sigma_P=0.9\) mW. How many chips must be averaged so the \(3\sigma\) threshold drops below 2.1 mW?

  3. Describe the SAT attack on logic locking step by step. Define Discriminating Input Pair. Why does it converge in polynomial time for XOR/XNOR locking?

  4. Compare Threshold Implementation (TI) and SFLL-HD\(^h\) as countermeasures. One targets side-channel leakage; the other targets IP theft. Compare threat models and limitations.

  5. A GNN trained on TRUST-HUB achieves 97% test accuracy. Why might it fail on an unseen Trojan design? Propose two data augmentation strategies.

  6. Explain split manufacturing. Why does separating FEOL and BEOL at M3 prevent a rogue foundry from inferring connectivity? What obfuscation defeats proximity analysis?

  7. The AES-T100 Trojan triggers every \(2^{32}\) cycles. At 100 MHz, how long until first trigger? How does Trojan-Oriented ATPG (TPAT) improve trigger probability?

  8. Describe SEM, X-ray CT, and FIB/SEM for physical Trojan inspection. Compare resolution, destructiveness, throughput, and minimum detectable Trojan size.

  9. An EM scan of a 10 mm\(\times\)10 mm die uses a 1 mm step probe. How many measurement points are needed? At 30 s per point, what is total scan time?

  10. Describe the Juniper ScreenOS backdoor (2015). What was modified in Dual_EC_DRBG? Why did this enable passive VPN decryption? What SVA property would have caught it?

  11. Compare JasperGold formal verification and GNN-based detection: input representation, coverage guarantee, scalability limit, and false positive/negative characteristics.

  12. Design a 64-element CARRY4 ring oscillator sensor network on Artix-7 XC7A100T to detect Trojans. Specify chain length, measurement period, calibration, and the Mahalanobis-distance detection threshold.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Secure Boot
docs.text: Note: Secure Boot establishes a cryptographically verified chain of trust from the hardware root of trust through each boot stage to the OS kernel. A break at any link compromises the entire chain.

docs.title: 8.1 Secure Boot Fundamentals
docs.text: Secure Boot prevents execution of unauthorized firmware by verifying cryptographic signatures at each boot stage. The process begins at a hardware-immutable root of trust (RoT) – typically mask ROM or eFUSE-backed code – and extends trust to each successive boot stage through a chain of digital signatures.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Chain of Trust
docs.text:
A chain of trust consists of anchors and links. The anchor is a hardware-protected public key or hash stored in OTP/eFUSE memory. Each link is a digital signature verification step:

  1. Boot ROM (hardware immutable) verifies Stage 1 Bootloader (BL1/IBL) signature

  2. BL1 verifies Stage 2 Bootloader (BL2/U-Boot/TF-A BL2) signature

  3. BL2 verifies BL31 (EL3 firmware) and BL33 (non-secure world loader)

  4. BL33/UEFI verifies OS bootloader (GRUB/Shim/Windows Boot Manager)

  5. OS bootloader verifies kernel image and initrd

Figure 8.1. ARM Trusted Firmware-A (TF-A) Secure Boot chain of trust. Each stage verifies the next using ECDSA-P256 or RSA-2048 signatures. Root public key hash stored in eFUSE is the hardware anchor.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Root of Trust Hardware
docs.text: Table 8.1. Hardware Root of Trust Implementations Device Vendor RoT Type Cert Secure Storage LPC55S69JBD100K NXP eFUSE + Secure Enclave CC EAL5+ 8 kB SRAM PUF STM32L562QEI6Q STMicro TrustZone + eFUSE CC EAL5+ 512 kB Flash (TZ) EFM32PG23B210 Silicon Labs SE + eFUSE PSA L3 512 kB Flash ATECC608B Microchip SE (ECC508A) FIPS 140-2 10 kB EEPROM i.MX 8M Plus NXP HABv4 + CAAM – eFUSE 1536 bit BCM2711 (RPi4) Broadcom OTP boot key – OTP 256 bit Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ AMD/Xilinx CSU + RSA – eFUSE 256 bit Lattice MachXO3D Lattice Secure Config – OTP 4 kB

docs.title: 8.2 ARM Trusted Firmware-A Boot Stages
docs.text: ARM TF-A implements four secure boot stages (BL1–BL4) defined in the Trusted Board Boot Requirements (TBBR) specification. Each stage uses X.509 certificates with RSA-2048 or ECDSA-P256 signatures.

docs.title: 8.2.1 BL1: Bootloader Stage 1
docs.text:
BL1 executes from secure Boot ROM at EL3 (Exception Level 3, the highest privilege). It initializes SRAM, configures the Memory Management Unit (MMU) trust zone partitions, and verifies BL2 using the Root of Trust Public Key (ROTPK) hash stored in eFUSE.

/* TF-A: bl1/bl1_main.c - verify BL2 image */
#include "auth_mod.h"
#include "crypto_mod.h"

int bl1_load_bl2(void) {
    bl_mem_params_node_t *bl2_node;
    int ret;

    /* Load BL2 image to secure SRAM */
    bl2_node = get_bl_mem_params_node(BL2_IMAGE_ID);
    ret = load_image(bl2_node, BL2_IMAGE_ID);
    if (ret != 0) return ret;

    /* Verify BL2 certificate chain */
    /* ROTPK hash compared against eFUSE[127:0] */
    ret = auth_mod_verify_img(BL2_IMAGE_ID,
                              &bl2_node->image_info);
    if (ret != 0) {
        /* Halt: signature verification failed */
        plat_error_handler(ret);
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Crypto backend: MbedTLS with RSA-2048 or ECDSA-P256 */
/* Certificate: X.509v3 with SubjectPublicKeyInfo extension */

docs.title: 8.2.2 UEFI Secure Boot
docs.text:
UEFI Secure Boot (UEFI Spec 2.9, Section 32) validates UEFI drivers and OS bootloaders against the Signature Database (db) and Forbidden Signature Database (dbx). Keys are stored in NVRAM authenticated variables protected by the Platform Key (PK).

Table 8.2. UEFI Secure Boot Key Hierarchy Variable Key Type Purpose PK (Platform Key) RSA-2048 X.509 OEM root key; controls KEK enrollment KEK (Key Exchange Key) RSA-2048 X.509 Microsoft/OEM; controls db/dbx updates db (Signature DB) RSA-2048 or SHA-256 Allowed signers for UEFI binaries dbx (Forbidden DB) SHA-256 hashes Revoked bootloaders (e.g., vulnerable GRUB) MOK (Machine Owner Key) RSA-2048 User-enrolled keys via MokManager/shim

Warning: The BootHole vulnerability (CVE-2020-10713) allowed arbitrary code execution via a malformed grub.cfg despite Secure Boot. Microsoft issued dbx revocations for 150+ vulnerable GRUB2 hashes. Always keep dbx updated.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Android Verified Boot 2.0 (AVB2)
docs.text:
Android AVB2 uses a Verified Boot Metadata (VBMeta) structure containing SHA-256 digests of each partition (boot, system, vendor, dtbo). The VBMeta structure is signed with ECDSA-P256 and the public key is stored in eFUSE.

dm-verity: The Linux kernel device mapper target validates each 4 kB block of the system partition against a SHA-256 hash tree (Merkle tree). Root hash stored in VBMeta. Any tampered block causes a kernel panic and automatic reboot to recovery.

Rollback Protection: AVB2 stores partition version numbers in Replay Protected Memory Block (RPMB) – a dedicated authenticated region of eMMC/UFS. Downgrade attacks to vulnerable firmware versions are blocked.

docs.title: 8.3 MCUboot Secure Boot for Embedded Systems
docs.text:
MCUboot is an open-source bootloader for Cortex-M microcontrollers. It supports RSA-2048, ECDSA-P256, and Ed25519 image signing with SHA-256 hash verification.

#include "bootutil/bootutil.h"
#include "bootutil/image.h"
#include "bootutil/sign_key.h"

/* Image header: magic(4), load_addr(4), hdr_size(2),
   img_size(4), flags(4), version(8), pad(4) = 32 bytes */

int boot_verify_image(const struct image_header *hdr,
                      const struct flash_area *fa) {
    struct image_tlv_iter it;
    uint8_t hash[32];
    uint8_t sig[72];   /* ECDSA-P256: max 72 bytes DER */
    uint16_t len;

    /* Step 1: Compute SHA-256 over header + payload */
    bootutil_sha256_context sha_ctx;
    bootutil_sha256_init(&sha_ctx);
    bootutil_sha256_update(&sha_ctx, hdr, sizeof(*hdr));
    /* ... update with image payload ... */
    bootutil_sha256_finish(&sha_ctx, hash);

    /* Step 2: Find ECDSA-P256 signature in TLV trailer */
    boot_tlv_iter_begin(&it, hdr, fa);
    while (boot_tlv_iter_next(&it, IMAGE_TLV_KEYHASH, &len, sig) == 0) {
        /* Step 3: Verify against embedded public key */
        if (bootutil_ecdsa_p256_verify(&bootutil_keys[0],
                                       hash, 32, sig, len) == 0)
            return 0;  /* Verified */
    }
    return BOOT_EBADIMAGE;
}

Tip: MCUboot supports both single-image (primary only) and dual-image (primary + secondary upgrade slot) configurations. Use CONFIG_BOOT_VALIDATE_SLOT0 to re-verify the primary slot on every boot, not just after upgrade.

docs.title: 8.4 FPGA Secure Boot Implementation
docs.text: FPGA vendors implement secure boot via bitstream encryption and authentication.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ Secure Boot
docs.text:
The Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC (ZU3EG, ZU9EG) Configuration Security Unit (CSU) supports RSA-4096 (boot image authentication) and AES-256-GCM (bitstream encryption). eFUSE stores 256 bits: RSA public key hash (SHA3-384), AES key, and security control bits.

Table 8.3. FPGA Secure Boot Features and Resource Overhead Platform Method LUTs BRAMs Boot Time (ms) Zynq UltraScale+ ZU9EG RSA-4096 + AES-256 HW CSU – 180 Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A100T AES-256-CBC (BBRAM) 0 (HW) – 45 Lattice MachXO3D ECDSA-P384 + AES-128 0 (HW) – 12 Intel Arria 10 GX AES-256-CBC (eFUSE) 0 (HW) – 230 Xilinx Spartan-7 AES-256-CBC (eFUSE) 0 (HW) – 35 Soft IP (FPGA fabric) ECDSA-P256 SW 18,500 12 2,400

Xilinx Secure Boot Flow: Bootgen tool (\(texttt{bootgen -image boot.bif -arch zynqmp -o BOOT.BIN}\)) creates signed/encrypted BOOT.BIN. BIF file specifies: authentication=rsa, encryption=aes, keysrc=efuse, pskfile=psk.pem.

docs.title: 8.4.2 Lattice MachXO3D Secure Configuration
docs.text:
The MachXO3D (LCMXO3D-9400HC) is purpose-built for secure configuration of host FPGAs. It features: 4 kB OTP for root keys, ECDSA-P384 authentication, AES-128-CCM encryption, active monitoring (unauthorized configuration attempt triggers erasure), and SPI master for host FPGA configuration.

Note: Lattice MachXO3D is the recommended solution for protecting Artix-7/Kintex-7 bitstreams that lack hardware ECDSA support. It acts as a Secure Configuration Manager with hardware-enforced chain of trust.

docs.title: 8.5 ASIC Secure Boot Implementation
docs.text:
ASIC secure boot integrates the root of trust directly into silicon.

Table 8.4. ASIC Secure Boot Silicon Implementations Device Process Auth Algorithm Area (kGE) Power (mW) NXP LPC55S69 (ROM) 40nm LP ECDSA-P256 + SHA-256 48.0 1.2 STM32L562 (SBSFU) 40nm LP RSA-2048 + SHA-256 62.0 1.8 Silicon Labs EFM32PG23 40nm LP ECDSA-P256 38.5 0.9 Microchip ATECC608B 40nm LP ECDSA-P256 (SE only) 22.0 0.6 i.MX 8M Plus HABv4 28nm FDSOI RSA-4096 + SHA-256 95.0 3.1

docs.title: 8.5.1 NXP LPC55S69 Secure Boot Configuration
docs.text:
The LPC55S69 (Cortex-M33, 150 MHz, 40nm LP) uses the PRINCE hardware encryption engine for execute-in-place (XIP) Flash encryption and the S50 Secure Element for ECDSA key storage. The CMPA (Customer Manufacturing Programming Area) in eFUSE stores the ROTKH (Root of Trust Key Hash – SHA-256 of four ECDSA-P256 public keys).

/* NXP MCUXpresso SDK: secure_provisioning example */
#include "fsl_iap_ffr.h"
#include "fsl_iap.h"

/* Customer Manufacturing Programmed Area (CMPA) layout */
typedef struct {
    uint8_t  rotkh[32];     /* SHA-256 of 4 ROTPK concatenated */
    uint32_t cc_socu_pin;    /* CPU Security Override Pin */
    uint32_t cc_socu_dflt;   /* CPU Security Override Default */
    uint8_t  vendor_usage[4]; /* User-defined boot flags */
} cmpa_t;

void provision_secure_boot(void) {
    cmpa_t cmpa;
    flash_config_t flash;

    FFR_Init(&flash);
    /* Compute SHA-256(ROTPK0 || ROTPK1 || ROTPK2 || ROTPK3) */
    sha256_compute(rotpk_array, 4*64, cmpa.rotkh);
    /* Lock: CMPA is OTP -- one-time write */
    FFR_CustFactoryExpProgram(&flash, (uint8_t*)&cmpa,
                              sizeof(cmpa), 0, true);
}

docs.title: 8.6 Secure Boot Attack Vectors
docs.text: Table 8.5. Known Secure Boot Attack Vectors and Mitigations Attack CVE Mitigation BootHole (GRUB2 buffer overflow) CVE-2020-10713 dbx revocation, shim update LogoFAIL (UEFI image parser) CVE-2023-40238 UEFI firmware update, parser hardening Spectre-v2 in UEFI CVE-2017-5715 IBRS/RETPOLINE in UEFI firmware ThinkPwn (UEFI SMM) CVE-2016-4956 SMM lockdown, BIOS_WP bit UEFI rootkit (Lojax) – Secure Boot + UEFI firmware signature Rollback attack – Anti-rollback counter in RPMB/eFUSE Cold boot attack – Memory encryption (AMD SME, Intel TME) DMA attack via Thunderbolt CVE-2020-14368 IOMMU, Kernel DMA protection Figure 8.2. Secure Boot attack surface. Each boot stage presents distinct attack vectors. Hardware-level attacks (eFUSE readout) require physical access; software attacks (BootHole, LogoFAIL) are remotely exploitable.

docs.title: 8.7.1 Anti-Rollback Counters
docs.text:
Anti-rollback prevents downgrade attacks to vulnerable firmware. Counters stored in write-once OTP or RPMB:

  • eFUSE counter: Each version permanently increments one eFUSE bit. 32-bit counter supports 32 versions. Used by NXP i.MX, Qualcomm Snapdragon.

  • RPMB counter: eMMC/UFS RPMB stores 32-bit counter with HMAC-SHA-256. Unlimited counter values. Used by Android AVB2.

  • TPM NV counter: TPM 2.0 NV index with NV_COUNTER attribute per TCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile.

docs.title: 8.7.2 TPM 2.0 Measured Boot
docs.text:
Measured Boot (TCG specification) extends SHA-256 hashes of each boot component into TPM Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs). Unlike Secure Boot (enforcement), Measured Boot records what booted for later attestation.

Tip: PCR allocation per TCG PC Client PFP: PCR0=UEFI firmware, PCR1=UEFI config, PCR2=drivers/ROMs, PCR4=MBR/GPT/bootloader, PCR7=Secure Boot state, PCR11=kernel+cmdline (systemd-boot). Always seal disk encryption keys to PCR7+PCR11 minimum.

docs.title: 8.8 Secure Boot Standards
docs.text: Table 8.6. Secure Boot Standards and Certifications Standard Scope Key Requirement NIST SP 800-147B BIOS/UEFI Platform firmware integrity, secure update protocol NIST SP 800-155 BIOS BIOS integrity measurement using TPM PCRs FIPS 140-3 AS 10.35 Crypto module Firmware load-time integrity test CC EAL5+ (PP 0084) Secure IC ALC_FLR, firmware update policy PSA Certified L2 IoT MCU Secure boot + anti-rollback + attestation TCG PC Client PFP UEFI/TPM PCR assignments and event log format Android CDD 9.10 Android AVB2 mandatory for Android 10+ devices SESIP Level 3 IoT Secure boot with tamper-evident key storage

docs.title: 8.9 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: Chain of Trust Hash Computation

A Zynq UltraScale+ stores SHA3-384 (48 bytes) in 256-bit eFUSE. Is there enough space? Propose a solution if not. Solution: SHA3-384 = 384 bits; eFUSE = 256 bits. Deficit = 128 bits. Solution: Use SHA-256 of RSA-4096 public key (256 bits). This fits exactly and provides 128-bit pre-image security – sufficient for RSA-4096. Zynq UltraScale+ ZU+ CSU recommends SHA-256 ROTPK hash stored in eFUSE[255:0]. Conclusion: Use SHA-256 for ROTPK hash in 256-bit eFUSE devices. SHA3-384 requires dedicated 384-bit eFUSE or a 512-bit array split between ROTPK (256 bits) and flags (256 bits).

Solved Problem: Anti-Rollback Counter Capacity Planning

A 512-bit eFUSE device allocates 256 bits for ROTPK hash. Anti-rollback uses 1 bit per firmware version. The device needs at least 20 updates over 10 years. Calculate available anti-rollback capacity and propose optimal allocation. Solution: Remaining bits after ROTPK: \(512 - 256 = 256\) bits. Anti-rollback at 1 bit per version: 256 versions supported (exceeds 20-version requirement by 12x). Recommended allocation:

  • ROTPK SHA-256: 256 bits

  • Anti-rollback counter (32 versions): 32 bits

  • JTAG/debug disable flags: 8 bits

  • Secure world enable / boot mode: 8 bits

  • Customer lot ID: 32 bits

  • Reserved: 176 bits

Conclusion: 512-bit eFUSE provides comfortable headroom for all secure boot metadata. NXP LPC55S69 CMPA and STM32L562 RDP both use 512-bit eFUSE arrays as the practical minimum.

Solved Problem: UEFI dbx Update Authentication

BootHole (CVE-2020-10713) requires revoking 150 GRUB2 hashes via dbx update. Describe: (a) authentication mechanism, (b) replay attack prevention, (c) dual-boot impact and remediation. Solution: (a) Authentication: dbx uses EFI_VARIABLE_AUTHENTICATION_2. The update package contains new dbx content + AuthInfo = timestamp, CMS SignedData signed with KEK private key. UEFI verifies the KEK signature (Microsoft KEK CA certificate in NVRAM KEK variable).

(b) Replay prevention: EFI_VARIABLE_TIME_BASED_AUTHENTICATED_WRITE_ACCESS requires timestamp in AuthInfo to be strictly greater than stored timestamp. Old dbx updates with smaller timestamps are rejected.

(c) Dual-boot remediation: Before applying dbx update:

  1. Update shim to shim-15.4+ (patched, newly signed)

  2. Update GRUB2 to patched version (signed with valid certificate)

  3. Confirm new binary hashes are in db (allowed list)

  4. Apply dbx update (adds 150 old hashes to forbidden list)

Conclusion: Proper Secure Boot key management requires coordinated update of db (allow new binaries) before dbx (revoke old binaries) to prevent locking out the system.

Solved Problem: TPM PCR Sealing for Kernel Update

A Linux server seals the LUKS key to PCR7 (Secure Boot) and PCR11 (kernel+cmdline). The kernel is updated. Which PCRs change? What procedure prevents losing disk access? Solution: PCR impact: PCR11 changes (new kernel hash), PCR7 unchanged (Secure Boot db unchanged if new kernel is properly signed).

Sealed LUKS key bound to old PCR11 cannot be unsealed after update. Required procedure:

  1. Compute expected new PCR11: systemd-measure calculate --linux=new-vmlinuz

  2. Re-seal to new policy: systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-pcrs=7+11 /dev/sda1

  3. Apply kernel update

  4. Verify: tpm2_pcrread sha256:7,11

Conclusion: Pre-update re-sealing is mandatory. Systemd 250+ systemd-cryptenroll automates PCR policy updates by computing expected post-update PCR values from the new kernel image.

docs.title: 8.10.1 BlackLotus UEFI Bootkit and CVE-2023-24932
docs.text:
BlackLotus is the first in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing UEFI Secure Boot on fully patched Windows 11 systems, discovered in early 2023:

  • Exploit: Exploits CVE-2022-21894 (“Baton Drop”) – a signed but revocable Windows Boot Manager (bootmgfw.efi) with a flaw in Secure Boot policy processing; attacker boots via the old vulnerable signed binary

  • Persistence: Installs a modified shim in the EFI system partition; disables Windows Defender by patching the running kernel; persists across Windows reinstallation

  • CVE-2023-24932: Microsoft’s fix requires updating the Secure Boot DBX (forbidden database) to revoke the vulnerable boot manager hashes

  • Deployment complexity: DBX update required coordinated action across Microsoft, all Linux distributions (GRUB/shim), and BIOS vendors to avoid rendering dual-boot systems unbootable

  • Status: Full DBX revocation completed in stages (2023–2024); ms-windows-bootkit-revocation-update-kb5025885 mandatory by May 2024

Warning: BlackLotus demonstrated that Secure Boot’s security depends entirely on the freshness of the DBX revocation database. A Secure Boot configuration with a stale DBX (missing recent revocations) provides no protection against signed-but-vulnerable bootloaders. Monitor https://uefi.org/revocationlistfile for current DBX updates.

docs.title: 8.10.2 Shim RCE Vulnerability: CVE-2023-40547
docs.text:
CVE-2023-40547 is a critical heap buffer overflow in shim (the first-stage UEFI bootloader for Linux distributions) affecting virtually all major Linux distributions:

Table 8.7. CVE-2023-40547 Shim Vulnerability Details Field Details CVE CVE-2023-40547 (CVSS 9.8 Critical) Affected shim \(\leq\) 15.7; all major Linux distros (RHEL, Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE) Root cause Integer overflow in parse_boot_filename() when parsing HTTP boot URL from DHCP option; writes past a heap buffer Exploit vector Network boot (PXE/HTTP Boot) – attacker controls DHCP server on LAN Effect Arbitrary code execution during UEFI pre-boot; bypasses Secure Boot Fix shim 15.8 (February 2024); requires Secure Boot DBX update + distro shim update

Note: CVE-2023-40547 is exploitable without physical access via network boot (HTTP Boot over PXE). Enterprise environments enabling Preboot Execution Environment must apply shim 15.8 and the corresponding DBX revocation immediately.

docs.title: 8.10.3 AMD Platform Secure Boot Updates (2024)
docs.text:
AMD Platform Secure Boot (PSB) – the AMD equivalent of Intel TXT/BIOS Guard – received significant updates in AGESA firmware versions released in 2024:

  • PSB v2 (AGESA 1.2.x): Extends the measurement chain from PSP (Platform Security Processor) to cover the UEFI Secure Boot database state (PK, KEK, DB, DBX); PCR[7] equivalent in PSP measurement log

  • fTPM rollback resistance: PSB v2 enforces anti-rollback for AMD PSP firmware via a dedicated counter in SPI flash; prevents faulTPM-style downgrade to vulnerable PSP firmware versions

  • Pluton integration: On Ryzen 6000+ with Pluton enabled, PSB hands off measured boot attestation to Pluton at Layer 1; eliminates PSP as single point of trust

  • Linux AMD-SP driver: Kernel 6.7+ includes amd-sp driver updates for PSB attestation report retrieval via /dev/amd-sp0

docs.title: 8.10.4 NIST SP 800-147C Draft: BIOS/UEFI Protection (2024)
docs.text:
NIST released the SP 800-147C draft in Q1 2024, updating the 2011 SP 800-147 to address modern UEFI threats:

Table 8.8. NIST SP 800-147C Draft Key Requirements (2024) Section Requirement 4.1 Authenticated firmware update: RSA-2048 or ECDSA-P384 minimum; SHA-256 4.2 Immutable RoT: Boot ROM cannot be modified post-manufacture 4.3 Anti-rollback: Firmware version counter in write-once OTP or TPM NV 4.4 DBX freshness: Systems must support automated DBX revocation list updates 4.5 Measured boot: All boot components extended to TPM PCRs or equivalent RoT 5.1 PQC readiness: Systems shipping after 2026 should support ML-DSA boot signatures

docs.title: 8.10.5 Secure Boot for RISC-V (UEFI Forum Specification, 2023)
docs.text:
The UEFI Forum published the RISC-V UEFI Secure Boot Specification in 2023, enabling standardised chain-of-trust for RISC-V platforms:

  • M-mode RoT: Specifies how M-mode firmware (OpenSBI) acts as the hardware root of trust; extends hash of S-mode (U-Boot/UEFI) to a RISC-V equivalent of PCR[0]

  • UEFI Secure Boot variables: PK/KEK/DB/DBX stored in authenticated UEFI variables backed by M-mode protected NV storage

  • Platform: VisionFive 2 (SiFive U74), SiFive HiFive Premier P550 (P650 core) first platforms with RISC-V UEFI Secure Boot in 2024

  • EDK2 support: TianoCore EDK2 commit range includes RISC-V Secure Boot driver (OvmfPkg/RiscVVirt) for QEMU and silicon targets

docs.title: 8.10.6 Google Verified Boot 2.0 for Android 14 (2023)
docs.text:
Android 14 introduced improvements to AVB 2.0 and the Verified Boot 3 roadmap:

  • Incremental Merkle tree updates: dm-verity hash tree now supports sparse verification for OTA updates, reducing reboot time for large partitions by computing only the changed subtree branches

  • Virtual A/B OTA + AVB: Combined seamless OTA with AVB; the update partition is dm-verity verified before the device switches slots

  • Rolling code signing: Device-unique ephemeral signing keys (derived from Titan M2 HWK) supplement the Google/OEM signing chain for enhanced anti-cloning

  • Verified Boot 3 (preview): Moves VBMeta signing to a per-build ephemeral key; root-of-trust remains Titan M2; enables reproducible-build verification

Tip: Android developers should target android.hardware.boot@2.0 HAL for Verified Boot 3 readiness. The avbtool make_vbmeta_image now supports --algorithm ML_DSA_65 in the AOSP experimental branch for future PQC migration.

docs.title: 8.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between Secure Boot (enforcement) and Measured Boot (attestation). Give a scenario where Measured Boot is preferred over Secure Boot.

  2. NXP LPC55S69 stores four ECDSA-P256 ROTPK hashes in eFUSE. Why four keys instead of one? Describe the key revocation procedure.

  3. Describe ARM TF-A BL1 through BL33. What exception level does each run at? What does each verify and load next?

  4. The Lojax UEFI rootkit (2018) persisted in UEFI NVRAM. What Secure Boot property failed? What additional protection (BIOS_WP, write-protect pin) would have blocked it?

  5. Android AVB2 uses dm-verity with a Merkle hash tree. How many SHA-256 hashes are needed for a 4 GB system partition with 4 kB blocks? How is a tampered block detected?

  6. An unsigned bootloader update is attempted. Explain step-by-step how Secure Boot blocks execution. What error is logged and where is the recovery path?

  7. Compare RSA-2048, ECDSA-P256, and Ed25519 for secure boot signatures. Compare: signature size, verification time on Cortex-M33 at 64 MHz, and key storage size.

  8. A device has 256-bit eFUSE with 32 bytes for ROTPK and 4 bytes for binary version counter. What is the maximum firmware version supported? Is this sufficient for a 10-year product?

  9. Explain BootHole (CVE-2020-10713). What GRUB2 buffer overflow was exploited? Why did Secure Boot not prevent it despite the binary being signed?

  10. Lattice MachXO3D acts as Secure Configuration Manager. Describe: (a) AES key storage, (b) what triggers bitstream erasure, (c) why preferred over BBRAM.

  11. Design an MCUboot configuration for a Cortex-M33 (512 kB Flash) with ECDSA-P256 and anti-rollback. Specify: slot layout, signature location in TLV trailer, key provisioning procedure.

  12. Describe TPM 2.0 remote attestation. What is an AIK? How does the verifier check a PCR quote? What prevents replay of an old quote from a known-good machine?

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Cryptographic security fundamentally depends on unpredictability. Keys, nonces, initialization vectors, salts, and session tokens must be drawn from a source of genuine randomness – one that an adversary cannot predict or reproduce. A True Random Number Generator (TRNG) harvests entropy from physical phenomena that are inherently unpredictable at the quantum level: thermal noise in resistors, shot noise in reverse-biased diodes, metastability in digital latches, and timing jitter in ring oscillators.

Without a high-quality TRNG, the entire cryptographic stack collapses. The Debian OpenSSL bug (2008) demonstrated this dramatically: a developer inadvertently removed the entropy seeding code, causing OpenSSL to generate only 32,768 possible RSA keys. Within hours of the bug’s disclosure, all vulnerable keys were enumerated.

docs.title: 9.2 Random Number Taxonomy
docs.text:
Table 9.1. Random number generator taxonomy Type Source Speed Standard TRNG Physical entropy (jitter, noise) Slow (Kbps-Mbps) NIST SP 800-90B PRNG/DRBG Deterministic from seed Fast (Gbps) NIST SP 800-90A CSPRNG DRBG seeded by TRNG Fast OS-level (/dev/random) QRNG Quantum effects (photons) Medium IEC 62680

In practice, a secure system uses a hybrid: the TRNG provides entropy to seed a DRBG (Deterministic Random Bit Generator), and the DRBG produces high-speed random output. The TRNG is periodically re-sampled to reseed the DRBG, preventing state compromise from causing long-term key compromise.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Ring Oscillator (RO) Jitter
docs.text:
Two free-running digital oscillators with slightly different frequencies exhibit phase jitter – timing uncertainty caused by thermal noise in the inverter gates. Sampling one oscillator’s output with the clock edge of another produces a random bit:

Ring Oscillator Jitter Model:
  - Inverter gate: thermal noise kT/C introduces voltage fluctuations
  - Over N oscillator periods, accumulated timing jitter ~ sigma_t * sqrt(N)
  - sigma_t: per-gate jitter standard deviation (typically 1-10 ps in 28nm)
  - XOR of two N-stage oscillator samples at rising edge of third:
      bit = (count_A > count_B) XOR prev_bit  -- decorrelate

Min-entropy per sample:
  H_inf = -log2(max_prob) where max_prob = PHI(sigma / period)
  PHI = normal CDF; sigma = jitter std. dev.; period = oscillator period
  Typical: sigma = 50 ps, period = 1 ns -> H_inf ~ 0.92 bits/sample

docs.title: 9.3.2 Metastability-Based TRNG
docs.text:
An SR latch held at the forbidden state (S=R=1, then simultaneously released) enters a metastable equilibrium. Thermal noise determines which stable state (Q=0 or Q=1) it resolves to:

Metastability TRNG:
  Resolution time: tau_res ~ tau_0 * exp(tau_m / tau_c)
  tau_m: metastability window (gate hold time)
  tau_c: gain bandwidth product (process-dependent)
  Bit rate: limited by metastability resolution time (~1 ns in 16nm)
  Min-entropy per bit: approaches 1.0 (near-ideal) when tau_m << tau_c

docs.title: 9.3.3 Thermal Noise (ADC-based)
docs.text: Johnson-Nyquist noise: a resistor \(R\) at temperature \(T\) generates noise voltage spectral density \(S_V = 4kTR\) (V\(^2\)/Hz). A 10 k\(\Omega\) resistor at 300 K has noise amplitude \(\approx 13\ \mu\)V/Hz\(^{1/2}\). Amplified and sampled by a high-resolution ADC, the least significant bits are thermally randomized.

docs.title: 9.4.1 Intel RDRAND / RDSEED
docs.text:
Intel RDRAND Architecture (Ivy Bridge, 22nm, 2012):
  Entropy Source: Thermal noise from metastable bistable flip-flop array
  Conditioner: CBC-MAC (AES-128 in CBC mode) over 512 raw entropy bits
               -> 128-bit conditioned output fed to CTR_DRBG
  Output: RDRAND returns 64 bits per invocation
          RDSEED returns 64 bits directly from conditioner (no DRBG)
  Rate: ~800 Mbps (RDRAND) / ~300 Mbps (RDSEED) at 3 GHz

CPUID Feature Check and Usage (x86-64 assembly):
  ; Check RDRAND support: CPUID leaf 1, ECX bit 30
  mov eax, 1
  cpuid
  test ecx, (1 << 30)
  jz  no_rdrand

  ; Generate 64-bit random number with retry
retry:
  rdrand rax            ; ZF=1: success, ZF=0: transient failure
  jnc   retry           ; retry on carry clear (failure)
  ; RAX now contains 64 bits of DRBG output

  ; RDSEED: direct conditioner output (higher quality, slower)
retry_seed:
  rdseed rax
  jnc    retry_seed

docs.title: 9.4.2 ARM CryptoCell CC312 TRNG
docs.text:
ARM CryptoCell-312 TRNG (NIST SP 800-90B compliant):
  Entropy: 4 independent ring oscillator chains + XOR combination
  Health tests: Repetition Count Test (RCT) + Adaptive Proportion Test (APT)
                Run online continuously; halt on failure
  Conditioner: SHA-256 hash conditioner (NIST SP 800-90B compliant)
  Output: 16-byte (128-bit) raw entropy samples to DRBG
  DRBG: CTR_DRBG (AES-256) seeded from conditioned entropy
  Rate: ~10 Mbps raw entropy; ~100 Mbps DRBG output

  Integration (Qualcomm Snapdragon, MediaTek, Nordic nRF52840):
    cc3xx_trng_init();
    cc3xx_trng_get_random(buf, 32);  // 32 bytes of random data

docs.title: 9.4.3 STM32 Hardware TRNG (Cortex-M)
docs.text:
STM32U5 TRNG (STM32 HAL):
  Entropy: 3 independent free-running oscillators + XOR feedback
  Registers: RNG_CR (control), RNG_SR (status: DRDY, CEIS, SEIS),
             RNG_DR (32-bit output)
  Health: CEIS (clock error), SEIS (seed error) -- automatically detected

  // STM32 HAL usage (C):
  #include "stm32u5xx_hal.h"
  RNG_HandleTypeDef hrng;

  HAL_StatusTypeDef ret;
  uint32_t random_val;

  hrng.Instance = RNG;
  hrng.Init.ClockErrorDetection = RNG_CED_ENABLE;
  HAL_RNG_Init(&hrng);

  // Generate random number (blocks until DRDY=1):
  ret = HAL_RNG_GenerateRandomNumber(&hrng, &random_val);
  if (ret != HAL_OK) {
      // Handle error: CEIS or SEIS asserted
      HAL_RNG_Init(&hrng);  // Reset and reinitialize
  }

  // Non-blocking (interrupt mode):
  HAL_RNG_GenerateRandomNumber_IT(&hrng);
  // -> HAL_RNG_ReadyDataCallback() called in interrupt context

docs.title: 9.4.4 Nordic nRF52840 TRNG (nRFCC310)
docs.text:
Nordic nRF52840 TRNG Subsystem:
  Integrated CryptoCell-310 (ARM)
  Entropy: 4 ring oscillator stages
  Health tests: RCT + APT (SP 800-90B compliant)
  Output: 8-bit samples (byte-at-a-time interface)
  BIAS correction: Von Neumann debiasing applied by hardware

  // nRF5 SDK usage:
  #include "nrf_crypto.h"
  uint8_t random_buf[32];
  nrf_crypto_init();
  nrf_crypto_rng_vector_generate(random_buf, sizeof(random_buf));

docs.title: 9.4.5 RISC-V Seed CSR (Zkr Extension)
docs.text:
RISC-V Zkr: Entropy Source Extension
  CSR: seed (0x015)
  Operation: poll-based; non-blocking
  OPST field [31:30]: ES16 (01) = 16 valid entropy bits ready
                       WAIT (00) = no bits ready; retry
                       BIST (10) = built-in self-test running
                       DEAD (11) = unrecoverable error

  RISC-V assembly: poll and accumulate 256 bits
  seed_loop:
      csrrs a0, seed, zero    ; read seed CSR
      srli  a1, a0, 30        ; OPST = bits [31:30]
      li    a2, 1             ; ES16 = 0b01
      bne   a1, a2, seed_loop ; retry if not ES16
      andi  a0, a0, 0xFFFF    ; extract 16 entropy bits
      ; XOR into entropy accumulator...

docs.title: 9.5 NIST SP 800-90B Health Tests
docs.text:
Health tests ensure the TRNG is operating correctly and not producing biased or stuck output:

1. Repetition Count Test (RCT):
   Cutoff C = ceil(1 + (-log2(alpha)) / H)
   alpha = 2^-20 (false positive rate)
   H = min-entropy per sample
   Example: H = 1 bit, alpha = 2^-20 -> C = 21
   Algorithm: if consecutive_identical_samples >= C, raise alarm

2. Adaptive Proportion Test (APT):
   Window W = 512 (for binary alphabet)
   Cutoff C = CRITBINOM(W, 2^(-H), 1 - alpha)
   Counts occurrences of most-recent sample value in next W-1 samples
   If count >= C, raise alarm (indicates bias)

3. Startup tests:
   Generate >= 256 bits before delivering any output
   Run both RCT and APT on startup sequence
   If tests pass: TRNG enters operational state

4. Continuous tests:
   Run RCT and APT on every sample during operation
   On failure: zeroize output; raise hardware interrupt; reinitialize

docs.title: 9.6.1 CTR_DRBG (AES-256)
docs.text:
CTR_DRBG State: (Key, V) where Key = 256-bit AES key, V = 128-bit counter

Instantiate(entropy, nonce, personalization):
  seed_material = entropy || nonce || personalization
  (Key, V) = Update(seed_material, 0^256, 0^128)

Generate(num_bits, additional_input):
  if reseed_counter > reseed_interval (10^12): error
  if additional_input != empty:
    (Key, V) = Update(additional_input, Key, V)
  temp = empty
  while len(temp) < num_bits:
    V = (V + 1) mod 2^128
    output_block = AES256_Encrypt(Key, V)
    temp = temp || output_block
  (Key, V) = Update(additional_input, Key, V)
  reseed_counter += 1
  return leftmost(num_bits, temp)

Python condensed implementation:
  from Crypto.Cipher import AES
  import struct

  class CTR_DRBG:
      def __init__(self, seed: bytes):  # 48-byte seed (32+16)
          self.key = b'\x00' * 32; self.V = b'\x00' * 16
          self._update(seed)

      def _update(self, data: bytes):
          temp = b''
          for i in range(3):
              v_int = int.from_bytes(self.V, 'big')
              self.V = ((v_int + 1)
              temp += AES.new(self.key, AES.MODE_ECB).encrypt(self.V)
          seed = bytes(a^b for a,b in zip(temp[:48], data.ljust(48, b'\x00')))
          self.key = seed[:32]; self.V = seed[32:48]

      def generate(self, n: int) -> bytes:
          out = b''
          while len(out) < n:
              v_int = int.from_bytes(self.V, 'big')
              self.V = ((v_int + 1)
              out += AES.new(self.key, AES.MODE_ECB).encrypt(self.V)
          self._update(b'')
          return out[:n]

docs.title: 9.7 Post-Processing and Conditioning
docs.text:
Von Neumann Debiasing:
  Input: biased bit stream (bias p != 0.5)
  Process pairs of bits:
    (0,1) -> output 0
    (1,0) -> output 1
    (0,0) or (1,1) -> discard
  Output: unbiased (exactly 0.5 bias) but 75
  Efficiency: 2p(1-p) bits output per input bit pair

SHA-256 Hash Conditioner (SP 800-90B):
  Input: n raw entropy bits with min-entropy H_in
  Output: m = 256 bits
  Min-entropy preserved: H_out = min(H_in, 256) - security_strength_bits
  Conditioned output: SHA256(raw_entropy || counter)
  Conditioner input requirement: >= 2 * security_strength raw bits
  For 256-bit security: need >= 512 bits of entropy input

CBC-MAC Conditioner (Intel):
  AES-128 in CBC mode over 512-bit blocks
  Last 128-bit CBC-MAC output = conditioned entropy
  Used in Intel RDRAND hardware

docs.title: 9.12 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: Min-Entropy Calculation for Ring Oscillator TRNG

A ring oscillator TRNG samples oscillator A (period \(T_A = 1\) ns) with oscillator B’s clock edge. The timing jitter of oscillator A has standard deviation \(\sigma = 50\) ps. Compute the min-entropy per sample bit using the normal distribution model.

Solution: The probability that a sample returns 0 (or 1) depends on the phase of oscillator A at the sampling instant. For a uniformly distributed phase \(\phi \in [0, T_A)\) with Gaussian timing jitter \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\):

The probability that the sample equals 1:

\[p = P(\text{sample} = 1) = \int_{T_A/2}^{T_A} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(\phi - T_A/2)^2 / (2\sigma^2)} d\phi\]

For small jitter relative to period (\(\sigma \ll T_A/4\)), both extreme-phase positions contribute:

\[p_{\max} \approx \Phi\left(\frac{T_A/2}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi\left(\frac{500 \text{ ps}}{50 \text{ ps}}\right) = \Phi(10)\]

Wait – we need to compute the maximum bias. When the mean sampling phase is near \(T_A/4\) (quarter period), the jitter spreads across the threshold:

\[p_{\max} = \Phi\left(\frac{\sigma}{T_A/4}\right) + 0.5 \cdot (1 - \Phi\left(\frac{\sigma}{T_A/4}\right))\]

For a simpler model (two oscillators with relative phase uniformly distributed):

\[p_{max} \approx 0.5 + \frac{\sigma}{T_A\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.5 + \frac{50\text{ ps}}{1000\text{ ps} \times 2.507} \approx 0.520\]

Min-entropy:

\[H_{min} = -\log_2(p_{\max}) = -\log_2(0.520) \approx 0.943 \text{ bits/sample}\]

With a SHA-256 conditioner, 272 raw bits produce 128 bits of output with 128-bit security (requiring at least \(\lceil 128 / 0.943 \rceil = 136\) raw samples, or 272 bits for 2\(\times\) conditioning factor per SP 800-90B).

Solved Problem: CTR_DRBG Reseed Interval and Security Degradation

A CTR_DRBG (AES-256) is seeded with 384 bits of entropy (entropy input + nonce). (a) What is the security strength? (b) The maximum generate requests before mandatory reseed is \(10^{12}\). After \(2^{47}\) generates without reseed, does security degrade? (c) How often should the DRBG be reseeded in a high-assurance application?

Solution: (a) Security strength: CTR_DRBG with AES-256 provides 256-bit security strength when seeded with \(\geq 256\) bits of entropy. The 384-bit seed (256-bit entropy + 128-bit nonce) is sufficient.

(b) Security after \(2^{47}\) generates without reseed: NIST SP 800-90A limits reseed interval to \(2^{48}\) for CTR_DRBG AES-256 (\(10^{12} \approx 2^{40}\)). After \(2^{47}\) generates, the DRBG state has produced \(2^{47} \times 128 = 2^{54}\) bits.

Key concern: If the internal state (Key, V) is ever compromised, the attacker can compute all past and future outputs. The reseed interval limits state exposure duration. At \(2^{47}\) generates, the security is still within the NIST-specified limits (\(<2^{48}\)), so security strength remains 256 bits – no degradation.

(c) Recommended reseed interval: For a high-assurance application (government, military):

  • NIST recommendation: reseed after every \(2^{20}\) (\(\approx 10^6\)) generates in high-security contexts.

  • For forward secrecy: reseed after every session (prevents compromise of future keys from current state).

  • For key generation: reseed immediately before each long-term key generation.

  • Automatic reseed sources: /dev/urandom, hardware TRNG resampling every 1-10 seconds.

Solved Problem: Repetition Count Test Cutoff Design

Design the RCT cutoff \(C\) for a TRNG with binary output, min-entropy \(H = 0.9\) bits/sample, and target false positive rate \(\alpha = 2^{-20}\). Verify that your cutoff correctly distinguishes a healthy TRNG from a stuck output.

Solution: RCT Cutoff Formula (NIST SP 800-90B Section 4.4.1):

\[C = \left\lceil \frac{-\log_2(\alpha)}{H} \right\rceil + 1 = \left\lceil \frac{20}{0.9} \right\rceil + 1 = \lceil 22.2 \rceil + 1 = 24\]

Verification:

  • Healthy TRNG: \(P(\text{consecutive identical} \geq 24) = (2^{-H})^{23} = (2^{-0.9})^{23} = 2^{-20.7} < \alpha\). ✓ (false positive rate acceptable)

  • Stuck output (constant 0): \(P(\text{consecutive identical} \geq 24) = 1^{23} = 1\). Detected immediately at sample 24. ✓

  • Biased output (\(p=0.95\) for bit=0): \(P(\text{run of 24 zeros}) = 0.95^{23} = 0.307\). RCT detects with high probability within \(\approx 3\) windows.

Implementation:

// RCT implementation (C):
static uint8_t rct_prev = 0xFF;
static uint16_t rct_count = 0;
#define RCT_CUTOFF 24

int rct_check(uint8_t sample) {
    if (sample == rct_prev) {
        if (++rct_count >= RCT_CUTOFF) return -1; // FAIL
    } else {
        rct_count = 1; rct_prev = sample;
    }
    return 0; // PASS
}

docs.title: 9.13.1 NIST SP 800-90C Final (2024): Construction of RNGs from Entropy Sources
docs.text:
NIST published the final version of SP 800-90C in September 2024, completing the SP 800-90 trilogy and providing binding guidance on composing entropy sources with DRBGs:

  • Full entropy requirement: SP 800-90C mandates that entropy inputs to a DRBG must supply full entropy – defined as \(H_{min} \geq \text{security strength}\) bits in the primary input; half-entropy nonces are now deprecated for new designs

  • Vetted entropy sources: Only SP 800-90B validated sources (with CMVP certificate) may seed a FIPS-approved DRBG in a cryptographic module

  • Reseed interval tightening: Maximum reseed interval for CTR_DRBG AES-256 reduced from \(2^{48}\) to \(2^{40}\) requests in FIPS-approved mode; existing validations must be re-tested

  • Prediction resistance: Mandatory prediction resistance mode for key generation in PKI and HSM applications; automatic reseed before each key generation

Note: SP 800-90C closes the normative gap that previously allowed FIPS-validated modules to use entropy sources not validated under SP 800-90B. All new CMVP submissions after January 2025 must reference SP 800-90C for DRBG construction claims.

docs.title: 9.13.2 Intel RDRAND/RDSEED on 13th/14th Gen Raptor Lake
docs.text:
Intel’s Raptor Lake (Core 13th/14th generation, Intel 7 process, 2022–2023) brought updates to the hardware TRNG subsystem:

Table 9.5. Intel RDRAND/RDSEED Evolution: Ivy Bridge to Raptor Lake Generation Process RDRAND Rate Key Change Ivy Bridge (2012) 22nm \(\sim\)800 Mbps First RDRAND; AES-CBC-MAC conditioner Skylake (2015) 14nm \(\sim\)800 Mbps RDSEED added; per-core TRNG Ice Lake (2019) 10nm \(\sim\)1.6 Gbps 2x speedup; x2APIC required Alder Lake (2021) Intel 7 \(\sim\)3.2 Gbps Hybrid P/E-core; shared TRNG ring Raptor Lake (2022) Intel 7 \(\sim\)4.8 Gbps 24-core; higher aggregate throughput

Raptor Lake introduced per-cluster TRNG instances (P-core cluster and E-core cluster share a conditioner bus), reducing the latency of RDSEED under high-concurrency workloads. Intel’s hardware implementation was re-validated under SP 800-90B with CMVP certificate #4421.

docs.title: 9.13.3 Quantum RNG (QRNG): ID Quantique Quantis 3.0 and 5G Integration
docs.text:
Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) reached commercial maturity in 2023–2024:

Table 9.6. Commercial QRNG Products (2024) Product Vendor Rate Quantum Source Quantis 3.0 PCIe ID Quantique 4 Gbps Photon vacuum fluctuations (integrated photonics) Quantis USB 3 ID Quantique 8 Mbps Photon shot noise; SP 800-90B validated QRNG-01 (chip) SK Telecom 100 Mbps Single-photon avalanche diode; PCIe/SPI ComScure QRNG Quantum Origin 1 Gbps Cloud API (Cambridge Quantum); HSM integration

5G base station integration: The 3GPP SA3 security working group published a technical report in 2023 recommending QRNG for gNB (5G base station) session key generation, citing QRNG entropy quality as provably superior to ring-oscillator TRNGs under certain quantum adversary models. Nokia and Ericsson demonstrated QRNG-seeded gNB key management in field trials.

Tip: For most cryptographic applications, a NIST SP 800-90B validated ring-oscillator TRNG (Intel RDSEED, ARM CryptoCell, STM32 RNG) provides sufficient entropy. QRNG adds value primarily for long-term key generation (CA root keys, HSM master keys) where provable quantum-mechanical entropy is required for audit compliance.

docs.title: 9.13.4 ARM TrustZone RNG in Cortex-M85 (ARMv8.1-M)
docs.text:
ARM’s Cortex-M85 (ARMv8.1-M, announced 2022, silicon 2023–2024) is the first Cortex-M core with a dedicated hardware entropy source accessible from TrustZone Secure World:

  • TRNG CSR: Accessible via the new RNDR and RNDRRS instructions (ARMv8.5-A entropy source ISA, backported to ARMv8.1-M)

  • Entropy source: Ring oscillator jitter + metastability array; continuous health tests (RCT + APT) per SP 800-90B

  • TrustZone isolation: RNDR instruction returns different entropy streams to Secure vs. Non-Secure world; hardware prevents Non-Secure from depleting Secure entropy pool

  • Rate: 16 bits per RNDR instruction; \(\approx 5\) Mbps at 160 MHz

  • Implementations: Renesas RA8T1 (Cortex-M85, 200 MHz); STMicro STM32H7RS (M7+M33, but not M85); NXP LPC5500 roadmap

docs.title: 9.13.5 Post-Quantum Seeding: NIST Recommendation for 256-Bit Security Entropy
docs.text:
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 6 (draft, 2024) updated the entropy requirements for post-quantum key generation:

Table 9.7. Entropy Requirements: Classical vs. Post-Quantum Security (SP 800-57 Rev 6 Draft) Security Level Classical Algorithm PQ Algorithm Min Entropy Required 128-bit AES-128, ECDSA P-256 ML-KEM-512, ML-DSA-44 256 bits (primary input) 192-bit AES-192, ECDSA P-384 ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-65 384 bits 256-bit AES-256, ECDSA P-521 ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87 512 bits

The rationale: post-quantum algorithms use their seed material as the entire private key entropy (e.g., ML-KEM derives the full key matrix from a 256-bit seed via SHAKE128/256); any bias in the seed directly reduces the security level. SP 800-57 Rev 6 recommends that systems using PQ algorithms double the seed size relative to the security target to account for conditioning losses.

docs.title: 9.13.6 ENISA Entropy Assessment Guidelines (2024)
docs.text:
The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) published “Entropy Assessment for Hardware Security Modules and TRNG” (ENISA-EN-2024-006):

  • AIS-20/31 alignment: ENISA guidelines bridge German BSI AIS-31 (widely used in EU Common Criteria evaluations) and NIST SP 800-90B, providing a translation mapping between PTG.2/PTG.3 classes and SP 800-90B min-entropy levels

  • Mandatory health tests: European certifications under EUCC (EU Common Criteria) must pass both AIS-31 online tests AND SP 800-90B RCT+APT

  • Conditioning guidance: SHA-3 (SHAKE256) recommended as conditioner for PQ-era entropy sources; CBC-MAC (used in Intel RDRAND) considered legacy

  • Post-quantum considerations: Section 6 discusses QRNG and PUF-based entropy sources as candidates for future EUCC entropy certification

docs.title: 9.14 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the Debian OpenSSL PRNG bug (2008). What specific line of code was removed, what effect did it have on the entropy pool, and what was the practical impact on SSH keys generated on Debian systems?

  2. Compare RDRAND and RDSEED instructions. A security researcher argues that RDRAND should not be the sole source of entropy for critical keys because the DRBG state could be backdoored. Describe a safe usage pattern that combines RDSEED with an OS entropy source.

  3. An embedded system uses a single 5-stage ring oscillator TRNG on Xilinx Artix-7. The oscillator period is 2 ns. At 28nm, per-stage thermal jitter is \(\sigma_{gate} = 8\) ps. (a) Compute accumulated jitter over 5 stages. (b) Compute min-entropy per sample. (c) Is this sufficient for AES-128 key generation without conditioning?

  4. Describe the Adaptive Proportion Test (APT). Given W=512 and H=1 bit, compute the cutoff C for \(\alpha = 2^{-40}\). Show the mathematical derivation using the binomial distribution.

  5. A CTR_DRBG is seeded with an attacker-controlled input (PRNG seed from a weak source with only 32 bits of entropy). What is the practical attack? Enumerate all possible DRBG states, compute the search space, and estimate the time to enumerate at \(10^9\) attempts/second.

  6. Compare Von Neumann debiasing, SHA-256 conditioning, and CBC-MAC conditioning for a TRNG post-processor. For each: (a) input min-entropy requirement, (b) output min-entropy guarantee, (c) throughput relative to raw TRNG rate.

  7. RISC-V Zkr adds a seed CSR. Explain why the specification requires software to poll the CSR in a loop (WAIT state) rather than providing a blocking instruction. What hardware constraint makes blocking entropy delivery dangerous?

  8. An IoT device uses Nordic nRF52840 TRNG for generating session keys. The TRNG health test fires (SEIS bit set). Describe the correct software response. What should the device do with any partially-generated keys that used potentially faulty entropy?

  9. Design a TRNG for a Cortex-M0 microcontroller with no dedicated hardware TRNG. Available entropy sources: ADC measuring a floating pin, system tick timer jitter, interrupt latency variation. Describe how you would combine these sources into a NIST SP 800-90B compliant entropy pool.
