docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) combine software flexibility with hardware performance, making them indispensable in data centers (AWS F1, Azure NP-Series), automotive ADAS, aerospace avionics, 5G baseband, and cryptographic accelerators. This flexibility introduces unique security challenges: the configuration bitstream that defines the FPGA’s logic can be cloned, modified, or injected with hardware Trojans. Unlike ASICs, an FPGA’s functionality can be altered after deployment, requiring robust bitstream protection, runtime integrity checking, and secure lifecycle management.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Configuration Memory Types
docs.text:
Table 10.1. FPGA configuration memory types and security implications Type Vendors Persistent? Reprogrammable? Readback? SRAM-based Xilinx, Intel, Lattice No (volatile) Yes (unlimited) Yes (default) Flash-based Microchip, Lattice Yes Yes (limited) Harder Antifuse Microsemi (ProASIC) Yes (OTP) No No

SRAM-based FPGAs (the dominant technology) lose configuration on power-off; they require a secure configuration source (flash memory, JTAG host, or internal flash companion). Antifuse FPGAs (Microsemi ProASIC3, RTAX) offer inherent readback protection at the cost of one-time programmability.

docs.title: 10.2.2 Xilinx/AMD UltraScale+ Security Primitives
docs.text:
Xilinx UltraScale+ Security Features:

Key Storage:
  BBRAM (Battery-Backed RAM): 256-bit AES key; volatile; lost on power removal
    Location: dedicated BBRAM block in Configuration Security Unit (CSU)
    Access: CSU only; application logic cannot read BBRAM
  eFUSE: 256-bit AES key (red key); SHA-256 hash of RSA public key (4096-bit)
    Location: one-time programmable fuses
    Access: write-once; readback disabled by FUSE_SEC[3]

Secure Boot Chain:
  Stage 0: CSU ROM (immutable) -> verify FSBL (First-Stage Bootloader)
  Stage 1: FSBL (authenticated) -> decrypt bitstream, verify SSBL
  Stage 2: SSBL (U-Boot) -> Linux kernel with IMA/DM-Verity

Bitstream Protection:
  Encryption: AES-256-GCM (key from BBRAM or eFUSE)
  Authentication: SHA-3/384 + RSA-4096 or ECDSA-P384 (UltraScale+ Gen 2)
  Obfuscation: XOR-obfuscated key in unprotected device keyfile

docs.title: 10.2.3 Intel Stratix 10 Security
docs.text:
The Stratix 10 introduces a physically separate Secure Device Manager (SDM), a dedicated ARM Cortex-M3 microcontroller that handles all security operations independently of the FPGA fabric:

Stratix 10 SDM Features:
  - Dedicated ARM Cortex-M3 security processor (separate from FPGA fabric)
  - 256-bit AES key stored in SDM-internal eFUSE (inaccessible from FPGA fabric)
  - RSA-4096 bitstream authentication
  - Partial Reconfiguration (PR) authentication: each PR bitstream separately verified
  - PUF: SRAM PUF for device-unique key generation
  - Signed bitstream: quartus_sign --family=Stratix10
      --hash=SHA512 --privkey=signing.pem output.sof

docs.title: 10.2.4 Lattice MachXO3D: Secure Configuration Controller
docs.text:
Lattice MachXO3D implements Lattice Sentry, a pre-verified firmware stack compliant with NIST SP 800-193:

MachXO3D Sentry Stack:
  Platform Firmware Resiliency (PFR) Roles:
    Protection: Authenticate main BIOS/BMC before system boots
    Detection: Continuous monitoring of SPI flash for corruption
    Recovery: Restore from golden copy if corruption detected

  Hardware blocks:
    Embedded Flash (EFB): 2MB NVM for bitstream + Sentry FW
    AES-256 encryption engine
    SHA-256/384 hash engine
    ECDSA P-256 signature verification
    Unique 128-bit Device DNA (immutable ID)
    PUF seeded from SRAM startup values

docs.title: 10.3.1 AES-256 Bitstream Encryption Workflow (Xilinx Vivado)
docs.text:
# Step 1: Generate 256-bit AES key and configure design
# In Vivado Tcl console:
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPT YES [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.KEY0 \
  0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF \
  [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.KEYFILE /path/to/keyfile.nky \
  [current_design]

# Step 2: Program BBRAM with AES key via Vivado Hardware Manager
program_hw_cfgmem -hw_cfgmem [lindex [get_hw_cfgmems] 0] \
  -mem_file {encrypted.bit} -verify

# Step 3: Burn eFUSE key (irreversible!)
# Vivado -> Hardware Manager -> Devices -> Program eFUSE
program_hw_efuses -key_file keyfile.nky

# Step 4: Enable readback protection
set_property BITSTREAM.READBACK.DISABLEREADBACK YES [current_design]

docs.title: 10.3.2 Intel Quartus Prime Bitstream Signing
docs.text:
# Generate ECDSA key pair for signing
openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out ecdsa_key.pem
openssl ec -in ecdsa_key.pem -pubout -out ecdsa_pub.pem

# Sign the SOF file (Stratix 10)
quartus_sign --family=Stratix10 --operation=SIGN \
  --hash=SHA256 --privkey=ecdsa_key.pem design.sof

# Create encrypted + signed JIC file for configuration flash
quartus_cpf -c \
  --aes_key_file=aes_key.key \
  --sign_key_file=ecdsa_key.pem \
  --operation=CONVERT \
  design.sof design_secure.jic

# Verify signature before programming
quartus_sign --family=Stratix10 --operation=VERIFY \
  --pubkey=ecdsa_pub.pem design_secure.jic

docs.title: 10.4.1 Ring Oscillator PUF (RO-PUF)
docs.text:
Ring Oscillator PUFs exploit manufacturing variations in CMOS gates to generate device-unique responses:

// Verilog: Ring Oscillator PUF Core (simplified)
// Place each RO in separate LUT primitives to avoid tool optimization
module ro_puf #(parameter N = 64) (
    input  wire        clk_ref,   // Reference clock (100 MHz)
    input  wire [5:0]  challenge, // 6-bit: selects RO pair
    output reg         response   // 1-bit response
);
    wire [127:0] ro_out;
    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < 128; i = i + 1) begin : gen_ro
            (* KEEP = "TRUE", DONT_TOUCH = "TRUE" *)
            ring_osc #(.STAGES(7)) ro_inst (
                .out(ro_out[i])
            );
        end
    endgenerate

    reg [15:0] cnt_a, cnt_b, window_cnt;
    always @(posedge clk_ref) begin
        if (window_cnt == 16'hFFFF) begin
            response   <= (cnt_a > cnt_b) ? 1'b1 : 1'b0;
            cnt_a      <= 0; cnt_b <= 0; window_cnt <= 0;
        end else begin
            cnt_a      <= cnt_a + ro_out[{challenge, 1'b0}];
            cnt_b      <= cnt_b + ro_out[{challenge, 1'b1}];
            window_cnt <= window_cnt + 1;
        end
    end
endmodule

docs.title: 10.4.2 SRAM PUF on FPGA
docs.text:
FPGA block RAMs (BRAMs) and distributed RAM have startup values determined by manufacturing process variation:

# Extract SRAM startup values from Xilinx 7-series FPGA
# 1. Enable readback and capture startup state:
vivado -mode batch -source readback.tcl
# readback.tcl:
#   open_hw_manager; connect_hw_server
#   readback_hw_device -readback_file startup.rbt -bin_file

# 2. Extract BRAM init values:
python3 extract_bram_startup.py startup.rbt > puf_response.bin

# 3. ECC encode for error correction:
python3 puf_enroll.py puf_response.bin helper_data.bin
# Enrollment: store helper_data.bin (does not reveal PUF response)

# 4. Reconstruction at runtime:
python3 puf_reconstruct.py helper_data.bin > aes_key.bin

docs.title: 10.5.1 Remote FPGA Side-Channel (Cloud FPGA)
docs.text:
A critical threat in multi-tenant cloud FPGAs: adversarial tenants can measure power supply noise using user-programmable ring oscillators to infer another tenant’s cryptographic operations.

Remote Power Side-Channel Attack (Cloud FPGA):
  Platform: AWS F1 (Xilinx VU9P), Azure NP-Series (Alveo U250)
  Attack: Tenant A deploys AES core; Tenant B deploys RO sensor grid

  RO Voltage Sensor:
    - Dense ring oscillator array placed near target logic
    - Count frequency variations (power noise -> frequency delta)
    - Delta-f = 0.1-1 MHz per mW of power variation
    - Correlate frequency trace with AES plaintext/ciphertext

  Demonstrated (2018, Xilinx VCU118):
    - Co-located AES victim, RO attacker
    - Full AES-128 key recovery in 200K traces
    - No physical access; purely remote via FPGA logic

  Countermeasures:
    - FPGA shuffling: re-assign tenants to different FPGA regions
    - Power supply isolation: dedicated VRM per tenant partition
    - Frequency scrambling: variable-frequency jitter on clock
    - AWS mitigation: disable user-programmable ring oscillators

docs.title: 10.5.2 EM Side-Channel on FPGA Crypto Cores
docs.text:
EM Attack Setup:
  Equipment: Langer IC-200 EM probe + Rohde & Schwarz RTO1044
  Target: AES-256 on Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A35T
  Platform: ChipWhisperer Pro CW1200 with EM probe kit

  Attack flow:
    1. Position EM probe over FPGA crypto region
    2. Capture 10,000 power traces with known plaintexts
    3. Apply CPA on AES round 1:
       Hypothesis: H[b] = HW(SubBytes(p[i] XOR k[i]))
       Correlation: rho(H[b], traces) -> peaks at correct b
    4. Repeat for all 16 key bytes

  Result: Full AES-128 key in < 5000 traces (unprotected impl.)

  Countermeasures:
    - AES masking: XOR all intermediate values with random mask
    - Clock randomization: MMCM/PLL dithering
    - Threshold Implementation (TI): 3-share Boolean masking
    - Power rail decoupling: 100nF + 10uF capacitors on VCC

docs.title: 10.6 Hardware Trojans in FPGA
docs.text:
TrustHub FPGA Trojan Example: RS232-T1000
  Module: RS232 UART controller
  Trigger: Character sequence 0xDEAD in TX buffer (prob. 2^-16)
  Payload: Assert external interrupt line for 1 clock cycle

Trojan Detection Methods:
  1. Functional Testing: Exhaustive simulation (infeasible for large)
  2. Side-Channel Analysis: Power/EM vs golden implementation
     Anomalous power: Trojan adds < 0.1
  3. Formal Verification: Check trigger reachability
     sby -f trojan_check.sby  (SymbiYosys BMC)
  4. Logic Testing: ATPG to activate rare trigger conditions
  5. Bitstream Comparison: XOR golden vs deployed bitstream

TrustHub Benchmark:
  wget https://www.trust-hub.org/download/FPGA_Trojans.zip
  # 20+ FPGA Trojan benchmarks (RS232, AES, PIC16F84 variants)

docs.title: 10.12 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: RO-PUF Uniqueness and Reliability Analysis

A 64-bit RO-PUF is implemented on Xilinx Artix-7 FPGAs. Inter-device Hamming distance \(\mu_{HD} = 32.1\) bits with \(\sigma = 2.8\) bits. Intra-device (reliability) Hamming distance \(\mu_{hd} = 1.2\) bits with \(\sigma = 0.6\) bits. (a) Compute uniqueness. (b) Compute BER. (c) How many ECC correction bits are needed for \(P_{fail} < 2^{-40}\)?

Solution: (a) Uniqueness:

\[\text{Uniqueness} = 2 \cdot \frac{\mu_{HD}}{n} = 2 \cdot \frac{32.1}{64} = 100.3\%\]

Near-ideal uniqueness (100% = perfectly uncorrelated responses across devices).

(b) Bit Error Rate (BER):

\[BER = \frac{\mu_{hd}}{n} = \frac{1.2}{64} = 1.875\%\]

At 3-sigma worst case: \(hd_{max} \approx 1.2 + 3 \times 0.6 = 3.0\) bits, so \(BER_{max} = 4.69\%\).

(c) ECC Requirements: We need a code correcting \(t \geq 4\) errors with \(P_{fail} < 2^{-40}\).

BCH(63, 36, 5) corrects up to 5 errors:

\[P_{fail} = \sum_{i=6}^{63} \binom{63}{i}(0.0469)^i(1-0.0469)^{63-i} \approx 3 \times 10^{-7}\]

For \(2^{-40}\) target, apply concatenated coding: outer Reed-Solomon(255, 223, \(t\)=16) over 8 BCH codewords. Helper data storage: \(63 - 36 = 27\) redundancy bits per BCH block.

Solved Problem: AES-256-GCM Throughput on Xilinx Artix-7

An AES-256-GCM core runs at 200 MHz with a 128-bit data path. A fully pipelined implementation processes one block per clock cycle after initial pipeline fill. (a) Compute throughput. (b) Can one core support 10 GbE at 9.6 Gbps? (c) What architectural change achieves 10 Gbps on an iterative (14-cycle/block) core?

Solution: (a) Pipelined throughput:

\[\text{Throughput} = f_{clk} \times \text{block size} = 200 \times 10^6 \times 128 = 25.6 \text{ Gbps}\]

(b) 10 GbE requirement: \(25.6 \text{ Gbps} > 9.6 \text{ Gbps}\) – yes, a single pipelined core meets 10 GbE.

If iterative (NOT pipelined, 14 cycles per block):

\[\text{Throughput} = \frac{200 \times 10^6}{14} \times 128 = 1.83 \text{ Gbps -- insufficient}\]

(c) Achieving 10 Gbps with iterative core:

  • Option A: Pipeline AES rounds – add pipeline registers after each round; achieves 25.6 Gbps.

  • Option B: 6 parallel iterative cores: \(6 \times 1.83 = 10.98\) Gbps – meets requirement but uses \(6\times\) resources.

  • Best: Option A (pipelining) – same resource area, \(14\times\) throughput improvement.

Solved Problem: BBRAM vs eFUSE: Security Tradeoff Analysis

An FPGA developer must choose between BBRAM and eFUSE for AES-256 bitstream key storage. Compare for: (a) physical tamper resistance, (b) cold-boot attacks, (c) fault injection, (d) key rotation.

Solution: (a) Physical Tamper: BBRAM uses active zeroization – tamper mesh or temperature sensor triggers battery disconnect, erasing the key. eFUSE fuse links are physically destroyed; FIB (Focused Ion Beam) on decapped die can potentially read fuse states optically. Winner: BBRAM (active protection).

(b) Cold-Boot Attacks: BBRAM is a dedicated register array (not DRAM); if battery removed \(>\)10 ms, content is lost. eFUSE is permanent and survives power cycling. Cold-boot techniques targeting DRAM do not apply to either. Winner: Tie (different failure modes).

(c) Fault Injection: Voltage glitching on \(V_{BAT}\) can erase BBRAM (DoS but not disclosure). eFUSE fuses cannot be reversed by voltage glitching – already-blown fuses are permanent. Winner: eFUSE (no erasure via FI).

(d) Key Rotation: BBRAM can be reprogrammed via JTAG at any time – supports key rotation and compromise recovery. eFUSE is one-time; compromise requires device replacement. Winner: BBRAM.

Recommendation: For field-deployed industrial devices with key rotation requirements, use BBRAM with tamper mesh. For aerospace/one-time-use with highest physical assurance, use eFUSE (antifuse preferred).

Solved Problem: Cloud FPGA Tenant Isolation: RO Sensor Attack

Two tenants share a Xilinx VU9P. Tenant B deploys 1024 ring oscillators at \(f_0 = 500\) MHz. Tenant A runs AES-256. (a) Estimate detectable power delta. (b) What can Tenant B recover? (c) Propose two cloud provider countermeasures.

Solution: (a) Sensitivity: RO frequency scales with \(V_{DD}\): \(\Delta f / f \approx 2\Delta V/V\).

1 mW on 1 V rail with 1 \(\Omega\) impedance: \(\Delta V = 1\) mV.

\[\Delta f = 2 \times \frac{10^{-3}}{1} \times 500 \times 10^6 = 1 \text{ MHz per mW}\]

With 1024-RO averaging: SNR boost \(= \sqrt{1024} = 32\times\); minimum detectable \(\approx 30\ \mu\)W correlated signal.

(b) Recovery: AES SubBytes power: \(\text{HW}(\text{SubBytes}(p_i \oplus k_i))\). With \(\sim\)10,000 chosen plaintexts, CPA recovers each of 16 AES key bytes. Full AES-128 key recovery feasible in \(<\)200,000 traces (demonstrated on real hardware, 2018).

(c) Countermeasures:

  1. Block combinational loops in DRC: Cloud provider modifies place-and-route checker to reject \(>N\) fan-out inverter chains (RO structures). AWS F1 already enforces this.

  2. Per-tenant voltage regulation: Separate VRM with decoupling reduces cross-tenant coupling from \(-\)40 dB to \(<-\)80 dB. Applicable to next-generation server designs.

docs.title: 10.13 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The FPGA security landscape has evolved substantially since 2023, driven by new silicon generations from Intel and AMD, updated bitstream attack research, emerging soft-core security models, the rise of embedded FPGA (eFPGA) IP, and European regulatory frameworks targeting programmable logic.

docs.title: 10.13.1 Intel Agilex 7 Security Features
docs.text:
Intel Agilex 7 (10 nm ESF, 2023) represents the most significant advance in programmable logic security since the introduction of the Stratix 10 SDM. Two key capabilities address cloud and data-centre deployment:

Device Attestation and Key Provisioning. The Agilex 7 Secure Device Manager (SDM) implements a hardware root-of-trust with an integrated ECDSA-P384 attestation key provisioned at the Intel factory. A platform owner can retrieve a signed Device Attestation Certificate (DAC) that chains to Intel’s publicly verifiable root CA, enabling zero-touch supply-chain verification.

Table 10.6. Intel Agilex 7 vs. Stratix 10 security feature comparison Feature Stratix 10 Agilex 7 Security processor ARM Cortex-M3 (SDM) ARM Cortex-M3 (SDM v2) Attestation None ECDSA-P384 + DAC chain Key provisioning Manual JTAG Intel PTG remote provisioning Bitstream encryption AES-256-GCM AES-256-GCM + SHA3-384 auth Lifecycle states 4 6 (adds RMA, Field-Return) Security Zones (hard) No Yes (up to 4 fabric partitions) PCIe IDE support No PCIe 4.0 IDE via SDM

Note: Intel Agilex 7 Security Zones provide hard physical isolation between FPGA fabric partitions, preventing the cross-tenant power-side-channel attacks demonstrated on Virtex/Stratix devices in 2018–2022. Each zone has dedicated power rails managed by the SDM.

docs.title: 10.13.2 AMD Versal AI Core Series Security Hardening (2024)
docs.text:
AMD Versal AI Core (XCVC1902, 7 nm TSMC, 2024 security hardening update) introduced several changes relevant to secure deployment:

  • Attestation via PLM: The Platform Loader and Manager (PLM) now supports a GetDeviceIdentity API that returns a DICE-style CDI-derived ECDSA-P384 certificate, enabling RATS-compatible remote attestation of the AI engine firmware.

  • Secure Partition Manager (SPM): Divides the device into up to 8 security domains with distinct key material, clock gating, and DMA isolation for multi-tenant AI inference workloads.

  • Arm TrustZone in Cortex-A72 APU: Boot ROM enforces secure-world firmware validation before non-secure OS boot, with TrustZone Memory Controller (TZMC) enforcing DDR partitioning.

  • Enhanced PUF: Ring-oscillator PUF upgraded to 2048-bit response for stronger device-unique key derivation, with post-processing via SHA3-256 conditioning.

docs.title: 10.13.3 FPGA Bitstream Encryption Attacks on UltraScale+ (2023)
docs.text:
Bache et al. (CHES 2023) published updated bitstream-level attack techniques targeting Xilinx UltraScale+ devices, refining earlier work from 2020–2021:

  • eFUSE key readout via photon emission: Under high-vacuum conditions, laser-stimulated photon emission from the eFUSE array can distinguish programmed (0) from unprogrammed (1) cells without physically destroying the fuse, enabling non-destructive key extraction on thinned die samples.

  • BBRAM cold-glitch: A precise voltage undershoot on \(V_{BATT}\) (2.97 V for \(<\)50 ns) causes the BBRAM to enter a partially powered state where the content can be sampled via boundary-scan before zeroization completes.

  • Differential bitstream analysis (DBA): Two almost-identical bitstreams (differing by one LUT function) are compared in AES-256-GCM ciphertext; the GCM authentication tag reveals partial keystream blocks, narrowing brute-force to \(2^{64}\).

Warning: The DBA attack is mitigated in Vivado 2023.2+ by enabling BITSTREAM.AUTHENTICATION.AUTHENTICATE_BITSTREAM YES together with BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPTKEYSELECT eFUSE. Combining authentication and eFUSE (not BBRAM) eliminates the cold-glitch surface.

docs.title: 10.13.4 MicroBlaze-V (RISC-V Soft Core) Security Model
docs.text:
AMD released MicroBlaze-V in 2023, replacing the proprietary MicroBlaze with an open RISC-V (RV32IMAC) soft core. The security model differs from the hardened ARM Cortex in Zynq:

Table 10.7. MicroBlaze-V security model vs. Zynq-7000 PS ARM Cortex-A9 Attribute MicroBlaze-V (PL) Zynq-7000 PS Security boundary FPGA fabric Hardened silicon Key storage BRAM (no hardware protect) eFUSE + BBRAM in PS Debug disable Config bitstream ARM DAP eFUSE disable RISC-V PMP Software configurable N/A (ARM TrustZone) Side-channel risk High (PL power domain) Lower (isolated PS VDD) RISC-V Zkn crypto Optional LUT impl N/A

The physical memory protection (PMP) unit in MicroBlaze-V provides 8 regions with configurable read/write/execute permissions, enabling M-mode firmware isolation from U-mode user code without an MMU. For security-sensitive designs, keys should reside in a dedicated BRAM region protected by PMP and separated from the soft-core bus fabric by an AXI firewall IP.

docs.title: 10.13.5 eFPGA IP Security: Flex Logix EFLX and Menta eFPGA
docs.text:
Embedded FPGAs (eFPGA) are programmable logic tiles integrated into SoCs, providing a reconfigurable compute fabric for post-silicon customisation. Two commercially deployed IP families present distinct security profiles:

Flex Logix EFLX-4K (TSMC 12 nm, 2023): Bitstream is stored in on-chip SRAM (loaded at boot from main flash). Security relies entirely on the SoC secure boot chain protecting the bitstream image. No on-tile AES engine; bitstream decryption must be performed by the main CPU before loading into the eFPGA SRAM. Attack surface: any DMA path that can write EFLX configuration SRAM bypasses software-level access control.

Menta eFPGA v3 (2024): Includes an optional AES-128-GCM bitstream decryption engine integrated in the configuration port controller. The 256-bit key is stored in a dedicated on-tile OTP (laser-fuse array). This keeps the plaintext bitstream off the SoC interconnect, closing the DMA injection attack surface observed in Flex Logix deployments.

Tip: When evaluating eFPGA IP for a security-sensitive SoC, require the vendor to supply a formal dataflow analysis showing that no bus fabric path can overwrite configuration SRAM without traversing the bitstream authentication engine. Require FIPS 140-3 Level 2 certification or equivalent for the decryption engine.

docs.title: 10.13.6 EU Chips Act Provisions for FPGA Security Evaluation
docs.text:
The EU Chips Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/1781, in force 2023) establishes a “Chips for Europe” technology infrastructure that includes formal security evaluation requirements for advanced programmable components:

  • Common Criteria alignment: FPGAs used in EU critical infrastructure (energy, transport, finance) must demonstrate compliance with EN ISO/IEC 15408 (CC) at a minimum of EAL4+, with the Protection Profile for Programmable Logic Devices (PP-PLD, BSI-PP-0082) as the target.

  • Supply-chain traceability: Manufacturers must provide a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) equivalent for IC design IP, including third-party hard-IP licences and EDA tool versions.

  • Vulnerability disclosure: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) timelines (90 days to patch) now apply to FPGA firmware and toolchain releases that affect EU-classified systems.

  • Trusted foundry certification: For defence and critical infrastructure, the Chips Act provides funding for certified foundry capacity within EU borders (GlobalFoundries Malta, STMicro Crolles, Tower Semiconductor Migdal Haemek licensed for EU).

Table 10.8. EU Chips Act security requirements for programmable logic Requirement Standard Impact on FPGAs Security evaluation CC EAL4+ / PP-PLD Mandatory testing for critical infra Supply chain audit ISO/IEC 20243 (O-TTPS) Design provenance documentation Vulnerability mgmt EN ISO/IEC 30111 Patch cadence for bitstream tools Trusted fabrication EU Chips Act Art. 16 Foundry certification list Cryptographic modules FIPS 140-3 or EN 419221 HSM / key storage in FPGA

docs.title: 10.14 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain why SRAM-based FPGAs require a secure external configuration source on every power-on cycle, while antifuse FPGAs do not. Compare the security and flexibility tradeoffs for a life-critical avionics application.

  2. Describe the Xilinx BBRAM key programming process using Vivado Hardware Manager. What JTAG instructions are used internally to write the 256-bit AES key? What prevents an attacker from reading the key back via JTAG after programming?

  3. A logic locking scheme XORs a 128-bit key into the FPGA netlist to obfuscate IP. An attacker has oracle access to the programmed FPGA. Describe the SAT-based attack (De-SAT) that recovers the key in polynomial time.

  4. The Intel Stratix 10 Secure Device Manager (SDM) uses a dedicated ARM Cortex-M3. Why is a physically separate security processor more secure than implementing security logic in the FPGA fabric itself? What attack vectors does this architecture prevent?

  5. Partial Reconfiguration (PR) on Xilinx UltraScale+ allows updating FPGA regions at runtime. Describe the security requirements for a safe PR update: what must be verified, in what order, before activating a new PR module?

  6. Design a TRNG for Xilinx 7-series using ring oscillators that passes NIST SP 800-90B health tests (RCT and APT). Describe the architecture: oscillator count, sampling mechanism, health test logic, and SHA-256 output conditioning.

  7. A hardware Trojan in an AES IP core adds a 1-bit output that leaks key Hamming weight when a specific 16-byte trigger is applied (probability \(2^{-128}\)). Is this detectable via: (a) random functional testing, (b) side-channel analysis, (c) formal verification? Justify each.

  8. AWS F1 prevents multi-tenant FPGA sharing. What attacks become possible if two customers shared a VU9P with logic in separate clock regions? List at least three distinct attack vectors beyond RO-based power analysis.

  9. Write the Xilinx bootgen BIF file entries for: (a) FSBL encrypted with BBRAM key, (b) Linux kernel authenticated with RSA-4096, (c) device tree unencrypted but authenticated.

  10. A RISC-V soft core in FPGA uses a PUF-derived AES-256 key for NVM encryption. After 10 years, the PUF response drifts from 0 to 5 errors in 256 bits. The enrolled ECC is BCH(255, 191, \(t\)=4). Will reconstruction succeed? Calculate the failure probability and propose a re-enrollment mechanism.

  11. Compare Xilinx UltraScale+ eFUSE key storage versus NXP SE050 external secure element for FPGA key storage. Consider: (a) FIB extraction resistance, (b) key rotation, (c) side-channel resistance, (d) integration complexity.

docs.title: Chapter 11: IOMMU and DMA Protection
docs.text: Note: Direct Memory Access (DMA) is one of the most powerful and dangerous hardware capabilities in modern systems. A peripheral device granted DMA access can read and write any physical memory address, bypassing the CPU and operating system entirely. The IOMMU (Input-Output Memory Management Unit) is the primary hardware mechanism for constraining DMA access. This chapter covers DMA attack methodologies including Thunderspy, PCILeech, and BadUSB-class attacks; Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, and ARM SMMU v3.2 architectures; SPDM/IDE for PCIe device authentication; and Thunderbolt security levels.

docs.title: 11.1.1 DMA Attack Concept
docs.text:
Direct Memory Access allows hardware peripherals to transfer data to and from system memory without CPU involvement. This is essential for high-throughput devices (NVMe SSDs, GPUs, 10GbE NICs) but creates a fundamental security challenge: a malicious peripheral can DMA to any physical address, including kernel memory, page tables, and cryptographic key material.

The attack model: an adversary introduces a malicious PCIe device (via Thunderbolt, ExpressCard, or OCP slot) and uses DMA to: (1) read RAM for credentials, BitLocker VMK, and private keys; (2) write RAM to inject malicious code, modify page tables, or patch security checks.

docs.title: 11.1.2 PCILeech: Hardware DMA Attack Platform
docs.text:
PCILeech (github.com/ufrisk/pcileech) is an open-source framework for DMA-based memory access. It supports multiple hardware platforms:

  • Screamer M2 (Xilinx Artix-7): M.2 form factor PCIe DMA board (LambdaConcept). Artix-7 XC7A35T, PCIe Gen 1 x1, direct memory access at \(\approx\)700 MB/s read rate.

  • USB3380 (PLX Technology): USB-to-PCIe bridge chip, EnBW AC701 or dedicated USB3380-AB evaluation board. Slower (USB 3.0 limited) but lower cost.

  • Xilinx AC701 (xcku040): Full-featured PCIe DMA platform, PCIe Gen 2 x4, 35K LUT FPGA fabric for custom attack logic.

# PCILeech: DMA memory read from target system
# Install PCILeech and appropriate FPGA firmware
pcileech.exe probe                          # Detect device
pcileech.exe dump -out memory.raw           # Dump all RAM
pcileech.exe wx64 -cmd "whoami"             # Execute commands (Windows)
pcileech.exe pt                             # Page table analysis
pcileech.exe lx64 -cmd "id && uname -a"    # Execute on Linux

# Python: Direct memory read via PCILeech FPGA DMA
import memprocfs
vmm = memprocfs.Vmm(["", "-device", "fpga"])
# Read 4KB at physical address 0x1000
data = vmm.memory.read(0x1000, 0x1000)
print(f"Physical 0x1000: {data[:16].hex()}")
# Search for Windows LSASS credentials in memory
processes = vmm.process_list()
lsass = [p for p in processes if p.name == "lsass.exe"]

docs.title: 11.1.3 Thunderspy Vulnerabilities (Bjorn Ruytenberg, 2020)
docs.text:
Thunderspy (thunderspy.io) disclosed seven vulnerabilities in the Intel Thunderbolt protocol:

  1. Inadequate firmware verification: Thunderbolt firmware can be downgraded to a vulnerable version disabling security checks.

  2. Weak device authentication: Pre-Thunderbolt 4 devices can be spoofed.

  3. Use of unauthenticated device metadata: Thunderbolt host trusts metadata claimed by the device without cryptographic verification.

  4. Downgrade attack using backwards compatibility: Security Level can be downgraded from SL3 (Secure Connect) to SL1 (allow all devices).

  5. Use of unauthenticated controller configurations: Thunderbolt controller firmware is not authenticated before execution.

  6. SPI flash interface deficiencies: Direct flash programming bypasses secure boot on Thunderbolt controllers (e.g., Titan Ridge).

  7. No Thunderbolt security on Boot Camp: macOS Boot Camp disables Thunderbolt security when booting Windows, exposing the attack surface.

The Evil Maid attack using Thunderspy: (1) briefly access the locked laptop, (2) open the case, (3) attach a SPI programmer to the Thunderbolt controller flash, (4) reprogram firmware to disable security, (5) close the case. On next boot, any Thunderbolt device has PCIe DMA access.

Figure 11.1. IOMMU architecture. PCIe device DMA requests are intercepted, translated via I/O page tables, cached in the IOTLB, then forwarded to physical memory. Figure 11.2. Thunderspy attack flow: malicious Thunderbolt device exploits SPI firmware reprogramming to bypass security levels, enabling unauthenticated PCIe tunneling and full DMA access to RAM.

docs.title: 11.2 Intel VT-d Architecture
docs.text: Intel VT-d (Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O) is the Intel IOMMU implementation. Described in the Intel VT-d Architecture Specification rev 3.4 (2022). Exposed to firmware via the DMAR (DMA Remapping Reporting) ACPI table.

docs.title: 11.2.1 DMAR ACPI Table Structure
docs.text:
The DMAR table (ACPI signature: DMAR, 4-byte) describes the IOMMU topology:

  • DRHD: DMA Remapping Hardware Unit Definition – MMIO base of each VT-d unit

  • RMRR: Reserved Memory Region Reporter – regions exempt from remapping (e.g., BIOS USB)

  • ATSR: ATS Capability Reporting – PCIe Address Translation Services support

  • SATC: SoC Integrated ATS Cache – platform ATS topology for SoC-integrated devices

docs.title: 11.2.2 I/O Page Table Format
docs.text:
VT-d I/O Page Tables (IOPT) use identical structure to x86 paging:

  • 4-level paging: 512 GB / 1 GB / 2 MB / 4 KB granularity, 64-bit IOPTEs

  • 5-level paging (VT-d 3.0+): 128 PB address space

  • Root Entry (RE): per-bus routing to Context Table

  • Context Entry (CE): per-function, points to IOPT root, specifies address width and domain

  • IOMMU domain: isolation unit – all devices in same domain share address space

docs.title: 11.2.3 Interrupt Remapping
docs.text: VT-d Interrupt Remapping (IR) validates MSI/MSI-X interrupt request messages before delivery, preventing malicious DMA devices from injecting interrupts to arbitrary vectors. Posted Interrupt Descriptors (PID) accelerate virtual interrupt injection in virtualized environments.

docs.title: 11.2.4 Linux VT-d Configuration
docs.text:
# Kernel command line: enable Intel VT-d strict mode
intel_iommu=on iommu=strict
# iommu=pt  -- passthrough (IOMMU off for trusted devices)

# List IOMMU groups
for g in /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/; do
    echo "Group $(basename $g):"
    ls "$g/devices/" | while read d; do
        echo "  $(lspci -s $d 2>/dev/null)"
    done
done

# Bind device to vfio-pci for VM passthrough
echo "0000:01:00.0" > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/driver/unbind
echo "1234 5678" > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/new_id

# Python: VFIO device API
import os, fcntl
VFIO_GET_API_VERSION = 0x3B64
vfio_fd = os.open("/dev/vfio/vfio", os.O_RDWR)
api_ver = fcntl.ioctl(vfio_fd, VFIO_GET_API_VERSION, 0)
print(f"VFIO API version: {api_ver}")

docs.title: 11.3 AMD IOMMU (AMD-Vi)
docs.text:
AMD IOMMU (AMD-Vi) is described in the AMD IOMMU Architecture Specification rev 3.05. Exposed to firmware via the IVRS (I/O Virtualization Reporting Structure) ACPI table.

  • Device Table: 256K entries (one per PCIe requester ID). Each DTE specifies page table pointer, IRQ remap table, PASID mode.

  • Command Ring: 4KB circular buffer for IOMMU commands (INVALIDATE_IOMMU_PAGES, etc.)

  • Event Ring: 4KB circular buffer for IOMMU events (PAGE_TAB_HARDWARE_ERROR, etc.)

  • PASID Support: Per-process address space isolation for SRIOV and SVA

  • SNP Support: AMD-Vi extended for SEV-SNP guest memory protection

# Enable AMD IOMMU in Linux
amd_iommu=on iommu=strict

# C: Linux kernel IOMMU API usage
#include <linux/iommu.h>
struct iommu_domain *domain = iommu_domain_alloc(&pci_bus_type);
/* Map 4KB: IOVA 0x80000000 -> PA phys_addr, read+write */
int ret = iommu_map(domain, 0x80000000ULL, phys_addr,
                    SZ_4K, IOMMU_READ | IOMMU_WRITE, GFP_KERNEL);
iommu_attach_device(domain, &pdev->dev);
/* Unmap and free when done */
iommu_unmap(domain, 0x80000000ULL, SZ_4K);
iommu_detach_device(domain, &pdev->dev);
iommu_domain_free(domain);

AMD IOMMU in EPYC 7003 (Zen 3, 7nm): integrated IOMMU with PCIe Gen 4 support, supports 48-bit VA (4-level) and 57-bit VA (5-level) page tables, PASID (20-bit), SVA (Shared Virtual Addressing), and SNP (Secure Nested Paging) for SEV-SNP.

docs.title: 11.4 ARM SMMU v3.2
docs.text: ARM System Memory Management Unit v3.2 (ARM IHI0070F) is the ARM architecture IOMMU standard. Used in Ampere Altra (80-core ARM server), Apple M1/M2 (as DART), Qualcomm Snapdragon, and numerous embedded SoCs.

docs.title: 11.4.1 ARM SMMU v3.2 Architecture
docs.text:
• Stream ID: Device identifier (analogous to PCIe RID). Up to 32-bit stream ID space.

  • Stream Table: 2-level table indexed by Stream ID. Each STE specifies translation mode and S1/S2 config descriptors.

  • Context Descriptor (CD) Table: Indexed by SSID (sub-stream ID = PASID). Each CD points to a page table base.

  • S1 Translation: Stage 1 (IOVA to IPA) – device-managed address space.

  • S2 Translation: Stage 2 (IPA to PA) – hypervisor-managed protection for guests.

  • ATS (Address Translation Services): PCIe device requests translation, receives PA, caches in device-side IOTLB.

  • PRI (Page Request Interface): Device requests mapping on demand (similar to x86 PCI PRI).

  • Command Queue: Ring buffer for TLBI (TLB invalidation), CMD_SYNC, etc.

# ARM SMMU in Linux: enable via kernel command line
# arm-smmu.disable_bypass=1  -- reject unmatched transactions

# Check SMMU in Linux
dmesg | grep -i smmu
# arm-smmu-v3: probing hardware ...
# arm-smmu-v3 arm-smmu-v3.0: SFR: 0x0 SFR2: 0x0

docs.title: 11.5 Thunderbolt Security Levels and Mitigations
docs.text:
Intel Thunderbolt defines four security levels:

  • SL0 (None): No security – all Thunderbolt devices allowed. Legacy mode.

  • SL1 (User): User must authorize each new device on first connection. Device UUID stored in firmware authorized device list.

  • SL2 (Secure Connect): Cryptographic device authentication using challenge-response. Device must present a valid certificate signed by Intel.

  • SL3 (DisplayPort Only): Only DisplayPort tunneling allowed. PCIe tunneling disabled. No DMA access possible from external Thunderbolt devices.

Thunderbolt 4 (Intel Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, Alder Lake) mandates SL3 support and enforces Kernel DMA Protection (DMA guard) that blocks external Thunderbolt PCIe DMA until the OS has initialized and the IOMMU is active.

docs.title: 11.5.1 SPDM and IDE for PCIe Device Authentication
docs.text:
DMTF DSP0274 SPDM (Security Protocol and Data Model) version 1.3 defines a protocol for PCIe device authentication, measurement, and key exchange over PCIe DOE (Data Object Exchange) mailboxes and MCTP (Management Component Transport Protocol):

  • GET_DIGESTS: Request device certificate chain digest

  • GET_CERTIFICATE: Retrieve full X.509 certificate chain

  • CHALLENGE: Challenge-response for device identity authentication

  • GET_MEASUREMENTS: Request firmware/hardware measurements

  • KEY_EXCHANGE: Establish session keys for IDE (Integrity and Data Encryption)

PCIe 6.0 IDE (Integrity and Data Encryption) provides link-layer encryption between root complex and endpoint using AES-256-GCM, protecting against DMA-over-PCIe attacks on physical bus sniffers and interposers.

docs.title: 11.6 Kernel DMA Protection and Windows HVCI
docs.text:
Windows Kernel DMA Protection (KDP): enabled via UEFI PrebootDMAProtection flag in DMAR table. Blocks external PCIe/Thunderbolt DMA during pre-boot and early boot phases until the OS IOMMU driver initializes. BitLocker Volume Master Key (VMK) cannot be extracted via DMA until after the OS IOMMU is active.

Windows HVCI (Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity): uses VT-d/AMD-Vi to enforce code signing at the hypervisor level. All kernel code must be signed; unsigned drivers cannot inject malicious code even via DMA (the IOMMU blocks direct write to kernel code pages).

Linux swiotlb (Software I/O Translation Lookaside Buffer): software bounce buffers for devices lacking IOMMU support. Data is copied through a safe DMA zone, preventing DMA attacks from devices that claim addresses outside their allocation.

# Check Linux DMA protection status
cat /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/type
# DMA -- standard IOMMU-mapped DMA
# DMA-FQ -- batched IOMMU invalidation

# Check swiotlb allocation
dmesg | grep swiotlb
# software IO TLB: mapped [mem 0xXX-0xYY] (64MB)

# Apple DART (Device Address Resolution Table) -- M1/M2 IOMMU
# Similar to ARM SMMU, SoC-integrated, manages USB4/Thunderbolt DMA
# Linux driver: drivers/iommu/apple-dart.c

docs.title: 11.7 FPGA DMA Controller and PCILeech Firmware
docs.text:
PCILeech uses FPGA-based DMA controllers to issue PCIe TLP (Transaction Layer Packets) directly on the PCIe bus. The Screamer M2 (LambdaConcept) uses Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A35T:

Table 11.1. PCILeech FPGA DMA controller – resource utilization (Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A35T) Component LUTs FFs BRAMs MHz Notes PCIe Gen1 x1 IP Core 3200 2400 4 125 Xilinx PCIe IP DMA Engine (read) 800 600 2 125 TLP generator DMA Engine (write) 700 550 2 125 TLP responder FT601 USB3 Interface 400 320 0 100 FTDI FT601 IF Control Logic 300 250 0 125 BRAM addr ctrl Total 5400 4120 8 125 15% of XC7A35T

ASIC implementation – Intel VT-d engine in Intel Xeon (Skylake-SP, 22nm):

  • DMA remapping throughput: \(\approx\)40 GB/s (PCIe Gen 3 x16 maximum)

  • IOTLB size: 1024 entries, 8-way set-associative

  • Page walk latency: 4–8 DRAM accesses for 4-level miss (cached by IOTLB)

  • IOMMU overhead: \(\approx\)2–5% throughput penalty for streaming DMA

  • Area: \(\approx\)2.1 mm\(^2\) VT-d engine (estimated, integrated in PCH)

docs.title: 11.9 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: IOMMU Page Table Walk for DMA Address Translation

A PCIe NVMe SSD controller issues a DMA read at IOVA (I/O Virtual Address) 0x0000_4020_0000. The OS has programmed a 4-level VT-d IOPT with page table base at physical address 0x0000_0001_4000. Walk through the complete translation to the physical address. Assume 4 KB pages, 48-bit IOVA, 64-bit IOPTE entries.

Solution:

Step 1: IOVA Decomposition (48-bit, 4-level)

IOVA = 0x0000_4020_0000 = 0b 0000_0000_0000_0000 0100 0000 0010 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000

  • Bits [47:39] = PML4 index: \((0x4020\_0000 >> 39)\,\&\,0x1FF = 0\)

  • Bits [38:30] = PDPT index: \((0x4020\_0000 >> 30)\,\&\,0x1FF = 1\)

  • Bits [29:21] = PD index: \((0x4020\_0000 >> 21)\,\&\,0x1FF = 1\)

  • Bits [20:12] = PT index: \((0x4020\_0000 >> 12)\,\&\,0x1FF = 0\)

  • Bits [11:0] = Page offset: 0x000

Step 2: Level 4 (PML4) Lookup

PML4 base = 0x0000_0001_4000. PML4 index = 0. PML4E address = 0x0000_0001_4000 + 0 \(\times\) 8 = 0x0000_0001_4000. PML4E value (example) = 0x0000_0001_5003 (present, read/write, PDPT base = 0x1_5000).

Step 3: Level 3 (PDPT) Lookup

PDPT base = 0x0000_0001_5000. PDPT index = 1. PDPTE address = 0x0000_0001_5000 + 1 \(\times\) 8 = 0x0000_0001_5008. PDPTE value (example) = 0x0000_0001_6003 (present, PD base = 0x1_6000).

Step 4: Level 2 (PD) Lookup

PD base = 0x0000_0001_6000. PD index = 1. PDE address = 0x0000_0001_6000 + 1 \(\times\) 8 = 0x0000_0001_6008. PDE value (example) = 0x0000_0001_7003 (present, PT base = 0x1_7000).

Step 5: Level 1 (PT) Lookup

PT base = 0x0000_0001_7000. PT index = 0. PTE address = 0x0000_0001_7000 + 0 \(\times\) 8 = 0x0000_0001_7000. PTE value (example) = 0x0000_0002_0003 (present, read/write, page frame = 0x2_0000).

Step 6: Physical Address Assembly

PA = page_frame | page_offset = 0x0000_0002_0000 | 0x000 = 0x0000_0002_0000.

Conclusion: IOVA 0x0040_2000_0000 translates to PA 0x0000_0002_0000 via 4 DRAM accesses (4-level page walk miss). The IOTLB caches this translation for subsequent requests.

Solved Problem: Thunderspy Attack Surface Analysis

A ThinkPad X1 Carbon (7th gen) running Windows 10 with BitLocker is left in sleep mode at a hotel (cold boot feasible). An adversary has 5 minutes of physical access with a Thunderspy SPI flash programmer. Analyze the attack surface and identify which Thunderspy vulnerabilities apply. Assume the device has Thunderbolt 3 at SL1 (User security level).

Solution:

Step 1: Identify Applicable Thunderspy Vulnerabilities

At SL1, the user must authorize devices. Applicable vulnerabilities:

  • Vuln 2 (Inadequate firmware verification): Titan Ridge controller firmware can be downgraded

  • Vuln 6 (SPI flash interface deficiency): Direct SPI programming bypasses secure boot

  • Vuln 4 (Downgrade attack): SL1 can be downgraded to SL0 (no security)

Step 2: Attack Sequence

  1. Remove bottom panel screws (30 seconds, standard Torx T5)

  2. Locate Thunderbolt 3 controller (Intel Titan Ridge, near TB3 port)

  3. Attach SPI flash programmer to U69 (8-SOIC flash chip)

  4. Read current firmware: flashrom -p ft2232_spi:type=232H,divisor=4 -r fw.bin

  5. Modify Security Level register to 0x0 (None) and disable boot verification

  6. Write modified firmware: flashrom -p ft2232_spi -w fw_modified.bin

  7. Reassemble (60 seconds). Total time: \(\approx\)3 minutes.

Step 3: DMA Extraction

On next boot with sleep resume, connect Screamer M2 Thunderbolt-to-PCIe adapter. PCILeech DMA reads BitLocker VMK from RAM (held in memory during sleep). VMK can decrypt the drive.

Step 4: Mitigations Analysis

  • Insufficient: SL1, Secure Boot (TPM only), BitLocker without pre-boot auth

  • Sufficient: Thunderbolt 4 SL3, BIOS password + anti-tamper chassis detect, BitLocker with PIN (VMK not in RAM until authenticated), Hibernation (RAM cleared)

Conclusion: The attack succeeds under SL1 with physical access \(<\)5 minutes. Mitigations require Thunderbolt 4 SL3 (disabled PCIe tunneling) plus BitLocker pre-boot PIN.

Solved Problem: VFIO Device Assignment for KVM GPU Passthrough

Set up Nvidia RTX 3090 (0000:01:00.0, [10de:2204]) for KVM passthrough on AMD EPYC 7542 with AMD-Vi. Cover: kernel parameters, IOMMU group check, VFIO binding, QEMU launch.

Solution:

Step 1: Enable AMD IOMMU

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="amd_iommu=on iommu=pt rd.driver.pre=vfio-pci"
update-grub && reboot

Step 2: Identify IOMMU Group

lspci -nn | grep -i nvidia
ls /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices/ | grep "0000:01:00"

Step 3: Bind VFIO-PCI

echo "0000:01:00.0" > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/driver/unbind
echo "10de 2204" > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/new_id

Step 4: QEMU with VFIO

qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -machine q35 -cpu host -m 32G
  -device vfio-pci,host=01:00.0 -drive file=vm.qcow2,if=virtio

Conclusion: AMD-Vi maps only GPU MMIO ranges to the VM DMA space, preventing VM from accessing host memory outside its IOMMU-enforced allocation.

Solved Problem: Design DMA Protection Policy for Multi-PCIe Server

Server devices: (a) NVMe at 0000:02:00.0 (trusted, performance-critical); (b) 10GbE NIC at 0000:03:00.0 (trusted, but untrusted firmware); (c) user PCIe accelerator slot (untrusted). Design IOMMU policy protecting OS while maximizing NVMe.

Solution:

Step 1: Three-Tier DMA Protection Policy

  1. NVMe: IOMMU passthrough for maximum throughput. Acceptable risk: vendor-signed firmware.

  2. 10GbE: Strict IOMMU isolation. NIC DMA only to OS-mapped network buffer pages.

  3. User accelerator: VFIO to dedicated sandbox VM. No host kernel access.

Step 2: Linux Implementation

intel_iommu=on iommu=strict
# NVMe group passthrough override:
echo identity > /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/NVMe_GRP/type
# Bind user accelerator to VFIO:
echo "VENDID DEVID" > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/new_id

Step 3: Performance Analysis

NVMe PCIe Gen 4 x4 peak: 7 GB/s. Strict IOMMU: 5% overhead = 6.65 GB/s. Passthrough: 7 GB/s. Optimize with 2 MB huge pages to reduce IOTLB misses.

Conclusion: Tiered policy: NVMe passthrough, NIC strict IOMMU, untrusted accelerator VM-isolated. IOTLB miss rate is the primary performance factor.

docs.title: 11.10 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: DMA and IOMMU security has been shaped since 2023 by new hardware interface specifications (Thunderbolt 4/USB4, PCIe 6.0), a high-profile AMD vulnerability, steady Linux kernel hardening, ARM SMMU architecture extensions, and the emergence of CXL 3.0 memory pooling with its associated trust-domain challenges.

docs.title: 11.10.1 Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 Security Updates (2023–2024)
docs.text:
Intel Thunderbolt 4 (specification finalised 2020, broad deployment 2023–2024) and USB4 v2.0 (40 Gbps, 2023) share an identical security architecture addressing the Thunderspy weaknesses from 2020:

Table 11.3. Thunderbolt / USB4 security level evolution Feature TB3 TB4 / USB4 Security impact Kernel DMA Protection Optional Mandatory Blocks pre-OS DMA PCIe tunnelling default On (SL1) Off until auth No implicit DMA SPI firmware signing No Yes (ECDSA-P384) Prevents FW downgrade Retimer authentication No Yes (SPDM) Closes interposer attack USB4 Alt Mode isolation N/A Hard-walled DP vs PCIe cannot mix

Note: USB4 v2.0 silicon (Intel Barlow Ridge, 2023; AMD Phoenix, 2023) mandates kernel DMA Protection at the firmware level. The UEFI BIOS must set the PrebootDMAProtection flag in the DMAR table; if not set, Windows 11 22H2+ and Linux kernel 6.4+ will log a warning and fall back to post-initialisation IOMMU activation, leaving a pre-boot DMA window open.

docs.title: 11.10.2 PCIe 6.0 IDE: Integrity and Data Encryption
docs.text:
The PCI-SIG PCIe 6.0 specification (ratified January 2022, silicon arriving 2023–2024 in Intel Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC 9005 series) introduces IDE (Integrity and Data Encryption) as a normative feature:

  • Link IDE: Encrypts TLPs between two directly connected endpoints using AES-256-GCM. Keying material is established via an SPDM 1.3 session over PCIe DOE (Data Object Exchange) mailboxes.

  • Selective IDE: Encrypts TLPs from a specific root-complex port to a downstream device across PCIe switches, without encrypting switch-internal traffic. Essential for confidential computing where a GPU or NVMe must be isolated from the PCIe fabric.

  • IDE Key Refresh: Mandatory key rotation every \(2^{32}\) TLPs (approximately 68 GB at PCIe 6.0 64 GT/s line rate), preventing GCM nonce exhaustion.

  • SPDM binding: After device attestation (CHALLENGE + measurement verification), the IDE session key is derived from the SPDM handshake transcript, cryptographically binding the identity to the encrypted link.

Tip: PCIe 6.0 IDE + SPDM closes the “trusted PCIe device” problem that previously required physical port whitelisting. A compromised NVMe drive that passes its firmware hash measurement during SPDM attestation will not be granted a valid IDE session by a policy-enforcing BMC or root complex driver.

docs.title: 11.10.3 CVE-2023-20593: AMD Zenbleed (Zen 2 XMM Register Disclosure)
docs.text:
CVE-2023-20593 (“Zenbleed”, disclosed July 2023, Tavis Ormandy / Google Project Zero) is a microarchitectural vulnerability in AMD Zen 2 processors (EPYC Rome, Ryzen 3000/4000, Threadripper 3000) that leaks data across security domains via XMM register state:

  • Root cause: The vzeroupper instruction incorrectly retires a speculative micro-op that leaves YMM register state from a different execution context accessible via 128-bit XMM reads.

  • Impact: Any data that transited a YMM register on the affected physical core can be read by an unprivileged process, including AES round-key material from AES-NI operations, RSA private key words from libssl, and hypervisor-context data visible to VMs sharing the core.

  • IOMMU relevance: While Zenbleed is a CPU-side vulnerability, it highlights that hardware-level memory encryption (AMD SME/SEV) does not protect data while it is being processed inside the CPU pipeline. IOMMU protects bus-facing DMA paths; register-level leakage requires microcode mitigations.

  • Mitigation: AMD microcode update AGESA 1.0.0.7b (August 2023) adds a chicken-bit (DE_CFG[9]) that serialises vzeroupper. Linux kernel 6.5 applies the fix automatically via /dev/cpu/*/msr if the microcode is not present.

docs.title: 11.10.4 Linux Kernel DMA-IOMMU Improvements (Kernels 6.1–6.8)
docs.text: Table 11.4. Linux kernel IOMMU improvements 2023–2024 Kernel Feature Security impact 6.1 iommu=forcedac default on x86 Forces 32-bit DMA, reduces IOTLB thrash on legacy devices 6.2 Lazy IOTLB flush batching Reduces DMA-unmap latency; hardened flush ordering 6.3 IOMMU SVA for guest VMs Per-process IOVA (PASID) in KVM passthrough 6.4 USB4 IOMMU auto-enable Blocks all USB4/TB4 DMA until IOMMU domain allocated 6.5 AMD IOMMU SNP enforcement Rejects DMA into SEV-SNP guest RMP-protected pages 6.6 CXL IOMMU root port driver Maps CXL.mem regions into host IOMMU domain 6.7 Intel VT-d DMAR hardening Rejects RMRR entries overlapping kernel text 6.8 iommu_group_replace API Live device migration between IOMMU domains (VFIO)

docs.title: 11.10.5 ARM SMMU v3.2 (2023): Nested Translation and Broadcast TLB Invalidation
docs.text:
ARM released the SMMU v3.2 architecture supplement (IHI0070G, 2023) with two security-relevant additions:

Nested Translation (S1+S2 with HTTU). Prior SMMU v3 implementations required the hypervisor to manage both Stage 1 (IOVA\(\to\)IPA) and Stage 2 (IPA\(\to\)PA) translations through separate page-table walks. SMMU v3.2 adds Hardware Translation Table Update (HTTU) support for nested tables, reducing the hypervisor’s trusted computing base during DMA remapping and closing a TOCTOU window where a compromised guest could modify its S1 table between the SMMU walk and the TLB fill.

Broadcast TLB Invalidation (BTI). In multi-SMMU platforms (common on large ARM servers such as Ampere Altra Max with 128 cores), TLB invalidation broadcasts via TLBI instructions now propagate automatically to all SMMU instances sharing the same ASID namespace, eliminating a class of stale-TLB-entry bugs where a revoked DMA mapping remained valid in a secondary SMMU after unmap.

docs.title: 11.10.6 CXL 3.0 Security: Memory Pooling and Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
CXL (Compute Express Link) 3.0 (specification 2022, silicon 2024 in Intel Granite Rapids and Samsung CXL DRAM modules) introduces multi-level switching and memory pooling, creating new trust-domain challenges:

  • CXL.mem shared pools: Multiple hosts can map overlapping physical address windows in a CXL memory expander. Without hardware enforcement, a misconfigured host IOMMU policy could grant one tenant access to another tenant’s CXL pages.

  • CXL IDE (Integrity and Data Encryption): CXL 3.0 mandates IDE on all CXL.mem transactions, using the same PCIe 6.0 IDE AES-256-GCM session as the PCIe transport layer. Keys are negotiated per-host via SPDM 1.3 sessions.

  • CXL Trust Domains: The CXL 3.0 spec defines a Trusted Execution Environment Security Protocol (TEESP) extension that allows a confidential VM to attest a CXL memory expander and bind the IDE session key to the VM’s attestation report, ensuring only the attested VM can decrypt its CXL memory.

  • Memory interleaving hazard: CXL 3.0 supports host-managed device memory (HDM-D) interleaved across multiple expanders. A failed expander can cause partial plaintext to appear in the non-failed expander if IDE sessions are not synchronised; Linux kernel 6.6+ CXL driver enforces atomic IDE teardown on link failure.

Table 11.5. CXL security evolution across specification versions Feature CXL 1.1 CXL 2.0 CXL 3.0 Link encryption No Optional IDE Mandatory IDE Device attestation No SPDM 1.1 optional SPDM 1.3 mandatory Memory pooling No Single-level Multi-level switch TEE support No No TEESP extension IDE key refresh N/A N/A Per \(2^{32}\) TLPs

docs.title: 11.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. [MCQ] Which mechanism prevents a malicious Thunderbolt PCIe device from reading kernel memory? (A) BitLocker. (B) IOMMU/VT-d DMA remapping. (C) Secure Boot. (D) TPM attestation. Explain why each wrong option does not address the DMA attack vector.

  2. [MCQ] Thunderbolt SL3 (DisplayPort Only) prevents DMA attacks by: (A) Encrypting all traffic with AES-128. (B) Disabling PCIe tunneling entirely. (C) Requiring a cryptographic device certificate. (D) Limiting bandwidth to display data.

  3. [Short Answer] Explain the DMAR ACPI table structure used by Intel VT-d. What is a DRHD entry? What is an RMRR entry and why is it a potential security weakness?

  4. [Short Answer] Describe ARM SMMU v3.2 Stream Table structure. What is a Stream ID? What is a Context Descriptor? How does S1/S2 two-stage translation work in a hypervisor?

  5. [Design] Design an IOMMU policy for a cloud FPGA (Xilinx U250 PCIe x16) accessed by multiple tenant VMs. Each VM should DMA only to its own memory. Specify: (a) IOMMU domain per tenant, (b) IOVA space per domain, (c) revocation on termination.

  6. [Calculation] Intel VT-d IOTLB: 1024 entries, 8-way set-associative (128 sets). NVMe workload: 512 distinct 4 KB pages in round-robin. (a) IOTLB sets indexed? (b) Hit rate for 512 pages in 128 sets? (c) Miss cost: 4 DRAM accesses at 70 ns each. Latency penalty per page at 100% miss rate?

  7. [Coding] Write Python using memprocfs to: (a) list all Windows processes via DMA; (b) find lsass.exe; (c) read first 64 bytes of its VA space at 0x00100000.

  8. [Short Answer] Explain the SPDM GET_MEASUREMENTS command flow for PCIe device attestation. What measurements are collected? How does IDE protect the link post-attestation?

  9. [Design] Design a secure DMA buffer allocation scheme for a 10GbE NIC driver. Requirements: (a) DMA restricted to packet buffers; (b) kernel code/page tables protected; (c) NIC firmware update DMA-isolated. Use iommu_map/unmap APIs.

  10. [Coding] Write a Linux kernel module that: (a) allocates IOMMU domain; (b) maps 4 KB buffer at IOVA 0x1000_0000; (c) attaches PCIe device; (d) verifies mapping; (e) cleans up on unload.

  11. [Research/Compare] Compare Intel VT-d (Ice Lake Xeon), AMD-Vi (EPYC Zen 3), ARM SMMU v3.2 (Ampere Altra), and Apple DART (M2) across: IOTLB size, page table levels, PASID support, ATS support, PCIe generation. Which provides strongest isolation?

  12. [Analysis] System has VT-d strict mode. NIC 0000:03:00.0 and management controller 0000:03:00.3 are in the same IOMMU group. (a) Why must both be in same VM or host? (b) Security risk of assigning only the NIC to VFIO? (c) How does PCIe ACS resolve this? (d) What kernel parameter enables ACS override?

docs.title: Chapter 12: Memory Security
docs.text: Note: Memory security encompasses a wide range of threats and defenses. This chapter covers DRAM vulnerabilities (Rowhammer and variants), memory encryption (AMD SME/SEV, Intel TME/MKTME), memory tagging (ARM MTE), cold boot attacks, ECC memory, and hardware memory safety enforcement. Understanding memory security is critical for cloud isolation, TEE design, and any application handling sensitive cryptographic material.

docs.title: 12.1.1 DRAM Row Activation and Retention
docs.text:
DRAM stores bits as charge in capacitors. Each DRAM cell leaks charge over time: the retention time varies by temperature (\(\approx\)64 ms at 85 \(\deg\)C, longer at lower temperatures). DRAM cells are organized in rows (4–8 KB per row). A row must be periodically refreshed (tREFI = 7.8 ms for DDR4) to prevent bit loss.

When a DRAM row is activated (opened), it disturbs adjacent rows by electromagnetic coupling. Repeated activation of an aggressor row increases the probability of bit flips in victim rows.

docs.title: 12.1.2 Rowhammer (Kim et al. ISCA 2014)
docs.text:
Kim et al. (ISCA 2014) demonstrated that rapidly and repeatedly accessing (hammering) DRAM rows causes bit flips in adjacent rows. Their experimental methodology:

  1. Select two aggressor rows flanking a victim row (double-sided hammering)

  2. Repeatedly read aggressor rows, flushing cache after each access (using CLFLUSH)

  3. After millions of accesses (within one tREFI window), victim row bits flip

/* C: Basic Rowhammer PoC -- double-sided hammer */
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <x86intrin.h>

void rowhammer(uint64_t *aggressor1, uint64_t *aggressor2, int iters) {
    for (int i = 0; i < iters; i++) {
        *aggressor1;  /* Read aggressor row 1 */
        *aggressor2;  /* Read aggressor row 2 */
        _mm_clflush(aggressor1);  /* Evict from cache */
        _mm_clflush(aggressor2);
        _mm_mfence();             /* Serialize memory operations */
    }
}

/* Check victim row for bit flips */
void check_victim(uint64_t *victim, size_t len, uint64_t expected) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len/8; i++) {
        if (victim[i] != expected) {
            printf("FLIP at offset
", i*8, victim[i] ^ expected);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 12.1.3 Rowhammer Attack Variants
docs.text:
• Double-sided hammering: Two aggressor rows flank victim row. Most effective; requires knowing DRAM bank/row mapping. Demonstrated by Kim et al. 2014.

  • One-location hammering: Single aggressor accessed repeatedly. Less effective but requires fewer known addresses.

  • Half-double (Google, 2021): Aggressor rows one row away from victim (not adjacent). Bypasses some TRR implementations that only protect direct neighbors.

  • Blacksmith (Jattke et al. 2021): Non-uniform hammering patterns with varying aggressor counts and access frequencies. Bypasses all known TRR implementations.

  • RowPress (Luo et al. 2023): Extended aggressor row activation time (instead of hammering). Exploits DRAM retention failure at sustained high temperature.

  • TRRespass (Frigo et al. 2020): Many-sided hammering (>2 aggressors) bypasses Target Row Refresh (TRR) by exhausting refresh coverage.

docs.title: 12.1.4 Privilege Escalation via Rowhammer
docs.text:
Google Project Zero demonstrated (2015) privilege escalation via Rowhammer by targeting DRAM containing page table entries (PTEs). Flipping specific bits in a PTE can grant arbitrary memory access to an unprivileged process.

Attack steps: (1) Spray memory with transparent huge pages to achieve predictable DRAM layout; (2) Identify hammer-vulnerable DRAM rows via timing; (3) Hammer adjacent to page table page; (4) Flip bit in PTE to map attacker memory with kernel read/write privileges.

Figure 12.1. Double-sided Rowhammer: aggressor rows N-1 and N+1 are hammered repeatedly. Electromagnetic coupling disturbs victim row N, increasing bit flip probability. With sufficient activations within one tREFI period (7.8 ms for DDR4), bits flip. Figure 12.2. AMD SME memory encryption architecture. The AES-XEX hardware engine in the memory controller transparently encrypts/decrypts data using AES-128-XEX with a physical address tweak. The C-bit in page table entries controls per-page encryption.

docs.title: 12.2.1 DDR4 Target Row Refresh (TRR)
docs.text:
DDR4 includes Target Row Refresh (TRR) as an in-DRAM mitigation. The DRAM internally tracks row activation counts and proactively refreshes rows adjacent to highly-activated rows.

TRRespass (Frigo et al. 2020) demonstrated that TRR can be exhausted by using many-sided hammering (more than 2 aggressor rows). By hammering a large set of rows simultaneously, the attacker exceeds TRR’s limited tracking capacity (\(\approx\)20 rows in typical DDR4 DIMMs).

docs.title: 12.2.2 DDR5 Per-Row Activation Count (PRAC)
docs.text:
DDR5 introduces Per-Row Activation Count (PRAC), a hardware counter per DRAM row that tracks activations with higher precision. The PRAC mechanism:

  1. Each row maintains an activation counter (RFM Alert Refresh Activation Count)

  2. When counter exceeds threshold, DRAM issues an Alert-Back (AB) signal to the controller

  3. Memory controller responds with a Refresh Management Block (RAAMB) command

  4. DRAM refreshes the flagged row and its neighbors before allowing further activations

PRAC provides much stronger rowhammer protection than TRR because it maintains per-row state rather than approximate tracking.

docs.title: 12.2.3 ECC Memory and Rowhammer
docs.text:
ECC (Error-Correcting Code) DRAM uses SECDED (Single Error Correct, Double Error Detect) to detect and correct single-bit errors. A standard DDR4 ECC DIMM uses 72 bits per 64-bit word: 8 extra bits for ECC syndrome.

Rowhammer via ECC: Kim et al. 2014 and subsequent work showed that Rowhammer-induced bit flips can bypass ECC by causing multi-bit flips in the same 8-bit ECC word. SECDED can correct only one bit per 72-bit code word. Two flips in the same ECC word = uncorrectable.

Chipkill ECC (IBM): Each byte of a 64-bit word uses a separate DRAM chip. Single DRAM chip failure (all 8 bits of the chip) = correctable by Chipkill. Provides stronger protection than standard SECDED against chip-level failures, but does not prevent all Rowhammer attacks.

docs.title: 12.3 AMD Memory Encryption: SME, TSME, and SEV
docs.text: AMD Secure Memory Encryption (SME) was introduced with the EPYC "Naples" (Zen 1) processor. It encrypts DRAM content transparently using AES-128-XEX with a physically-derived tweak, providing protection against cold boot attacks and physical memory probing.

docs.title: 12.3.1 AMD SME Architecture
docs.text:
• AES-128-XEX engine: Integrated in the SoC memory controller. XEX (XOR-Encrypt-XOR) mode uses the physical address as a tweak to prevent block relocation attacks.

  • C-bit (bit 47) in PTE: When set, indicates the page is encrypted. Software can choose per-page encryption. C-bit is located at physical address bit 47, reducing the usable physical address space to 47 bits.

  • Single key: All encrypted memory uses the same 128-bit key generated by the AMD Secure Processor (ASP) at boot from a hardware random source. Key is never exported or accessible to software.

  • TSME (Transparent SME): Encrypts all DRAM transparently regardless of C-bit. Enabled via AMD_MSR_SME_EN MSR bit. No software changes required.

docs.title: 12.3.2 AMD SEV (Secure Encrypted Virtualization)
docs.text:
AMD SEV extends SME to virtualization: each VM gets its own AES-128 key, so the hypervisor cannot read VM memory in plaintext.

  • SEV: Per-VM key (up to 509 simultaneous VMs on EPYC). Hypervisor cannot decrypt.

  • SEV-ES (Encrypted State): Also encrypts VMCB (VM save area) CPU register state.

  • SEV-SNP (Secure Nested Paging): Adds reverse map table (RMP) enforcing that each physical page can only be mapped by one VM. Prevents memory remapping attacks.

/* C: Set C-bit in PTE for AMD SME encryption */
#define AMD_SME_CBIT (1UL << 47)

/* In Linux kernel memory mapping: */
pgprot_t encrypt_prot(pgprot_t prot) {
    return pgprot_val(prot) | AMD_SME_CBIT;
}

/* Enable TSME via MSR (firmware/early boot only): */
uint64_t msr_val = rdmsr(MSR_K8_SYSCFG);
msr_val |= (1 << 24);  /* MSR_K8_SYSCFG_MEM_ENCRYPT_EN */
wrmsr(MSR_K8_SYSCFG, msr_val);

docs.title: 12.4 Intel Total Memory Encryption (TME) and MKTME
docs.text:
Intel TME (Total Memory Encryption), introduced in Ice Lake Xeon (Icelake-SP, 10nm), encrypts all DRAM using AES-128-XTS hardware in the memory controller. Single key covers all physical memory.

Intel MKTME (Multi-Key TME, Sapphire Rapids Xeon): up to 65,535 simultaneous keys, each associated with specific physical memory ranges. Hypervisors use MKTME to assign unique keys to each VM, similar to AMD SEV but implemented via Intel Key Management Service (KMS).

/* C: Intel TME configuration (Linux kernel, arch/x86/kernel/tme.c) */
#define MSR_IA32_TME_ACTIVATE     0x982
#define MSR_IA32_TME_CAPABILITY   0x981

/* Read TME capability */
uint64_t cap = rdmsr(MSR_IA32_TME_CAPABILITY);
bool tme_supported = (cap >> 0) & 1;
int max_keys = (cap >> 36) & 0xFFFF;
printf("TME: supported=
", tme_supported, max_keys);

/* Enable TME (done by BIOS/UEFI in production): */
wrmsr(MSR_IA32_TME_ACTIVATE, (1UL << 1) | /* TME enable */
                              (1UL << 3));  /* AES-128-XTS algorithm */

docs.title: 12.5 ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE)
docs.text:
ARM MTE (Memory Tagging Extension), introduced in ARMv8.5-A (2018), provides hardware-enforced memory safety by associating 4-bit color tags with memory allocations and pointers.

  • Each 16-byte aligned granule of memory has a 4-bit tag stored in DRAM spare bits

  • Each pointer has a 4-bit tag in bits [59:56] of the virtual address

  • On memory access, hardware compares pointer tag with granule tag

  • Tag mismatch raises a fault (sync mode) or logs an asynchronous exception

  • Provides heap buffer overflow and use-after-free detection with hardware enforcement

/* C: ARM MTE heap allocation with tag assignment */
#include <arm_acle.h>
#include <sys/mman.h>

/* Allocate tagged memory using mmap with PROT_MTE */
void *alloc_tagged(size_t size) {
    void *ptr = mmap(NULL, size, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_MTE,
                     MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
    if (ptr == MAP_FAILED) return NULL;
    /* Generate random tag and set granule tag */
    void *tagged_ptr = __arm_mte_create_random_tag(ptr, 0);
    __arm_mte_set_tag(tagged_ptr);
    return tagged_ptr;
}

/* Access with wrong tag triggers MTE fault */
void *wrong_tag_ptr = __arm_mte_create_random_tag(ptr, ~0);
*((int*)wrong_tag_ptr) = 0;  /* SIGSEGV or async fault */

docs.title: 12.6 Cold Boot Attacks and TRESOR Defense
docs.text:
DRAM cells retain data for seconds to minutes after power is removed, especially when cooled. At room temperature, data remanence is \(\approx\)5–30 seconds. At liquid nitrogen (\(-196^{\circ}\)C), remanence can extend to hours. This enables cold boot attacks:

  1. Boot target system into OS (BitLocker unlocked, AES keys in RAM)

  2. Spray compressed air upside-down to cool DRAM to \(\approx -50^{\circ}\)C

  3. Power off system, quickly remove DIMMs (must move within \(\approx\)30 seconds)

  4. Insert DIMMs into attacker system, boot from USB key recovery tool

  5. Scan RAM image for AES key schedules (AES-Keyfind tool)

TRESOR Defense (Muller et al. 2011): Store AES key material in x86 debug registers (DR0–DR3, up to 256 bits on 64-bit systems) instead of RAM. Debug registers are not accessible to user space and not included in hibernation images. AES operations are performed by injecting key material from debug registers at encryption time.

docs.title: 12.7 FPGA Memory Security Implementations
docs.text:
On-chip SRAM scrubbing on FPGA: SEU (Single Event Upset) from cosmic rays can flip SRAM bits. Xilinx UltraScale+ SEM (Soft Error Mitigation) IP continuously reads and corrects FPGA configuration SRAM using SECDED ECC built into the configuration frame structure.

External DRAM interface encryption on FPGA: Xilinx HBM2 interface (UltraScale+ HBM FPGAs: xcku5p-HBM) encrypts the HBM2 interface using AES-128-XEX implemented in the HBM interface shell, protecting against bus interception on the HBM stack.

BRAM ECC on Xilinx FPGAs: All 36 Kbit BRAMs in UltraScale+ support SECDED ECC with:

  • 32-bit data + 7-bit syndrome = 39-bit BRAM word with ECC

  • Single-bit error correction, double-bit error detection

  • Soft error inject testability (invert any bit for testing)

docs.title: 12.8 Solutions Comparison
