docs.title: 14.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: TPM 2.0 PCR Extension Chain Calculation

A system boots with PCR[4] = 0x00...00 (32 zero bytes). Three measurements are extended in order: MBR (M1 = SHA256 of MBR image = a1b2...), GRUB stage 2 (M2), Linux kernel (M3). Compute the final PCR[4] value using the recursive formula. What property does this provide?

Solution: PCR extension formula: \(\text{PCR}_{new} = \text{SHA256}(\text{PCR}_{old} \| M_i)\)

\[\begin{align*} \text{PCR}^{(0)} &= \texttt{0x00...00} \quad \text{(32 bytes)} \\ \text{PCR}^{(1)} &= \text{SHA256}(\text{PCR}^{(0)} \| M_1) = \text{SHA256}(\texttt{00..00} \| M_1) \\ \text{PCR}^{(2)} &= \text{SHA256}(\text{PCR}^{(1)} \| M_2) \\ \text{PCR}^{(3)} &= \text{SHA256}(\text{PCR}^{(2)} \| M_3) \end{align*}\]

Security properties:

  1. Order dependency: Swapping \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) produces a different final PCR value. A verifier knows not just which components were measured but in what order.

  2. Collision resistance: An attacker cannot find \(M_1' \neq M_1\) such that the final PCR matches the golden value (SHA-256 preimage resistance).

  3. Binding: The TPM’s signature on the PCR value cryptographically binds the entire boot sequence. Any modification to any stage changes all subsequent PCR values.

Practical computation with tpm2-tools:

# Simulate PCR extension:
tpm2_pcrextend 4:sha256=<hex_M1>
tpm2_pcrextend 4:sha256=<hex_M2>
tpm2_pcrextend 4:sha256=<hex_M3>
tpm2_pcrread sha256:4  # Verify final PCR[4]

Solved Problem: AMD SEV-SNP: Decode Policy Bits

An AMD SEV-SNP guest reports POLICY = 0x00000000000B0000 (hex). Decode the policy fields and determine: (a) Is debug mode allowed? (b) Is SMT permitted? (c) Minimum ABI version?

Solution: AMD SEV-SNP POLICY field (AMD ABI Spec Section 4.3):

POLICY = 0x00000000000B0000
Binary: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000
        0000 0000 0000 1011 0000 0000 0000 0000

Bit mapping:
  [15:8]   ABI_MINOR = 0x00 = 0
  [23:16]  ABI_MAJOR = 0x0B = 11  <- minimum platform firmware SVN
  [24]     SMT  = 0 -- SMT NOT required (can run on single-thread CPU)
  [25]     MIG  = 0 -- migration NOT allowed
  [26]     DBG  = 0 -- DEBUG NOT allowed (no debug decryption)
  [27]     SINGLE_SOCKET = 0 -- multi-socket allowed

(a) Debug mode: Bit[26] = 0 – debug mode is NOT allowed. A platform in debug mode cannot run this guest (POLICY check fails at VMRUN).

(b) SMT: Bit[24] = 0 – SMT is not required. The guest can run on a CPU with SMT disabled.

(c) Minimum ABI: ABI_MAJOR = 11 (0x0B). The platform’s ABI major version must be \(\geq 11\) (SNP firmware v1.11+).

Solved Problem: SPDM Challenge-Auth: Verify Signature

A SPDM CHALLENGE_AUTH response contains: Cert chain SHA384 digest, nonce echo (32 bytes), 0 measurement summary bytes, opaque data (0 bytes), and ECDSA P-384 signature (96 bytes). Describe the complete verification procedure the requester must execute.

Solution: SPDM CHALLENGE_AUTH signature covers (DSP0274 v1.3 Section 11.4):

\[\text{Signature} = \text{ECDSA-P384}\left(\text{Signing\_key},\ \text{SHA384}(\text{A} \| \text{B} \| \text{C})\right)\]

Where:

  • \(A\) = “responder-challenge_auth signing” (context string, 38 bytes)

  • \(B\) = concatenation of all prior SPDM message transcripts (VCA: VERSION + CAPABILITIES + ALGORITHMS + DIGESTS + CERTIFICATE + CHALLENGE)

  • \(C\) = CHALLENGE_AUTH response body (without signature field)

Verification steps:

  1. Certificate chain validation: Parse CERTIFICATE response; verify chain from leaf cert to trusted root CA (manufacturer’s anchor). Check key usage: leaf must have “digital signature” extension.

  2. Nonce echo check: CHALLENGE contained 32-byte requester nonce; verify CHALLENGE_AUTH echoes the same nonce (anti-replay).

  3. Cert digest check: Verify SHA384 of received cert chain matches DIGESTS response.

  4. Transcript hash: Compute SHA384 over concatenated VCA transcript (Steps 1-7 of SPDM session negotiation).

  5. Signature verification: Using leaf certificate ECDSA P-384 public key, verify ECDSA-P384 signature over the transcript hash.

  6. Policy check: Verify leaf certificate attributes: subject name matches device identity, not expired, not revoked (OCSP or CRL check against DMTF certificate authority).

Solved Problem: DICE CDI Forgery Resistance

An attacker compromises a DICE Layer 1 device (bootloader) and attempts to forge a CDI_1 that matches the golden value. (a) What is the computational difficulty? (b) If the attacker knows UDS, can they forge CDI_0? (c) What protocol check prevents the Alias Certificate from being accepted after firmware replacement?

Solution: (a) Forging CDI_1: \(\text{CDI}_1 = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{CDI}_0, H_1)\) where \(H_1 = \text{SHA256}(\text{Layer1\_FW})\).

To forge CDI_1 with a different Layer 1 firmware \(H_1'\), the attacker needs:

\[\text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{CDI}_0, H_1') = \text{CDI}_1\]

This requires finding \(H_1'\) such that HMAC produces the same output – a second preimage of HMAC-SHA256. Assuming HMAC-SHA256 is a PRF, this requires \(2^{256}\) operations (brute-force of 256-bit output). Computationally infeasible.

(b) Forging CDI_0 with known UDS: \(\text{CDI}_0 = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{UDS}, H_0)\).

If the attacker has compromised the Layer 1 and knows UDS, they can compute CDI_0 with any firmware hash (they control \(H_0'\)). They could compute a valid \(\text{CDI}_0' = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{UDS}, H_0')\).

However: UDS is stored in OTP fuses, physically inaccessible from software. A Layer 1 compromise does NOT give software access to the UDS – the hardware enforces this isolation.

(c) Protocol check – Alias Certificate rejection: The verifier checks that the firmware measurement in the Alias Certificate extension matches the Reference Value (known-good firmware hash). A new firmware hash \(H_1' \neq H_1\) is in the certificate and is detected by the verifier. Even if the attacker tries to use an old Alias Certificate (replay), the verifier includes a freshness nonce in the attestation request that must be signed by the current Alias key.

Solved Problem: Intel TDX: Attestation Report Fields

An Intel TDX attestation verifier receives a TD Quote. List and explain 5 specific fields it must validate, and describe what each field proves about the Trust Domain.

Solution: Required TD Quote validation (Intel TDX Attestation Architecture v1.0):

  1. MRTD (TD Measurement Register, 384 bits): SHA-384 of initial TD memory contents at launch. Verifier compares against a reference build hash (from CI/CD build pipeline). Proves: the TD runs the expected, unmodified code image.

  2. RTMR[0-3] (Runtime Measurement Registers, 384 bits each): Software-extended registers capturing UEFI, bootloader, kernel, application measurements. Verifier checks each RTMR against known-good values from the software supply chain. Proves: the complete software stack is unmodified.

  3. REPORTDATA (512 bits): Guest-supplied nonce (64 bytes, typically challenge from verifier + session ID). Verifier checks this matches the nonce it sent. Proves: freshness – the quote was generated on demand for this session, not replayed.

  4. TD Attributes (debug bit): Must be 0 for production deployments. If debug bit is 1, memory is not encrypted with production key. Proves: the TD is not in debug mode (which would allow memory inspection).

  5. Intel PCK Certificate chain: Leaf PCK cert -> Intel PCK CA -> Intel Root CA (offline root). Verifier validates the chain using Intel’s public root certificate. Proves: the attestation key is genuinely bound to Intel SGX/TDX hardware on the specific platform (CPU model, security version identified by CPUSVN in cert).

docs.title: 14.14 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: Hardware attestation has moved from experimental to production-scale deployment between 2022 and 2026. IETF RATS RFC 9334 is now widely implemented, TCG DICE Endorsement Architecture has been standardised, NVIDIA Hopper introduced the first GPU-level confidential computing attestation, SPDM 1.3 governs PCIe device identity, Microsoft Azure Attestation Service v2 targets cloud-scale verification, and Keylime v7 brings IMA-based attestation to large Linux fleets.

docs.title: 14.14.1 IETF RATS Architecture RFC 9334 (2022, Deployed 2023–2024)
docs.text:
IETF RFC 9334 (Remote ATtestation procedureS, March 2022) was ratified over a background of confidential computing deployments; broad ecosystem adoption materialised in 2023–2024:

  • Passport model deployments: FIDO Alliance FIDO2/WebAuthn attestation (900M+ monthly authentications in 2024) implements the RATS Passport model. The authenticator (attester) presents an attestation statement to a FIDO server (relying party) whose verification logic acts as a verifier consuming FIDO Metadata Service endorsements.

  • Background-check model in cloud: All three major cloud providers (AWS Nitro, Azure Confidential VMs, Google Confidential GKE) implement the Background-Check model where a tenant submits evidence (SGX quote, TDX quote, SEV-SNP report) to a verifier service that returns an Attestation Result consumed by the relying-party workload before secret injection.

  • EAT (Entity Attestation Token, RFC 9542): Deployed in Arm SystemReady IR 2.1 certified devices (2024) as the standard claim format for boot-time measurements, replacing vendor-specific TPM quote formats in new platform designs.

Table 14.5. RATS RFC 9334 deployment status by ecosystem (2024) Ecosystem Model Evidence format FIDO2 / WebAuthn Passport CBOR attestation statement Intel TDX cloud Background-check ECDSA-P256 TD Quote AMD SEV-SNP cloud Background-check ECDSA-P384 SNP report AWS Nitro Enclave Passport CBOR-COSE signed document ARM CCA (Realm) Background-check CCA realm token (EAT) IoT (Arm Corstone) Background-check EAT CBOR/COSE

docs.title: 14.14.2 TCG DICE Endorsement Architecture for Devices (2023)
docs.text:
TCG published the DICE Endorsement Architecture for Devices (TCG DICE ENDA, version 1.00, October 2023), extending the DICE CDI derivation chain with a formal endorsement hierarchy:

  • Endorsement Certificate Authority (ECA): The device manufacturer operates an ECA that signs DeviceID endorsement certificates at the factory. Each endorsement certificate binds the DeviceID public key to the hardware serial number and a set of certified hardware capabilities (e.g., FIPS 140-3 TRNG, tamper detection active).

  • Endorsed DICE Chain: The verifier can now distinguish a factory-provisioned DeviceID (endorsed by manufacturer ECA) from a self-signed DeviceID, enabling trust-level differentiation in RATS-compliant verification policies.

  • Alias Certificate Endorsement: For renewable firmware, the Alias Certificate (per-firmware) is also endorsable: the manufacturer signs an expected alias certificate hash into the endorsement, allowing offline pre-validation of known-good firmware releases.

  • Hardware deployments: Google Titan M2 (Pixel 8, 2023), Microsoft Pluton (AMD Ryzen 7040, 2023), and OpenTitan 0.9 all implement TCG DICE ENDA-compatible certificate chains.

docs.title: 14.14.3 NVIDIA Hopper Confidential Computing Attestation (H100 CC, 2023)
docs.text:
NVIDIA H100 (Hopper architecture, TSMC 4 nm) introduced Confidential Computing (CC) mode in 2023, the first GPU-class attestation deployment:

  • Attestation root: Each H100 is factory-provisioned with a GPC (GPU Platform Certificate) signed by NVIDIA’s root CA (ECDSA-P384). The certificate binds the GPU serial number to the RIM (Reference Integrity Manifest) for the on-GPU CC firmware (FWID = SHA-384 of GSP-RM firmware).

  • Local attestation report: The CC firmware generates a RIM Report containing FWID, nonce, driver version, and a hardware-signed digest (HMAC-SHA384 keyed by the GPU’s internal HSM key), accessible via the NVIDIA CC SDK nvml API.

  • Remote attestation: The local RIM Report is sent to NVIDIA’s Hopper Attestation Service (OCSP-style REST API) which verifies the GPC chain and returns a signed Attestation Result (AR) in JWT format, consumable by RATS-based relying parties.

  • Security model: In CC mode, all GDDR6 traffic is encrypted with a session key negotiated with the attestation-verified driver. The CPU host cannot read GPU memory in plaintext, and the GPU firmware hash must match the RIM before the CC session activates.

Note: NVIDIA Hopper CC attestation integrates with Intel TDX (for the host-side Trust Domain) to create end-to-end confidential AI inference: the TDX-attested VM receives an NVIDIA CC attestation report and verifies both the CPU memory encryption (TDX) and the GPU memory encryption (H100 CC) before injecting model weights.

docs.title: 14.14.4 SPDM 1.3 (2023): PCIe and CXL Device Authentication
docs.text:
DMTF DSP0274 SPDM 1.3 (October 2023) adds several features relevant to hardware attestation deployments in data-centre and edge environments:

  • Mutual authentication (MutAuth): Both requester and responder exchange certificates and challenge each other, enabling the device to verify the authenticity of the host management controller before revealing sensitive measurements.

  • Multi-key certificate slots: Up to 8 simultaneous certificate chains per device, supporting separate keys for identity, attestation, and IDE session establishment.

  • Extended measurements: Measurement blocks now support structured data (OID-tagged firmware component hashes, configuration digests, and runtime event logs), aligning SPDM measurements with TCG DICE Alias Certificate extensions.

  • CXL support: CXL 3.0 specifies SPDM 1.3 as the mandatory attestation protocol for TEESP-capable memory expanders.

docs.title: 14.14.5 Microsoft Azure Attestation Service v2 (2024)
docs.text:
Microsoft Azure Attestation (MAA) Service v2 (GA March 2024) is a RATS-compliant Background-Check model verifier operating at cloud scale:

Table 14.6. Azure Attestation Service v2 supported evidence types Evidence type Format Verifier anchor Intel SGX DCAP ECDSA-P256 quote Intel PCK cert chain (PCCS) Intel TDX ECDSA-P256 TD quote Intel PCK cert chain AMD SEV-SNP ECDSA-P384 report AMD ARK/ASK chain (KDS) ARM CCA Realm EAT CBOR/COSE ARM Veraison reference values TPM 2.0 PCR quote (RSA/ECC) Microsoft CA (Pluton / UEFI EK) NVIDIA H100 CC JWT RIM report NVIDIA root CA (OCSP)

MAA v2 returns JSON Web Tokens (JWT) containing the Attestation Result (AR) with claims: x-ms-isolation-tee (TEE type), x-ms-runtime (runtime claims from the attested environment), and cnf (confirmation key binding). The JWT is signed by an MAA service certificate verifiable against Microsoft’s public PKI.

docs.title: 14.14.6 Keylime Remote Attestation v7.x (Linux Foundation, 2024)
docs.text:
Keylime (Linux Foundation, v7.x released 2024) is the leading open-source TPM-based remote attestation framework for Linux fleets:

  • Architecture: Keylime Registrar maintains a database of enrolled devices (EK + AK certificates). Keylime Verifier continuously polls agents (running on each attested host) for fresh TPM quotes covering PCR[10] (IMA log) and compares against allowlists.

  • IMA integration: Linux IMA (Integrity Measurement Architecture) extends PCR[10] with SHA-256 hashes of every executed file, loaded kernel module, and accessed configuration file. Keylime v7 adds policy-as-code allowlists in JSON-LD format, enabling per-workload IMA policies.

  • RATS compliance: Keylime v7 implements IETF RATS Background-Check model: the Keylime Verifier acts as a RATS Verifier; the agent generates EAT evidence; the Verifier produces a signed AR in JWT format consumed by deployment orchestrators (Kubernetes, Ansible).

  • Post-quantum readiness: Keylime 7.2 (2024) adds support for TPM 2.0 ECC-based AKs (ECDSA-P384) as default, replacing the legacy RSA-2048 AK, reducing quote size from 256 B to 96 B signature.

docs.title: 14.15 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between local attestation and remote attestation in Intel TDX. When is each used? What prevents a verifier from being deceived by a replayed quote from a previous session?

  2. Compare AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX attestation from the following perspectives: (a) Root signing key ownership, (b) Certificate retrieval endpoint, (c) Measurement register semantics, (d) VM live migration attestation support.

  3. An ICS (industrial control) device running a PLC firmware needs hardware attestation for OT network admission. Design the attestation system: (a) HRoT hardware selection, (b) measurement strategy (what to measure), (c) attestation protocol for non-IP industrial protocols.

  4. SPDM v1.3 adds secure session establishment (after attestation, encrypted channel). Describe the key exchange mechanism, ciphersuite negotiation, and how attestation evidence is bound to the session key.

  5. The Keylime open-source attestation system uses TPM 2.0 + IMA. Explain how IMA extends PCR[10] for each file executed. If an attacker injects a malicious shared library that is never directly executed, can Keylime detect it?

  6. A manufacturer uses DICE to provision 10 million IoT devices. The DeviceID private key never leaves the chip, but the DeviceID certificate must be stored in the manufacturer’s database. What database design prevents a rogue insider from creating fraudulent DeviceID certificates for non-existent devices?

  7. An SPDM responder (NVMe SSD) returns measurements that include hash of its firmware, configuration, and logical block address mapping table. Explain why the LBA mapping table measurement is security-critical. What attack does it prevent?

  8. Compare EAT (Entity Attestation Token, RFC 9542) in CBOR/COSE format vs JWT format for: (a) implementation complexity on constrained devices, (b) interoperability, (c) transport overhead. Which would you recommend for a BLE-connected IoT sensor?

  9. Veraison is a CCC project providing RATS verifier services. Describe how a new hardware platform (e.g., a custom RISC-V HRoT) integrates with Veraison to enable remote attestation. What pluggable components must be implemented?

  10. An AMD SEV-SNP MEASUREMENT field contains the SHA-384 hash of the initial guest memory. If the hypervisor loads a guest VM from a pre-built image file, how does the pre-launch measurement process work? What guarantee does it provide about the initial guest state?

  11. Design a zero-trust network access (ZTNA) architecture that uses TPM-based attestation for endpoint verification. Specify: (a) enrollment flow (first boot), (b) continuous verification (per-connection), (c) policy decision point integration, (d) response to failed attestation.

  12. IEEE 802.1AR distinguishes IDevID (factory) and LDevID (locally significant). Why can LDevID have a shorter validity period and simpler certificate chain than IDevID? How does the 802.1AR enrollment protocol prevent an attacker from enrolling a stolen IDevID certificate on a different device?

docs.title: Chapter 15: Automotive Hardware Security
docs.text: Note: Automotive cybersecurity became a regulatory requirement in 2022 when UN ECE WP.29 Regulation 155 took effect. Over 100 million vehicles now contain embedded HSMs implementing SHE or EVITA specifications.

docs.title: 15.1 Automotive Threat Landscape
docs.text: Modern vehicles contain 50–150 ECUs and expose attack surfaces across multiple wireless interfaces. The 2015 Jeep Cherokee exploit by Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek exploited a Sprint cellular IP port 6667 QNX D-Bus vulnerability, pivoting to rewrite DPIM CAN firmware – enabling remote brake, throttle, and steering control at highway speed with no physical access. The attack caused a 1.4 million vehicle recall, the first ever for a cybersecurity issue.

docs.title: 15.1.1 Remote Attack Surface
docs.text:
• OBD-II port (SAE J1979): 16-pin DLC connector. CAN pins 6/14. Full UDS (ISO 14229) access. Service 0x27 Security Access, 0x34/0x36 firmware download. No authentication. Aftermarket 4G/BLE dongles create persistent remote access.

  • V2X (DSRC/C-V2X): DSRC IEEE 802.11p at 5.9 GHz. C-V2X 3GPP PC5 sidelink. BSM (PSID 0x20) broadcast at 10 Hz. Pre-2019 deployments lacked certificate validation.

  • Cellular TCU: 4G LTE/5G NR modems in TCUs. Qualcomm MDM9615 CVEs (2014–2016). Cellular often connected to infotainment CAN.

  • Bluetooth: A2DP, HFP, BLE GATT. BlueBorne 2017 (CVE-2017-0781): RCE without pairing.

  • WiFi 802.11ac: WPA2-TKIP downgrade, PMKID, KRACK (CVE-2017-13077). Tesla Model 3 WiFi exploit at Pwn2Own 2019.

  • Key fob/PASE: LF 125 kHz + UHF 315/433/868 MHz. Relay attacks extend to 100 m. Keeloq broken (Courtois 2008).

  • CCC Digital Key/UWB: NFC ISO 14443 + UWB IEEE 802.15.4z for centimeter ranging. Apple CarKey, Android NFC key.

Warning: The OBD-II port provides completely unauthenticated access to all vehicle CAN networks. A rogue 4G-enabled dongle provides persistent remote access to safety systems with no way for the driver to detect the compromise.

docs.title: 15.2 Automotive E/E Architecture
docs.text:
Three E/E architecture generations define automotive security:

  • Distributed ECU (pre-2015): 80–150 dedicated ECUs on separate CAN segments. Gateway ECU (NEC V850, Renesas RH850) routes between segments with no security filtering. Wiring harness 40–60 kg.

  • Domain-based (2015–2025): Domain Controller ECUs. Domains: Powertrain, Chassis/Safety, ADAS, Infotainment, Body, V2X. Central Gateway NXP S32G274A provides CAN-to-Ethernet bridging with firewall rules. Wiring 30–40 kg.

  • Zone-based (2025+): Zone ECUs by physical region. 1000BASE-T1 backbone. Software-Defined Vehicle. VW MEB/SSP, Tesla S/X (2021+), GM Ultium. Wiring target under 20 kg.

docs.title: 15.2.1 AUTOSAR Classic and Adaptive
docs.text:
• Classic CP: OSEK/VDX RTOS. BSW: COM stack (PDUR, CANIF, SecOC), Memory (NvM, FEE), Crypto (CSM, CRYIF, CRY/SHE driver). ASIL-D brakes, steering, airbag.

  • Adaptive AP: POSIX Linux/QNX. ara::com (SOME/IP), ara::crypto API. ADAS, OTA, V2X stack. Supports OCI containers.

Figure 15.1. Domain-based Automotive E/E Architecture. Blue double arrows = 1000BASE-T1 Ethernet. Red dashed = CAN bus 500 kbps. Central Gateway NXP S32G274A enforces SecOC MAC verification and firewall. Domain ECUs use AURIX TC397 SHE+.

docs.title: 15.3 CAN Bus Security
docs.text:
CAN (ISO 11898, Bosch 1986) has no built-in security: no source authentication (any node can forge any arbitration ID), broadcast topology (all nodes receive all frames), plaintext payloads (no encryption), no replay protection, and bus-off DoS via error frame injection.

Table 15.1. CAN Attack Vectors and Countermeasures Attack Mechanism Target Countermeasure Frame injection Forge arb ID Any ECU SecOC AES-CMAC UDS replay Record 0x27 seed/key Security access Freshness counter ISO-TP FC inject Forge flow ctrl Multi-frame sessions Session state machine Bus-off DoS Error frame flood Safety ECUs Error recovery Firmware reflash UDS 0x34/0x36/0x37 All ECUs ECDSA signed firmware DTC erasure UDS 0x14 All ECUs HSM audit log CAN fuzzing Random injection All ECUs CAN firewall rules

docs.title: 15.4 CAN SecOC – Secure Onboard Communication
docs.text: AUTOSAR SecOC (SWS_SecuredOnboardCommunication, R20-11) adds AES-128-CMAC authentication to CAN, LIN, FlexRay, and Automotive Ethernet PDUs without protocol changes.

docs.title: 15.4.1 SecOC MAC Operation
docs.text:
1. MAC input: DataID[15:0] (16-bit PDU identifier) \(\|\) AuthenticPDU \(\|\) FreshnessValue[63:0].

  2. MAC compute: AES-128-CMAC(SecOC_KEY, MAC_input). SecOC_KEY in SHE KEY_n slot.

  3. Truncate: First N bits of 128-bit CMAC (N = 24–64 bits per AUTOSAR config).

  4. Assemble: Secured PDU = AuthPDU \(\|\) TruncFreshness[3:0] \(\|\) TruncMAC.

  5. Receive: Expand truncated freshness using stored counter + accept window, verify MAC.

Table 15.2. SecOC Configuration by CAL Level Tier CAL MAC bits Fresh bits Accept Window Safety-critical (ABS, EPS) CAL 3–4 48–64 8 4 Chassis (TPMS, suspension) CAL 2–3 32 8 8 Powertrain (engine, trans) CAL 2 24 4 16 Body (lights, HVAC, doors) CAL 1 24 4 16

docs.title: 15.5 SHE – Secure Hardware Extension
docs.text:
HIS SHE Specification v1.1 (2009) developed by BMW, Bosch, Continental, Volkswagen. AES-128-only embedded HSM targeting cost-sensitive ECUs where full EVITA HSM is not economically justified.

Table 15.3. SHE Key Slot Architecture (HIS SHE v1.1 + SHE+ extensions) Slot ID Name Purpose Flags 0x00 SECRET_KEY Internal KDF, never exposed Always locked 0x01 MASTER_ECU_KEY Authorize key updates WRITE_PROTECT 0x02 BOOT_MAC_KEY Verify secure boot CMAC BOOT_PROTECT 0x03 BOOT_MAC Stored boot firmware MAC BOOT_PROTECT 0x04 KEY_1 SecOC / user AES-128 Configurable 0x05–0x0E KEY_2 to KEY_11 User AES-128 keys Configurable 0x0F KEY_12 Debug/calibration DEBUGGER_PROTECT 0x10–0x1F (SHE+ extensions) AES-256, ECC, RSA slots Configurable Table 15.4. SHE v1.1 Command Reference Command Operation Key Slot CMD_LOAD_KEY (0x01) Provision via M1/M2/M3 MASTER_ECU_KEY CMD_LOAD_PLAIN_KEY (0x02) Load volatile RAM key None CMD_EXPORT_RAM_KEY (0x03) Export encrypted RAM key MASTER_ECU_KEY CMD_ENC_ECB (0x04) AES-128-ECB encrypt/decrypt KEY_1..KEY_12 CMD_ENC_CBC (0x05) AES-128-CBC encrypt/decrypt KEY_1..KEY_12 CMD_GENERATE_MAC (0x06) AES-128-CMAC compute KEY_1..KEY_12 CMD_VERIFY_MAC (0x07) AES-128-CMAC verify KEY_1..KEY_12 CMD_INIT_RNG (0x0A) Initialize PRNG SECRET_KEY CMD_EXTEND_SEED (0x0B) Mix entropy into PRNG SECRET_KEY CMD_RND (0x0C) Generate 128 random bits PRNG state CMD_GET_STATUS (0x0F) Read 8-bit status register None CMD_GET_ID (0x10) Read 96-bit UID + CMAC MASTER_ECU_KEY CMD_BOOT_FAILURE (0x11) Signal boot verify failure BOOT_MAC_KEY CMD_BOOT_OK (0x12) Signal successful boot verify BOOT_MAC_KEY CMD_CANCEL (0x13) Cancel blocking operation None

docs.title: 15.5.1 CMD_LOAD_KEY Protocol: M1/M2/M3
docs.text: Figure 15.2. SHE CMD_LOAD_KEY Protocol. M1 identifies key slots and ECU UID. M2 is AES-CBC-encrypted new key with monotonic counter preventing replay. M3 authenticates M1+M2 via CMAC proving AuthKey possession. M4+M5 are SHE confirmation messages.

docs.title: 15.7 AURIX TC3xx HSM – Infineon TriCore
docs.text:
• Main CPU: 6x TriCore TC1.8E at 300 MHz (3 lockstep pairs, ASIL-D), 16 MB flash, 6.9 MB SRAM.

  • HSM core: ARM Cortex-M0+ at 200 MHz. Hardware-isolated from TriCore via MPU (8 regions). Inaccessible at any TriCore privilege level.

  • HSM Flash: 256 KB at 0xAF500000. No read/write/execute from TriCore.

  • HSM SRAM: 32 KB with hardware access control.

  • AES engine: AES-128/256 (ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM, CMAC). Throughput 1.28 Gbps AES-128-ECB at 200 MHz.

  • Asymmetric: RSA-2048 (sign 30 ms, verify 1 ms), RSA-4096 (sign 200 ms), ECC P-256 (scalar mul 2 ms), ECC P-384 (scalar mul 5 ms).

  • Hash: SHA-256 at 400 MB/s, SHA-384/SHA-512 at 280 MB/s.

  • TRNG: Ring-oscillator entropy, AIS-31 PTG.2, conditioned via AES-256-CTR-DRBG.

  • SHE+: HIS SHE v1.1 plus AES-256, ECC, RSA, up to 20 key slots.

  • Secure Boot: ECDSA-P256 verification of TriCore firmware before CPU release.

  • IPC: 32 mailbox registers: HSM_HSTx (host to HSM) + HSM_HTSx (HSM to host).

  • Lifecycle: DEVELOPMENT (writable) to PRODUCTION (eFUSE; Flash locked, debug off).

  • ASIC: 28nm FDSOI, STMicro Crolles fab. BGA-416, 27x27 mm. AEC-Q100 Grade 1.

docs.title: 15.8.1 IEEE 1609.2 Certificate Format
docs.text: IEEE 1609.2-2022 SignedData: hashId (SHA-256 or SHA-384), tbsData, signer (certificate or HashedId8), signature (EcdsaP256Signature: r = compressed point 33B, s = 32B). Certificate size: approximately 145–200 bytes COER encoded.

docs.title: 15.8.2 SCMS Architecture
docs.text:
• Root CA: ECDSA-521, offline, 20+ year validity. Thales Luna HSM 7 air-gapped facility. Operated by USDOT-designated CAMP.

  • Enrollment CA (ECA): 5-year Enrollment Certificates (EC) issued at manufacturing. EC proves vehicle legitimacy to PCA.

  • Pseudonym CA (PCA): 1-week Pseudonym Certificates (PC) via butterfly key expansion. Blind issuance: PCA cannot link EC to PC.

  • LA1 + LA2: Independent linkage seed components. LV = PRF(s1, s2, cert_id) embedded in each PC. Both LAs required to de-anonymize.

  • Misbehavior Authority (MA): Investigates reports, requests seeds from LA1+LA2 jointly.

Table 15.7. V2X Hardware Platform Comparison Platform Vendor Radio Crypto Target SAF5100 RoadLink NXP DSRC 802.11p + C-V2X ECDSA-256 HSM OEM TCU CRATON2 Autotalks Dual DSRC+C-V2X ECDSA-256, AES OEM+Aftermarket Cohda MK5 OBU Cohda 802.11p, GPS, CAN IEEE 1609.2 HSM RSU + OBU Cohda MK6 OBU Cohda C-V2X PC5, ETH IEEE 1609.2 HSM OEM OBU SXGA3040 Savari DSRC 5.9 GHz IEEE 1609.2 Road-side unit

docs.title: 15.9 Uptane – OTA Security
docs.text:
Uptane (Linux Foundation Automotive, IEEE/ISTO, production: BMW, GM, Rivian):

  • Director Repository: Signs Targets binding image hashes to ECU serial numbers. Director alone cannot install arbitrary images.

  • Image Repository: Offline-signed (air-gapped HSM) Targets with image hashes. Timestamp: 24-hour expiry. Prevents freeze attacks.

  • Primary ECU: Fetches + verifies both repositories. Distributes to Secondaries.

  • Secondary ECUs: Independent crypto verification. Hardware rollback counter (AURIX SMU, eMMC RPMB).

  • ECU Manifest: Signed firmware inventory report sent to Director periodically.

docs.title: 15.10 ISO/SAE 21434 and UN ECE WP.29 Regulation 155

docs.title: 15.14 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: SHE CMD_LOAD_KEY M1/M2/M3 Calculation

Provision KEY_1 (slot 0x04) into AURIX TC397. MASTER_ECU_KEY = 0x000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F, UID (15 bytes) = 0x01234567890ABCDEF012340000000000, new KEY_1 = 0x404142434445464748494A4B4C4D4E4F, counter = 1, flags = 0x04. Derive K1, construct M1, describe M2 structure, specify M3 input.

Solution: Step 1: KDF Constants (HIS SHE v1.1, Table 1)

CONST_ENC = 01 01 53 48 45 00 80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 B0

CONST_MAC = 01 02 53 48 45 00 80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 B0

Step 2: Derive K1 – Miyaguchi-Preneel Compression

\(K_1 = \text{AES}(\text{AuthKey}, \text{CONST\_ENC}) \oplus \text{CONST\_ENC} \oplus \text{AuthKey}\)

Step 3: Build M1 (16 bytes)

Byte 15 = \((0x04 \ll 4) \mid 0x01 =\) 0x41. M1 = 01 23 45 67 89 0A BC DE F0 12 34 00 00 00 00 41

Step 4: M2 Plaintext (32 bytes)

Word 0 = \((\text{counter} \ll 4) \mid \text{flags} = (1 \ll 4) \mid 4 = \texttt{0x14}\). Bytes 0–3: 00 00 00 14. Bytes 4–19: new key. Bytes 20–31: zero.

Step 5: Encrypt M2 = AES-128-CBC(K1, IV=0, M2plain)

Block 1 input = M2plain[0..15] XOR 0x00..00. Block 2 input = M2plain[16..31] XOR Block1 ciphertext (CBC chaining).

Step 6: M3 = AES-128-CMAC(K2, M1 \(\|\) M2)

48 bytes (3 AES blocks). CMAC output: 16-byte authentication tag proving possession of AuthKey.

Step 7: SHE Verification

SHE re-derives K2, verifies M3 CMAC, re-derives K1, decrypts M2, checks counter (1 > 0), stores KEY_1, returns M4+M5 confirmation.

Solved Problem: CAN SecOC Freshness Counter Design for EPS ECU

Design SecOC freshness for EPS ECU: 100 Hz CAN, 8-byte frame, 6-byte authentic PDU, 2-byte SecOC trailer. Requirements: no cross-ignition replay, tolerate 5 missed messages.

Solution: Step 1: Trailer Space Analysis

Available: 8 - 6 = 2 bytes = 16 bits for SecOC trailer (TruncFreshness + TruncMAC).

Step 2: Full Freshness Counter Structure (64-bit, NvM-persisted)

  • Bits 63..48: Trip counter (16 bits). Incremented at ignition ON. NvM-persisted.

  • Bits 47..40: ECU reset counter (8 bits). Incremented at ECU reset within trip.

  • Bits 39..32: Reserved (8 bits, zero).

  • Bits 31..0: Message counter (32 bits, 100 Hz). Capacity: \(2^{32}/100 \approx 497\) days.

Step 3: Truncation for 16-bit Trailer

TF (Truncated Freshness): 4 bits = bits 3..0 of message counter. TM (Truncated MAC): 12 bits = bits 127..116 of CMAC. Byte 6: TF[3:0] | TM[11:8]. Byte 7: TM[7:0].

Step 4: Accept Window

Window = 8: accepts [N, N+7] mod 16. Tolerates 7 missed messages \(\geq 5\). Satisfied.

Step 5: Cross-Ignition Replay Prevention

NvM persist at ignition OFF. Ignition ON: increment trip bits 63..48, zero bits 31..0, write NvM. Captured frames from trip T have trip counter T. In trip T+1 MAC input includes trip counter T+1, so old MAC fails verification.

Step 6: Security Analysis

12-bit MAC: brute force probability 1/4096 per attempt. At 100 Hz: 100/4096 = 2.4% per second. For CAL-3 (safety-critical EPS): upgrade to CAN FD 12-byte, use 24-bit MAC (3 bytes). Brute force: 100/16777216 = 0.0006% per second. Meets CAL-3 requirement.

Solved Problem: V2X Pseudonym Certificate Pool Sizing

Fleet of 500,000 vehicles: urban 2 hr/day (10 rotations/hr), highway 2 hr/day (1 rotation/hr), 5-day weekday + weekend. Cert size 200 bytes. Calculate certs/vehicle/week, PCA signing rate, storage/vehicle.

Solution: Step 1: Rotations per Vehicle per Week

Urban weekday: \(10 \times 2 \times 5 = 100\). Highway weekday: \(1 \times 2 \times 5 = 10\). Weekend urban (2 days, 2 hr each): \(10 \times 2 \times 2 = 40\). Weekend highway: \(1 \times 2 \times 2 = 4\). Total: \(100 + 10 + 40 + 4 = 154\). With 20% margin: \(\lceil 154 \times 1.2 \rceil = 185\) certs/vehicle/week.

Step 2: PCA Backend Signing Rate

Fleet weekly demand: \(500{,}000 \times 185 = 92.5\text{M}\) certs/week. Average rate: \(92.5\text{M} / 604{,}800 \approx 153\) ECDSA-P256 signs/second. Peak factor 5x (Monday morning): \(153 \times 5 = 765\) signs/second. Thales Luna HSM 7 ECDSA-P256: 10,000 ops/sec. Required: 1 HSM. Deploy 3 for HA.

Step 3: Storage per Vehicle

Certificates: \(185 \times 200 = 37{,}000\) bytes = 36 KB. Private keys (32B each): \(185 \times 32 = 5{,}920\) bytes = 5.8 KB. Metadata: \(185 \times 20 = 3{,}700\) bytes = 3.6 KB. Total: 46.6 KB. Private keys in NXP SE050 (50 KB NVM). Certs + metadata in eMMC RPMB partition.

Solved Problem: TARA Analysis: Rogue OBD-II Dongle Attack

Perform ISO/SAE 21434 Clause 15 TARA for: rogue OBD-II dongle (ESP32+SIM800L+TJA1050, $15 BOM) shipped to fleet manager. Provides bidirectional 4G CAN bus access to attacker C2. Identify assets, STRIDE threats, attack path, damage, risk value, countermeasures.

Solution: Step 1: Asset Identification

Safety: ABS, ESP, EPS, engine management, airbag. Privacy: GPS trip history, driver behavior, VIN. Financial: odometer, insurance telemetry. Operational: fleet routing, maintenance data.

Step 2: STRIDE Threats

  • S: Inject arb ID 0x1A0 (wheel speed cluster), data=0x00x8. ABS deactivates at 100 km/h.

  • T: UDS 0x34/0x36/0x37 ECU reflash if 0x27 seed/key is XOR-based.

  • R: UDS 0x14 ClearDTC erases all DTCs and event data records.

  • I: UDS 0x22 reads VIN (0xF190), odometer (0xF4B1), GPS, key handles.

  • D: Error frame flood drives ABS ECU TEC above 255. Bus-Off state.

  • E: UDS 0x27 brute-force XOR seed/key. Engineering session unlock.

Step 3: Attack Path

C2 \(\to\) 4G \(\to\) ESP32 \(\to\) TJA1050 \(\to\) OBD-II pins 6/14 \(\to\) ID=0x1A0, data=0x00x8 at 100 Hz. ABS sees zero wheel speed. Driver brakes at 100 km/h. Wheels lock. Vehicle crashes.

Step 4: Damage

Severity S3 (ISO/SAE 21434): severe injuries or fatalities. Controllability C3: not controllable by average driver.

Step 5: Feasibility

Elapsed time: \(< 1\) day. Expertise: Advanced. Knowledge: Restricted-to-Public (opendbc). Equipment: ?. Attack potential: HIGH (4/5 EVITA scale).

Step 6: Risk Value

ISO/SAE 21434 5x5 matrix: Impact = 5 (S3), Feasibility = 4 (HIGH). Risk Level = 5 (Unacceptable). CAL requirement = CAL 4.

Step 7: Countermeasures and Residual Risk

C1: CAN SecOC CMAC on all safety PDUs (0x1A0, 0x200). Unsigned frames rejected. Stops injection. C2: OBD-II CAN firewall (NXP S32G): whitelist diagnostic PIDs only. C3: UDS 0x27 via ECDSA HSM challenge-response. Cannot brute-force. C4: CAN IDPS anomaly detection. C5: Physical OBD-II port lock (NFC release). Residual risk after C1+C2+C3: Risk Level 2 (Acceptable).

docs.title: 15.15 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The period 2023–2026 marks the transition from voluntary automotive cybersecurity measures to mandatory regulatory enforcement, with new V2X hardware generations, the Tesla HW4 security architecture, advanced HSM silicon, hardware-enforced OTA security, and AUTOSAR SecOC hardware requirements standardised for zone-based E/E architectures.

docs.title: 15.15.1 ISO/SAE 21434:2021 and UNECE WP.29 R155 Enforcement (2024)
docs.text:
UNECE Regulation 155 (R155) required all new vehicle type approvals in the European Union, Japan, and South Korea to demonstrate a certified Cybersecurity Management System (CSMS) from July 2022. The critical 2024 enforcement milestone extended this requirement to all newly manufactured vehicles (not just new type approvals):

Table 15.10. R155 / ISO 21434 enforcement timeline and hardware implications Date Requirement Hardware impact Jul 2022 New type approvals: CSMS mandatory (EU/JP/KR) HSM mandatory for CAL 3+ ECUs Jul 2024 All new vehicles (EU/JP/KR): CSMS mandatory SHE+ or EVITA in all safety ECUs 2025+ China GB/T 44464 equivalent (draft) Domestic HSM requirements expected 2026 R156 (OTA): signed update mandatory globally RPMB / hardware rollback counter

Note: ISO/SAE 21434:2021 does not mandate specific hardware; it requires that the TARA outcome drives hardware selection. In practice, CAL 3 and CAL 4 items (safety-critical brake, steering, engine management ECUs receiving external inputs) universally require hardware HSMs (SHE+ or EVITA Medium/Full) to achieve the cryptographic protection strength required.

docs.title: 15.15.2 V2X PKI: C-V2X (5G NR-V2X) vs. DSRC Hardware Comparison
docs.text:
The V2X hardware ecosystem bifurcated in 2023–2024 between legacy DSRC (IEEE 802.11p, OBD-deployed) and C-V2X (3GPP Rel-16 NR-V2X PC5) in new OEM deployments:

Table 15.11. C-V2X vs. DSRC hardware security comparison (2024 production) Feature DSRC (802.11p) C-V2X (NR-V2X PC5) Radio 5.9 GHz, 10 MHz channels 5.9 GHz PC5 Rel-16 Hardware NXP SAF5100, Cohda MK5 Qualcomm FSM10055, NXP SAF5400 HSM Integrated ECDSA-P256 Integrated ECDSA-P256 + SEV Pseudonym certs IEEE 1609.2 (COER) IEEE 1609.2 (same format) Latency \(<\)2 ms (no network dep.) 1–4 ms (Uu-free PC5) Certificate issuance latency SCMS offline batch SCMS online (\(<\)100 ms) CNSA 2.0 readiness Requires upgrade to P-384 P-384 in Rel-18 draft

The NXP SAF5400 (C-V2X, 2023) integrates the IEEE 1609.2 certificate management and signing engine into a single SoC with dedicated HSM (Arm Cortex-M7 at 400 MHz), supporting concurrent ECDSA-P256 signing at 5,000 ops/s for dense-traffic 10 Hz BSM broadcast scenarios (\(\approx 500\) simultaneous peer vehicles per intersection).

docs.title: 15.15.3 Tesla Full Self-Driving Computer HW4 (2023) Security Architecture
docs.text:
Tesla Hardware 4 (HW4, introduced in Model S/3/X/Y from late 2022, widely deployed 2023) represents the current state-of-the-art in OEM FSD security:

  • SoC: Samsung 7 nm dual-chip configuration, each with two FSD neural network accelerators (ASIC NPUs), ARM Cortex-A72 application cluster, and an isolated security domain.

  • Secure Boot: Four-stage measured boot (BootROM \(\to\) BL1 \(\to\) TF-A \(\to\) FSD OS) with per-stage ECDSA-P384 signature verification. Boot measurements are extended into an internal PCR-equivalent register and signed with the device’s unique key before any network connection is permitted.

  • Camera pipeline isolation: Camera ISP data paths are routed through SMMU-protected DMA channels; the FSD NPU can only DMA from designated camera buffer regions, preventing cross-sensor data leakage.

  • OTA attestation: Each OTA delta package is verified by an ECDSA-P384 Tesla production key. HW4 adds a monotonic hardware counter (in SEC NVM) that prevents downgrade to a previous signed version even if the attacker presents a valid old signature.

  • Tamper detection: HW4 implements a silicon-level physical tamper detector (differential voltage monitor on SEC domain VDD) that triggers erasure of the device attestation key if VDD deviation exceeds \(\pm\)3% for more than 10 \(\mu\)s.

docs.title: 15.15.4 Automotive HSM: Infineon SHE+ and NXP SE050 Automotive Grade
docs.text:
Two HSM products targeting emerging automotive requirements (post-quantum readiness, EVITA Full performance, and ISO 26262 ASIL-B/D qualification):

Infineon SHE+ v1.2 (2024 firmware, AURIX TC3xx): Adds optional ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204) verification to the existing ECDSA-P384 secure boot chain via an HSM firmware extension, enabling hybrid classical + post-quantum firmware signature verification for vehicles with a 2035 end-of-life target aligned with CNSA 2.0.

NXP SE050 Automotive (AEC-Q100 Grade 2, 2023): Extends the commercial SE050 secure element with:

  • Operating range: \(-40\) to \(+105\) \(^\circ\)C (Grade 2)

  • AEC-Q100 qualification: 1000 h HTOL, 85\(^\circ\)C/85% RH THB

  • I2C interface: 1 MHz Fast-Mode+, fault-tolerant framing for CAN gateway integration

  • Key capacity: 12 ECDSA-P256 key slots, 4 ECC-P384, 3 AES-256

  • Certifications: CC EAL6+ (same as commercial SE050), ISO 26262 ASIL-B for safety-relevant key operations (secure boot signing key management)

docs.title: 15.15.5 OTA Hardware Security: Signed Rollback Protection
docs.text:
UNECE R156 (Software Update Management System, SUMS) requires hardware-enforced rollback prevention as a mandatory feature of OTA update systems from 2024. Hardware rollback counter implementations in production:

Table 15.12. Automotive OTA rollback prevention hardware mechanisms Mechanism Hardware Security property eMMC RPMB (Replay Protected Memory Block) eMMC 5.1 (Micron, Kioxia) 32-bit counter signed by device-unique HMAC key AURIX TC3xx NvM SMU Infineon TriCore SMU 32-bit monotonic NvM counter, HSM-protected eFUSE version counter Multiple MCUs Blow-once per update: irreversible version lock Uptane hardware counter AURIX + eMMC RPMB Dual-source mutual verification

Warning: eFUSE-based version counters are irreversible – each software update permanently blows one fuse bit. For a vehicle with 150 ECUs and 25-year lifetime, a 32-bit eFUSE counter supports at most 32 updates per ECU. Uptane with eMMC RPMB provides equivalent security with unlimited update cycles and is preferred for gateway and infotainment ECUs.

docs.title: 15.15.6 AUTOSAR SecOC Hardware Requirements for Zone E/E Architectures
docs.text:
The AUTOSAR R22-11 SecOC specification (Secure Onboard Communication) has been updated for zone-based E/E architectures (2024 baseline):

  • Ethernet SecOC: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) is now the mandatory link-layer security for 1000BASE-T1 backbone links in zone-based architectures, replacing per-PDU CMAC for backbone traffic. Zone ECUs must include a MACsec-capable Ethernet PHY (NXP TJA1120, 2023).

  • CAN FD SecOC latency: For safety-critical PDUs at 10 ms cycle time, the SecOC CMAC computation must complete within 2 ms. This requires hardware AES-CMAC acceleration; software-only implementations on Cortex-M4 at 120 MHz cannot meet this requirement for 64-bit MAC lengths.

  • Key freshness via HSM: The freshness value provider (FvP) must be backed by a hardware monotonic counter in the HSM, not a software counter, to prevent FvP manipulation by a compromised host CPU.

  • Hardware crypto requirement: AUTOSAR R22-11 formally mandates that AES-CMAC for CAL 3 and CAL 4 PDUs must be computed in an HSM subsystem isolated from the main CPU, citing the SHE+ or EVITA Light specification as the minimum acceptable implementation.

docs.title: 15.16 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Describe the three fundamental security weaknesses of CAN (ISO 11898). For each, provide a specific attack with the exact arbitration ID, injected payload, affected ECU, and resulting vehicle behavior.

  2. SHE mandates AES-128 only. Grover algorithm reduces post-quantum security to 64-bit effective. Assess whether AES-128 SecOC keys are adequate for vehicles in service until 2045 and describe the SHE+ migration path.

  3. Design a complete SecOC configuration table for 20 CAN PDUs across three security tiers (safety 5 ms, chassis 20 ms, body 100 ms). Specify CAN FD payload, authentic PDU size, truncated freshness bits, truncated MAC bits, accept window, and brute-force attack time for each tier.

  4. A factory provisioned 50,000 AURIX TC397 ECUs with the same MASTER_ECU_KEY value. An attacker extracts the key via fault injection. Assess the blast radius and design a remote re-keying procedure using only CMD_LOAD_KEY.

  5. Reconstruct the 2015 Jeep Cherokee attack chain: (a) Sprint cellular IP port 6667, (b) QNX D-Bus IPC escalation, (c) Harman HU firmware update, (d) DPIM CAN firmware rewrite. Identify CVSS v3.1 score for each step.

  6. IEEE 1609.2 uses ECDSA P-256 (64-byte sig). A post-quantum extension proposes ML-DSA-44 (2420-byte sig). Calculate maximum V2X vehicles per km2 broadcasting BSMs at 10 Hz on DSRC 10 MHz channel at 6 Mbps, 50% efficiency. Compare P-256 vs. ML-DSA-44.

  7. Explain the SCMS butterfly key expansion scheme. Show how a single enrollment certificate request produces 20 unique pseudonym keypairs without the PCA learning the vehicle identity.

  8. Uptane requires Director + Image repository dual signatures. Construct a specific attack where Director is fully compromised but Image repository (offline keys) prevents arbitrary firmware installation. Show the verification failure sequence.

  9. Perform TARA for V2X BSM spoofing: attacker broadcasts 50 phantom BSMs claiming braking at 0 km/h on a highway on-ramp. Identify damage scenarios for ADAS cooperative collision avoidance. Propose countermeasures at PHY, MAC, and ADAS application layers.

  10. The AURIX TC397 HSM IPC uses 32 mailbox registers. Identify the TOCTOU vulnerability where TriCore modifies command buffer between HSM reading header and parameters. Describe the parameter snapshotting mitigation.

  11. UN ECE Regulation 155 requires OEMs to report cybersecurity incidents. An OEM discovers a remotely exploitable buffer overflow in 800,000 production vehicles. Write the complete incident response plan from T+0 to T+72h including regulatory notification and patch deployment strategy.

  12. Implement in Python using the cryptography library a SHE CMD_VERIFY_MAC function: given 16-byte key, message (hex string), reference MAC (hex string), and truncation N bytes (1–16), compute AES-128-CMAC and return VERIFICATION_PASSED or VERIFICATION_FAILED. Validate against NIST SP 800-38B test vector 1: key=2B7E151628AED2A6ABF7158809CF4F3C, empty message, expected MAC=BB1D6929E95937287FA37D129B756746.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Post-Quantum Cryptography Hardware
docs.text: Note: NIST finalized four post-quantum standards in August 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), FIPS 206 (FN-DSA). NSA CNSA 2.0 mandates migration to PQC for all National Security Systems by 2033.

docs.title: 16.1 Quantum Threat to Classical Cryptography
docs.text:
Shor’s algorithm (1994) solves integer factorization in polynomial time \(O(n^3)\), breaking RSA-2048 ( 4096 logical qubits needed) and ECDSA P-256 ( 2330 qubits). Grover’s algorithm (1996) provides quadratic speedup, halving symmetric key strength: AES-128 post-quantum = 64 bits, AES-256 post-quantum = 128 bits.

Table 16.1. Quantum Algorithm Impact on Cryptographic Primitives Primitive Classical Security Post-Quantum Action RSA-2048 112 bits Broken (Shor) Replace immediately ECDSA P-256 128 bits Broken (Shor) Replace immediately ECDH P-384 192 bits Broken (Shor) Replace immediately AES-128 128 bits 64 bits (Grover) Upgrade to AES-256 AES-256 256 bits 128 bits (Grover) Acceptable SHA-256 256 bits 128 bits (Grover) Acceptable ML-KEM-768 178 bits 128 bits NIST FIPS 203 approved ML-DSA-44 128 bits 128 bits NIST FIPS 204 approved

docs.title: 16.2 NIST PQC Standards – FIPS 203/204/205/206
docs.text: Table 16.2. NIST PQC Standards (Finalized August 2024) FIPS Algorithm Base Problem Type Key Sizes FIPS 203 ML-KEM (Kyber) Module-LWE KEM 800B/1184B/1568B FIPS 204 ML-DSA (Dilithium) Module-LWE+SIS Signature 1312/1952/2592B FIPS 205 SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) Hash function Signature 32/48/64B sk FIPS 206 FN-DSA (Falcon) NTRU lattice Signature 897B/1793B

docs.title: 16.3 ML-KEM (Kyber) – Module Learning With Errors KEM
docs.text: ML-KEM is based on the hardness of the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem over the polynomial ring \(R = \mathbb{Z}_q[x]/(x^{256}+1)\) with \(q = 3329\).

docs.title: 16.3.1 Parameter Sets
docs.text:
• ML-KEM-512: \(k=2\), \(\eta_1=3\), \(\eta_2=2\). Security level 1 (AES-128 equivalent). Public key 800 bytes, secret key 1632 bytes, ciphertext 768 bytes.

  • ML-KEM-768: \(k=3\), \(\eta_1=2\), \(\eta_2=2\). Security level 3 (AES-192 equivalent). Public key 1184 bytes, secret key 2400 bytes, ciphertext 1088 bytes. CNSA 2.0 recommended.

  • ML-KEM-1024: \(k=4\), \(\eta_1=2\), \(\eta_2=2\). Security level 5 (AES-256 equivalent). Public key 1568 bytes, secret key 3168 bytes, ciphertext 1568 bytes.

docs.title: 16.3.2 Number Theoretic Transform (NTT)
docs.text:
The NTT is the key performance-critical operation in ML-KEM. It transforms polynomial multiplication from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(n \log n)\) using the prime field \(\mathbb{Z}_{3329}\).

NTT butterfly unit computes: \((a, b) = (a + \omega \cdot b \bmod q, \; a - \omega \cdot b \bmod q)\)

where \(\omega\) is a root of unity modulo \(q = 3329\), and modular reduction uses Montgomery or Barrett methods.

Montgomery reduction: given \(t = a \cdot b\), compute \(t \cdot R^{-1} \bmod q\) where \(R = 2^{16}\) for \(q = 3329\). Uses only additions and shifts – no division.

docs.title: 16.3.3 ML-KEM Operations
docs.text:
1. KeyGen: Sample matrix \(A \in R_q^{k \times k}\) from seed \(\rho\). Sample secret \(s\), error \(e\) from centered binomial distribution. Public key \(pk = As+e\).

  2. Encaps: Sample \(r\) from seed. Compute \(c = \text{Enc}(pk, m; r)\). Return ciphertext \(c = (u, v)\) and shared key \(K = H(m)\).

  3. Decaps: Compute \(m' = \text{Dec}(sk, c)\). Re-encapsulate: \(K = H(m')\) if valid, else \(K = H(z \| c)\) (implicit rejection).

Figure 16.1. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) KeyGen, Encaps, and Decaps flow. The NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) over polynomial ring \(\mathbb{Z}_q[x]/(x^{256}+1)\) with \(q=3329\) enables efficient polynomial multiplication. Implicit rejection in Decaps prevents chosen-ciphertext attacks.

docs.title: 16.4 NTT Butterfly Unit Hardware
docs.text: Figure 16.2. NTT Butterfly Unit for ML-KEM. Twiddle factor w multiplied with input b using Montgomery reduction (no division, just shifts and adds). Results a’ = a + wb mod q and b’ = a - wb mod q. Hardware implementation on Artix-7: 1 DSP48E1 + 120 LUTs at 200 MHz.

docs.title: 16.5 ML-DSA (Dilithium) Hardware
docs.text:
ML-DSA (FIPS 204, based on Dilithium) uses Module-LWE and Module-SIS problems with rejection sampling for signature generation.

Table 16.3. ML-DSA Parameter Sets (FIPS 204) Level Variant PK size SK size Sig size Security NIST 2 ML-DSA-44 1,312 B 2,528 B 2,420 B 128 bits NIST 3 ML-DSA-65 1,952 B 4,032 B 3,293 B 192 bits NIST 5 ML-DSA-87 2,592 B 4,896 B 4,595 B 256 bits

docs.title: 16.6 SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) Hardware
docs.text:
SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is stateless hash-based signature scheme using FORS (Forest of Random Subsets) and Hypertree (HT) structure. No lattice mathematics – all operations are hash function calls (SHAKE-256 or SHA-256 variants).

Table 16.4. SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) Variants and Signature Sizes Variant Hash PK Sig size Security SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s SHAKE-256 32 B 7,856 B 128 bits SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f SHAKE-256 32 B 17,088 B 128 bits (fast) SLH-DSA-SHAKE-192s SHAKE-256 48 B 16,224 B 192 bits SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s SHAKE-256 64 B 29,792 B 256 bits SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s SHA-256 32 B 7,856 B 128 bits

Warning: SLH-DSA signatures are very large (7,856–49,856 bytes) compared to ECDSA (64 bytes) or ML-DSA (2,420–4,595 bytes). For bandwidth-constrained applications (V2X BSM at 5.9 GHz, TLS handshake), SLH-DSA is impractical. ML-DSA is preferred for general-purpose signatures; SLH-DSA is recommended only where stateless signatures are required and bandwidth is not a concern (e.g., firmware signing with offline key).

docs.title: 16.7 FN-DSA (Falcon) Hardware Challenges
docs.text:
FN-DSA (FIPS 206, Falcon) uses NTRU lattice with Fast Fourier Sampling (FFS) for compact signatures (897 bytes for Falcon-512, 1793 bytes for Falcon-1024). However, it is hardware-unfriendly:

  • Gaussian sampler: Requires discrete Gaussian sampling over \(\mathbb{Z}\). Hardware implementation requires constant-time floating-point or fixed-point arithmetic to prevent timing side-channels.

  • FFT-based NTRU solver: Uses complex floating-point FFT for key generation. Not suitable for resource-constrained hardware without dedicated FPU.

  • Side-channel vulnerability: Gaussian sampler timing leaks discovered in early Falcon implementations (Guerreau et al. 2022, USENIX Security). Constant-time implementation adds 20–40% overhead.

docs.title: 16.8 Hybrid KEM: X-Wing and ECDH+ML-KEM
docs.text:
Hybrid KEMs combine classical and post-quantum algorithms to maintain security against both classical and quantum adversaries during the transition period:

  • X-Wing: X25519 + ML-KEM-768. IETF draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem. Combined shared secret \(= (\text{X25519\_ss} \| \text{MLKEM768\_ss} \| \text{X25519\_pk} \| \text{MLKEM768\_pk})\). Security: classical OR quantum adversary must break both components.

  • TLS 1.3 Hybrid: ECDH P-256 + ML-KEM-768 via NamedGroup extension. Google Chrome + Cloudflare deployed in 2023 (CECPQ2). BoringSSL, AWS-LC support.

  • Dual-PRF combiner: \(K = \text{PRF}(K_1, K_2)\) where \(K_1\) = classical KEM output, \(K_2\) = PQ KEM output. Provides security if either KEM is secure.

For ML-KEM-768 on UltraScale+, 300 MHz operation with 2,800 LUTs enables 3.5 Mbps keygen – 3.5x faster than Artix-7 due to higher DSP efficiency and lower routing delay.

docs.title: 16.11 Side-Channel Attacks on PQC
docs.text:
PQC algorithms introduce new side-channel attack surfaces:

  • NTT timing leaks: Non-constant-time modular reduction in NTT. Barrett reduction requires a branch or multiply-accumulate that leaks via power trace. Montgomery reduction is branch-free but may still leak via operand-dependent power consumption.

  • ML-DSA rejection sampling: The signing loop repeats if the generated signature fails the norm check (probability  30%). Repeated iterations leak timing information. Mitigation: constant-time norm check + always execute fixed number of iterations.

  • Falcon Gaussian sampler: Table-based discrete Gaussian sampling produces observable power patterns. Guerreau et al. (USENIX Security 2022) demonstrated full key recovery from 1000 power traces.

  • ML-KEM implicit rejection: The implicit rejection path in Decaps must execute the same computations as the accept path to prevent timing oracle. Verified in FIPS 203 specification as a constant-time requirement.

docs.title: 16.12 PQC Software and Hardware Solutions
