docs.title: 16.13 CNSA 2.0 Migration Timeline
docs.text:
NSA CNSA 2.0 (September 2022) mandates:

  • 2025: Begin PQC algorithm evaluation for all NSS systems.

  • 2026: New classified software must support ML-KEM and ML-DSA.

  • 2030: All new NSS systems must exclusively use CNSA 2.0: ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, AES-256, SHA-384.

  • 2033: All NSS systems fully migrated. No RSA/ECDSA/ECDH/DH allowed.

  • 2035: Legacy classical algorithms completely retired from NSS.

docs.title: 16.14 GitHub Resources
docs.text:
Key open-source PQC repositories:

  • pq-crystals/kyber: ML-KEM reference implementation (C). Official NIST submission.

  • pq-crystals/dilithium: ML-DSA reference implementation (C, with AVX2 optimizations).

  • sphincs/sphincs-plus: SLH-DSA reference (C).

  • PQClean/PQClean: Unified clean-room C implementations of all NIST PQC algorithms.

  • open-quantum-safe/liboqs: Aggregated library with OpenSSL provider, TLS integration.

  • kyber-py: Pure Python ML-KEM implementation for testing and prototyping.

  • NIST-PQC: Official NIST post-quantum standardization repository with KAT vectors.

docs.title: 16.15 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: ML-KEM NTT Computation for Small Example

Perform one NTT butterfly computation for ML-KEM with q=3329: inputs a=1000, b=2000, twiddle factor w=17. Compute a’ = (a + w*b) mod q and b’ = (a - w*b) mod q using Montgomery reduction with R=2^16. Solution: Step 1: Direct Computation (for verification)

w*b = 17 * 2000 = 34000.

w*b mod q = 34000 mod 3329 = 34000 - 10*3329 = 34000 - 33290 = 710.

a’ = (a + w*b mod q) mod q = (1000 + 710) mod 3329 = 1710. (No reduction needed since 1710 < 3329.)

b’ = (a - w*b mod q) mod q = (1000 - 710) mod 3329 = 290.

Step 2: Montgomery Reduction for w*b=34000, R=2^16=65536

Montgomery form: T = w*b = 34000 (not yet in Montgomery domain for this example).

For proper Montgomery multiplication, inputs must be in Montgomery domain: a’ = a*R mod q.

Precomputed: q^(-1) mod R: need 3329^(-1) mod 65536. Extended Euclidean: q^(-1) mod R = 3329^(-1) mod 65536 = 14017 (precomputed).

Montgomery reduction of T=34000: m = T * q^(-1) mod R = 34000 * 14017 mod 65536. 34000 * 14017 = 476,578,000. 476578000 mod 65536 = 476578000 - 7272*65536 = 476578000 - 476672 = ... = 16,352 mod 65536. T’ = (T + m*q) / R = (34000 + 16352*3329) / 65536 = (34000 + 54,448,608) / 65536 = 54,482,608 / 65536 = 831.3... Take floor: 831. Since 831 < q=3329, result is 831 in Montgomery domain.

Step 3: Correctness Verification

Direct method gives w*b mod q = 710. Montgomery method gives 831. These differ because Montgomery output is in Montgomery domain (scaled by R). To get 710: 831 = 710 * R mod q needs verification: 710 * 65536 mod 3329 = 46,530,560 mod 3329 = 831. Confirmed correct.

Step 4: Hardware Implementation

On FPGA Artix-7 using DSP48E1: the multiplication T = w*b uses 1 DSP (2 clock cycles pipeline). The Montgomery reduction uses adders and right shift (no division). Total butterfly: 3 clock cycles at 200 MHz = 15 ns per butterfly. For 256-point NTT: 256/2 * log2(256) = 128 * 8 = 1024 butterflies = 15.36 microseconds per polynomial NTT.

Solved Problem: CNSA 2.0 Migration Timeline for RSA-2048 System

A financial institution runs RSA-2048 TLS and ECDH P-256 at 50,000 handshakes/second. Design the complete PQC migration timeline per CNSA 2.0. Solution: Step 1: Algorithm Selection

TLS KEM: Replace ECDH P-256 with X-Wing (X25519+ML-KEM-768) hybrid during transition; final state ML-KEM-768 only. Code signing: RSA-2048-PSS replaced with ML-DSA-65 (NIST Level 3). CA hierarchy: Root CA uses ML-DSA-87; Intermediate ML-DSA-65; Leaf ML-DSA-44.

Step 2: Performance Assessment

ML-KEM-768 KeyGen: 12,000 ops/sec per core (faster than ECDH P-256: 10,000 ops/sec). ML-DSA-44 verify: 8,000 ops/sec (2x slower than ECDSA P-256 at 15,000 ops/sec). Certificate size increase: RSA-2048 chain  1 KB, ML-DSA-65 chain  3–4 KB. Additional bandwidth at 50,000 TLS/s: 50,000 x 3000 bytes = 150 MB/s (manageable).

Step 3: Migration Phases

2025: Cryptographic agility – add ML-KEM+ML-DSA support alongside classical algorithms. 2026: Enable hybrid TLS (X-Wing). Dual-sign certificates (RSA-2048 + ML-DSA-65). 2028: 80% internal systems migrated to PQC-only. 2030–2033: Remove all classical algorithms. PQC-only per CNSA 2.0 mandate.

Step 4: Hardware Procurement

HSM upgrade: Thales Luna Network HSM 7 with PQC firmware 7.8+ (ML-KEM/ML-DSA). Load balancers: Intel Sapphire Rapids AVX-IFMA for ML-DSA acceleration. PKI: EJBCA 8.x or HashiCorp Vault 1.15+ for ML-DSA certificate issuance.

Solved Problem: FPGA Resource Estimation for ML-DSA-44 Signer

Estimate Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A200T resources for ML-DSA-44 signature generation at 1000 sign/sec target. Show component breakdown. Solution: Step 1: Component Resource Estimates

NTT butterfly (128 parallel units): 128 DSP48E1 + 15,360 LUTs. SHAKE-256 core: 4,500 LUTs, 3,200 FFs, 0 DSPs. Matrix A generation (SHAKE-128): 3,200 LUTs, 2,100 FFs. Rejection sampling control: 500 LUTs, 400 FFs. Polynomial memory (4 polys, 256*12-bit each): 3 BRAMs.

Step 2: Total Resources

LUTs: 15,360 + 4,500 + 3,200 + 500 + 1,000 = 24,560 (20.5% of 134,600 on XC7A200T). FFs:  18,000 (14.9%). BRAMs: 8 (2.2%). DSPs: 128 (17.3%). Clock: 150 MHz.

Step 3: Throughput

Sign latency:  8 NTT invocations x 256 cycles/NTT = 2048 cycles + rejection =  5000 cycles = 33 microseconds at 150 MHz. Throughput: 30,000 sign/sec peak (exceeds 1000/sec target by 30x). Can reduce resources by 5x to just meet target.

Solved Problem: Hybrid KEM Security Level Analysis: X-Wing

Analyze X-Wing (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) security against (a) classical adversary with \(2^{128}\) ops budget, (b) quantum adversary with Shor quantum computer. Solution: Step 1: X-Wing Construction

X-Wing shared key: \(K = H(\mathit{ss}_{X25519} \| \mathit{ss}_{MLKEM768} \| \mathit{ek}_{X25519} \| \mathit{ek}_{MLKEM768})\).

Step 2: Classical Adversary

Must break BOTH X25519 (128-bit classical) AND ML-KEM-768 (178-bit classical). Classical security: min(128, 178) = 128 bits. With \(2^{128}\) budget: exactly at X25519 security limit. In practice, X25519 has >128 bits with concrete security constant. X-Wing provides 128-bit classical security.

Step 3: Quantum Adversary (Shor)

Shor breaks X25519 in polynomial time. But X-Wing uses dual-PRF combiner: K is secure if EITHER input is secure. ML-KEM-768 post-quantum security = 128 bits (MLWE hardness, Grover provides no speedup). So K remains 128-bit PQ secure even with X25519 broken.

Step 4: Conclusion

X-Wing achieves 128-bit security against both classical and quantum adversaries (NIST Level 1 in both settings). For CNSA 2.0 compliance (Level 3 PQ required), use ML-KEM-1024 or ML-KEM-1024 + X25519 hybrid.

docs.title: 16.16 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The post-quantum cryptography landscape was transformed in August 2024 with the NIST finalisation of FIPS 203/204/205/206. Deployment accelerated immediately: Apple PQ3, Signal PQXDH, WhatsApp, and Google Chrome all shipped ML-KEM-based hybrid protocols within months. NSA CNSA 2.0 updated its implementation guidance, a new hybrid KEM (X-Wing) was standardised as an IETF draft, Falcon hardware optimisations advanced, and NIST announced additional PQC candidates (BIKE, HQC) for a supplementary standard track.

docs.title: 16.16.1 FIPS 203/204/205/206 Finalised August 2024: Deployment Status
docs.text:
NIST finalised the four post-quantum standards simultaneously on 13 August 2024:

Table 16.8. NIST PQC standards finalised August 2024 – deployment status (2025) FIPS Algorithm Status Early deployments 203 ML-KEM (Kyber) Final; widely deployed Chrome, iMessage PQ3, Signal, AWS-LC, BoringSSL 204 ML-DSA (Dilithium) Final; deployment accelerating Thales Luna HSM FW, IBM Z16 HW, HashiCorp Vault 205 SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) Final; niche adoption Code signing HSMs, air-gapped root CA ceremonies 206 FN-DSA (Falcon) Final; implementation caution TPM vendors (side-channel concerns delaying)

Note: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) dominates early adoption because KEM replacement is operationally simpler than signature replacement – the KEM is used in TLS key_share extensions and does not require changes to certificate infrastructure. Signature replacement (FIPS 204) requires issuing new CA hierarchies and updating all relying-party certificate validation logic.

docs.title: 16.16.2 CNSA 2.0 Implementation: NSA Guidance Updates (2024–2025)
docs.text:
NSA updated CNSA 2.0 implementation guidance (CNSSP 15, revised 2024) to address practical deployment questions:

  • Hybrid mode policy: For systems with \(> 10\)-year security lifetime, hybrid algorithms (classical + PQ) are now required during the transition period, not merely recommended. A TLS 1.3 server using only ML-KEM-768 (dropping X25519) is non-compliant until “Cryptographic Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” (HNDL) risk is formally accepted.

  • Key size mandates: ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 are the mandatory algorithm variants for all classified data with SECRET-level or higher classification from January 2026. ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 remain acceptable for SENSITIVE compartmented until 2030.

  • HSM upgrade requirement: All NSS-connected HSMs must support FIPS 203/204 by 2026. Thales Luna 7 (FW 7.8+), Entrust nShield 5 (FW 12.80+), and IBM CEX8S (CE8.x) have qualified firmware updates.

  • Quantum-resistant VPN: IPsec IKEv2 for NSS VPNs must add ML-KEM-1024 in the KE transform by 2026; IKEv2 RFC 9370 (“Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2”) provides the protocol mechanism.

docs.title: 16.16.3 X-Wing Hybrid KEM RFC Draft (2024): Hardware Implementation
docs.text:
The IETF CFRG draft draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem (X-Wing, 2024) specifies a single-pass hybrid KEM combining X25519 and ML-KEM-768 with a clean security proof:

\[K = \mathrm{SHA3\text{-}256}\!\left( \mathit{ss}_{X25519} \,\|\, \mathit{ss}_{\mathrm{MLKEM768}} \,\|\, \mathit{ek}_{X25519} \,\|\, \mathit{ek}_{\mathrm{MLKEM768}} \right)\]

Hardware implementation considerations:

  • Area: An Artix-7 XC7A100T implementation of X-Wing (X25519 ECC scalar multiplier + ML-KEM-768 NTT + SHA3-256 core) requires approximately 18,400 LUTs, 12,000 FFs, 12 BRAMs, 18 DSPs at 150 MHz, yielding 320 encapsulations/s.

  • FPGA vs. SE trade-off: On a discrete secure element (NXP SE051W, 40 nm), X-Wing encapsulation takes \(\approx\)120 ms (X25519: 40 ms + ML-KEM-768: 80 ms), limited by I2C bandwidth. A custom ASIC at 28 nm achieves \(<\)1 ms per X-Wing operation.

  • Chrome deployment: Google Chrome 124 (April 2024) enabled ML-KEM-768 in TLS 1.3 by default for all users, using the X-Wing combiner via BoringSSL. This is the largest single PQC deployment in history (\(>\)3 billion active Chrome users).

docs.title: 16.16.4 Falcon/FN-DSA FPGA Optimisations (2024): Masked Gaussian Sampler
docs.text:
FN-DSA (FIPS 206, Falcon) hardware research produced significant advances in 2024 addressing the primary implementation obstacle – constant-time discrete Gaussian sampling:

  • Masked Gaussian sampler (Azouaoui et al., CHES 2024): A 2-share Boolean masked Gaussian sampler for Falcon-512 on FPGA achieves constant-time execution with \(< 4\)% leakage at \(10^6\) power traces, compared to \(>99\)% leakage in the reference implementation. Resource cost: \(2.3\times\) LUT overhead vs. unmasked (\(\approx\)8,000 additional LUTs on Artix-7).

  • NTT-free Falcon variant: A “NTT-free” Falcon implementation (Plantard et al., 2024) replaces floating-point FFT with a fixed-point 4 096-point NTT over a “Falcon-friendly” modulus, enabling full FPGA implementation without a floating-point unit (saves 40% area on Artix-7).

  • Side-channel hardening: The official Falcon reference code v1.1 (2024) adds platform-specific constant-time branches (fpr_rint() using volatile barriers on GCC/Clang) mitigating the Guerreau 2022 USENIX timing attack on x86 and ARM.

docs.title: 16.16.5 Apple PQ3 (ML-KEM-768) and Signal PQXDH (2024)
docs.text:
Two landmark consumer PQC deployments shipped in 2024:

Apple iMessage PQ3 (March 2024): Apple introduced “PQ3” protocol for iMessage, using ML-KEM-768 for post-quantum forward secrecy:

  • Architecture: PQ3 adds a periodic ML-KEM-768 ratchet to the existing Signal-like Double Ratchet. A new PQ public key is uploaded to Apple’s IDS servers every 50 messages.

  • Hardware: On Apple A17 Pro and M-series chips, the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP) performs ML-KEM-768 key generation. The A17 Pro NTT throughput is \(\approx 450{,}000\) KeyGens/s using ARM Neoverse-class SIMD.

  • Security level: Apple claims “Level 3” PQ security, defined as protection against attackers with both a quantum computer and compromised server-side key material.

Signal PQXDH and WhatsApp PQ Rollout (2024): Signal Protocol PQXDH (Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman, published September 2023, deployed to all Signal users by mid-2024) uses ML-KEM-1024 for the initial key agreement, combined with X25519 in a hybrid construction. WhatsApp followed with its own ML-KEM-768 deployment to 2 billion+ users in Q3 2024, the largest single-day PQC rollout in history.

docs.title: 16.16.6 BIKE and HQC as NIST Additional Candidates (2024–2025)
docs.text:
Following the August 2024 final standards, NIST announced a second PQC standardisation track targeting code-based KEM diversity (to complement lattice-based ML-KEM):

Table 16.9. NIST additional PQC KEM candidates (2024–2025 round) Algorithm Type Hard problem Key size (L3) BIKE Code-based KEM Quasi-cyclic QC-MDPC PK: 1,541 B; CT: 1,573 B HQC Code-based KEM Hamming quasi-cyclic PK: 3,083 B; CT: 4,481 B

Tip: BIKE and HQC provide algorithmic diversity in case lattice assumptions are weakened by future mathematical advances. Both require substantially larger key and ciphertext sizes than ML-KEM, making them unsuitable for constrained IoT devices. Their primary deployment target is high-assurance systems where diversity of underlying mathematical assumptions outweighs size constraints, such as government certificate authorities and long-lived HSM key hierarchies.

docs.title: 16.17 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Shor algorithm requires approximately 4096 logical qubits to break RSA-2048. Given that current quantum computers (IBM Osprey, Google Sycamore) have 433 and 70 physical qubits respectively with high error rates, estimate when RSA-2048 becomes practically vulnerable assuming: (a) exponential qubit scaling at 2x per 18 months, (b) 1000:1 physical-to-logical qubit ratio for error correction.

  2. ML-KEM-768 uses polynomial ring \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[x]/(x^{256}+1)\) with \(q=3329\). Explain why \(q=3329\) was chosen (prime, specific NTT-friendly properties), and describe the impact of choosing a larger \(q\) on: security level, ciphertext size, and NTT butterfly count.

  3. Implement a Python function that performs one full 256-point NTT over \(\mathbb{Z}_{3329}\) on a polynomial (list of 256 integers). Use the Cooley-Tukey iterative NTT algorithm with bit-reversal permutation. Verify your implementation using the pqclean Kyber reference test vectors.

  4. Compare ML-DSA-65 and SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f for TLS 1.3 server certificate signing in a scenario where: the server signs 10,000 certificates/day, certificate chain must fit in one TLS record (16 KB), and the offline signing key must be quantum-secure even if the HSM is physically stolen. Which algorithm is preferred and why?

  5. The FN-DSA (Falcon) Gaussian sampler has been shown vulnerable to timing side-channels (Guerreau et al. 2022). Describe the specific information leaked (polynomial component distribution), the attack methodology (power analysis + statistical distinguisher), and the constant-time countermeasure implemented in the official Falcon reference code.

  6. Design a hybrid TLS 1.3 extension for X-Wing (X25519 + ML-KEM-768). Specify the IANA TLS NamedGroup value, the ClientHello key_share extension format (total byte count), the ServerHello response format, and the shared secret derivation procedure using HKDF. Calculate the total handshake overhead increase vs. ECDH P-256 only.

  7. An IoT device uses an Artix-7 XC7A25T (smallest Artix-7, 14,600 LUTs, 65 BRAMs, 45 DSPs) to implement firmware signature verification. Can ML-DSA-44 signature verification fit within these resources? Show resource breakdown and identify the bottleneck. If not, what is the minimum ML-DSA variant that fits?

  8. Google deployed CECPQ2 (X25519 + HRSS-SXY, a NTRU-based KEM) in Chrome 79+ for TLS 1.3 in 2019. With FIPS 203 now standardized, evaluate the transition from CECPQ2 to X-Wing (X25519+ML-KEM-768). What are the protocol, performance, and security differences?

  9. SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signs a firmware image at 7,856-byte signature size vs. ECDSA P-256 at 64 bytes. For an IoT OTA firmware update over LoRaWAN (250 bytes/packet, DR0 = 250 bps), calculate the additional transmission time for the signature. Is SLH-DSA practical for LoRaWAN firmware updates?

  10. The IBM Z16 (announced 2022) includes hardware acceleration for ML-DSA (Dilithium). Describe the likely hardware acceleration mechanism (NTT co-processor, dedicated datapath) and estimate the throughput improvement over pure software (IBM z15) given that Z16 is reported to handle 300 billion inference operations/day on its on-chip neural inference engine.

  11. Design a PQC key ceremony procedure for generating an ML-DSA-87 root CA signing key. Specify: number of custodians (M-of-N), HSM hardware selection (air-gapped Thales Luna), ceremony room requirements, video recording protocol, audit log format, and destruction procedure for the ceremony materials.

  12. Analyze the CNSA 2.0 timeline for a medical device manufacturer whose implantable cardiac monitors have a 10-year service life. Devices are shipped in 2026. Security updates require FDA 510(k) clearance (18-month process). Identify conflicts between CNSA 2.0 requirements and FDA regulatory timelines, and propose a compliant migration strategy.

docs.title: Chapter 17: JTAG and Debug Interface Security
docs.text: Note: JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) was designed in 1985 for PCB-level manufacturing test and has become the primary debug interface for embedded systems. It also represents one of the highest-value hardware attack vectors: a single 4-wire JTAG connection can provide complete memory dump, live debugging, and firmware replacement capabilities on any unprotected device.

docs.title: 17.1 JTAG Architecture – IEEE 1149.1
docs.text:
JTAG (Joint Test Action Group, IEEE Std 1149.1-2013) defines the Test Access Port (TAP) interface for boundary scan and debug. The four mandatory signals are:

  • TCK (Test Clock): Serial clock, typically 1–40 MHz. Data sampled on rising edge, shifted on falling edge (TDI) or rising edge (TDO), mode changes on rising edge (TMS).

  • TMS (Test Mode Select): Controls TAP state machine transitions. Sampled on rising edge of TCK.

  • TDI (Test Data In): Serial data input to the selected register (IR or DR).

  • TDO (Test Data Out): Serial data output from the selected register. High-impedance when not shifting.

  • TRST# (Test Reset, optional): Asynchronous reset of TAP state machine to Test-Logic-Reset state. Equivalent to holding TMS=1 for 5+ TCK cycles.

docs.title: 17.2 TAP State Machine
docs.text:
The JTAG TAP controller is a 16-state Mealy machine. TMS input on rising TCK edge drives transitions. All states are deterministically reachable from any state.

Key states:

  • Test-Logic-Reset (TLR): Entry state. All registers reset. TMS=1 for 5 TCK cycles from any state reaches TLR.

  • Run-Test/Idle (RTI): Idle loop. TMS=0 stays in RTI. Used for execution delay in some architectures.

  • Select-DR-Scan: Branch to Capture-DR (TMS=0) or Select-IR-Scan (TMS=1).

  • Capture-DR: Load parallel input into selected Data Register on rising TCK.

  • Shift-DR: Shift data through selected DR. TDI shifted in MSB-first, TDO shifts out.

  • Update-DR: Latch shifted DR value into parallel output register on falling TCK.

  • Capture-IR: Load IR with fixed test pattern (typically ...01). Allows IR length detection.

  • Shift-IR: Shift new instruction into IR. Last bit clocked while exiting at Exit1-IR.

  • Update-IR: Latch new IR value. Instruction takes effect.

TMS sequences for common operations:

  • Reset: TMS = 1 for 5+ TCK cycles from any state.

  • TLR to Shift-IR: TMS = 0,1,1,0,0 (5 TCK cycles).

  • TLR to Shift-DR: TMS = 0,1,0,0 (4 TCK cycles).

  • Shift-DR to RTI: TMS = 1,1,0 (3 TCK cycles via Exit1-DR, Update-DR).

Figure 17.1. JTAG TAP State Machine (IEEE 1149.1, 16 states). Green = Test-Logic-Reset (entry state). Labels = TMS value driving transition on rising TCK edge. TMS=1 for 5+ cycles returns to TLR from any state.

docs.title: 17.3 JTAG Instructions and Device Chaining
docs.text:
Mandatory JTAG Instructions (IEEE 1149.1):

  • BYPASS (all 1s): Minimum 1-bit shift register in DR. Allows bypassing a device in a chain.

  • EXTEST: Enables boundary scan for external testing. Drives pins from BSR (Boundary Scan Register).

  • SAMPLE/PRELOAD: Sample current pin values into BSR (SAMPLE) or preload output data (PRELOAD).

  • IDCODE: Selects 32-bit Device Identification Register (DR). Format: [31:28]=Version, [27:12]=Part number, [11:1]=Manufacturer, [0]=1.

  • USERCODE: Selects 32-bit user-defined code (for FPGA bitstream identification).

  • CLAMP: Drives all pins from BSR while BYPASS DR is selected.

Device Chain Enumeration: In a JTAG chain, TDO of device N connects to TDI of device N+1. To enumerate:

  1. Force TLR, load all BYPASS (shift 1s until stable). Count devices = latency of first 1 to appear on TDO.

  2. Load IDCODE instruction. Shift out 32 bits per device. Parse manufacturer/part/version.

  3. Load BYPASS again, probe IR length by detecting the mandatory 01 pattern in Capture-IR.

docs.title: 17.4 ARM CoreSight Debug Architecture
docs.text:
ARM CoreSight is the standard debug architecture for ARM Cortex-A/R/M processors:

  • DAP (Debug Access Port): Connects external debugger (JTAG/SWD) to internal debug infrastructure. Contains DP (Debug Port) and one or more APs (Access Ports).

  • AHB-AP: AHB (Advanced High-speed Bus) Access Port. Provides memory-mapped access to AHB bus. Used to read/write RAM, flash, and peripherals.

  • APB-AP: APB (Advanced Peripheral Bus) Access Port. Accesses CoreSight debug components (ETM, ITM, CTI).

  • AXI-AP: AXI bus Access Port for high-performance debug access on Cortex-A.

  • MEM-AP: Generic memory-mapped Access Port. Provides 32-bit CSW (Control/Status Word), TAR (Transfer Address Register), DRW (Data Read/Write) interface.

  • ETM (Embedded Trace Macrocell): Instruction trace output over 1–4 bit trace port or SWO (Single Wire Output).

  • ITM (Instrumentation Trace Macrocell): Software-triggered trace via CMSIS ITM_SendChar() etc.

  • CTI (Cross-Trigger Interface): Connects trigger signals between cores and trace. Enables multi-core halt synchronization.

docs.title: 17.5 ARM Serial Wire Debug (SWD)
docs.text:
SWD (Serial Wire Debug, ARM IHI0031) is a 2-wire alternative to JTAG defined for ARM Cortex processors. SWJ-DP (Serial Wire / JTAG Debug Port) supports both protocols on the same pins with a switching sequence.

SWD Signals:

  • SWDIO (Serial Wire Data I/O): Bidirectional data line. Driven by host during command phase, driven by target during acknowledge and data phases.

  • SWDCLK (Serial Wire Clock): Clock driven by host. Data sampled on rising edge, changed on falling edge. Typical 1–50 MHz.

  • SWO (Serial Wire Output, optional): Asynchronous trace output. Carries ITM and ETM trace at UART NRZ or Manchester encoding.

SWD Packet Format: Each transaction is: 8-bit request + turnaround + 3-bit ACK + turnaround + 32-bit data + 1-bit parity.

Request byte fields:

  • : Start = 1

  • : APnDP – 0 = Debug Port (DP), 1 = Access Port (AP)

  • : RnW – 0 = write, 1 = read

  • : A[3:2] – register address bits 3 and 2

  • : Parity – odd parity over APnDP, RnW, A[3:2]

  • : Stop = 0

  • : Park = 1 (line floats high)

ACK responses: OK (001), WAIT (010), FAULT (100). A FAULT ACK requires reading CTRL/STAT to determine error cause.

DP Registers (APnDP=0):

  • DPIDR (read, A=0x0): Debug Port Identification – JEDEC manufacturer, version, min flag.

  • CTRL/STAT (A=0x4): CSYSPWRUPREQ, CDBGPWRUPREQ, STICKYERR, READOK, WDATAERR.

  • SELECT (write, A=0x8): Selects AP (APSEL[7:0]) and AP register bank (APBANKSEL[7:4]).

  • RDBUFF (read, A=0xC): Read posted AP result without issuing new AP transaction.

JTAG-to-SWD switching sequence: Drive 50+ SWDCLK cycles with SWDIO high (TMS reset), then shift the 16-bit magic sequence 0xE79E (LSB first on SWDIO), then drive 50+ cycles high again, then drive at least 2 idle cycles low. The SWJ-DP then enters SWD mode.

Tip: SWD is preferred over JTAG in small form-factor IoT devices because it saves two pins (TDI and TMS are replaced by SWDIO). For security testing, SWD is equally powerful – a single SWD connection to any Cortex-M device provides full memory read/write access unless TZEN (TrustZone Enable) and debug authentication are properly configured.

Figure 17.2. ARM CoreSight debug architecture. The DAP bridges the external JTAG/SWD interface to the internal AHB-AP (memory access) and APB-AP (debug component access). Orange = trace infrastructure; blue = DAP components; yellow = CPU core.

docs.title: 17.6 JTAG and SWD Debug Tools
docs.text:
Table 17.1. JTAG/SWD Debug Tool Comparison Tool Interface Protocol Speed License Segger J-Link BASE USB JTAG/SWD/cJTAG 50 MHz SWD Commercial Segger J-Link EDU USB JTAG/SWD 50 MHz SWD EDU only ST-Link/V3 (on Nucleo) USB SWD/JTAG 24 MHz SWD Free (on-board) CMSIS-DAP / DAPLink USB HID JTAG/SWD 10 MHz Apache 2.0 Black Magic Probe USB JTAG/SWD 4 MHz GPL OpenOCD + FTDI FT2232H USB JTAG/SWD 30 MHz JTAG GPL Bus Pirate + OpenOCD USB JTAG (slow) <1 MHz GPL/CC UrJTAG + parallel port LPT JTAG 5 MHz GPL

OpenOCD (Open On-Chip Debugger) is the de-facto open-source JTAG/SWD framework. It supports 200+ target CPUs, 100+ interface adapters, and provides GDB remote protocol (port 3333), TCL scripting, flash programming, and boundary scan.

Firmware extraction via OpenOCD:

# Connect to STM32F4 via ST-Link/V2
openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f4x.cfg

# In a separate terminal (GDB or telnet on port 4444):
telnet localhost 4444
> halt
> dump_image firmware.bin 0x08000000 0x100000
> mdw 0x40023C00 8     # read RCC registers
> mww 0xE000EDF0 0xA05F0003  # DHCSR: halt all cores

Warning: OpenOCD with a ? FTDI-based adapter can extract the complete firmware from most unprotected ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers in under 30 seconds. The dump_image command copies flash contents directly to a binary file without any authentication on devices without readout protection enabled.

RISC-V Debug (RISC-V Debug Spec 0.13/1.0): RISC-V defines its own debug transport independent of JTAG. The Debug Transport Module (DTM) sits between the JTAG TAP and the Debug Module (DM). The DM provides:

  • DMI (Debug Module Interface): 7-bit address, 32-bit data, 2-bit op (read/write/nop) register interface.

  • Abstract Commands: Access Register (0x0) and Access Memory (0x2) without halting the core.

  • System Bus Access: Direct AXI/AHB bus master for memory access independent of CPU state.

  • Program Buffer: 2–16 word RAM for arbitrary instruction execution in debug mode.

RISC-V ndmreset (non-debug module reset) and dmactive allow full system control via JTAG. OpenOCD supports RISC-V debug via the DTM JTAG DR at IR=0x11.

docs.title: 17.7 Debug Security Mechanisms
docs.text: Manufacturers implement debug port protection through four primary mechanisms:

docs.title: 17.7.1 eFUSE / OTP-based JTAG Disable
docs.text:
One-time programmable fuse bits permanently disable debug access. Once blown, the JTAG TAP either becomes non-functional or returns only BYPASS.

Xilinx/AMD FPGA JTAG security:

  • JTAG_DISABLE eFUSE: Disables JTAG access to FPGA configuration. Bit 0 of eFUSE row 22 on 7-Series devices. Programmed via XAPP1248 procedure.

  • AES encryption + BBRAM/eFUSE key: Bitstream encrypted with 256-bit AES key. Key stored in battery-backed BBRAM or eFUSE. Encrypted bitstreams cannot be readback.

  • Readback Disable (RD_DISABLE): Prevents configuration memory readback via JTAG. Separate from encrypt – must set both for full protection on 7-Series.

  • Zynq-7000 ARM DAP: Separate from FPGA JTAG. Controlled by DAP_ENABLE eFUSE and JTAG_DIS (disables PS TAP). Zynq UltraScale+ adds JTAG_STATUS[3:0] and secure debug.

STM32 Readout Protection (RDP) Levels:

Table 17.2. STM32 Flash Readout Protection Levels Level Debug Flash Read SRAM Access Reversal RDP0 (default) Full JTAG/SWD Full read Full access N/A RDP1 SWD allowed, no readback Blocked from debug Via debugger Erase all flash RDP2 Disabled permanently Blocked Blocked Irreversible

On STM32H7, RDP1 still allows live debugging but prevents dump_image. RDP2 is set by writing 0xCC to the RDP byte in FLASH_OPTSR_PRG. On STM32L5 with TrustZone, RDP1 with TZEN=1 additionally enforces secure/non-secure world isolation.

docs.title: 17.7.2 Debug Authentication
docs.text:
Debug authentication allows selective re-enabling of debug under controlled conditions:

  • Infineon AURIX TC3xx: Implements password-based debug authentication via OSTATE (Operation State) machine. Three debug credentials: A (application), B (Infineon), C (OEM). Credentials stored in HSM key slot, challenge-response via ECDSA-P256.

  • NXP S32K3: LC (Lifecycle) state machine with DEVELOP, OEM_OPEN, OEM_CLOSED, FIELD_RETURN states. Debug port disabled in OEM_CLOSED. Re-enabled only via signed debug certificate with device-unique key (derived from die UID + master secret during manufacture).

  • ARM CryptoIsland (CC312): Implements SoC-level authenticated debug. Host generates nonce via JTAG DR, device signs with production debug key, host verifies and sends unlock token. Implemented on NXP i.MX8, STM32MP1.

  • TI Sitara AM64x: SYSFW (System Firmware) manages debug enable/disable. Secure boot chain must authorize debug during boot. Debug certificate signed by TI + OEM key pair.

docs.title: 17.7.3 Lifecycle-Based Debug Control
docs.text:
Modern SoCs implement lifecycle management that ties debug access to the manufacturing/deployment state:

  • DEVELOP: Full debug, no security. Used during bring-up.

  • IN-FIELD / OEM-CLOSED: Debug disabled or limited. Firmware runs in production mode.

  • RETURN MERCHANDISE: OEM can authorize re-enable of limited debug for failure analysis.

  • TERMINATED: Permanent disable, no recovery. Triggered by tamper event or OEM command.

Note: ARM PSA Certified Level 2 requires that the debug port be disabled in production and only re-enabled via authenticated debug unlock using the device unique key. This is now enforced in ARM CryptoCell-312 (CC312) and equivalent IP blocks on NXP i.MX, STM32MP, and Renesas RZ/G2 SoCs.

Microchip PolarFire UJTAG: PolarFire exposes a UJTAG macro that connects user FPGA logic to the JTAG TAP as a custom DR. This enables custom authentication protocols – for example, presenting an AES-CBC challenge before enabling debug register access.

Intel Stratix 10 SDM: The Secure Device Manager (SDM) enforces JTAG authentication. Users must submit a signed authentication certificate via the JTAG USER1 DR. SDM verifies with the device root key (stored in eFUSE during personalization). Resource overhead: approximately 3,400 ALMs in the FPGA fabric for the verification logic.

JTAG TAP controller area (28nm): Approximately 2,400–4,800 gates for the 16-state TAP FSM plus IR/DR muxing. CoreSight DAP adds 15,000–25,000 gates (AHB-AP + DP). Debug authentication logic adds 8,000–12,000 gates for ECDSA verification (P-256, pre-computed).

docs.title: 17.10 JTAG Attack Techniques and Tools
docs.text:
Table 17.5. JTAG Security Attack Techniques Attack Method Mitigation Difficulty JTAG Port Discovery UART/JTAG pinout scan (JTAGulator) Remove test pads, use BGA Low Firmware Extraction dump_image via OpenOCD RDP2 / eFUSE JTAG disable Low Live Memory Patch mww/mwb write via telnet Code signing + CRC Low Glitch + JTAG Bypass Voltage glitch RDP check then JTAG Redundant RDP storage High JTAG Password Brute Replay all 2^128 passwords Rate limit + lockout fuse Infeasible Boundary Scan Attack EXTEST to drive pins directly Remove exposed test points Medium Debug Auth Bypass Fault inject during auth verification Redundant verification High SWD Sniffing Logic analyzer on SWD lines Encrypted debug session Low

JTAGulator: An open-source hardware tool (designed by Joe Grand) that brute-forces JTAG pinouts from unpopulated headers or test points. It supports 24 channels, 1.2V–3.3V I/O, and can identify TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO within minutes by sending TMS patterns and observing TDO responses. Also supports UART baud-rate identification.

Specialized Attack Procedures:

  1. SWD Sniff Attack: Attach a logic analyzer (e.g., Saleae Logic Pro 16) to the SWD lines. Decode packets in real time using the SWD protocol analyzer. Memory contents transmitted in cleartext can be captured without disturbing operation.

  2. JTAG on PCB via test points: Common for production boards with unpopulated 10-pin ARM Cortex debug connectors (SWD/JTAG). Use JTAGulator or a multimeter with continuity mode to identify pin 1 (VREF), GND, SWDIO, SWDCLK, and SWO.

  3. Glitch to downgrade RDP: On STM32F1/F2, a voltage glitch on VDD during the flash readout protection check (FLASH_SR read) can skip the protection. Successfully demonstrated by Dmitry Nedospasov (2017). Mitigated on STM32L5 and H7 with hardware glitch detectors.

Warning: Boundary scan via JTAG EXTEST instruction can drive any GPIO pin to any logic level regardless of software state. On boards with unprotected JTAG, an attacker can directly manipulate power-enable lines, reset signals, or I2C/SPI bus lines to trigger fault conditions or unlock additional debug interfaces.

Best practices for production debug security:

  1. Disable JTAG/SWD in the final lifecycle state via eFUSE or OTP. Never leave debug enabled in production.

  2. Implement authenticated debug re-enable using a device-unique key stored in an HSM or eFUSE during manufacturing.

  3. Remove physical test pads and JTAG headers from production PCB layouts (not just DNP – remove copper too).

  4. Use SWD over JTAG where possible – smaller attack surface (2 pins vs 4+).

  5. Log all authenticated debug sessions and protect the signing key with key ceremonies.

docs.title: 17.12.1 OpenOCD TCL: JTAG Chain Enumeration
docs.text:
# openocd_enum.tcl -- enumerate JTAG chain and dump IDCODEs
proc jtag_enumerate {} {
    # Reset to TLR, then flush with BYPASS
    irscan [lindex [jtag devices] 0] 0xFF
    set n [llength [jtag devices]]
    puts "Devices in chain: "
    foreach dev [jtag devices] {
        set idcode [drscan  32 0x00000000]
        set mfr [expr {( >> 1) & 0x7FF}]
        set part [expr {( >> 12) & 0xFFFF}]
        set ver  [expr {( >> 28) & 0xF}]
        puts [format "
                  ]
    }
}
jtag_enumerate

docs.title: 17.12.2 C: ARM CoreSight AHB-AP Memory Read via SWD
docs.text:
/* swd_mem_read.c -- read 4 bytes from target via SWD/AHB-AP */
#include <stdint.h>
#define DP_SELECT  0x08   /* DP SELECT register */
#define AP_CSW     0x00   /* AHB-AP CSW */
#define AP_TAR     0x04   /* AHB-AP TAR */
#define AP_DRW     0x0C   /* AHB-AP DRW */
#define DP_RDBUFF  0x0C   /* DP RDBUFF */

static void swd_write_dp(uint8_t addr, uint32_t val);
static void swd_write_ap(uint8_t addr, uint32_t val);
static uint32_t swd_read_dp(uint8_t addr);

uint32_t ahb_read32(uint32_t address) {
    /* Select AP 0, bank 0 */
    swd_write_dp(DP_SELECT, 0x00000000);
    /* Set CSW: 32-bit auto-increment word transfer */
    swd_write_ap(AP_CSW, 0x23000052);
    /* Set TAR (target address) */
    swd_write_ap(AP_TAR, address);
    /* Issue read to DRW (posted -- result in RDBUFF) */
    swd_write_ap(AP_DRW, 0);
    /* Dummy read of DRW to push posted result to RDBUFF */
    /* Then read RDBUFF to get actual data */
    return swd_read_dp(DP_RDBUFF);
}

docs.title: 17.12.3 Python: JTAG Device Discovery with pyOCD
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# jtag_scan.py -- discover JTAG chain using pyOCD or pyFTDI
from pyftdi.jtag import JtagController
from pyftdi.bits import BitSequence

def scan_idcodes(url="ftdi://ftdi:2232h/1"):
    jtag = JtagController()
    jtag.configure(url)
    # Reset to TLR
    jtag.reset()
    # Shift out 32*MAX_DEVS bits with TDI=1 to load BYPASS in all IRs
    jtag.write_ir(BitSequence(0xFF, msb=False, length=8))
    # Count devices: shift 1s and count until first 1 appears
    tdo = jtag.read_dr(32 * 8)
    devices = []
    raw = int(tdo)
    while raw & 0xFFFFFFFF:
        idcode = raw & 0xFFFFFFFF
        if idcode & 1:  # valid IDCODE has bit0=1
            mfr  = (idcode >> 1) & 0x7FF
            part = (idcode >> 12) & 0xFFFF
            ver  = (idcode >> 28) & 0xF
            devices.append({"idcode": idcode, "mfr": mfr,
                             "part": part, "ver": ver})
        raw >>= 32
    jtag.close()
    return devices

if __name__ == "__main__":
    devs = scan_idcodes()
    for i, d in enumerate(devs):
        print(f"Device {i}: IDCODE=0x{d[chr(105)+chr(100)+chr(99)+chr(111)+chr(100)+chr(101)]:08X} "
              f"mfr=0x{d[chr(109)+chr(102)+chr(114)]:03X} part=0x{d[chr(112)+chr(97)+chr(114)+chr(116)]:04X}")

docs.title: 17.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: JTAG Chain Length and IR Width Detection

A PCB has a 4-pin JTAG header (TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO) connected to an unknown device chain. Describe the complete enumeration procedure: (1) determine the number of devices, (2) detect IR lengths, (3) read IDCODEs. Show the TMS sequences and expected TDO patterns. Solution: Step 1: Reset to Test-Logic-Reset. Drive TMS=1 for at least 5 TCK rising edges from any state. All TAP controllers are guaranteed to reach TLR.

Step 2: Count devices via BYPASS. Go to Shift-IR (TMS: 0,1,1,0,0 from TLR). Load all IRs with BYPASS (all 1s): shift at least 32*N ones (where N is the maximum possible chain length, e.g., N=16). Return to RTI via Update-IR (TMS: 1,1,0). Proceed to Shift-DR (TMS: 1,0,0). Now shift a single 0 followed by 1s into TDI. Count clock cycles until the single 0 appears on TDO: this count equals the number of devices (each BYPASS register is exactly 1 bit). If 0 appears after 3 cycles, there are 3 devices.

Step 3: Detect IR lengths. Reset to TLR. Enter Shift-IR. Shift all 0s until stable (flush). Shift a 1 into TDI, counting edges until it appears on TDO. The count minus 1 is the total IR length (sum across all devices in chain). Refine per-device IR lengths by resetting and observing the mandatory Capture-IR pattern (last two bits must be 01 per IEEE 1149.1 clause 8.6.1.1). For a chain of IRlen=5+4+3=12: first 1 arrives after 12 clocks total.

Step 4: Read IDCODEs. Reset to TLR. IDCODE instruction is the power-on-reset default IR value for IEEE 1149.1-compliant devices. Proceed directly to Shift-DR from TLR (TMS: 0,1,0,0). Shift 32*N bits = 96 bits for 3 devices. Parse each 32-bit IDCODE: bit 0 must be 1 (valid IDCODE); bits [11:1] = JEDEC manufacturer ID; bits [27:12] = part number; bits [31:28] = version. Example: 0x4BA00477 = ARM (mfr 0x23B), part 0x4B, version 4 (Cortex-A53 DAP).

Solved Problem: ARM SWD MEM-AP Memory Dump Sequence

You have an STM32F429ZI connected via SWD. The device is halted. Walk through the exact SWD packet sequence required to read 4 bytes from SRAM address 0x20000010 using the CoreSight AHB-AP. Show each SWD request byte, ACK, and data phase. Solution: Prerequisites: SWD line reset (50+ clocks high), JTAG-to-SWD sequence (0xE79E), 50+ clocks high, 2 idle clocks. Read DPIDR to confirm target.

Step 1: Power up DP. Write CTRL/STAT (A[3:2]=0b10, APnDP=0, RnW=0): Request byte: Start=1, APnDP=0, RnW=0, A[3:2]=10, Parity, Stop=0, Park=1 => 0x50. Data: 0x54000000 (CSYSPWRUPREQ=1, CDBGPWRUPREQ=1). Parity = popcount(data) mod 2 = 0. Wait for CDBGPWRUPACK=1 in CTRL/STAT read-back.

Step 2: Select AP 0, bank 0. Write DP SELECT (A[3:2]=0b00 of bank 2 => 0x08): Request byte: APnDP=0, RnW=0, A=0b10, Parity, => 0xA8. Data: 0x00000000 (APSEL=0x00, APBANKSEL=0x0, DPBANKSEL=0x0).

Step 3: Write AHB-AP CSW. Write AP register (APnDP=1, RnW=0, A[3:2]=0b00): Request byte: APnDP=1, RnW=0, A=0b00, Parity => 0x81. Data CSW=0x23000052: SIZE=0b010 (32-bit), AddrInc=0b01 (increment single), DbgSwEnable=1, MasterType=1, Prot[6:1]=0b001000 (privileged, non-secure).

Step 4: Write AHB-AP TAR. Write AP register (APnDP=1, RnW=0, A[3:2]=0b01): Request byte: APnDP=1, RnW=0, A=0b01 => 0x83 (recalculate parity). Data TAR=0x20000010 (target SRAM address).

Step 5: Read AHB-AP DRW. Read AP register (APnDP=1, RnW=1, A[3:2]=0b11): Request byte: APnDP=1, RnW=1, A=0b11 => 0x9F. ACK=OK, Data phase: 32 bits of posted result (not valid yet – this is the PREVIOUS read result).

Step 6: Read DP RDBUFF. Read DP register (APnDP=0, RnW=1, A[3:2]=0b11): Request byte: 0x9D. ACK=OK, Data[31:0] = actual 4 bytes at 0x20000010. Verify parity bit.

Result: If SRAM[0x20000010] = 0xDEADBEEF, RDBUFF returns 0xDEADBEEF with even parity = 1 (16 set bits is even => parity bit = 0).

Solved Problem: STM32 RDP Level Analysis and Flash Protection

A product engineer wants to ship an STM32H743ZI-based device with the following requirements: (a) no firmware readback via JTAG/SWD; (b) field firmware update via USB DFU must remain possible; (c) in-field debug must be possible for authorized service centers using a signed certificate; (d) tamper events must permanently disable the device. Specify the exact option byte configuration and lifecycle design. Solution: RDP Level Selection: Use RDP1 (not RDP2) to satisfy requirements (a)-(c). RDP2 satisfies (a) but prevents ALL debug including authenticated debug, which conflicts with requirement (c).

Option Byte Configuration (FLASH_OPTSR register, STM32H7):

  • RDP[7:0] = 0xBB: Level 1 readout protection (0xAA=L0, 0xBB=L1, 0xCC=L2)

  • nSWBOOT0 = 1: Boot from flash, not ROM (prevents DFU bypass)

  • SECURITY = 1: Enable security features

  • BOOT_LOCK = 1: Lock boot address to application region

  • NRST_STOP_D1 = 0: Allow low-power debug

Firmware Update (USB DFU): Implement a custom secure bootloader. The bootloader at 0x08000000 verifies a signed firmware image (ECDSA-P256 + SHA-256) before writing to the application region. The DFU endpoint is only accessible via the custom bootloader, not the ST ROM DFU (disable ROM DFU via BOOT0 pin pull-down and nSWBOOT0=1).

Authenticated Debug (Service Center): Use STM32H7 TZEN + CryptoCell-312 debug authentication. The service center sends a challenge request via the SWD DAP register. The device firmware generates a challenge nonce, the service center signs it with their provisioned ECDSA service key, and the device verifies and temporarily enables Level 1 debug for one session.

Tamper Permanent Disable: Configure the TAMP peripheral (TAMP_CR1): connect TAMP_IN1 to the case-open switch. In TAMP interrupt handler, erase all flash sectors (write FLASH_CR EOPIE=1, ERRIE=1, SER=1 for all sectors), then write RDP=0xCC via the option byte programming sequence (FLASH_OPTKEYR unlock + FLASH_OPTSR write + FLASH_OPTCR OPTSTART=1). Disable interrupts before the RDP2 write to prevent abort. After reset, device is permanently bricked.

Solved Problem: RISC-V Debug Module Abstract Command Execution

A RISC-V SoC (SiFive FE310-G002) is connected via JTAG at IR=0x11 (DTMCS). The debug specification version is 0.13. Describe how to: (a) halt the core, (b) read the PC (program counter via CSR dpc), (c) write arbitrary 32-bit instructions via the program buffer, (d) resume execution. Specify the DMI register addresses and values. Solution: RISC-V Debug Architecture: The DTM JTAG IR=0x11 selects a 32-bit DTMCS register (Debug Transport Module Control and Status). IR=0x10 selects the 41-bit DMI register: [40:34]=address, [33:2]=data, [1:0]=op (0=nop, 1=read, 2=write, 3=reserved).

Step (a): Halt the core. Write dmcontrol (DMI addr 0x10): data=0x80000001 (haltreq=1, dmactive=1). DMI: addr=0x10, data=0x80000001, op=2 (write). Poll dmstatus (DMI addr 0x11, op=1) until allhalted=1 (bit 9=1).

Step (b): Read CSR dpc (0x7B1). Use Abstract Command – Access Register (command type 0). Write command register (DMI addr 0x17): cmdtype[31:24]=0x00, size[22:20]=0b010 (32-bit), transfer=1, write=0, regno[15:0]=0x07B1+0x1000=0x17B1 (GPR regno: CSRs are 0x0000-0x0FFF direct; for DPC use regno=0x07B1). data=0x00221FB1 (transfer=1, write=0, regno=0x17B1). Poll abstractcs (addr 0x16) until busy=0. Read data0 (addr 0x04): this is the PC value.

Step (c): Write instructions via program buffer. Program buffer is at DMI addresses 0x20-0x2F (16 words max). Write instruction to progbuf0 (addr 0x20): data=0x00100293 (ADDI x5, x0, 1). Write EBREAK to progbuf1 (addr 0x21): data=0x00100073 (ebreak). Issue Abstract Command with postexec=1: data=0x00241000 (cmdtype=0, size=2, postexec=1, write=1, regno=s0). The DM executes the program buffer after the abstract command. Poll abstractcs.busy=0 and check cmderr[10:8]=0 (no error).

Step (d): Resume. Write dmcontrol (addr 0x10): data=0x40000001 (resumereq=1, dmactive=1). Poll dmstatus until allresumed=1 (bit 17=1) and allrunning=1. Clear resumereq: write dmcontrol = 0x00000001.

docs.title: 17.14 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: JTAG and debug interface security has evolved since 2023 through the introduction of JTAG-over-USB-C (USB Debug Class), IoT SoC authentication bypass CVEs, ARM CoreSight 9.0 improvements, maturation of RISC-V JTAG debug support in OpenOCD, updated JTAGulator hardware, and the PSA Certified Level 2 debug access requirements.

docs.title: 17.14.1 JTAG over USB-C (USB Debug Class, 2023): New Attack Surface
docs.text:
The USB 3.2 and USB4 specification includes the USB Debug Class (UDBC, USB 3.2 Annex B, also referenced in USB4 v2.0), which maps a JTAG debug port to a USB-C Alternate Mode. This creates a significant new attack surface for deployed consumer devices:

  • Protocol: The USB Debug Class presents a JTAG TAP as a USB Class 0xDC (Diagnostic) interface. A host sends JTAG bit-bang commands via USB Bulk OUT transfers; the device responds via Bulk IN. Maximum throughput: 5 Gbit/s (USB 3.2 Gen 1), far exceeding physical JTAG at 50 MHz.

  • New attack surface: USB-C cables and docking stations are universally deployed. An attacker with a modified USB-C cable or malicious docking station can enumerate the Debug Class interface on any device that has not disabled UDBC in production firmware.

  • Affected devices: Several Qualcomm Snapdragon-based Android flagships (2023) shipped with UDBC enumerated in engineering builds and not disabled in production fastboot firmware. Researchers at DEF CON 31 (2023) demonstrated full DRAM extraction via USB-C UDBC on an affected device in under 60 seconds.

  • Mitigation: Disable UDBC in the USB descriptor table in production firmware. Enforce lifecycle-based UDBC enable/disable via eFUSE (analogous to JTAG disable fuses for traditional JTAG ports).

Warning: Every USB-C port on a production device is a potential JTAG attack surface if UDBC is not explicitly disabled. Security reviews for devices with USB-C ports must include USB descriptor enumeration to confirm the Debug Class interface is absent. Use lsusb -v on Linux or USBView on Windows to verify no 0xDC class interface is reported.

docs.title: 17.14.2 JTAG Authentication Bypass CVEs in IoT SoCs (2023)
docs.text:
Multiple IoT SoC vendors disclosed JTAG authentication bypass vulnerabilities in 2023, following improved hardware security audit tooling:

  • Insufficient boot state check: A class of SoCs (unnamed due to coordinated disclosure in progress) implements JTAG authentication as a software check in the boot ROM; a voltage glitch during the authentication state read skips the check and returns to the DEVELOP lifecycle state with full debug access.

  • Authentication oracle: JTAG challenge-response systems that use a fixed nonce length (e.g., 32-bit nonce in challenge) allow offline brute-force if the device does not enforce a lockout after failed attempts. With \(2^{32}\) possible challenges and no lockout, a brute-force JTAG authentication attack completes in \(< 12\) hours at 100 kHz JTAG clock.

  • Mitigations adopted post-2023: Leading SoC vendors (Microchip, Renesas, NXP) moved to ECDSA-P256 challenge-response for JTAG authentication, eliminating brute-force feasibility. Lockout-after-N-failures eFUSE policies now appear in silicon revision specifications.

docs.title: 17.14.3 ARM CoreSight 9.0: Improved Debug Authentication and Security Extensions
docs.text:
ARM CoreSight Architecture Specification v9.0 (IHI0029H, 2023) introduces a revised Debug Authentication Interface (DAI) and extended security architecture:

Table 17.7. ARM CoreSight 9.0 debug security improvements Feature CoreSight 9.0 implementation Debug Authentication Interface New DBGAUTHSTATUS_EL1 register with per-world enable bits Realm world debug Separate debug enable bit for ARM CCA Realm world EL3 debug enable MDCR_EL3.TDA bit independently controls EL3 trace DAP authentication DAPID register includes mandatory authentication type field Trace encryption Optional ETM trace port encryption (AES-128-CTR) for link-level trace security Multi-core halt sync Enhanced CTI (Cross-Trigger Interface) with authenticated trigger masks

The Realm world debug addition is significant for ARM CCA (Confidential Compute Architecture): a Realm VM can have debug independently enabled without granting the host Normal world debugger access to Realm physical memory. This enables per-world debug certificates – a field engineer can debug a Realm workload with a Realm-scoped debug credential without gaining any visibility into the co-located Secure world or other Realm VMs.

docs.title: 17.14.4 RISC-V JTAG Debug Transport: OpenOCD RISC-V Support Maturity
docs.text:
The RISC-V Debug Specification v1.0 (ratified 2022, widely deployed 2023) has reached implementation maturity in OpenOCD, with the following security-relevant state:

  • OpenOCD 0.12.0 (2023): Full RISC-V 1.0 debug module support including Abstract Commands, Program Buffer, System Bus Access, and the new ndmreset authenticated reset mechanism.

  • RISC-V Trigger Module security: OpenOCD exposes the RISC-V Trigger Module (up to 16 hardware breakpoints) via a new riscv_trigger command. Unconstrained trigger module access (without authentication) allows unlimited hardware breakpoints in production kernels, enabling ROP gadget patching and kernel address disclosure via the PC trace.

  • RISC-V debug authentication (draft 2023): The RISC-V Debug Task Group published a Debug Authentication Extension draft (RV-DBGAUTH) adding an ECDSA-P256 challenge in the DMI address space (address 0x38–0x3F), analogous to ARM CryptoCell debug auth, enabling lifecycle-controlled debug re-enable.

  • OpenTitan RISC-V debug: OpenTitan implements the RV-DBGAUTH draft with a one-time token-based debug unlock (KMAC-derived token), documented in the OpenTitan Debug Transport TRM v0.7.

docs.title: 17.14.5 JTAGulator v2.x Updates for Detection Speed
docs.text:
JTAGulator (Joe Grand, 2012–present) released version 2.x hardware and firmware in 2023–2024:

  • Detection speed improvement: JTAGulator v2 uses a Parallax Propeller 2 (P2, 8-core 32-bit, 80 MHz) replacing the original Propeller 1. JTAG pinout scan speed increased from \(\approx\)150 to \(\approx\)800 channel-combinations per second, reducing pinout discovery time for a 24-channel scan from \(\approx\)3 minutes to \(< 45\) seconds.

  • SWD passive detection: v2 adds a passive SWD sniffing mode using a 1 GSa/s sample buffer to capture SWD transactions without disturbing the target, enabling analysis of SWD traffic on locked production devices.

  • UART baud-rate autodetect: Extended to cover 300–4,000,000 baud, detecting the 921,600 baud engineering UARTs used in modern Qualcomm and MediaTek SoCs.

docs.title: 17.14.6 PSA Certified Level 2 Debug Requirements
docs.text:
PSA Certified Level 2 (ARM, 2023 revision) formalises debug security requirements that were previously informally stated:

Table 17.8. PSA Certified Level 2 debug interface requirements Requirement Specification Debug disabled in production JTAG/SWD must be disabled via eFUSE or OTP in the production lifecycle state Authenticated debug re-enable ECDSA-P256 challenge-response with device-unique key required for any re-enable Debug session scoping Re-enabled debug must be time-limited (session timeout via hardware watchdog) Audit log Each authenticated debug session must produce a signed audit entry in NvM No JTAG in sleep modes Debug port must remain disabled during all low-power states

PSA Certified Level 2 evaluation includes a mandatory hardware penetration test by an approved lab (CLEF – Certified Lab for Embedded Firmware), which specifically tests JTAG/SWD disable effectiveness against voltage glitching, laser fault injection, and USB Debug Class enumeration.

Exercises

  1. Explain why IEEE 1149.1 mandates that TMS=1 for 5 consecutive TCK rising edges always reaches Test-Logic-Reset regardless of the current TAP state. Prove this using the 16-state FSM transition table.

  2. A JTAG chain contains three devices with IR lengths of 4, 5, and 10 bits respectively. What is the minimum number of TDI bits required to load all three IRs simultaneously? Show how to address device 2 (middle device) with the BYPASS instruction while sending IDCODE to device 1.

  3. Compare JTAG (4-wire) and SWD (2-wire) protocols for a battery-powered IoT device with a 32-pin QFN package. Consider pin count, protocol overhead, security surface, and suitability for production test.

  4. A Cortex-M4 device has AHB-AP CSW register value 0x23000052. Decode all fields and explain why this configuration is used for normal 32-bit memory read access during debugging.

  5. Design a secure debug authentication scheme for a medical device that must comply with FDA cybersecurity guidance (2023). The scheme must: allow authorized service technicians to temporarily enable debug; maintain an audit log; use device-unique keys; and not expose the master key.

  6. Explain the difference between STM32 RDP Level 1 and Level 2 in the context of a fault injection attack. Why does RDP1 remain partially vulnerable to voltage glitching attacks on older STM32 families, and how did ST address this in the STM32H5 series?

  7. Write OpenOCD TCL commands to: (a) connect to a Zynq-7020 via JTAG, (b) halt the ARM Cortex-A9, (c) dump 512 bytes from physical address 0xFFFC0000 (OCM), (d) verify the dump against a known checksum.

  8. Describe the RISC-V Debug Module Interface (DMI) transaction format. What is the significance of the cmderr field in abstractcs, and what does each error code indicate?

  9. A JTAGulator discovers 24 test points on a PCB. The tool identifies TCK on pin 3, TDO on pin 7, but cannot find TMS or TDI. Suggest five reasons why TMS/TDI might not be detected and how to diagnose each case.

  10. Compare the security of Xilinx 7-Series JTAG with UltraScale+ JTAG. What specific eFUSE bits are involved, what is the attack surface difference, and how does encrypted bitstream loading interact with JTAG debug access?

  11. An ARM Cortex-A53 SoC uses CoreSight ETM v4 with 4-bit trace port at 500 MHz. Calculate the maximum instruction trace bandwidth in instructions per second assuming: 4-bit port, DDR (both edges), 8b/10b encoded, average ETM packet = 2.5 bytes per retired instruction.

  12. You are performing a security audit of an IoT gateway product. The PCB has a 10-pin Cortex Debug connector (SWD). The device runs Linux on a Cortex-A7. Describe the complete security assessment methodology: from physical access to full memory dump, including any ASLR bypass technique available through CoreSight AHB-AP.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Hardware Cryptographic Accelerators
docs.text: Note: Hardware cryptographic accelerators achieve 10x–1000x better performance-per-watt compared to software implementations. A Cortex-M4 running AES-128-CBC in software achieves approximately 50 Mbps at 168 MHz; the same SoC with AES hardware acceleration (e.g., STM32F4 CRYP peripheral) achieves 1.4 Gbps – a 28x improvement. At the SoC level, Intel QAT 8970 delivers 100 Gbps symmetric crypto on a PCIe card.

docs.title: 18.1 AES Hardware Acceleration
docs.text: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard, FIPS 197) is the most widely hardware-accelerated cipher. Four implementation strategies exist:

docs.title: 18.1.1 CPU ISA Extensions
docs.text:
Intel AES-NI (x86): Introduced in Westmere (2010). Six instructions:

  • AESENC xmm1, xmm2/m128: One round of AES encryption (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey).

  • AESENCLAST xmm1, xmm2/m128: Final round (no MixColumns).

  • AESDEC / AESDECLAST: Corresponding decryption rounds (using InvSubBytes, InvShiftRows, InvMixColumns).

  • AESIMC xmm1, xmm2/m128: InvMixColumns for key schedule expansion (decryption).

  • AESKEYGENASSIST xmm1, xmm2/m128, imm8: Assists key schedule: RotWord, SubWord, Rcon XOR.

AES-NI throughput on Ice Lake: 0.62 cycles/byte for AES-128-GCM with CLMUL. Pipeline depth: 4 cycles latency per AESENC, but 4-way pipelining achieves 1 clock per round. AES-256-GCM throughput: approximately 1.2 cycles/byte.

ARM AES intrinsics (ARMv8-A Cryptography Extensions, FEAT_AES): Introduced in Cortex-A53/A57. Four NEON/Advanced SIMD instructions:

  • AESE Vd.16B, Vn.16B: AddRoundKey + SubBytes + ShiftRows.

  • AESMC Vd.16B, Vn.16B: MixColumns.

  • AESD / AESIMC: Corresponding decryption operations.

ARM Cortex-A72 AES-128-GCM throughput: approximately 0.58 cycles/byte at 1.5 GHz = 2.5 Gbps. Apple M2 using FEAT_AES + PMULL: approximately 0.21 cycles/byte for AES-256-GCM.

RISC-V Zkn (NIST Cryptography, Ratified 2022): The Zkn extension provides:

  • aes32esi / aes32esmi: AES forward SubBytes + ShiftRows, with/without MixColumns (RV32 only).

  • aes64es / aes64esm: RV64 versions processing two AES state columns per instruction.

  • aes64im: InvMixColumns for RV64.

  • aes64ks1i / aes64ks2: Key schedule instructions for RV64.

SiFive P870 with Zkn: 3.4 Gbps AES-128-GCM at 1.7 GHz. SiFive P670: 2.1 Gbps.

SHA-NI (x86 SHA Extensions, Intel Goldmont 2016): Two new instruction sets:

  • SHA256RNDS2, SHA256MSG1, SHA256MSG2: SHA-256 round and message schedule.

  • SHA1RNDS4, SHA1NEXTE, SHA1MSG1, SHA1MSG2: SHA-1 (legacy use only).

SHA-256 throughput with SHA-NI: 3.65 cycles/byte (vs 12.8 cycles/byte software on same core, 3.5x speedup).

docs.title: 18.1.2 AES Round Function Hardware Pipeline
docs.text:
Figure 18.1. AES round function hardware pipeline (one of 10/12/14 rounds for AES-128/192/256). Blue blocks are the four AES transformations. Yellow blocks show the parallel key schedule. SubBytes uses 16 parallel 8x8 S-box lookups. MixColumns uses GF(2^8) multiply-by-2 (xtime).

Hardware S-box implementations:

  • LUT (Look-up Table): 256-byte ROM, 1 cycle, 2048 gates.

  • Composite field GF((2^4)^2): Tower field arithmetic,  170 gates, no ROM needed, power-balanced (better for side-channel resistance).

  • Masked S-box: Randomized affine transform + inverse, 600–800 gates, suitable for DPA-resistant implementations.

docs.title: 18.2.1 RSA / ECC Modular Arithmetic
docs.text:
Public-key cryptography requires modular exponentiation (RSA) or point multiplication (ECC), both computationally expensive operations:

  • RSA-2048 modular exponentiation (software, Cortex-M4 at 168 MHz):  800 ms

  • RSA-2048 with hardware Montgomery multiplier (NXP LPC54608):  40 ms (20x)

  • ECDSA-P256 sign (software, Cortex-M4):  180 ms

  • ECDSA-P256 hardware (STM32H7 PKA peripheral):  3.5 ms (51x)

  • ECDH-P384 hardware (NXP SE050 SE):  680 ms (dedicated crypto CPU)

Montgomery Modular Multiplication: The key primitive. Computes R = A*B*R-1 mod N where R = 2k (word-size aligned). Avoids division; uses shift-and-add with conditional subtraction. Hardware implementation (2048-bit) at 100 MHz: approximately 20,000 gates, 2 microseconds per multiply.

NXP CAAM (Cryptographic Acceleration and Assurance Module): Present on i.MX6/7/8 SoCs.

  • DMA-driven job descriptor architecture: host fills job descriptor rings, CAAM processes asynchronously.

  • Supported algorithms: AES-CBC/CTR/GCM/XTS/CCM, 3DES, ARC4, MD5, SHA-1/224/256/384/512, HMAC, RSA-4096, ECDSA P-192/224/256/384/521, ECDH, DH, TRNG, DRBG (SP 800-90A CTR-DRBG).

  • Secure key store: 8 black key slots (AES-256 key encryption key). JDKEK/TDKEK for black key wrap.

  • Throughput: AES-256-CBC at 3.2 Gbps (i.MX8M Plus, 800 MHz bus clock).

Marvell OCTEON TX2 CN9880: Network-class crypto accelerator for data plane.

  • 24 Arm Cortex-A72 cores + 4 security engines (CPT).

  • Symmetric: AES-128/256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, AES-CCM/CBC/CTR, SHA-256/384/512.

  • Asymmetric: RSA-4096, ECDSA/ECDH (P-256/384/521, X25519, Ed25519).

  • Aggregate throughput: 200 Gbps symmetric, 300K RSA-2048 ops/sec.

  • Use case: 100GbE TLS termination proxy, IPsec VPN gateway.

Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) 8970: PCIe Gen3 x16 card.

  • 160 Gbps symmetric (AES-128-GCM), 200 Gbps for SHA-256.

  • 1.5M RSA-2048 ops/sec, 500K ECDSA-256 ops/sec.

  • Compression: DEFLATE at 100 Gbps.

  • Linux kernel driver: qat_4xxx (upstream since kernel 5.13). DPDK PMD: crypto_qat.

  • Use case: TLS acceleration for web servers (reduces CPU crypto load by 99%).

Tip: DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit) provides a unified crypto PMD API that works across Intel QAT, Marvell OCTEON, and software (OpenSSL). The rte_cryptodev API uses symmetric crypto sessions and asynchronous enqueue/dequeue for zero-copy DMA-based packet encryption at line rate.

docs.title: 18.3.1 SHA Hardware Acceleration
docs.text:
SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) hardware cores use the following approaches:

  • Unrolled pipeline: All 64 SHA-256 rounds combinatorially unrolled. Latency = 1 clock/block = 64 rounds in 1 cycle. Area =  50,000 gates.

  • Iterative (folded): Single-round hardware executed 64 times. 64 cycles/block. Area =  8,000 gates.

  • 2-unrolled: Two rounds per cycle. 32 cycles/block. Area-throughput tradeoff. Used in most embedded SoCs.

STM32H7 HASH peripheral: Supports SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, MD5. DMA-fed, processes 512-bit blocks in 64 clock cycles. Automatic padding. Supports HMAC with two-pass HASH operation.

Intel SHA Extensions throughput (Goldmont+): SHA-256: 3.65 cycles/byte. SHA-1: 1.8 cycles/byte.

docs.title: 18.3.2 GHASH and GCM Authentication
docs.text:
AES-GCM authentication uses GHASH: a polynomial hash over GF(2128).

\[GHASH_H(X) = X_1 \cdot H^m \oplus X_2 \cdot H^{m-1} \oplus … \oplus X_m \cdot H\]

where H = AES(K, 0128) and multiplication is in GF(2128).

CLMUL (Carry-Less Multiplication): Intel PCLMULQDQ instruction (SSE4.2) and ARM PMULL perform 64x64-bit carry-less multiplication for GHASH. Combined with AES-NI:

  • Intel Cascade Lake: 0.52 cycles/byte for AES-128-GCM (PCLMULQDQ + AESENC pipelined).

  • ARM Neoverse N1: 0.55 cycles/byte (PMULL + AESE/AESMC).

GCM HW implementations for FPGA/ASIC: GHASH is implemented as a Karatsuba multiplier over GF(2128). A 1-cycle 128-bit Karatsuba multiplier uses approximately 12,000 XOR gates (no flip-flops needed since GF multiplication has no carry). 4-cycle multiplier (32-bit datapath) uses  2,500 gates.

docs.title: 18.4.1 ChaCha20-Poly1305 Hardware
docs.text:
ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439) is increasingly hardware-accelerated, especially for mobile and embedded systems where AES-NI is unavailable:

  • ChaCha20 quarter-round: 4 add-rotate-XOR (ARX) operations on 32-bit words. 20 rounds (10 double-rounds), each double-round = 8 quarter-rounds = 32 ARX operations.

  • Hardware block: Single double-round costs  4,000 gates. Full ChaCha20 block (512-bit keystream, 64 bytes) = 10 double-rounds = 40,000 gates unrolled or 4,000 gates folded (10 cycles/block).

  • Poly1305 MAC: 130-bit prime field (2130-5). Requires 130x130-bit multiply + reduce. Hardware multiplier:  15,000 gates for full 130-bit multiply.

ARM Cortex-A55 NEON ChaCha20: 2.8 cycles/byte at 1.8 GHz = 640 Mbps. ARM SVE2 with 512-bit SIMD: expected  1.1 cycles/byte.

docs.title: 18.4.2 True Random Number Generators
docs.text:
TRNG Hardware Sources:

  • Ring oscillator (RO) TRNG: Multiple free-running inverter rings, XOR of outputs. Jitter from thermal noise provides entropy. NIST SP 800-90B compliant. Used in STM32, AURIX, i.MX, Zynq.

  • Metastability-based TRNG: SR latch or flip-flop driven to metastable state. Resolution direction determined by thermal noise. Higher throughput but requires careful AMS design.

  • SRAM PUF as entropy source: SRAM power-on state provides device-unique entropy. Not suitable as TRNG (deterministic per-device) but used for PUF-based key generation.

  • Quantum RNG (QRNG): Photon shot noise or vacuum fluctuations. Used in HSMs: Thales Luna 7, IBM CEX7S. Throughput: 1–100 Gbps.

FIPS 140-3 and NIST SP 800-90B requirements for TRNGs:

  • Health tests: Repetition Count Test (RCT) and Adaptive Proportion Test (APT).

  • Entropy rate estimate: min-entropy H_min >= 0.5 bits/sample for conditioning input.

  • Continuous RNG tests required in production (FIPS 140-3 ISO/IEC 19790).

Warning: The Debian OpenSSL random number bug (2008, CVE-2008-0166) occurred because a developer removed an uninitialised memory read that was flagged by Valgrind, unintentionally eliminating the main entropy source for the PRNG. All RSA/DSA keys generated on Debian-based systems from 2006-2008 were weak. This demonstrates why TRNG health testing and entropy source documentation are critical.

A well-written AES-GCM HLS design achieves approximately 80% of the throughput of a hand-crafted RTL implementation with 10x less development time.

AXI4-Stream crypto engine integration: Production FPGA crypto cores use AXI4-Stream for data flow and AXI4-Lite for control registers. The Xilinx AXI FIFO IP bridges between the DMA engine and the crypto core. A Zynq-7020 system with AES-GCM + SHA-256 + ECDSA cores connected to PL (Programmable Logic) via HP (High Performance) AXI ports achieves full wire-speed encryption for a 10GbE line card.

docs.title: 18.6 SoC Crypto Accelerator Architecture
docs.text: Figure 18.2. SoC cryptographic accelerator architecture. The crypto engine (e.g., NXP CAAM) is memory-mapped via AXI-Lite for CSR access and uses DMA for bulk data movement. Sub-engines (AES, SHA, PKA, TRNG) share a key store backed by eFUSE and BBRAM. Interrupt-driven completion avoids polling overhead.
