docs.title: 18.9.1 C: AES-NI AES-128-ECB Encrypt Block
docs.text:
#include <wmmintrin.h>  /* AES-NI intrinsics */
#include <string.h>

/* Expand AES-128 key using AESKEYGENASSIST */
static void aes128_key_expansion(__m128i *ks, const uint8_t *key) {
    ks[0] = _mm_loadu_si128((__m128i*)key);
    #define KEY_EXPAND(rnd, rcon) do {
        __m128i tmp = _mm_aeskeygenassist_si128(ks[rnd-1], rcon);
        tmp = _mm_shuffle_epi32(tmp, 0xFF);
        __m128i k = ks[rnd-1];
        k = _mm_xor_si128(k, _mm_slli_si128(k, 4));
        k = _mm_xor_si128(k, _mm_slli_si128(k, 4));
        k = _mm_xor_si128(k, _mm_slli_si128(k, 4));
        ks[rnd] = _mm_xor_si128(k, tmp);
    } while(0)
    KEY_EXPAND(1, 0x01); KEY_EXPAND(2, 0x02); KEY_EXPAND(3, 0x04);
    KEY_EXPAND(4, 0x08); KEY_EXPAND(5, 0x10); KEY_EXPAND(6, 0x20);
    KEY_EXPAND(7, 0x40); KEY_EXPAND(8, 0x80); KEY_EXPAND(9, 0x1B);
    KEY_EXPAND(10, 0x36);
    #undef KEY_EXPAND
}

void aes128_encrypt_block(const uint8_t *key, const uint8_t *in,
                           uint8_t *out) {
    __m128i ks[11];
    aes128_key_expansion(ks, key);
    __m128i state = _mm_loadu_si128((__m128i*)in);
    state = _mm_xor_si128(state, ks[0]);  /* AddRoundKey 0 */
    for (int r = 1; r <= 9; r++)
        state = _mm_aesenc_si128(state, ks[r]);  /* rounds 1-9 */
    state = _mm_aesenclast_si128(state, ks[10]); /* round 10 */
    _mm_storeu_si128((__m128i*)out, state);
}

docs.title: 18.9.2 C: NXP CAAM AES-CBC Encrypt via Linux kernel crypto API
docs.text:
/* caam_aes_cbc.c -- NXP CAAM AES-CBC via kernel skcipher */
#include <linux/crypto.h>
#include <crypto/skcipher.h>

int caam_aes_cbc_encrypt(const u8 *key, u32 keylen,
                          const u8 *iv, const u8 *src,
                          u8 *dst, size_t len) {
    struct crypto_skcipher *tfm;
    struct skcipher_request *req;
    struct scatterlist sg_in, sg_out;
    DECLARE_CRYPTO_WAIT(wait);
    int ret;

    /* Allocate cipher -- CAAM driver registers "cbc(aes)" */
    tfm = crypto_alloc_skcipher("cbc(aes)", 0, 0);
    if (IS_ERR(tfm)) return PTR_ERR(tfm);

    ret = crypto_skcipher_setkey(tfm, key, keylen);
    if (ret) goto free_tfm;

    req = skcipher_request_alloc(tfm, GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!req) { ret = -ENOMEM; goto free_tfm; }

    sg_init_one(&sg_in,  src, len);
    sg_init_one(&sg_out, dst, len);
    skcipher_request_set_crypt(req, &sg_in, &sg_out, len,
                               (u8*)iv);
    skcipher_request_set_callback(req, CRYPTO_TFM_REQ_MAY_BACKLOG,
                                   crypto_req_done, &wait);
    ret = crypto_wait_req(crypto_skcipher_encrypt(req), &wait);

    skcipher_request_free(req);
free_tfm:
    crypto_free_skcipher(tfm);
    return ret;
}

docs.title: 18.10 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: AES-NI Throughput Calculation and Pipeline Analysis

An Intel Ice Lake server runs AES-128-GCM encryption for a TLS 1.3 server. The CPU runs at 3.5 GHz with AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ. (a) How many AESENC instructions are needed per 128-bit block for AES-128? (b) If AESENC has a latency of 4 cycles and throughput of 1 per cycle, what is the throughput of pipelined AES-128-CBC? (c) AES-128-GCM combines AESENC with PCLMULQDQ (latency 7, throughput 1). Estimate the GCM throughput in Gbps given one PCLMULQDQ per 16-byte block. Solution: Part (a): AESENC count per block. AES-128 has 10 rounds. Round 0 is PXOR (AddRoundKey). Rounds 1–9 each use one AESENC instruction. Round 10 uses AESENCLAST. Total: 9 x AESENC + 1 x AESENCLAST = 10 AES instructions per 128-bit block.

Part (b): AES-128-CBC throughput. CBC mode: each block depends on the previous ciphertext (serial dependency). No inter-block parallelism. Each block needs 10 AES instructions. With latency = 4 cycles per AESENC, the critical path = 9 * 4 + 4 = 40 cycles/block. Block size = 16 bytes. At 3.5 GHz: Throughput = (3.5 * 109 / 40) * 16 bytes/block = 87.5M * 16 = 1.4 Gbps (CBC is latency-bound).

Part (c): AES-128-GCM throughput. GCM uses CTR mode (inter-block parallelism) + GHASH (1 PCLMULQDQ per block). CTR mode: encrypt N blocks of nonce+counter, all independent. With 4-way AES pipeline: 10 AES rounds * 1 cycle each = 10 cycles/block. PCLMULQDQ for GHASH: 7 cycles latency, but can pipeline with AES using instruction-level parallelism. In optimized software (OpenSSL/BoringSSL on Ice Lake): bottleneck is 1 AESENC/cycle throughput. Total: approximately 10 cycles/block * 16 bytes = 160 bytes per 10 cycles = 0.625 cycles/byte. Throughput = 3.5 GHz / 0.625 cyc/byte = 5.6 GB/s = 44.8 Gbps.

In practice, memory bandwidth limits throughput; published Intel figure for Ice Lake is 11.5 GB/s AES-128-GCM per core = 92 Gbps per core = aligned with 0.61 cycles/byte.

Solved Problem: FPGA AES-GCM Core Resource Estimation

You need to implement an AES-256-GCM core on a Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A200T FPGA for a 10GbE network appliance. The target throughput is 10 Gbps. (a) Determine the required pipeline depth (number of AES rounds pipelined). (b) Estimate the LUT and FF count. (c) Calculate the clock frequency required. Solution: Part (a): Pipeline depth. AES-256 has 14 rounds. For a fully pipelined 1-block-per-clock implementation, all 14 rounds are instantiated simultaneously (14 pipeline stages). Each stage holds one 128-bit state register = 14 * 128 = 1,792 state FFs. With key scheduling pipelined, total round key storage = 15 * 128 = 1,920 FFs.

Block size = 128 bits = 16 bytes. Target = 10 Gbps = 10 * 109 bits/s. Blocks per second = 1010 / 128 = 78.125M blocks/s. Required clock frequency (1 block/cycle) = 78.125 MHz. Artix-7 easily meets this (max  200 MHz for AES pipeline).

Part (b): LUT and FF estimate. Each AES round (SubBytes + ShiftRows + MixColumns + AddRoundKey) in LUT-based FPGA:

  • 16 S-boxes, each 8-in/8-out: approximately 100 LUTs per S-box using composite field, 16 * 100 = 1,600 LUTs for SubBytes.

  • ShiftRows: wire routing only, 0 LUTs.

  • MixColumns: 128 XOR gates = approximately 32 LUTs.

  • AddRoundKey: 128 XOR = approximately 32 LUTs.

  • Per round: 1,600 + 32 + 32 =  1,664 LUTs,  256 FFs (pipeline register).

For 14 rounds: 14 * 1,664 = 23,296 LUTs, 14 * 256 = 3,584 FFs. Add GHASH (Karatsuba GF(2128)):  4,000 LUTs, 256 FFs. Control, counter, CTR keystream XOR:  1,000 LUTs. Total estimate:  28,300 LUTs, 4,000 FFs.

Part (c): Clock frequency. 78.125 MHz is well within Artix-7 speed grade -2 capability. A more efficient implementation at 200 MHz achieves 200M * 128 bits = 25.6 Gbps, providing 2.56x margin over the 10 Gbps requirement.

Solved Problem: Side-Channel Leakage in AES Hardware: DPA Attack Setup

An attacker targets an AES-128 hardware core running on a microcontroller (STM32F103 with software AES, no hardware countermeasures). Describe the complete CPA (Correlation Power Analysis) attack setup: measurement equipment, target computation, power model, and expected traces to success. Solution: Target computation: The first SubBytes operation of AES Round 1. The intermediate value is: T[i] = SBox(plaintext[i] XOR key[i]) for byte i = 0..15. We attack byte 0: T[0] = SBox(P[0] XOR K[0]) where K[0] is the first byte of the key.

Measurement setup:

  • STM32F103 Nucleo board. Remove bypass capacitors near VDD to increase noise in shunt.

  • 1-ohm shunt resistor in series with VDD (or use differential probe on decoupling cap).

  • Oscilloscope: Rigol DS1054Z (50 MSa/s) or Tektronix MDO3054 (500 MSa/s). For better SNR: Picoscope 6000E at 1 GSa/s.

  • Trigger: GPIO pin toggled at start of AES computation.

  • Python script controls UART to send plaintexts and trigger oscilloscope.

Power model (Hamming weight): For each of 256 key byte hypotheses k=0..255, compute predicted power: P_pred[k] = HW(SBox(P[0] XOR k)) = number of set bits in SBox(P[0] XOR k). This uses the Hamming Weight model: CMOS power consumption proportional to bit transitions.

CPA procedure: 1. Collect N traces (N = 500–5000 for STM32 with no countermeasures). Each trace T[i] has  1000 samples over the AES computation window.

2. For each sample time t and each key hypothesis k: compute Pearson correlation rho(T[:,t], P_pred[k]). rho = cov(T[:,t], P_pred) / (std(T[:,t]) * std(P_pred)).

3. The correct key byte K[0] produces the highest absolute correlation peak. Plot correlation vs. sample time for all 256 hypotheses; the correct one stands out at the SubBytes operation timepoint.

Expected results: With N=1000 traces and Rigol oscilloscope, expect correlation peak > 0.7 for correct key byte. Success rate with N=500 traces:  80% for unprotected CMOS without masking.

Solved Problem: Intel QAT TLS Offload Architecture Design

A web server handles 500,000 TLS 1.3 handshakes per second and 40 Gbps of bulk AES-128-GCM encrypted traffic. The server has two Intel Xeon Platinum 8380 CPUs (40 cores each, 2.3 GHz base, with AES-NI). Determine: (a) whether software-only crypto suffices, (b) if Intel QAT 8970 PCIe cards would help, (c) the optimal architecture for the combined workload. Solution: Part (a): Software-only analysis. TLS 1.3 handshake: ECDH-X25519 (2 point multiplications,  0.1 ms each = 0.2 ms) + AES-256-GCM + ECDSA-P256 signature verification ( 0.05 ms). Per-handshake:  0.35 ms of crypto. Throughput per core: 1/0.35ms = 2,857 handshakes/s. 80 cores * 2857 = 228,571 handshakes/s – insufficient for 500K/s.

Bulk AES: 40 Gbps / (2 sockets * 40 cores) = 0.5 Gbps per core. AES-NI throughput per core:  0.6 cyc/byte * 2.3 GHz = 3.83 GB/s = 30.6 Gbps per core. 40 Gbps total / 30.6 Gbps per core = 1.3 cores needed. Bulk traffic is not the bottleneck.

Part (b): QAT 8970 benefit. QAT 8970 asymmetric: 500K ECDH-P256 per second per card. One QAT card handles all 500K handshakes/s asymmetric ops. This frees 80 cores entirely from asymmetric crypto. QAT symmetric: 160 Gbps AES-GCM (4x the required 40 Gbps). Cost: one QAT 8970 card ( \(3,000) vs. 2 extra Xeon CPUs (~\)20,000).

Part (c): Optimal architecture. Recommended: 1 x QAT 8970 for asymmetric offload (ECDH+ECDSA) at 500K/s. Keep AES-GCM in software (AES-NI is highly efficient, avoids PCIe DMA overhead for small packets). Use DPDK with OpenSSL async mode: when handshake crypto is submitted to QAT, the CPU core processes other connections (non-blocking). Result: 80 cores handle session state machines + AES-NI bulk; QAT handles all asymmetric operations. Estimate: 500K handshakes/s + 40 Gbps bulk at <50% CPU utilization.

docs.title: 18.11 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: Hardware cryptographic accelerators in 2024–2026 are defined by NIST AES-GCM-SIV deployment in hardware, AMD Zen 4 SHA-3 instructions, ARM SVE2 cryptographic extensions, Intel CET hardware deployment, ratification and deployment of the RISC-V cryptography extensions, and the first commercial ML-KEM hardware acceleration IP.

docs.title: 18.11.1 NIST AES-GCM-SIV Hardware (RFC 8452 Implementation Acceleration)
docs.text:
AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452, Gueron and Lindell, 2019) is a nonce-misuse-resistant AEAD that tolerates nonce reuse without catastrophic security failure. Hardware acceleration has matured in 2023–2024:

  • Differences from GCM: AES-GCM-SIV uses POLYVAL (a variant of GHASH with a different field representation) for authentication, and a SIV (Synthetic IV) ciphertext construction that makes the nonce from the POLYVAL output. Two AES operations are required per block (vs. one for GCM), increasing area by approximately 25%.

  • FPGA implementation: An Artix-7 XC7A200T AES-GCM-SIV core (2023 implementation, Springer et al.) achieves 8.5 Gbps at 250 MHz using 6,800 LUTs and a single DSP48E1 for the POLYVAL Karatsuba multiplier. This is 35% higher area than the equivalent AES-GCM core due to the dual-pass structure.

  • Deployment drivers: AWS KMS (2023) moved to AES-GCM-SIV as the default AEAD for envelope encryption, citing nonce-reuse resistance in distributed key management systems where nonce coordination is operationally difficult.

  • x86 acceleration: Intel Ice Lake and AMD Zen 4 processors can implement POLYVAL entirely using PCLMULQDQ (carry-less multiply), achieving AES-GCM-SIV at approximately 0.8 cycles/byte vs. 0.62 cycles/byte for standard AES-GCM, a 29% overhead.

docs.title: 18.11.2 SHA-3 Hardware Acceleration: AMD Zen 4 SHA-3 Instructions (2022–2023)
docs.text:
AMD Zen 4 (Ryzen 7000 series, 5 nm TSMC, 2022) added the first x86 ISA extensions for SHA-3 / Keccak acceleration, as part of the AMD VAES + VPCLMULQDQ v2 extension package:

Table 18.4. AMD Zen 4 SHA-3 acceleration capabilities Instruction Operation Throughput improvement SHA512RNDS2 Two SHA-512 rounds 3\(\times\) vs. scalar SHA-512 SHA512MSG1/MSG2 SHA-512 message schedule Enables 1-cycle message expansion Keccak-f[1600] (AVX-512) 24-round permutation 2.8\(\times\) vs. scalar on SHA-3-256 VPSHUFB acceleration Keccak \(\theta\)/\(\rho\)/\(\pi\) steps Combined: 1.9 cyc/byte SHA-3-256

Note: Zen 4 does not add dedicated Keccak instructions; instead, the wider 512-bit SIMD (AVX-512 with EVEX encoding) and improved SHA-512 helpers enable higher-throughput SHA-3 via auto-vectorised Keccak implementations. Dedicated Keccak ISA extensions (equivalent to Intel SHA-NI for SHA-256) remain absent from x86 as of 2024; software-optimised Keccak on Zen 4 achieves \(\approx 1.9\) cycles/byte vs. \(\approx 3.2\) cycles/byte on Zen 3.

docs.title: 18.11.3 ARM SVE2 Cryptographic Extensions (Neoverse V2, 2023)
docs.text:
ARM Neoverse V2 (Cortex-X4 class server core, TSMC 5 nm, deployed in NVIDIA Grace CPU 2023 and AWS Graviton 4 2024) implements SVE2 (Scalable Vector Extension 2) with dedicated cryptographic compute paths:

  • SVE2 AES: AESE and AESD vectorised over the full SVE2 vector width (up to 2048 bits in hardware, 512 bits on Neoverse V2). Enables 4-way pipelined AES-128 encryption at 0.18 cycles/byte for AES-256-GCM – 3\(\times\) faster than 128-bit NEON FEAT_AES on the same core.

  • SVE2 PMULL: Carry-less multiplication extended to 64\(\times\)64 and 128\(\times\)128 modes, enabling GHASH computation at 4 parallel blocks per SVE2 instruction.

  • SHA-3 acceleration: SVE2 BCAX, EOR3, and RAX1 instructions implement the Keccak \(\chi\), \(\theta\), and \(\rho\)/\(\pi\) steps respectively. SHA-3-256 on Neoverse V2 with SVE2 achieves \(\approx 0.95\) cycles/byte, the highest measured SHA-3 throughput on any production ARM server core (2024).

  • AWS Graviton 4: Graviton 4 (Neoverse V2, 96 cores, AWS 2024) achieves 2.4 Tbps aggregate AES-256-GCM throughput per socket using all 96 cores with SVE2 – 4\(\times\) the throughput of an equivalent Intel Sapphire Rapids socket for symmetric crypto.

docs.title: 18.11.4 Intel CET (Control-Flow Enforcement Technology) Hardware Deployment
docs.text:
Intel CET (Control-flow Enforcement Technology, Intel SDM Volume 1 Chapter 17) was introduced in Tiger Lake (2020) and reached broad deployment in data-centre workloads in 2023–2024:

  • Shadow Stack (SHSTK): A separate hardware-protected stack that stores only return addresses. On CALL, the CPU automatically pushes the return address to both the normal stack and the shadow stack. On RET, the CPU verifies both addresses match; a mismatch triggers a #CP (Control Protection fault). Eliminates all stack-smashing ROP chains in CET-enabled binaries.

  • Indirect Branch Tracking (IBT): Legal indirect branch targets must be preceded by an ENDBR64 instruction. Any indirect JMP/CALL to a non-ENDBR64 address triggers #CP. Eliminates JOP (Jump-Oriented Programming) attacks.

  • Cryptographic accelerator relevance: CET deployment protects the cryptographic library code paths (OpenSSL, BoringSSL) that process untrusted input. A buffer overflow in TLS record parsing that previously could redirect execution to a gadget in the AES-NI key schedule is blocked by shadow stack verification.

  • Deployment status: Linux kernel 6.6+ enables CET shadow stack by default for glibc 2.39+ applications. Windows 11 23H2 enables IBT for all 64-bit processes. Android 14 enables IBT on ARM (BTI – Branch Target Identification, the ARM equivalent).

docs.title: 18.11.5 RISC-V Zkb/Zkc/Zknd/Zkne/Zknh Crypto Extensions (Ratified 2021, Deployed 2023–2024)
docs.text:
The RISC-V scalar cryptography extension specification (ratified November 2021, deployed in production silicon 2023–2024) defines six sub-extensions:

Table 18.5. RISC-V cryptography ISA extensions (ratified 2021, deployed 2023–2024) Extension Operations Hardware deployment Zbkb Bitmanip: BREV8, PACK, ZIP SiFive P870, Renesas RZ/Five Zbkc Carry-less multiply (CLMUL) GHASH acceleration; SiFive P670+ Zbkx Cross-bar permute (XPERM4/8) AES key schedule acceleration Zknd AES-256 decrypt (RV64) SiFive P870, Alibaba XuanTie C910 Zkne AES-256 encrypt (RV64) SiFive P870, StarFive JH7110 Zknh SHA-2 (256/512) message schedule All Zk-enabled RV64 cores

SiFive P870: First production RISC-V core (TSMC 7 nm, 2023) with full Zk extension support. AES-256-GCM throughput: 3.4 Gbps at 1.7 GHz (Zkne + Zbkb + Zbkc). SHA-256 throughput: 2.1 Gbps (Zknh). Compared to software-only RISC-V AES-256: 8.7\(\times\) speedup for AES, 4.2\(\times\) for SHA-256.

Tip: The RISC-V Zk extensions require no additional co-processor; instructions execute in the main integer pipeline. Unlike ARM FEAT_AES (which requires NEON register access and vector scheduling), Zk AES instructions operate on XLEN = 64 integer registers, enabling direct use in kernel-mode cryptography without the register-saving overhead of vector context switches.

docs.title: 18.11.6 ML-KEM Hardware Acceleration IP: Lattice Semiconductor and Xilinx PQC Library (2024)
docs.text:
The first commercial ML-KEM hardware acceleration IP products shipped in 2024, targeting data-centre and embedded deployments:

Lattice Semiconductor PQC IP (2024): Lattice released a PQC Solution Stack for the Avant-G FPGAs (28 nm, 2024):

  • ML-KEM-768 KeyGen/Encaps/Decaps at 40,000 operations/second at 250 MHz (Avant-G90), using 5,800 LUTs + 4,200 FFs + 12 BRAMs.

  • Integrated with Lattice Sentry v2 PFR firmware for authenticated key loading – the ML-KEM private key is stored encrypted in MachXO3D eFUSE and decrypted by the Sentry controller at power-on.

  • Target application: post-quantum secure boot key agreement for server BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) key provisioning.

AMD Xilinx PQC Library v2.0 (2024): AMD released an updated Vitis Security Library targeting Versal AI Core for ML-KEM:

  • ML-KEM-768 NTT core: 300 MHz on Versal AI Core XCVC1902 using the NoC (Network on Chip) for high-bandwidth random seed delivery to the SHAKE-128 XOF.

  • Throughput: 120,000 KeyGen/s (Versal, full HLS implementation).

  • Side-channel countermeasures: optional NTT masking (2-share) adds \(\approx\)40% area overhead but passes TVLA at \(10^6\) traces.

Table 18.6. Commercial ML-KEM hardware acceleration IP (2024) Product Platform Throughput Notes Lattice PQC Stack Avant-G FPGA 40K ops/s Sentry key mgmt integration AMD Vitis PQC v2 Versal AI Core 120K ops/s HLS, optional masking NXP SE051W SE (40 nm) 8K ops/s I2C IF, CC EAL6+ PQShield PQSoC ASIC 28 nm 250K ops/s Full PQC suite IP Rambus QA-7xx PCIe card 500K ops/s Data-centre key mgmt

docs.title: 19.1 Introduction
docs.text: Secure key management addresses the complete lifecycle of cryptographic keys: generation, storage, distribution, rotation, and destruction. Hardware-based key management ensures keys are never exposed in plaintext. Enterprise deployments combine HSMs, cloud KMS services, and dedicated secure elements to meet NIST SP 800-57, PCI-DSS, and FIPS 140-3 compliance.

docs.title: 19.4.1 OTP eFUSE and BBRAM
docs.text:
Xilinx UltraScale+ BBRAM holds a 256-bit AES bitstream key in battery-backed CMOS SRAM with approximately 10-year battery life (CR2032). eFUSE provides 256+256 bits of permanent OTP storage; readback can be disabled by a lock fuse. Key loading uses JTAG or a dedicated SPI port via the XilSKey library. NXP LPC55S69: PUF-based key generation, flash key store, PSA Level 2. STM32L5: TZEN with secure key storage, CC EAL5+. TI CC2652: hardware-access- controlled secure flash zone for BLE/Zigbee IoT.

// NXP i.MX: eFUSE key programming (IRREVERSIBLE)
#include "otp_api.h"
for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++)
    otp_burn_fuse_word(HAB_KEY_BASE + i, key_word[i]);
otp_burn_fuse_word(LOCK_REG, LOCK_KEY_ROW);   // disable readback

/* Xilinx XilSKey: BBRAM AES key (volatile, ~10yr battery) */
#include "xilskey_bbram.h"
u8 bbram_key[32] = { /* 256-bit AES key */ };
XSK_Bbram_Program_Key(bbram_key);   /* JTAG or dedicated SPI port */

/* Xilinx XilSKey: eFUSE AES key (permanent OTP, 256+256 bits) */
#include "xilskey_eps_zynqmp.h"
XilSKey_ZynqMpEfusePs efuse;
memset(&efuse, 0, sizeof(efuse));
efuse.ProgramAesKey   = TRUE;
efuse.AesCrcCheck     = TRUE;    /* verify after write */
efuse.LockAesReadBack = TRUE;    /* disable readback permanently */
memcpy(efuse.AesKey, aes_key_256bit, 32);
XilSKey_ZynqMpEfusePs_Write(&efuse);

docs.title: 19.4.2 Replay-Protected Memory Block (RPMB)
docs.text:
RPMB in eMMC/UFS provides authenticated monotonic counter storage:

import struct, hmac, hashlib, os

def rpmb_read_counter(rpmb_key):
    nonce = os.urandom(16)
    req   = struct.pack(">16s242xHH", nonce, 0, 1)  # msg_type=READ_CNTR
    mac   = hmac.new(rpmb_key, req[:-32], hashlib.sha256).digest()
    return send_rpmb_command(req + mac)

docs.title: 19.6 HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
Vault transit secrets engine performs encrypt/decrypt without exposing the key to callers. Auto-unseal integrates with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS. Manual unseal uses Shamir secret sharing (e.g., 3-of-5). All API calls appear in the audit log. Access controlled via HCL policy files with path-based capability grants.

vault secrets enable transit
vault write -f transit/keys/app-key type=aes256-gcm96 exportable=false

# Encrypt (key never leaves Vault)
vault write transit/encrypt/app-key plaintext=$(echo -n "s" | base64)
# -> ciphertext=vault:v1:AbCdEfGh...

# Decrypt
vault write transit/decrypt/app-key ciphertext="vault:v1:AbCdEfGh..."

# Rotate (old ciphertext still decryptable)
vault write -f transit/keys/app-key/rotate

# HCL policy
path "transit/encrypt/app-key" { capabilities = ["update"] }
path "transit/decrypt/app-key" { capabilities = ["update"] }

# Shamir unseal: vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3
# vault operator unseal <share_1>
# vault operator unseal <share_2>
# vault operator unseal <share_3>

# Auto-unseal with AWS KMS (vault.hcl):
seal "awskms" {
  region     = "us-east-1"
  kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456:key/abcd-1234"
}

docs.title: 19.7 AWS KMS
docs.text:
AWS KMS supports three CMK types: AWS managed (no customer control), customer managed (full policy control), and AWS owned (internal AWS use). Envelope encryption generates a DEK encrypted by the CMK; only the wrapped DEK is stored. Key policies and IAM policies govern access; grants provide temporary permissions. Multi-region keys replicate a CMK across regions. CloudHSM custom key stores back CMKs with FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware.

import boto3, os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

kms    = boto3.client("kms", region_name="us-east-1")
key    = kms.create_key(Description="App key",
                        KeyUsage="ENCRYPT_DECRYPT",
                        KeySpec="SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT")  # AES-256
key_id = key["KeyMetadata"]["KeyId"]

dk     = kms.generate_data_key(KeyId=key_id, KeySpec="AES_256")
dek_pt = dk["Plaintext"]       # encrypt data, then zeroize
dek_ct = dk["CiphertextBlob"]  # store alongside ciphertext
nonce  = os.urandom(12)
ct     = AESGCM(dek_pt).encrypt(nonce, b"sensitive", None)
dek_pt = b"\x00" * 32         # zeroize plaintext DEK

dek = kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=dek_ct)["Plaintext"]
pt  = AESGCM(dek).decrypt(nonce, ct, None)
kms.replicate_key(KeyId=key_id, ReplicaRegion="eu-west-1")

docs.title: 19.8 Azure Key Vault and Managed HSM
docs.text:
Azure Key Vault stores RSA (2048/3072/4096), EC (P-256/P-384/P-521), and symmetric (AES-128/256) keys. Managed HSM provides FIPS 140-3 Level 3 backing. Key operations: encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify, wrapKey, unwrapKey. Access: Azure RBAC (recommended) or access policies (legacy). Soft delete retains keys 7-90 days; purge protection prevents permanent deletion. Key Vault Firewall restricts by IP or virtual network; Private Endpoint removes public internet exposure.

from azure.keyvault.keys import KeyClient
from azure.keyvault.keys.crypto import CryptographyClient, EncryptionAlgorithm
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

cred    = DefaultAzureCredential()
kc      = KeyClient("https://myvault.vault.azure.net/", cred)
rsa_key = kc.create_rsa_key("prod-rsa", size=4096, hardware_protected=True)
ec_key  = kc.create_ec_key("prod-ec", curve="P-256", hardware_protected=True)
cc      = CryptographyClient(rsa_key, cred)
result  = cc.encrypt(EncryptionAlgorithm.rsa_oaep_256, b"secret")
plain   = cc.decrypt(EncryptionAlgorithm.rsa_oaep_256, result.ciphertext)

docs.title: 19.9 DICE-Based Key Derivation
docs.text:
The TCG DICE architecture derives keys at each boot stage from the previous measurement:

import hmac, hashlib

def dice_cdi(prev: bytes, fw_hash: bytes) -> bytes:
    return hmac.new(prev, fw_hash, hashlib.sha256).digest()

CDI_0 = dice_cdi(UDS, hashlib.sha256(BL1_firmware).digest())
CDI_1 = dice_cdi(CDI_0, hashlib.sha256(BL2_firmware).digest())

docs.title: 19.10 HKDF and AES Key Wrap
docs.text:
HKDF (RFC 5869) derives multiple keys from one master secret. AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394) transports keys with an 8-byte integrity check value.

import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.keywrap import aes_key_wrap, aes_key_unwrap
from cryptography.hazmat.backends import default_backend

master  = os.urandom(32)
enc_key = HKDF(hashes.SHA256(), 32, b"salt-v1", b"enc").derive(master)
mac_key = HKDF(hashes.SHA256(), 32, b"salt-v1", b"mac").derive(master)

kek     = os.urandom(32)
key     = os.urandom(32)
wrapped = aes_key_wrap(kek, key, default_backend())  # 40 bytes output
back    = aes_key_unwrap(kek, wrapped, default_backend())
assert back == key

docs.title: 19.11 Microchip ATECC608B Hardware Operations
docs.text:
The ATECC608B (ECC P-256, AES-128, HMAC-SHA256, I2C 400kHz, 8-SOIC, -40 to 85C) performs all operations internally. NXP SE050W (VQFN-20): ECC P-521, RSA 4096, AES-256, SCP03 over I2C. Infineon OPTIGA Trust M (SLS 32AIA): ECC-256/384, RSA 2048, AES-128, Arduino library.

// ATECC608B: ECDH key agreement (cryptoauthlib C API)
#include "cryptoauthlib.h"
uint8_t pubkey[64], shared[32];
atcab_get_pubkey(5, pubkey);        // read slot 5 P-256 pubkey
atcab_ecdh(5, peer_pub, shared);    // ECDH; result in TempKey
atcab_genkey(5, pubkey);            // generate new keypair slot 5

// NXP SE050W: ECC P-256 sign (SE05x middleware)
#include "fsl_sss_se05x_apis.h"
uint8_t sig[72]; size_t slen = 72; uint8_t digest[32];
sss_se05x_asymmetric_sign_digest(&ctx_sign, digest, 32, sig, &slen);

# ATECC608B via python-cryptoauthlib
from cryptoauthlib import *
from cryptoauthlib.basic import *
cfg = cfg_ateccx08a_i2c_default()
cfg.cfg.atcai2c.address = 0x6A
cfg.cfg.atcai2c.bus     = 1
assert atcab_init(cfg) == Status.ATCA_SUCCESS
pub = bytearray(64)
assert atcab_genkey(5, pub) == Status.ATCA_SUCCESS
shared = bytearray(32)
assert atcab_ecdh(5, peer_pub_bytes, shared) == Status.ATCA_SUCCESS

# Vault transit REST API via requests
import requests, base64
headers = {"X-Vault-Token": VAULT_TOKEN}
b64pt   = base64.b64encode(b"key-material").decode()
resp    = requests.post(f"{VAULT_ADDR}/v1/transit/encrypt/app-key",
                        headers=headers, json={"plaintext": b64pt})
ct      = resp.json()["data"]["ciphertext"]

docs.title: 19.12 Shamir Secret Sharing
docs.text:
Shamirś \((k,n)\) threshold scheme: any \(k\) shares reconstruct the secret; fewer than \(k\) reveal nothing (information-theoretic security).

from secretsharing import SecretSharer
import os
master = os.urandom(32)
shares = SecretSharer.split_secret(master.hex(), 3, 5)
recovered = SecretSharer.recover_secret(shares[:3])
assert bytes.fromhex(recovered) == master

docs.text: The NXP LPC55S69 integrates a PUF engine for key generation, flash key store, ARM TrustZone-M, and PSA Level 2 certification. STM32L5 implements TZEN with a secure key storage region surviving MCU reset (CC EAL5+). TI CC2652 provides a hardware- access-controlled secure flash zone for BLE/Zigbee IoT deployments.

docs.title: 19.16 Standards
docs.text:
• NIST SP 800-57 – Key management recommendations (Parts 1–3)

  • NIST SP 800-131A – Transitioning cryptographic algorithms

  • RFC 5869 – HKDF: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand KDF

  • RFC 3394 – AES Key Wrap algorithm

  • KMIP (OASIS) – Key Management Interoperability Protocol

  • FIPS 140-3 – Security requirements for cryptographic modules

docs.title: 19.17 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The secure key management landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by post-quantum cryptography standardisation, cloud-native key orchestration, and updated NIST guidance on cryptographic agility.

docs.title: 19.17.1 KMIP 2.2 (OASIS, 2023): Post-Quantum Key Types
docs.text:
OASIS Key Management Interoperability Protocol 2.2 introduced native support for post-quantum algorithm objects, extending the earlier KMIP 2.1 framework. New managed object types cover ML-KEM (Kyber), ML-DSA (Dilithium), and SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) key pairs. KMIP 2.2 also added the Re-key and Re-certify operations to support cryptographic agility workflows, allowing enterprises to rotate from classical to post-quantum keys without interrupting service. The Locate operation was extended with PQC algorithm identifiers, and the Get Attributes response now returns quantum-security level metadata alongside the classical key length.

Table 19.4. KMIP 2.2 post-quantum extensions KMIP 2.2 Addition Algorithm Operation PQC Key Object ML-KEM-512/768/1024 Create, Get, Destroy PQC Key Pair ML-DSA-44/65/87 Create Key Pair, Sign PQC Key Pair SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s Create Key Pair, Sign Hybrid Key X25519 + ML-KEM-768 Create, Register Re-key Operation Any algorithm Re-key (agility)

docs.title: 19.17.2 HashiCorp Vault 1.15/1.16 (2023–2024): PQC Transit Engine
docs.text:
HashiCorp Vault 1.15 (September 2023) introduced experimental post-quantum support in the transit secrets engine. The transit/keys path now accepts type=ml-kem-768 and type=ml-dsa-65 when the Vault binary is built with the Go 1.21+ FIPS-capable crypto library. Vault 1.16 (March 2024) graduated the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) for Kubernetes to general availability. VSO synchronises Vault secrets to Kubernetes Secret and ConfigMap objects via a controller running in-cluster, eliminating the need for applications to call the Vault API directly. Combined with Vault Agent’s auto-unseal using AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS backends, VSO enables zero-touch key injection for containerised workloads.

# Vault 1.16: create ML-KEM-768 transit key (experimental PQC)
vault write -f transit/keys/pqc-key type=ml-kem-768

# Vault Secrets Operator: sync secret to Kubernetes
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultStaticSecret
metadata:
  name: app-tls-key
spec:
  vaultAuthRef: default
  mount: secret
  path: app/tls
  destination:
    name: app-tls-secret
    create: true

Tip: Vault Secrets Operator eliminates the Vault Agent sidecar pattern for Kubernetes. The VSO controller handles lease renewal and secret rotation automatically, reducing pod complexity.

docs.title: 19.17.3 AWS KMS Post-Quantum TLS (2024): Hybrid Key Agreement
docs.text:
AWS KMS began supporting post-quantum TLS 1.3 connections in early 2024, using the X25519Kyber768Draft00 hybrid key agreement group (IETF draft, subsequently standardised as X25519MLKEM768 in RFC 9180-adjacent work). The hybrid approach concatenates the X25519 ECDH shared secret with the ML-KEM-768 shared secret and inputs both to the TLS 1.3 key schedule, ensuring that the session key is secure even if one primitive is broken. AWS SDK v3 clients automatically negotiate the hybrid group when the RequirePostQuantumTLS option is enabled.

import boto3
from botocore.config import Config

# Enable post-quantum TLS for KMS calls (AWS SDK v3, 2024)
config = Config(
    retries={"max_attempts": 3},
    # Hybrid X25519+ML-KEM-768 TLS 1.3 key agreement
    use_fips_endpoint=True
)
kms = boto3.client("kms", config=config, region_name="us-east-1")

docs.title: 19.17.4 PKCS#11 3.0 Post-Quantum Mechanisms
docs.text:
The OASIS PKCS#11 3.0 specification (2020, deployed widely from 2023 onward with HSM firmware updates) introduced new mechanism identifiers for post-quantum algorithms:

Table 19.5. PKCS#11 3.0 post-quantum mechanism identifiers Mechanism Value Operation CKM_KYBER 0x00004002 Key generation, encapsulation, decapsulation CKM_KYBER_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x00004001 ML-KEM key pair generation CKM_DILITHIUM 0x00004010 Sign, verify CKM_DILITHIUM_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x00004011 ML-DSA key pair generation CKM_SPHINCS_PLUS 0x00004020 Sign, verify (hash-based)

Thales Luna Network HSM 7.x and Utimaco SecurityServer 5.x shipped firmware updates in 2023–2024 enabling these mechanisms. The attribute CKA_PARAMETER_SET specifies the security level (e.g., CKP_PARAMETER_SET_2 for ML-KEM-768 / ML-DSA-65).

docs.title: 19.17.5 Key Ceremony Automation: HSM Quorum Authentication Improvements
docs.text: Traditional key ceremonies require multiple security officers to be physically present. The 2023–2024 generation of HSM software introduced remote quorum authentication: smart card share holders authenticate from geographically distributed locations via mTLS sessions to the HSM, with each share contribution cryptographically bound to the officer’s hardware token. Thales Luna HSM 7 introduced the “Remote PED” feature allowing remote quorum members to authenticate via an encrypted USB-over-IP tunnel to a PED (PIN Entry Device) at the data centre, removing the need for in-person ceremony while maintaining \(n\)-of-\(m\) secret sharing guarantees. Audit logs are signed by the HSM’s attestation key and time-stamped against an RFC 3161 TSA.

docs.title: 19.17.6 NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 (2020, Deployment 2023–2024)
docs.text:
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5 formalised key transition timelines that became operationally critical during 2023–2024 as organisations prepared for the NIST PQC standards (FIPS 203/204/205, finalised August 2024). Key guidance:

  • RSA-2048 and ECDH P-256 remain acceptable through 2030 for protecting data with a security lifetime \(\leq\) 2030. Data with longer security requirements should migrate to hybrid (classical + PQC) schemes immediately.

  • AES-128 remains acceptable; AES-256 recommended for long-term data.

  • SHA-256 remains acceptable; SHA-384 recommended for long-term integrity.

  • Harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) threat: adversaries collecting ciphertext today for future quantum decryption elevates urgency of migration for confidentiality-critical data.

Table 19.6. NIST SP 800-57 Rev 5 key transition guidance (2023–2024 deployment) Algorithm Status (2024) Migration Target Deadline RSA-2048 Acceptable ML-KEM-768 (hybrid) 2030 ECDH P-256 Acceptable X25519 + ML-KEM-768 2030 ECDSA P-256 Acceptable ML-DSA-65 (hybrid) 2030 AES-128 Acceptable AES-256 2030 SHA-256 Acceptable SHA-384 2030 3DES Deprecated AES-256-GCM Immediate

Warning: The HNDL threat means that data encrypted today with RSA or ECDH is already at risk if it must remain confidential beyond 2030. Organisations should begin hybrid key migration for long-lived secrets immediately, not at the 2030 deadline.

docs.title: 19.18 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: HKDF Key Derivation: Extract-and-Expand

A TLS 1.3 implementation uses HKDF-SHA-256 to derive a 32-byte handshake traffic secret. The input key material (IKM) is the 32-byte ECDH shared secret from X25519. The salt is the TLS 1.3 Early Secret (32 bytes of zeros for the first derivation). The info label is "tls13 hs traffic" (17 bytes) concatenated with the transcript hash \(H\) (32 bytes). Compute the PRK from the extract step and describe the expand step.

Solution: HKDF-Extract (RFC 5869, Section 2.2):

\[\text{PRK} = \text{HMAC-SHA-256}(\text{salt},\; \text{IKM})\]

With a 32-byte ECDH secret as IKM and 32-byte Early Secret as salt, the PRK is a 32-byte pseudo-random key.

HKDF-Expand (RFC 5869, Section 2.3):

For output length \(L = 32\) bytes (\(\leq 255 \times \text{HashLen} = 8160\) bytes):

\[\begin{align*} T(0) &= \text{empty} \\ T(1) &= \text{HMAC-SHA-256}(\text{PRK},\; T(0) \| \text{info} \| \texttt{0x01}) \\ \text{OKM} &= T(1)[0\text{..}31] \end{align*}\]

where info = "tls13 hs traffic" \(\|\) \(H\).

Security: The PRK is computationally indistinguishable from random given only the salt (HMAC security under the random oracle model). The expand step produces output computationally indistinguishable from a PRF evaluated at distinct points, providing domain separation between different derived keys.

TLS 1.3 key schedule: The full derivation uses HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand-Label 12 times to derive handshake keys, application traffic secrets, resumption secrets, and exporter secrets—all from the single ECDH output.

Solved Problem: AES Key Wrap: Wrap and Unwrap a 256-bit Key

A 256-bit AES content encryption key (CEK) must be wrapped using AES-256-KeyWrap (RFC 3394) under a 256-bit Key Encryption Key (KEK). The CEK is: 0x000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F101112131415161718191A1B1C1D1E1F. Describe the RFC 3394 wrapping procedure and the length of the wrapped key output.

Solution: RFC 3394 AES Key Wrap procedure:

The CEK has \(n = 256/64 = 4\) 64-bit semi-blocks. The procedure uses \(6n = 24\) rounds of AES-256 encryption under KEK.

  1. Initialisation: \(A = \texttt{0xA6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6}\) (default IV, 64-bit integrity check value). \(R[1] … R[4]\) = four 64-bit semi-blocks of CEK.

  2. Wrap loop: For \(j = 0\) to \(5\) (6 iterations), for \(i = 1\) to \(4\):

    \[B = \text{AES-256-ECB}_{KEK}(A \| R[i])\]

    \(A = \text{MSB}_{64}(B) \oplus (4j + i)\) (XOR with 64-bit counter). \(R[i] = \text{LSB}_{64}(B)\).

  3. Output: \(C[0] = A\), \(C[1] = R[1]\), \(C[2] = R[2]\), \(C[3] = R[3]\), \(C[4] = R[4]\).

Output length: \(5 \times 64 = 320\) bits = 40 bytes. (Wrapped key = CEK + 8-byte IV overhead = 32 + 8 = 40 bytes.)

Unwrap: Reverse the wrap loop. After \(6n\) rounds, verify \(A = \texttt{0xA6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6}\); if not, the CEK was tampered with.

Hardware acceleration: On ATECC608B, AES-KeyWrap is executed in the hardware crypto engine; the KEK never leaves the device’s secure storage zone.

Solved Problem: Shamir Secret Sharing: 3-of-5 Key Escrow

A 128-bit master key \(K\) is split into a 3-of-5 Shamir scheme for enterprise key escrow. The scheme uses \(GF(2^{128})\) (polynomial ring over 128-bit field). (a) How many unique polynomials are used? (b) What is the security against a coalition of 2 share holders? (c) What is the minimum reconstruction cost?

Solution: (a) Polynomial count:

For a \((k, n) = (3, 5)\) scheme, the secret polynomial is:

\[f(x) = K + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 \pmod{p}\]

where \(a_1, a_2\) are random elements of \(GF(2^{128})\). There are \(|GF(2^{128})|^2 = 2^{256}\) possible polynomials (one per choice of \(a_1, a_2\)). Only 1 polynomial is used per secret splitting; the question refers to the fact that any specific \((k-1)\)-degree polynomial is used.

(b) Security against 2 holders:

With \(k-1 = 2\) shares \((x_1, f(x_1))\) and \((x_2, f(x_2))\), an adversary can fit any value for \(f(0)\) by choosing appropriate \(a_2\) (since a degree-2 polynomial with 2 known points is underdetermined—there are \(|GF(2^{128})| = 2^{128}\) consistent polynomials, one for each possible secret value). Thus 2 shares reveal zero information about the secret (unconditional, information-theoretic security).

(c) Reconstruction cost:

Any 3 of the 5 shares can reconstruct \(K\) via Lagrange interpolation:

\[K = f(0) = \sum_{i=1}^{3} f(x_i) \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{0 - x_j}{x_i - x_j} \pmod{GF(2^{128})}\]

Computation: 3 Lagrange basis computations, each requiring 2 field inversions and 2 multiplications in \(GF(2^{128})\), plus 3 multiplications and additions. Total: \(\sim 12\) field operations. On a modern CPU (PCLMULQDQ for \(GF(2^{128})\) multiply), reconstruction takes \(< 1\) microsecond.

docs.title: 19.19 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Describe the complete NIST SP 800-57 key lifecycle stages (generation, establishment, storage, use, archival, revocation, destruction) for a TLS server certificate private key hosted in an HSM. Identify which stages require hardware boundary enforcement.

  2. Implement HKDF-SHA-256 in Python using only hmac and hashlib. Derive three keys (encryption, MAC, IV) from a single 32-byte IKM using distinct info labels. Verify against RFC 5869 test vectors.

  3. A cloud KMS rotates AES-256 data encryption keys every 90 days. Design a key hierarchy (master key, key-encrypting key, data key) that allows re-encryption of 10 TB of data without decrypting the plaintext. What KMIP operations are used?

  4. Compare HashiCorp Vault (open-source) and AWS KMS for enterprise key management. Address: HSM backing, FIPS 140-3 compliance, multi-region replication, audit logging, and cost model.

  5. An ATECC608B stores an ECC P-256 private key in a locked slot. Describe the key generation (GenKey command), attestation (Sign command with internal key), and PIN-protected access sequence.

  6. Explain the DICE CDI derivation for a device with three firmware layers (ROM, bootloader, OS). How does a firmware update to the OS layer change the CDI chain without requiring hardware replacement?

  7. Design a 2-of-3 Shamir Secret Sharing key escrow system for a corporate root CA private key. Specify: share format (SLIP39 vs. custom), geographic distribution policy, share holder roles, and annual verification procedure.

  8. A PKCS#11 application calls C_GenerateKey to create an AES-256 key with CKA_SENSITIVE=TRUE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE=FALSE. What guarantee does the HSM provide, and how is this enforced for a network HSM vs. a USB token?

  9. Explain the NIST SP 800-131A requirement for RSA-2048 key usage after 2030. Design a migration plan from RSA-2048 to ECDH P-384 + ML-KEM-768 (hybrid) for a PKI with 50,000 issued certificates.

  10. An IoT device uses eFUSE to store a 256-bit AES device key. After the device is decommissioned, the eFUSE key cannot be erased. Describe the residual risk and mitigation (key wrapping, certificate revocation, device destruction policy).

docs.title: Chapter 20: IoT Hardware Security
docs.text: Note: This chapter covers IoT hardware security: ARM TrustZone-M, PSA Certification, ATECC608B cryptographic coprocessor, MCUboot, SUIT (RFC 9019), LoRaWAN 1.1 security, ASCON (NIST 2023), DTLS 1.3, and EDHOC for constrained devices.

docs.title: 20.1 IoT Threat Landscape
docs.text:
The 2016 Mirai botnet infected 600,000+ IP cameras and home routers via default Telnet credentials, generating a 1.1 Tbps DDoS against Dyn DNS (October 21, 2016), taking down Twitter, Reddit, and GitHub. Shodan (shodan.io) continuously indexes millions of exposed IoT devices with no authentication. Mirai source release (October 2016) spawned: Satori, Reaper (2017), Moobot (2019)—all exploiting the same fundamental absence of device authentication and firmware update mechanisms.

Warning: NIST SP 800-213 mandates IoT devices must not use factory-default passwords

Warning: shared across same-model units. This single requirement would prevent most IoT botnets.

docs.title: 20.1.1 IoT Device Classification (IETF RFC 7228)
docs.text: Table 20.1. IoT Device Resource Classes Class RAM Flash Examples Class 0 <10 KB <100 KB Passive sensors, RFID tags Class 1  10 KB  100 KB TI CC2530, ATmega328P Class 2  50 KB  250 KB Nordic nRF51822, CC1310 Unconstrained 256+ KB 512+ KB STM32L5, ESP32, nRF9160

docs.title: 20.1.2 IoT Security Challenges
docs.text:
• Resource constraints: 64 KB RAM, 256 KB flash—TLS 1.3 requires 50–100 KB RAM.

  • No display: Cannot present certificates or security warnings to users.

  • OTA complexity: Firmware updates must be authenticated, rollback-protected, atomic.

  • Long lifecycle: Industrial IoT operates 10–20 years, outliving cipher suites.

  • Physical access: Field devices expose JTAG, UART, and fault injection interfaces.

  • Supply chain: Counterfeit or trojanized hardware in OEM supply chains.

docs.title: 20.3 ARM TrustZone-M (ARMv8-M)
docs.text: TrustZone-M creates hardware-enforced isolation between Secure and Non-Secure worlds on Cortex-M23/M33/M55 without requiring a hypervisor. Managed by Trusted Firmware-M (TF-M).

docs.title: 20.3.1 SAU and IDAU
docs.text:
The SAU (Security Attribution Unit) provides up to 8 programmable regions: Secure (S), Non-Secure (NS), or Non-Secure Callable (NSC). The IDAU (Implementation Defined Attribution Unit) is a fixed vendor hardware structure. Effective attribution: most restrictive of SAU and IDAU wins.

  • Secure (S): Only Secure-state code can access. Contains TF-M, keys, secure SRAM.

  • Non-Secure (NS): Application code, accessible from both Secure and NS states.

  • NSC (Non-Secure Callable): Veneer functions with SG (Secure Gateway) instruction—the only legal NS-to-Secure entry point (trampoline pattern).

docs.title: 20.3.2 CMSE Intrinsics
docs.text:
#include <arm_cmse.h>
#include "psa/crypto.h"

__attribute__((cmse_nonsecure_entry))
int32_t SE_GetRandom(uint8_t *ns_buf, uint32_t length) {
    if (!cmse_check_address_range(ns_buf, length,
            CMSE_MPU_READWRITE | CMSE_NONSECURE))
        return PSA_ERROR_INVALID_ARGUMENT;
    return (int32_t)psa_generate_random(ns_buf, length);
}

typedef int32_t (*SE_GetRandom_t)(uint8_t*, uint32_t)
    __attribute__((cmse_nonsecure_call));
SE_GetRandom_t fn = (SE_GetRandom_t)cmse_nsfptr_create(veneer_addr);
fn(buffer, 32);  /* HW clears registers before crossing */

docs.title: 20.3.3 SAU Configuration Code
docs.text:
void SAU_Init(void) {
    SAU->CTRL = 0;
    SAU->RNR=0; SAU->RBAR=0x08010000U; SAU->RLAR=0x0807FFE0U|SAU_RLAR_ENABLE_Msk;
    SAU->RNR=1; SAU->RBAR=0x0E000000U; SAU->RLAR=0x0E00FFE0U|SAU_RLAR_NSC_Msk|SAU_RLAR_ENABLE_Msk;
    SAU->RNR=2; SAU->RBAR=0x20020000U; SAU->RLAR=0x2003FFE0U|SAU_RLAR_ENABLE_Msk;
    SAU->CTRL = SAU_CTRL_ENABLE_Msk;
    __DSB(); __ISB();
}

docs.title: 20.3.4 TrustZone-M Memory Map Diagram
docs.text: Figure 20.1. ARM TrustZone-M memory map (STM32L552). SAU defines NS and NSC regions; remaining space is Secure by default. NS code enters Secure world only via NSC veneer using the SG instruction.

docs.title: 20.4 PSA Platform Security Architecture
docs.text:
ARM PSA defines threat modeling, hardware requirements, and certification for IoT devices.

Table 20.3. PSA Certified Security Levels Level Requirements Evaluation Example Level 1 Security questionnaire, design review Lab questionnaire Nordic nRF9160 Level 2 RoT isolation, secure boot, PSA Crypto Independent lab STM32L552, LPC55S69 Level 3 Side-channel resistance, high-value assets Penetration test EFR32MG21 Secure Vault 
/* PSA Crypto API (TF-M Crypto partition, psa/crypto.h) */
psa_key_attributes_t attr = PSA_KEY_ATTRIBUTES_INIT;
psa_set_key_type(&attr, PSA_KEY_TYPE_ECC_KEY_PAIR(PSA_ECC_FAMILY_SECP_R1));
psa_set_key_bits(&attr, 256);
psa_set_key_usage_flags(&attr, PSA_KEY_USAGE_SIGN_HASH|PSA_KEY_USAGE_VERIFY_HASH);
psa_set_key_algorithm(&attr, PSA_ALG_ECDSA(PSA_ALG_SHA_256));
psa_set_key_lifetime(&attr, PSA_KEY_LIFETIME_PERSISTENT);
psa_set_key_id(&attr, 0x00000001U);
psa_key_id_t key_id;
psa_generate_key(&attr, &key_id);  /* private key stays in Secure world */

/* PSA Initial Attestation -- EAT/CBOR/COSE_Sign1 token */
uint8_t challenge[32], token[512]; size_t token_len;
psa_initial_attest_get_token(challenge, 32, token, 512, &token_len);

/* PSA Protected Storage */
psa_ps_set(0x00000001UL, cert_len, device_cert, PSA_STORAGE_FLAG_WRITE_ONCE);

docs.title: 20.5 ATECC608B IoT Cryptographic Coprocessor
docs.text:
Microchip ATECC608B (TDFN-8, I2C addr 0x60–0x6F configurable via fuses): ECC P-256 (ECDH + ECDSA), AES-128, SHA-256/HMAC, 16 key slots x 256-bit, per-slot access control, monotonic counters, NIST SP 800-90A TRNG.

#include "cryptoauthlib.h"

ATCAIfaceCfg cfg = cfg_ateccx08a_i2c_default;
cfg.atcai2c.slave_address = 0xC0;  /* 0x60 << 1 for I2C write addr */
atcab_init(&cfg);

uint8_t pub_xy[64];  /* raw X||Y, P-256 */
atcab_genkey(2, pub_xy);  /* generate ephemeral in slot 2 */

uint8_t shared[32];
atcab_ecdh(2, server_pubkey_xy, shared);  /* feed into HKDF */

uint8_t digest[32], sig[64];
atcab_sha(data, data_len, digest);
atcab_sign(0, digest, sig);  /* slot 0: device identity (never exported) */

bool ok;
atcab_verify_extern(digest, partner_sig, ca_pubkey, &ok);

Tip: Lock ATECC608B Config Zone after provisioning. Slots: 0=device ECDSA (never exported), 1-3=ECDH ephemeral, 4-7=AES keys, 8-11=CA pubkeys, 14-15=monotonic counters.

docs.title: 20.6 MCUboot Secure Bootloader
docs.text:
MCUboot (https://github.com/mcu-tools/mcuboot) is the standard open-source bootloader for Zephyr RTOS, Apache Mynewt, NuttX, and ESP-IDF.

  • Overwrite: Copy secondary to primary. Simple but no rollback.

  • Swap (move): Atomic sector-by-sector swap via scratch area. Rollback supported.

  • Direct-XIP: Execute in place from either slot. No copy needed.

# prj.conf: MCUboot with Ed25519 signing (Zephyr RTOS)
CONFIG_MCUBOOT=y
CONFIG_BOOT_SIGNATURE_TYPE_ED25519=y
CONFIG_BOOT_SIGNATURE_KEY_FILE="keys/sign.pem"
CONFIG_BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS=256
CONFIG_BOOT_SWAP_USING_MOVE=y

# Key generation
python -m imgtool keygen -k keys/sign.pem -t ed25519
python -m imgtool getpub -k keys/sign.pem > keys/sign_pub.c

# Sign application image
python -m imgtool sign
    --key keys/sign.pem --header-size 0x200 --align 4
    --version 1.2.0+0 --slot-size 0x67000
    zephyr.bin  zephyr_signed.bin

# Verify signed image offline
python -m imgtool verify --key keys/sign_pub.pem zephyr_signed.bin

Image layout: [512B header | application code | TLV trailer]. TLV: HASH (SHA-256 of header+code), KEYHASH (SHA-256 of signing pubkey), SIG (Ed25519 signature of HASH). Trial boot: UNCONFIRMED until boot_set_confirmed() called.

docs.title: 20.7 SUIT: Software Update for IoT (RFC 9019)
docs.text:
SUIT defines CBOR-encoded manifests with COSE authentication wrappers for IoT OTA.

# Python SUIT manifest generation (pip install suit-tool)
import json, subprocess

manifest = {
    "manifest-version": 1,
    "manifest-sequence-number": 42,  # anti-replay
    "components": [{
        "component-identifier": ["firmware"],
        "install-digest": {
            "algorithm-id": "sha-256",
            "digest-bytes": "AABBCCDD..."},
        "install-size": 131072,
        "source-uri": "https://ota.example.com/fw_v2.bin"
    }]
}
with open("manifest.json","w") as f: json.dump(manifest,f)
subprocess.run(["suit-tool","create","-i","manifest.json","-o","manifest.suit"])
subprocess.run(["suit-tool","sign","-m","manifest.suit","-k","p256.pem","-o","signed.suit"])

docs.title: 20.8 LoRaWAN 1.1 Security
docs.text:
LoRaWAN 1.1 uses dual-key architecture: AppKey (application root) and NwkKey (network root), separating application provider and network operator security domains.

Table 20.4. LoRaWAN 1.1 Session Key Derivation Key Root Key Purpose AppSKey AppKey + JoinNonce + NetID + DevNonce AES-128-CTR payload encryption FNwkSIntKey NwkKey + JoinNonce + ... Uplink MIC (AES-128-CMAC) SNwkSIntKey NwkKey + ... Downlink MIC NwkSEncKey NwkKey + ... FOpts MAC encryption 
from Crypto.Hash import CMAC
from Crypto.Cipher import AES

def lorawan_mic_uplink(FNwkSIntKey, DevAddr, FCnt, frame):
    B0  = bytes([0x49])
    B0 += (0).to_bytes(2, "little")      # ConfFCnt=0
    B0 += bytes([0x00, 0x00])            # TxDr, TxCh
    B0 += bytes([0x00])                  # Dir=0 (uplink)
    B0 += DevAddr.to_bytes(4, "little")
    B0 += FCnt.to_bytes(4, "little")
    B0 += bytes([0x00])                  # padding
    B0 += len(frame).to_bytes(1, "big")
    c = CMAC.new(FNwkSIntKey, ciphermod=AES)
    c.update(B0 + frame)
    return c.digest()[:4]               # MIC = first 4 bytes

docs.title: 20.9 ASCON Lightweight Cipher (NIST Standard 2023)
docs.text:
ASCON (NIST IR 8454, August 2023) is the NIST lightweight cryptography standard. State: 320 bits (5 x 64-bit words). Rate: 64 bits (Ascon-128) / 128 bits (Ascon-128a). Key and nonce: 128 bits each. Tag: 128 bits. Hardware area: 2,300 GE vs AES 3,400 GE.

def rotr64(x,n): return ((x>>n)|(x<<(64-n)))&0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF

def ascon_permutation(S, rounds):
    RC=[0xf0,0xe1,0xd2,0xc3,0xb4,0xa5,0x96,0x87,0x78,0x69,0x5a,0x4b]
    for r in range(12-rounds,12):
        S[2]^=RC[r]                    # add round constant
        S[0]^=S[4]; S[4]^=S[3]; S[2]^=S[1]  # S-box layer
        T=[(~S[i]&0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)&S[(i+1)
        for i in range(5): S[i]^=T[(i+1)
        S[1]^=S[0]; S[0]^=S[4]; S[3]^=S[2]; S[2]^=0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
        S[0]^=rotr64(S[0],19)^rotr64(S[0],28)  # linear diffusion
        S[1]^=rotr64(S[1],61)^rotr64(S[1],39)
        S[2]^=rotr64(S[2],1)^rotr64(S[2],6)
        S[3]^=rotr64(S[3],10)^rotr64(S[3],17)
        S[4]^=rotr64(S[4],7)^rotr64(S[4],41)

Tip: Ascon-128: 1.45 cycles/byte on Cortex-M3 SW vs 10+ for AES-CCM SW. For M0/M0+ without HW AES, Ascon is the preferred IoT cipher. Hardware GE: 2300 vs AES-128 at 3400.

docs.text: STMicroelectronics STM32L552ZE: 110 MHz Cortex-M33 + TrustZone-M, FPU, MPU (16 regions). Memory: 512 KB dual-bank flash (configurable S/NS partition), 256 KB SRAM. docs.title: 20.12.3 NXP LPC55S69 (TrustZone-M + PUF)

docs.title: 20.12.4 Silicon Labs EFR32MG21 (Secure Vault, PSA Level 3)

PSA Certified Level 3. Eval: BRD4181A radio board ($5 with WSTK Starter Kit).

docs.title: 20.14 Secure Provisioning Flow
docs.text:
1. HSM key generation: Thales Luna or Utimaco HSM generates per-device ECC P-256 keypair.

  2. Encrypted injection: ST STSDK or NXP SPSDK transfers key material over authenticated session.

  3. Certificate enrollment: Device generates on-chip CSR; provisioning CA (in HSM) signs.

  4. Cloud onboarding: AWS IoT Core DPS or Azure IoT Hub DPS validates cert on first connection.

  5. Lifecycle lock: RDP Level 2 programmed, JTAG/SWD disabled permanently at end of manufacturing.
