docs.title: 20.17 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: TrustZone-M SAU Configuration for STM32L552

Given STM32L552: Secure TF-M at 0x08000000–0x0800FFFF (64 KB), NSC veneer at 0x0E000000–0x0E00FFFF (64 KB), NS app at 0x08010000–0x0807FFFF (448 KB), NS SRAM at 0x20020000–0x2003FFFF (128 KB). Write the complete SAU configuration and verify access control. Solution: Step 1: Identify SAU entries.

SAU only marks NS and NSC regions; Secure is the default for all other space. Required: SAU[0]=NS flash, SAU[1]=NSC veneer, SAU[2]=NS SRAM.

Step 2: RBAR and RLAR values.

SAU[0]: RBAR=0x08010000, RLAR=0x0807FFE0|0x01=0x0807FFE1  (NS, enable)
SAU[1]: RBAR=0x0E000000, RLAR=0x0E00FFE0|0x03=0x0E00FFE3  (NSC, enable)
SAU[2]: RBAR=0x20020000, RLAR=0x2003FFE0|0x01=0x2003FFE1  (NS, enable)

Step 3: C implementation.

void SAU_Init(void) {
    SAU->CTRL=0;
    SAU->RNR=0; SAU->RBAR=0x08010000U; SAU->RLAR=0x0807FFE1U;
    SAU->RNR=1; SAU->RBAR=0x0E000000U; SAU->RLAR=0x0E00FFE3U;
    SAU->RNR=2; SAU->RBAR=0x20020000U; SAU->RLAR=0x2003FFE1U;
    SAU->CTRL=SAU_CTRL_ENABLE_Msk;
    __DSB(); __ISB();
}

Step 4: Verification.

NS -> 0x08000000 (S TF-M): SecureFault
NS -> 0x0E000100 via SG:   Switch to Secure state (allowed)
S  -> 0x20020000 (NS SRAM): Allowed (Secure can access NS)
NS -> 0x20000000 (S SRAM): SecureFault

Solved Problem: LoRaWAN 1.1 MIC Verification Step-by-Step

LoRaWAN 1.1 uplink: MHDR=0x40, DevAddr=0xABCD1234, FCnt=5, frame=[0x40,0x34,0x12,0xCD,0xAB,0x00,0x05,0x00]. FNwkSIntKey=16 zero bytes. Received MIC=0xAABBCCDD. Is the frame valid? Solution: Step 1: Construct B0 block (16 bytes).

B0[0]=0x49           block type indicator
B0[1:2]=0x00 0x00    ConfFCnt=0 (unconfirmed uplink)
B0[3]=0x00 TxDr=0, B0[4]=0x00 TxCh=0
B0[5]=0x00           Dir=0 (uplink)
B0[6:9]=34 12 CD AB  DevAddr little-endian
B0[10:13]=05 00 00 00  FCnt=5 little-endian
B0[14]=0x00          padding
B0[15]=0x08          len(frame)=8 bytes

Step 2: Compute AES-128-CMAC.

Input = B0 (16 bytes) || frame (8 bytes) = 24 bytes total. CMAC-AES-128(key=16x0x00, B0||frame). MIC = first 4 bytes of output.

Step 3: Compare.

Computed MIC differs from received 0xAABBCCDD. REJECT. Frame dropped silently (no error response, avoids oracle). Possible causes: wrong FNwkSIntKey, replay (FCnt mismatch), or payload tampering.

Solved Problem: MCUboot Image Signing and Verification Process

Describe the complete MCUboot Ed25519 workflow: key generation, prj.conf configuration, imgtool invocation, image format, and boot-time verification including rollback protection. Solution: Step 1: Key generation.

python -m imgtool keygen -k sign.pem -t ed25519
python -m imgtool getpub -k sign.pem > sign_pub.c
# sign_pub.c compiled into MCUboot binary

Step 2: prj.conf.

CONFIG_BOOT_SIGNATURE_TYPE_ED25519=y
CONFIG_BOOT_SIGNATURE_KEY_FILE="sign.pem"
CONFIG_BOOT_SWAP_USING_MOVE=y

Step 3: Sign image.

python -m imgtool sign --key sign.pem --header-size 0x200 --align 4
    --version 1.2.0+0 --slot-size 0x67000
    zephyr.bin  zephyr_signed.bin
# Layout: [512B header | app code | TLV: HASH+KEYHASH+SIG]

Step 4: Boot-time verification.

1. Check header magic (0x96F3B83D)
2. SHA-256(header+app) vs TLV HASH entry
3. Verify TLV SIG (Ed25519) vs embedded pubkey
4. Check version >= minimum (anti-rollback)
5. Swap secondary->primary, set UNCONFIRMED, reboot
6. App calls boot_set_confirmed() OR MCUboot reverts

Solved Problem: PSA Certified Level 2 Requirements for STM32L552

A product team targets PSA Certified Level 2 on STM32L552. Map each mandatory PSA Level 2 requirement to the specific STM32L552 hardware or TF-M software feature that satisfies it. Solution: Requirement mapping:

  1. Verified Boot (RQ_A_SECBOOT): MCUboot Ed25519. TZEN=1 option byte.

  2. Crypto (RQ_A_CRYPTO): STM32L5 PKA+AES+SHA via TF-M Crypto partition PSA API.

  3. Secure Storage (RQ_A_STORAGE): TF-M ITS (Secure SRAM) + TF-M PS (AES-256-GCM).

  4. Attestation (RQ_A_ATTEST): TF-M Initial Attestation (EAT/CBOR/COSE_Sign1).

  5. Isolation: SAU + IDAU + MPU via TF-M firmware configuration.

  6. Lifecycle: STM32L5 RDP 0/1/2 + TF-M lifecycle CSR states.

  7. Debug control: RDP Level 2 disables JTAG/SWD permanently.

Certification: Submit to accredited lab (Riscure, Brightsight). Architecture review + TF-M source review + basic fault injection test. Certificate valid 3 years.

docs.title: 20.18 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: IoT hardware security has matured significantly, driven by new protocol standards, updated certification schemes, and major regulatory mandates.

docs.title: 20.18.1 Matter 1.2/1.3 (2023–2024): Hardware Security Requirements
docs.text:
The Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA) released Matter 1.2 (October 2023) and Matter 1.3 (May 2024), adding hardware security requirements beyond the original Matter 1.0 specification. Matter mandates a Device Attestation Certificate (DAC) stored in a Secure Element or equivalent tamper-resistant hardware; the DAC private key must be generated on-chip and never exported. The attestation flow uses CASE (Certificate-Authenticated Session Establishment) with ECDSA P-256, with the Device Attestation public key certified by the vendor’s Product Attestation Intermediate (PAI) certificate.

Matter 1.2 added nine new device categories (refrigerators, robot vacuums, smoke detectors, etc.) and reinforced that each must carry a hardware-protected DAC. Matter 1.3 introduced Enhanced Setup Code for NFC-based commissioning and Device Energy Management (DEM) with security bindings to prevent unauthorised energy schedule modifications. Thread 1.3 (the underlying mesh protocol) now requires hardware-backed Operational Credentials.

Table 20.10. Matter 1.3 hardware security requirements by credential type Matter Security Element Hardware Requirement Storage Device Attestation Certificate On-chip generation, no export SE / OTP DAC Private Key CC EAL5+ or equivalent SE NVM Node Operational Certificate Rotatable per fabric SE or PSA L2 PASE Passcode Printed QR / NFC tag Non-secure storage OK CASE Session Keys Ephemeral (ECDH) Transient SRAM

docs.title: 20.18.2 PSA Certified Level 3 (2023): New Evaluation Methodology
docs.text:
Arm PSA Certified Level 3 received a revised methodology in 2023, adding mandatory physical attack testing to the existing architectural and implementation reviews. Level 3 evaluations now require:

  • Resistance to non-invasive side-channel analysis (DPA, EM analysis) on cryptographic operations—the first PSA level to mandate physical testing.

  • Resistance to fault injection attacks (voltage/clock glitching, laser FI) on security-critical code paths (PIN verification, boot verification).

  • An independently accredited laboratory (e.g., Riscure, Brightsight, CESTI) must perform the penetration testing phase.

Silicon Labs EFR32MG21 Secure Vault High and Nordic nRF5340 achieved PSA Certified Level 3 under the revised methodology in 2023. The evaluation scope explicitly covers the secure enclave’s cryptographic engines and the secure boot chain.

docs.title: 20.18.3 EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA 2024): IoT Hardware Security Mandates
docs.text:
The EU Cyber Resilience Act was formally adopted in 2024 (Regulation 2024/2847), entering into force with a 36-month transition period. The CRA imposes mandatory cybersecurity requirements on all hardware and software products with digital elements sold in the EU. For IoT devices, the key hardware-level requirements include:

  • Secure by default: No universal default passwords; credentials must be unique per device or generated on first use.

  • Unique device identity: Each device must have a hardware-rooted cryptographic identity (e.g., X.509 certificate backed by a secure element).

  • Secure update mechanism: OTA updates must be authenticated and integrity-checked; rollback to vulnerable firmware must be prevented.

  • Vulnerability disclosure: Manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA within 24 hours.

  • Class I devices (standard IoT): Self-assessment conformity. Class II devices (critical, e.g., industrial gateways): Third-party conformity assessment mandatory.

Note: The CRA explicitly references ETSI EN 303 645 and NIST IR 8259 as candidate technical standards. IoT manufacturers targeting the EU market must align hardware designs with these requirements by 2027.

docs.title: 20.18.4 NIST IR 8259D: IoT Device Cybersecurity Profile for Enterprise (2023)
docs.text:
NIST IR 8259D (Profile Using the IoT Core Baseline for the Industrial Internet of Things) was published in 2023 as a companion to the foundational IR 8259A. It defines security capability baselines for enterprise IoT deployments, with hardware- specific requirements including:

  • Device identity: Hardware-rooted unique identifier (UID) that is immutable and cryptographically bound to device certificates.

  • Cryptographic key protection: Private keys must reside in hardware- protected storage (HSM, SE, or TPM) inaccessible via software interfaces.

  • Physical access protection: Anti-tamper mechanisms that zeroize keys upon case opening (relevant for Class II industrial IoT).

  • Software update integrity: Hardware-verified signature check before any firmware is applied; rollback counter enforced in hardware.

docs.title: 20.18.5 RP2350 (Raspberry Pi Pico 2, 2024): Dual-Architecture Security
docs.text:
The RP2350 (announced August 2024) introduces a dual-architecture design: two ARM Cortex-M33 cores and two RISC-V Hazard3 cores (only one architecture active at a time, selected at boot). Security features represent a major step beyond the RP2040:

  • ARM TrustZone-M: Full TrustZone-M support on the Cortex-M33 cores, enabling secure/normal world isolation as described in this chapter.

  • OTP (One-Time Programmable) memory: 4096 bits of on-chip OTP for key storage, boot configuration, and lock bits. The OTP includes an error correction code (ECC) engine.

  • Secure Boot: Hardware boot signature verification using an ECC P-256 key hash stored in OTP; unsigned firmware is rejected when secure boot is enabled.

  • GLITCH DETECTORS: Voltage glitch detection circuitry that triggers a system reset, mitigating fault injection attacks that were trivially effective on the RP2040.

  • RISC-V security: When booting in RISC-V mode (Hazard3 cores), the PMP (Physical Memory Protection) unit provides memory isolation analogous to TrustZone-M.

Tip: RP2350’s dual-architecture capability enables interesting use cases: ARM Cortex-M33 with TrustZone-M can run the secure world, while RISC-V Hazard3 cores run the normal world application. The architecture selection is fixed at boot time by an OTP bit.

docs.title: 20.18.6 ESP32-S3 Secure Boot v2 and Flash Encryption Improvements
docs.text: Espressif Systems updated the ESP32-S3 security subsystem in 2023 with Secure Boot v2 enhancements. Secure Boot v2 uses RSA-3072 with PSS padding (replacing the older ECDSA-based scheme) for firmware image verification, with the public key digest stored in eFuse. Up to three public keys can be enrolled simultaneously, enabling key rotation without hardware access: if a signing key is compromised, the corresponding eFuse digest bit is revoked, and the next enrolled key takes over. Flash encryption improvements include support for XTS-AES-256 (versus the previous XTS-AES-128), with the encryption key stored in a dedicated eFuse key block that is inaccessible after eFuse programming with the DIS_DOWNLOAD_ICACHE and DIS_DOWNLOAD_DCACHE fuses set.

docs.title: 20.18.7 Nordic nRF9160/nRF5340 PSA Certified Certification
docs.text:
Nordic Semiconductor received PSA Certified Level 2 for the nRF9160 (LTE-M/NB-IoT SiP) and nRF5340 (dual Arm Cortex-M33 SoC) in 2023 under the revised PSA Certified Methodology v3.0. The nRF5340’s dual-core architecture—a 128 MHz application core (Cortex-M33) and a 64 MHz network core (Cortex-M33)—maps naturally to PSA’s isolation model: the application core runs TF-M (Trusted Firmware-M) in the secure world, while the network core handles radio protocol stacks in isolation. The CryptoCell-312 hardware cryptographic accelerator (AES-128, SHA-256, ECC P-256, TRNG) is accessible only from the secure world, satisfying the PSA Level 2 requirement for hardware-isolated cryptographic services.

Table 20.11. Recent IoT platform security certifications (2023–2024) Platform MCU PSA Level Key Security Features RP2350 (Pico 2, 2024) Dual Cortex-M33 + dual RISC-V Level 1 capable TrustZone-M, OTP, glitch detect ESP32-S3 (2023 update) Xtensa LX7 Not PSA Secure Boot v2, XTS-AES-256 Nordic nRF5340 Dual Cortex-M33 Level 2 CryptoCell-312, TF-M Nordic nRF9160 Cortex-M33 Level 1 CryptoCell-310, LTE-M SL EFR32MG21 Secure Vault Cortex-M33 Level 3 DPA-resist, anti-tamper mesh

Exercises

  1. (MCQ) In ARM TrustZone-M NSC region, which instruction switches from Non-Secure to Secure state? (a) BLX, (b) SG, (c) SMC, (d) SVC.

  2. (MCQ) LoRaWAN 1.1 encrypts the application payload using which session key? (a) NwkKey, (b) FNwkSIntKey, (c) AppSKey, (d) NwkSEncKey.

  3. (Short Answer) Explain the difference between SAU and IDAU in TrustZone-M. What is the effective attribution when SAU marks a region NS but IDAU marks it Secure?

  4. (Short Answer) Describe the MCUboot trial boot mechanism. What happens if the application never calls boot_set_confirmed() before the next watchdog reset?

  5. (Design) Design a PSA-compliant secure provisioning flow for 100,000 IoT devices: HSM key generation, encrypted key injection, certificate enrollment, cloud zero-touch provisioning. Address security guarantees if a device is stolen during shipping.

  6. (Design) A LoRaWAN 1.0.x deployment uses a single AppKey. List the specific attacks this enables and explain how LoRaWAN 1.1 dual-key architecture closes each vulnerability.

  7. (Coding) Write a C function with cmse_nonsecure_entry that validates an NS buffer, performs AES-256-GCM encryption via PSA Crypto API using persistent key ID 0x1, and writes ciphertext + 16-byte tag to the NS caller buffer.

  8. (Coding) Write a Python script using cbor2 and pycose to generate a SUIT RFC 9019 manifest: firmware v2.1.0, SHA-256 image digest, sequence number 42, HTTPS fetch URI, COSE_Sign1 signed with ECDSA-P256.

  9. (Analysis) Design an ATECC608B (16 slots x 256-bit) slot assignment for a TLS 1.3 mutual-auth IoT client: device ECDSA identity key, ECDH ephemeral, CA public key, AES-128 session key, anti-replay counter. Specify read/write/auth policy for each slot.

  10. (Analysis) Compare Ascon-128 (10 cy/B SW) vs AES-128-CCM (55 cy/B SW) on a 16 MHz Cortex-M0+. Calculate CPU load for 100-byte CoAP payloads per second. At what frequency does AES-CCM exceed 80% CPU load?

  11. (Research) EFR32MG21 Secure Vault achieves PSA Level 3 via DPA resistance. Explain: (a) what physical quantities DPA measures, (b) how hardware masking counters DPA, (c) why TrustZone-M isolation alone cannot achieve Level 3.

  12. (Design) Design a complete Matter 1.3 security architecture for a smart thermostat: DAC, PAI, CD, PASE commissioning, CASE session establishment, OTA with SUIT. Specify hardware for each element, factory provisioning flow, and security guarantee.

docs.title: Chapter 21: Secure Elements and Smart Cards
docs.text: Note: This chapter covers secure elements (SEs) and smart cards: ISO 7816, ISO 14443, JavaCard, GlobalPlatform, SCP03, EMV, PIV, ePassport (ICAO 9303), MIFARE Classic attacks, NFC security, and hardware including NXP JavaCard, STMicro ST31, Infineon SLE 97.

docs.title: 21.1 Secure Element Definition and Form Factors
docs.text:
A secure element (SE) is a tamper-resistant hardware platform with secure storage and cryptographic execution, isolated from the host processor. Key form factors:

  • ISO 7816 contact card (ID-1): Standard credit card size (85.6 x 54 mm), 6-8 gold contacts.

  • ISO 7816 ID-000 (SIM): Mini SIM plug (25 x 15 mm), same electrical interface.

  • ISO 14443 contactless: 13.56 MHz NFC interface, Type A or B modulation.

  • Embedded SE (eSE): Discrete chip soldered to PCB, I2C/SPI interface. NXP SE050.

  • iSIM/eSIM: SE IP block integrated into application processor SoC. GSMA SGP.22.

docs.title: 21.1.1 Smart Card Architecture
docs.text: A smart card contains: CPU (8-bit 8051 or 32-bit ARM), ROM (OS code,  128 KB), EEPROM/Flash (applets + data, 64–640 KB), RAM (working memory, 4–32 KB), crypto coprocessor (DES, AES, RSA, ECC hardware engines), and I/O controller implementing ISO 7816 T=0 or T=1 protocol.

docs.title: 21.2.1 Physical Layer and ATR
docs.text: ISO 7816-3 defines 8 contacts (C1–C8): C1=VCC (1.8/3/5V), C2=RST, C3=CLK (1–5 MHz), C4=RFU, C5=GND, C6=VPP (programming voltage, mostly unused), C7=I/O (half-duplex serial), C8=RFU. The Answer To Reset (ATR) is sent by the card after reset, conveying: supported protocols (T=0, T=1), historical bytes, and interface character bytes.

docs.title: 21.2.2 APDU Structure
docs.text:
Application Protocol Data Units (APDUs) are the communication language of smart cards.

Table 21.1. APDU Command and Response Structure Field Command APDU Response APDU Size (bytes) CLA Class byte N/A 1 INS Instruction byte N/A 1 P1 P2 Parameters N/A 2 Lc Data length N/A 0-3 DATA Command data Response data 0-255 Le Expected response length N/A 0-3 SW1 SW2 N/A Status word 2 
/* Java: construct APDU to SELECT application by AID */
byte[] selectCmd = {
    (byte)0x00, (byte)0xA4, (byte)0x04, (byte)0x00,  /* CLA INS P1 P2 */
    (byte)0x07,                                        /* Lc: AID length */
    (byte)0xA0,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x03,0x00,0x00,         /* AID */
    (byte)0x00                                         /* Le */
};

/* Python: pyscard (PC/SC) */
from smartcard.System import readers
r = readers()[0]
conn = r.createConnection()
conn.connect()
data, sw1, sw2 = conn.transmit(list(selectCmd))
print(f"SW: {sw1:02X}{sw2:02X}")  /* 9000 = success */

docs.title: 21.3 JavaCard Platform
docs.text: JavaCard is a subset of Java that executes on smart card CPUs. The JavaCard Virtual Machine (JCVM) provides bytecode interpretation and garbage collection. The JavaCard Runtime Environment (JCRE) manages applet lifecycle and inter-applet communication.

docs.title: 21.3.1 JavaCard Applet Lifecycle
docs.text:
• install(): Called when applet is installed on the card. Create persistent objects.

  • select(): Called when host selects this applet via SELECT APDU. Initialize session state.

  • process(APDU): Called for each subsequent APDU. Main command handler.

  • deselect(): Called when another applet is selected. Clean up session state.

  • uninstall(): Called when applet is deleted. Remove all persistent objects.

/* JavaCard ECDH Key Agreement Applet */
import javacard.framework.*;
import javacard.security.*;
import javacardx.crypto.*;

public class ECDHApplet extends Applet {
    private KeyPair kp;
    private KeyAgreement ecdh;
    private byte[] sharedSecret;

    protected ECDHApplet() {
        kp = new KeyPair(KeyPair.ALG_EC_FP, KeyBuilder.LENGTH_EC_FP_256);
        kp.genKeyPair();  /* generate on-card ECC P-256 key */
        ecdh = KeyAgreement.getInstance(KeyAgreement.ALG_EC_SVDP_DH_PLAIN, false);
        sharedSecret = JCSystem.makeTransientByteArray((short)32, JCSystem.CLEAR_ON_DESELECT);
    }

    public void process(APDU apdu) {
        byte[] buf = apdu.getBuffer();
        if (apdu.isISOInterswitch()) return;
        switch(buf[ISO7816.OFFSET_INS]) {
        case (byte)0x10:  /* GET PUBLIC KEY */
            ECPublicKey pub = (ECPublicKey)kp.getPublic();
            short len = pub.getW(buf, (short)0);
            apdu.setOutgoingAndSend((short)0, len);
            break;
        case (byte)0x20:  /* DO ECDH: Lc bytes = peer public key */
            short lc = apdu.setIncomingAndReceive();
            ecdh.init(kp.getPrivate());
            ecdh.generateSecret(buf, ISO7816.OFFSET_CDATA, lc,
                                sharedSecret, (short)0);
            break;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 21.4 GlobalPlatform Security
docs.text: GlobalPlatform (GP) defines the card management infrastructure for Java Card platforms, including Security Domains (ISD, SSD, DAP), Secure Channel Protocols (SCP02/SCP03), and Delegated Management (DAP).

docs.title: 21.4.1 GlobalPlatform Security Domain Hierarchy
docs.text: Figure 21.1. GlobalPlatform Security Domain hierarchy. The Issuer Security Domain (ISD) manages the card. Supplementary Security Domains (SSDs) are created by service providers. Each SSD manages its own applets independently.

docs.title: 21.4.2 SCP03: Secure Channel Protocol 3
docs.text:
SCP03 replaces SCP02 (3DES-based) with AES-128-based session key derivation and authenticated encryption. Three session keys derived from static base keys:

Table 21.2. SCP03 Session Keys Key Static Base Derivation Purpose S-ENC Enc Key AES-CMAC(Enc-Key, data) Command/response encryption S-MAC MAC Key AES-CMAC(MAC-Key, data) Command MAC (C-MAC) S-RMAC RMAC Key AES-CMAC(RMAC-Key, data) Response MAC (R-MAC) 
# SCP03 session key derivation (Python)
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
from Crypto.Hash import CMAC

def scp03_derive(base_key, derivation_data, context):
    """Derive SCP03 session key using AES-CMAC derivation"""
    # Derivation data: 12 bytes label + derivation constant + 2 bytes len
    data = derivation_data + context
    c = CMAC.new(base_key, ciphermod=AES)
    c.update(data)
    return c.digest()  # 16-byte session key

# Host challenge: 8 bytes random
# Card challenge: 8 bytes from card
host_challenge = os.urandom(8)
# After mutual authentication:
S_ENC  = scp03_derive(enc_base_key,  b"\x04"+host_challenge+card_challenge, b"\x00\xc2\x80")
S_MAC  = scp03_derive(mac_base_key,  b"\x06"+host_challenge+card_challenge, b"\x00\xc2\x80")
S_RMAC = scp03_derive(rmac_base_key, b"\a"+host_challenge+card_challenge, b"\x00\xc2\x80")

docs.title: 21.5 EMV (Europay/Mastercard/Visa)
docs.text:
EMV 4.3 specification defines the global standard for chip-based payment cards.

Table 21.3. EMV Authentication Methods Method Acronym How it works Online/Offline Static Data Authentication SDA Card signs static data with issuer key Offline only Dynamic Data Authentication DDA Card signs terminal challenge dynamically Offline only Combined DDA/App Crypto CDA DDA combined with application cryptogram Offline Offline PIN – PIN verified by card chip, not network Offline

docs.title: 21.5.1 EMV DDA Verification
docs.text:
DDA (Dynamic Data Authentication) uses the card’s unique RSA private key to sign a challenge from the terminal. The terminal verifies with the card’s public key, certified by the issuer, certified by the scheme (Visa/Mastercard) certification chain.

# EMV DDA verification steps:
# 1. GET PROCESSING OPTIONS: card returns AIP+AFL
# 2. READ RECORD: card returns signed static data (SSD)
# 3. INTERNAL AUTHENTICATE: terminal sends 8-byte challenge
#    Card returns SDAD = RSA_sign(card_priv, hash(challenge||data))
# 4. Terminal:
#    a) Verify issuer cert chain (scheme CA -> issuer -> card pubkey)
#    b) Verify SDAD using card public key
#    c) Check SDAD contains terminal challenge
# Successful DDA proves card is genuine (not cloned)

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

# Verify SDAD (RSA-2048 PKCS#1 v1.5 signature)
card_pubkey.verify(
    sdad_bytes, challenge_and_data,
    padding.PKCS1v15(), hashes.SHA1()  # EMV uses SHA-1
)

docs.title: 21.6 PIV – Personal Identity Verification
docs.text:
PIV (FIPS 201-3) mandates smart card credentials for US federal employees and contractors. The card holds X.509 certificates in four key slots plus a retired-key store.

Table 21.4. PIV Key Slots Slot Alias Key Algorithm Purpose 9A PIV Authentication RSA-2048 / ECC P-384 Authenticate card and cardholder 9C Digital Signature RSA-2048 / ECC P-384 Sign documents and emails 9D Key Management RSA-2048 / ECC P-256 Decrypt and key establishment 9E Card Authentication ECC P-256 Contactless authentication, no PIN required 82-95 Retired Key 1-20 RSA-2048 / ECC P-384 Historical key management records 
# Python PIV APDU: authenticate with slot 9A (ECC P-384)
# GENERAL AUTHENTICATE command
cla, ins = 0x00, 0x87
p1, p2 = 0x14, 0x9A  # alg=ECC-P384, slot=9A
# Build Dynamic Authentication Template
dat = bytes([0x7C, len_challenge+4, 0x82, 0x00, 0x81, len_challenge]) + challenge
apdu = bytes([cla, ins, p1, p2, len(dat)]) + dat + bytes([0x00])
resp = card.transmit(apdu)
# Response: 7C tag contains 0x82 (response) with signature bytes

The CHUID (Card Holder Unique Identifier) contains a FASC-N (Federal Agency Smart Credential Number) encoded in BCD, a UUID, an expiration date, and an asymmetric signature over those fields for authenticity checking by physical access readers.

docs.title: 21.7 ePassport – ICAO Doc 9303
docs.text:
ICAO Doc 9303 defines the Machine Readable Travel Document (MRTD) standard used in over 150 countries. The chip stores DG1 (MRZ data), DG2 (facial image), DG7 (signature), DG14 (Active Authentication public key), and DG15 (AA public key for EAC).

Table 21.5. ePassport Access Control Protocols Protocol Standard Protection Key Length BAC ICAO 9303 Part 11 Basic Access Control (3DES) 56-bit effective PACE ICAO 9303 Part 11 Password Authn. Connection Estab. AES-128/256 AA ICAO 9303 Part 11 Active Authentication (RSA/ECDSA) 1024-4096 bits EAC v1 BSI TR-03110 Chip+Terminal Auth (EU) AES-128 + ECC P-256 EAC v2 BSI TR-03110 PACE + CA + TA AES-128/256 + ECC SAC ICAO 9303 Part 11 Supplemental AC (replaces BAC) AES-128/256 
# PACE protocol simplified flow (ICAO 9303 Part 11 Section 4.4):
# Step 1: Get Nonce -- encrypted with Kenc derived from MRZ
ENC_NONCE = card.sendAPDU(0x00,0x86,0x00,0x00, [0x7C,0x02,0x80,0x00])
# Step 2: Map Nonce -- ECDH ephemeral key exchange
# Step 3: Perform Key Agreement -- second ECDH
# Step 4: Mutual Authentication -- compute/verify auth tokens
# Result: session keys KSenc, KSmac for Secure Messaging

docs.title: 21.7.1 Logical Data Structure (LDS)
docs.text:
The LDS organises data groups DG1-DG16 plus SOD (Security Object Document). SOD contains hash values of all DGs signed by the issuing state DS (Document Signer) certificate, which chains to the CSCA (Country Signing CA) certificate.

Warning: Clone-resistant only with AA/EAC: BAC-only passports can be cloned because the chip does not prove its identity; AA adds a device-bound RSA/ECDSA key.

docs.title: 21.8 MIFARE Classic Attacks
docs.text: MIFARE Classic (NXP) uses the proprietary CRYPTO1 stream cipher. Karsten Nohl reverse-engineered it in 2008; Garcia et al. published the full specification in 2009. A standard 1K card has 16 sectors x 4 blocks; each sector protected by 48-bit Key A and 48-bit Key B stored in Sector Trailer (block 3/7/11/...). A 6-byte UID is transmitted unencrypted; some cards use random 4-byte UIDs (anti-cloning).

docs.title: 21.8.1 CRYPTO1 Weaknesses
docs.text:
CRYPTO1 has a 48-bit LFSR state. Three published attacks break it:

  • Nested Authentication: knowing one sector key, recover adjacent sector keys using the nonce correlation. MFOC (Mifare OFfline Cracker) tool automates this.

  • Darkside Attack: obtain key from the tag error response when the random nonce leaks keystream bits through parity. Tools: mfkey32, Proxmark3 darkside.

  • Hardnested: works against cards with random UIDs; exploits LFSR linearity to recover keys with  50k authentication attempts.

# MFOC nested authentication -- simplified key recovery loop:
# Requires: one known key for any sector
# 1. Authenticate sector 0 with known key -> get encrypted nonce nt1
# 2. Predict nt2 (timing-correlated): brute-force 65536 candidates
# 3. For each candidate: solve CRYPTO1 state, derive target sector key
# Tool command line:
#   mfoc -O dump.mfd
# Proxmark3 hf mf nested 1 0 A FFFFFFFFFFFF d

Warning: MIFARE Classic must not be used for physical access control: the attack tool Proxmark3 (open hardware) can clone most MIFARE Classic cards in under 20 seconds.

Tip: MIFARE DESFire EV3 uses AES-128 with mutual authentication (ISO 7816-4 / ISO 14443-4), transaction MAC, and proximity check (ISO 14443-3 timing). It is not vulnerable to CRYPTO1 attacks.

docs.title: 21.9 NFC Security
docs.text:
NFC (ISO 14443, ISO 15693, ISO 18092) operates at 13.56 MHz with typical read range 3-5 cm (ISO 14443-A) to 1 m (ISO 15693). Security threats include:

  • Eavesdropping: passive attacker captures reader-to-card RF field. Range up to 1 m with a directional antenna.

  • Relay Attack: NFC proxy (NFCGate, Proxmark3 relay) forwards commands between victim card and distant reader. Defeated by distance bounding (ISO 14443-3 frame timing <1 ms RTT = 22 cm).

  • Power Analysis (SPA/DPA): measuring power envelope during AES key schedule leaks key bytes. NXP P60 includes built-in SPA/DPA countermeasures (randomised scheduling, dual-rail logic).

  • Fault Injection: voltage/clock glitching or laser fault injection can skip PIN verification branches. CC EAL5+ evaluation requires resistance to fault attacks.

Table 21.6. NFC Security Comparison Protocol Frequency Range Authentication Encryption ISO 14443-A/B 13.56 MHz <10 cm Challenge-Response AES-128/TDES ISO 15693 13.56 MHz <1 m None (basic) None ISO 18092 (NFCIP-1) 13.56 MHz <20 cm Mutual (NFC-DEP) AES-128 FeliCa (JIS 6319-4) 13.56 MHz <10 cm Mutual (SESN) AES-128 MIFARE DESFire EV3 13.56 MHz <10 cm Mutual ISO 7816 AES-128+MAC

docs.title: 21.10.1 NXP P60D080PVE
docs.text:
The NXP P60 family (SmartMX3) is a JavaCard 3.0.5 / GlobalPlatform 2.3.1 secure element with CC EAL 6+ (EN 419211) certification. The P60D080PVE variant integrates:

  • 80 KB user EEPROM (expandable to 150 KB with extended memory model)

  • 16 KB RAM + 640 KB ROM (JCRE + OS)

  • RSA-4096, ECC P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519, AES-256, DES/TDES, SHA-512 hardware accelerators

  • ISO 14443-A/B NFC interface at 848 kbps + ISO 7816 contact interface

  • Active shield mesh, voltage/frequency monitors, light sensor, temperature sensor

  • 40 nm NXP process node; 25 mm2 die area

docs.title: 21.10.2 STMicroelectronics ST31G480
docs.text:
The ST31G480 (ST33G1M2 family) targets eGovernment/ePassport applications:

  • 480 KB EEPROM, 32 KB RAM, 1.5 MB ROM; JavaCard 3.0.4 + GP 2.2.1

  • Hardware AES-128/256, RSA-4096, ECC, SHA-256/384/512

  • SWP (Single Wire Protocol) interface for UICC/SIM applications

  • CC EAL 5+ certified; 28 nm CMOS process; operating at 1.2 V core / 3 V I/O

docs.title: 21.10.3 Infineon SLE 97144
docs.text:
SLE 97 integrates a 16/32-bit security controller (Infineon SLE 9670) with 144 KB NVM:

  • Contact + contactless (ISO 14443-A/B, ISO 15693) dual interface

  • Public Key Unit (PKU): RSA-4096 in 300 ms, ECC-256 in 200 ms at 10 MHz

  • CC EAL 6+ with AVA_VAN.5 (vulnerability analysis); qualified for banking + ePassport

  • 40 nm Infineon CMOS; I-block protocol for T=1 with EDC and anti-tearing support

docs.title: 21.10.4 NXP SE050
docs.text:
SE050 is a plug-and-play IoT secure element in 2.5 x 2.5 mm WLCSP package:

  • ECC P-256/P-384/P-521/Ed25519, RSA-2048/4096, AES-256, HMAC-SHA256

  • I2C interface (400 kHz / 3.4 MHz); 50 KB persistent memory

  • Arm M0+ core, CC EAL 6+; Python library: se05x (NXP EdgeLock)

  • Used in: Google Titan, NXP LPC55S69 dev boards, Raspberry Pi security hats

docs.text:
Table 21.9. Smart Card and Secure Element Solutions Solution Type Standard Use Case Open Source NXP P60 (SmartMX3) Hard SE JavaCard/GP/EMV Banking, ePassport, ID No (SDK only) Infineon SLE 97 Hard SE JavaCard/GP/EMV ePassport, Banking No STMicro ST31G480 Hard SE JavaCard/GP UICC/SIM, eGov No NXP SE050 IoT Hard SE GP SCP03 IoT device identity Partial (TF-M) Microchip ATECC608B Crypto coprocessor PKCS#11 IoT keys, WiFi devices No (lib only) GlobalPlatform TEE Software SE GP TEE 1.0 Mobile DRM, keys No (spec only) OP-TEE Software TEE GP TEE 1.0 Linux+TrustZone-A Yes (BSD-2) JavaCard RI Soft JavaCard JavaCard 3.0.5 Development/testing Yes (GPL v2) jCardSim JavaCard sim JavaCard 3.0.5 Unit testing applets Yes (Apache 2) Proxmark3 NFC research hw ISO 14443/15693 SE research, pentesting Yes (GPL v3) Chameleon Mini NFC emulator hw ISO 14443 Field research Yes (MIT) MFOC Attack tool CRYPTO1 MIFARE Classic audit Yes (GPL v2)

Solved Problem: Constructing an ISO 7816 SELECT + READ BINARY APDU Sequence

A Java Card applet stores a 16-byte secret in EF (Elementary File) 0x0001. An off-card host must (1) SELECT the applet by AID=A0000000030000, (2) SELECT EF 0x0001, then (3) READ BINARY the 16 bytes. Write each APDU in hex and state the expected SW1-SW2 response. Solution: Step 1 – SELECT by AID (CLA=00, INS=A4, P1=04, P2=00): AID = A0 00 00 00 03 00 00 (7 bytes), Lc=07, Le=00. APDU: 00 A4 04 00 07 A0 00 00 00 03 00 00 00 Expected response: 90 00 (success) with optional FCI template.  Step 2 – SELECT EF by ID (P1=00, P2=00 for first occ.): File ID = 00 01 (2 bytes), Lc=02. APDU: 00 A4 00 00 02 00 01 Expected response: 90 00.  Step 3 – READ BINARY (INS=B0, P1=0x00, P2=0x00 = offset 0): Le = 0x10 (16 bytes requested). APDU: 00 B0 00 00 10 Expected response: 16 data bytes + 90 00.  Error codes: 6A82 = file not found; 6982 = security status not satisfied; 6C10 = wrong Le (use Le=10).

Solved Problem: SCP03 Session Key Derivation

A GlobalPlatform SCP03 channel uses a base key set: ENC=4041424344454647 48494A4B4C4D4E4F, MAC=4041424344454647 48494A4B4C4D4E4F (same for simplicity). Host challenge H=0102030405060708 and card challenge C=0807060504030201. Derive the Session ENC key S-ENC and confirm its first 4 bytes. Solution: SCP03 Key Derivation (Section 4.1.5 of GP Amend D): Derivation data = [derivation_constant] || [counter=0] || H || C For S-ENC: constant = 0x04; for S-MAC: constant = 0x06; for S-RMAC: constant = 0x07.  Step 1: Build 32-byte derivation input: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 04 80 00 80 bits 0-11: zeros; bit 96: derivation constant (0x04 for ENC); bit 112-127: length=128, then H || C appended.  Step 2: AES-CMAC(ENC_base_key, derivation_data) Python: from Crypto.Hash import CMAC; from Crypto.Cipher import AES c = CMAC.new(enc_key, ciphermod=AES); c.update(deriv_data); s_enc = c.digest() Result: S-ENC first 4 bytes = E7 A1 C2 D3 (illustrative). The session keys encrypt C-APDU data (S-ENC) and compute C-MAC/R-MAC (S-MAC/S-RMAC).

Solved Problem: EMV DDA Offline Dynamic Authentication

During an EMV DDA transaction the terminal sends an INTERNAL AUTHENTICATE command. The card signs a 4-byte terminal random number (UN=AABBCCDD) concatenated with card-specific data using its ICC Private Key (RSA-2048). Describe the full verification steps the terminal performs to authenticate the card. Solution: Step 1 – Retrieve ICC Public Key: READ RECORD -> Application file contains ICC Public Key Certificate. Decrypt certificate with Issuer Public Key -> recover ICC PK (n_icc, e_icc).  Step 2 – Send INTERNAL AUTHENTICATE: APDU: 00 88 00 00 04 AA BB CC DD 00 Card computes: SignedDynamicAppData = RSA_sign(ICC_priv, hash_data) where hash_data = Hash(ICC_dynamic_number || pad || UN).  Step 3 – Verify Signature: 1. RSA_verify(ICC_pub, SignedDynamicAppData) -> recovered hash. 2. Recompute SHA-1(card_dynamic_data || UN). 3. Compare: if equal, card possesses ICC private key -> authentic card.  Step 4 – Verify Certificate Chain: Issuer PK Certificate signed by CA PK (from terminal AID-keyed CA key table). ICC PK Certificate signed by Issuer PK. Full chain: CA -> Issuer -> ICC.  Security: DDA prevents card skimming (static SDA data cannot be replayed because ICC dynamic number increments per transaction).

Solved Problem: MIFARE Classic MFOC Nested Authentication Attack

You have a MIFARE Classic 1K card. You know Key A=FFFFFFFFFFFF for sector 0. Using the nested authentication vulnerability, derive the Key A for sector 1. Explain each step of the MFOC algorithm and the time/space complexity. Solution: Background: CRYPTO1 is a 48-bit LFSR. The nested attack exploits that when the reader re-authenticates to a second sector while already authenticated, the card nonce nt2 is encrypted with the CRYPTO1 keystream (which depends on nt1).  Step 1 – Authenticate sector 0 with known Key A: Reader sends: AUTHREQ(block 0) -> card sends nonce nt1 (32-bit random). Reader sends: {nr, ar} encrypted -> session established (CRYPTO1 state S0).  Step 2 – Collect nested nonce nt2: Without resetting, reader sends: AUTHREQ(block 4, sector 1). Card responds with nt2 XOR ks2 (nt2 encrypted with CRYPTO1 keystream ks2). Also: parity bits are encrypted -> 8 extra keystream bits known.  Step 3 – Exploit timing for nt2 prediction: MIFARE RNG is a 16-bit LFSR clocked by field pulses (32-bit internal state). After  200 timed acquisitions, nt2 space reduces from 232 to  216.  Step 4 – Brute-force CRYPTO1 state: For each candidate nt2: CRYPTO1_init(Key?, uid, nt2) -> check 8 parity bits. Matching state reveals Key A for sector 1.  Complexity: Time O(232/timing_reduction)  = O(216); Space O(1); real-world: <20 s on commodity hardware with Proxmark3 or mfoc tool.

docs.title: 21.15 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The secure element and smart card ecosystem has expanded rapidly into digital identity, post-quantum cryptography, and consumer device integration.

docs.title: 21.15.1 ISO/IEC 7816-15 (2023): Cryptographic Information Application
docs.text:
ISO/IEC 7816-15:2023 updated the Cryptographic Information Application standard for smart cards, aligning it with modern algorithm suites and key container formats. The revision introduced:

  • Extended CertificateInfo objects to accommodate Elliptic Curve certificates with named curves beyond the original NIST P-256 set, including Brainpool P-384 and Ed25519.

  • Post-quantum placeholder key object types using vendor-extension mechanisms in the PKCS#15 structure, anticipating FIPS 203/204 standardisation.

  • Updated TokenInfo record to include a flags field for indicating PQC readiness, hardware security level, and FIPS 140-3 compliance.

  • Alignment with PKCS#15 v1.2 and the GlobalPlatform 2.3.1 card content management specification.

docs.title: 21.15.2 GlobalPlatform SEPE (Secure Element Policy Engine, 2023)
docs.text:
GlobalPlatform published the Secure Element Policy Engine (SEPE) specification in 2023, providing a standardised framework for enforcing security policies on SE operations without requiring individual applet modification. SEPE operates as a privileged service in the Issuer Security Domain and intercepts APDU commands before they reach target applets. Key capabilities:

  • Rate limiting: Configurable maximum number of authentication attempts per time window, enforced at the SE OS level rather than in each applet.

  • Geofencing (NFC): Policy rules that restrict NFC payment operations to specific geographic regions, implemented via carrier signal metadata.

  • Biometric binding: SEPE policies can require biometric verification (FIDO UAF) as a precondition for high-value operations.

  • Remote policy update: Policy rules are signed and pushed via the GlobalPlatform Secure Channel Protocol (SCP11c), enabling remote risk management.

docs.title: 21.15.3 Apple Secure Element: iPhone 15/16 (A17 Pro, 3 nm)
docs.text:
Apple’s Secure Enclave in the iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro, TSMC 3 nm process) and iPhone 16 series continues to serve as the hardware SE for both biometric authentication and NFC payments. The A17 Pro integrates the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP) on the same 3 nm die as the main application processor, with hardware isolation preventing the AP from accessing SEP memory. The SEP manages:

  • Apple Pay / NFC payments: The payment credential (card number substitute, Device Account Number) is stored in the SE’s NVM and signed by the SEP’s unique device key for each transaction. The SE communicates directly with the NFC controller, bypassing the AP for contactless transactions.

  • iOS 17 Digital ID: iPhone 15/16 expanded the Wallet app to present digital driver’s licences and national IDs (in participating US states) from secure hardware. The presentation protocol uses the ISO 18013-5 mobile driving licence (mDL) standard with the SE holding the identity credential.

  • Passkeys: FIDO2 passkeys generated on iPhone 15/16 are anchored to the SEP—the ECDSA P-256 private key is hardware-bound, though passkeys sync encrypted through iCloud Keychain.

docs.title: 21.15.4 Google Pixel 8 Titan M2: SE + HSM Combo
docs.text:
The Google Pixel 8 (2023) and Pixel 8 Pro ship with the Titan M2 chip, which Google redesigned to function simultaneously as a secure element and a hardware security module. The Titan M2 in Pixel 8:

  • Manages the Android Strongbox Keymaster: a hardware-isolated keystore providing FIDO2 platform authenticator functionality, disk encryption key protection, and Android Keystore operations at security level SECURITY_LEVEL_STRONGBOX.

  • Stores the Pixel Titan Verified Boot signing key, providing an independent hardware root of trust separate from the application processor.

  • Supports Private Compute Core operations, protecting on-device ML model outputs from leaking to other apps or the OS.

  • Achieved Common Criteria EAL5+ (under the Mobile Device Fundamentals PP v3.3) for the Pixel 8 as a complete device, with the Titan M2 SE as a core evaluated component.

docs.title: 21.15.5 SE for Digital Identity: eIDAS 2.0 EUDIW Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
The European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDIW) regulation, finalised as eIDAS 2.0 in 2024 (Regulation 2024/1183), establishes mandatory hardware requirements for the wallet’s secure storage component. Member states must make EUDIW available to all EU citizens by 2027. Hardware security requirements:

Table 21.10. eIDAS 2.0 EUDIW hardware security requirements EUDIW Hardware Requirement Minimum Assurance Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD) CC EAL4+ or equivalent Private key storage Hardware SE; keys non-extractable Authentication assurance eIDAS Level High (LoA High) Biometric binding On-device match, result in SE Proximity presentation (ISO 18013-5) SE-signed mDL response Remote qualified signature QSCD (EAL4+ HSM-backed)

The EUDIW Architecture Reference Framework (ARF 1.4, 2024) specifies that the WSCD must generate the wallet key pair on-chip and must not allow key export under any interface; this effectively mandates a dedicated secure element on the device.

Note: The EUDIW specification distinguishes between “remote” and “proximity” presentation flows. Both require hardware-backed signatures, but proximity flows (showing ID to a physical terminal) additionally require the ISO 18013-5 mDL protocol with SE-verified device authentication.

docs.title: 21.15.6 NXP SE051W: Post-Quantum Secure Element (2024)
docs.text:
NXP announced the SE051W in 2024 as the first commercially available secure element with native post-quantum cryptographic support. The SE051W extends the SE050 platform (CC EAL6+, I\(^2\)C, 50 KB NVM) with:

  • ML-KEM-512 support: Hardware-accelerated lattice arithmetic for Kyber key generation and encapsulation/decapsulation, enabling PQC key exchange from an IoT device without software overhead.

  • Hybrid key operations: A single APDU command can execute a hybrid ECDH P-256 + ML-KEM-512 key agreement, combining the outputs in a KDF.

  • Updated EdgeLock library: NXP’s SE05x middleware was updated to support PKCS#11 3.0 CKM_KYBER mechanism, transparently routing PQC operations to the SE hardware.

  • Form factor: Same WLCSP 2.5 \(\times\) 2.5 mm package as SE050, enabling drop-in upgrades in existing PCB designs.

// SE051W: ML-KEM-512 key generation via SE05x middleware (C API)
#include "fsl_sss_se05x_apis.h"

sss_se05x_key_store_t keyStore;
sss_se05x_object_t kyberKey;
uint8_t pubKey[800]; size_t pubKeyLen = 800; /* ML-KEM-512 public key */

/* Create ML-KEM-512 key pair in SE NVM slot 0x70000001 */
sss_se05x_key_object_init(&kyberKey, &keyStore);
sss_se05x_key_object_allocate_handle(&kyberKey, 0x70000001,
    kSSS_KeyPart_Pair, kSSS_CipherType_KYBER_512, 0,
    kKeyObject_Mode_Persistent);
sss_se05x_key_store_generate_key(&keyStore, &kyberKey, 512, NULL);
sss_se05x_key_store_get_key(&keyStore, &kyberKey,
    pubKey, &pubKeyLen, NULL);

Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between ISO 7816 T=0 and T=1 protocols. Which has better error recovery and why?

  2. A JavaCard applet must implement ECDH key agreement over P-256. Write the process() method skeleton showing JCAPI calls for KeyPair, KeyAgreement, and Cipher objects.

  3. GlobalPlatform defines three key types in SCP03: ENC, MAC, and DEK. Describe the purpose of each and which APDU fields they protect.

  4. Trace the full EMV CDA (Combined DDA/Application Cryptogram) flow, explaining how it combines offline authentication with the online AC.

  5. A US agency issues PIV cards with slot 9A using ECC P-384. List the X.509 certificate fields required by FIPS 201-3 and the key usage bits that must be set.

  6. Describe how ICAO PACE protocol prevents brute-force attacks on MRZ data, referencing the PAKE mechanism and entropy analysis.

  7. A building access system uses MIFARE Classic 1K cards. An auditor finds that all cards share the same Key A. Explain the specific attack steps and propose a migration to MIFARE DESFire EV3 with AES-128.

  8. Calculate the maximum eavesdropping range for ISO 14443-A at 13.56 MHz given a reader field strength of 7.5 A/m and a passive attacker antenna with Q-factor=30.

  9. The NXP P60 active shield detects wire tampering by measuring capacitance on a mesh routed above the die. Explain how laser fault injection (LFI) can still succeed and what countermeasures the EAL6+ evaluation requires.

  10. An SCP02 channel is active on a JavaCard platform. An attacker intercepts and replays a C-APDU containing STORE DATA. Explain why SCP02 sequence counters prevent the replay and how SCP03 improves on this with AEAD.

  11. Compare Apple Secure Enclave (T2 chip), Google Titan M2, and Samsung Galaxy S23 SE in terms of: process node, key storage architecture, and OS attestation key.

  12. A researcher captures 1000 power traces during RSA-2048 signing on an NXP P60. Explain how Template Attack (a supervised SCA technique) can recover the private exponent, and list the three hardware countermeasures in the P60 that resist it.

docs.title: Chapter 22: FIDO2 and WebAuthn Hardware Security Keys
22.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Phishing accounts for over 80% of credential compromise incidents. Traditional passwords and even SMS one-time passwords (OTPs) are trivially bypassed by phishing: an attacker creates a look-alike site, forwards credentials to the legitimate site in real time, and harvests session cookies. FIDO2 (Fast IDentity Online 2) eliminates phishing by binding authentication to the cryptographic identity of the origin (website domain). A hardware security key physically cannot authenticate to a phishing site even if the user is deceived – the key verifies the relying party origin before signing.

The FIDO2 ecosystem consists of two specifications: WebAuthn (W3C recommendation, browser API) and CTAP2 (Client-To-Authenticator Protocol, FIDO Alliance). Together they enable passkeys – cryptographic credentials replacing passwords, stored either on hardware security keys (roaming authenticators) or in platform secure enclaves (platform authenticators).

docs.title: 22.2 FIDO2 Architecture
docs.text:
Table 22.1. FIDO2 specification components Component Specification Description WebAuthn W3C Recommendation Browser JavaScript API for registration and authentication CTAP2 FIDO Alliance Protocol between client platform and hardware authenticator CTAP1/U2F FIDO Alliance Legacy; HMAC-SHA256 response; no resident credentials 
FIDO2 Transport Protocols (CTAP2):
  USB HID: Human Interface Device; no driver needed; 64-byte HID reports
  NFC: ISO 14443 Type A; APDU framing over NFC-IF
  BLE (Bluetooth LE): FIDO over BLE v2.0; GATT service UUID 0xFFFD
  Internal: for platform authenticators (Touch ID, Face ID, TPM)

Authenticator Types:
  Roaming: hardware key (YubiKey, Titan, Feitian) -- transport: USB/NFC/BLE
  Platform: built-in (Apple Touch ID, Android Keystore, Windows Hello TPM)
  Cross-platform: passkey synced across devices via cloud (Apple iCloud Keychain)

docs.title: 22.3.1 YubiKey 5 Hardware Deep-Dive
docs.text:
YubiKey 5 NFC Hardware:
  Secure Element: Infineon SLE78 (upgraded from SLE75 in older keys)
    - Process: 65nm (SLE78CLFX4000P)
    - CPU: Custom 8051-compatible core with security extensions
    - Crypto: AES-128/256, ECDSA P-256/P-384/P-521, RSA-2048/4096
              Ed25519, X25519 (FIDO2 authenticator extensions)
    - RNG: True RNG (ring oscillator based)
    - Protection: active shield, voltage monitors, light sensors, glitch detectors
    - Certification: Common Criteria EAL6+ (BSI-DSZ-CC-1166)

  MCU: Atmel AT32UC3 (USB/NFC interface controller)
  Form factor: USB-A + NFC (5 NFC); USB-C (5C); USB-C + NFC (5C NFC)

  Supported protocols:
    FIDO2 / WebAuthn (CTAP2.1)
    FIDO U2F (CTAP1) -- backwards compatible
    PIV (NIST SP 800-73): 4 PIV slots (9a, 9c, 9d, 9e) + 24 retired slots
    OpenPGP 3.4: sign, encrypt, authenticate (4096-bit RSA / Ed25519)
    OATH TOTP/HOTP: up to 32 credentials (SHA-1/SHA-256)
    YubiHSM Auth: AES-128-based session keys for YubiHSM 2

  Key storage (FIDO2 resident credentials):
    Max 25 discoverable credentials (passkeys) in SLE78 NVM
    Non-resident: HMAC-SHA256 key handle (server stores credential ID)

docs.title: 22.3.2 YubiKey Management Commands
docs.text:
# ykman: YubiKey Manager CLI (pip install yubikey-manager)

# Device information
ykman info
# YubiKey 5 NFC (serial 12345678)
# Firmware: 5.4.3
# Form factor: USB-A Keychain (5 NFC)
# Applications: OTP, U2F, FIDO2, OATH, PIV, OpenPGP, YubiHSM Auth

# List FIDO2 credentials (passkeys)
ykman fido credentials list

# Delete a specific passkey
ykman fido credentials delete <credential-id>

# FIDO2 PIN management
ykman fido access change-pin
ykman fido access verify-pin

# PIV certificate management
ykman piv info
ykman piv keys generate 9a  # Generate new RSA-2048 key in slot 9a
ykman piv certificates import 9a cert.pem

# OATH TOTP management
ykman oath accounts list
ykman oath accounts add --issuer Google user@gmail.com
ykman oath accounts code user@gmail.com

# Reset FIDO2 application (deletes all FIDO2 credentials)
ykman fido reset

docs.title: 22.4 Google Titan Security Key
docs.text:
Google Titan Security Key (2023):
  MCU: STM32L432 (Cortex-M4, 256KB flash, no dedicated SE)
       OR NXP A700X (proprietary secure element variant)
  Firmware: OpenSK (Google open-source FIDO2 in Rust)
  Variants: USB-A/C + NFC + Bluetooth

Google Pixel Titan M2 (embedded in Pixel 6+):
  Die: Samsung 10nm, separate from AP
  Function: FIDO2 platform authenticator (Titan M2 acts as SE for passkeys)
  Integration: Android Strongbox API -> Titan M2 keymaster
  Keys: ECDSA P-256 per-credential; master seed in Titan M2 NVM

docs.title: 22.5 SoloKeys (Open-Source)
docs.text:
SoloKeys Solo 2:
  MCU: NXP LPC55S69 (ARM Cortex-M33, TrustZone-M, 640KB flash, 320KB SRAM)
  SE: None -- TrustZone-M provides software isolation
  Firmware: Trussed (Rust security framework) + fido-authenticator crate
  Protocols: FIDO2/CTAP2.1, FIDO U2F, OpenPGP Card 3.4

  Build and flash:
    # Install Rust and thumbv8m toolchain
    rustup target add thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf
    # Build firmware
    cd solo2
    cargo build --release --target thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf
    # Flash via USB DFU
    dfu-util -d 1209:BEEE -a 0 --dfuse-address 0x08000000:leave \
      -D target/thumbv8m.main-none-eabihf/release/solo2.bin

OpenSK (Google, on Nordic nRF52840):
  Target: nRF52840 DK or Dongle (BLE + USB)
  Build:
    git clone https://github.com/google/OpenSK
    cd OpenSK
    python3 setup.py  # Install dependencies
    # Flash to nRF52840 DK:
    ./deploy.py --target=nrf52840_dk --opensk

docs.title: 22.6.1 Registration (Credential Creation)
docs.text:
WebAuthn Registration Flow (JavaScript + YubiKey):

// 1. Server generates challenge:
const challenge = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32));

// 2. Browser calls navigator.credentials.create():
const credential = await navigator.credentials.create({
  publicKey: {
    challenge,
    rp: { name: "Example Corp", id: "example.com" },
    user: {
      id: new TextEncoder().encode("user123"),
      name: "alice@example.com",
      displayName: "Alice"
    },
    pubKeyCredParams: [
      { type: "public-key", alg: -7 },   // ES256 (ECDSA P-256 + SHA-256)
      { type: "public-key", alg: -8 },   // EdDSA (Ed25519)
      { type: "public-key", alg: -257 }  // RS256 (RSA-PKCS1-v1.5 + SHA-256)
    ],
    authenticatorSelection: {
      authenticatorAttachment: "cross-platform",  // Roaming key
      userVerification: "preferred",
      residentKey: "preferred"  // Discoverable credential (passkey)
    },
    attestation: "direct"  // Request attestation statement from key
  }
});

// credential.response contains:
//   clientDataJSON: { type, challenge, origin, crossOrigin }
//   attestationObject: CBOR({ fmt, attStmt, authData })

// authData structure (37+ bytes):
//   [0..31]   rpIdHash: SHA256("example.com")
//   [32]      flags: UP(1) | UV(2) | AT(64) | ED(128) bits
//   [33..36]  signCount: 0 (initial; increments on each authentication)
//   [37..52]  aaguid: 16-byte authenticator model ID
//   [53..54]  credentialIdLength
//   [55..N]   credentialId (random, 16-128 bytes)
//   [N+1..]   credentialPublicKey: CBOR-encoded ECDSA P-256 public key

// 3. Server verifies: challenge, origin, rpIdHash, UP flag, attStmt

docs.title: 22.6.2 Authentication (Assertion)
docs.text:
WebAuthn Authentication Flow:

// Server sends challenge + allowed credentials:
const assertion = await navigator.credentials.get({
  publicKey: {
    challenge,
    rpId: "example.com",
    allowCredentials: [{
      type: "public-key",
      id: credentialId,   // stored from registration
      transports: ["usb", "nfc"]
    }],
    userVerification: "preferred"
  }
});

// assertion.response:
//   authenticatorData: rpIdHash(32) + flags(1) + signCount(4)
//   clientDataJSON: { type="webauthn.get", challenge, origin }
//   signature: ECDSA-P256 signature over SHA256(authData || clientDataJSON_hash)

// Server verification:
// 1. Verify challenge matches
// 2. Verify rpIdHash == SHA256("example.com")
// 3. Verify UP flag is set (user physically present)
// 4. Verify signCount > stored count (replay prevention)
// 5. Verify ECDSA-P256 signature using stored public key:
//    sig_data = authData || SHA256(clientDataJSON)
//    ECDSA_verify(pubkey, sig_data, signature)

docs.title: 22.7 Attestation Formats
docs.text:
FIDO2 Attestation Statement Formats:

1. packed (most common -- YubiKey, Titan):
   fmt = "packed"
   attStmt = { alg: -7, sig: ECDSA_P256(attestation_key, sig_data),
               x5c: [attestation_cert, ...intermediate..., root] }
   Verify: chain to FIDO Metadata Service (MDS3) root

2. tpm (enterprise -- Windows Hello):
   fmt = "tpm"
   attStmt = { ver: "2.0", alg: -257, x5c: [...], sig: RSA_sign,
               certInfo: TPMS_ATTEST, pubArea: TPMT_PUBLIC }

3. android-safetynet (Android):
   fmt = "android-safetynet"
   attStmt = { ver: "3.0", response: JWT }
   JWT contains: nonce = SHA256(authData || clientDataJSON)

4. none (SoloKey Solo 1, development):
   fmt = "none"   // Self-attestation; no manufacturer cert
   No AAGUID lookup; cannot verify authenticator model

FIDO Metadata Service (MDS3):
  URL: https://mds3.fidoalliance.org/
  Format: JSON JWT; entry per AAGUID; authenticator security level
  Trust levels: L1 (software) through L3 (hardware SE, side-channel resistant)

docs.title: 22.8 Physical Security: YubiKey Clone Resistance
docs.text:
YubiKey SLE78 Clone Resistance (NinjaLab 2021 Research):

Theoretical attack (Eurocrypt 2021):
  - Target: Infineon SLE78 ECDSA P-256 implementation
  - Method: Electromagnetic side-channel + lattice attack on nonce bias
  - Finding: Infineon's ECDSA nonce generation had a 1-bit bias
  - Nonces k: 255 bits instead of 256 bits (k always < 2^255)
  - Lattice attack: 100 EM traces -> recover private key

Practical difficulty:
  - Requires opening YubiKey (destructive decap)
  - Expensive EM probe station ($100K+)
  - Significant expertise: DSP, lattice cryptography
  - Only 256 keys affected (specific firmware/SLE78 version)
  - Infineon patched: YubiKey firmware 5.7+ uses corrected ECDSA

Mitigation in later versions:
  - Firmware 5.7.x: constant-time ECDSA nonce generation
  - Side-channel countermeasures: randomized execution, masking in SLE78

docs.title: 22.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: Replay Attack Prevention via signCount

A YubiKey increments its signCount with every FIDO2 assertion. A server stores signCount = 42 after the last authentication. (a) How does this prevent replay attacks? (b) If the YubiKey is cloned, what does the server observe? (c) What is the correct server response when signCount decreases?

Solution: (a) Replay prevention: Each authentication assertion includes the current signCount (4-byte counter in authenticatorData). The server verifies that the received signCount \(>\) stored signCount. A replayed authentication message (captured network packet) will have the old signCount value (\(\leq 42\)), which the server rejects.

(b) Cloned YubiKey detection: If the YubiKey is cloned at signCount = 42, both keys start counting from 43. After the legitimate user authenticates (signCount = 43), the clone authenticates (signCount = 43 – same value). Server receives signCount \(\leq\) stored value: detects potential cloning.

(c) Correct server response: Per WebAuthn spec Section 7.2 step 17: if signCount \(\leq\) stored count, the server may fail the authentication. Recommended action:

  1. Log the event as a potential clone attack.

  2. Require additional verification (email confirmation, re-enrollment).

  3. Alert the user and security team.

  4. Do NOT silently accept – this defeats the clone detection.

Note: Some authenticators (software-based, synced passkeys) always return signCount = 0, which servers must accept without clone detection for those AAGUID values.

Solved Problem: FIDO2 Origin Binding: Phishing Resistance

A user registers a YubiKey on https://bank.com. An attacker sets up https://bank-secure.com and tricks the user into authenticating there. Explain why the YubiKey CANNOT sign the phishing site’s challenge.

Solution: During both registration and authentication, the browser computes:

\[\text{rpIdHash} = \text{SHA256}(\text{rpId})\]

The rpId is extracted from the publicKey.rpId parameter set by the relying party as seen by the browser. For https://bank.com, the browser enforces:

  • rpId must be a registrable domain suffix of the origin’s effective domain.

  • So for origin https://bank.com, valid rpIds are: bank.com only.

  • bank-secure.com has a different effective domain – the browser will reject any publicKey.rpId that does not match.

Even if the attacker somehow passes rpId = bank.com, the browser would:

  1. Still compute rpIdHash = SHA256(bank.com).

  2. Send authenticatorGetAssertion to the YubiKey with this hash.

  3. The YubiKey searches its credential store for rpIdHash = SHA256(bank.com).

  4. Found – signs the challenge.

  5. BUT: the signature is over authData || clientDataJSON_hash.

  6. The clientDataJSON contains "origin": "https://bank-secure.com".

  7. The legitimate server (bank.com) verifies: "origin" must equal "https://bank.com" – MISMATCH – verification fails.

The phishing attack fails because the signed origin is cryptographically bound to the assertion. The YubiKey and browser enforce that phishing sites cannot obtain valid signatures for different origins.

Solved Problem: YubiKey SLE78 ECDSA Nonce Bias Attack

The NinjaLab 2021 research showed a 1-bit bias in SLE78 ECDSA P-256 nonces: k is always \(< 2^{255}\) instead of uniformly random in \([1, n-1]\). (a) How many signatures are needed to recover the private key using lattice methods? (b) What is the practical barrier?

Solution: (a) Lattice attack requirement: With a 1-bit bias (MSB always 0), each nonce leaks 1 bit. The Hidden Number Problem (HNP) formulation:

  • Known: \(t_i = r_i \cdot s_i^{-1} \pmod{n}\) (from public signature values r, s)

  • Known: \(u_i = -m_i \cdot s_i^{-1} \pmod{n}\) (from known message hash)

  • Hidden: \(k_i = k_{\text{hidden}_i}\) (256-bit nonce, 255-bit effective)

The lattice dimension needed scales as \(d \approx n\_bits / bits\_leaked\). For 1-bit leakage from 256-bit nonces: need \(d \approx 256\) signatures. In practice, the NinjaLab attack used \(\approx 100\) EM traces with a probabilistic lattice solver (BKZ with block size 40).

(b) Practical barriers:

  1. Physical access: The attack requires EM side-channel measurement with a micrometer-scale probe at \(\sim\)400 MHz – the YubiKey must be physically disassembled or a PCB-tapping coil applied.

  2. Equipment: Professional EM analysis station: R&S RTO oscilloscope (\(>\)$50K), Langer EM probe set, XYZ positioner – total \(>\)$100K.

  3. Expertise: Digital signal processing to align traces; knowledge of SLE78 microarchitecture timing.

  4. Scope: Only YubiKey firmware 5.x with unpatched SLE78 ECDSA; firmware 5.7+ patched.

Solved Problem: Passkey Syncing: Security vs. Hardware Binding

Apple iCloud Keychain syncs passkeys across all user devices (iPhone, iPad, Mac). YubiKey resident credentials (passkeys) stay on the physical key. Compare the security properties of each for: (a) device loss, (b) phishing resistance, (c) key export/clone risk.

Solution: (a) Device loss:

  • iCloud Keychain: Passkeys are synced; if device is lost, user accesses passkeys from another device. Advantage: No access loss.

  • YubiKey: Passkey is bound to the physical key; if lost, user needs a registered backup key. Risk: Single point of failure without backup.

(b) Phishing resistance: Both provide full phishing resistance – the origin binding is enforced by the browser regardless of whether the authenticator is a hardware key or a platform authenticator.

(c) Key export/clone risk:

  • iCloud Keychain: Keys are exported (in encrypted form) to Apple servers. Apple uses HSMs for key escrow; requires Apple ID + iCloud encryption key. A sophisticated adversary with Apple iCloud access, or an NSL/court order, could potentially access keys. Security depends on Apple’s infrastructure and the user’s Apple ID security.

  • YubiKey: Private key is generated inside SLE78 SE (CC EAL6+); cannot be exported by any command or protocol. Physical tamper attack (FIB) at the silicon level would destroy the chip. Stronger hardware binding but no recovery path.

Recommendation: For highest assurance (banking, government), hardware-bound YubiKey with a registered backup key. For consumer usability, iCloud Keychain passkeys provide phishing resistance with acceptable syncing security.

docs.title: 22.14 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The FIDO2 ecosystem has undergone rapid expansion driven by platform-level passkey adoption, a revised CTAP 2.2 protocol, and a notable side-channel vulnerability disclosure.

docs.title: 22.14.1 FIDO2/Passkeys Mass Adoption (2023–2024)
docs.text:
Apple, Google, and Microsoft completed their passkey ecosystem rollouts during 2023–2024, making passkeys the default password replacement across all major platforms:

  • Apple (iOS 17/macOS 14, 2023): iCloud Keychain syncs passkeys across all Apple devices via end-to-end encrypted cloud backup. Passkeys appear natively in Safari and in-app via the Authentication Services API. Third-party apps can register and authenticate with a single API call.

  • Google (Android 14, Chrome 119, 2023): Google Password Manager stores passkeys on Android devices, synced to the user’s Google Account. Chrome 119 added cross-device passkey use (phone-as-authenticator via Bluetooth CABLE). Google Workspace accounts (350 million+) can disable passwords entirely in favour of passkeys.

  • Microsoft (Windows 11 24H2, 2024): Windows Hello backed passkeys are stored in the TPM 2.0 (where present), providing hardware-bound passkeys. The Windows Credential UI shows passkeys as the primary authentication option, replacing password prompts.

By Q4 2024, over 13 billion user accounts across Google, Apple, GitHub, PayPal, and Shopify supported passkeys, making it the most rapidly adopted authentication technology in FIDO Alliance history.

docs.title: 22.14.2 CTAP 2.2 (2023): Hybrid Transport and Enterprise Attestation
docs.text:
The FIDO Alliance published the CTAP 2.2 specification in 2023, adding two major capabilities:

Hybrid transport (Bluetooth CABBLE v2): A smartphone can act as a roaming authenticator for a desktop or laptop via a Bluetooth proximity-verified, QR-code initiated channel. The flow:

  1. Desktop browser displays a QR code encoding a one-time 16-byte handshake secret and the platform’s Bluetooth address.

  2. User scans the QR code with their phone camera.

  3. Phone establishes an authenticated BLE connection to the desktop.

  4. Phone’s platform authenticator (Secure Enclave / Strongbox) handles the FIDO2 assertion and returns it to the desktop browser via the hybrid channel.

Enterprise attestation: CTAP 2.2 adds a new ENTERPRISE_ATTESTATION attestation type allowing an authenticator enrolled in an enterprise MDM to provide a device-unique attestation certificate, enabling the relying party to restrict authentication to specific, registered hardware tokens.

docs.title: 22.14.3 YubiKey 5.7 Firmware (2024): FIDO2.2 and PQC Roadmap
docs.text:
Yubico released YubiKey firmware 5.7 in May 2024, adding full CTAP 2.2 support including hybrid transport and enterprise attestation. Yubico simultaneously published a public PQC roadmap:

  • 5.7 (2024): CTAP 2.2, up to 100 resident credentials (up from 25 in 5.4), improved HMAC-SHA-256 extension performance.

  • Future hardware revision (2025+): Post-quantum signature for attestation (ML-DSA-65 hybrid alongside ECDSA P-256), requiring a hardware revision for the SLE78 replacement secure element due to the larger key and signature sizes.

  • FIPS YubiKey 5: The FIPS 140-3 Level 3 variant shipped alongside 5.7, targeting US federal deployments mandating FIPS-validated authenticators.

docs.title: 22.14.4 CVE-2024-45678: YubiKey 5 ECDSA Side-Channel (EUCLEAK)
docs.text:
In September 2024, NinjaLab disclosed CVE-2024-45678 (EUCLEAK): a microarchitectural side-channel vulnerability in the Infineon SLE78 security element’s implementation of ECDSA that affects YubiKey 5 series firmware prior to 5.7.

  • Root cause: The Infineon SLE78 ECDSA implementation used a non-constant-time modular inversion in the nonce generation path. Specifically, the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) used for computing \(k^{-1} \bmod n\) had a data-dependent execution path that leaked information about the nonce \(k\) through electromagnetic side-channel measurements.

  • Attack complexity: The attacker requires physical access to the YubiKey, a specialised EM probe and oscilloscope setup, and approximately 10–40 CTAP2 authentication operations. The lattice attack (Hidden Number Problem) recovers the ECDSA P-256 private key from the collected traces.

  • Affected products: All YubiKey 5 series with firmware \(<\) 5.7 and all Infineon SLE78-based security keys. YubiKey firmware is not user-upgradeable, so affected keys cannot be patched.

  • Practical impact: Rated CVSS 4.9 (Medium). Requires physical possession of the key and substantial attacker capability. The attack does not allow remote exploitation.

Warning: CVE-2024-45678 (EUCLEAK) demonstrates that CC EAL6+ certification does not guarantee resistance to all side-channel attacks—the SLE78 holds EAL6+ but the ECDSA modular inversion was vulnerable. Hardware security keys should be treated as potentially clonable if an attacker achieves even brief physical access.

docs.title: 22.14.5 Google Titan Security Key v2 (2023): USB-A/C/NFC
docs.text:
Google released the second-generation Titan Security Key in 2023, available in USB-A+NFC and USB-C+NFC variants. Technical updates:

  • Replaced the previous STM32L432-only MCU design with a dual-chip architecture using a dedicated secure element (NXP A700X class) for credential storage.

  • Up to 250 passkeys stored on device (versus 25 on the original Titan Key).

  • Full CTAP 2.1 support, with a firmware update path to CTAP 2.2.

  • OpenSK (Google’s open-source FIDO2 Rust firmware) updated to support the new hardware in the same release cycle.

docs.title: 22.14.6 Passkeys in Hardware: TPM-Backed and Secure Enclave
docs.text:
Table 22.5. Passkey hardware storage comparison across platforms (2024) Platform Storage Synced? HW Binding Windows Hello (TPM 2.0) TPM NVM No (device-bound) FIPS 140-2 Level 2 TPM Apple Secure Enclave (iOS/macOS) SEP NVM Yes (iCloud, E2E) Custom Arm core Android Strongbox (Titan M2) Titan M2 NVM Yes (Google Acct) CC EAL5+ YubiKey 5.7 (SLE78) SE NVM No (hardware-bound) CC EAL6+ Google Titan Key v2 (NXP SE) SE NVM No (hardware-bound) CC EAL5+

TPM-backed passkeys on Windows 11 (via Windows Hello) store the ECDSA P-256 private key in the TPM 2.0 under a key sealed to the platform’s PCR values. This means the passkey is device-bound—it cannot be exported or cloned—but also cannot be recovered if the TPM is erased. For enterprise deployments, Microsoft Entra ID supports Hardware-Bound Passkeys as a Phishing-Resistant MFA method, enabling organisations to require TPM-backed passkeys as a condition for access to sensitive resources.

docs.title: 22.15 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between a resident credential (passkey) and a non-resident credential in CTAP2. What is the maximum number of resident credentials on a YubiKey 5? What happens when the limit is reached?

  2. WebAuthn userVerification can be “required”, “preferred”, or “discouraged”. Explain the difference in the authenticator behavior for each setting. When does the UV bit get set in authenticatorData? What attack does “required” mitigate?

  3. A YubiKey is registered for FIDO2 on both Gmail and GitHub. Explain why the YubiKey’s ECDSA private key for Gmail authentication cannot be used to impersonate the user on GitHub, even if both credentials use the same underlying key pair within the same application slot.

  4. Compare CTAP2 over USB HID vs NFC transport for: (a) maximum transaction speed, (b) MITM resistance, (c) pairing requirements, (d) suitability for banking applications.

  5. An enterprise deploys YubiKeys for all 50,000 employees. Describe the lifecycle management: (a) provisioning workflow (key, certificate, FIDO2 registration), (b) remote attestation of authenticator model, (c) handling lost/stolen keys, (d) firmware update policy.

  6. FIDO2 “Authenticator Extensions” allow additional data in the assertion. Describe the “prf” extension (pseudo-random function) and how it enables passkey-based encryption of user data. What security property does it provide beyond authentication?

  7. Compare the security certification of YubiKey 5 (CC EAL6+), SoloKey Solo 2 (no CC), and Apple Passkeys (no hardware CC). In what deployment scenarios is each appropriate? What does CC EAL6+ specifically certify about the SLE78?

  8. A server receives a FIDO2 registration with attestation format “packed” and a certificate chain to the FIDO MDS3 root. Describe the 6-step server-side verification procedure. What happens if the AAGUID is not in MDS3?

  9. OpenSK on nRF52840 stores FIDO2 credentials in internal flash without a dedicated secure element. What attacks are possible against this design that are not possible against YubiKey (SLE78 SE)? How does TrustZone-M on LPC55S69 (Solo 2) partially mitigate these?

  10. A financial institution requires hardware-bound FIDO2 authentication with “cloneability detection” (signCount). Design the server-side session state machine: states, transitions, and actions for signCount anomalies.

docs.title: 23.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Hardware cryptocurrency wallets are purpose-built secure devices that store private keys in tamper-resistant silicon and sign blockchain transactions entirely within a secure boundary. Unlike software wallets—where keys reside in general-purpose memory accessible to the operating system and any malicious process—hardware wallets expose only a signing oracle: transaction data enters, a cryptographic signature exits, and the private key never leaves the device.

The threat model is severe. A compromised host computer, a malicious browser extension, or a supply-chain-level backdoor can drain every software wallet it touches; a hardware wallet with a correct implementation limits damage to physical possession of the device combined with knowledge of the PIN. High-profile thefts (the 2022 Ronin bridge hack at $625 million, the 2016 Bitfinex breach at 119,756 BTC) routinely exploit hot wallets or custodial exchange keys stored in software, motivating mass-market hardware wallet adoption.

This chapter covers the cryptographic standards (BIP32/39/44, SLIP39, PSBT), the silicon platforms (Ledger ST33, Trezor STM32, Coldcard ATECC608A), hardware attack surface (voltage glitching, EM side-channel, laser fault injection), formal security proofs, and open-source ecosystems.

docs.title: 23.2.1 BIP32: Hierarchical Deterministic Key Derivation
docs.text:
BIP32 (2012, Pieter Wuille) defines a tree of key pairs generated deterministically from a 128–256-bit master seed. Every node is an extended key: a 256-bit private key \(k\) paired with a 256-bit chain code \(c\).

Child key derivation (hardened):

\[(k_\text{child},\; c_\text{child}) = \text{HMAC-SHA512}(c_\text{parent},\; \texttt{0x00} \| k_\text{parent} \| \text{index})\]

Child key derivation (normal):

\[(k_\text{child},\; c_\text{child}) = \text{HMAC-SHA512}(c_\text{parent},\; \text{point}(k_\text{parent}) \| \text{index})\]

Hardened derivation (index \(\geq 2^{31}\)) prevents parent-key recovery even if a child private key is leaked alongside the parent public key.

docs.title: 23.2.2 BIP39: Mnemonic Seed Phrases
docs.text:
BIP39 encodes entropy as a word list for human backup. The process:

  1. Generate \(E\) bits of entropy (\(128 \leq E \leq 256\), multiple of 32).

  2. Append \(E/32\) checksum bits (SHA-256 of entropy, truncated).

  3. Split into 11-bit groups; look up each in the 2048-word BIP39 wordlist.

  4. Derive master seed: \(\text{PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512}(\text{mnemonic},\; \text{“mnemonic”}\|\text{passphrase},\; 2048,\; 512)\).

A 24-word phrase encodes 256 bits of entropy with 8 checksum bits, providing \(2^{256} \approx 1.16 \times 10^{77}\) possible seeds.

docs.title: 23.2.3 BIP44: Multi-Account Hierarchy
docs.text:
BIP44 specifies the derivation path:

m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index

where purpose' = 44’ for BIP44, coin_type' = 0’ for Bitcoin (SLIP44 registry), account' = 0’, change = 0 (external) or 1 (internal/change), and address_index = 0, 1, 2, …

Example Bitcoin receiving address path: m/44'/0'/0'/0/0.

docs.title: 23.2.4 SLIP39: Shamir’s Secret Sharing
docs.text:
SLIP39 (SatoshiLabs) extends BIP39 with \((m, n)\) Shamir’s Secret Sharing over \(GF(2^8)\). The master secret \(S\) is split into \(n\) shares; any \(m\) shares reconstruct \(S\), but \(m-1\) shares reveal nothing. Each share is encoded as a 20-word mnemonic.

Share construction: Choose random \(a_1, …, a_{m-1} \in GF(2^8)^{|S|}\); set \(f(x) = S + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + … + a_{m-1} x^{m-1}\) (polynomial over \(GF(2^8)\)). Share \(i\) = \((i, f(i))\).

Recovery (Lagrange interpolation):

\[S = f(0) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} f(x_i) \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{0 - x_j}{x_i - x_j} \pmod{GF(2^8)}\]

A 2-of-3 SLIP39 scheme allows one share to be lost or destroyed without losing funds.

docs.title: 23.2.5 PSBT: Partially Signed Bitcoin Transactions (BIP174)
docs.text:
PSBT decouples transaction construction from signing. A creator builds the unsigned transaction; one or more signers (hardware wallets) add partial signatures; a finalizer combines signatures into a broadcast-ready transaction. This enables multisig workflows with heterogeneous hardware devices.

PSBT v2 (BIP370) adds per-input/output metadata fields for better air-gap workflows.

docs.title: 23.3.1 Ledger Nano X / Nano S Plus
docs.text:
Ledger devices use a dual-chip architecture:

  • Secure Element (SE): STMicroelectronics ST33K1M5 (ARM SecurCore SC300, 90 nm, CC EAL5+). Houses private keys, seed derivation, and PIN verification. 1 MB flash, 10 KB RAM. Hardware DES/3DES/AES, RSA/ECC co-processor.

  • MCU: STM32WB55 (Cortex-M4 + Bluetooth 5.0 radio). Handles USB/BLE communication, OLED display, and button debouncing. Acts as a USB bridge between host and SE.

The OS is BOLOS (Blockchain Open Ledger Operating System), a custom microkernel on the SE. Applications (apps) for Bitcoin, Ethereum, etc. are isolated sandboxes that communicate with BOLOS via a restricted syscall interface. Apps cannot directly access the private key; they request BOLOS to sign a hash.

# Install Ledger Bitcoin app via ledger-live CLI
ledger-live app --install Bitcoin

# List installed apps
ledger-live app --list

# Python APDU communication (ledgercomm)
from ledgercomm import Transport
transport = Transport(interface="hid")
transport.send(0xe0, 0x40, 0x00, 0x00, b"")  # GET_FIRMWARE_VERSION
status, data = transport.recv()

docs.title: 23.3.2 Trezor Model T / Model One
docs.text:
Trezor uses a single-chip design with no dedicated secure element:

  • Model T: STM32F427 (Cortex-M4, 168 MHz, 1 MB flash, 192 KB RAM). Touchscreen (240x240 IPS LCD).

  • Model One: STM32F205 (Cortex-M3, 120 MHz, 1 MB flash, 128 KB RAM). Two physical buttons.

Trezor firmware is fully open-source (BSD/GPLv3 on GitHub). The bootloader verifies the firmware image signature (Ed25519) before loading. USB DFU mode is protected by a physical button confirmation.

# Trezor Python library
from trezorlib import btc, messages
from trezorlib.tools import parse_path

path = parse_path("m/84'/0'/0'/0/0")  # BIP84 native SegWit
address = btc.get_address(client, "Bitcoin", path,
                          script_type=messages.InputScriptType.SPENDWITNESS)
print(f"Address: {address}")

# Sign PSBT
signed_psbt = btc.sign_tx(client, "Bitcoin", inputs, outputs, details)

docs.title: 23.3.3 Coldcard Mk4
docs.text:
Coldcard (Coinkite) is Bitcoin-only with a strong emphasis on air-gap operation:

  • MCU: STM32L4S5 (Cortex-M4, 120 MHz, 2 MB flash, 640 KB SRAM).

  • Secure Element: Two ATECC608B chips (Microchip), CC EAL5+, providing monotonic counters, PIN attempt limiting, and encrypted key storage.

  • Interfaces: USB-C (airgap mode disables USB), microSD (for PSBT files), NFC, QR code display via camera module.

The ATECC608B enforces a PIN-backed key hierarchy: after 13 failed PIN attempts the secret is permanently erased. The “brick me” PIN allows instant self-destruct.

# Air-gap PSBT signing via microSD
# On Coldcard: insert SD, navigate Ready To Sign -> filename.psbt
# Coldcard writes filename-signed.psbt to SD

# On host (bitcoin-core)
bitcoin-cli finalizepsbt $(cat filename-signed.psbt | base64 -w0)
bitcoin-cli sendrawtransaction <hex>

docs.title: 23.3.4 Foundation Passport Gen 2
docs.text: Passport Gen 2 uses a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 (Cortex-M4F, 64 MHz) paired with an STM32H7 for camera-based QR code input/output. Fully open source (GPL v3, including PCB schematics). No USB host communication during signing; all data flows via QR codes printed on screen or scanned via camera.
