docs.title: 25.14.5 UK DSIT Digital Security by Design Programme Outcomes (2024)
docs.text:
The UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) published the final outcomes of the Digital Security by Design (DSbD) programme in 2024:

  • GBP 190 million invested: Over 100 industrial and academic organisations participated in the programme, receiving Morello SDP boards and access to CHERI toolchains.

  • Commercial pathway: Arm announced that CHERI capability features are planned for future Arm IP licensing, enabling SoC vendors to incorporate CHERI into production silicon without waiting for a full Morello-class processor.

  • CHERIoT commercial deployment: Microsoft announced that CHERIoT-based hardware is under evaluation for Azure IoT Edge devices, potentially making CHERIoT the first commercially deployed CHERI variant.

  • Standards: BSI (British Standards Institution) published PAS 1885:2024 (“CHERI-based security in embedded systems”), the first national standard referencing CHERI capability hardware.

docs.title: 25.14.6 Arm CHERI Morello: Capability Bounds Violations in Production Code
docs.text:
The Arm Morello evaluation team published analysis of capability bounds violations detected when running real production software on Morello in purecap mode. Findings:

  • OpenSSL 3.0.x: 4 capability faults detected in the ASN.1 parser and the BIGNUM arithmetic routines, caused by pointer arithmetic that assumed contiguous memory layout across separately allocated objects.

  • SQLite 3.x: 2 capability faults in the page cache eviction code, where a pointer was incremented past the end of a buffer in an unused code path.

  • zlib 1.2.x: 1 capability fault in the Huffman decompression loop when processing a malformed input—the fault would have been exploitable as an out-of-bounds read in a non-CHERI build.

  • Python 3.11: 11 capability faults in CPython’s object allocator and the struct module, reflecting assumptions about memory layout that are valid on x86-64 but not guaranteed by the C standard.

These real-world results validate the CHERI capability model’s effectiveness: vulnerabilities that would have been silent memory corruptions on conventional hardware were converted to deterministic, debuggable faults on Morello.

docs.title: 25.15 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Draw the CHERI CC128 capability structure for a heap allocation at address 0x10000 of size 512 bytes. Specify the address, bounds encoding (exponent, B, T), permissions (R/W only), and tag bit value.

  2. Compare CHERI capability enforcement with Intel MPX (Memory Protection Extensions) and ARM MTE (Memory Tagging Extension) in terms of: granularity, performance overhead, type-safety guarantees, and hardware requirements.

  3. Explain why CHERI’s monotonicity property is essential for security. Give a concrete attack scenario that would be possible if software could widen a capability’s bounds.

  4. The CHERI Flute core on Kintex-7 achieves 110 MHz. A vanilla (non-CHERI) RISC-V core on the same device runs at 160 MHz. Calculate the clock frequency overhead and explain what microarchitectural additions cause it.

  5. Describe the CHERIoT compartment model for embedded RTOS use cases. How does CHERIoT differ from the server-class Morello in terms of capability register width and memory granularity?

  6. A shared library libpng processes untrusted PNG files and is compartmentalised in CheriBSD. Describe how CHERI prevents a heap buffer overflow in libpng from leaking the application’s private keys stored in a separate heap region.

  7. Analyse the performance overhead of CHERI purecap for pointer-intensive workloads (linked list traversal vs. sequential array access). Which workload sees more overhead and why?

  8. The Sail formal model of CHERI-RISC-V specifies the capability bounds check semantics. Write a Sail-like pseudocode for the CHERI load instruction CLC, including tag bit retrieval and bounds checking.

  9. Explain the “use-after-free” vulnerability class. How does CHERI’s tag bit—cleared by free()—prevent a dangling capability from being dereferenced after memory is released?

  10. Research the SOAAP (Security-Oriented Analysis of Application Programs) tool. How can it be used to identify which parts of a C++ application are good candidates for CHERI compartmentalisation?

  11. Calculate the tag RAM bandwidth overhead for a system with a DDR4-3200 memory controller (51.2 GB/s peak bandwidth) and a 10% tag cache miss rate. Tag RAM accesses are 64 bytes per miss (cache line granularity).

docs.title: 26.1 Introduction
docs.text:
RISC-V is an open, royalty-free instruction set architecture (ISA) whose modular extension model has made it uniquely amenable to hardware security innovation. Unlike x86 or ARMv8, where security features must negotiate decades of legacy compatibility, RISC-V implementers can adopt exactly the security extensions their threat model demands—whether that is physical memory protection for microcontrollers, cryptographic acceleration for IoT nodes, or Trusted Execution Environments for server-class chips.

The RISC-V Foundation (RISC-V International as of 2020) ratified numerous security extensions: the H (Hypervisor) extension for virtualisation isolation, the Smepmp/Zisslpcfi extensions for software privilege separation and control-flow integrity, the Zkr TRNG seed CSR, the Zk* scalar cryptographic extensions, and PMP/ePMP for physical memory protection.

Commercial implementations include SiFive (E21/E76, X280), Alibaba T-Head C906/C910, Western Digital SweRV, Microchip PolarFire SoC (Cortex-M + RISC-V), and ESWIN EIC7700 (Spacemit K1 series with AI accelerator + security processor).

This chapter covers the RISC-V privilege architecture, PMP/ePMP, Keystone and CURE TEE frameworks, cryptographic extensions (Zk*), CFI extensions, and side-channel mitigations.

docs.title: 26.2.1 Privilege Modes
docs.text:
RISC-V defines four privilege levels:

  • U-mode (User): Untrusted application code. Least privileged.

  • S-mode (Supervisor): OS kernel and hypervisor guest.

  • HS-mode (Hypervisor-extended Supervisor): Host hypervisor.

  • M-mode (Machine): Firmware (OpenSBI), highest privilege. Executes before the OS and configures security policies.

The trust hierarchy is M > HS > S > U. In TEE architectures, the security monitor runs in M-mode and enforces world isolation between a normal OS (S-mode) and a secure OS (S-mode in a separate hart context, or via WorldGuard extension).

docs.title: 26.2.2 Physical Memory Protection (PMP)
docs.text:
PMP restricts M-mode from delegating physical memory access to S/U-mode. Up to 64 PMP regions are supported (RISC-V spec v1.12). Each region is defined by:

  • pmpaddr: The address register (one per region).

  • pmpcfg: Configuration bits: R (read), W (write), X (execute), A (address matching mode: OFF/TOR/NA4/NAPOT), L (locked).

Address matching modes:

  • NAPOT (Naturally Aligned Power-of-Two): Region size \(2^k\) bytes, base aligned to \(2^k\). Most common.

  • TOR (Top Of Range): Region is [pmpaddr[i-1], pmpaddr[i]).

  • NA4: 4-byte granule, special case.

// OpenSBI PMP configuration (M-mode firmware)
// Protect 2 MB DRAM region for secure world (addr=0x80200000, size=0x200000)
// NAPOT encoding: pmpaddr = (base >> 2) | ((size/2 - 1) >> 2)
//               = (0x80200000 >> 2) | (0xFFFFF >> 2)
//               = 0x200800000 | 0x3FFFF = 0x2008FFFF... (simplified for illustration)

// Using OpenSBI domain API
struct sbi_domain_memregion reg = {
    .base  = 0x80200000,
    .order = 21,  // 2^21 = 2 MB
    .flags = SBI_DOMAIN_MEMREGION_READABLE |
             SBI_DOMAIN_MEMREGION_EXECUTABLE,
};
sbi_domain_root_add_memregion(&reg);

// In firmware (assembly): configure pmp0 for read-only secure region
// pmpaddr0 = NAPOT encoding for [0x80000000, 0x80200000)
// pmpcfg0  = 0x9F (L|A=NAPOT|X|W|R -> locked RWX)
csrw pmpaddr0, a0
csrw pmpcfg0,  a1

docs.title: 26.2.3 ePMP (Enhanced PMP, Smepmp)
docs.text:
The Smepmp extension (ratified 2022) adds M-mode self-restriction: M-mode code can mark PMP entries as machine-mode deny, preventing even M-mode from accessing certain physical regions. Key new configuration bit: mseccfg.MML (Machine Mode Lockdown).

With MML=1:

  • Locked PMP entries (L=1) apply to M-mode as well as S/U-mode.

  • An M-mode firmware can lock itself out of a secure region containing cryptographic keys, preventing any post-boot access.

docs.title: 26.3 RISC-V Scalar Cryptographic Extensions (Zk*)
docs.text:
The RISC-V scalar cryptographic extensions (ratified 2021) add hardware-accelerated cryptographic instructions to the base ISA:

  • Zkn (NIST algorithm suite): AES-128/192/256 (Zknd for decryption, Zkne for encryption), SHA-256/512 (Zknh), GHASH (for GCM).

  • Zks (ShangMi suite): SM4 block cipher, SM3 hash.

  • Zkr (Entropy Source): seed CSR — a 32-bit CSR that returns raw entropy from a hardware TRNG. The opcode csrrw rd, seed, x0 reads one 16-bit entropy word per access.

  • Zkt (Data-Independent Execution Latency): Declares that Zk instructions have constant execution time regardless of operand values. Critical for preventing timing side-channels in crypto code.

// RISC-V AES-128 single-round example (Zkne/Zknd instructions)
// aes32esmi: AES round function mix + sub (encoding mode)
// rd = aes32esmi(rs1, rs2, bs) where bs selects byte

// AES-128 key schedule (Zkne)
.macro AES128_KSC rd, rs1, rnum
    aes32esi  \rd, \rs1, \rs1, 0  // SubWord on byte 0
    xori      \rd, \rd, aes_rcon_\rnum
.endm

// GCM: GHASH using clmul (Zbc extension)
// GHASH(H, X) = X * H over GF(2^128)
clmul   a4, a0, a2    // low 64 bits of product
clmulh  a5, a0, a2    // high 64 bits

// TRNG: read entropy via Zkr seed CSR
read_entropy:
    csrrw   a0, seed, x0   // Read 16 bits of entropy + status
    srli    a1, a0, 30     // Extract status bits [31:30]
    li      a2, 1          // OPST_ES16 = 0b01 (valid entropy)
    bne     a1, a2, read_entropy  // Retry if not valid
    andi    a0, a0, 0xFFFF  // Extract 16-bit entropy word
    ret

AES throughput: On SiFive X280 (rv64gcv + Zkne, 1 GHz), AES-128-CBC achieves 2.1 Gbps using Zkne instructions—versus 0.18 Gbps using table-based AES. An 11.7\(\times\) speedup.

docs.title: 26.4 Keystone TEE Framework
docs.text:
Keystone is an open-source RISC-V TEE framework developed at UC Berkeley. It uses PMP to isolate an enclave (secure application) from the OS and other software:

  1. Security Monitor (SM): Runs in M-mode. Manages enclave lifecycle: ECREATE, EADD, EINIT, EENTER, EEXIT, EDESTROY.

  2. Enclave: U/S-mode trusted application + runtime library. Mapped to a PMP-protected physical region.

  3. Host OS: S-mode untrusted Linux. Communicates with SM via SBI (Supervisor Binary Interface) calls.

  4. Attestation: SM signs an attestation report over the enclave’s SHA-256 measurement using an Ed25519 key provisioned at manufacture time.

// Keystone host application: create and run enclave
#include "keystone.h"

Keystone::Enclave enclave;
Keystone::Params params;
params.setFreeMemSize(4 * 1024 * 1024);    // 4 MB enclave memory
params.setUntrustedMem(UNTRUSTED_START, 4096);
params.setEnclaveEntry(0x10000);

enclave.init("enclave.eapp", "runtime.eyrie", params);

// Get remote attestation report
Keystone::Report report;
enclave.getReport(&report, nonce, nonce_len);
// report contains SM signature over hash(enclave + nonce)

enclave.run();
enclave.destroy();

docs.title: 26.5 WorldGuard Memory Protection
docs.text:
The SiFive WorldGuard extension (proprietary, based on the RISC-V Trusted Execution Environment ratified work) assigns a world ID (WID) to every memory transaction. A WorldGuard checker at the bus interconnect filters transactions based on WID:

  • WID 0 = Normal World.

  • WID 1 = Secure World (TEE).

  • The security monitor controls world transitions by writing the WID CSR.

This mirrors ARM TrustZone’s NS bit but integrates cleanly with RISC-V privilege levels and PMP. SiFive X280 and FU740 implement WorldGuard.

docs.title: 26.6 Control-Flow Integrity: Zisslpcfi and Zicfilp
docs.text:
The RISC-V CFI extensions address ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) and JOP (Jump-Oriented Programming) attacks:

  • Zicfilp (Landing Pads): Every indirect branch target must be a LPAD (Landing Pad) instruction; branching to any other address traps. Equivalent to ARM BTI (Branch Target Identification) or Intel IBT.

  • Zicfiss (Shadow Stack): A separate, protected shadow stack stores return addresses. SSPUSH saves the return address; SSPOP and SSCOMPARE verify return addresses on function return. Equivalent to Intel CET Shadow Stack or ARM GCS.

  • Smepmp + CFI: CFI is effective only when combined with W^X (Write XOR Execute) enforcement via PMP entries, preventing code injection.

// Function with shadow stack (Zicfiss) compiler output (conceptual)
my_function:
    sspush  ra           // Push return address to shadow stack
    addi    sp, sp, -16
    sd      ra, 8(sp)
    // ... function body ...
    ld      ra, 8(sp)
    addi    sp, sp, 16
    sscompare ra         // Compare with shadow stack (trap if mismatch)
    ret

// Landing pad at indirect call target (Zicfilp)
callback_target:
    lpad    0            // Must be first instruction; label ID = 0
    // ... callback code ...
    ret

docs.title: 26.8.1 Spectre and Meltdown on RISC-V
docs.text:
Out-of-order RISC-V processors (e.g., BOOM, Rocket with prefetch, Alibaba C910) are susceptible to Spectre-class attacks:

  • Spectre-PHT (v1): Bounds-check bypass using branch predictor. Mitigation: FENCE instruction as speculation barrier; compiler -mspeculative-load-hardening.

  • Spectre-BTB (v2): Branch target injection. Mitigation: retpoline sequences; predictor flush on privilege transition.

  • Meltdown: RISC-V processors with strict privilege checks in the pipeline do not exhibit classic Meltdown (unlike early Intel), but microarchitectural variants may still exist.

The RISC-V FENCE.I (Instruction Fence) and FENCE (Data Fence) provide ordering guarantees but are not speculation barriers. A SFENCE.VMA (Supervisor memory-management Fence) flushes TLB and is used after page table updates.

docs.title: 26.8.2 Data-Independent Execution Latency: Zkt
docs.text:
The Zkt extension declares that the scalar cryptographic instructions (Zkne/Zknd AES, Zknh SHA, Zkb bitmanip, Zbc clmul) have data-independent execution latency: execution time is the same regardless of operand values.

This guarantee prevents timing attacks on cryptographic implementations. Compilers and assemblers can rely on Zkt to emit constant-time cryptographic code without additional FENCE barriers.

docs.text:

  • RISC-V TEE AP-TEE TG — Active task group (2023) standardising RISC-V TEE interface for confidential computing (competing with Keystone, CURE).

  • FIPS 140-3 — Cryptographic module validation for commercial RISC-V security processors requiring certification.

  • TCG DICE — Device Identifier Composition Engine used by OpenTitan (RISC-V based) for hardware-rooted attestation.

docs.title: 26.14 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: PMP Configuration: Protect Secure Enclave Region

A RISC-V M-mode firmware must configure a PMP entry to restrict S/U-mode from accessing a 512 KB secure enclave region at physical address 0x80400000. Compute the NAPOT-encoded pmpaddr value and the pmpcfg byte for a read-execute-only (R, X; no W) locked region.

Solution: NAPOT encoding:

NAPOT encodes a region of size \(2^k\) starting at an aligned base as:

\[\text{pmpaddr} = \frac{\text{base}}{4} \Bigg| \frac{2^k / 2 - 1}{1} = \frac{\text{base} + 2^{k-1} - 1}{4}\]

(In other words: shift base right 2 to get word address, then set the lower \((k-2)\) bits to 1.)

For base = 0x80400000 and size = \(2^{19}\) = 512 KB (\(k=19\)):

\[\begin{align*} \text{pmpaddr} &= \frac{\texttt{0x80400000}}{4} \Bigg| \frac{2^{18} - 1}{1} \\ &= \texttt{0x20100000} \;|\; \texttt{0x0003FFFF} \\ &= \texttt{0x2013FFFF} \end{align*}\]

pmpcfg byte:

Bit fields: [7:6] = A[1:0] (address mode), [5] = L (lock), [2] = X, [1] = W, [0] = R.

  • A = 11b (NAPOT) \(\to\) bits [7:6] = 11

  • L = 1 (locked, applies to M-mode too) \(\to\) bit 5 = 1

  • X = 1, W = 0, R = 1 \(\to\) bits [2:0] = 101

\[\text{pmpcfg} = \underbrace{11}_{A}\underbrace{1}_{L}\underbrace{00}_{rsvd} \underbrace{101}_{X,W=0,R} = \texttt{0x9D}\]

Result: Set pmpaddr0 = 0x2013FFFF and pmpcfg0[7:0] = 0x9D. S/U-mode can read and execute from 0x80400000–0x8047FFFF but cannot write. M-mode is also locked out (L=1 with Smepmp MML=0 means L restricts S/U only; to also restrict M-mode, set mseccfg.MML=1).

Solved Problem: Zkr TRNG: Min-Entropy Estimation

A RISC-V Zkr seed CSR returns 16-bit entropy words. The hardware TRNG has a measured min-entropy of 0.97 bits per bit (slightly below ideal due to a biased ring oscillator stage). A 256-bit AES key is needed. How many csrrw seed reads are required to gather sufficient entropy, and what health test should be applied?

Solution: Min-entropy per 16-bit word:

\[H_\infty(\text{word}) = 16 \times 0.97 = 15.52 \text{ bits}\]

Words required for 256 bits of min-entropy:

\[N_\text{words} = \left\lceil \frac{256}{15.52} \right\rceil = \lceil 16.49 \rceil = 17\]

17 reads of the seed CSR provide \(17 \times 15.52 = 263.8\) bits of min-entropy, which is sufficient for a 256-bit key (with \(\sim 7.8\) bits margin).

Post-processing: The 17 words (272 raw bits) must be passed through a NIST SP 800-90B-compliant conditioner (e.g., SHA-256 of the concatenated words). SHA-256 of 272 raw bits yields 256 bits with min-entropy: \(\min(256, 263.8) = 256\) bits.

Health tests: Per NIST SP 800-90B:

  • Repetition Count Test (RCT): Flag error if the same 16-bit value repeats \(C\) times consecutively, where \(C = 1 + \lceil -\log_2(\alpha) / H_\infty \rceil = 1 + \lceil 20.9 / 15.52 \rceil = 3\) (for \(\alpha = 2^{-20}\)).

  • Adaptive Proportion Test (APT): Over a window of \(W = 512\) samples, the most-frequent value should not exceed \(C_\text{APT} = 324\) (for \(\alpha = 2^{-20}\), 16-bit alphabet).

The Zkr specification requires a compliant implementation to run these tests and report OPST_BIST (failing test) or OPST_DEAD (entropy source failure) in the status bits of the seed CSR.

Solved Problem: Keystone Attestation: Enclave Measurement

A Keystone enclave is built from two pages: a code page at physical address 0x82000000 (SHA-256 hash \(H_1\)) and a data page at 0x82001000 (SHA-256 hash \(H_2\)). The security monitor computes the enclave measurement as \(M = \text{SHA-256}(H_1 \| H_2 \| \text{nonce})\). Explain how this measurement enables remote attestation and what an attacker must do to forge a valid attestation.

Solution: Measurement chain:

  1. During ECREATE and EADD, the SM hashes each physical page added to the enclave. The running hash extends over all pages in order.

  2. During EINIT, the SM finalises the measurement \(M\) by mixing in the attestation nonce (provided by the remote verifier).

  3. The SM signs \((M, \text{nonce}, \text{timestamp})\) using its Ed25519 device key (provisioned at fabrication): \(\sigma = \text{Ed25519.Sign}(K_\text{SM}, M \| \text{nonce})\).

  4. The signature \(\sigma\) is returned to the enclave application, which forwards it to the remote verifier.

Remote verifier checks:

  1. Verify \(\sigma\) using the SM’s Ed25519 public key (pinned or from the chip vendor’s certificate).

  2. Verify that \(M\) matches the expected measurement of the legitimate enclave binary (computed offline by the verifier: \(M^* = \text{SHA-256}(H_1^* \| H_2^* \| \text{nonce})\)).

  3. Verify nonce freshness to prevent replay.

Forging a valid attestation requires:

  1. Compromising the SM’s Ed25519 private key: Requires physical access to a chip with a laser/EM side-channel attack on M-mode execution, or a pre-fabrication supply-chain attack.

  2. Collision attack on SHA-256: Finding \((H_1', H_2')\) such that \(\text{SHA-256}(H_1' \| H_2' \| n) = M^*\). Computationally infeasible (\(2^{128}\) security).

Conclusion: Attestation is unforgeable assuming the SM key is secure and SHA-256 is collision-resistant.

docs.title: 26.15 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: RISC-V security extensions have moved from ratification to commercial silicon deployment, with cryptographic instructions, enhanced memory protection, and new domain isolation mechanisms reaching production SoCs.

docs.title: 26.15.1 RISC-V Zk* Cryptographic Extensions: Commercial SoC Deployment (2023–2024)
docs.text:
The RISC-V scalar cryptographic extensions (Zkn, Zks, Zkr), ratified in 2021, reached broad commercial SoC availability in 2023–2024:

Table 26.4. Commercial RISC-V SoCs with Zk* cryptographic extension deployment (2023–2024) SoC Vendor Zk Extensions AES Throughput X280 (RV64GCV) SiFive Zkn, Zks, Zkr, Zkt 2.1 Gbps @ 1 GHz C906 (RV64GCV) Alibaba T-Head Zkn, Zkr 1.8 Gbps @ 1.2 GHz C910 (RV64GCV) Alibaba T-Head Zkn, Zks, Zkr 2.4 Gbps @ 1.5 GHz EIC7700 (Spacemit K1) ESWIN Zkn, Zkr 1.6 Gbps @ 1 GHz JH7110 (VisionFive 2) StarFive Zkn 1.2 Gbps @ 1 GHz

GCC 13 and LLVM 17 added full Zk* code generation support, enabling the -march=rv64gc_zkn_zks_zkr flag to auto-generate AES and SHA instructions without manual assembly. The Linux kernel arch/riscv/crypto/ subtree was updated in kernel 6.5 (August 2023) to include AES-CBC, AES-GCM, and SHA-256/512 optimised implementations using Zkne/Zknd/Zknh instructions.

docs.title: 26.15.2 RISC-V PMP Updates: Smepmp (2023) and ePMP Enforcement
docs.text:
The Smepmp extension (Machine-mode Security Enhancement for PMP), ratified by RISC-V International in 2022 and deployed in commercial SoCs from 2023, resolved a critical limitation of classical PMP: M-mode code was never restricted by PMP entries. The mseccfg.MML (Machine Mode Lockdown) bit enables:

  • M-mode code is subject to PMP checks when MML=1. A firmware can lock a cryptographic key region with L=1 and R=0,W=0,X=0, making the region inaccessible even to M-mode exception handlers after initial configuration.

  • RLB (Rule Lock Bypass) bit: When RLB=0 (cleared at end of initialisation), no further changes to locked PMP entries are permitted, providing an immutable security configuration.

  • OpenSBI 1.3 (2023) added full Smepmp support in its domain abstraction layer, allowing platform firmware to configure M-mode restricted regions for secure enclaves.

ePMP enforcement in commercial hardware: The StarFive JH7110 (used in VisionFive 2 SBC) implements 64 PMP entries (the maximum per RISC-V spec) with ePMP TOR (Top Of Range) and NAPOT modes, enabling fine-grained protection of the M-mode security monitor region and OpenSBI domain boundaries.

docs.title: 26.15.3 SiFive X280 (2023): Vector Crypto Extensions and Security Monitor
docs.text:
The SiFive X280 is a 64-bit out-of-order RISC-V core supporting RV64GCV (G = IMAFD, C = compressed, V = vector) with cryptographic extensions:

  • Zvk (Vector Cryptography) extensions: The X280 implements Zvkned (AES-128/256 in ECB/CTR), Zvknhb (SHA-512 via vector), and Zvbc (carry-less multiply via vector), enabling throughput of \(>\)20 Gbps AES-256-GCM on a single X280 core at 1 GHz using 256-bit vector operations.

  • WorldGuard security monitor: The X280 implements SiFive WorldGuard natively, with WID (World Identifier) bits propagated through the TileLink interconnect to memory controllers and peripherals.

  • SiFive Shield: A hardware security module IP block accompanying the X280 in SiFive’s Freedom platform provides an OTBN-like coprocessor for constant-time big-number arithmetic (RSA/ECC key operations) isolated from the main core pipeline.

docs.title: 26.15.4 RISC-V WorldGuard: Hardware Domain Isolation (2024 Spec)
docs.text:
The RISC-V WorldGuard specification was updated in 2024 by the RISC-V International TEE Task Group, aligning it more closely with the RISC-V AP-TEE (Application Processor TEE) standard:

  • WID assignment: Up to 16 World Identifiers (WIDs) per hart, compared to 4 in the original SiFive specification. Each WID corresponds to a distinct hardware domain (Normal World, Secure World, multiple trusted VMs, etc.).

  • Checker topology: WorldGuard checkers are placed at every TileLink or AXI interconnect crossbar, filtering memory transactions by WID. The checker configuration (which WIDs can access which physical address ranges) is programmed by M-mode firmware during boot and locked with the same mseccfg.RLB mechanism as Smepmp.

  • Interrupt isolation: WorldGuard 2024 adds WID tagging to interrupt delivery, ensuring that an interrupt intended for Secure World cannot be delivered to Normal World and vice versa.

docs.title: 26.15.5 Allwinner D1-H RISC-V: Secure Boot Deployment
docs.text:
The Allwinner D1-H (XuanTie C906 RISC-V core, 1 GHz) became one of the first mass-market RISC-V SoCs with a production secure boot chain:

  • Secure Boot: The D1-H boot ROM verifies a SHA-256 hash of the first-stage bootloader stored in eFUSE, refusing to execute unsigned code when the BOOT_VERIFY eFUSE bit is programmed.

  • eFUSE key store: 256-bit AES key and 256-bit RSA key hash stored in OTP eFUSEs; the AES key is used for optional encrypted bootloader storage in eMMC/NAND.

  • Deployment: The Nezha RISC-V SBC and MangoPi MQ Pro (widely used in the RISC-V developer community) incorporate the D1-H with secure boot configurable via the Allwinner secure boot toolchain.

docs.title: 26.15.6 StarFive JH7110 (VisionFive 2): Security Boot and TrustZone Analog
docs.text:
The StarFive JH7110 (RISC-V SiFive U74-MC quad-core, 1 GHz) used in the VisionFive 2 SBC demonstrates the RISC-V equivalent of an application processor security stack:

  • Secure boot chain: ZSBL (Zero-Stage BootLoader) in mask ROM verifies FSBL (First-Stage BootLoader) using Ed25519 signatures, with the verification public key stored in OTP.

  • M-mode security monitor (OpenSBI): OpenSBI 1.3 running in M-mode implements Smepmp domain isolation, providing a security boundary analogous to ARM Secure World without requiring TrustZone hardware.

  • Penglai TEE: The JH7110 supports the Penglai enclave framework (developed by IPADS, Shanghai Jiao Tong University), which uses Smepmp-based physical memory isolation to create hardware-protected enclaves without dedicated TrustZone silicon.

  • OP-TEE port: An experimental OP-TEE (Open Portable TEE) port to the JH7110 was published in 2024, demonstrating GlobalPlatform TEE API compatibility on RISC-V using PMP-based isolation rather than TrustZone.

Table 26.5. RISC-V security developments 2023–2024 Development Year Extension Key Milestone Zk* commercial SoCs 2023–24 Zkn/Zks/Zkr Linux kernel 6.5 crypto drivers Smepmp in OpenSBI 1.3 2023 Smepmp M-mode self-restriction SiFive X280 Zvk 2023 Zvkned/Zvknhb 20+ Gbps AES via vector WorldGuard spec 2024 2024 WorldGuard 16-WID domain isolation Allwinner D1-H secure boot 2023 – Mass-market RISC-V secure boot JH7110 Penglai TEE 2024 Smepmp PMP-based enclave, OP-TEE port

docs.title: 26.16 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Configure two PMP entries to: (a) allow S/U-mode read-write access to DRAM region [0x80000000, 0x88000000) (128 MB NAPOT), and (b) deny all access to a 64 KB secure enclave at 0x87F00000. Which PMP entry must have higher priority and why?

  2. Write a RISC-V assembly routine that reads 32 bytes of entropy from the Zkr seed CSR, handles OPST_BIST and OPST_DEAD error states, and passes the collected entropy through SHA-256 to produce a 256-bit key seed.

  3. Explain the difference between Zicfilp (landing pads) and Zicfiss (shadow stack) in terms of the attack classes each addresses. Can Zicfilp alone prevent ROP attacks?

  4. A CVA6 out-of-order core implements ePMP with Smepmp MML=1. Describe how an M-mode firmware can use this to “seal” its own cryptographic keys in a DRAM region that no subsequent code (including M-mode exception handlers) can read.

  5. Compare the Keystone, CURE, and Sanctum TEE frameworks for RISC-V. What are the key microarchitectural assumptions of each, and which protects against cache-timing attacks?

  6. Implement the RISC-V Zkne AES-128 key schedule in C using the __builtin_riscv_aes32esi intrinsics. Verify correctness against the FIPS 197 test vectors.

  7. The WorldGuard extension uses WIDs (World IDs) rather than PMP regions. Explain the scalability advantage of WorldGuard over PMP when the number of isolated domains exceeds 16.

  8. A RISC-V IoT device uses FreeRTOS with ePMP for task isolation. Task A (S-mode) manages TLS keys; Task B (U-mode) handles MQTT. Design the PMP region layout to prevent Task B from reading Task A’s keys, while allowing both to share a common read-only flash region for firmware.

  9. Explain how the RISC-V Zkt extension declaration enables constant-time AES-GCM in a software TLS stack without FENCE barriers between AES rounds.

  10. Calculate the throughput improvement of Zkne-accelerated AES-128-CBC over a table-based software AES implementation on a 1 GHz RISC-V core. Assume: software AES requires 120 cycles per 16-byte block; Zkne AES requires 11 rounds \(\times\) 4 instructions/round = 44 instructions at 1 cycle/instruction plus pipeline overhead of 8 cycles.

docs.title: Chapter 27: Formal Verification of Hardware Security
27.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Hardware security vulnerabilities discovered after fabrication are catastrophic. A bug in Register Transfer Level (RTL) code, once committed to silicon, cannot be patched with firmware updates alone; it may require full chip respins costing millions of dollars and months of schedule delay. High-profile incidents—the Pentium FDIV bug (1994), Meltdown and Spectre (2018), Rowhammer DRAM attacks, and numerous TrustZone bypass exploits—demonstrate that simulation and testing alone are insufficient to guarantee security properties.

Formal verification mathematically proves that a hardware design satisfies a specification for all possible inputs and states, not just the test cases the engineer thought to simulate. Key techniques include:

  • Model Checking: Exhaustive state-space exploration using symbolic algorithms (BDD, SAT, SMT).

  • Theorem Proving: Human-guided proof construction in proof assistants (Coq, Isabelle/HOL, ACL2).

  • Equivalence Checking: Verifying that two circuit representations (RTL vs. gate-level netlist, or original vs. optimised) are functionally identical.

  • Security Property Verification: Checking information flow properties (non-interference, IFC) and cryptographic primitive correctness.

Industrial adoption is accelerating: Arm formally verifies its TrustZone isolation properties; Intel uses formal methods for microcode; Galois and DARPA’s BESSPIN programme verified processor security properties; OpenTitan uses formal tools for its HMAC and AES RTL.

docs.title: 27.2.1 Linear Temporal Logic (LTL)
docs.text:
LTL expresses properties over infinite linear traces of states. Key operators:

  • \(\mathbf{G}\, p\) (Globally): \(p\) holds in all future states.

  • \(\mathbf{F}\, p\) (Finally): \(p\) holds in some future state.

  • \(\mathbf{X}\, p\) (neXt): \(p\) holds in the next state.

  • \(p\, \mathbf{U}\, q\) (Until): \(p\) holds until \(q\) holds.

Security property examples:

\[\begin{align*} &\mathbf{G}(\texttt{priv\_mode} = U \Rightarrow \neg \texttt{access\_secure\_mem}) \quad \text{(memory isolation)} \\ &\mathbf{G}(\texttt{key\_exposed} \Rightarrow \mathbf{F}\,\texttt{system\_reset}) \quad \text{(zeroisation on leak)} \\ &\mathbf{G}(\texttt{boot\_valid} \Rightarrow \mathbf{X}\,\texttt{os\_load}) \quad \text{(secure boot progress)} \end{align*}\]

docs.title: 27.2.2 Computation Tree Logic (CTL)
docs.text:
CTL extends LTL to branching time, allowing reasoning over trees of execution:

  • \(\mathbf{AG}\, p\): For All paths, Globally \(p\).

  • \(\mathbf{EF}\, p\): there Exists a path where Finally \(p\).

  • \(\mathbf{AF}\, p\): For All paths, Finally \(p\).

  • \(\mathbf{EG}\, p\): there Exists a path where Globally \(p\).

CTL is particularly useful for verifying:

  • \(\mathbf{AG}(\neg \texttt{key\_accessible\_from\_ns\_world})\): The cryptographic key is never accessible from the normal world on any execution path.

  • \(\mathbf{AF}(\texttt{attestation\_complete})\): Every boot sequence eventually completes attestation.

docs.title: 27.2.3 PSL and SVA: Hardware Property Languages
docs.text:
IEEE 1850 PSL (Property Specification Language) and SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) bring LTL/CTL-like properties into RTL design flows:

// SystemVerilog Assertion: memory isolation property
// U-mode cannot read secure_mem_reg
property u_mode_no_secure_read;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (priv_mode == U_MODE) |-> (secure_mem_read == 1'b0);
endproperty
assert property (u_mode_no_secure_read)
    else $error("SECURITY VIOLATION: U-mode read of secure memory");

// Liveness: after a key load, within 10 cycles it becomes ready
property key_load_liveness;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    key_load_en |-> ##[1:10] key_ready;
endproperty
assert property (key_load_liveness);

// AES output determinism: same key+plaintext always same ciphertext
property aes_determinism;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (aes_start && (key == key_saved) && (pt == pt_saved))
    |-> ##[1:$] (ct == ct_expected);
endproperty

docs.title: 27.3.1 SAT/SMT-Based Bounded Model Checking
docs.text:
Bounded Model Checking (BMC) unrolls the circuit for \(k\) time steps and encodes the reachability question as a SAT/SMT instance. For a design \(M\) and property \(\varphi\):

\[\text{BMC}(M, \varphi, k) \equiv I(s_0) \wedge \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k-1} T(s_i, s_{i+1}) \wedge \neg \varphi(s_0, …, s_k)\]

If the formula is SAT, a counterexample of depth \(\leq k\) exists. If UNSAT for all \(k\) up to the completeness threshold, the property holds.

Tools: SymbiYosys (open-source, uses Yosys + solvers: Boolector, Bitwuzla, Z3), JasperGold (Cadence), Questa Formal (Mentor/Siemens), VC Formal (Synopsys).

docs.title: 27.3.2 IC3/PDR: Property Directed Reachability
docs.text:
IC3 (Incremental Construction of Inductive Clauses), also called PDR (Property Directed Reachability), is the dominant industrial model checker. It maintains a sequence of over-approximations \(F_0 \subseteq F_1 \subseteq … \subseteq F_N\) of states reachable in \(0, 1, …, N\) steps, refining them by blocking counterexample traces. IC3 converges without explicit bound \(k\), making it complete for many hardware properties.

# SymbiYosys formal verification flow
# File: secure_boot.sby

[options]
mode prove          # Formal proof (unbounded)
depth 50            # BMC depth for bounded checks

[engines]
smtbmc boolector    # SMT engine (Boolector SMT solver)
abc pdr             # IC3/PDR engine via ABC

[script]
read -formal secure_boot.sv
read -formal pmp_check.sv
hierarchy -top secure_boot_top
proc; opt; memory; opt
flatten

[files]
secure_boot.sv
pmp_check.sv

# Run: sby -f secure_boot.sby
# Output: PASS (property proved) or FAIL (counterexample trace)

docs.title: 27.3.3 BDD-Based Model Checking
docs.text:
Binary Decision Diagrams (BDDs) represent Boolean functions as canonical DAGs. The symbolic model checker computes the set of reachable states as a BDD and checks properties via BDD operations. BDDs work well for control-heavy designs (FSMs) but suffer state-space explosion for large data paths.

CUDD (Colorado University Decision Diagrams) is the standard open-source BDD library. NuSMV and Spin (for software models) use BDD-based model checking.

docs.title: 27.4.1 HOL4 and Galois’s RISC-V Verification
docs.text:
The RISC-V ISA Formal Spec in HOL4 (funded by DARPA BESSPIN) provides a machine-readable, mechanically checked specification of the RISC-V privileged architecture. The HOL4 model:

  • Defines the RISC-V state machine: registers, CSRs, memory, privilege modes.

  • Specifies all instruction semantics as HOL4 functions.

  • Proves security properties: e.g., that PMP configurations correctly isolate physical memory regions across privilege level transitions.

(* HOL4 snippet: PMP access check theorem (illustrative pseudocode) *)
(* "U-mode cannot access a locked PMP region with L=1, A=NAPOT, R=0" *)

Theorem pmp_u_mode_deny :
  !s addr.
    (priv_level s = U_MODE) /\
    pmp_entry_matches s.pmpaddr0 addr /\
    pmp_cfg_locked s.pmpcfg0 /\
    ~pmp_cfg_readable s.pmpcfg0
    ==>
    access_check s addr Read = AccessFault
Proof
  rw[priv_level_def, pmp_entry_matches_def, access_check_def]
  (* ... proof steps ... *)
QED

docs.title: 27.4.2 Coq and CHERI Formal Verification
docs.text:
The Sail formal model of CHERI generates Coq proof obligations from the CHERI ISA specification. Key theorems proven in Coq:

  • Monotonicity: Every CHERI instruction either preserves or narrows capability bounds and permissions. No instruction can widen them.

  • Tag integrity: If a memory location’s tag bit is 0, no sequence of CHERI instructions can produce a valid (tagged) capability from it.

  • Spatial safety: Any capability dereference is within bounds, or a trap is raised.

These proofs constitute a mechanised guarantee—not just a design goal.

docs.title: 27.4.3 ACL2 and Microcode Verification
docs.text:
Intel uses the ACL2 theorem prover to verify floating-point and division microcode, following the Pentium FDIV incident. ACL2 provides:

  • A Lisp-based logic for hardware models.

  • Automated induction and rewriting.

  • Verified: IEEE 754 compliance of floating-point units, division algorithms (SRT, radix-16), and x87 transcendental approximations.

docs.title: 27.5.1 Non-Interference
docs.text:
Non-interference formalises information flow: a system \(S\) is non-interfering if high-security inputs cannot influence low-security outputs:

\[\forall s_1, s_2 :\; (s_1 =_L s_2) \Rightarrow (\text{run}(S, s_1) =_L \text{run}(S, s_2))\]

where \(=_L\) means “equal in the low-security projection”.

For a TrustZone processor: normal-world outputs must be identical regardless of secure-world memory contents (and vice versa). Proving non-interference requires quantifying over all possible secure-world states, which is infeasible by simulation but tractable by model checking over small data widths.

docs.title: 27.5.2 Cryptographic Correctness
docs.text:
Formal verification of cryptographic hardware:

  • AES correctness: Prove that the hardware AES engine computes the FIPS 197 standard AES function for all 128-bit keys and plaintexts. Approach: equivalence checking against a reference Verilog model.

  • SHA-256 correctness: Model check all 64 rounds against NIST test vectors; prove the message schedule and compression function.

  • ECDSA constant-time: Prove that the scalar multiplication execution time is independent of the scalar value (data-oblivious property).

docs.title: 27.5.3 Secure Boot Properties
docs.text:
// SVA: Secure boot cannot load an unsigned image
property no_unsigned_os_load;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    os_load_trigger |-> sig_verified;
endproperty
assert property (no_unsigned_os_load);

// SVA: Hash measurement extends before PCR register changes
property pcr_extends_in_order;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    pcr_extend_en |-> (hash_engine_done ##1 pcr_updated);
endproperty
assert property (pcr_extends_in_order);

docs.title: 27.6.1 Formal Verification Flow
docs.text: Figure 27.1. Formal hardware verification flow. RTL and security properties are fed to a formal tool; multiple engines (BMC, IC3/PDR, BDD) are invoked in parallel. A counterexample triggers RTL revision.

docs.title: 27.6.2 Information Flow: Non-Interference Model
docs.text: Figure 27.2. Non-interference model for hardware information flow security. High-security inputs (secret keys, secure world state) must not influence low-security outputs observable by the normal world.

docs.title: 27.7 Equivalence Checking
docs.text:
Combinational and sequential equivalence checking (SEC/EC) verifies that synthesis, place-and-route, and optimisation transformations preserve functional equivalence:

  1. RTL vs. Gate-Level: After synthesis, check that the optimised gate-level netlist computes the same function as the RTL. Essential for detecting synthesis bugs that could introduce backdoors.

  2. Pre-vs-Post-Layout: Verify timing-aware gate-level after place-and-route vs. the pre-layout netlist. Identifies ECO (Engineering Change Order) errors.

  3. Cryptographic Cores: For AES, the optimised implementation (e.g., composite-field S-box, tower-field multiplication) must be equivalent to the FIPS reference model.

Tools: Cadence Conformal, Synopsys Formality, Mentor OneSpin, Yosys/ABC (open-source, limited to combinational for free version).

# Yosys/ABC equivalence check (RTL vs gate-level AES S-box)
yosys << 'EOF'
read_verilog aes_sbox_reference.v
hierarchy -top aes_sbox_ref
synth -top aes_sbox_ref -flatten
write_blif aes_ref.blif

read_verilog aes_sbox_optimized.v
hierarchy -top aes_sbox_opt
synth -top aes_sbox_opt -flatten
write_blif aes_opt.blif
EOF

abc -c "cec aes_ref.blif aes_opt.blif"
# Output: Networks are equivalent.

docs.title: 27.8.1 Data-Oblivious Property Verification
docs.text:
A hardware operation is data-oblivious if its execution time (and resource usage trace) is independent of secret data. Formally:

\[\forall d_1, d_2 \in \mathcal{D} :\; \text{trace}(d_1) = \text{trace}(d_2)\]

where \(\mathcal{D}\) is the set of secret data values.

CacheAudit (INRIA) performs abstract interpretation of x86/RISC-V binaries to bound cache-based information leakage. It computes an upper bound on the number of bits leaked per cache miss pattern.

ct-verif (Barthe et al.) uses Boogie and Z3 to verify constant-time properties of C code compiled to LLVM IR, then mapped to hardware.

docs.title: 27.8.2 Formal Verification of Power Side-Channel Resistance
docs.text:
TVLA (Test Vector Leakage Assessment) is a statistical method; formal methods complement it:

  • COCO (Coco Formal Tool, TU Graz): Verifies that a masked hardware implementation (boolean masking) correctly prevents first-order DPA. It checks that no intermediate signal is statistically dependent on unmasked secret bits.

  • SILVER (Bloem et al.): Verifies compositionality of masked gadgets at RTL level using SAT/SMT.

  • Formal t-SNI proof: The \((t, n)\)-probing model: an adversary probing \(t\) wires learns nothing about the secret. Tools prove this for \(t\)-share masked implementations.

docs.title: 27.9 OpenTitan Formal Verification Case Study
docs.text:
OpenTitan (lowRISC) uses formal verification for its hardware security IP:

  • HMAC core: SVA properties verify that hmac_done is only asserted after exactly 64 SHA-256 compression rounds, and that the output matches the FIPS 198-1 test vector.

  • AES core: SymbiYosys proves that the AES core’s key schedule FSM correctly sequences all 11 round key derivations (128-bit mode) without skipping or repeating steps.

  • CSRNG (CTR_DRBG): IC3/PDR proves that the internal state is never output directly and that reseed_cnt overflows trigger a re-seed before the 248 byte output limit.

  • Alert Handler: Formal analysis proves that every hardware alert eventually propagates to the CPU within a bounded number of cycles.

# OpenTitan formal verification target (HMAC core)
# File: hw/ip/hmac/data/hmac.hjson (formal targets defined here)
# Run SymbiYosys from project root:
cd /path/to/opentitan
./hw/ip/hmac/dv/hmac_sby.sh

# Equivalent manual invocation:
cd hw/ip/hmac/formal
sby -f hmac_securitycheck.sby

# Example security property in hmac_securitycheck.sv:
// hmac key register never accessible from software after key_clear
property hmac_key_clear_security;
    @(posedge clk_i) disable iff (!rst_ni)
    key_clear_i |=> (reg2hw.key[0].q == 32'h0);
endproperty
assert property (hmac_key_clear_security);

docs.title: 27.13 Standards and Specifications
docs.text:
• IEEE 1800-2017 (SystemVerilog) — SystemVerilog language standard; includes SVA (SystemVerilog Assertions) for property specification.

  • IEEE 1850-2010 (PSL) — Property Specification Language; LTL/CTL semantics for hardware properties.

  • IEC 61508 — Functional Safety for Programmable Electronic Systems. Recommends formal methods at SIL 3/4.

  • ISO 26262 — Automotive functional safety; formal verification recommended at ASIL D.

  • Common Criteria (ISO 15408) — Security evaluation; formal models (formal specification and verification) required at EAL5–7.

  • DO-254 (EUROCAE ED-80) — Airborne electronic hardware design assurance; formal methods for DAL A/B hardware.

  • NIST SP 800-193 — Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines; formal verification of boot integrity properties recommended.

  • FIPS 140-3 / ISO 19790 — Cryptographic module security; formal security policy models required at Levels 3 and 4.

  • CHERI ISA Specification + Sail model — Formal ISA model with Coq and HOL4 proof targets for capability monotonicity.

  • RISC-V Sail ISA model — Machine-readable formal spec of RISC-V privileged architecture; generates Isabelle/HOL4 proof obligations.

docs.title: 27.14 Famous Repositories and Tools
docs.text:
• YosysHQ/sby (GitHub) — SymbiYosys: front-end for formal hardware verification using Yosys and open-source solvers.

  • YosysHQ/yosys (GitHub) — Yosys synthesis and formal flow. Includes smtbmc, formalff, and equiv passes.

  • chipsalliance/opentitan (GitHub) — OpenTitan RoT; contains formal testbenches for AES, HMAC, CSRNG, alert handler, OTP controller.

  • Boolector/boolector (GitHub) — Boolector SMT solver; default engine for SymbiYosys smtbmc mode.

  • bitwuzla/bitwuzla (GitHub) — Next-generation SMT solver for bit-vectors and floating-point.

  • coq/coq (GitHub) — Coq proof assistant; used for CHERI Sail formal proofs and cryptographic algorithm verification.

  • rems-project/sail (GitHub) — Sail ISA specification language; generates Coq, HOL4, and Isabelle theorems from RISC-V and CHERI specs.

  • microsoft/Z3 (GitHub) — Z3 SMT solver; used in COCO, ct-verif, and VC Formal.

  • TUGraz-IIS/coco (GitHub) — COCO tool for formal DPA verification of masked hardware implementations.

  • ucb-bar/firrtl (GitHub) — FIRRTL IR; formal analysis passes used in Chisel-generated RISC-V designs.

docs.title: 27.15 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: BMC Depth: Verifying a 4-Bit Counter with Overflow

A 4-bit up-counter resets when it reaches 15 (0xF). Write an SVA property that the counter never exceeds 15, and determine the BMC depth required to guarantee the property over all reachable states. The initial state is counter = 0.

Solution: SVA property:

property counter_no_overflow;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (counter <= 4'hF);  // counter is 4-bit so this is trivially true
                        // Real property: after reset, counter reaches 15 and resets
endproperty

// More interesting: counter wraps correctly (reaches 15 then 0)
property counter_wrap;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (counter == 4'hF) |=> (counter == 4'h0);
endproperty
assert property (counter_wrap);

BMC depth analysis:

The counter cycles through states \(0 \to 1 \to … \to 15 \to 0\). The state space has 16 states. To verify counter_wrap, the BMC must explore at least one full cycle: starting from state 15, observe the transition to 0.

If the initial state is 0 (reset), the property counter == 15 |=> counter == 0 first becomes relevant at step \(k = 15\) (after 15 clock edges from reset). Therefore, BMC depth \(k = 16\) is sufficient to observe the wrap event.

IC3/PDR: For IC3, no explicit bound is needed. IC3 discovers the inductive invariant: “counter \(\leq\) 15 \(\wedge\) (counter = 15 \(\Rightarrow\) next(counter) = 0)” and proves the property without unrolling 16 steps.

State space: 16 reachable states (4-bit counter). BDD-based model checking trivially handles this with a 4-variable BDD.

Solved Problem: Non-Interference Check: Two-Domain Register File

A register file has 8 registers: R0–R3 are “low” (L) and R4–R7 are “high” (H). A combinational ALU reads any two registers and writes to any register. Define the non-interference property and describe what BMC step count is needed to check it.

Solution: Non-interference formalisation:

Define two initial states \(s_1, s_2\) that agree on all L registers but may differ on H registers:

\[s_1 =_L s_2 \iff s_1.\text{R0} = s_2.\text{R0} \wedge … \wedge s_1.\text{R3} = s_2.\text{R3}\]

The property: for all instructions that write to an L register (R0–R3), the result must depend only on L registers:

\[\forall \text{instr} :\; \text{dst} \in \{0,1,2,3\} \Rightarrow (\text{result depends only on } s.\text{R0}, …, s.\text{R3})\]

SVA formulation (product construction):

// Run two copies of the ALU with identical L inputs, different H inputs
// Check that L outputs agree
property noninterference;
    @(posedge clk)
    // If both copies execute same instruction with same L inputs
    ((alu1.src_sel_L == alu2.src_sel_L) && (alu1.L_regs == alu2.L_regs))
    // and destination is L register
    && (alu1.dst < 4)
    // Then results must be equal
    |-> (alu1.result == alu2.result);
endproperty

BMC depth: For a combinational ALU (no pipeline), \(k = 1\) (one clock cycle) is sufficient to check all write operations. For a pipelined design with 3-stage pipeline, \(k = 3\). IC3/PDR proves this without a bound.

Key insight: Non-interference in hardware is a 2-safety property (quantifies over two execution traces). Standard model checkers need the “product construction” (running two copies simultaneously) to handle 2-safety. HyperLTL and HyperCTL* are the appropriate logics for such properties.

Solved Problem: Equivalence Checking: Optimised vs Reference AES S-Box

An optimised AES S-box uses a composite field \(GF(2^4)^2\) decomposition (tower field) to reduce area. Describe the equivalence checking workflow and what the equivalence checker must verify to establish cryptographic correctness.

Solution: Reference model: FIPS 197 defines the S-box as:

\[\text{SubBytes}(b) = \text{Affine}(b^{-1} \text{ in } GF(2^8)) \oplus 0x63\]

The reference Verilog uses a lookup table (256\(\times\)8-bit ROM).

Optimised model: Uses Canright’s composite field decomposition: \(GF(2^8) \cong GF((2^4)^2) / (x^2 + x + \phi)\) where \(\phi\) is a primitive element of \(GF(2^4)\). Inversion in \(GF(2^8)\) is mapped to two squarings, one inversion in \(GF(2^4)\), and two multiplications—fewer gates than a full \(GF(2^8)\) inverter.

Equivalence checking workflow:

  1. Read both Verilog models (aes_sbox_rom.v, aes_sbox_composite.v).

  2. Flatten and technology-map both to AND/XOR/NOT primitives.

  3. Invoke Yosys/ABC cec command (Combinational Equivalence Checking).

  4. ABC’s CEC: builds a miter circuit (XOR of both outputs) and checks if the miter is satisfiable (SAT = not equivalent, UNSAT = equivalent).

What must be verified:

  • For all 256 input values \(b \in \{0, …, 255\}\): the output of the optimised S-box equals the reference.

  • This is a purely combinational 8-input, 8-output function; BDD/SAT handles it in milliseconds.

Result: If ABC reports Networks are equivalent, the optimised S-box is provably correct for all inputs—no test vectors needed.

Solved Problem: IC3/PDR: Verify PMP Isolation Invariant

Specify an inductive invariant for a RISC-V PMP unit that guarantees: “A U-mode load to address \(A\) is permitted only if some PMP entry \(i\) covers \(A\) and its R bit is set.” Sketch how IC3 would prove this invariant.

Solution: Invariant formulation (in pseudo-SMT):

Let \(\text{PMP\_MATCH}(i, A)\) = true iff PMP entry \(i\)’s address range covers \(A\) according to its NAPOT/TOR encoding, and \(\text{PMP\_R}(i)\) = the R permission bit of entry \(i\).

\[\begin{align*} \text{Invariant} \equiv \;& \forall A, \text{priv} = U :\\ & \text{load\_granted}(A) \Rightarrow \exists i \in [0..15] : \text{PMP\_MATCH}(i, A) \wedge \text{PMP\_R}(i) \end{align*}\]

IC3 proof sketch:

  1. Initiation: In the reset state, all PMP entries are disabled (A=0, pmpcfg=0x00); no loads are granted (\(\text{load\_granted}(A) = \text{false}\) for all \(A\)). Invariant holds vacuously.

  2. Consecution: Consider any state \(s\) satisfying the invariant and any transition \(s \to s'\):

    • If an M-mode write changes a pmpcfg entry to enable R permission, then \(\text{PMP\_R}(i)\) becomes true; loads from the covered range are now permitted, and the invariant witness (entry \(i\)) exists.

    • If an M-mode write clears R permission on entry \(i\), then \(\text{load\_granted}\) must also be false for that range (the PMP checker immediately denies access).

    • U-mode instructions cannot modify PMP CSRs (privilege check trap).

  3. IC3 discovers the inductive clause “\(\text{priv} = U \wedge \neg(\exists i : \text{PMP\_MATCH}(i,A) \wedge \text{PMP\_R}(i)) \Rightarrow \neg\text{load\_granted}(A)\)” and adds it to the frame sequence \(F_k\).

  4. The clause sequence converges (no new counterexamples), proving the invariant.

Practical tooling: Encode the PMP state machine in Verilog with SVA assertions, and run with SymbiYosys mode prove + ABC IC3 engine. Proof typically completes in \(<60\) seconds for a 16-entry PMP.

docs.title: 27.16 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: Formal verification of hardware security has matured from academic research into industrial practice, with AI-assisted tooling, large-scale open-source verification campaigns, and mechanised proofs of real silicon security properties.

docs.title: 27.16.1 OpenTitan Formal Verification Results (2023–2024): 100K+ Assertions
docs.text:
The OpenTitan project (lowRISC, Google, and partners) has operated the most comprehensive open-source formal hardware security verification programme in existence. By 2024, the repository contained:

  • 100,000+ SVA assertions across the AES, HMAC, CSRNG, KMAC, OTBN, Key Manager, Alert Handler, OTP Controller, Flash Controller, and ROM Controller IP blocks.

  • Nightly SymbiYosys runs: All formal targets are verified nightly in the OpenTitan CI pipeline (GitHub Actions + internal compute cluster). Any regression causes a CI failure, preventing RTL changes that break security properties.

  • OTBN formal proofs: The OpenTitan Big Number accelerator (OTBN, used for RSA/ECC operations) has formal proofs that the instruction sequencer never executes instructions when the secure wipe operation is pending, and that the internal register file is zeroed within a bounded number of cycles after a wipe request.

  • OTP Controller: IC3/PDR proofs verify that once an OTP partition is locked, subsequent write attempts generate an alert and do not modify OTP state, for all possible sequences of lock and write commands.

# OpenTitan: run all formal targets for the HMAC block
cd $OPENTITAN_ROOT
./hw/ip/hmac/dv/hmac_sby.sh
# Runs: hmac_securitycheck (key_clear, output_suppress),
#        hmac_prim_verify (round_count, done_sequencing)
# Expected: PASS on all targets in ~10 min on 8-core host

docs.title: 27.16.2 Cadence JasperGold 2024: AI-Assisted Property Generation
docs.text:
Cadence JasperGold 2024 introduced Jasper PropGen (Property Generator), an AI-assisted feature that analyses RTL designs and suggests SVA properties:

  • LLM-guided suggestion: PropGen uses a fine-tuned language model trained on a corpus of verified hardware designs and their associated properties to suggest safety and liveness properties for new RTL modules.

  • Property clustering: Suggested properties are clustered by type (information flow, protocol correctness, temporal ordering) and ranked by estimated verification effort (trivial to state-space explosion risk).

  • Iterative refinement: The engineer accepts, rejects, or refines suggestions; accepted properties are automatically added to the formal testbench and run through JasperGold’s IC3/PDR engine.

  • Security mode: A dedicated “Security Analysis” mode focuses property generation on non-interference, key accessibility, and privilege boundary properties, using domain annotations in the RTL (/ secure / comments or explicit security-level attributes).

Tip: AI-assisted property generation addresses the “blank page problem” in formal verification: engineers know their design should be correct but struggle to articulate the properties. PropGen’s suggestions serve as a starting point that domain experts then refine, typically reducing property writing time by 40–60% according to Cadence’s 2024 user studies.

docs.title: 27.16.3 Synopsys VC Formal 2024.03: Security Path Verification
docs.text:
Synopsys VC Formal 2024.03 added a dedicated Security Path Verification (SPV) mode for hardware designs:

  • Taint tracking: SPV instruments the design with symbolic taint labels on designated secret signals (key registers, seed values) and automatically generates information-flow assertions: no tainted signal should appear in any output observable from a specified trust domain.

  • Power side-channel pre-silicon: SPV integrates with Synopsys PrimeTime PX to compute the correlation between power estimates and secret-dependent intermediate values, flagging RTL lines that create exploitable power signatures before tape-out.

  • SPDM/TLS protocol FSM verification: A new protocol mode verifies that the design’s authentication FSM matches the SPDM 1.3 or TLS 1.3 state machine specification, catching implementation deviations that could allow downgrade attacks.

docs.title: 27.16.4 CHERI Formal Proofs: HOL4 Mechanised Proofs of CHERI-MIPS (2023)
docs.text:
The Cambridge REMS (Rigorous Engineering of Mainstream Systems) project published mechanised HOL4 proofs of CHERI-MIPS safety properties in 2023:

  • Spatial safety (formally proved): For any sequence of CHERI-MIPS instructions, every memory access is within the bounds of the capability used as the base register, or a CHERI exception is raised. Stated as a HOL4 theorem over the full CHERI-MIPS instruction set.

  • Monotonicity (formally proved): No CHERI-MIPS instruction produces a tagged capability with wider bounds or more permissions than its inputs. The proof proceeds by case analysis over all 42 CHERI instructions.

  • Tag integrity (formally proved): If a memory location’s tag is 0, no finite execution sequence can produce a tagged capability pointing to that location without M-mode intervention.

  • Proof size: The HOL4 proofs span approximately 25,000 lines across the Sail-generated HOL4 definitions and hand-written proof scripts. They are mechanically checked by HOL4’s kernel, providing the highest assurance level (EAL7-equivalent for the ISA model).

docs.title: 27.16.5 seL4 Verified Microkernel on RISC-V (2023): Full Verification Complete
docs.text:
The seL4 microkernel (Data61/CSIRO, UNSW) completed full functional correctness verification on RISC-V (RV64) in 2023:

  • What is verified: The C implementation of seL4 on RISC-V is proved to be a refinement of the abstract specification (in Isabelle/HOL), meaning every system call behaves exactly as specified for all possible inputs and kernel states.

  • Security properties: The RISC-V seL4 proof includes: integrity (a process cannot modify objects it does not have write capability to), confidentiality (information can only flow along authorised capability paths), and availability (no process can prevent another from making progress given sufficient CPU time).

  • Proof artefacts: Available at github.com/seL4/l4v; the RISC-V-specific refinement proof adds \(\sim\)15,000 lines to the existing ARM/x86 proof base.

  • Security-critical deployments: DARPA and NIWC Pacific have evaluated seL4 on RISC-V for embedded avionics; the verified RISC-V port enables DO-178C DAL A qualification paths for safety-critical aerospace hardware.

docs.title: 27.16.6 RISC-V Sail Model: Formal ISA Specification for Hardware Compliance
docs.text:
The RISC-V Sail model (maintained by the RISC-V International Sail/ISA working group) serves as the authoritative formal specification of the RISC-V privileged and unprivileged ISA:

  • Hardware compliance: RISC-V International now uses Sail model execution as a component of official ISA compliance testing (riscv-arch-test suite). Processors submitted for RISC-V certification must pass tests derived from the Sail operational semantics.

  • Proof generation: The Sail compiler generates Isabelle/HOL and Coq theorem prover representations from the Sail model, enabling formal proofs of security properties directly over the hardware specification.

  • Smepmp and Zk extensions: The 2023 Sail model update includes full operational semantics for Smepmp (including MML/RLB CSR interactions) and all Zkn/Zks/Zkr instructions, enabling formal proofs of PMP isolation and cryptographic instruction correctness.

  • CHERI-RISC-V in Sail: The rems-project/sail-cheri-riscv repository provides a Sail model of CHERI-RISC-V that generates both HOL4 and Coq proof targets, used as the foundation for the CHERI formal proofs described above.

Table 27.4. Formal verification hardware security developments 2023–2024 Development Year Key Result OpenTitan 100K+ assertions 2023–24 Nightly CI formal verification JasperGold PropGen (AI) 2024 40–60% property writing speedup VC Formal 2024.03 SPV 2024 Taint tracking, power SCA pre-silicon CHERI-MIPS HOL4 proofs 2023 Spatial safety, monotonicity mechanised seL4 on RISC-V full proof 2023 Integrity + confidentiality on RV64 RISC-V Sail compliance 2023 Smepmp/Zk in formal ISA spec

docs.title: 27.17 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Write two SVA assertions for a TPM 2.0 PCR register: (a) once locked, the PCR cannot be reset except by a full system reset; and (b) the PCR extends operation completes within 100 clock cycles of the extend command.

  2. Explain the difference between safety properties (\(\mathbf{AG}\,p\)) and liveness properties (\(\mathbf{AF}\,p\)) in the context of hardware security. Give a real hardware security example of each.

  3. The CHERI Sail model proves capability monotonicity. Write the theorem statement in pseudocode: “For any CHERI instruction, the output capability’s bounds are a subset of the input capability’s bounds.” What proof technique is used (induction, case analysis, etc.)?

  4. Use SymbiYosys to verify a simple 2-input multiplexer (mux) property: the output equals input A when sel=0 and input B when sel=1. Write the .sby configuration file and the SVA property.

  5. Describe the product construction for verifying HyperLTL property \(\forall \pi_1 \forall \pi_2 : \mathbf{G}(\text{out}[\pi_1]_L = \text{out}[\pi_2]_L)\) (non-interference over all trace pairs). How many copies of the system does the model checker instantiate?

  6. An AES-128 core has a 10-round pipeline (one round per stage). Write a BMC-based strategy to verify that the first round key equals the original 128-bit key. What is the minimum BMC depth?

  7. Explain what a “counterexample trace” is in formal verification and how it helps engineers locate RTL bugs. Give an example of a counterexample to the property: “The secret key register is zeroed within 5 cycles of a zeroisation command.”

  8. The COCO tool verifies that a masked AES implementation is first-order DPA resistant. Describe what it checks at the RTL level and what output it produces when a masking error is found.

  9. Compare model checking and theorem proving for hardware security verification in terms of: automation level, decidability, scalability, and what class of properties each handles best.

  10. An OpenTitan alert handler has 5 alert sources. Write SVA properties to verify: (a) no alert is permanently silenced (liveness), and (b) an alert reaching the alert handler is forwarded to the CPU within 10 cycles (bounded response).

  11. Research the DARPA BESSPIN programme. What RISC-V processors were evaluated, what security properties were formally verified, and what vulnerability classes were discovered through formal analysis that simulation missed?

docs.title: 28.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Hardware supply chain security encompasses the policies, technologies, and procedures required to protect electronic components and systems from adversarial compromise at every stage of their lifecycle. Unlike software vulnerabilities, which can often be patched after deployment, hardware-level compromises may be permanent, undetectable by software means, and catastrophically impactful to national security and critical infrastructure. The supply chain for a modern integrated circuit spans multiple continents, dozens of organizations, and thousands of individual process steps, each representing a potential insertion point for malicious modification.

The scope of hardware supply chain threats is broad: a threat actor may insert a Hardware Trojan during chip design at an untrusted IP vendor, alter the netlist during fabrication at an offshore foundry, substitute counterfeit components during PCB assembly, or intercept finished systems during logistics for physical implant installation. Each attack surface demands distinct detection and mitigation strategies. High-profile incidents such as the alleged Supermicro server board modifications reported in 2018, the DARPA SHIELD program responding to counterfeit component proliferation, and the documented sale of recycled military-grade ICs through gray-market channels have elevated supply chain security to a top-tier national security concern.

This chapter provides a comprehensive technical treatment of hardware supply chain threats, detection methodologies, cryptographic authentication architectures, trusted manufacturing programs, and relevant international standards. Specific chip families, part numbers, process nodes, and evaluation boards are referenced throughout to ground abstract concepts in engineering practice.

docs.title: 28.2.1 Attack Stages
docs.text:
The hardware supply chain can be decomposed into six principal stages, each with distinct threat actors and attack vectors.

Figure 28.1. Hardware supply chain attack surface across six lifecycle stages with representative threats at each stage.

docs.title: 28.2.2 Design-Phase Threats
docs.text:
Third-party IP cores, procured from commercial vendors or open-source repositories such as OpenCores, are integrated into SoC designs without exhaustive verification. A malicious IP vendor can embed a Hardware Trojan triggered by a rare operand sequence, a specific GPIO state, or a timer-based condition. Notable examples include:

  • Trust-Hub Benchmark Trojans: The Trust-Hub consortium maintains a library of 97 documented Trojan benchmarks in synthesizable RTL, including the AES-T100 through AES-T2000 series, covering combinational and sequential trigger types.

  • DARPA TIC Program: The Trusted Integrated Circuit program funded logic testing research that demonstrated sub-10 gate Trojans undetectable by functional simulation.

  • Rogue EDA Plugins: Synthesis tool plugins for Synopsys Design Compiler or Cadence Genus can silently alter timing constraints or insert scan chain backdoors.

docs.title: 28.2.3 Fabrication-Phase Threats
docs.text: Offshore foundries operating at advanced nodes such as TSMC 5nm (N5), Samsung 4LPE, or GlobalFoundries 12LP provide the manufacturing capacity for the majority of high-performance ICs used in defense and commercial sectors. A compromised foundry can modify the GDSII layout to add a Trojan cell cluster occupying fewer than 0.1% of die area, overproduce authorized die and sell excess units through gray-market channels, or alter doping profiles in critical transistors to reduce device lifetime through time-bomb degradation.

docs.title: 28.2.4 Assembly and Distribution Threats
docs.text: Contract Electronics Manufacturers (CEMs) such as Foxconn, Jabil, and Flex assemble PCBs using components sourced from authorized distributors (Arrow, Avnet, Mouser) but also from gray-market brokers when parts are scarce. Interdiction attacks involve intercepting shipments and inserting passive monitoring implants on the PCB before resealing packaging.

docs.title: 28.3 Counterfeit Component Categories
docs.text:
The Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) and ERAI classify counterfeit components into five primary categories:

  1. Remarked: A lower-grade or different device with the part marking altered to represent a higher-specification or scarce part. Example: An STM32F103C8T6 (64KB Flash) remarked as STM32F103RBT6 (128KB Flash).

  2. Recycled: Components harvested from scrapped PCBs, re-tinned, and sold as new. Detectable by lead-free solder on leaded-specification parts, mixed solder paste on balls, and evidence of prior thermal excursions.

  3. Cloned: Functionally compatible but manufactured without authorization using a reverse-engineered die design. Often produced at unlicensed fabs in regions with lax IP enforcement.

  4. Overproduced: Authentic die from a legitimate foundry produced in excess of the authorized quantity and diverted to unauthorized distribution channels. These are functionally identical and hardest to detect.

  5. Defective/Out-of-Spec: Failed parts regraded and sold as fully functional, or parts from the tails of process distributions that do not meet full operating range specifications.

docs.title: JTAG-Based Identification
docs.text:
Every IEEE 1149.1-compliant device exposes a 32-bit IDCODE register via the JTAG TAP controller. The IDCODE encodes manufacturer ID (11 bits, JEDEC JEP106), part number (16 bits), and version (4 bits). A remarked device will present the IDCODE of its true silicon, not the false marking:

# OpenOCD: read JTAG IDCODE from suspect device
openocd -f interface/ftdi/ft2232h_breakout.cfg \
        -f target/stm32f1x.cfg \
        -c "init; scan_chain; exit"

# Expected for genuine STM32F103C8:
#   TapName       Enabled  IdCode     Expected   IrLen
#   stm32f1x.cpu  1   0x1ba01477  0x1ba01477    4

# Xilinx XC7A35T legitimate IDCODE:
#   0x0362D093  (bits[27:12] = 0x362D -> 35T)
# XC7A100T IDCODE should be:
#   0x03631093  (bits[27:12] = 0x3631 -> 100T)
# Mismatch -> remarked counterfeit confirmed

docs.title: 28.4.1 Cryptographic Device Identity
docs.text:
Establishing unforgeable device identity requires hardware-rooted cryptographic credentials. The Microchip ATECC608B secure element implements ECDSA P-256/P-384 signing and verification, ECDH key agreement for session key derivation, hardware SHA-256/HMAC, monotonic counters for anti-replay, locked key slots preventing extraction, and a Physically Unclonable Function for device-unique root key generation.

Figure 28.2. Hardware authentication architecture using ATECC608B secure element and SPDM protocol.

docs.title: 28.4.2 SPDM Protocol (DSP0274 v1.2)
docs.text:
DMTF DSP0274 defines SPDM, a standardized protocol enabling authenticated communication between system components without relying on software-only trust. SPDM v1.2 supports the following message exchanges:

  • GET_DIGESTS / DIGESTS: Retrieves SHA-384 digests of certificate chains stored in the device.

  • GET_CERTIFICATE / CERTIFICATE: Retrieves X.509 DER-encoded certificate chain.

  • CHALLENGE / CHALLENGE_AUTH: Nonce-based challenge-response using ECDSA-384 or EdDSA.

  • GET_MEASUREMENTS / MEASUREMENTS: Retrieves TPM PCR-equivalent firmware measurements signed by the device attestation key.

  • KEY_EXCHANGE: Establishes a session using ECDH for encrypted subsequent communication.

SPDM operates over MCTP (DSP0236) tunneled over PCIe VDM, I2C/SMBus, USB, or TCP/IP. The PCIe CXL 3.0 specification mandates SPDM for component authentication.

# spdm-emu: run SPDM requester against hardware component
./spdm_requester_emu --trans PCI_DOE \
    --slot-id 0 \
    --measurement-hash-algo SHA_384 \
    --base-asym-algo ECDSA_ECC_NIST_P384 \
    --base-hash-algo SHA_384 \
    --req-cap CERT,CHAL,ENCRYPT,MAC,MUT_AUTH,KEY_EX,MEAS \
    --exe-conn DIGEST,CERT,CHAL,MEAS

# Typical output on authentic device:
# Measurement[0]: DMTF_SPEC_MEAS_HASH_EXTEND = SHA384(FW_image)
# Measurement[1]: DMTF_SPEC_MEAS_RAW_BIT_STREAM = Config regs
# CHALLENGE_AUTH signature: verified OK (ECDSA-384)

docs.title: 28.4.3 PUF-Based Device Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Physically Unclonable Functions exploit manufacturing process variations to generate device-unique, unclonable bit strings. The SRAM PUF is the most widely deployed type: on power-up, uninitialized SRAM cells settle to a device-specific pattern determined by threshold voltage mismatch between cross-coupled inverter pairs.

Key commercial PUF implementations:

  • Intrinsic ID SRAM PUF: Licensed to NXP (LPC55S69), Renesas (RX65N), and Samsung; provides 256-bit root key with helper data stored in NVM. Evaluation board: LPCXpresso55S69-EVK (OM13089).

  • Microsemi PolarFire SoC PUF: Used in PolarFire SoC FPGA (MPFS250T-FCVG484E) for RTK generation, integrated into the MSS security subsystem.

  • ICTK Via-PUF: Via hole PUF in 180nm CMOS process. FAR and FRR both below \(10^{-6}\). Used in Korean national ID card chips.

  • Arbiter PUF: Path delay race condition; demonstrated in Xilinx XC7A35T-1CSG324C configuration logic, 64-bit response from 64-bit challenge.

docs.title: 28.5 in-toto Attestation Framework
docs.text:
The in-toto framework provides a supply chain attestation specification where each step in the build pipeline is recorded as a signed link metadata file. The framework ensures that every artifact was produced by an authorized functionary and that the build pipeline was not subverted.

# in-toto: define hardware design supply chain layout
# layout.json (key fields)
{
  "expires": "2027-12-31T00:00:00Z",
  "steps": [
    {
      "name": "rtl-design",
      "functionaries": [{"keyid": "designer_ed25519_key"}],
      "expected_materials": [],
      "expected_products": [
        ["CREATE", "src/aes_core.v"],
        ["CREATE", "src/top.v"]
      ],
      "run": []
    },
    {
      "name": "synthesis",
      "functionaries": [{"keyid": "cicd_key_id"}],
      "expected_materials": [
        ["MATCH", "src/*.v", "WITH", "PRODUCTS", "FROM", "rtl-design"]
      ],
      "expected_products": [["CREATE", "netlist/top_synth.v"]]
    },
    {
      "name": "pnr",
      "functionaries": [{"keyid": "cicd_key_id"}],
      "expected_materials": [
        ["MATCH", "netlist/top_synth.v", "WITH", "PRODUCTS",
         "FROM", "synthesis"]
      ],
      "expected_products": [["CREATE", "impl/top.bit"]]
    }
  ]
}

# Generate link metadata during synthesis step:
in-toto-run --step-name synthesis \
  --signing-key cicd_key.pem \
  --materials src/*.v \
  --products netlist/top_synth.v \
  -- dc_shell -f synth.tcl

# Verify entire hardware supply chain:
in-toto-verify --layout layout.root.link \
  --layout-keys root_key.pub \
  --link-dir ./links/

docs.title: 28.6 SLSA Framework for Hardware
docs.text:
Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) defines four levels of supply chain integrity. Applied to hardware design flows:

Table 28.2. SLSA Levels Applied to Hardware Design Supply Chain Level Requirement Hardware Analog SLSA 1 Build process documented Synthesis script in version control SLSA 2 Version controlled + build service Git-tagged RTL, Jenkins CI build SLSA 3 Non-falsifiable provenance in-toto signed link metadata per step SLSA 4 Two-party review + hermetic build Dual-sign RTL commits, isolated EDA env

Achieving SLSA 4 for hardware requires isolated EDA tool environments (containerized Synopsys or Cadence runs with no network access), cryptographically signed synthesis reports, and a two-person approval gate for any netlist modification. The DARPA AISS (Automated Implementation of Secure Silicon) program funds research toward SLSA 4 equivalent for ASIC flows.

docs.title: 28.7.1 Software Bill of Materials
docs.text: The White House Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) mandated SBOM for federal software procurement. NTIA defines three SBOM formats: SPDX 2.3 (Linux Foundation, ISO/IEC 5962:2021), CycloneDX 1.4 (OWASP, supports HBOM extensions), and SWID Tags (ISO/IEC 19770-2, used in US DoD CMMC context).

docs.title: 28.8.1 DoD Trusted Foundry (DMEA)
docs.text:
The Defense Microelectronics Activity (DMEA) operates the Trusted Foundry Program (TFP), accrediting domestic U.S. foundries and design houses to produce ICs for classified and sensitive military systems.

  • Category 1A (Trusted Fab): Full GDSII-to-packaged-die production. Accredited: IBM/GlobalFoundries Malta NY (180nm–12nm), SkyWater Technology (90nm, FOSS-capable), Northrop Grumman (200mm SOI for HBT/SiGe), OnSemi Gresham OR (0.35um–0.18um analog/mixed-signal).

  • Category 1B (Trusted Design): RTL through GDSII tape-out. Accredited: Raytheon Microelectronics (El Segundo), BAE Systems MicroElectronics, General Dynamics Mission Systems.

  • Category 2 (Trusted Distributor): Procures from Trusted Suppliers, maintains chain of custody. Accredited: Arrow Electronics Federal, Avnet Federal.

docs.title: 28.8.2 GlobalFoundries Trusted (Fab 8, Malta NY)
docs.text: GF Fab 8 at Malta, New York manufactures on 14nm FinFET (14LPP) and 12nm (12LP) nodes for TFP. GF Trusted provides U.S.-citizen-only fab floor access for designated production lots, GDSII-to-packaged-device chain of custody documentation, lot traceability linking wafer ID to die to package via laser-marked serial number, and side-channel resistant library cells for cryptographic IP.

docs.title: 28.8.3 Samsung Austin Semiconductor
docs.text: Samsung Austin Semiconductor operates a 300mm fab (S1) in Austin, Texas at 14nm (14LPP). The facility operates under U.S. ITAR controls for export-sensitive designs. The SAS 8nm SF8T node (FinFET) is used for commercial military-grade SoCs including some Qualcomm defense-variant products.

docs.title: 28.8.4 TSMC Arizona (Fab 21)
docs.text: TSMC Fab 21 in Phoenix, Arizona produces at 4nm (N4P) and 3nm (N3E) process nodes with CHIPS Act funding. U.S. government procurement requirements are expected to drive TFP alignment certification.

docs.title: 28.9 FPGA-Based Supply Chain Monitoring
docs.text:
FPGAs implement real-time supply chain monitoring logic including PUF enrollment, secure boot measurement, and tamper detection. The supply chain monitor IP core comprises: SRAM PUF enrollment and reconstruction (BCH error correction), SHA-256 pipeline for SBOM hash verification, ECDSA-256 signature verification using Montgomery curve point multiplier, and a secure boot state machine compatible with the DICE architecture.
