docs.title: 28.11.1 Holographic Labels and Laser Marking
docs.text: OEM manufacturers apply physical authentication features to packaged ICs including holographic overlabels (3M Confirm series) with micro-text visible under 10x magnification, fiber laser engraving directly onto package mold compound, 2D DataMatrix (ISO/IEC 16022) encoding lot number, date code, and serial number, and chemical DNA taggants mixed into epoxy mold compound verifiable with field-deployable PCR kits.

docs.title: 28.11.2 Secure Key Injection at Manufacturing
docs.text:
# Microchip ATECC608B: secure manufacturing provisioning
# Step 1: Initialize configuration zone
atcab_init(&cfg_ateccx08a_i2c_default);

# Step 2: Write configuration zone (slot configs, I2C addr, etc.)
uint8_t config_data[128] = {
    /* SN[0:3] read-only, SN[4:8] read-only */
    0x83, 0x20,  /* Slot 0: P-256 keypair, external sign enabled */
    0x87, 0x20,  /* Slot 1: Internal sign only                   */
    0x8F, 0x20,  /* Slot 2: Secret key (HMAC operations)         */
};
atcab_write_config_zone(config_data);

# Step 3: Lock config zone (irreversible operation)
atcab_lock_config_zone();

# Step 4: Generate keypair in Slot 0 (private key never leaves)
uint8_t public_key[64];
atcab_genkey(0, public_key);
/* Send public_key to factory HSM via TLS -> HSM issues X.509 cert */

# Step 5: Write device certificate (DER encoded) to data zone
atcab_write_bytes_zone(ATCA_ZONE_DATA, CERT_SLOT, 0,
                       cert_der, cert_len);

# Step 6: Lock data zone
atcab_lock_data_zone();
/* Device is now personalized and ready for field deployment */

docs.title: 28.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: Identifying a Remarked Component via JTAG IDCODE

A procurement inspector receives a batch of ICs labeled as Xilinx XC7A100T-2FGG484C (Artix-7, 100K LUT, -2 speed grade). Using a JTAG probe, the IDCODE registers return 0x0362D093. Determine whether these components are genuine and specify the remediation steps.

Solution: The Xilinx IDCODE format: bits [31:28] = version, bits [27:12] = part number, bits [11:1] = manufacturer (0x049 = Xilinx per JEDEC JEP106), bit [0] = 1.

Parsing 0x0362D093:

  • Bits [11:1] = 0x049 = Xilinx (correct manufacturer)

  • Bits [27:12] = 0x362D -> cross-reference Xilinx UG470 Table 6-2

  • 0x362D corresponds to XC7A35T, not XC7A100T

  • XC7A100T should return IDCODE 0x03631093 (bits [27:12] = 0x3631)

Conclusion: The returned IDCODE 0x0362D093 conclusively identifies the silicon as XC7A35T (33,650 LUT6 equivalent) sold as XC7A100T (101,440 LUT6 equivalent) – a 3x capacity downgrade. These are remarked counterfeits.

Remediation steps:

  1. Quarantine the entire lot immediately.

  2. File a counterfeit alert with ERAI (Electronic Resellers Association International).

  3. Perform SEM cross-section: XC7A35T die area is approximately 3.14 mm\(^2\) vs. 8.0 mm\(^2\) for XC7A100T in TSMC 28nm HPL.

  4. Conduct XRF on package marking to detect sanding evidence.

  5. Report to supplier and initiate formal counterfeit reporting per SAE AS5553B.

  6. If purchased under government contract, notify DCSA (Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency).

Solved Problem: SRAM PUF Reliability and ECC Budget Analysis

An SRAM PUF implementation on an STM32L562 (Cortex-M33, 40nm) uses 2048 bits of startup SRAM. Laboratory characterization shows a raw intra-HD (within-device across temperature \(-40\) to \(+85\) degrees C) of 6.2% and inter-HD (between devices) of 49.8%. Determine whether BCH(255,245) with \(t=10\) error correction is sufficient to achieve FRR below \(10^{-6}\).

Solution: The raw bit error rate within a device: \(p = 0.062\).

For BCH(\(n=255, k=245, t=10\)), we use 255-bit codewords. The expected number of errors per codeword: \(\mu = 255 \times 0.062 = 15.81\).

Since \(\mu = 15.81 > t = 10\), the BCH code is under-dimensioned. Using the binomial tail probability:

\[P_\text{fail,block} = \sum_{i=11}^{255} \binom{255}{i} (0.062)^i (0.938)^{255-i}\]

By Poisson approximation (\(\lambda = 15.81\)): \(P(X > 10) \approx 1 - F_\text{Poisson}(10; 15.81) \approx 0.93\).

This is catastrophically high. For 2048 PUF bits using \(\lfloor 2048/255 \rfloor = 8\) codewords, all 8 must succeed. But individual block failure probability is 93%, so the approach completely fails.

Corrective design: Move to BCH(511, 466, \(t=22\)). With \(\mu = 511 \times 0.062 = 31.7\) errors per codeword and \(t=22\): this still fails. The proper approach is a two-step process:

  1. Reliability masking during enrollment: Perform PUF reads at \(-40\), \(+25\), and \(+85\) degrees C. Retain only bits that are stable across all three (typically 60–70% of cells). This reduces effective \(p\) to approximately 1.5%.

  2. With stable subset (\(p=0.015\)): Using BCH(511, 493, \(t=10\)), \(\mu = 511 \times 0.015 = 7.67 < t = 10\). \(P(X > 10 | \lambda = 7.67) \approx 4.3 \times 10^{-2}\). Still too high.

  3. Final solution: BCH(255, 223, \(t=16\)) with stable subset (\(p=0.015\)): \(\mu = 3.83\), \(P(X > 16) < 10^{-9}\). FRR \(< 10^{-6}\) is achieved with \(\geq 7\) codewords.

Conclusion: BCH(255,245) with \(t=10\) is insufficient. A reliability-masked PUF combined with BCH(255,223,\(t=16\)) meets the \(10^{-6}\) FRR target.

Solved Problem: in-toto Link Metadata Verification and Tamper Detection

An RTL synthesis step produces netlist top_synth.v with SHA-256 hash H1. The in-toto link metadata records H2 for the same file. A verifier later computes H3 from the file on disk. Describe the verification logic and the security implication of \(H1 = H2 \neq H3\).

Solution: The in-toto verification algorithm:

  1. Load signed link metadata for the synthesis step. Verify the Ed25519 signature using the functionary’s public key (embedded in the layout). If the signature is invalid, abort immediately: supply chain integrity violation.

  2. Extract the recorded artifact hash H2 from the link’s products field for top_synth.v.

  3. Compute H3 = SHA-256(top_synth.v) from the current file on disk.

  4. Compare H2 and H3: if equal, the file is unmodified since the authorized synthesis step completed.

In the scenario where \(H1 = H2 \neq H3\): the link metadata was correctly signed at synthesis time (H1 = H2 confirms the recorded hash matches what the CI/CD functionary computed). However, the current file hash H3 differs, meaning top_synth.v was modified after the synthesis step completed.

Security implication: This is a post-synthesis tampering event. The netlist may contain an inserted Hardware Trojan or unauthorized functional modification introduced at the place-and-route stage or during artifact storage. The entire fabrication pipeline downstream of this step must be treated as untrusted. Required actions: (1) Re-synthesize from audited RTL under in-toto monitoring. (2) Perform differential analysis between H2-version and H3-version netlist to identify the modification. (3) Initiate incident response to identify the compromised CI/CD stage or storage system.

Solved Problem: HBOM Completeness Audit for a Hardware Security Module

A system integrator provides a CycloneDX 1.4 HBOM for a hardware security module listing 47 components. Physical X-ray inspection of the PCB reveals 52 distinct component reference designators. Classify the risk categories for the 5 unlisted components and specify the corrective action required.

Solution: Audit process:

  1. Extract all reference designators from the PCB via X-ray tomography and optical inspection. Record manufacturer part number from silkscreen, XRF material analysis, and JTAG IDCODE where applicable.

  2. Map each reference designator to a HBOM entry using part number cross-reference.

  3. For each of the 5 unlisted components, determine: component type (active IC, passive, connector), signal path location relative to cryptographic interfaces, and whether the part number appears on the approved vendor list (AVL).

Risk classification for unlisted components (ordered by severity):

  • Critical – Active IC on cryptographic bus: An unaccounted active IC placed on the SPI or I2C bus between the host MCU and the secure element. This could be a bus interposer performing man-in-the-middle key extraction. Requires immediate quarantine, decapsulation, and forensic analysis of the unknown IC.

  • High – Unaccounted power management IC: An unlisted DC-DC converter or LDO on the VDD_CORE rail could introduce a glitching attack surface to bypass secure boot voltage fault detection. Requires AVL check, electrical characterization, and replacement with approved part.

  • Medium – Passive on sensitive data line: An undocumented ferrite bead or capacitor on a data signal line. Possibly a BOM revision not reflected in the HBOM; characterize impedance and confirm no active silicon content.

  • Low – Mechanical/non-electrical: EMI shielding clips or mounting hardware not affecting electrical function. Update HBOM for completeness.

  • Low – Optical indicator: LED in a non-sensing status indicator path. Verify no photodetection capability on cryptographic side channels.

The integrator is in violation of NIST SP 800-161r1 and must issue a corrective action report. System acceptance is blocked until the HBOM is updated and all unlisted active ICs are accounted for through documented chain of custody.

Solved Problem: Recycled Component Detection via C-SAM Analysis

A defense contractor receives 500 units of NXP T2080NXE7PQAB (PowerPC e6500, QorIQ, PBGA896) procured from an unauthorized broker. C-SAM inspection is ordered. Describe the procedure, the specific indicators of recycling, and the accept/reject criteria per AS6171.

Solution: C-SAM Procedure: Operate the Sonoscan D9600 at 75 MHz for PBGA die-substrate interface scanning. Perform C-mode (amplitude) scan at die-attach interface, die-to-substrate underfill, and BGA ball-to-PCB pad interface.

Indicators of recycled components:

  1. Delamination at die-attach: Dark (low-reflectance) regions at the die-epoxy interface indicating voiding from thermal cycling during prior use. Accept criterion: \(<2\%\) void area per JEDEC JESD22-B112.

  2. Package corner delamination: PBGA corners experience highest thermal stress from coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch (silicon 3 ppm/K vs. BT substrate 15 ppm/K). Delamination extending \(>0.5\) mm from any corner edge is rejectable.

  3. BGA ball height bimodality: Reformed solder balls from re-balling operations show inconsistent height distribution. New part nominal ball height: \(0.60 \pm 0.05\) mm. Recycled-and-re-balled: \(0.45 \pm 0.12\) mm with high standard deviation detectable in A-mode scan.

  4. Intermetallic compound thickness: IMC thickness at solder-pad interface correlates with number of prior reflow cycles. New parts: \(<3\) um Cu\(_3\)Sn / Cu\(_6\)Sn\(_5\). After one reflow cycle: 4–5 um. Two or more cycles: \(>7\) um detectable by cross-section SEM/EDS.

  5. Prior solder residue: Inkjet dot patterns or solder mask residue from previous PCB attachment visible in C-SAM as surface artifact.

Sampling and decision per AS6081 / AS6171:

  • Sample size from lot of \(N = 500\): \(\lceil\sqrt{500}\rceil + 1 = 24\) units.

  • Accept/Reject: If \(\geq 2\) units show delamination \(> 2\%\) or IMC \(> 5\) um, reject the entire lot.

  • Escalation: Rejected lots must be reported to ERAI, quarantined with lot serialization, and the supplier reported to GIDEP (Government-Industry Data Exchange Program).

docs.title: 28.15 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The hardware supply chain security landscape shifted fundamentally between 2022 and 2026, driven by landmark legislation, new X-ray inspection capabilities, and the emergence of the Hardware Bill of Materials as a procurement requirement.

docs.title: 28.15.1 CHIPS and Science Act — US Domestic Fabrication Incentives
docs.text:
The Creating Helpful Incentives to Produce Semiconductors (CHIPS) and Science Act (Public Law 117-167, August 2022) appropriated $52.7 billion for domestic semiconductor manufacturing, of which $39 billion targeted fabrication facility construction grants. Implementation through the CHIPS Program Office (within US Department of Commerce) commenced in 2023–2025 with the following security implications for supply chains:

  • Security requirements for grant recipients: Facilities receiving CHIPS Act grants must submit Technology Access Plans (TAPs) to the Department of Defense and agree to restrictions on technology transfer to “countries of concern” (People’s Republic of China, Russia, Iran, North Korea). Recipients are prohibited from expanding leading-edge capacity in restricted countries for ten years.

  • TSMC Fab 21 (Phoenix, AZ): TSMC received $6.6 billion in direct funding under the CHIPS Act (announced April 2024). Fab 21 Phase 1 (N4P process) began production in 2024; Phase 2 (N2 process, 2 nm) is targeted for 2026. This provides the first domestic source of leading-edge nodes for US defense programs.

  • Intel 18A at Ohio (Fab 52/62): Intel received up to $8.5 billion (announced March 2024) for Ohio “Silicon Heartland” fabs at Intel 18A (1.8 nm-class, gate-all-around CFET technology).

  • Samsung Taylor, Texas: Samsung received approximately $6.4 billion for expansion of its Taylor, Texas fab to the 4 nm SF4X process node.

Note: CHIPS Act security requirements do not yet mandate DMEA Trusted Foundry Program accreditation for commercial grant recipients. DoD programs requiring TFP must still use DMEA-accredited Category 1A facilities. CHIPS Act fabs may seek TFP alignment in subsequent phases.

docs.title: 28.15.2 NIST SP 800-161 Revision 1 — C-SCRM Practices
docs.text:
NIST Special Publication 800-161 Revision 1 (C-SCRM Practices for Systems and Organizations) was published in May 2022 and saw widespread federal adoption through 2023–2024 under OMB Memorandum M-22-18. Key technical additions over the original 800-161 include:

Table 28.7. NIST SP 800-161r1 Key C-SCRM Practice Families Practice Family Requirement Summary Hardware Supply Chain Relevance SR-1: Policy Agency-level C-SCRM policy with executive commitment Requires explicit hardware procurement security clauses SR-2: C-SCRM Plan Multi-level plan (enterprise, program, project) Maps to HBOM maintenance obligations SR-3: Supply Chain Controls Contractual flow-down to sub-tier suppliers Requires HBOM disclosure from sub-tier EMS providers SR-4: Provenance Document hardware component provenance JEDEC JEP106 ID + lot traceability records SR-5: Acquisition Strategies Risk-based sourcing; avoid sole-source dependencies Dual-source critical ICs; authorized distributor only SR-6: Supplier Assessments Annual third-party audits of critical suppliers AS6496 Trusted Supplier accreditation as evidence SR-10: Inspection of Systems Physical and logical inspection of delivered hardware C-SAM, XRF, JTAG IDCODE verification per AS6171 SR-11: Component Authenticity Verify authenticity of system components PUF-based or SPDM attestation before commissioning

The 2023–2024 adoption wave was accelerated by CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 23-01, which required federal civilian agencies to implement C-SCRM programs aligned with SP 800-161r1 by April 2024.

docs.title: 28.15.3 EU Chips Act — European Semiconductor Sovereignty
docs.text:
The European Chips Act (Regulation EU 2023/1781, published September 2023) established a €43 billion investment framework for European semiconductor manufacturing:

  • Pillar 1 – Research and innovation: €3.3 billion for the KDT (Key Digital Technologies) Joint Undertaking to develop 2 nm-class process technology within the EU by 2030.

  • Pillar 2 – Secure supply: Facilitates first-of-a-kind fab construction in EU member states. TSMC announced a €10 billion fab in Dresden, Germany (ESMC – European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company) targeting 28/22 nm FD-SOI and 12/16 nm FinFET; production targeted for 2027.

  • Pillar 3 – Monitoring and crisis response: Establishes a European Semiconductor Board with authority to coordinate emergency measures (invoking crisis stage) and require priority orders during supply disruptions. This directly addresses the 2021–2022 automotive chip shortage lesson.

Tip: The EU Chips Act Pillar 3 crisis monitoring mechanism can compel semiconductor manufacturers operating in the EU to prioritize orders for critical applications (medical, defense, automotive). Supply chain engineers should monitor the European Semiconductor Board’s “alert” and “crisis” stage declarations as part of operational continuity planning.

docs.title: 28.15.4 X-ray CT for IC Inspection — Bruker and Zeiss Systems
docs.text:
Industrial X-ray computed tomography became a mainstream counterfeit detection tool in 2023–2024, replacing destructive decapsulation for initial screening. Two systems dominate the market for IC inspection:

Bruker SkyScan 1275:

  • Source: microfocus X-ray tube, 20–100 kVp, \(5~\mu\)m focal spot

  • Detector: 11 Mpixel CMOS flat-panel, \(16 \times 16\) cm field of view

  • Resolution: \(3~\mu\)m voxel in high-resolution mode

  • Use case: BGA package inspection – detecting re-balling, voiding, foreign objects; die stack verification in PoP (Package-on-Package) devices

  • Scan time: 4–8 minutes per component for full 3D reconstruction

Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa:

  • Source: synchrotron-quality lab X-ray with Fresnel zone plate optics

  • Resolution: \(500\) nm voxel (sub-micron tomography)

  • Use case: Die-level metallization layer inspection for Hardware Trojan detection; cross-section of wire bonds; via structure analysis

  • Detection capability: foreign conductive inclusions down to \(2~\mu\)m diameter detectable in 28 nm-node metallization stack

The combination of Bruker SkyScan (package-level, fast) and Zeiss Xradia (die-level, high-resolution) provides a two-tier inspection pipeline matching the AS6171 testing methodology: gross physical anomaly screening followed by high-resolution die analysis on suspect samples.

docs.title: 28.15.5 JEDEC JEP106 and JESD89 — Traceability Improvements
docs.text:
JEDEC JEP106 (Manufacturer Identification Code, 2023 revision) extended the manufacturer ID table with 47 new entries covering emerging fabless design houses and ODM manufacturers in Southeast Asia. Key improvements relevant to counterfeit detection:

  • Extended Continuation Codes: JEP106 now supports up to bank 11 (previous maximum bank 9), accommodating 176 additional manufacturer entries. The JTAG IDCODE bits [11:1] encode the manufacturer; cross-referencing against the updated JEP106 table detects device identity mismatches in remarked parts.

  • JESD89C (Measuring and Reporting Single Event Effects): Updated 2023 to require lot-specific SEU characterization data from manufacturers, enabling traceability from wafer lot to published radiation test results.

  • JEP-STD-153: New JEDEC standard (2024) for unique electronic component identification using 2D DataMatrix symbology, encoding: manufacturer bank+ID, part number, lot code, date code, and serial number in a machine-readable format compatible with automated optical inspection (AOI) lines.

docs.title: 28.15.6 HBOM — Hardware Bill of Materials as an Emerging Standard
docs.text:
The Hardware Bill of Materials concept evolved from concept to emerging procurement requirement between 2023 and 2024:

  • NTIA HBOM Framework (October 2023): The National Telecommunications and Information Administration published a preliminary discussion document on HBOM minimum elements, mirroring the SBOM minimum elements from NTIA’s 2021 guidance. Proposed minimum fields: component name, component version, manufacturer, unique identifier (purl or CPE), HBOM author, timestamp, and dependency relationships.

  • CycloneDX 1.5 Hardware Extension (2023): CycloneDX 1.5 (OWASP, released June 2023) strengthened HBOM support with new component metadata fields: manufacturer.contact, releaseNotes, and externalReferences types including bom-link for cross-referencing between software SBOM and hardware HBOM artifacts.

  • DoD CMMC 2.0 and HBOM: The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification 2.0 (final rule published October 2024) Level 2 and Level 3 requirements for supply chain risk management (Practice SR.2.111) are interpreted by DCSA as requiring HBOM documentation for hardware components in scope.

Warning: HBOM standards remain in flux as of 2025. CycloneDX and SPDX are competing for adoption in different verticals. Programs implementing HBOM pipelines should maintain format-agnostic tooling capable of generating both CycloneDX 1.5 and SPDX 2.3 outputs from the same underlying component database.

docs.title: 28.15.7 Google Project Zero Supply Chain Findings (2023–2024)
docs.text:
Google Project Zero published two significant supply chain security findings relevant to hardware security practitioners:

  • Samsung Exynos Baseband Vulnerabilities (March 2023): Project Zero disclosed 18 zero-day vulnerabilities in Samsung Exynos modems (used in Pixel 6/7, Galaxy S22, Galaxy A series). Four of the vulnerabilities allowed silent remote code execution over the baseband without user interaction. The supply chain implication: OEMs integrating third-party modem silicon may be exposed to vulnerabilities in subsystems they do not control. Mitigation adopted by Google: disabling Wi-Fi calling and Voice-over-LTE on affected Pixel devices via software while awaiting firmware patches.

  • Mali GPU Driver Vulnerabilities (2023 series): Project Zero identified multiple kernel driver vulnerabilities in Arm Mali GPU drivers (CVE-2023-4211, CVE-2023-33200, CVE-2023-34970) affecting devices from MediaTek, Samsung, and Qualcomm. The attack surface spans the hardware–software boundary: the GPU driver communicates directly with the Mali G-series hardware via memory-mapped registers, and a kernel driver bug can expose the entire GPU memory region, enabling cross-process weight extraction on shared AI inference hardware.

docs.title: 28.16 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. A batch of Texas Instruments CC2652R7 (IEEE 802.15.4 SoC, VQFN-48) is purchased from a gray-market broker. Design a three-stage test plan combining electrical, optical, and cryptographic methods to confirm authenticity. Specify which characteristics of the CC2652R7 enable discrimination from counterfeit candidates.

  2. The SPDM GET_MEASUREMENTS response from a PCIe NVMe SSD returns Measurement[0] as SHA-384 of the firmware image. An auditor computes a local hash of the firmware binary obtained from the vendor portal and finds a mismatch. List four possible causes in order of severity and the investigation steps for each cause.

  3. A secure key injection station uses a Thales Luna HSM to provision ECDSA P-256 private keys into 10,000 IoT device secure elements per production day (8 hours). Each provisioning operation (keygen + ECDSA sign of CSR + write certificate) consumes 12 ms of HSM compute time. Calculate the minimum number of HSM partitions required, including a 20% utilization headroom.

  4. Analyze the SLSA threat model for an FPGA bitstream compilation pipeline. Map the four SLSA levels to specific controls in a Xilinx Vivado-based build system covering version control, build server isolation, provenance generation, and two-party review. What additional controls does SLSA 4 require beyond a standard DevOps CI/CD pipeline?

  5. A HBOM for a medical imaging system lists a component with entry: purl: pkg:generic/xilinx/xcku115@2.0. Explain what supply chain risks are not captured by this entry and specify the additional CycloneDX fields that should be added to address foundry provenance, lot traceability, and firmware version attestation.

  6. An arbiter PUF is instantiated on a Xilinx XC7A35T with 64 challenge-response pairs enrolled during manufacturing. An attacker captures 56 CRPs through an SPDM measurement side channel. Using the Linear Additive Delay model for arbiter PUFs, estimate the minimum number of CRPs needed for a logistic regression attacker to achieve above 95% prediction accuracy on unseen CRPs, and discuss two hardware defenses.

  7. Compare overproduced silicon (authentic die, unauthorized distribution) versus cloned silicon (unauthorized fab, reverse-engineered die) as supply chain threats. For each: describe physical detection methods, estimated probability of detection using standard AS6171 tests, and legal/regulatory consequences for the party responsible.

  8. A DoD program requires NSA-approved Type 1 encryption on an embedded processor. The program office must choose between a DMEA-accredited trusted foundry ASIC and a commercial FPGA solution. Using the DMEA TFP Category definitions (1A, 1B, 2), describe the procurement path for each option including applicable ITAR and MIL-STD-3018 obligations.

  9. The in-toto framework requires link metadata signed by the authorized functionary key. Describe an attack scenario where an adversary who compromises the CI/CD signing private key can subvert supply chain attestation while avoiding detection, and propose a mitigation using HSM-bound Yubikey 5C NFC with PKCS#11 interface.

  10. A PUF enrollment is performed at 25 degrees C. Field deployment spans \(-40\) to \(+85\) degrees C. The device uses BCH(255,235) with \(t=10\) error correction. Characterization data shows intra-device HD peaks at 11.4% at temperature extremes. Calculate the codeword failure probability and determine whether the ECC budget is adequate. Propose a modified enrollment strategy to achieve FRR \(< 10^{-6}\).

  11. Design a counterfeit detection acceptance sampling plan for a lot of 1000 units of Analog Devices ADUM4160 (USB isolator, QSOP-16). Specify the AS6081 sampling size, the inspection methods appropriate for this package type and component function, the accept/reject criteria, and the ERAI/GIDEP reporting escalation path if the lot fails.

  12. Explain how a sequential Hardware Trojan can be designed to evade both functional simulation with standard test vectors and post-silicon burn-in testing, yet be reliably triggered after a specific number of clock cycles in field deployment. Propose a detection methodology based on Statistical Analysis of Sequential (SAS) trigger patterns combined with differential power analysis.

docs.title: 29.1 Introduction
docs.text:
5G and telecommunications hardware security encompasses the silicon security of base stations, core network processors, subscriber identity modules, and the network function virtualization infrastructure that runs the 5G core. Unlike general IT systems, telecom hardware must authenticate billions of subscribers at millisecond latency while resisting sophisticated nation-state adversaries who have physical access to the radio interface and may control intermediate network elements. The introduction of Open RAN (O-RAN), which disaggregates hardware and software from different vendors, introduces new attack surfaces at software-hardware interfaces that previously existed only within a single-vendor proprietary stack.

Security threats to 5G span the full protocol stack: the UICC/eSIM hardware storing the subscriber’s permanent identity, the air interface over which the UE exchanges authentication vectors, the gNodeB (gNB) base station that must be protected from software tampering, the 5G Core network functions implemented as cloud-native workloads, and the legacy SS7 and Diameter signaling protocols that remain interoperable with 5G for roaming. Each layer requires hardware-specific security controls that go beyond software configuration.

This chapter provides a comprehensive technical treatment of 5G authentication hardware, UICC and eSIM security, base station secure boot and attestation, O-RAN security architecture, legacy signaling vulnerabilities, network function virtualization security, and quantum-safe migration paths. Specific chipsets, evaluation platforms, and protocol message flows are referenced throughout.

docs.title: 29.2 5G Network Architecture and Security Domains
docs.text:
Figure 29.1. 5G network architecture with security domains at UE, access network, 5G core, and home network.

The 5G architecture per 3GPP TS 23.501 separates security into three main domains:

  • Access Security: Protection of the NR-Uu interface between UE and gNB, including SUPI/SUCI privacy, NAS and RRC ciphering (128-AES-EEA, 128-SNOW3G, 128-ZUC), and integrity protection (128-AES-EIA, 128-SNOW3G, 128-ZUC).

  • Network Domain Security: IPsec ESP (AES-256-GCM) on N2, N3, Xn interfaces between network functions, and TLS 1.3 on SBA (Service Based Architecture) HTTP/2 interfaces.

  • User Plane Security: End-to-end encryption between UE and UPF using a session-specific key derived from the 5G-AKA exchange.

docs.title: 29.3.1 Physical UICC Architecture
docs.text:
The Universal Integrated Circuit Card (UICC) is a tamper-resistant smart card implementing the 3GPP USIM application. Hardware security features include:

  • JavaCard OS: UICC firmware runs on JavaCard 3.0.4 with GlobalPlatform 2.3.1 security domain management. The USIM applet is loaded into an isolated security domain.

  • Cryptographic Accelerators: AES-128/256 for MILENAGE and TUAK; ECC P-256 for eSIM profile authentication; SHA-256/384 for integrity; TRNG meeting AIS-31 statistical requirements.

  • Physical Protection: Active mesh of fine conductors over the die surface detecting probe attempts; light sensors triggering zeroization on decapsulation; frequency monitors rejecting clock glitching; voltage detectors rejecting supply manipulation.

  • PIN/PUK Protection: After 3 consecutive wrong PIN entries, the USIM application is locked. After 10 wrong PUK entries, the card is permanently blocked per 3GPP TS 31.102.

docs.title: 29.3.2 SIM Cloning Attacks
docs.text:
Historical SIM cloning attacks exploited weak cryptographic implementations in 2G (A3/A8 COMP128v1). The COMP128v1 algorithm was broken in 1998 by Briceno et al., requiring only 150,000 adaptive chosen challenges. Modern UICC using MILENAGE (AES-128) or TUAK (Keccak-f[1600]) is not practically clonable; however, physical hardware attacks remain concerns for high-value targets:

  • Power Analysis: DPA on MILENAGE AES-128 requires approximately \(10^4\) traces; countermeasure is masking with random shares.

  • Fault Injection: Laser fault injection on ECC key operations during eSIM profile installation; mitigated by computation redundancy checks.

  • eSIM Profile Extraction: Extraction of the ECIES private key from an unprotected eUICC flash using microprobing; mitigated by dedicated secure memory with hardware encryption.

docs.title: 29.3.3 IMSI Catchers (Stingrays)
docs.text:
IMSI catchers exploit the lack of network-to-UE authentication in 2G and partially in 4G (no NAS integrity for Attach Request before security mode). In 5G, the SUCI mechanism encrypts the SUPI (IMSI) on the air interface using the home network’s public key, preventing IMSI harvesting:

# SUCI construction (3GPP TS 33.501, Sec. 6.12.2)
# UE generates ephemeral ECDH key pair using Curve25519 or secp256r1
# Home network public key K_hnpub is pre-provisioned in USIM

# ECIES-based SUCI encryption (Curve25519 profile A):
ephemeral_privkey = generate_x25519_private()
ephemeral_pubkey  = X25519(ephemeral_privkey, G)  # base point

# Shared secret via ECDH:
shared_secret = X25519(ephemeral_privkey, K_hnpub)

# Key derivation (ANSI X9.63 KDF with SHA-256):
icb  = KDF(shared_secret || ephemeral_pubkey, 16)  # enc key
MAC  = KDF(shared_secret || ephemeral_pubkey, 32)  # MAC key

# Encrypt MSIN (mobile subscriber ID number, 5-10 digits):
encrypted_MSIN = AES-128-CTR(icb, MSIN)
mac_value      = HMAC-SHA256(MAC, encrypted_MSIN)[0:8]

# SUCI = MCC | MNC | routing_indicator | protection_scheme_id
#        | ephemeral_pubkey | encrypted_MSIN | mac_value

Only the home network’s SIDF (Subscription Identifier De-concealing Function), which holds the private key corresponding to K_hnpub, can decrypt the SUCI and recover the SUPI. This cryptographically defeats passive IMSI catchers.

docs.title: 29.4.1 Protocol Message Flow
docs.text: Figure 29.2. 5G-AKA protocol message flow between UE (USIM), SEAF (AMF), and UDM/AUSF.

docs.title: 29.4.2 MILENAGE Algorithm Details
docs.text:
MILENAGE (3GPP TS 35.206) uses AES-128 as a block cipher core. Given subscriber permanent key K (128 bits) and operator key OPc (128 bits, derived from OP by XOR with AES_K(OP)):

# MILENAGE core computation (3GPP TS 35.206 Annex 3)
# Input: K (128-bit), RAND (128-bit), SQN (48-bit), AMF (16-bit)
# OPc = AES_K(OP) XOR OP  (configured in USIM at personalization)

# Compute TEMP = AES_K(RAND XOR OPc)
TEMP = AES128(K, RAND ^ OPc)

# f1: Network Authentication Code (MAC-A, 64-bit)
IN1  = SQN[47:0] || AMF[15:0] || SQN[47:0] || AMF[15:0]
# rotate and XOR with OPc, then AES
MAC_A = AES128(K, rotate_left(TEMP^OPc, r1) ^ c1^OPc)[0:64]

# f2: Response (RES, 64-bit)
RES   = AES128(K, rotate_left(TEMP^OPc, r2) ^ c2^OPc)[64:128]

# f3: Cipher Key (CK, 128-bit)
CK    = AES128(K, rotate_left(TEMP^OPc, r3) ^ c3^OPc)

# f4: Integrity Key (IK, 128-bit)
IK    = AES128(K, rotate_left(TEMP^OPc, r4) ^ c4^OPc)

# f5: Anonymity Key (AK, 48-bit) -- conceals SQN in AUTN
AK    = AES128(K, rotate_left(TEMP^OPc, r5) ^ c5^OPc)[0:48]

# AUTN = SQN ^ AK || AMF || MAC_A
AUTN  = (SQN ^ AK) || AMF || MAC_A

# 5G key derivation from CK, IK:
KAUSF = HMAC_SHA256(CK||IK, "5G AKA" || SQN^AK || SN_name)
KSEAF = HMAC_SHA256(KAUSF, "K_seaf" || SN_name)
KAMF  = HMAC_SHA256(KSEAF, "K_amf"  || GUAMI || separation_bit)

docs.title: 29.4.3 5G Key Derivation Hierarchy
docs.text:
The 5G key hierarchy produces session-specific keys from a single root K stored in the USIM HSM:

K (permanent, 128-bit, HSM-protected in USIM)
  |
  +-- KAUSF  (derived per AKA run, known to AUSF and USIM)
       |
       +-- KSEAF  (serving network anchor key, SEAF only)
            |
            +-- KAMF  (AMF anchor key)
                 |
                 +-- KNASenc  (NAS encryption: AES-128, SNOW3G, ZUC)
                 +-- KNASint  (NAS integrity: AES-128-EIA2)
                 +-- KgNB    (gNB anchor key)
                      |
                      +-- KRRCenc  (RRC ciphering)
                      +-- KRRCint  (RRC integrity)
                      +-- KUPenc   (User Plane ciphering)
                      +-- KUPint   (User Plane integrity, optional)

docs.title: 29.5.1 SM-DP+ and ISD-P Architecture
docs.text:
The GSMA SGP.22 Consumer eSIM specification defines a secure profile download architecture involving the SM-DP+ (Subscription Manager Data Preparation Plus) server and the eUICC (embedded UICC):

# SGP.22 Profile Download Sequence (simplified)
# Step 1: Device requests eSIM activation
GET /gsma/rsp2/es9plus/initiateAuthentication
  -> SM-DP+ returns: serverSigned1 (ECDSA-P256 signed)

# Step 2: eUICC authenticates SM-DP+
GET /gsma/rsp2/es9plus/authenticateClient
  Body: euiccInfo2 (eUICC capabilities, certificate)
  SM-DP+ verifies eUICC certificate chain:
    eUICC_cert -> EUM_cert -> CI_cert (GSMA root CA)

# Step 3: Profile package preparation
# SM-DP+ encrypts profile with eUICC public key:
# Profile_encrypted = ECIES_P256(eUICC_pubkey, Profile)
# Profile_signed    = ECDSA_P256(SM-DP+ key, Profile_hash)

# Step 4: Profile installation on eUICC
# eUICC decrypts profile in ISD-P (Issuer Security Domain Profile)
# ISD-P is a separate secure domain per operator:
#   - Cannot access other operators' ISD-P
#   - Controlled by Controlling Authority Security Domain (CASD)
#   - Profile contains: USIM application, operator credentials,
#     MILENAGE K, OPc, algorithm preferences

docs.title: 29.5.2 ISD-P Isolation
docs.text: Each operator profile installs into a dedicated ISD-P (Issuer Security Domain Profile) on the eUICC. The CASD controls creation and deletion of ISD-Ps. GlobalPlatform 2.3.1 security domain hierarchy ensures cryptographic isolation between profiles: operator A’s USIM applet cannot read operator B’s key material even if both are installed on the same eUICC.

docs.title: 29.6.1 TPM 2.0 Integration
docs.text:
3GPP TS 33.117 requires base stations to implement platform integrity attestation before connecting to the 5G Core. A representative gNB hardware platform (Ericsson AIR 6449, Samsung RU for O-RAN) implements:

  • TPM 2.0 (Infineon SLB9670): Stores the Endorsement Key (EK) and Attestation Identity Key (AIK). PCR registers 0–7 measure firmware boot stages.

  • Measured Boot Sequence: UEFI/BIOS -> bootloader -> OS kernel -> 5G L1/L2 software stack. Each layer extends the appropriate PCR before executing the next.

  • Remote Attestation to 5GC: The AMF verifies the gNB’s TPM Quote (PCR set signed by AIK) against known-good values before accepting N2 registration.

# gNB TPM 2.0: Generate attestation quote for 5GC verification
# Using tpm2-tools on Linux

# Step 1: Create AIK (Attestation Identity Key) in TPM
tpm2_createak -G rsa2048 -g sha256 -s rsassa \
    -C 0x81010001 -c ak.ctx -u ak.pub -n ak.name

# Step 2: Certify AIK with Endorsement Key (TPM proof of AIK)
tpm2_makecredential -e ek.pub -s ak.name -n ak.name \
    -o credential.blob

# Step 3: At boot, extend PCRs with firmware measurements
tpm2_pcrevent -i /boot/vmlinuz sha256

# Step 4: Generate TPM Quote (signed PCR values for N2 attestation)
tpm2_quote -c ak.ctx -l sha256:0,1,2,3,4,7 \
    -q $(openssl rand -hex 20) \  # nonce from AMF
    -m quote.msg -s quote.sig -o pcrs.out

# Step 5: AMF verifies quote using gNB's certified AK public key
# Expected PCR[7] = SHA256(Secure_Boot_Policy || signing_cert_hash)

docs.title: xApp Isolation in Near-RT RIC
docs.text:
The O-RAN near-real-time RAN Intelligent Controller (near-RT RIC) hosts xApps from multiple vendors. Security isolation requirements per O-RAN WG11 specifications:

  • Container Isolation: Each xApp runs in a Kubernetes pod with dedicated namespace, NetworkPolicy restricting E2 interface access, and PodSecurityPolicy enforcing read-only root filesystem.

  • E2 Interface Authentication: TLS 1.3 mutual authentication between E2 termination in the near-RT RIC and the E2 node (O-DU/O-CU), using certificates issued by the O-RAN CA.

  • A1 Policy Security: Non-RT RIC to near-RT RIC A1 interface uses TLS 1.3 with RBAC to restrict which xApps can receive policy updates.

  • xApp SDK Sandboxing: O-RAN SC (Software Community) xApp SDK provides a secure API abstraction; direct memory access to E2AP protocol buffers is prohibited.

docs.title: O-RU Authentication
docs.text:
Open Fronthaul (eCPRI/7-2x split) authentication between O-DU and O-RU uses IEEE 802.1X EAP-TLS. MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) provides layer-2 encryption and integrity protection on the fronthaul:

# O-RU MACsec configuration (Linux wpa_supplicant + ip macsec)
# On O-DU side:

# Step 1: 802.1X EAP-TLS authentication of O-RU
wpa_supplicant -i oru_fronthaul0 \
    -c /etc/wpa_supplicant/oru.conf &

# wpa_supplicant config for O-RU:
# network={
#   key_mgmt=IEEE8021X
#   eap=TLS
#   ca_cert="/etc/ssl/oran-ca.pem"
#   client_cert="/etc/ssl/oru-cert.pem"
#   private_key="/etc/ssl/oru-key.pem"
# }

# Step 2: After 802.1X auth, configure MACsec
ip link add link oru_fronthaul0 macsec0 type macsec \
    cipher suite GCM-AES-256 icvlen 16 encrypt on
ip macsec add macsec0 rx port 1 address AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF
ip macsec add macsec0 rx port 1 address AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF \
    sa 0 pn 1 on key 0A abc123...  # 256-bit SAK
ip macsec add macsec0 tx sa 0 pn 1 on key 0B def456...

docs.title: 29.7.1 SS7 Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
SS7 (Signaling System No. 7) was designed in 1975 with no authentication; any entity with SS7 access can impersonate any network element. Critical attacks documented by Positive Technologies and exploited by nation-state actors:

  • Location Tracking: MAP_PROVIDE_SUBSCRIBER_INFO (PSI) returns subscriber Cell-ID and geographic location to any SS7 node that sends the request. Defense: SS7 firewall filtering PSI from non-home networks.

  • Call Interception: MAP_REGISTER_SS registers a call forwarding number controlled by the attacker. All incoming calls are silently forwarded before reaching the victim’s phone.

  • SMS Interception: MAP_SEND_ROUTING_INFO_FOR_SM reveals the HLR and MSC serving the target; MAP_MT_FORWARD_SHORT_MESSAGE redirects the SMS to the attacker.

  • OTP Bypass: The above SMS interception enables bypass of SMS-based two-factor authentication – documented in attacks on mTAN banking systems (Germany, 2017).

# SS7 attack example: Location tracking via MAP PSI
# Using SigPloit (research/educational framework)

from scapy.contrib.sigtran import *
from scapy.contrib.ss7.map import *

# Build MAP PSI request (attacker impersonates MSC)
psi_req = MAP_provide_subscriber_info_arg(
    subscriberIdentity=IMSI("123456789012345"),
    requestedInfo=requestedInfo(
        locationInformation=None,  # Request location
        subscriberState=None       # Request activity state
    )
)

# SS7 defense: Per GSMA FS.11 baseline
# - Block PSI from foreign networks for home subscribers
# - Whitelist: Only allow MAP operations from known GT (global titles)
# - Anomaly detection: Sudden location change = alert
# - 5G migration: Replace MAP with SBA HTTP/2 (no SS7 exposure)

docs.title: 29.7.2 Diameter Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
4G/LTE uses Diameter protocol (IETF RFC 6733) for Cx, Sh, S6a, and Gx interfaces. Like SS7, Diameter was designed without strong authentication of the requesting node:

  • Cancel-Location Attack: Diameter Cancel-Location-Request (CLR) sent to HLR forces the victim’s device to re-register, enabling IMSI exposure during the re-attach procedure.

  • Insert-Subscriber-Data: Modifies subscriber profile to redirect services.

  • Authentication-Information-Request: Extracts authentication vectors from HLR if the attacker’s Diameter node is not properly authenticated.

Defense: IPsec between all Diameter nodes, Diameter Application-layer Security (IETF RFC 6733 + TLS), and Diameter firewall (Evolvent, Mobileum) filtering messages by AVP content, origin-realm validation, and rate limiting.

docs.title: 29.8 Network Function Virtualization Hardware Security
docs.text:
5G core network functions (AMF, SMF, UPF, UDM, AUSF) run as containerized microservices on COTS server hardware. Hardware security considerations include:

  • Intel TXT (Trusted Execution Technology): Measures BIOS, bootloader, and hypervisor into PCR registers before launching the 5GC workload. Used in Ericsson Cloud Core on Intel Xeon Scalable (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids) platforms.

  • AMD SEV-SNP (Secure Encrypted Virtualization – Secure Nested Paging): Encrypts VM memory with VM-specific keys in AMD EPYC 7003/9004 (Genoa) processors. Enables encrypted containers for UDM (which stores K values) even from the hypervisor.

  • Intel SGX: Provides Trusted Execution Environments for AUSF/SIDF operations involving SUCI decryption. Nokia Cloud BTS uses SGX enclaves for AMF NAS layer.

  • SmartNIC Security: NVIDIA BlueField-3 DPU (200 GbE, Arm Cortex-A78) implements IPsec offload for N3/N9 GTP-U tunnels, removing crypto from the host CPU and providing hardware-enforced packet filtering.

docs.title: 29.9 FPGA-Based 5G Baseband Security

docs.title: 29.11 Quantum-Safe 5G Migration
docs.text:
The Mosca theorem states that if quantum computers capable of breaking ECDH-256 and RSA-2048 become available within \(y\) years, and the system has a \(t\)-year security lifetime, migration must begin at least \((y - t)\) years before the quantum threat materializes. For 5G infrastructure with a 15–20 year lifecycle, PQC migration is urgent:

  • SUCI Protection: Current ECIES with Curve25519 is vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm. NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 (Kyber-768) replaces the ECDH key encapsulation. SUCI size increases from approximately 50 bytes (Curve25519) to approximately 1250 bytes (ML-KEM-768), which requires 5G NAS message fragmentation support.

  • AKA Root Keys: K is AES-128 (MILENAGE) or Keccak (TUAK). AES-128 has 64-bit security against Grover’s algorithm. Migration to AES-256 MILENAGE (proposed in 3GPP Rel-20) provides 128-bit post-quantum security.

  • TLS Certificates: ECDSA P-256 certificates on SBA, N2, N3 interfaces replaced with NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 (Dilithium-3) certificates. Certificate size: 3.3 KB vs. 64 bytes for ECDSA.

  • 3GPP Standardization Timeline: 3GPP TR 33.700-01 (Rel-19) initiated PQC study item; Rel-20 (2027+) expected to normatively specify PQC algorithms.

# Hybrid PQC + classical key exchange for 5G SBA interfaces
# Using OQS-OpenSSL provider (Open Quantum Safe project)

# Configure nginx (AMF HTTP/2 server) with hybrid KEM:
# nginx.conf:
ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;
ssl_ciphers  TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384;

# OQS provider enables hybrid groups:
# X25519_kyber768 (classical + PQC hybrid)
ssl_ecdh_curve X25519Kyber768Draft00:X25519:P-256;

# Certificate: Dilithium3 leaf signed by ECDSA P-384 (hybrid)
ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/amf-dilithium3.crt;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/amf-dilithium3.key;
ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/nginx/oran-ca-hybrid.crt;

# Verify client (SMF, UDM) certificates
ssl_verify_client on;
ssl_client_certificate /etc/nginx/oran-ca-hybrid.crt;

docs.title: 29.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: SUCI Decryption Failure Analysis

A 5G UE sends a Registration Request containing a SUCI encrypted with the home network’s Curve25519 public key (profile A). The AUSF/SIDF reports a decryption failure. List five possible causes and the diagnostic procedure for each.

Solution: Possible causes of SUCI decryption failure at the SIDF:

  1. Wrong home network public key provisioned in USIM: The eUICC received an incorrect K_hnpub during profile download or the SM-DP+ provisioned a stale key. Diagnostic: Extract the ephemeral public key from the SUCI, attempt ECDH with all known historical K_hnpriv versions. If one succeeds, trigger USIM reprovisioning via OTA update. Mitigation: Include K_hnpub version indicator in the SUCI routing indicator field.

  2. SIDF key rollover race condition: The home network rotated K_hnpriv after the USIM was provisioned but before the key propagated to all SIDF instances. Diagnostic: Check SUCI timestamp against key rotation log. Mitigation: Maintain at least two active K_hnpriv versions during rollover period.

  3. SUCI bit error over NR-Uu interface: The SUCI ephemeral public key (32 bytes for Curve25519) arrived corrupted, causing ECDH to produce garbage. Diagnostic: Check NAS layer CRC error counters; the NAS layer provides integrity protection only after security mode command, so initial Registration Request is unprotected. The UE should retransmit after 5GMM timer T3510 expiry.

  4. Protection scheme mismatch: The USIM uses profile B (secp256r1 ECIES) but the SIDF is configured only for profile A (Curve25519). Diagnostic: Parse SUCI protection scheme ID byte; compare with SIDF capability configuration in UDM.

  5. Tampering or MITM: An active IMSI catcher attempted to decrypt the SUCI (which it cannot since it lacks K_hnpriv) and relayed a corrupted SUCI. This attack is self-defeating but causes a denial of service. Diagnostic: Check if the correlation between SUCI failures and specific gNB cells shows spatial clustering, suggesting a rogue base station.

Solved Problem: 5G-AKA Key Hierarchy Derivation Exercise

Given a subscriber with K = 0x0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF and a RAND of all-zeros (for calculation purposes), and assuming OPc = 0xCDC202D5123E20F62B6D676AC72CB318, compute the expected KSEAF key structure step by step.

Solution: This derivation follows 3GPP TS 33.501 Annex A and MILENAGE (TS 35.206):

Step 1: MILENAGE produces CK and IK:

\[\text{TEMP} = \text{AES}_{K}(\text{RAND} \oplus \text{OPc})\]

With RAND = 0x00...00 and OPc = 0xCDC202..., TEMP = AES\(_{K}\)(OPc).

Step 2: CK = \(f_3(K, \text{RAND})\) and IK = \(f_4(K, \text{RAND})\), both 128-bit outputs of AES applied with rotations \(r_3, r_4\) and constants \(c_3, c_4\) from TS 35.206.

Step 3: Compute KAUSF from 3GPP TS 33.501 Annex A.2:

\[\text{KAUSF} = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{CK} \| \text{IK},\ S)\]

where \(S = \text{FC=0x6A} \| \text{SN-name} \| \text{len(SN-name)} \| (\text{SQN} \oplus \text{AK}) \| \text{len=6}\).

Step 4: Compute KSEAF from Annex A.6:

\[\text{KSEAF} = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{KAUSF},\ \text{FC=0x6C} \| \text{SN-name} \| \text{len(SN-name)})\]

Step 5: Compute KAMF from Annex A.7:

\[\text{KAMF} = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{KSEAF},\ \text{FC=0x6D} \| \text{SUPI} \| \text{GUAMI} \| \text{uplink\_counter})\]

Security properties: Each key is computationally independent of its siblings given the HMAC one-way function. Forward secrecy is achieved by the per-AKA-run derivation: a compromised KSEAF does not reveal K or enable decryption of past sessions. The UE and AUSF independently derive KAUSF from the same CK||IK, with no explicit transfer of KAUSF over the network.

Solved Problem: SS7 SMS Interception Attack and Defense Design

An operator has detected anomalous MAP_SEND_ROUTING_INFO_FOR_SM (SRI-SM) requests originating from foreign SS7 point codes for domestic subscribers. Design an SS7 firewall rule set to block this attack while preserving legitimate international SMS delivery.

Solution: Attack analysis: SRI-SM from a foreign SS7 network should only be sent by a legitimate SMS Service Centre (SMSC) to deliver an SMS originating from that network. An attacker spoofing an SMSC sends SRI-SM to harvest MSC/VLR routing information and subscriber HLR addresses, enabling targeted SMS interception.

Firewall rule set (per GSMA FS.11 baseline, Category 2 rules):

  1. Rule 1 – SRI-SM origin validation: Allow SRI-SM only from GT (Global Title) addresses matching the official SMSC address range for the originating PLMN, validated against the GSMA Roaming Registry (AA.19 database). Block all SRI-SM from GT addresses not in the registry.

  2. Rule 2 – SRI-SM rate limiting: Allow maximum 10 SRI-SM requests per foreign PLMN per second for a given MSISDN. Sustained queries above this threshold indicate automated enumeration; block and alert.

  3. Rule 3 – SRI-SM response filtering: Filter outbound SRI-SM responses to suppress the subscriber’s VLR address (replace with proxy VLR address). The SMSC only needs the MSRN (Mobile Subscriber Roaming Number) for delivery, not the raw VLR GT.

  4. Rule 4 – Correlated attack detection: Correlate SRI-SM with subsequent MT-Forward-SM within 60 seconds. If SRI-SM is followed by no MT-FSM, flag as reconnaissance. Block the foreign GT if this pattern repeats \(>5\) times within 10 minutes.

  5. Rule 5 – International SMSC whitelist: Maintain a whitelist of authorized international SMSCs from MNO bilateral roaming agreements. Any SRI-SM from non-whitelisted GT is dropped and logged.

Legitimate SMS delivery is preserved because authorized foreign SMSCs appear on the whitelist (Rule 5) and have delivery-correlated patterns (Rule 4). Long-term mitigation: migrate to 5G SBA using HTTP/2 with mTLS for SMS delivery (3GPP TS 24.547 SMS over NAS), eliminating SS7 exposure.

docs.title: 29.15 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The 5G security landscape evolved rapidly between 2023 and 2026, with accelerating 5G Standalone deployments exposing new attack surfaces, and post-quantum cryptography migration entering the 3GPP standardisation agenda.

docs.title: 29.15.1 5G SA Deployment Acceleration and Security Advantages
docs.text:
5G Non-Standalone (NSA) architecture (3GPP Release 15) anchors the 5G NR air interface to the legacy 4G LTE core. 5G Standalone (SA) mode, deploying the full 5G Core (5GC), became commercially predominant in 2023–2024 with meaningful security advantages:

  • SUPI privacy via SUCI: 5G SA mandates SUCI encryption of the subscriber permanent identifier (SUPI/IMSI). NSA mode optionally supports this only when the 5G NR anchor is connected to a 4G EPC with SUPI privacy extensions – a gap exploited by IMSI catchers on NSA deployments.

  • NAS integrity protection from first message: 5G SA secures NAS messages (registration, service request) from the initial attach, whereas 4G LTE NAS integrity is applied only after the Security Mode Command. This eliminates several redirection and fingerprinting attack vectors documented against 4G.

  • User Plane Integrity (UPI): 5G SA standardises optional user-plane integrity protection (KUPint, AES-128-EIA2) between UE and gNB. NSA provides no equivalent. Network operators enabling UPI prevent bit-flip attacks on unencrypted UDP payloads in the PDCP layer.

docs.title: 29.15.2 GSMA FS.40 — 5G Hardware Security Guidelines (2024)
docs.text:
GSMA FS.40 (5G Cybersecurity Knowledge Base, updated 2024) added a dedicated hardware security annex covering:

  • gNB hardware root of trust: FS.40 mandates that base stations supporting operator trust programs implement a hardware TPM 2.0 or equivalent HSE (Hardware Security Engine) with measured boot. The attestation report must cover BIOS, bootloader, OS kernel, and 5G L1/L2 software stack PCR measurements.

  • SIM/eSIM supply chain requirements: FS.40 Section 5.8 requires that UICC and eUICC personalisation (K value injection) occurs at GSMA-accredited Subscription Management facilities using FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs. This directly addresses supply chain K-extraction scenarios at unaccredited SIM personalisation bureaux.

  • Network slice hardware isolation: For network slices carrying mission-critical traffic (public safety, industrial IoT), FS.40 recommends physical hardware isolation (separate DPU/SmartNIC processing paths) rather than software-only VLAN/namespace isolation to prevent cross-slice data leakage at the hypervisor layer.

docs.title: 29.15.3 O-RAN Alliance WG11 Security Specifications (2023–2024)
docs.text:
O-RAN Alliance Working Group 11 (WG11) published the Security Requirements and Controls Specification v4.0 (O-RAN.WG11.Security-Reqs-and-Controls-v04.00, June 2023) and supplementary Security Test Specifications:

Table 29.5. O-RAN WG11 Key Security Controls (2023–2024) Interface Security Control Hardware Relevance Open Fronthaul (eCPRI) MACsec GCM-AES-256 mandatory O-RU must include MACsec engine (hardware offload required at 25G rates) E2 (near-RT RIC) TLS 1.3 mutual auth, RBAC per xApp E2 termination in O-DU must use HSM-stored private key O1 Management TLS 1.3, NETCONF over SSH O-DU/O-CU management plane key protected by TPM A1 (non-RT to near-RT) TLS 1.3, policy signing Policy objects signed by non-RT RIC private key O-RU Boot Secure boot with ECDSA-384 signing O-RU bootloader must verify firmware before bringing up RF chains SMO (Service Mgmt) Certificate-based service mesh Service account certificates issued by O-RAN PKI with short lifetimes

WG11’s 2024 Security Test Specification (O-RAN.WG11.Security-Test-Spec) introduced penetration testing requirements for Open Fronthaul MACsec implementations, mandating that vendors provide test harness access to security evaluators before commercial deployment in Tier 1 operator networks.

docs.title: 29.15.4 5G Redirection and Downgrade Attacks — IMSI Catchers on 5G NR
docs.text:
Research published at IEEE Security & Privacy 2023 (“5G-Spector: An O-RAN Compliant Layer-3 5G Cellular Attack Detection System”) documented that 5G NR NSA deployments remain vulnerable to redirection attacks:

  • RRC Connection Release with Redirection: A rogue 5G NR base station (implemented on USRP B210 + OAI gNB software at approximately $3,000 hardware cost) can broadcast a fake 5G NR cell at higher power than the legitimate network, capture UE RRC connections, then issue an RRCRelease message with a redirectedCarrierInfo field pointing to a target 4G LTE cell controlled by the attacker. The UE silently drops to 4G where IMSI catchers operate.

  • SUCI Stripping: In 5G SA, rogue base stations cannot recover the SUPI because they lack the home network private key. However, if the network operator misconfigures the AMF to fall back to SUPI (not SUCI) for “interoperability” with legacy equipment, SUPI privacy is completely defeated. 3GPP TS 33.501 Section 6.12.5 forbids this fallback but compliance is operator-dependent.

  • Countermeasures: The 5G-Spector system deploys monitoring xApps in the near-RT RIC to detect anomalous RRC Release patterns; GSMA FS.40 recommends subscriber-side UE configuration locking (Android 14+ “5G Only” network mode) to prevent downgrade.

Warning: 5G NSA deployments do not provide SUCI privacy in the downlink direction. Mobile network operators claiming “5G security” for NSA-only networks should disclose that IMSI-catcher-resistant subscriber identity protection requires full 5G SA architecture with an operational SIDF in the 5GC.

docs.title: 29.15.5 Post-Quantum 5G — 3GPP SA3 PQC Work Item (2024–2025)
docs.text:
3GPP Security Working Group SA3 initiated a formal study item on post-quantum cryptography for 5G (3GPP TR 33.700-01, Release 19) in 2024. Key technical decisions:

  • SUCI PQC migration: Current Curve25519/secp256r1 ECIES in SUCI will be replaced with ML-KEM-768 (NIST FIPS 203). SUCI size increases from approximately 50 bytes (Curve25519) to approximately 1,184 bytes (ML-KEM-768 ciphertext + encapsulation overhead), requiring 5G NAS message fragmentation support and eUICC flash storage expansion on USIM personalisation.

  • 5G-AKA root key upgrade: AES-128 MILENAGE provides 64-bit post-quantum security (Grover). 3GPP SA3 agreed to specify AES-256 MILENAGE in Release 20 (normative expected 2027), requiring USIM re-personalisation programmes.

  • Hybrid classical+PQC: For the transition period (2025–2030), SA3 recommends hybrid key exchange combining ECDH P-256 with ML-KEM-768 for SBA interface TLS sessions (X25519Kyber768Draft00 group). This provides security against both classical and quantum adversaries simultaneously.

  • Hardware impact: ML-KEM-768 NTT arithmetic (polynomial multiplication over \(\mathbb{Z}_q\), \(q=3329\), degree \(n=256\)) requires approximately \(18,000\) clock cycles on Cortex-A55 without hardware acceleration. USIM execution time increases from \(< 1\) ms (ECIES Curve25519) to approximately 15 ms (ML-KEM-768) on current smart card silicon, impacting mass authentication events (stadium events, transportation hubs).

docs.title: 29.15.6 Ericsson and Nokia RAN Hardware Security — Secure Boot and Attestation in BBUs
docs.text:
Commercial RAN vendors integrated hardware security features into Baseband Units (BBUs) in response to GSMA FS.40 and national security authority requirements:

Ericsson Radio System (2024): Ericsson’s 5G RAN products (AIR 6449, AIR 3219) include a dedicated Security Processing Unit (SPU) implemented as a hardened ASIC subsystem:

  • Measured boot chain: ROM \(\to\) UEFI \(\to\) Linux kernel \(\to\) Ericsson 5G L1/L2. Each stage hash extends TPM 2.0 PCR registers before next stage executes.

  • Remote attestation to Ericsson Cloud Infrastructure Manager (ECIM) via IETF RATS (RFC 9334) EAT (Entity Attestation Token) format.

  • Physical tamper evidence: epoxy-filled module housing with embedded tamper mesh; field detection of mechanical intrusion attempts.

Nokia AirScale (2024): Nokia’s AirScale base station platforms (AirScale Indoor Radio, ASIK) deployed:

  • Platform Attestation Service (PAS): Nokia-proprietary attestation framework providing PCR-based measurements to Nokia NetAct network management.

  • Secure key storage: ASIC-integrated OTP fuses for EK (Endorsement Key) anchoring, preventing key extraction through JTAG or debug interfaces post-provisioning.

  • Software-defined radio security: RF parameter bounds enforcement in hardware – transmission power, frequency range, and modulation format are hardware-constrained to prevent regulatory non-compliance even if software is compromised.

docs.title: 29.16 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. An O-RAN deployment uses a near-RT RIC hosting xApps from three different vendors (Nokia, Mavenir, and Viavi). Describe the Kubernetes security controls (NetworkPolicy, PodSecurityAdmission, OPA/Gatekeeper) that enforce isolation between xApps on the E2 interface, and explain what happens if one xApp’s container is compromised by a supply chain attack.

  2. A 5G subscriber’s SUCI is intercepted by a passive adversary on the NR-Uu interface. The SUCI uses profile A (Curve25519, AES-128-CTR, HMAC-SHA256). What cryptographic guarantee prevents the adversary from recovering the SUPI? How many bits of classical security does this provide, and what is the post-quantum security level against a CRQC running Shor’s algorithm?

  3. An operator observes a sudden spike in MAP_PROVIDE_SUBSCRIBER_INFO requests for a specific subscriber’s IMSI from 47 different foreign SS7 point codes over a 2-hour window. Classify this as one of the documented attack types, describe the likely adversary goal, and design a coordinated response involving the SS7 firewall, law enforcement notification, and subscriber protection steps.

  4. A gNodeB running an open-source 5G stack (OAI or srsRAN) is deployed without TPM 2.0 integration. The AMF requires platform integrity attestation per 3GPP TS 33.117. Describe a software-only attestation alternative using IMA (Integrity Measurement Architecture) and remote attestation via IETF RATS, including its limitations compared to hardware TPM attestation.

  5. A 5G-AKA authentication vector contains AUTN = SQN_XOR_AK || AMF || MAC-A. The UE detects that the received SQN_XOR_AK does not match the expected sequence number range (delta \(> 2^{28}\) from stored SQN). What 5G-AKA procedure does the UE initiate, what message does it send, and what does this response reveal to a passive eavesdropper? Propose a privacy enhancement.

  6. Compare the security of SMS-based OTP (via SS7 delivery) versus FIDO2 hardware token (YubiKey 5 NFC) versus SIM-based authentication (3GPP TS 33.222 GAA/GBA) for a mobile banking application. Evaluate each mechanism against SS7 interception, SIM swap, and phishing attacks, and identify the hardware security properties that distinguish FIDO2.

  7. An eSIM profile downloaded via SGP.22 fails to install on a Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra (Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 with integrated eSIM). The eUICC returns error code 3.8 (Confirmation Code Error). Describe the complete SGP.22 error handling procedure, which cryptographic operation likely failed, and the recovery path without requiring a new eSIM profile from the SM-DP+.

  8. Design a MACsec key rotation scheme for an O-RAN fronthaul with 100 O-RU units connected to a single O-DU. Specify the SAK (Secure Association Key) lifetime, the key rotation trigger mechanism (time-based vs. packet-count-based), the MKA (MACsec Key Agreement) protocol parameters, and the failover behavior when a SAK negotiation fails mid-session.

  9. The Qualcomm FSM100xx 5G RAN SoC (7nm, ARM Cortex-A55 cluster + DSP) implements hardware-accelerated PDCP ciphering. A side-channel attacker performs EM (electromagnetic) analysis on 10,000 PDCP packets ciphered with AES-128-EEA2. Estimate the feasibility of key recovery using correlation electromagnetic analysis (CEMA), and describe the hardware countermeasures available in the FSM100xx security subsystem.

  10. The 3GPP Rel-17 SNPN (Stand-alone Non-Public Network) specification allows an enterprise to deploy a private 5G network without roaming agreements. Describe the authentication architecture for SNPN: which 5GC NFs are required, how subscriber credentials are provisioned without a traditional SIM, and what hardware root-of-trust mechanisms are appropriate for an IoT industrial use case.

docs.title: 30.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Medical device hardware security is uniquely life-critical: a compromised insulin pump can deliver a lethal dose, a hacked pacemaker can induce cardiac arrest, and ransomware on hospital imaging networks can delay critical diagnoses. Unlike enterprise IT security, medical device security must balance robust cryptographic protection against extreme constraints on power (implantables operate on batteries with 5–15 year lifetimes), latency (real-time closed-loop drug delivery cannot tolerate authentication delays), and update frequency (regulatory resubmission may be required for firmware changes classified as design modifications).

The threat landscape has evolved dramatically. Barnaby Jack’s 2011 demonstration of remote wireless attacks against implantable drug delivery systems, the 2016 Abbott/St. Jude Medical pacemaker vulnerabilities (CVE-2016-9563 and related advisories), and the 2021 Medtronic MiniMed insulin pump recalls represent concrete, documented exploitations of medical device hardware. The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack disabled MRI scanners and CT systems in UK NHS hospitals, demonstrating that even non-networked medical devices are affected by hospital network security failures.

This chapter provides a comprehensive technical treatment of medical device security architecture, regulatory requirements, specific embedded hardware platforms, wireless security for physiological monitoring devices, secure firmware update mechanisms, hospital network segmentation, and relevant international standards.

docs.text: Table 30.1. Medical Device Categories, Representative Hardware, and Primary Attack Surfaces Category Device Example Hardware Attack Surface Implantable Cardiac pacemaker ASIC + RF (MICS 402–405 MHz) Wireless, physical access Implantable ICD (defibrillator) Custom SoC + HV capacitor RF command injection Implantable Neurostimulator ARM Cortex-M4 + BLE 5.2 BLE stack, firmware Wearable CGM (glucose monitor) nRF52840 + BLE BLE pairing, data spoof Wearable Insulin pump STM32L4 + BLE/RF Dose command replay Networked Ventilator i.MX6 + Ethernet Network, firmware update Networked Infusion pump Cortex-A9 + WiFi Dosing parameter modify Imaging MRI / CT scanner x86 Xeon + DICOM PACS network, ransomware Lab Hematology analyzer Cortex-A53 + USB USB payload, LIS interface
