docs.title: 31.16 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: Stuxnet OB35 Detection Strategy

A Siemens Step7 / S7-PLCSIM environment is being audited for potential Stuxnet contamination. Describe a detection strategy that does not rely on antivirus signatures, targeting the OB35 injection technique specifically. The auditor has access to the Step7 project files and a JTAG-connected hardware debugger.

Solution: Stuxnet detection strategy without antivirus signatures:

  1. Direct PLC memory readback via S7comm protocol (bypass hooked DLL): Stuxnet’s key evasion technique hooks S7OTBXDX.DLL to hide OB35 from the Step7 IDE. However, a direct S7comm connection using a modified client (Siemens S7comm-plus protocol) that does not go through the hooked DLL can read the actual OB35 block from the PLC memory:

    # Using Snap7 library (bypasses S7OTBXDX.DLL):
import snap7
client = snap7.client.Client()
client.connect("192.168.1.100", 0, 1)
ob35_data = client.upload(client.BlocksList())
# Compare ob35_data with Step7 project source -> discrepancy = Trojan

  2. Hash comparison of OB35: Extract OB35 from both the Step7 project (from the .s7p file, decompiled) and directly from the PLC via Snap7. Compute SHA-256 of both. Any difference indicates tampering.

  3. VFD frequency command audit: Stuxnet modifies frequency setpoint writes to Profibus-connected VFDs. A timing analysis of Profibus DP traffic between the S7-315 and the frequency converters (Vacon or Fararo Paya model) shows anomalous frequency changes (1410 Hz / 2 Hz) outside the expected operating range. Deploy a Profibus TAP (passive monitor) to capture raw Profibus DP frames.

  4. JTAG hardware debug: Halt the S7-315 CPU via JTAG (Siemens uses a proprietary debug interface on the front panel). Read OB35 directly from CPU SRAM at the known address (extracted from Step7 documentation). This bypasses all DLL hooking and provides a ground-truth view of the running program.

  5. S7OTBXDX.DLL integrity check: On the engineering workstation, compute SHA-256 of C:\Siemens\Step7\Bin\S7OTBXDX.DLL and compare against known-good hash from Siemens. Stuxnet replaces this file; file size will be 346 KB (malicious) vs. 149 KB (genuine).

Solved Problem: TRITON Threat Mitigation Design

Following the 2017 TRITON attack, a petrochemical plant must harden its Triconex-based SIS architecture. Design a defense-in-depth architecture that addresses the three root causes identified by Dragos: (1) no authentication on TriStation 1131 protocol, (2) DIP switch PROGRAM mode accessible remotely, (3) no logging of programming access. Specify hardware and network controls for each.

Solution: Defense-in-depth architecture addressing each root cause:

Root Cause 1 – No TriStation authentication:

  • Install the Schneider Electric Trident Nexus Security Module (NSM) on all Tricon chassis. The NSM enforces HMAC-SHA256 authentication on all TriStation 1131 connections.

  • Deploy a dedicated, isolated engineering network for SIS access (separate physical switches, not VLAN-separated from DCS network). This network has no routing to the corporate IT network.

  • Implement a hardware firewall (Hirschmann EAGLE40) on the SIS engineering network permitting TriStation traffic (UDP 1502) only from a single, authorized engineering workstation IP.

Root Cause 2 – DIP switch PROGRAM mode:

  • Physical lockout: Install a keyed security enclosure over the Tricon chassis front panel. The DIP switch is accessible only with a physical key held by the SIS engineer.

  • Process control: Require a Management of Change (MoC) work order plus two-person authorization before the DIP switch is placed in PROGRAM mode. The key is held in a tamper-evident safe with access logged.

  • NSM enforcement: Configure the NSM to require a separate authentication credential (hardware token, e.g., Yubikey 5C) even when the DIP switch is in PROGRAM mode. Remote programming without physical presence at the chassis is disabled.

Root Cause 3 – No programming access logging:

  • NSM logging: The Nexus Security Module cryptographically signs and timestamps all programming access events. Logs are transmitted via unidirectional data diode (Waterfall Security) from the SIS network to a read-only historian on the DCS network.

  • Behavioral monitoring: Deploy Nozomi Networks Guardian on the SIS engineering network segment. Any TriStation protocol traffic outside authorized maintenance windows triggers an immediate alert.

  • Physical access logging: Door access control (badge + PIN) to the SIS control room is logged to a centralized SIEM with correlation: DIP switch mode change must coincide with authorized personnel badge access within 5 minutes.

Solved Problem: Modbus TCP Function Code Whitelist Design

A water treatment plant SCADA system uses Modbus TCP to communicate between a SCADA master (IP 10.1.1.10) and 15 RTUs controlling pump stations (IPs 10.1.2.1–10.1.2.15). Design a Modbus TCP firewall rule set that restricts communication to the minimum necessary function codes for normal operations while detecting and blocking attack function codes.

Solution: Modbus TCP firewall rule design:

Normal operation analysis:

  • SCADA reads sensor data: FC03 (Read Holding Registers) from each RTU – water level, flow rate, pressure.

  • SCADA reads pump status: FC01 (Read Coils) – pump running/stopped.

  • SCADA writes pump commands: FC05 (Write Single Coil) – pump start/stop during authorized operation windows.

  • SCADA writes setpoints: FC16 (Write Multiple Registers) – flow rate setpoints, alarm thresholds.

Firewall rule set (implemented in Fortinet FortiGate with Modbus AppID):

# Modbus TCP firewall policy (FortiGate CLI):

config firewall policy
  edit 10
    set name "SCADA-to-RTU-READ"
    set srcintf "SCADA_VLAN"
    set dstintf "OT_VLAN"
    set srcaddr "SCADA_MASTER_10.1.1.10"
    set dstaddr "RTU_POOL_10.1.2.0/24"
    set service "MODBUS_READ"  # FC01,FC02,FC03,FC04 only
    set schedule "always"
    set action accept
    set logtraffic all
  next
  edit 11
    set name "SCADA-to-RTU-WRITE-AUTHORIZED"
    set srcaddr "SCADA_MASTER_10.1.1.10"
    set dstaddr "RTU_POOL_10.1.2.0/24"
    set service "MODBUS_WRITE"  # FC05,FC06,FC16 only
    set schedule "OPERATIONAL_HOURS"  # 06:00-22:00 only
    set action accept
    set logtraffic all
  next
  edit 12
    set name "BLOCK-DANGEROUS-FC"
    # Block FC08 (Diagnostics), FC43 (Device ID), FC64-72 (user-defined)
    set service "MODBUS_DANGEROUS"
    set action deny
    set logtraffic all  # Alert on any attempt
  next
  edit 13
    set name "BLOCK-UNAUTHORIZED-MODBUS"
    # Any Modbus traffic not from SCADA master -> deny and alert
    set dstaddr "RTU_POOL_10.1.2.0/24"
    set service "MODBUS_TCP"
    set action deny
    set logtraffic all
  next

Detection: Nozomi Networks passive monitoring generates an alert for: FC08 from any source; FC05/FC16 outside operational hours; Modbus traffic from any IP other than 10.1.1.10; FC43 (device enumeration preceding targeted attack); rapid sequential writes to the same register address (coil cycling indicating manipulation).

Solved Problem: IEC 62443 Security Level Assessment for Power Substation

A utility company must assess the Security Level achieved by their 138kV transmission substation. The substation uses: SEL-421 protection relays (DNP3 over Ethernet, no SAv5), ABB RTU500 SCADA gateway (IEC 104, no authentication), Cisco IE3400 switch with VLAN segmentation (no 802.1X), and a T-Mobile cellular backup link (no VPN). Determine the achieved SL and the gap to SL-2.

Solution: IEC 62443-3-3 Security Level assessment against SR (Security Requirement) families:

Current State Analysis:

SR 1.1 – Human User Identification and Authentication: FAILED. DNP3 and IEC 104 have no user authentication; any device can send commands. Current SL: SL-0.

SR 1.3 – Account Management: FAILED. No per-user accounts on RTU or protection relays. Current SL: SL-0.

SR 2.1 – Authorization Enforcement: FAILED. All Modbus/DNP3/IEC104 clients have read+write access; no role-based restriction. Current SL: SL-0.

SR 3.1 – Communication Integrity: FAILED. DNP3 without SAv5 and IEC 104 without IEC 62351-5 have no message authentication. Current SL: SL-0.

SR 3.3 – Security Functionality Verification: PARTIAL. Physical access to relays allows manual verification. No automated integrity check. Current SL: SL-1.

SR 5.1 – Network Segmentation: PARTIAL. VLANs exist but without 802.1X; VLAN spoofing is possible. Current SL: SL-1.

SR 5.2 – Zone Boundary Protection: FAILED. Cellular backup link with no VPN provides an unauthenticated path to the OT network. Current SL: SL-0.

Achieved Overall SL: SL-0 to SL-1 (below SL-2 target).

Gaps to SL-2 and Remediation:

  1. Enable DNP3 SAv5 on SEL-421 relays (SEL firmware supports SAv5 from version 3.0): provides HMAC message authentication.

  2. Upgrade ABB RTU500 to support IEC 62351-5 (authenticated IEC 104), or deploy a protocol proxy (Schweitzer Engineering SEL-3620) that adds authentication.

  3. Enable 802.1X on Cisco IE3400 with MAB for relays that cannot support 802.1X supplicant.

  4. Deploy IPsec VPN on T-Mobile cellular link (Cisco ASR 901 with FlexVPN, AES-256-GCM, IKEv2 with certificate authentication).

  5. Cost-benefit: Implementation cost is approximately $180K; the substation supports 40,000 customers. NERC CIP-005 also mandates these controls for transmission substations.

Solved Problem: CRASHOVERRIDE GOOSE Attack Defense

The CRASHOVERRIDE malware sent malicious GOOSE (Generic Object Oriented Substation Event) messages on an IEC 61850 station bus to trip circuit breakers. Design a protection relay configuration and network security control that detects and blocks unauthorized GOOSE messages without disrupting legitimate protection operations.

Solution: GOOSE attack characteristics: GOOSE messages are multicast (Ethernet layer 2, no IP), sent to the multicast MAC 01:0C:CD:01:XX:XX, with no authentication in IEC 61850 Ed.1/Ed.2. The attacker sends CB_OFF (circuit breaker open) GOOSE messages with high priority (StNum=1, SqNum=0, T=current time) that protection relays accept as legitimate.

Defense architecture:

Layer 1 – GOOSE subscription whitelist per relay: Configure each protection relay (SEL-451, GE Multilin L90) to subscribe to GOOSE messages only from specific publisher MAC addresses:

# SEL-451 Relay: GOOSE Subscription Configuration
# Only accept GOOSE from the specific Bus Protection IED (L90):
GSE_SUB 1:
  APPID = 0x0001
  SrcMAC = 00:A0:7A:12:34:56  # L90 IED MAC address
  GoCBRef = "L90LD0/LLN0$GO$GGIO_CB_Status"
  AllowTrip = YES
# Any GOOSE from other MAC address is ignored

Layer 2 – GOOSE rate limiting and anomaly detection: Deploy a managed switch (GE Multilin D400 or ABB FOX-U) with GOOSE traffic inspection. Configure: maximum 5 GOOSE messages per second per APPID (legitimate protection GOOSE during a fault: \(<\)3 per second). More than 5 GOOSE/second from any source: switch drops excess and generates SNMP trap. An attacker’s GOOSE flood (CRASHOVERRIDE sent hundreds per second) triggers the rate limiter.

Layer 3 – IEC 61850 Ed.2 GOOSE Authentication (future): IEC 62351-6 defines HMAC authentication for GOOSE using AES-128-GMAC appended to the GOOSE frame. This requires: hardware crypto accelerator in the IED (most modern relays support it), key management infrastructure for substation (pairwise keys between publishers and subscribers), and a key update procedure that avoids gaps in protection during key rotation.

Layer 4 – Behavioral baseline anomaly: Nozomi Networks Guardian baseline: CB_OFF GOOSE messages are expected only during fault conditions (correlates with relay analog inputs showing overcurrent, overvoltage, or differential current). A CB_OFF GOOSE with no correlated analog fault event = anomaly alert within 500ms.

docs.title: 31.18 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: ICS and SCADA security entered a period of heightened national security focus between 2023 and 2025, driven by Chinese state-sponsored intrusions into critical infrastructure and NIST’s updated OT security guidance.

docs.title: 31.18.1 CISA ICS-CERT Advisories 2023–2024 — Siemens and Rockwell Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
CISA published a significant volume of ICS-CERT advisories targeting major PLC vendors:

Siemens SIMATIC S7-1500 / SIMATIC S7-1200 (2023–2024):

  • CVE-2023-28831 (CVSS 9.8): Heap buffer overflow in the SIMATIC S7-1500 OPC UA server allows unauthenticated remote code execution. Affected versions: V3.0.0 to V3.0.1. Siemens Security Advisory SSA-892048 (July 2023) recommended firmware update to V3.0.2.

  • CVE-2023-44318 (CVSS 6.5): Web server on SIMATIC S7-1200 and S7-1500 CPUs allows directory traversal to read arbitrary files from the PLC filesystem, including private key material if TLS certificates are stored on the PLC flash.

  • SIMATIC S7 PROFINET discovery: Multiple 2024 advisories (SSA-711928, SSA-953287) documented that PROFINET Discovery and Configuration Protocol (DCP) enabled unauthenticated device renaming and IP address modification, effectively enabling denial-of-service against any SIMATIC device on the PROFINET segment.

Rockwell Automation ControlLogix (2023):

  • CVE-2023-3595 (CVSS 9.8) and CVE-2023-3596: Remote code execution vulnerabilities in Allen-Bradley ControlLogix EtherNet/IP communication module (1756-EN2T series). Attackers with network access to the EtherNet/IP port could execute arbitrary code in the communication module’s firmware, modifying ladder logic execution without the engineering workstation detecting the change. CISA ICSA-23-221-01 (August 2023) identified active exploitation in the wild.

  • Impact: ControlLogix is deployed in approximately 40% of US petrochemical and power generation facilities. The vulnerability’s high CVSS and active exploitation prompted immediate patch guidance from CISA.

Warning: CVE-2023-3595 was discovered by Dragos researchers as part of an investigation into active ICS threat group activity. The vulnerability had been exploited in the wild before public disclosure. Unpatched ControlLogix 1756-EN2T modules connected to networks accessible from corporate IT segments are a critical exposure.

docs.title: 31.18.2 Volt Typhoon — Chinese APT Targeting Critical Infrastructure Hardware
docs.text:
CISA, NSA, and FBI issued a joint Cybersecurity Advisory (AA23-144A, May 2023) on Volt Typhoon (also tracked as Bronze Silhouette), a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor conducting long-term persistent access to US critical infrastructure OT networks:

  • Target sectors: Communications, energy, transportation, and water and wastewater systems. Particular focus on pre-positioning within OT networks that could cause disruption in a Taiwan conflict scenario.

  • Living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques: Volt Typhoon avoided malware by using legitimate system administration tools (wmic, ntdsutil, netsh, PowerShell) to enumerate OT networks, avoiding detection by signature-based IDS. Hardware devices targeted included:

    • Cisco and Fortinet edge routers (initial access, VPN credential harvesting)

    • SCADA historian servers (OPC DA data exfiltration)

    • Operational Technology-specific hardware: Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories (SEL) protective relays accessed via DNP3 after lateral movement from IT to OT networks

  • Hardware-targeted persistence: In some intrusions, Volt Typhoon operators installed firmware modifications on Cisco RV320/325 small business routers (CVE-2019-1653) to maintain persistent covert access to operational technology sites even after corporate network cleanup.

  • Duration: CISA assessed that Volt Typhoon had been present in some victim networks for 5 years prior to detection.

docs.title: 31.18.3 NIST SP 800-82 Revision 3 — Updated OT Security Guide (2023)
docs.text:
NIST Special Publication 800-82 Revision 3, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security” (September 2023) substantially updated the OT security framework:

  • Zero Trust Architecture for OT: SP 800-82r3 introduces ZTA concepts for OT environments, acknowledging that traditional Purdue Model perimeter-based security is insufficient against advanced persistent threats that have already bridged the IT/OT air gap. Micro-segmentation of OT device communications is recommended.

  • Hardware security controls for legacy PLCs: New Section 6.2.5 addresses compensating controls for PLCs with no native authentication (Modbus RTU, DNP3 without SAv5), including unidirectional security gateways (Waterfall Security, OWL Cyber Defense) as hardware-enforced data-diode solutions.

  • Firmware integrity for ICS: SP 800-82r3 recommends firmware signing and verification for all new ICS hardware procurement, aligned with NIST SP 800-193 Platform Firmware Resilience guidelines. Legacy devices without secure boot should be compensated with network-level anomaly detection.

docs.title: 31.18.4 IEC 62443-3-3 SL-3 Hardware Requirements (2023 Update)
docs.text:
IEC 62443-3-3 (System Security Requirements and Security Levels), 2023 amendment, clarified Security Level 3 (SL-3) hardware requirements for industrial control systems defending against sophisticated adversaries (nation-state level threats):

Table 31.8. IEC 62443-3-3 SL-3 Hardware-Specific Requirements (2023) Security Requirement SL-3 Specification Hardware Implementation SR 1.1 Human Auth Hardware multi-factor authentication Smart card + PIN for all engineering access SR 3.1 Communication Integrity AES-128-CMAC per message with replay prevention DNP3 SAv5 or IEC 62351-5 hardware authenticator SR 3.8 Session Integrity All sessions authenticated and integrity protected TLS 1.3 hardware offload at SCADA gateway SR 5.2 Zone Boundary Hardware-enforced unidirectional flow between zones Data diode for historian connections SR 7.6 Network / Security Config Settings Physical lockout of network configuration Hardware key switch on switch/router front panel SR 7.8 Control System Component Inventory Automated hardware inventory with anomaly detection Passive network tap + hardware fingerprinting

docs.title: 31.18.5 Dragos Year in Review 2023 — ICS Threat Groups Targeting Hardware
docs.text:
Dragos’s 2023 Year in Review report identified 21 active threat groups targeting industrial control systems. Hardware-focused activities included:

  • CHERNOVITE (Industroyer2): Continued development of ICS-specific malware targeting Siemens SIMATIC and ABB RTU hardware via IEC 104 and IEC 61850 protocols. CHERNOVITE demonstrated capability to issue direct IED (Intelligent Electronic Device) control commands bypassing the SCADA master.

  • BENTONITE: Targeted oil and gas upstream equipment – Emerson DeltaV DCS, Honeywell Experion PKS – with initial access through VPN gateway compromise, followed by OPC-UA enumeration to identify controllable hardware assets.

  • Hardware asset discovery: Multiple threat groups were observed using Shodan, ZoomEye, and active scanning to identify internet-exposed OT hardware prior to targeted intrusions. Exposed assets include: Siemens S7-300/400 PLCs with S7comm accessible on TCP/102 (approximately 4,200 globally Internet-exposed as of Q4 2023).

docs.title: 31.18.6 OT Hardware Security — Claroty and Nozomi Hardware Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Passive OT asset visibility platforms evolved to include hardware-level fingerprinting:

Claroty xDome (2023–2024):

  • Protocol-based fingerprinting: passive analysis of PROFINET DCP, BACnet Who-Is/I-Am, DNP3 Data Link Layer identify hardware vendor and model without active scanning. Model confidence score \(>95\%\) for 847 OT device types.

  • Firmware version extraction: Claroty passively extracts firmware version strings from unencrypted protocol responses (Modbus FC43 Device Identification, EtherNet/IP Identity Object Attribute 3), enabling CVE correlation without credentialed access.

Nozomi Networks Guardian (2024):

  • ML-based hardware anomaly detection: trained on 200+ million OT device communication baseline samples. Detects hardware replacement attacks (physical swap of a PLC with a Trojanised unit) by identifying deviations in process variable timing patterns and protocol microsecond-timing signatures unique to specific hardware variants.

  • Vantage platform: cloud-based aggregation of Guardian sensor telemetry enables cross-site hardware anomaly correlation – if a firmware upgrade anomaly is detected at one site, similar patterns at peer sites generate pre-emptive alerts.

docs.title: 31.19 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. A Siemens S7-300 PLC (CPU 315-2 DP) controlling a water pump station has no security features beyond a physical key switch. The plant manager asks for an upgrade path to IEC 62443-3-3 SL-2 compliance without replacing the PLC hardware. Describe the compensating controls that can achieve SL-2 equivalent protection at the network and physical layer, and identify which SL-2 requirements cannot be met without hardware replacement.

  2. Modbus TCP is used on an OT network with no function code restrictions. An attacker on a compromised engineering workstation sends FC08 (Diagnostics, sub-function 01 – Restart Communications Option) to all 24 RTUs simultaneously. Describe the physical impact on the process, the detection capability of each OT monitoring platform (Dragos, Claroty, Nozomi), and the network-level control that would have blocked this command.

  3. The TRITON malware exploited the Triconex Tricon Model 3008 via the TriStation 1131 protocol. The Triconex implements Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) with 2-of-3 voting. Explain why the TMR architecture failed to prevent the TRITON attack from disabling the SIS (hint: consider what happens when TRITON’s buggy code causes two of three CPUs to enter fail-safe state simultaneously), and propose a defense that uses the TMR architecture itself as a detection mechanism.

  4. A CRASHOVERRIDE-style attack targets a 230kV substation using unauthorized IEC 60870-5-104 commands sent from a compromised engineering workstation. The substation has 8 RTUs controlling transformer tap changers and 12 RTUs controlling feeder circuit breakers. Design an incident response playbook for the first 15 minutes after detection, specifying: isolation steps that preserve substation stability, forensic data collection from network TAPs, and the NERC CIP incident reporting timeline requirements.

  5. Allen-Bradley ControlLogix 5580 (1756-L85E) implements CIP Security for EtherNet/IP using DTLS 1.2 for Class 1 (implicit) messaging. A plant engineer claims that the DTLS handshake adds 50ms latency, making it unacceptable for a PLC I/O scan cycle of 10ms. Evaluate this claim: calculate the actual DTLS handshake overhead for a pre-established session versus a new session establishment, and propose the Session ID resumption configuration that eliminates per-packet handshake overhead.

  6. A data diode (Waterfall Security Unidirectional Security Gateway) is deployed between the OT historian (Levels 2/3) and the enterprise network (Level 4). The OT team needs to send firmware updates from Level 4 to Level 2 PLCs. Explain why a strict data diode architecture cannot support this requirement, and design a secure alternative that maintains the security properties of the OT network while enabling controlled firmware distribution.

  7. The Honeywell Safety Manager (HSM) post-TRITON security update requires firmware to be cryptographically signed before installation. Describe the complete key management architecture for a petrochemical plant with 5 HSM controllers: how the signing keys are generated and stored (HSM vendor, plant, or end user?), the signing ceremony process, the key distribution to controllers, and the revocation procedure if the signing key is compromised.

  8. IEC 62351-6 defines optional authentication for IEC 61850 GOOSE messages using AES-128-GMAC. A protection relay engineer argues that implementing GOOSE authentication will cause protection operations to exceed the allowable operating time of 100ms specified in IEC 61850-5 for Class P3 (Performance Level 3). Evaluate this claim by calculating the GMAC computation latency for a 200-byte GOOSE frame on an Arm Cortex-M7 running at 216 MHz (with hardware AES acceleration), and determine whether authentication is feasible within the timing constraint.

  9. A SCADA historian (OSIsoft PI Server) at Level 3 must push process data to an enterprise data lake (Level 4) in real time for machine learning model training. The security team requires a data diode; the OT team requires bi-directional PI replication. Research and evaluate two architectures that satisfy both requirements: (1) Waterfall Secure Bypass with time-limited supervised channel, and (2) OSIsoft PI Replication over data diode with event queuing. Compare their security properties and failure modes.

  10. MITRE ATT&CK ICS technique T0857 (System Firmware) involves an attacker installing malicious firmware on an industrial PC running a SCADA HMI (Windows 10 LTSC 2019, Intel Core i5-8500). Describe: the attack vector (UEFI firmware vulnerability or bootkit), the persistence mechanism, the detection challenge compared to SCADA application-layer attacks, and the hardware-based defense using Intel Boot Guard + Intel TXT measured boot.

  11. A natural gas pipeline SCADA system uses DNP3 over satellite (VSAT) links to communicate with compressor station RTUs at 9600 baud. The RTU engineer reports that enabling DNP3 SAv5 (Secure Authentication version 5) increases the per-command overhead from 24 bytes to 156 bytes (due to HMAC and challenge messages). Calculate the impact on communication latency and throughput at 9600 baud, and propose an optimization that maintains SAv5 security while minimizing bandwidth overhead.

  12. After the 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack (which compromised IT systems, not OT systems directly), the company preemptively shut down OT systems for 6 days. Design a network architecture and detection system that would allow an operator to: (1) confirm that OT systems are not compromised even if IT systems are, (2) continue OT operations during an IT network compromise, and (3) safely resume IT/OT connectivity after IT remediation. Specify the hardware components (firewalls, data diodes, monitoring) and detection mechanisms for each goal.

docs.title: Chapter 32: Biometric Hardware Security
docs.text: Biometric authentication systems embed cryptographic-grade identity verification directly into silicon, fusing sensor physics, signal processing, and secure element architectures into a single attack surface that spans both the physical and digital worlds. Unlike password-based systems, a compromise of biometric data is permanent: a user cannot change their fingerprint. This chapter examines the hardware architectures, implementation details, attack surfaces, and defences for modern biometric systems deployed in consumer devices, border control, and enterprise access control.

docs.title: 32.1 Biometric System Architecture
docs.text:
A biometric system comprises four functional stages executed in sequence: data capture, feature extraction, template comparison, and access decision. Each stage introduces unique hardware security requirements.

Figure 32.1. Biometric system pipeline: sensor acquisition, liveness detection (PAD), feature extraction, TEE-isolated matching, and decision logic.

docs.title: 32.2.1 Capacitive Sensors
docs.text:
Apple Touch ID Generation 1 uses the AuthenTec AE2 capacitive array: 88x88 pixels at 500 dpi, thin-film passivation layer, scan frequency 62.5 kHz, connected to the A7 SoC via SPI at 8 MHz. The sensor communicates exclusively with the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP) over an encrypted channel; the Application Processor never sees raw minutiae or image data.

Touch ID Generation 2 (iPhone 6 / 6 Plus) increased resolution to 96x96 pixels and added a second-generation sapphire cover lens, improving wet-finger performance. Maximum template storage: 5 fingerprints, each encoded as a 512-byte AES-256-GCM encrypted blob inside the Secure Enclave’s EEPROM partition.

Synaptics ClearPad FS7600: 256x360 pixel active capacitive array, SentryPoint security subsystem running on an ARM Cortex-M4F at 48 MHz, on-chip AES-128 encryption, anti-spoof liveness detection based on perspiration analysis at 10 Hz frame rate, SPI interface at 8 MHz.

docs.title: 32.2.2 Optical Under-Display Sensors
docs.text:
Goodix GD3238 (2019): 128x96 pixel CMOS image sensor optimised for OLED displays, 1080 dpi effective resolution, PDAF autofocus assist, I2C/SPI dual interface, operating voltage 1.8 V / 3.3 V, area 7.9 mm \(\times\) 5.0 mm.

Goodix GD3288 (2021): 192x192 pixel, 1080 dpi, integrated DSP running a 3-layer CNN for minutiae extraction, 10 ms acquisition-to-result latency, SPI 48 MHz, compatible with Samsung OLED panels at up to 120 Hz refresh rate.

docs.title: 32.2.3 Ultrasonic PMUT Sensors
docs.text:
Qualcomm 3D Sonic QFS1080 (Snapdragon Fingerprint 3D Sonic): Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer (PMUT) array, operating frequency 20 MHz, fabricated on TSMC 28 nm CMOS process, 64x172 element array, active area 8.0 mm \(\times\) 4.0 mm, acoustic signal propagates through the display glass, sub-epidermis imaging captures internal ridge structure (sub-dermis layer at 0.3 mm depth), defeating 2D spoofs and many silicone molds.

Qualcomm QFS2530 (3D Sonic Max, 2020): active area enlarged to 20 mm \(\times\) 30 mm (8\(\times\) larger than QFS1080), supporting two-finger simultaneous capture, 28 nm CMOS, ultrasound frequency 25 MHz, Z-axis resolution 10 microns, deployable under 1.2 mm glass or OLED panels. Integrated in Snapdragon 865 and 888 devices.

# QFS1080 register map (SPI, 8-bit address space)
0x00  CHIP_ID          RO  0x10    (silicon revision)
0x01  SOFT_RESET       WO  bit[0] = 1 triggers reset
0x10  SCAN_MODE        RW  0x00 = fingerprint, 0x01 = nav
0x11  SCAN_FREQ        RW  0x00 = 20 MHz, 0x01 = 25 MHz
0x20  IMAGE_DATA[N]    RO  64 * 172 bytes raw acoustic frame
0x30  RESULT_SCORE     RO  match score [0..1000] (TEE-visible only)
0x40  LIVENESS_STATUS  RO  0x01 = live, 0x00 = spoof detected

docs.title: 32.2.4 Fingerprint Matching Algorithms
docs.text:
NIST BOZORTH3 (from NBIS v5.0.0): landmark-based minutiae matching, graph-based comparison using inter-minutiae distance and angle triplets, ANSI/NIST ITL 1-2011 data format (Type-9 record), open source under public domain.

DeepPrint (Michigan State University, 2019): ResNet-50 backbone trained on 650k fingerprints, outputs 192-dimensional fixed-length embedding, cosine similarity matching, EER 0.1% on FVC2004, inference at 12 ms on Snapdragon 855 DSP.

# BOZORTH3 invocation (NIST NBIS v5.0.0)
$ mindtct -m1 finger.pgm finger_minutiae
$ bozorth3 -A outfmt=spscores probe.xyt gallery.xyt
# Output: integer score [0..1000]; authentication threshold typically 40
# Identification mode (1:N)
$ bozorth3 -A outfmt=spscores probe.xyt gallery_dir/*.xyt | sort -rn | head -1

docs.title: 32.3.1 Apple Face ID TrueDepth Camera System
docs.text:
Apple Face ID (iPhone X, 2017) TrueDepth module hardware components:

  • Dot Projector: 30,000 infrared VCSEL (Vertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting Laser) dots at 940 nm wavelength; diffractive optical element (DOE) distributes the pattern across the face surface for structured-light depth reconstruction.

  • Infrared Camera: 1280x960 pixel InGaAs CMOS array, 30 fps capture rate, images the deformed dot pattern for stereo depth map computation.

  • Flood Illuminator: broadfield 940 nm IR LED array for ambient illumination compensation and initial face detection trigger.

  • A11 Bionic Neural Engine: 2-core ML processor, 600 GOPS, executes face detection, depth map processing, and feature encoding at enrol and match time.

  • Secure Enclave (SEP T1): ARM TrustZone-based isolated processor, AES-256 hardware accelerator, SHA-2 accelerator, TRNG, 4 MB internal SRAM; stores AES-256-GCM encrypted face template.

Face ID template adaptation: after each successful match, the model is incrementally updated (up to 4 revisions retained) to accommodate appearance changes such as aging, glasses, and beard growth. If match score drops below EER threshold, the template is not updated, preventing a gradual drift attack.

docs.title: 32.3.2 Iris Recognition – Daugman IrisCode
docs.text:
John Daugman’s IrisCode (Cambridge, 1994, updated 2009): Gabor wavelet decomposition of the normalised iris image (rubber-sheet model: 64 rows \(\times\) 512 columns polar grid), each complex Gabor coefficient binarised to 2 bits (sign of real, sign of imaginary), yielding a 2048-bit binary code stored in 256 bytes.

Matching uses normalised Hamming distance:

\[d_H = \frac{\| (C_A \oplus C_B) \wedge M_A \wedge M_B \|} {\| M_A \wedge M_B \|}\]

where \(M_A, M_B\) are masking bitmaps excluding eyelid occlusion. Authentication threshold: \(d_H \leq 0.32\). False match probability at this threshold: \(\approx 10^{-11}\), derived from the binomial distribution over 2048 independent coin-flip bits.

docs.title: 32.4 Presentation Attack Detection (PAD) and Liveness
docs.text:
ISO 30107-3 defines the PAD evaluation methodology with two primary metrics:

  • BPCER: Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate (genuine user rejected as attack)

  • APCER: Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (attack accepted as genuine)

docs.title: 32.4.1 Fingerprint PAD Techniques
docs.text:
Texture analysis (software PAD): Local Binary Pattern (LBP) histograms, 256-bin computed on 8x8 pixel blocks, SVM classifier trained on LivDet-2021 dataset (22,000 samples, 12 sensor types); APCER \(< 3\%\) against gelatin spoofs.

Perspiration analysis (hardware PAD): Genuine fingers exhibit 1–5% contrast variation at 62.5 Hz due to sweat pore activity; artificial materials show static reflectance. Synaptics FS7600 implements this at hardware level via 10-Hz multi-frame differential capture.

3D acoustic structure (hardware PAD): QFS1080/2530 ultrasonic sensors image sub-dermal layers (sweat ducts, dermal papillae). Silicone and gelatin artifacts show different acoustic impedance: \(Z_{gel} \approx 1.42\) MRayl vs. \(Z_{skin} \approx 1.70\) MRayl at 20 MHz. Combined surface + sub-surface texture achieves APCER \(< 0.1\%\) against silicone molds.

docs.title: 32.4.2 Face Anti-Spoofing
docs.text:
Structured-light depth map: Apple Face ID structured-light provides a 3D point cloud; a printed photograph has zero Z-variance across the entire face region, triggering the flat-surface rejection test built into the Neural Engine inference pipeline.

Micro-texture classification: ResNet-18 binary classifier (live vs. spoof) trained on NUAA + MSU-MFSD datasets, APCER 0.5% and BPCER 0.5%, inference latency 8 ms on A14 Neural Engine.

Temporal blink detection: Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR) threshold: EAR drop \(> 0.2\) within a 200 ms window; replay attacks on flat screens fail because the video frame rate cannot reproduce the randomised challenge-response blink timing.

Challenge-response: IDEMIA IDAFace issues randomised gaze direction, head pose, or lip-movement prompts at runtime. The biometric sensor captures the response and verifies 3D head motion consistency with the prompt before accepting the match.

docs.title: 32.5 Cancelable Biometrics and Template Protection
docs.text:
A cancelable biometric transform \(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{f}, k)\) is applied to raw features \(\mathbf{f}\) before storage; only the transformed template \(\mathbf{f}' = \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{f}, k)\) is stored. Revocation replaces key \(k\) with a new \(k'\).

Figure 32.2. Cancelable biometric template protection: revocable transform with secure storage and TEE-isolated comparison. Revocation regenerates key \(k'\).

docs.title: 32.5.1 BioHashing
docs.text:
BioHashing (Jin, Ling, Goh, 2004): given feature vector \(\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^N\) and a user-specific random seed \(s\), generate orthonormal random matrix \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times L}\) via PRNG seeded with \(s\) and Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation, then binarise: \(h_i = 1\) if \((\mathbf{f}^T \mathbf{r}_i) > 0\), else \(h_i = 0\).

import numpy as np

def biohash(feature_vec, seed, L=512):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    R   = rng.randn(len(feature_vec), L)
    R, _ = np.linalg.qr(R)          # Gram-Schmidt via QR decomp.
    h   = feature_vec @ R
    return (h > 0).astype(np.uint8) # L-bit BioHash

# Enrolment
template = biohash(fp_embedding, token_seed, L=512)

# Revocation: generate new seed from TRNG and re-enrol
new_template = biohash(fp_embedding, new_seed, L=512)

docs.title: 32.5.2 Fuzzy Vault and Secure Sketch
docs.text:
Fuzzy Vault (Juels & Sudan, 2002): locks secret \(K\) (e.g., AES-256 key) with biometric set \(A\) (minutiae coordinates). Polynomial \(p(x)\) encodes \(K\) as coefficients; vault \(V = \{(a_i, p(a_i)) : a_i \in A\} \cup \{\text{chaff}\}\). Unlocking requires query set \(B\) with \(|A \cap B| \geq t\) (error-correction threshold).

Secure Sketch (Dodis et al., 2004): for bit strings with Hamming noise, sketch \(SS(w) = w \oplus \text{BCH\_encode}(w)\). Recovery: \(\hat{w} = \text{BCH\_decode}(w' \oplus SS(w))\) when \(d_H(w, w') \leq t\) (BCH correction capability).

docs.title: 32.6.1 Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)
docs.text:
ARM TrustZone partitions the processor into Normal World and Secure World (TEE). On Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, the Qualcomm Trusted Execution Environment (QTEE) runs on a dedicated Cortex-A55 core at 300 MHz in the Secure World. Biometric templates are stored as AES-256-GCM encrypted blobs in the TEE’s RPMB (Replay Protected Memory Block) partition on UFS 3.1 storage.

RPMB authentication uses HMAC-SHA-256 with a device-unique key fused into OTP eFUSE at manufacturing time; each RPMB read/write carries a monotonic counter in the MAC input, preventing replay attacks even if the NAND flash is cloned.

docs.title: 32.6.2 Secure Element (SE)
docs.text:
Apple Secure Enclave Processor (SEP, present from A7 onwards): embedded ARC processor running sepOS, hardware AES engine, SHA-2 engine, TRNG, 4 MB internal SRAM. Communication with the Application Processor occurs only via a mailbox register; no DMA path exists between Application Processor memory and SEP SRAM. Face ID and Touch ID templates are encrypted with a SEP-derived 256-bit key that never leaves the SEP silicon boundary.

Samsung Knox: embedded Secure Element (Infineon SLE97144, EAL5+ certified) stores template encryption keys. Biometric data is AES-256 encrypted and stored in TrustZone Trusted Storage (TZDRAM), key management handled by Knox Vault SE.

docs.title: 32.10 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: Hamming Distance Authentication Decision

An iris recognition system stores a 2048-bit IrisCode template. During an authentication attempt, 620 bits of the query code differ from the stored template. Of the 2048 bits, 200 bits are masked (eyelid occlusion) in both templates. Determine whether the user should be authenticated (threshold \(d_H \leq 0.32\)) and compute the Hamming distance.

Solution: Step 1: Effective bit count. Masked bits excluded from comparison: \(N_{mask} = 200\). Effective bits: \(N_{eff} = 2048 - 200 = 1848\).

Step 2: Differing bits in unmasked region. Assuming all 620 differing bits fall in the unmasked region (worst case for the system): \(\delta = 620\).

Step 3: Normalised Hamming distance.

\[d_H = \frac{\delta}{N_{eff}} = \frac{620}{1848} \approx 0.335\]

Step 4: Authentication decision. Threshold \(d_H \leq 0.32\). Since \(0.335 > 0.32\), the user is REJECTED.

Step 5: Physical interpretation. The false match probability at \(d_H = 0.32\) is \(\approx 10^{-11}\) (one in 100 billion random IrisCode pairs). A distance of 0.335 indicates insufficient overlap; this is consistent with a different individual or poor image quality (e.g., contact lens, dilation mismatch).

Solved Problem: BioHashing Revocation Security Analysis

A fingerprint system uses BioHashing with \(L=512\) output bits and a user-specific 128-bit random token. An attacker obtains the stored BioHash but does not know the token. (a) Can the attacker recover the original fingerprint features? (b) What is the brute-force security level against token search? (c) Describe the revocation procedure.

Solution: (a) Feature recovery: The BioHash \(\mathbf{h} = \text{sign}(\mathbf{f}^T \mathbf{R})\) applies a sign function after a random projection. Even with known \(\mathbf{R}\) (derivable if the attacker knew the token), recovering \(\mathbf{f}\) from 512 binary sign bits requires solving a system of 512 half-space inequalities in \(\mathbb{R}^{192}\) (for a 192-dimensional DeepPrint embedding). This is an NP-hard phase-recovery problem in the random projection setting. Conclusion: No practical recovery is possible.

(b) Brute-force token search: Token space: \(|\mathcal{K}| = 2^{128}\). Per-token cost: PRNG(192\(\times\)512) + QR decomposition + dot-product \(\approx 10^5\) operations. Total: \(2^{128} \times 10^5 \approx 2^{145}\) operations. At \(10^{15}\) operations/second: \(2^{145}/2^{50} = 2^{95}\) seconds. Age of the universe \(\approx 2^{59}\) seconds. Security level: 128-bit, computationally infeasible.

(c) Revocation procedure:

  1. Detect compromise event (breach notification or user request).

  2. Generate new random token \(k'\) via hardware TRNG (NIST SP 800-90B compliant).

  3. Re-enrol: capture fresh biometric sample, compute \(\mathbf{h}' = \text{BioHash}(\mathbf{f}, k')\).

  4. Overwrite the stored template with \(\mathbf{h}'\) in SE/TEE RPMB.

  5. Securely erase old token \(k\) from all storage (zero-fill + RPMB counter increment).

The old BioHash \(\mathbf{h}\) is now useless because all future comparisons use \(k'\).

Solved Problem: Ultrasonic Spoof Detection via Acoustic Impedance

The QFS1080 PMUT sensor operates at 20 MHz. Genuine skin has acoustic impedance \(Z_{skin} = 1.70\) MRayl. A silicone spoof has \(Z_{spoof} = 1.42\) MRayl. The PMUT membrane has \(Z_{mem} = 4.0\) MRayl. Calculate the reflection coefficient at the membrane-to-finger interface for both genuine and spoof, and assess whether the 12-bit ADC can distinguish them.

Solution: Step 1: Reflection coefficient formula.

\[\Gamma = \frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\]

Step 2: Genuine skin.

\[\Gamma_{skin} = \frac{1.70 - 4.0}{1.70 + 4.0} = \frac{-2.30}{5.70} = -0.4035\]

Step 3: Silicone spoof.

\[\Gamma_{spoof} = \frac{1.42 - 4.0}{1.42 + 4.0} = \frac{-2.58}{5.42} = -0.4760\]

Step 4: Reflected power difference. \(|\Gamma_{skin}|^2 = 0.1628\); \(|\Gamma_{spoof}|^2 = 0.2266\). Power difference: \(\Delta P = 0.0638\) (6.38% of incident power).

Step 5: ADC resolution check. 12-bit ADC: \(2^{12} = 4096\) levels over full scale. Minimum detectable difference: \(100\%/4096 = 0.024\%\). A 6.38% power difference is \(6.38/0.024 \approx 266\) ADC counts – highly resolvable. Additionally, secondary sub-dermal echoes (sweat ducts at 0.1–0.3 mm depth) appear in genuine fingers and are absent in silicone, providing a second independent detection channel. Conclusion: Reliable spoof detection is achievable.

Solved Problem: FAR/FRR Operating Point and EER Estimation

A face recognition system has three measured operating points: \(\tau = 0.65\): FAR = 0.50%, FRR = 2.0%; \(\tau = 0.70\): FAR = 0.10%, FRR = 5.0%; \(\tau = 0.75\): FAR = 0.01%, FRR = 12.0%.

(a) A high-security data center requires FAR \(< 0.1\%\) and FRR \(< 10\%\). Choose the threshold. (b) An airport fast-lane requires FAR \(< 1\%\) and FRR \(< 3\%\). Choose the threshold. (c) Estimate the EER and the corresponding threshold using linear interpolation.

Solution: (a) Data center: \(\tau = 0.70\): FAR = 0.10% (satisfies \(\leq 0.1\%\)), FRR = 5.0% (satisfies \(< 10\%\)). \(\tau = 0.75\): FRR = 12% – fails. Use \(\tau = 0.70\).

(b) Airport fast-lane: \(\tau = 0.65\): FAR = 0.50% (\(< 1\%\), satisfies), FRR = 2.0% (\(< 3\%\), satisfies). \(\tau = 0.70\): FRR = 5.0% – fails. Use \(\tau = 0.65\).

(c) EER estimation: At \(\tau = 0.65\): FAR (0.50%) \(<\) FRR (2.0%), so EER lies below \(\tau = 0.65\). Parameterise below this point assuming linear behaviour with slope derived from the data: From \(\tau = 0.65\) to \(\tau = 0.70\): \(\Delta\)FAR \(= -0.40\%\), \(\Delta\)FRR \(= +3.0\%\) per \(\Delta\tau = 0.05\). Rate: FAR changes \(-8\%\)/unit, FRR changes \(+60\%\)/unit. Extrapolating below \(\tau = 0.65\): FAR(\(\tau\)) \(\approx 0.50 + 8(0.65 - \tau)\), FRR(\(\tau\)) \(\approx 2.0 - 60(0.65 - \tau)\). Setting FAR = FRR: \(0.50 + 8\delta = 2.0 - 60\delta \Rightarrow 68\delta = 1.50 \Rightarrow \delta = 0.022\). EER threshold: \(\tau_{EER} \approx 0.65 - 0.022 = 0.628\). EER value: \(\approx 0.50 + 8 \times 0.022 = 0.676\%\). EER \(\approx 0.68\%\) at \(\tau \approx 0.63\).

docs.title: 32.11 Standards
docs.text:
• ISO/IEC 19794: Biometric data interchange formats – Part 2: Finger minutiae data, Part 4: Finger image data, Part 5: Face image data, Part 6: Iris image data.

  • ISO/IEC 30107-3: Presentation Attack Detection – Part 3: Testing and reporting (APCER and BPCER evaluation methodology).

  • NIST SP 800-76-2: Biometric Specifications for Personal Identity Verification; fingerprint image quality (NFIQ 2.0 score 0–100).

  • ANSI/NIST ITL 1-2011 (NIST SP 500-290): Data Format for the Interchange of Fingerprint, Facial, and Scar/Mark/Tattoo Information. Type-9 record defines minutiae data structure.

  • IEEE 2410-2021: Standard for Biometric Open Protocol; RESTful API for biometric system interoperability.

  • FIDO2 / WebAuthn W3C Recommendation: FIDO2 CTAP2 protocol enables biometric authenticators (platform or roaming) to replace passwords; biometric match occurs on-device, cryptographic assertion is sent to relying party.

  • FIDO UAF 1.1: Universal Authentication Framework for mobile biometrics; used by Samsung Pass, Qualcomm Snapdragon Sense ID.

  • Common Criteria PP-0117: Biometric Verification Mechanisms Protection Profile; EAL4+ certification for Touch ID and Windows Hello hardware.

  • GDPR Article 9: Biometric data classified as special-category personal data in the European Union, requiring explicit consent and data minimisation.

  • NIST SP 800-181 Rev. 1: National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE) Workforce Framework; includes biometric system security roles.

docs.title: 32.12 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: Biometric hardware security advanced across multiple fronts from 2023 to 2026: deepfake-driven presentation attacks challenged existing PAD testing frameworks, Apple refreshed its Face ID silicon, and the EU AI Act established landmark prohibitions on real-time biometric mass surveillance.

docs.title: 32.12.1 Deepfake Attacks on Biometric Hardware — ISO/IEC 30107-3 PAD Updates (2023)
docs.text:
The proliferation of generative adversarial network (GAN) and diffusion-model deepfake tools lowered the cost of high-quality presentation attacks to near-zero, prompting ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 37 to revise the PAD evaluation methodology:

  • ISO/IEC 30107-3 Amendment 1 (2023): Added Attack Type 3 (Adversarial Example attacks) and Attack Type 4 (Generative AI synthetic presentations) to the PAD evaluation taxonomy. Attack Type 3 covers perturbation- based attacks that fool CNN-based liveness classifiers while remaining imperceptible to humans. Attack Type 4 covers deepfake video presentations against 2D face recognition systems.

  • APCER thresholds tightened: For Attack Type 4 (deepfake video), the revised methodology requires APCER \(<~0.3\%\) at BPCER = 1% for Class 1 (high-security) applications. Previous thresholds (APCER \(<~1\%\)) were set before commercial diffusion models existed.

  • Hardware implications: 3D structured-light systems (Apple Face ID) maintain strong resistance because a 2D deepfake video presents a flat depth map. Optical under-display fingerprint sensors (Goodix GD3288) remain vulnerable to 3D-printed spoof fingers generated from deepfake-reconstructed minutiae maps.

Tip: The most effective defence against generative AI presentation attacks is sensor diversity: requiring simultaneous presentation to two physically distinct sensor modalities (face + fingerprint, or iris + face) dramatically increases the cost of a coordinated synthetic attack, as both modalities must be spoofed independently.

docs.title: 32.12.2 Apple Face ID — A17 Pro Improvements and Neural Engine Updates
docs.text:
Apple’s A17 Pro SoC (3 nm TSMC N3B process, iPhone 15 Pro, September 2023) delivered material improvements to Face ID security:

  • Neural Engine (6th generation): 35 TOPS performance (vs. 17 TOPS in A15), enabling a deeper liveness detection CNN with more temporal frames processed per authentication attempt. The increased compute budget allows the liveness model to analyse 60 fps infrared video rather than sparse frame sampling.

  • Secure Enclave (SEP) refresh: A17 Pro includes an updated SEP with a post-quantum-ready key derivation function based on CRYSTALS-Kyber in hybrid mode, anticipating future OS updates that will transition biometric template encryption keys to PQC algorithms.

  • FAR improvement: Apple reports Face ID FAR of \(1\) in \(1{,}000{,}000\) (unchanged from A14/A15). The A17 improvements primarily target FRR reduction in challenging lighting, glasses, and mask-wearing scenarios rather than FAR tightening.

  • Face ID on Apple Watch Ultra 2 (2023): Not deployed. Apple Watch Ultra 2 uses Passcode + wrist-detection presence sensing. The TrueDepth module’s spatial requirement (minimum 25 cm capture distance) is incompatible with wrist-mounted form factor.

docs.title: 32.12.3 FIDO2 Biometric Authenticator Certification (2024)
docs.text:
The FIDO Alliance Biometric Component Certification program (launched November 2023, first certifications awarded 2024) establishes hardware-level FAR/FRR requirements for FIDO2 platform authenticators:

Table 32.5. FIDO Alliance Biometric Certification Tiers (2024) Tier FAR Requirement Hardware Test Requirement Biometric Component (BC) 1 FAR \(\leq\) 0.01% Vendor self-declaration on accredited test set Biometric Component (BC) 2 FAR \(\leq\) 0.001% Third-party lab (NIST FRVT or equivalent) evaluation Biometric Component (BC) 3 FAR \(\leq\) 0.0001% Lab evaluation + PAD testing per ISO 30107-3

FIDO2 BC certification requires that biometric matching occur exclusively within a TEE or dedicated Secure Element — the biometric feature vector must never pass through the Rich OS application processor in plaintext. This mandates hardware-isolated matching engines (Apple SEP, Qualcomm QTEE, Samsung Knox Vault SE).

docs.title: 32.12.4 EU AI Act Biometric Provisions (2024)
docs.text:
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act, published August 2024) classifies certain biometric hardware systems as prohibited or high-risk AI:

  • Prohibited: Real-time remote biometric identification (RBI) in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement (with narrow exceptions for terrorism search, missing children). Systems using face recognition cameras in city centres, transit stations, or stadiums for real-time identification are prohibited.

  • High-risk: Biometric categorisation systems inferring sensitive characteristics (political opinion, religious belief, sexual orientation) from biometric data. Under the EU AI Act Annex III, these require conformity assessment including a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA).

  • Hardware implication: Camera systems with embedded face recognition processing (Axis Communications, Bosch cameras with on-edge AI) sold into the EU market may be classified as prohibited AI systems if their inference pipeline performs real-time RBI. Vendors are required to disable real-time identification features or obtain specific law enforcement deployment authorisation.

Warning: The EU AI Act prohibition on real-time RBI does not apply to post-event forensic identification (recorded video analysis) or to workplace access control systems with explicit employee consent. Manufacturers should clearly document the latency between capture and identification in their technical file to demonstrate that on-device processing does not constitute “real-time” operation.

docs.title: 32.12.5 Under-Display Fingerprint Spoofing — Qualcomm 3D Sonic Max Gen 2
docs.text:
Research published at USENIX Security 2024 analysed the Qualcomm 3D Sonic Max Gen 2 (QFS2630, used in Samsung Galaxy S23/S24 series) and documented improved but non-zero vulnerability to advanced spoofs:

  • Gelatin spoof defeat: QFS2630’s expanded active area (30 mm \(\times\) 20 mm) and improved sub-dermal imaging at 25 MHz confirmed APCER \(<~0.05\%\) against gelatin mold spoofs (improved from QFS2530’s \(<~0.1\%\)).

  • 3D-printed ABS spoof: High-resolution 3D printing at 100-micron layer height of ABS plastic (acoustic impedance \(Z_{ABS} \approx 2.7\) MRayl) produced a spoof that the acoustic impedance discriminator classified as suspicious. However, by applying a thin (0.2 mm) silicone overcoat (\(Z_{sil} \approx 1.05\) MRayl), researchers created a composite spoof with blended impedance signature within the live-skin acceptance window. APCER for this composite attack: \(\approx 3\%\).

  • Vendor response: Qualcomm released a PAD algorithm update (liveness model revision 4.1) in November 2023 via Android Security Update, improving composite spoof rejection. Hardware-level mitigation requires higher-frequency operation (50 MHz target in next generation for finer sub-dermal resolution).

docs.title: 32.12.6 Iris Recognition in AI PCs — Intel RealSense ID F455
docs.text:
Intel RealSense ID F455 (updated 2024 firmware) for Windows Hello enterprise deployments:

  • Hardware: Intel RealSense ID module (940 nm VCSEL flood illuminator, 1280\(\times\)800 NIR camera sensor, Intel Movidius neural processing unit running the Daugman IrisCode pipeline in a hardware-isolated domain).

  • Security updates (firmware 3.25, Q1 2024): Added on-device ISO 30107-3 PAD testing with APCER \(<~0.4\%\) against paper prints and low-quality printed iris replicas. Template storage fully encrypted with AES-256-GCM; ECDSA P-384 attestation key for Windows Hello challenge-response.

  • AI PC integration: Intel launched a reference design for “AI PCs” in 2024 integrating the F455 sensor with Intel Core Ultra (Meteor Lake) processors. The Neural Processing Unit (NPU) in Meteor Lake runs the iris feature extraction at \(<~100\) ms end-to-end latency while the F455’s dedicated Movidius processor handles PAD. This hardware partitioning ensures that a compromised application processor cannot inject a spoofed iris template – the feature extraction and liveness results are signed by the F455’s attestation key before transmission to Windows Hello.

docs.title: 32.13 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. A fingerprint sensor has FAR = 0.001% at threshold \(\tau_1\) and FRR = 0.1% at threshold \(\tau_2\). Assuming linear FAR/FRR trade-off curves between these two operating points, compute the threshold \(\tau_{EER}\) and the EER value.

  2. The Apple Secure Enclave stores biometric templates encrypted with a 256-bit key derived from the device UID, which is fused into OTP silicon and never readable by software. Explain why an attacker who physically dumps the NAND flash cannot decrypt the stored templates even with unlimited computational resources. What hardware property provides this guarantee?

  3. Describe the complete attack chain for fingerprint spoofing against a capacitive sensor. Include: (a) obtaining a latent fingerprint, (b) photolithographic transfer to gelatin or silicone, (c) presenting the artifact to the sensor, and (d) explain specifically why this attack fails against the QFS1080 ultrasonic sensor.

  4. An IrisCode has \(N_{eff} = 1900\) effective bits after eyelid masking. Impostor pairs follow an approximately normal distribution with \(\mu = 0.46\) and \(\sigma = 0.02\). Calculate the probability that a random impostor pair achieves \(d_H \leq 0.32\), expressing the answer as a \(z\)-score and a tail probability.

  5. Compare BioHashing and Fuzzy Vault across four dimensions: (a) computational complexity during matching, (b) revocability when the token is compromised, (c) cross-database linkability, (d) security under a stolen-token model where the attacker has both the BioHash/vault and the token.

  6. A face recognition system uses 128-dimensional L2-normalised embeddings. An adversarial example attack adds \(\ell_\infty\) perturbation \(\epsilon = 4/255\) pixel-wise to a face image to cross the decision boundary. Propose two hardware-level defences (not software model patches) that reduce this attack’s effectiveness, and explain the mechanism for each.

  7. Explain the Daugman rubber-sheet normalisation for iris recognition. Why is polar coordinate remapping necessary before Gabor encoding? Quantify the effect on IrisCode Hamming distance when the iris is captured at two different pupil dilation levels (\(r_1 = 1.2\) mm and \(r_2 = 2.4\) mm) with an outer iris boundary fixed at \(R = 5.5\) mm.

  8. A 1:N border control system processes 1000 iris comparisons per second against a gallery of 5,000,000 templates. Each IrisCode is 256 bytes. Calculate: (a) minimum memory bandwidth in MB/s, (b) number of XOR-popcount operations per second, (c) whether the gallery fits in the BRAM budget of a Xilinx ZU9EG (912 BRAMs x 36 Kb each).

  9. The Fuzzy Vault scheme using fingerprint minutiae requires an overlap of \(t\) genuine minutiae between the enrolled set \(A\) (80 points) and the query set \(B\) (70 points) to recover the secret polynomial. If the genuine minutia overlap follows a binomial distribution and the attacker must pick \(t = 20\) correct points from \(|V| = 200\) vault points (80 genuine + 120 chaff), estimate the brute-force search complexity assuming \(t = 20\) is the minimum necessary.

  10. Federated biometric verification splits a template \(T\) into two shares \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) stored on separate servers \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). Describe a secure two-party computation (2PC) protocol using garbled circuits that allows \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) to jointly compute whether a query embedding \(Q\) matches \(T\) without either server learning the full template or the query vector.

  11. ISO 30107-3 reports APCER = 2% and BPCER = 1% for a PAD module. In a deployed system, 0.1% of all authentication attempts are presentation attacks. Compute the overall effective system FAR and FRR, accounting for the PAD module’s effect on both attack and genuine presentations.

docs.title: Chapter 33: Satellite and Aerospace Hardware Security
docs.text: Satellite and aerospace systems operate in environments of extreme physical hostility – high-energy particle radiation, electromagnetic interference, and thermal cycling – while simultaneously requiring strong cryptographic assurance against adversaries capable of sophisticated signal manipulation, spoofing, and uplink jamming. This chapter covers the hardware architectures used to address both the environmental and adversarial threat landscape, from radiation-hardened processor design through GPS anti-spoofing, avionics bus security, and post-quantum satellite communications.

docs.title: 33.1 Space Radiation Environment
docs.text: The near-Earth radiation environment is dominated by three populations of energetic particles: (1) trapped protons and electrons in the Van Allen radiation belts, (2) galactic cosmic rays (GCR), and (3) solar energetic particles (SEP) from flares and coronal mass ejections.

docs.title: 33.1.1 Van Allen Radiation Belts and Orbit Comparison
docs.text:
The inner Van Allen belt (1,000–6,000 km altitude) contains protons with energies up to 600 MeV and electrons up to several MeV. The outer belt (13,000–40,000 km) is primarily electrons up to 10 MeV. Table 33.1 compares radiation dose and SEU rates by orbit.

Table 33.1. Radiation environment by orbit altitude and belt region. Orbit Altitude (km) TID/year (krad Si) SEU rate (err/bit/day) Shield. (mm Al) LEO (ISS) 400 5–10 \(10^{-8}\) 10 LEO (Sun-sync) 600 10–30 \(10^{-7}\) 10 LEO inner belt 1,200 50–200 \(10^{-6}\) 20 MEO (GPS) 20,200 500–2000 \(10^{-5}\) 40 GEO 35,786 100–500 \(10^{-6}\) 15 HEO (Molniya) 500–40,000 200–3000 \(10^{-5}\) 30

docs.title: 33.1.2 Single-Event Effects
docs.text:
A Single-Event Upset (SEU) occurs when a single energetic particle deposits enough charge to flip a memory bit. The critical charge \(Q_c\) (in femtocoulombs) and LET (Linear Energy Transfer, in MeV\(\cdot\)cm\(^2\)/mg) threshold characterise the sensitivity of a device. For modern SRAM at 28 nm: \(Q_c \approx 1\) fC, LET threshold \(\approx 1\) MeV\(\cdot\)cm\(^2\)/mg, cross-section \(\sigma \approx 10^{-8}\) cm\(^2\)/bit.

Single-Event Latch-up (SEL) is destructive: a parasitic thyristor latches into a low-impedance state, drawing destructive current. Radiation-hardened designs use Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) process nodes to eliminate the parasitic path, or implement current-limit fuses per memory block.

docs.title: 33.2 Radiation-Hardened Processor Hardware
docs.text: Figure 33.1. Satellite system architecture: ground station to spacecraft to mission control, showing the CCSDS SDLS authentication path from payload to ground.

docs.title: 33.2.1 BAE Systems RAD750
docs.text:
The BAE Systems RAD750 is the radiation-hardened PowerPC 750 derivative:

  • Process: IBM 0.25 \(\mu\)m CMOS SOI (rad-hard design rules, enclosed transistors)

  • Clock: 33–200 MHz; typical mission frequency 133 MHz

  • TID tolerance: 1 Mrad (Si), SEL immune (SOI substrate eliminates parasitic thyristor)

  • SEU rate: \(< 10^{-10}\) errors/bit/day in GEO (ECC-protected caches)

  • Power: 5 W at 133 MHz, 3.3 V core; rad-hard 64-bit bus

  • Deployed on: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Kepler, MAVEN, New Horizons, MESSENGER

docs.title: 33.2.2 Cobham Gaisler GR740
docs.text:
The CAES (formerly Cobham) GR740 quad-core SPARC V8 processor:

  • Process: TSMC 65 nm rad-hard CMOS (RHBD standard cells)

  • Cores: 4\(\times\) LEON4FT with hardware FPU, 1 GHz maximum

  • TID tolerance: 300 krad (Si)

  • SEU mitigation: EDAC on all memories, TMR on flip-flops in cache controller

  • Interfaces: SpaceWire (ECSS-E-ST-50-12C), CAN 2.0, MIL-STD-1553B

  • Deployed on: ESA future missions, CNES satellites

docs.title: 33.2.3 Microchip RTG4 FPGA
docs.text:
The Microchip (formerly Microsemi) RTG4 radiation-hardened FPGA:

  • Process: 130 nm CMOS radiation-hardened (proton and heavy ion tested)

  • Logic: 151,824 LUT-4 cells, 462 user I/Os, 64\(\times\) SERDES (3.125 Gbps)

  • TID tolerance: 100 krad (Si); SEU immune logic (RHBD flip-flops)

  • Non-volatile: flash-based configuration, no scrubbing required (unlike SRAM FPGAs)

  • Crypto: hardware AES-256 and SHA-256 fabric cores supported

  • Deployed on: cubesats, small GEO payloads, NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative

docs.title: 33.3 Radiation Mitigation Techniques
docs.text:
Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR): Three identical circuit instances compute in parallel; a majority voter selects the result. Any single SEU in one instance is masked. FPGA implementation overhead: \(3\times\) LUT utilisation plus voter logic (\(\approx 5\%\) additional).

-- VHDL TMR voter for safety-critical register
architecture rtl of tmr_voter is
begin
  process(A, B, C)
  begin
    -- Majority vote: output asserted if 2 of 3 inputs agree
    Q <= (A and B) or (B and C) or (A and C);
  end process;
end rtl;

DICE (Dual Interlocked storage Cell): A bistable cell with two storage nodes that are mutually interlocked; a single-node upset cannot propagate to flip the cell state. Used in rad-hard SRAM and flip-flop libraries. Area overhead vs. standard cell: \(\approx 2.5\times\); no speed penalty.

EDAC (Error Detection and Correction): SECDED (Single Error Correct, Double Error Detect) Hamming codes applied to all memory arrays. For a 64-bit data word: 7 check bits, covering \(2^7 = 128\) syndrome patterns. Typical EDAC latency: 1–2 clock cycles for correction.

Memory Scrubbing: For SRAM-based FPGAs (e.g., Xilinx QV Virtex-5QV), configuration bits can be upset by radiation. A scrubber periodically reads the configuration frame, computes CRC, and rewrites corrected frames to prevent accumulated errors from causing functional failure. Scrub rate: typically 1 full bitstream per 100 ms.

/* Xilinx Virtex-5QV ICAP scrubber (C pseudocode) */
while (1) {
    for (frame = 0; frame < TOTAL_FRAMES; frame++) {
        read_frame_via_ICAP(frame, buf);
        if (ecc_check(buf) != ECC_OK) {
            correct_and_write_frame(frame, buf);
            log_seu_event(frame, timestamp);
        }
    }
    sleep_ms(100);
}

docs.title: 33.4 CCSDS Space Data Link Security (SDLS)
docs.text:
CCSDS 352.0-B-2 (Space Data Link Security, 2019) defines authenticated encryption for Telecommand (TC) and Telemetry (TM) frames using:

  • Authenticated Encryption: AES-256-GCM (IETF RFC 5288 variant adapted for space)

  • Digital Signature: ECDSA P-256 (NIST FIPS 186-4) for command authentication

  • Key Management: CCSDS 351.0-M-1 defines the Space Key Management Protocol (SKMP)

CCSDS TC frame structure with SDLS security header/trailer:

TC Frame (CCSDS 232.0-B-4 + SDLS 352.0-B-2):
+------------------+----------+-----------+----------+---------+
| Primary Header   | Sec. Hdr | Sec. Data | Sec. Tlr | ECF     |
| 5 bytes          | 6 bytes  | variable  | 16 bytes | 2 bytes |
+------------------+----------+-----------+----------+---------+
  Sec. Hdr: SPI (2B) + IV (4B)
  Sec. Tlr: AES-256-GCM authentication tag (128-bit)
  ECF: Error Control Field (CRC-16-CCITT)

Key management: Master Key pre-loaded into spacecraft Key Management Facility (KMF) during ground testing; session keys derived per-link using ECDH P-256 ephemeral exchange or wrapped with the master key (key transport mode).

CCSDS 351.0-M-1 Space Key Management Protocol: Defines procedures for initial key load (physical delivery to launch facility), operational key exchange, key revocation (zeroisation command authenticated with current key), and key recovery from backup KMF.

docs.title: 33.5 GPS Signal Structure and Spoofing Attacks
docs.text: Figure 33.2. GPS spoofing attack versus OSNMA and RAIM defence architecture. The spoofer transmits counterfeit GPS signals; OSNMA cryptographic authentication and RAIM consistency checking detect the attack.

docs.title: 33.5.1 GPS Signal Structure
docs.text:
• L1 C/A: 1575.42 MHz, BPSK modulated, C/A code 1023 chips at 1.023 Mchip/s, 50 bps navigation message. No authentication – spoofable without cryptographic keys.

  • L2C: 1227.60 MHz, civil signal, BPSK(1) + BPSK(10), L2 CM + CL codes.

  • L5: 1176.45 MHz, BPSK(10), 10.23 Mchip/s, safety-of-life signal (ICD-GPS-705).

  • M-Code: encrypted military signal on L1 and L2, BOC(10,5) modulation, PRN code classified, requires SAASM (Selective Availability Anti-Spoofing Module) or PPS-SM for reception.

docs.title: 33.5.2 Galileo OSNMA – Open Service Navigation Message Authentication
docs.text:
Galileo OSNMA (ICD Issue 1.1, 2023) applies the TESLA (Timed Efficient Stream Loss-tolerant Authentication) delayed key disclosure protocol:

  1. Satellite pre-computes hash chain: \(K_0 \leftarrow K_1 \leftarrow \cdots \leftarrow K_n\) using HMAC-SHA-256, root key \(K_0\) signed with ECDSA P-256.

  2. At epoch \(i\): satellite broadcasts data \(D_i\) + HMAC-SHA-256(\(K_i\), \(D_i\)) as MAC.

  3. At epoch \(i+1\): satellite discloses \(K_i\).

  4. Receiver verifies: \(K_i\) hashes to \(K_{i-1}\) (chain integrity), then verifies MAC on \(D_i\).

A spoofer cannot forge the authentication tag without knowing future keys (one-way chain property). OSNMA key size: 128-bit TESLA key, 256-bit ECDSA root key, 32-byte MAC per subframe.

docs.title: 33.5.3 Military GPS: M-Code and SAASM
docs.text:
M-Code (Modernized Military GPS Signal): BOC(10,5) modulation centred at L1/L2, spectral separation from C/A for anti-jam. Receiver requires SAASM (Selective Availability Anti-Spoofing Module, NSA TYPE-1 certified) or Security Module (SM) for PPS (Precise Positioning Service).

KGX-750 (General Dynamics): an NSA-certified GPS security module providing M-Code decryption and zeroisation on tamper detection (> 45 g shock, 0.1 V/m EMI). JDAM (Joint Direct Attack Munition) guidance: embedded KGX-750 equivalent for GPS-guided munitions, zeroises under physical compromise within 1 ms.

docs.title: 33.5.4 Spoofing Detection Techniques
docs.text:
AGC Monitoring: Automatic Gain Control voltage drop indicates sudden strong signal source (spoofer overpowering legitimate signal). Threshold: AGC change \(> 3\) dB in \(< 100\) ms triggers alert.

Multipath Indicators: Code-carrier divergence monitor; spoofed signals often show zero multipath (perfect signal), unlike genuine urban environment signals.

RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring): Consistency check across all visible satellites: compute position from each \(\binom{N}{N-1}\) subset, compare residuals; a spoofed satellite produces outlier. ARAIM (Advanced RAIM) extends to multi-constellation (GPS + Galileo + GLONASS + BeiDou).

Multi-constellation cross-check: GPS L1 C/A spoofable; simultaneously receiving authenticated Galileo OSNMA signal and cross-checking position (\(\Delta\)pos \(< 1\) m expected) detects GPS-only spoof.

INS/IMU fusion: Inertial Navigation System maintains dead-reckoning trajectory between GPS epochs. Sudden GPS position jump inconsistent with IMU-measured accelerations (Kalman filter innovation check) triggers spoofing alert.

docs.title: 33.6 Anti-Jamming Hardware
docs.text:
Controlled Reception Pattern Antenna (CRPA): A phased array of 7 antenna elements (CRPA-7 standard, IEC 62386). Digital beamforming null-steers interference sources while maintaining gain in satellite directions. Null depth: \(> 40\) dB rejection. Used on: military aircraft, warships, ground vehicles.

Null Steering (Spatial Processing): Adaptive algorithm (LCMV – Linearly Constrained Minimum Variance beamformer) computes weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\) minimising jammer power subject to unit gain constraint toward satellites: \(\min_{\mathbf{w}} \mathbf{w}^H \mathbf{R}_{xx} \mathbf{w}\) subject to \(\mathbf{w}^H \mathbf{a}(\theta_s) = 1\).

docs.title: 33.7.1 MIL-STD-1553B
docs.text:
MIL-STD-1553B (1978, amendment B 1993): dual-redundant 1 Mbit/s serial bus using Manchester-II encoding, 31 Remote Terminals (RT) per bus, Bus Controller (BC) arbitration. Security limitation: no authentication, no encryption. Physical Manchester encoding provides 0 error detection beyond parity bit. Attack surface: any RT node can inject frames if physically connected.

# MIL-STD-1553 frame format (Manchester-II encoded, 20-bit word)
Sync (3 bit-times) | Data/Command (16 bits) | Parity (1 bit)
Command word: RT_address(5) | T/R(1) | Subaddress(5) | Word_count(5)
Maximum bus speed: 1.0 Mbps, max stub length 0.3 m (T connector)

docs.title: 33.7.2 ARINC 429 and ARINC 664 (AFDX)
docs.text:
ARINC 429: 100 kbps (Lo) or 12.5 kbps (Hi) unidirectional broadcast bus, 32-bit words (label 8b + SDI 2b + data 19b + SSM 2b + parity 1b), no authentication or encryption. Used by Boeing 737NG, Airbus A320.

ARINC 664 / AFDX (Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet): Based on IEEE 802.3 Gigabit Ethernet with deterministic Virtual Links (VL), bandwidth allocation per VL, redundant star topology (dual network A/B). Security additions: VLAN segregation (IEEE 802.1Q), no encryption in ARINC 664 Part 7 (AFDX) base spec; encryption extensions under development. DO-326A mandates security assessment of AFDX networks.

docs.title: 33.7.3 DO-326A / ED-202A Airworthiness Security
docs.text:
DO-326A (RTCA, 2014) and its European counterpart ED-202A (EUROCAE, 2014) define the airworthiness security process for certification:

  • Security Risk Assessment (SRA) analogous to Safety Risk Assessment

  • Threat Condition (TC) classification: TC1 (catastrophic) through TC5 (no safety effect)

  • Security controls mapped to DO-178C / DO-254 development assurance levels

  • Penetration testing requirements for TC1 and TC2 functions

docs.title: 33.8 UAV and Drone Security
docs.text:
MAVLink 1.0 vulnerabilities: MAVLink (Micro Air Vehicle Link) protocol uses a 6-byte header + payload + 2-byte CRC. No authentication in MAVLink 1.0: any RF node within range can inject commands (COMMAND_LONG message, e.g., MAV_CMD_DO_LAND). CRC uses CRC-16/MCRF4XX (not a security primitive). Demonstrated attack: ground station spoof via 900 MHz ISM.

MAVLink 2.0 signing (RFC, 2020): Optional signing extension: 13-byte signature block appended to each packet. Format: link_id(1B) + timestamp(6B) + SHA-256_HMAC_truncated(6B). Pre-shared key distribution out-of-band (QR code or physical link). Limitation: replay window only 6 bytes of timestamp (microsecond counter).

# MAVLink 2.0 packet structure with signing
MAGIC(1) | LEN(1) | INCOMPAT_FLAGS(1) | COMPAT_FLAGS(1)
| SEQ(1) | SYS_ID(1) | COMP_ID(1) | MSG_ID(3)
| PAYLOAD(LEN bytes) | CRC(2) | SIGNATURE(13 bytes)

# Signature: link_id(1) + timestamp_us(6) + HMAC-SHA256[:6](5)
# HMAC key: 32-byte pre-shared secret, provisioned at pairing

docs.title: 33.9 Quantum-Safe Satellite Communications
docs.text:
CCSDS PQC Working Group (2023–present) is evaluating NIST PQC standard algorithms for insertion into CCSDS 352.0-B-X (next revision):

  • ML-KEM-1024 (CRYSTALS-Kyber, FIPS 203): key encapsulation for session key establishment, replacing ECDH P-256 in SKMP. Public key 1568 bytes, ciphertext 1568 bytes – requires larger CCSDS key management frames.

  • ML-DSA-65 (CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FIPS 204): digital signature for command authentication, replacing ECDSA P-256. Signature 3293 bytes – significant overhead for TC frame structure.

  • SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+, FIPS 205): stateless hash-based signatures as alternative; 50 kB signature is impractical for real-time telemetry.

  • Timeline: CCSDS 352.0-B-3 with PQC options expected 2026–2028.

Challenges for space deployment:

  • Larger key/signature sizes strain limited uplink bandwidth (S-band TC: 2 kbps typical)

  • ML-KEM arithmetic (NTT over \(\mathbb{Z}_q\), \(q=3329\)) requires dedicated hardware accelerator for energy efficiency on spacecraft (5 W power budget)

  • Radiation-hardened PQC accelerator: not yet commercially available; FPGA implementation on RTG4 feasible (11,000 LUTs for ML-KEM-512)
