docs.title: 37.8 Confidential Computing Ecosystem
docs.text: Solution Vendor Description TDX + DCAP Intel TDX-enabled Xeon; DCAP attestation library (open source) SEV-SNP AMD EPYC Milan/Genoa; snp-guest driver in Linux 5.19+ CCA / TF-RMM ARM Neoverse N3/V3 platform; TF-RMM open source Secure Execution IBM z15/z16 LinuxONE; KVM host Confidential Containers CNCF kata-containers + CC backends (TDX/SEV/CCA) Azure CVM Microsoft AMD SEV-SNP and TDX; vTPM 2.0 AWS Nitro Enclaves Amazon Nitro security chip; isolated EC2 enclaves GCP Confidential VMs Google AMD SEV-SNP; Shielded VM Enarx Enarx Project Cross-platform CC runtime (TDX/SEV/SGX) Gramine Gramine Project Library OS for SGX/TDX app shielding Veraison Linux Foundation Attestation verification service (RATS)

docs.title: 37.9.1 Confidential AI: TEE + GPU Convergence
docs.text:
The convergence of Confidential Computing with AI accelerators is a defining trend of 2024–2025:

  • NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing (GA 2023): AES-XTS-256 HBM3 memory encryption, PCIe TDX/SEV-SNP attestation. H200 (2024) extends with HBM3e 141 GB/s bandwidth encryption.

  • AMD MI300X + SEV-SNP (2024): GPU and CPU memory encryption unified, enabling confidential LLM inference.

  • Intel Gaudi 3 Confidential AI (2024): ECDSA attestation of HPU, AES-256 HBM encryption.

Tip: Confidential AI workloads require end-to-end confidentiality: CPU memory (SEV-SNP/TDX), GPU memory (H100 CC), the PCIe link (IDE – PCIe Integrity and Data Encryption), and the attestation chain must all be verified before running a confidential model.

docs.title: 37.9.2 CCA Deployment in Mobile and Edge
docs.text:
ARM CCA silicon shipped in:

  • Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (2023): First mobile SoC with RME

  • MediaTek Dimensity 9300 (2023): CCA-capable

  • Samsung Exynos 2400 (2024): CCA with Samsung Knox integration

Use cases: private ML inference on-device, digital identity (eIDAS 2.0 EUDIW credentials in Realm), mobile payments.

docs.title: 37.9.3 TEE-I/O: Confidential Peripherals
docs.text:
PCIe IDE (Integrity and Data Encryption, PCIe 6.0 spec) enables a TDX or SEV-SNP VM to establish an encrypted, authenticated channel directly to a PCIe device (NIC, NVMe SSD, GPU), bypassing the hypervisor:

  • SPDM 1.3 (DMTF, 2023): device identity and measurement protocol used to authenticate PCIe devices before granting them access to a TD

  • Intel TDX Connect (2024): production deployment of TDX + PCIe IDE

  • CXL 3.0 Security: trusted memory pooling with integrity checks

Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between a process-level TEE (Chapter 4) and a VM-level confidential computing environment like TDX or SEV-SNP. What is the TCB for each?

  2. AMD SEV-SNP uses a Reverse Map Table (RMP). Explain how the RMP prevents a hypervisor from injecting data into a guest VM. What fault is raised on violation?

  3. In ARM CCA, what is the role of the Root world? Why is EL3 (Monitor) placed in Root rather than Secure world?

  4. A cloud customer wants to run a confidential ML inference workload. List all the hardware security components required end-to-end (CPU, GPU, interconnect, attestation).

  5. Describe the DCAP attestation flow for Intel TDX. What is the PCCS and why is it needed?

  6. CacheWarp (2023) exploited AMD SEV’s cache behaviour to revert encrypted memory to a stale state. Explain the mechanism and why the fix required a microcode update.

  7. Compare the throughput-to-security trade-offs of AES-XTS-128 vs AES-XTS-256 in a memory encryption engine operating at DDR5-6400 bandwidth (\(\sim\)51 GB/s).

docs.title: Chapter 38: Hardware Security Design Flow and EDA Tools
docs.text:
Note: Designing secure hardware requires more than correct functionality. Security must be designed in from the first RTL line, verified at every step of the EDA flow, and validated against physical attacks before tape-out. This chapter covers the complete design-for-security (DFS) flow from specification to silicon.

The hardware security design flow integrates three disciplines: (1) secure architecture definition, (2) formal and simulation verification of security properties, and (3) physical security validation against side-channel and fault attacks. This chapter provides the methodology and tools to build new secure hardware technologies from scratch.

docs.title: 38.1 Threat Modelling for Hardware
docs.text:
Before any RTL is written, a hardware threat model must be established. The standard methodology is STRIDE-HW (adapted from Microsoft STRIDE for hardware assets):

Threat Hardware Example Countermeasure Spoofing Cloned device presenting false identity PUF-based device ID, X.509 provisioning Tampering Glitch attack on secure boot Voltage/clock monitors, ECC on config Repudiation No audit trail in secure enclave Monotonic counters, TPM event log Information Disclosure Side-channel key leakage Masking, hiding, constant-time logic Denial of Service Fault injection disabling security Redundant checks, watchdog timers Elevation of Privilege Bypassing privilege fence PMP/MPU hardware enforcement

Tip: Use the MITRE ATT&CK for ICS / Hardware framework alongside STRIDE. Map each hardware component (SoC bus, debug port, crypto engine) to relevant attack techniques.

docs.title: 38.1.1 Security Asset Identification
docs.text:
A security asset is anything that must be protected. Examples:

  • Root keys (Device Identity Key, Attestation Key)

  • Secure boot measurement registers

  • Privilege level state machines (e.g., bus master ID)

  • Monotonic counters (anti-replay)

  • Debug enable/disable fuses (OTP)

docs.title: 38.2.1 Principle of Least Privilege in Hardware
docs.text:
Every bus master (CPU, DMA, debug interface) should be granted the minimum privilege needed. Use a hardware memory protection unit (MPU) or bus firewall to enforce access control:

module bus_firewall (
    input  logic        clk, rst_n,
    input  logic [31:0] addr,
    input  logic        rnw,        // 1=read, 0=write
    input  logic [3:0]  master_id,  // 0=CPU, 1=DMA, 2=Debug
    input  logic        valid,
    output logic        grant,
    output logic        deny_irq
);
    // Key RAM: 0x4000_0000 -- 0x4000_0FFF
    localparam KEY_RAM_LO = 32'h4000_0000;
    localparam KEY_RAM_HI = 32'h4000_0FFF;
    localparam DEBUG_ID   = 4'd2;

    always_comb begin
        grant    = 1'b1;
        deny_irq = 1'b0;
        if (valid &&
            (addr >= KEY_RAM_LO) && (addr <= KEY_RAM_HI) &&
            (master_id == DEBUG_ID)) begin
            grant    = 1'b0;   // Block debug access to key RAM
            deny_irq = 1'b1;   // Raise security interrupt
        end
    end
endmodule

docs.title: 38.2.2 Constant-Time Hardware
docs.text:
Hardware is inherently data-dependent in timing unless explicit measures are taken. Secure hardware design rules:

  1. No secret-dependent branches: Multiplexers, not if-else trees driven by key bits

  2. No secret-dependent memory accesses: Use dual-port RAM with pre-fetching all candidates, or bitsliced implementations

  3. Fixed latency pipelines: All operations complete in the same number of clock cycles regardless of input

// BAD: data-dependent multiplexer select creates power side-channel
// if (key_bit) result = a; else result = b;

// GOOD: constant-time select using Boolean logic
module ct_select #(parameter W = 32) (
    input  logic          sel,      // secret bit
    input  logic [W-1:0]  a, b,
    output logic [W-1:0]  result
);
    // Both paths evaluated; select bit determines output
    // Power consumption identical regardless of sel value
    assign result = ({W{sel}} & a) | ({W{~sel}} & b);
endmodule

docs.title: 38.2.3 Secure State Machine Design
docs.text:
Security-critical FSMs must be:

  • One-hot encoded to detect glitch-induced invalid states

  • Hamming-distance hardened: secure states differ by \(\geq\)3 bits from all other states

  • Error-detecting: any undefined state immediately triggers a security alert and zeroization

typedef enum logic [4:0] {
    ST_IDLE    = 5'b00001,
    ST_AUTH    = 5'b00010,
    ST_ACTIVE  = 5'b00100,
    ST_LOCK    = 5'b01000,
    ST_ZEROIZE = 5'b10000
} secure_state_t;

secure_state_t state, next;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) state <= ST_IDLE;
    else        state <= next;

// Illegal state detector
always_comb begin
    if (state != ST_IDLE   && state != ST_AUTH  &&
        state != ST_ACTIVE && state != ST_LOCK  &&
        state != ST_ZEROIZE) begin
        // Glitch or fault injection detected
        security_alert = 1'b1;
        next = ST_ZEROIZE;
    end
end

docs.title: 38.3.1 Simulation and Functional Verification

docs.title: 38.3.3 Security-Specific EDA: Information Flow Tracking
docs.text:
Information Flow Tracking (IFT) is the most important security analysis in hardware EDA. It answers: Can a secret input ever affect an observable output?

Tools:

  • Cadence JasperGold SPV: Formally proves non-interference between tainted (secret) signals and outputs

  • GLIFT (Gate-Level IFT): Computes a shadow logic per gate to track information propagation

  • Maki: Open-source hardware IFT tool (MIT, 2022)

  • SecVerilog: Type-system for Verilog enforcing information-flow security at synthesis time (Cornell 2015, still used in 2024)

// JasperGold-style SVA property
// Mark key_reg as secret (tainted) source
// Assert: encrypted_out has no direct information flow from key_reg
// This uses SPV "taint source" / "taint sink" methodology

// Taint source declaration (in JasperGold SPV script):
//   taint_source key_reg -type secret

// Taint sink check:
//   taint_check plaintext_bus_out -expect no_taint

// Equivalent SVA non-interference property:
property key_noninterference;
    // For all pairs of runs differing only in key_reg,
    // the plaintext_bus_out must be equal
    // (expressed as a 2-safety property in SPV)
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    !$changed(key_reg) |-> !$changed(plaintext_bus_out);
endproperty
assert property (key_noninterference);

docs.title: 38.3.4 Physical Design and DRC/LVS Security Checks
docs.text:
Security-aware physical design requires additional checks beyond standard DRC/LVS:

  • Power mesh isolation: Separate power domains for secure and non-secure logic to prevent power side-channel cross-domain leakage

  • Shielded routing: Critical signal nets (key buses, secure boot signals) routed on metal layers shielded above and below with ground planes

  • Active shield mesh: Top-level metal mesh connected to tamper detection logic; any cut triggers zeroization

  • Fill cell security: Unused silicon area filled with active (not just filler) standard cells to prevent FIB circuit edit

docs.title: 38.4.1 Pre-Silicon Power Analysis
docs.text: TVLA at RTL Run Test Vector Leakage Assessment on gate-level simulations using annotated switching activity (VCD/SAIF files). Tool: Cadence Conformal Equality Checker with power annotation. ELMO (Estimated Leakage for Microcontrollers) Power leakage model for Cortex-M0/M3 cores; available on GitHub. Predicts DPA success rate before silicon. Gate-Level Power Simulation Synopsys PrimeTime PX: annotate switching activity from simulation, compute per-cell power, detect high-leakage cells in crypto datapaths.

docs.title: 38.4.2 Automated Masking Insertion
docs.text:
Manual masking of AES S-boxes is error-prone. Automated tools:

  • SILVER (Ruhr University Bochum): Formal verification of masked implementations; checks d-probing security

  • maskVerif: Verifies that a masked circuit is \(t\)-probing secure

  • AGEMA (2022): Automated Generation of Masked Implementations; synthesises a masked AES from unmasked RTL

docs.title: 38.5 Fault Injection Analysis in Design Flow
38.5.1 Fault Models
docs.text: Fault Model Physical Attack Design Countermeasure Bit-flip Laser fault injection, EM glitch ECC on registers; dual-rail logic Stuck-at-0/1 Power glitch Temporal redundancy (double compute) Transient clock Clock glitch Clock monitor + anomaly detector Instruction skip Laser on pipeline Redundant PC check; hash of instruction stream

docs.title: 38.5.2 FIPAC: Fault-Injection Protected Architecture
docs.text:
FIPAC (TU Graz 2022) instruments an RISC-V binary at compile time to detect instruction-skip attacks. It inserts a signature (XOR of instruction addresses) updated at every basic block and verified at branches.

/* Signature variable in dedicated register (e.g., t6 on RISC-V) */
extern volatile uint32_t __signature;

/* Macro inserted by FIPAC pass at each basic block entry */
#define FIPAC_UPDATE(expected_sig) \
    if (__signature != (expected_sig)) { security_fault(); }

void secure_check(uint32_t val) {
    FIPAC_UPDATE(0xDEAD1234UL);
    if (val == SECRET_MAGIC) {
        FIPAC_UPDATE(0xBEEF5678UL);
        grant_access();
    }
    FIPAC_UPDATE(0xCAFE9ABCUL);
}

docs.title: 38.6 FPGA Prototyping for Security Validation
docs.text:
FPGA prototyping is essential for pre-silicon security validation:

  1. Implement the design on a ChipWhisperer-compatible target (CW305 Artix-7)

  2. Run TVLA test campaigns: 100K–1M traces for t-test leakage detection

  3. Perform laser fault injection using a focused ion beam station or ChipSHOUTER platform

  4. Iterate on masking/hiding countermeasures before tape-out

Warning: FPGA power side-channels differ from ASIC due to the routing fabric. An FPGA implementation that passes TVLA may still leak on ASIC due to different parasitic capacitances. Always validate on the final ASIC process node.

docs.title: 38.7 Chip Tapeout Security Checklist
docs.text: Security Check Stage Responsible Tool/Method Threat model complete, all assets identified Pre-RTL Architecture review Formal non-interference (IFT) proof RTL JasperGold SPV / GLIFT Constant-time datapath verified RTL SILVER / maskVerif FSM illegal-state detection RTL Formal reachability check Bus firewall policy complete Gate-level Simulation + formal TVLA \(t < 4.5\) (no leakage) Gate-level PrimeTime PX + TVLA Fault injection coverage \(> 95\%\) Gate-level FIPAC / FiSim Active shield mesh routed Physical Custom DRC deck Shielded routing on key buses Physical Custom DRC Fill cells: no FIB-exposed polysilicon Physical DRC layer check OTP fuse programming verified Functional ATE test vector Debug interface disabled in production Functional ATE fuse readback

docs.title: 38.8 Creating New Hardware Security Technologies: Research-to-Silicon
docs.text: This section provides the complete flow for developing a novel hardware security primitive from concept to tape-out:

docs.title: 38.8.1 Step 1 – Security Architecture Definition
docs.text:
1. Define the security goal (e.g., “prevent software from reading attestation keys even with kernel-level compromise”)

  2. Enumerate assets and adversary capabilities (hardware attacker, software attacker, insider threat)

  3. Choose a hardware primitive (PUF, crypto engine, TEE, RoT)

  4. Design the trust boundary: what is inside vs. outside the HW security perimeter

docs.title: 38.8.2 Step 2 – RTL Implementation
docs.text:
Tools and languages:

  • SystemVerilog or VHDL for register-transfer level

  • Chisel (Scala-based HDL): used in RISC-V ecosystem, OpenTitan

  • Amaranth (Python HDL): increasingly popular for security research

  • CIRCT: MLIR-based hardware compiler; enables formal IR for security

docs.title: 38.8.3 Step 3 – Security Verification
docs.text:
1. Write security assertions (SVA properties) for every security invariant

  2. Run formal proof (SymbiYosys or JasperGold)

  3. Perform IFT analysis (GLIFT or JasperGold SPV)

  4. Verify masking correctness (SILVER/maskVerif)

  5. FPGA prototype + TVLA

docs.title: 38.8.4 Step 4 – Physical Design for Security
docs.text:
1. Synthesis (Synopsys DC / Cadence Genus / Yosys)

  2. Power domain planning: isolate sensitive logic

  3. Place and Route (Cadence Innovus / Synopsys ICC2)

  4. Apply shielding and active mesh

  5. Run security DRC checks

docs.title: 38.8.5 Step 5 – Silicon Validation
docs.text:
1. ATE (Automatic Test Equipment): Teradyne UltraFlex or Advantest T2000

  2. Side-channel lab: ChipWhisperer, Langer probe, oscilloscope

  3. Physical penetration testing: FIB, X-ray tomography, laser fault injection

  4. Common Criteria evaluation (CC EAL4+ or EAL6+)

Note: The full research-to-silicon timeline for a novel security primitive: architecture (2–4 months), RTL + verification (4–8 months), physical design (3–6 months), tape-out, manufacturing, and validation (6–12 months). Total: 15–30 months and $1M–$50M depending on process node.

docs.title: 38.10 Recent Developments (2024–2026)
docs.text: The hardware security design flow has seen significant advances in AI-assisted verification, open-source EDA tooling, and new security-specific HDLs since 2023.

docs.title: 38.10.1 AI-Assisted Security Property Generation
docs.text:
Manual writing of security assertions is the primary bottleneck in formal verification. New AI tools are changing this:

  • Cadence JasperGold PropGen (2024): LLM-assisted SVA property suggestion. Given an RTL module and natural-language security description (“key register must not flow to unencrypted output”), PropGen suggests candidate SVA properties. Engineers report 40–60% reduction in property authoring time for crypto datapaths.

  • Synopsys VC Formal AI (2024): Automated counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) with ML-driven witness generation; reduces state explosion in large bus fabric formal proofs.

  • AutoSVA (2023, Stanford): Open-source LLM-to-SVA pipeline; generates assume/assert pairs from Verilog comments using GPT-4.

Note: AI-generated assertions must be reviewed by a security engineer. LLMs can generate syntactically correct but semantically wrong properties — asserting the negation of a security invariant compiles and runs fine but provides zero protection.

docs.title: 38.10.2 Open-Source EDA Security Flow Maturity (2024)
docs.text: Tool Version 2024 Security Advances Yosys 0.40 (2024) Formal IFT plugin (GLIFT); improved synthesis for security-hardened netlists SymbiYosys 0.12 (2024) BMC + k-induction + PDR in single run; cover statements for security reachability Verilator 5.x (2024) Timing-accurate simulation; SVA assertion support; security lint rules OpenROAD 2024.x Open-source P&R; shielding-aware routing plugin (UMich, 2024) OpenTitan Earl Grey (2024) First open-source silicon security chip; full RTL + formal + DV suite public CIRCT 1.x (2024) MLIR hardware IR; enables formal security analysis on hardware IR nodes

docs.title: 38.10.3 Amaranth HDL and Security-Oriented HDLs
docs.text:
Amaranth (formerly nMigen, Python-based HDL) has gained adoption in security research due to its expressive type system and Python ecosystem integration:

  • Signal typing: Amaranth’s Shape system makes bit-width mismatches a compile-time error — eliminating a class of security bugs from implicit truncation

  • SoC integration: Amaranth SoC library builds bus fabrics with explicit memory-map access control, making bus firewall policy part of the HDL source rather than a separate document

  • Used in production: VexRiscv security extensions, LUNA USB security core

docs.title: 38.10.4 NIST PQC Hardware Implementation Guidance (2024)
docs.text:
Following FIPS 203/204/205/206 finalization (August 2024), NIST published SP 800-235 (draft, late 2024): Guidelines for Migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptographic Standards, which includes hardware-specific guidance:

  • Side-channel requirements for NTT butterfly units in ML-KEM hardware

  • Masking requirements: minimum 2-share masking for key generation path

  • ATE test vector requirements for PQC co-processors

  • Formal verification coverage requirements for PQC state machines

docs.title: 38.10.5 EU Cyber Resilience Act: Hardware Design Obligations (2024)
docs.text:
The EU CRA (effective October 2024, compliance deadline October 2027) imposes design-process requirements directly relevant to this chapter:

CRA Requirement Design Flow Implication Security by design (Art. 13) Threat model documented before RTL; security properties must be traceable to implementation No known exploitable vulnerabilities Formal verification of critical security properties required for Class II products Secure development process IEC 62443-4-1 or ISO/IEC 27034 SDL compliance; design review artifacts retained for 10 years Vulnerability disclosure CVE assignment process must be established before product ships; hardware CVEs now tracked in NVD

Exercises

  1. A designer uses if (key_bit) result = A; else result = B; in Verilog. Explain why this creates a power side-channel and rewrite it using constant-time techniques.

  2. Write an SVA property that asserts a 32-bit register secret_key never appears on a 32-bit AHB data bus ahb_hrdata in an unencrypted form. (Hint: use an information-flow tracking approach.)

  3. A one-hot FSM has 5 states (5 bits). An attacker glitches the device, flipping 2 bits simultaneously. Which resulting states are illegal? How would you detect them?

  4. Explain why a masked AES implementation must be formally verified with SILVER or maskVerif in addition to passing simulation tests.

  5. Design a bus firewall table for a SoC with: CPU (master 0), DMA (master 1), Debug (master 2); secure ROM (0x0000–0x7FFF), key RAM (0x8000–0x8FFF), peripheral AHB (0xA000–0xFFFF). Which accesses should be blocked?

  6. What is the difference between TVLA at RTL level and post-silicon TVLA? Why might a design pass RTL TVLA but fail post-silicon?

  7. Describe the complete EDA tool chain to take a new PUF circuit design from SystemVerilog RTL to a TSMC 7nm GDSII ready for tape-out, noting which security-specific checks are required at each step.

docs.title: Chapter 39: Chiplet and Heterogeneous Integration Security
docs.text:
Note: Chiplets disaggregate a monolithic SoC into multiple dies connected by a high-speed die-to-die interconnect. While enabling cost-effective scaling, chiplet architectures introduce new trust boundaries, supply chain risks, and physical attack surfaces that monolithic designs do not face.

The chiplet revolution—driven by TSMC’s CoWoS, Intel Foveros, and AMD’s EMIB— fundamentally changes the hardware security landscape. When a single package contains dies from multiple vendors, manufactured in different fabs, across different continents, each die-to-die link becomes a potential trust boundary and attack surface.

docs.title: 39.1.1 Key Interconnect Standards
docs.text: Standard Bandwidth Range Security Support UCIe 1.1 (2023) 32 Gb/s/mm \(<\)2mm Optional AES-256-GCM encryption+auth BoW (Open) 112 Gb/s \(<\)1mm No native security AIB (Intel) 2 Gb/s/pin \(<\)10mm Integrity bits only HBM3 1.2 TB/s Stacked Per-channel ECC; no encryption CXL 3.0 256 GB/s \(<\)10m PCIe AES-256-GCM IDE encryption

docs.title: 39.1.2 Trust Zones in a Chiplet Package
docs.text: Figure 39.1. Chiplet package trust zones: different dies have different trust levels requiring appropriate interconnect security.

docs.title: 39.2.1 Die-to-Die (D2D) Interconnect Attacks
docs.text:
Unlike monolithic on-chip buses, die-to-die interconnects are accessible with physical probing equipment:

Passive Probing High-bandwidth oscilloscope (100+ GHz Keysight DSA-Z or Tektronix DPO70000SX) with ground-signal probes can capture UCIe or BoW signals at the package edge if the interposer is exposed. Active Interposer Substitution Replace a legitimate passive interposer with a malicious active interposer that intercepts, modifies, or replays die-to-die transactions. Demonstrated by researchers at MIT Lincoln Labs (2022). Differential Power Analysis on D2D The simultaneous switching of 1000+ UCIe lanes creates measurable power signatures correlating with bus data.

Warning: Unencrypted die-to-die interconnects (BoW, early AIB) expose all data exchanged between chiplets to an attacker with package-level physical access. For security-sensitive data (keys, plaintext, attestation) always mandate UCIe with AES-256-GCM or a CXL IDE-equivalent link.

docs.title: 39.2.2 Supply Chain Threats Specific to Chiplets
docs.text: Threat Chiplet-Specific Vector Countermeasure Malicious third-party chiplet Untested chiplet from untrusted fab inserted into multi-die package SPDM attestation of each die; AS6081 procurement Counterfeit chiplet Legitimate chiplet replaced with lower-grade die PUF-based die identity; X-ray verification Malicious interposer Active silicon interposer with embedded hardware Trojan Electrical testing; X-ray CT of assembled package Side-channel via shared substrate Thermal or EM crosstalk between dies exposes secrets Physical isolation; thermal shield layers Memory chiplet extraction HBM3 stacked die removed and read off-chip Per-granule encryption on memory die

docs.title: 39.2.3 HBM Security
docs.text:
High Bandwidth Memory (HBM3, JEDEC JESD238) is stacked directly on the die using Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs). Security concerns:

  • HBM3 does not natively encrypt data. An attacker with access to the package (FIB, interposer probing) can read memory contents.

  • NVIDIA H100’s Memory Encryption Engine (MEE) provides AES-XTS-256 between the SXM5 die and HBM3 stacks, implementing inline encryption in the memory controller.

  • AMD MI300X (2024) integrates CPU+GPU dies in the same package, sharing HBM3; AMD SEV-SNP encryption covers the HBM3 address space.

docs.title: 39.3 UCIe Security (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express)
docs.text: UCIe 1.1 (2023) defines an optional but strongly recommended security layer above the physical/adapter layer. The security stack uses:

docs.title: 39.3.1 UCIe Security Architecture
docs.text:
1. Die Authentication (D-Auth): ECDSA-P384 or CRYSTALS-Dilithium identity proof at link initialization. Each die presents a certificate chain to its peer.

  2. Link Encryption: AES-256-GCM with a 96-bit nonce per packet. Key agreement via X25519 (or CRYSTALS-Kyber for post-quantum).

  3. Replay Protection: 48-bit sequence number; out-of-order packets generate security alerts.

  4. Key Refresh: Session keys rotated every \(2^{32}\) packets (\(\sim\)4 billion) to maintain GCM nonce uniqueness.

/* Die A (initiator) initiates secure session with Die B */

/* Step 1: Exchange ephemeral X25519 keys */
uint8_t eph_privA[32], eph_pubA[32];
x25519_keygen(eph_privA, eph_pubA);
ucie_send(DIE_B, MSG_KEY_EXCHANGE, eph_pubA, 32);

uint8_t eph_pubB[32];
ucie_recv(DIE_B, MSG_KEY_EXCHANGE, eph_pubB, 32);

/* Step 2: ECDH shared secret */
uint8_t shared[32];
x25519(shared, eph_privA, eph_pubB);

/* Step 3: HKDF to derive AES-256-GCM keys */
uint8_t key_A2B[32], key_B2A[32];
hkdf_sha256(shared, "UCIe-D2D-A2B", key_A2B, 32);
hkdf_sha256(shared, "UCIe-D2D-B2A", key_B2A, 32);

/* Step 4: Authenticate dies (ECDSA-P384 certificate exchange) */
ucie_send_certificate(DIE_B, die_cert_chain);
ucie_verify_certificate(recv_cert, trusted_CA_pubkey);

/* All subsequent UCIe packets encrypted + authenticated */

docs.title: 39.4 Chiplet Identity and Attestation
docs.text: Each chiplet must have a unique, unforgeable identity. The proposed architecture (IEEE P3164 Chiplet Security Working Group, 2023–2024):

docs.title: 39.4.1 DICE-based Chiplet Identity
docs.text:
The TCG DICE (Device Identity Composition Engine) Layering Architecture maps naturally to chiplet stacks:

  1. Layer 0 – Immutable Die Identity: PUF-derived root key burned at wafer sort. Certificate issued by the fab.

  2. Layer 1 – Package-Level Composition: The host die’s security controller measures all peer dies via D2D authentication and composes a compound device identity (CDI).

  3. Layer 2 – System-Level Attestation: The CDI is bound to a TPM/RoT attestation chain, proving the full chiplet composition to a remote verifier.

Figure 39.2. DICE-based chiplet identity layering: fab-rooted die identity composes into a system attestation quote.

docs.title: 39.8.1 UCIe 2.0 Security Enhancements (2025)
docs.text:
The UCIe 2.0 specification (expected Q2 2025) adds:

  • Post-quantum key agreement (X-Wing hybrid: X25519 + ML-KEM-768) as default in the security handshake

  • Multi-party authentication: packages with 3+ chiplets establish a group session key with a single handshake round

  • Hardware attestation integration: UCIe security controller exports SPDM 1.3 measurements to the host RoT

  • Die revocation: signed revocation lists distributed to UCIe controllers to block known-compromised chiplet certificates

docs.title: 39.8.2 IEEE P3164 Chiplet Security Standard (2024 Draft)
docs.text:
IEEE P3164 Working Group (formed 2023) published its first draft standard in 2024, covering:

  • Mandatory PUF-based die identity for Class A (secure) chiplets

  • D2D link encryption requirements at three assurance levels

  • Test-access security: blocking JTAG chain traversal across trust domains

  • Supply chain traceability: die-level serialization and certificate issuance

docs.title: 39.8.3 CHIPS Act Trusted Fab Certification
docs.text:
The US CHIPS and Science Act (2022) created a Trusted Foundry certification programme administered by NSTC (National Semiconductor Technology Center):

  • DoD-grade chiplets must originate from TSMC Arizona, Intel Ohio, or Samsung Texas fabs (all receiving CHIPS Act funding with security requirements)

  • Fab security requirements: secure design data transfer, cleared personnel for classified designs, anti-tamper measures on process equipment

  • Chiplet provenance chains must be cryptographically signed by the fab and included in HBOM (Hardware Bill of Materials)

Note: The HBOM (Hardware Bill of Materials) concept, analogous to SBOM for software, is gaining traction in 2024–2025. NTIA is developing HBOM guidance under the Biden/Biden-Harris Executive Order on supply chain security. An HBOM for a chiplet-based CPU would include: die manufacturer, fab, process node, mask set revision, and cryptographic die certificate hash.

Exercises

  1. A chiplet package contains a CPU die (trusted fab) connected to a memory controller die (overseas fab) via an unencrypted BoW interconnect. Describe three attack vectors this creates and suggest mitigations for each.

  2. UCIe 1.1 uses AES-256-GCM for link encryption. At 32 Gb/s bandwidth, calculate the maximum number of packets before nonce reuse occurs, assuming a 96-bit nonce with 32-bit sequence numbers and 128-bit packet granularity.

  3. Explain the DICE layering model for chiplet attestation. If Die B (memory controller) is compromised after manufacture, how would Layer 1 composition detect this during system boot?

  4. Compare the security implications of HBM3 stacked in a 2.5D interposer vs. 3D stacked directly on the die using TSVs. Which is harder to probe and why?

  5. An attacker replaces a legitimate UCIe-attached AI accelerator chiplet with a malicious clone that supports the same D2D interface. What UCIe security feature (introduced in UCIe 1.1) would detect this substitution? What is the root of trust for this detection?

  6. The AS6081 standard defines counterfeit electronic parts avoidance. List three specific measures an OEM assembling a chiplet-based server SoC should implement to comply with AS6081.

  7. Design a security architecture for a chiplet-based SoC destined for a satellite payload. The SoC contains: compute die (trusted US fab), RF transceiver die (European fab), memory die (Taiwanese fab). Define the trust model, D2D encryption requirements, and attestation chain.
